title: Democrat Hakeem Jeffries is nominated to become House speaker, a historic first
text:
Democrat Hakeem Jeffries is nominated to become House speaker, a historic first
Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black American with the gavel.
Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.
He ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media posts have been flooding the offices of Democrats and the newly elected, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.
Ahead of Wednesday's vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. He met with the caucuses that make up the House Democrats and talked to almost all members in what will be their large majority.
“I embrace those conversations," he said.
Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.
Jeffries will face a separate roll call of the whole House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.
Skeptics question whether leaders are up to the job
Wednesday’s vote was the first of their careers for dozens of members-elect, before they’re even sworn into office in January. With one of the biggest incoming majorities in decades, Jeffries will have room to spare.
Rep.-elect Brad Lander of New York announced he would support Jeffries when he launched his campaign for Congress. Rep.-elect Randy Villegas of California has said he was supporting whoever would help him best deliver for his Central Valley district.
Returning Rep. Emily Randall of Washington said she heard questions about House leadership during town halls in her district and had been watching direct messages stream into her Instagram feed about the leadership election. So she decided to start dialing them back.
“People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the House,” she said, referring to the Vermont independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. “Technically, yes, and it would be probably difficult.”
(It's true that the House can elect anyone speaker, but it's unlikely to be Sanders because he already has his day job in the Senate.)
On one call, Randall said, she listened to the constituent's concerns and then replied, “Truthfully, not like blowing smoke, whoever is our speaker — and I think it is going to be Hakeem Jeffries, and I am supporting Hakeem Jeffries for speaker — I think we will accomplish a lot of the things that he was asking us to.”
Lawmakers pointed to the livestream that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York did trying to explain the role of the speaker.
“There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the Capitol. “I think that everyone is far more concerned what that leadership means, what is it promising.”
First leaders of a post-Pelosi era
Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders of the post-Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.
When Rep. Nancy Pelosi of California decided to step aside from leadership in 2022 after the party's electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era. Pelosi, No. 2 Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland and Rep. James Clyburn of South Carolina had often moved together, rising, and then stepping back, from their long-held positions.
A similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland.
Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House “are quite different.”
She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others. “His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction,” Ansari said.
"It is more productive to focus on preparing on what we're going to do in the majority and what we need and want to get done in those first 100 days," she said.
Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who pulled off a stunning victory in a redrawn district favoring the Republican candidate, said before the vote that he'd be supporting Jeffries.
“It’s not even like a complex question,” he said about Jeffries, who he said “led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation.”
“I’m not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history," he said.

title: Eight County Teams Turn Regional Week Into Something Special
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 3: Eight Teams, Seven Finals, Five Titles
There are some weeks during a season when it feels like everything is happening at once.
Regional championship week was definitely one of those.
For two straight days, Aroostook County teams seemed to be everywhere. By the time it was over, eight different County teams had played in seven regional championship games, five had won, and five were still playing when state championship Saturday arrived.
That’s a pretty good reason for this one to land at No. 3 in my five stories that defined the fall.
It started Tuesday with Fort Kent and Wisdom.
Both schools sent their boys and girls teams into regional finals, and all four came home as Northern Maine champions.
Fort Kent’s girls beat Orono 3-0 to win their fourth straight Class C North title. The Fort Kent boys needed overtime against top-seeded Orono, with Dominic Cyr scoring the tying goal and then converting the game-winner just 36 seconds into overtime.
Wisdom had its own championship double.
The girls beat Dexter 3-1 behind three goals from Ellie Cyr, while the boys somehow found a way through one of the craziest games of the fall.
Cayden Hargrove scored four times in the second half against Piscataquis, Wisdom built a 4-1 lead, watched it disappear, and then Zeek Cyr scored with 13 seconds left to win it 5-4.
So by the end of Tuesday, Fort Kent and Wisdom had gone four-for-four in regional championship games.
And there was still another full day to go.
Wednesday brought three more regional finals involving four County teams.
Presque Isle’s girls reached the Class B North championship before falling to John Bapst. Fort Fairfield’s girls made it to the Class D North final before their run ended against Penobscot Valley.
Then Madawaska and Fort Fairfield met for the Class D North boys title, which meant the County was guaranteed one more regional champion either way.
Madawaska won that one 2-0, giving Aroostook County its fifth Northern Maine soccer championship in two days.
That’s when the numbers really started to stand out.
Eight County teams had reached regional championship games. Seven regional finals had at least one County team involved. Five championships came home, and five teams were headed to state championship games on the same Saturday.
Fort Kent sent both its boys and girls.
Wisdom sent both its boys and girls.
Madawaska sent its boys.
For one Saturday, five Aroostook County teams had a chance to bring home a Gold Ball.
Four finished as state runners-up, and one finished the job.
We’ll get to that one later in the countdown.
But what I’ll remember most about that week is just how much County soccer was represented when the season got down to its biggest games.
Presque Isle was there. Fort Fairfield was there. Madawaska was there. Fort Kent and Wisdom each had both teams still alive deep into the tournament.
For a couple of days, it really did feel like almost every regional championship had an Aroostook County team in the middle of it.
Eight teams. Seven regional finals. Five Northern Maine championships. Five chances at a Gold Ball.
That’s why this week of County soccer is No. 3 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.

title: Maine peer support service seeks to break mental health stigma for first responders
text:
Peer support service in Maine seeks to break mental health stigma for first responders
The recent deaths of two first responders in Maine have sparked conversations about what services are available to people who work in emergency services.
The Professional Firefighters of Maine wants those who are struggling to know that it’s okay to ask for help.
"Behavioral health is a serious problem, and we're doing a better job today than we did years ago in trying to break the stigma, but it's still out there," said Michael Crouse, who is the secretary of the PFFMaine Peer Support Team.
The labor union’s peer support team is filled with nearly 50 trained members who help other first responders navigate trauma. The peers themselves have been through traumatic experiences, too.
"We found that by having another firefighter that understands behavioral health and the resources that are available to those members, that trust is already built," Crouse said.
Crouse says peer members respond across the state.
The Professional Firefighters of Maine website provides several avenues for support, including how to recruit more peer support team members and how to cope with grief and loss.
Crouse says he wants more fire chiefs and local union officers to create their own peer teams so they can see early signs of distress among their staff.
The Kittery Fire Department is taking action. Chief Randall Trull says the department is working to develop a wellness initiative to better support the mental health needs of its own staff.
"When somebody says, 'I have a problem, and I need help,' that's strength. That's a positive strength. It's not a weakness," Trull said. "I think that's the stigma we have to get over."
Building the program is still in the early stages, but Trull says the town has shown its support for it.
If you’re a first responder looking to speak to a peer support provider, you can call 207-752-1520. If you or a loved one is in crisis, you can call the suicide crisis lifeline at 988.

title: Looksmaxxing influencer known as Clavicular indicted on rape charges
text:
Looksmaxxing influencer known as Clavicular indicted on rape charges in Massachusetts
Braden Peters, the 20-year-old "looksmaxxing" influencer known online as "Clavicular," now faces two felony counts of rape in a Massachusetts superior court.
Video above from October: Influencer 'Clavicular' appears in court on rape charge
Hearst Television sister station WCVB found court records indicating that he was indicted on Nov. 13 on the rape counts and one misdemeanor count of providing alcohol to an underage person.
Peters was in Orleans District Court last month to face a rape charge. He pleaded not guilty, posted $10,000 bail, and had to surrender his passport.
Additionally, the judge ordered Peters to stay away from the victim and prohibited him from posting online about the case.
According to the criminal complaint from the district court case, the accuser told police Peters gave her alcohol at his family’s home while he was live-streaming on Twitch. Police said an officer who reviewed clips from the livestream heard the teen tell Peters, "Wait, I'm so drunk though."
The teen also told Chatham police she woke up the next morning to Peters sexually assaulting her.
Court records reviewed Wednesday in the superior court case indicate that no hearings are yet scheduled for that case.
Peters built an online following through the online looksmaxxing subculture, which is focused on changing and optimizing one's physical appearance.

title: More Clouds Today... Lots of Sunshine Returns Thursday — Beautiful Fall Weather Continues
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - No changes to the going forecast as strong high pressure continues to dominate our weather as it remains locked in over the Eastern U.S. This will keep us storm-free with dry conditions and above average temperatures sticking around through the upcoming weekend.
Our day today will feature more cloudiness than yesterday as moisture associated with a stalled out front well to our north moves on through. Expect partly to mostly cloudy skies today with the bulk of the clouds across the northern half of our state and brighter conditions closer to the coast. Despite more clouds/less sunshine... temperatures will be a bit warmer than yesterday with highs mainly in the low to mid-50s north and mid-50s to around 60° elsewhere. Skies will clear out tonight with low temperatures dropping to the 30s.
We’ll see more sunshine returning to the forecast Thursday as moisture with the stalled out front pushes further north. We’ll see mostly sunny skies Thursday with highs in the mid-50s to low 60s. Friday looks awesome with mostly sunny skies and high temperatures again topping off in the mid-50s to low 60s. This beautiful fall weather continues into the weekend with sunshine Saturday and highs in the 50s. We’ll see a bit more cloudiness Sunday leading to a mix of sun and clouds with highs in the 50s to around 60°. Thursday and Friday look fantastic with sunshine and highs in the 50s to low 60s.
Our next best chance of any rainfall will arrive Sunday night into Monday as a cold front moves through... bringing us a chance of showers. At the same time... there is a storm system forecast to pass out to sea south of the area Monday. How far north this system comes will determine whether or not we see some steadier rain move in... especially for areas closer to the coast. We’ll keep an eye on it as it gets closer. Regardless as to how far north the storm comes... as it moves to our east Monday night... it will draw much colder air south from Eastern Canada leading to temperatures being about 15°-20° colder by Tuesday with highs mainly in the 30s. It looks like that colder weather will stick around through the remainder of next week.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly cloudy... most clouds north. Highs mainly in the 50s. West wind 5-15 MPH with gusts to 20 MPH possible.
Tonight: Clearing skies. Lows in the 30s. Light west wind.
Thursday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to low 60s. Southwest wind 5-10 MPH.
Friday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to low 60s.
Saturday: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to near 60°.
Sunday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the 50s to near 60°.

title: China select board makes changes to employees’ health plan
text:
After a second discussion at their Nov. 16 meeting, China select board members voted narrowly to lower the employees’ health insurance plan, while increasing payments from their HRA (Health Reimbursement Account) so not all out-of-pocket expenses will rise (see the Nov. 12 issue of The Town Line, p. 2).
The vote to transfer from the Maine Municipal Association’s “Katahdin Plan” to its “Moosehead Plan” was carried by Blane Casey, Natasha Littlefield and Thomas Rumpf. Brent Chesley was opposed and Edwin Bailey abstained.
The more than $28,000 in premium savings will be split between the employee HRA and the town, with $14,000 being added to the current HRA amount.
Most members of the audience for the Nov. 16 meeting were town employees. During the public comment period, which came 10 minutes and several agenda items after the health insurance decision, Amber French, wife of codes officer Nicholas French (who had a conflicting event), read a prepared statement.
French said town employees’ share of health insurance is already more than some can afford, and emphasized the importance of a good health care plan in attracting and keeping employees.
Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood, who recommended the Moosehead Plan, agreed a good health care plan is vital. She plans to review effects of the change repeatedly over the next months.
Other actions at the Nov. 16 meeting took less time. Board members:
— Re-elected Chesley board chairman and Rumpf board secretary.
— Rehired consultant Paul Froman for another three to four months to help prepare a transition of the current China Rescue Unit to a municipal department.
— Rehired town attorney Amanda Meader for another year.
— Re-elected Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood to the Hampden-based Municipal Waste Hub board of directors.
— Authorized resident Kyle Pierce to decorate the exterior of the former Weeks Mills school house for the holidays.
Hapgood reminded those present that all town departments will be closed Thursday and Friday, Nov. 26 and 27, for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Select board meetings for the remainder of the year are scheduled for 6 p.m., Nov. 30, Dec. 14 and Dec. 28, in the town office meeting room.

title: Paramedic mom unknowingly responds to scene where son was crushed to death while working on car
text:
(Gray News) - A paramedic in Utah unknowingly responded to an emergency involving her son after a car he was working on fell on him, authorities said.
The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said Logan Mumford, a father of two from Sigurd, was helping a woman repair her car on Nov. 16 when it fell from the jack supporting it, trapping him underneath.
A neighbor who had been helping had briefly gone across the street to get additional lighting and a floor jack when he heard the car fall.
He tried to pull Mumford out and lift the car but couldn’t.
The neighbor returned with a floor jack as deputies arrived. Together, they raised the car enough to remove Mumford, who was unresponsive and had suffered significant head trauma. First responders immediately began lifesaving efforts.
One of the paramedics sent to the scene was Mumford’s mother, who did not know her son was the patient until she heard his name.
“Behind every emergency call is a family, a story, and a community forever changed,” the sheriff’s office said. “Last night, this tragedy became far too personal for one of our own.”
Mumford was taken to a hospital where he was pronounced dead. He leaves behind a 3-year-old son and a 1-year-old daughter.
Authorities described Mumford as “someone who was always willing to lend a hand and help others.”

title: High surf washes couple’s engagement ring away minutes after dream proposal
text:
SAN CLEMENTE, Calif. (KCAL/KCBS) - A dream beach proposal in California took an unexpected turn when high surf washed away the couple’s engagement ring.
Jace Harrick proposed to his girlfriend Sunday with a beautiful diamond engagement ring. The picturesque proposal, with the sunset blanketing Calafia State Beach in San Clemente, seemed perfect – until the surf washed onto the shore around the couple.
“Initially, I’m like, ‘OK, this is fine. Let’s lift her up,’” Harrick said. “I didn’t want her to get swept away because we have El Niño. We know that can be a bit aggressive.”
As he picked up his fiancée, Harrick lost his grip on the ring box. The 4-carat ring fell into the knee-high water, and the couple hasn’t seen it since.
Jessica Licon and her family were on the beach that day and said the surf was rough. Her husband heard all the commotion a few feet away, thinking that everyone was celebrating the proposal.
“That’s when I told him, ‘No, the ring is gone. Everyone’s looking for it,’” Licon said. “Everyone was looking for the ring… but nobody found anything.”
A few treasure hunters with metal detectors searched the sand but had no luck.
Harrick plans to replace the ring. He said the silver lining in all of this is the proposal was perfect up to that last moment and that his soon-to-be wife is safe.
“Let’s control what we can control right now, and that’s our attitude,” Harrick said. “I’m just grateful she’s OK. That’s what’s important.”
A diver has offered to come out and search for the lost ring. Harrick plans to offer a reward to anyone who can find it.

title: A place to call home: Bangor mother, daughter receive keys to Habitat for Humanity house
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Habitat for Humanity is celebrating 50 years of making homeownership accessible, and the Bangor affiliate celebrated Wednesday for accomplishing just that.
Bangor resident Angie Works is now a proud homeowner, as she and her five-year-old daughter, Hope, received the keys to their new Grove Street home from Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor.
“I was living in a one-bedroom apartment for the last few months after my divorce,” explained Works. “When I was looking for permanent housing, I just thought, ‘Well, you can’t get anything you don’t apply for, so...’”
Qualified applicants who earn 30% to 80% of the area’s median income can apply. After getting approved for an affordable mortgage, Habitat helps close the financial gap.
“They are the homeowners. They are purchasing this home and will have a mortgage payment,” Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor’s Executive Director Melissa Huston said. “It’s just that Habitat partners with them and helps bridge the gap between what they can afford and the appraised value of the home.”
For Works, Habitat for Humanity’s involvement was critical, saying “there would have been no home without Habitat.”
“This area, Maine in general, is pretty high with the real estate costs and not very high with the incomes. There is a big divide between people that can afford the homes and the people that need the homes,” Works described. “So, for me, being a single mom, not having two incomes in the house, it wasn’t going to be feasible for a long time. So, this really helped with that.”
She added that Hope is excited to decorate her own bedroom, already painted a unique shade of purple that Works surprised her with.
Works’ Grove Street home is the 31st house constructed by Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor.
For the past 11 houses, Habitat has partnered with students at Eastern Maine Community College to build the frame, install insulation and more before having it delivered to the lot for finishing touches.
“I think it just brings a great opportunity for people to learn how to build a house, especially in a trade like this,” said Kason White, an EMCC student who helped build Works’ home. “Here we are with a whole house behind us, and it’s just cool to be able to donate to the community and help and just make a house for someone to live in.”
White was joined by other EMCC students to see the house fully painted and complete, which was done by volunteers, partner contractors and the homeowner as part of “sweat equity” required for the property.
As rents rise and starter homes become harder to find, organizers say Habitat makes the dream of homeownership a reality.
“It’s understandable why for-profit developers aren’t spending their time and their energy on small starter homes because they really just can’t turn a profit on it. As a non-profit, that is not our mission,” Huston described. “Our mission is to partner with those that wouldn’t be able to realize the dream of homeownership.”
Works said what homeownership ultimately provides is stability for her and her daughter: “Being able to have a home and know where you’re going to be and that you can afford that home, the stability of that just takes a lot of weight off your shoulders, especially in this market.”
Works was able to complete about 10% of her sweat equity before the home was ready, so she will be one of many volunteers for the next Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor home.
Lucky for her, it’s planned to go right next door!

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley (Clinton)
text:
Doctors in Clinton, 1800s
Your writer has now made an arbitrary jump from Augusta to the northeastern edge of Kennebec County to see what information is available about early doctors in Clinton, Albion and Benton. This article covers Clinton during about the first half of the 1800s.
Henry Kingsbury, in his chapter on the medical profession in his 1892 Kennebec County history, and other sources offered many names of 19th-century doctors practicing in these towns. Your writer found a fair amount of information (though, as usual, not about medical practices) on a few; bits of information on more; and no information at all on others.
* * * * * *
Various sources included among doctors said to have practiced in Clinton: Abram Frees (settled at Pishon’s Ferry on the Kennebec about 1815), Albert R. Lincoln, Seward Garcelon, William Albee and Dr. Thorndike.
In his chapter on the town of Clinton, Kingsbury mentioned Dr. Thorndike, dating him about 1848, and added William Guptill (about 1849; built what was in 1892 the Methodist parsonage); Richard Williams and Benjamin Clement (late 1850s); and Pitt M. Whitten and Daniel Moody (early 1860s).
Your writer’s on-line search yielded no information about Drs. Frees, Albee, Thorndike, Guptill, Williams, Whitten or Moody. Fortunately, Major General Carleton Edward Fisher’s history of Clinton was somewhat more informative.
Dr. Benjamin Clement moved around so much that he could have been in Clinton in the late 1850s, but your writer has no proof beyond Kingsbury. Here’s a summary of FamilySearch’s summary of his life:
Dr. Clement was born in 1787 in Hopkinton, New Hampshire, son of a doctor. On Sept. 10, 1812, in Sidney, he married Sylvia Pullen; their only child, a daughter they named Ann Sylvia, was born in Harmony (about 45 miles north of Sidney). In 1850, he was living in Monson (almost another 30 miles north). He died in Hanover, New Hampshire, part-way back to his birthplace, on March 9, 1865.
An on-line search for Albert R. Lincoln brought three references to a doctor with that name, who was born in Perry, in downeast Maine, in 1831 and died in 1899.
Ancestry says his middle name was Robinson, and his wife was Deborah Reynolds (Foster), born in 1832 and died in 1901. This source says the Lincolns were in Dennysville, near Perry, when their son, Harry, was born Aug. 31, 1867.
Further search led to a letter Dr. Lincoln wrote to Maine Governor Israel Washburn on Dec. 8, 1862. He inquired about getting commissioned as a surgeon or assistant surgeon in the 18th Maine Regiment, saying officers of the regiment had asked him to apply.
The letter says it was sent from Pembroke, a town about six miles from Perry.
On Feb. 25, 1865, Colonel Russell Shepherd, of the First Maine Heavy Artillery, wrote to Governor Samuel Cony recommending assistant surgeon Albert R. Lincoln for promotion to surgeon. “He has the reputation of being one of the most capable and efficient medical officers in the corps,” Shepherd wrote.
True, no doubt; but the persistence of evidence that the Lincolns remained in far eastern Maine makes Dr. Lincoln’s presence in Clinton highly unlikely.
* * * * * *
One doctor from this early list whose Clinton practice your writer confirmed was Seward Garcelon. On-line sources provide a fair amount of information about Garcelon and his family, especially his wife and her younger brother, Samuel Merritt.
Garcelon, born in Lewiston in 1806, followed older brother Daniel (born in 1795) in graduating from the Medical School of Maine at Bowdoin College, Class of 1830. The same year, he opened a medical practice in Clinton, where, on Aug. 26, 1833, he married Catherine Merritt.
In 1861, Garcelon retired. He and Catherine moved to Oakland, California, to join her brother Samuel Merritt. Garcelon died there on Feb. 5, 1877
When Merritt, a physician and businessman, died in 1890, Wikipedia says he was believed to be “the richest man in Oakland.” He left much of his wealth to his sister.
Catherine Merritt Garcelon lived until Dec. 9, 1891. According to one website, in 1890 she began distributing her property (a distribution that survived a legal challenge claiming she was not of sound mind).
She gave Bowdoin College $400,000 for scholarships for medical school students (the Merritt-Garcelon Scholarship). Bowdoin no longer includes a medical school; the scholarships are still awarded annually to Bowdoin graduates for continuing education in health care.
She gave the City of Oakland $600,000 “to build and operate a teaching hospital” in honor of her brother. Samuel Merritt College (now Samuel Merritt University, “focused on health sciences”) and Merritt Hospital (now part of a larger Oakland facility) were founded in 1909, the web says.
When Catherine Merritt Garcelon died, her net worth was estimated at between $2 and $3 million. She, her husband Seward and her brother Samuel are buried in Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery.
* * * * * *
A later list of Clinton physicians is included in Major General Carleton Edward Fisher’s 1970 history of the town. He opens his chapter on Professional and Civic Leaders with these names of doctors who practiced, at least briefly, before and during the Civil War: Ezekiel Brown, Jr.; John Bowman; Whiting Robinson; Abraham Freeze; Albert Carlton Thayer; Albert Thorndike; William Guptill; Benjamin Clement; Richard Williams; Rufus R. Williams; Daniel Moody; Charles Rowell; and Parker M. Whitten.
Seward Garcelon is not on Fisher’s list of Clinton doctors. Fisher did mention him: as a Clinton school committee member in 1833 and 1834 and 1836 through 1840, and as captain of the militia company that he and others got approved and organized in April 1841, in which he served until May 1848.
Abraham Freeze was apparently Kingsbury’s Abram Frees. Drs. Clement, Guptill, Moody, Thorndike, Whitten and Richard Williams appear on both early and later lists, and Fisher found bits of information on all of them.
Fisher dismissed several of the doctors on his and other lists as not staying long enough in Clinton to make an impression. Albert Thorndike and William Guptill both came in 1850, Benjamin Clement in 1856, Richard Williams and probably Charles Rowell in 1857, Rufus Williams in 1860.
* * * * * *
Fisher had trouble finding information about Freeze. He’s named Clinton’s third resident doctor, arriving at Pishon’s Ferry around 1817 (close enough to 1815). He had a wife named Hannah. Two girls named Barbory and Sarah might have been their daughters.
Clinton’s Old Village Cemetery has two stones marking the graves of Abraham and Hannah Freeze. Find a Grave says Abraham (whose gravestone calls him Mr. Abram Frees) was born in 1781 and died Aug. 11, 1840; Hannah (on her gravestone, wife of Abraham Freese) was also born in 1781 and died May 23, 1854.
* * * * * *
According to Fisher, Ezekiel Brown, Jr., was the first doctor in Clinton. He was born in Concord, Massachusetts, in 1743 (or 1745, according to Find a Grave). In 1772, he was granted a lot in Clinton, and was probably briefly in town then.
He returned to Concord before May 1774, when his wife, Mary (Barron, born in 1752, married Feb. 28, 1770) delivered their second child (of 10; all but the last, a boy born in 1797, lived to adulthood). Fisher surmised Brown studied medicine in Concord, because by 1776 he was qualified to “be commissioned a surgeon’s mate in the military service.”
He rose to the rank of surgeon and served until Jan. 1, 1781.
In or around 1789 the Browns came back to Clinton and settled at what was Brown’s Corner and is now Benton Station, on the Kennebec. Typically, Fisher wrote nothing about Brown’s medical practice. Instead, observing that as one of the town’s better-educated men, he would inevitably be chosen for government offices, Fisher listed those: town meeting moderator, selectman, town clerk, tax collector, holder of “several other minor town offices,” justice of the peace.
In 1812, Fisher wrote, Brown “lost the use of his left arm,” limiting his medical practice. He died June 30, 1824; Mary died May 6, 1832. Both are buried in Ames Cemetery, now in Benton (since Benton and Clinton became separate towns in 1842).
* * * * * *
Dr. John Bowman Fisher identified as Clinton’s second doctor, coming to town before 1807, the year he was first elected a selectman. He was re-elected in 1808 and 1810; he died April 14, 1810, “leaving no kin in the county.”
He had a wife named Jane B. Reed, born in 1797. Beyond that information, your writer is stymied, as Fisher evidently was, too.
* * * * * *
Dr. Whiting Robinson was Clinton’s third doctor, according to Fisher. He was born, Find a Grave says, Sept. 21, 1782, in Windham, Connecticut. He served as a surgeon’s mate in the Plimpton, Massachusetts, militia, and moved to Clinton in 1812. Here he was again a surgeon’s mate in the area militia, promoted to surgeon May 3, 1823, Fisher wrote.
His wife was Jane Bellknapp (Reed), born in 1796 or 1797.
Fisher listed Robinson as a member of Clinton’s first three-person school committee in 1821, serving through 1824 and again in 1829; as Clinton town clerk in 1823 and from 1825 to 1835; and as a Clinton selectman in 1832 and 1833.
Robinson died Feb. 24, 1852. Like Dr. Bowman, he lived in the part of Clinton that became Benton; he is buried in Benton’s Reed Cemetery, with his widow, Jane, who died Sept. 11, 1881.
* * * * * *
Dr. Albert Carlton Thayer was only briefly in Clinton, but Fisher shared a paragraph of information about him, and an on-line genealogy provided more.
Thayer was a Vassalboro native, born March 3, 1809, who graduated from Colby in 1828, went to Bowdoin Medical School and got a degree from Columbia’s medical school in 1831. In 1832 he was in practice in “the lower part” of Clinton, but “about 1833” he moved to Skowhegan, Fisher wrote; the on-line source says he practiced in Benton and Skowhegan.
The on-line genealogy names his wife as either Ann C. Putnam or Ann Atwood; Fisher said he married Elizabeth Atwood, from Pittston. He died Dec. 28, 1834, in Skowhegan (genealogy) or July 3, 1882, in Newport (Fisher).
Find a Grave confirms the former, with a photo of his stone in Skowhegan’s North Cemetery beside the stone of his wife, identified as Ann E. Putnam Thayer. Below Dr. Thayer’s information is the name “Little Albert,” a son who died Sept. 8, 1837, aged two years and two months, whom – if the gravestone dates are correct – his father never met.
* * * * * *
Dr. Daniel Moody was born in Limington, Fisher said, and opened a practice in Clinton “about 1862” (Clinton is about 100 miles northeast of Limington; Fisher offered no explanation for his choice. About 1865, he married Jennie Fly.
Fisher said Moody “took an active part in town affairs” until his death, but he is not on any of Fisher’s lists of elected town officials.
Moody died in 1889, according to Fisher.
An on-line Moody genealogy confirms Daniel and younger brother Simon, born in Limington to Joseph Moody. Neither their mother’s name nor their birthdates are provided.
* * * * * *
Dr. Parker M. Whitten, Fisher wrote, first studied at Bowdoin and then “graduated in medicine at Berkshire, Massachusetts, in 1864.”
(Wikipedia offers Berkshire Medical College, in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, which started in 1823 as part of Williams College, the still existing liberal arts college, and was “disbanded” in 1867. Berkshire, according to Wikipedia, was the first United States medical school to have a “professorship in mental diseases,” and the first to grant a medical degree to an African American.)
Fisher surmised Whitten came directly to Clinton, because he was “well enough settled” by 1868 to marry Clara Flood. If they had children, Fisher did not mention them, and your writer failed to find on-line information.
Whitten practiced in Clinton for 15 years, Fisher said, “but then his health failed and he moved to Elgin, Illinois, [no explanation given for this choice] where he died 5 April 1885.”
Main sources
Fisher, Major General Carleton Edward, History of Clinton, Maine (1970)
Kingsbury, Henry D., ed., Illustrated History of Kennebec County Maine 1625-1892 (1892)
Websites, miscellaneous.

title: LIVE: Mullin heads to Congress to face questions over flight disruptions, football trip and immigration
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.
The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.
A look at some of the highlights:
Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions
Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.
“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”
Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.
“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.
Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin’s Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.
That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.
Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling
Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.
Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.
Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.
“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.
Mullin defends ground stop response
Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.
The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.
At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn’t giving the public clear answers.
“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success,” Mullin said.
Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny
Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring spree, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The hiring rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.
Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.
The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump’s immigration agenda.
Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths.
“You are killing people,” McIver replied.
“No ma’am. That’s your opinion,” Mullin said, ending the exchange.
Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.
Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.
Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff.
___
Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.

title: Fisheries regulator cuts menhaden catch limit, adopting uneasy compromise proposed by Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Debate has raged up and down the East Coast this year over a small fish that plays a mighty role in the marine ecosystem: Atlantic menhaden, also known as bunker or pogies.
Last week, the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission voted to reduce the total menhaden catch limit along the Atlantic coastline, beginning with a 9% cut in 2027 and rising to a 17% cut in 2028, compared with the current limit. The measure was proposed by Maine’s delegation to the commission as a compromise between the status quo supported by commercial fishermen and steeper cuts sought by conservationists. At its next meeting in January, the commission will discuss how to allocate the new quota state by state.
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission regulates nearshore fisheries shared by the East Coast states from Maine to Florida.
Menhaden are an important food source for larger marine species such as striped bass and for birds of prey such as ospreys. The Atlantic striped bass population has been failing to reproduce for nearly a decade, and ospreys have also recently shown signs of decline. As a result, concern has been mounting about the management of the menhaden fishery.
The reduced catch limit “is a step in the right direction” to protect menhaden and those that depend on it, said Nick Lund, Maine Audubon’s advocacy and outreach manager. “We will continue to look to science to determine the correct next steps.”
Menhaden have become the preferred bait for lobster fishermen as herring quotas have been cut. As a result, New England fishermen have been catching and buying more and more menhaden in recent years. The fish are more affordable than frozen bait imported from other countries, and provide extra income for people who catch both lobster and menhaden.
Patrice McCarron, executive director of the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, told The Maine Monitor she was disappointed that the commission reduced the overall catch limit but relieved that the compromise was less restrictive than other proposals.
Splitting the reduction across two years will help the fishery adjust, McCarron added. “To have to take the full cut in one year would be very difficult,” she said.
While the bait fish industry is growing, it’s still small compared with a different industry in Virginia that reduces or cooks down menhaden to produce oil for omega-3 fatty acid supplements and protein for pet food. The industry has a long history in the United States, but only one facility is left: a processing plant in Reedville, Virginia, owned by Omega Protein, a subsidiary of Canada’s Cooke Inc.
The coastwide catch limit for menhaden in 2026 is 186,840 metric tons, down from 233,550 in 2025. In reality, commercial fishermen had caught a little less than 147,000 metric tons in 2025. Conservationists attributed this shortfall to a lack of menhaden in the ocean, while fishermen said they had fewer fishing days due to bad weather.
The limit in 2027 will be 170,000 metric tons, falling to 155,000 in 2028.
States are allocated their portions according to their historic fishing patterns. Maine is currently entitled to 4.8% of the total quota. Virginia is entitled to the vast majority of the catch, at just over 75%.
Maine has been fishing well above its quota for the past several years, which it is allowed to do by receiving quota transfers from other states and by taking advantage of “episodic events” when more menhaden were found in Maine waters than expected. In 2025, Maine’s actual landings were nearly 10% of the coastwide total.
Weighing ecology and economy
In the months leading up to last week’s meeting, the ASMFC received more than 48,000 public comments about how the menhaden fishery should be regulated over the next few years. Most were in favor of lowering the coastwide fishing quota by 40% as well as placing special limits on fishing in Chesapeake Bay, the nursery habitat for both menhaden and its predators.
Those who work in and around the commercial fishing industry spoke up in favor of keeping the status quo.
Suzannah Raber, a bait dealer who owns the New England Fish Company in Portland, said at the meeting that cutting the catch limit would cause a serious bait shortage in Maine and New England. She pointed out that many lobster fishermen have come to depend on menhaden as a second source of income.
“The lobstermen very much need menhaden to survive. It accounts for a lot of their income now,” she said.
Several New Englanders who spoke said they had seen plenty of fish in the Gulf of Maine and hypothesized that climate change is sending menhaden north.
“The fish are moving north. The waters are warming,” said Doug McQuarrie, a menhaden harvester in Maine.
Because of menhaden’s role in the ecosystem, the fishery is not meant to be managed in isolation but in tandem with other species such as striped bass. The 40% catch reduction supported by many who submitted public comment, as well as some of the states, would have minimized the probability of menhaden fishing negatively impacting striped bass and other predators.
The catch limit that was ultimately approved “abandoned” that ecological framework, Tony Friedrich, president and policy director of the American Saltwater Guides Association, said in an interview. He criticized the commission as caving in to pressure from the commercial fishing industry, saying the organization has let other fisheries it managed collapse in the past, such as cod and Northern shrimp.
“If we just give Mother Nature a chance, things can come back unless you exploit them to a tipping point,” Friedrich said.
Some commissioners, particularly those from Virginia, argued that the menhaden fishery is already managed conservatively. Several commissioners spoke about the need to balance ecological needs with the socioeconomic impact of their decision. Virginia, as well as Maine, had initially wanted to keep the current coastwide catch limit.
Ultimately, a narrow majority of states — Maine, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Virginia, South Carolina and Georgia, along with representatives from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Potomac River Fisheries Commission — voted for the 17% cuts by 2028.
States that had wanted steeper cuts — Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, Maryland, North Carolina and Florida — voted against the measure.
The commission reconvened on Nov. 11 to discuss a special cap for fishing within Chesapeake Bay and voted to set this cap at 21.8% of the total coastwide limit. Only Virginia and the representatives from federal agencies voted against this measure.
Many acknowledged that this cap is a precaution and that more scientific research on menhaden is needed.
Congress recently appropriated $2.5 million for research on these fish and their role in the ecosystem and the economy, to be distributed to scientists through the commission. The commission will issue a request for proposals in the next few weeks and will coordinate with the Virginia Institute for Marine Science, which is receiving $2 million appropriated from the Virginia state legislature for similar research. Preliminary findings are expected in 2028.

title: Democrats flipped 9 US Senate seats in the midterms — the most in almost 70 years
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) - Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s competitive U.S. Senate race has flipped a ninth Republican-held seat to the Democrats, giving Peltola’s party its biggest midterm gain in nearly 70 years.
Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term. That year, Democrats wrested away 13 Republican-held seats and also won both of Alaska’s newly created seats, for a total gain of 15 seats.
Peltola’s victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the Senate in 16 years. Democrats held 58 Senate seats in the waning days of the 111th Congress, which concluded on Jan. 3, 2011.
“56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in statement posted on social media. “Most people didn’t think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle.”
Even without Alaska, Democrats would have secured their largest majority since January 2015, when Republicans took control after flipping nine Democratic seats in the 2014 midterms during President Barack Obama’s second term.
Democrat Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate victory Wednesday in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race gave his party its eighth Republican-held seat. That win delivered Democrats their most midterm pickups since President Ronald Reagan’s second midterm election 40 years ago.
Democrats also reclaimed the House, picking up 42 seats as of Tuesday. The gains continued a historical trend of midterm losses for the president’s party.
The Senate has tended to be less susceptible to the midterm effect than the House. In seven of the last 16 midterms prior to 2026, the president’s party either held its ground or gained seats in the Senate, though all but one of those midterms occurred in the president’s first term. A president’s second midterm tends to be more punishing.
By comparison, the president’s party had gained House seats in only two midterms since the end of World War II.

title: Trump gets a personal tarmac welcome from Xi after landing in China
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
So at the start of the second day of Trump’s trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump’s behalf. He told reporters there was “zero” evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
“Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you’ve identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption,” said Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It’s a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
The White House said that Trump would have two separate meetings on Wednesday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.
As leaders were introduced on Wednesday night ahead of an APEC group photo, Putin approached Trump. They shook hands and traded greetings.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia’s invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump’s aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
“I think it’s very close to getting it done,” Trump said. “We’re going to have a good meeting on that.”
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. But neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for “working very hard.”
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
“Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes,” Trump said. “I love what you’ve done here.”
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines’ current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 “People Power” uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines’ strongman leader.
Trump called her “always the most beautiful” and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
What’s on the agenda for Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America’s largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China’s trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump’s close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China’s access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
___
Price reported from Manila, Philippines. AP writers Darlene Superville in Washington and Jim Gomez in Manila contributed to this report.

title: What new automatic enrollment rules mean for your retirement savings
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - The Treasury Department and the IRS have finalized new rules intended to make saving for retirement easier.
The final regulations implement a key part of the SECURE 2.0 Act, which required many new 401(k) and 403(b) workplace plans to automatically enroll eligible employees.
“With the SECURE 2.0 regulations in place, American families will be able to boost their savings and keep more of their hard-earned money through their automatic enrollment in a retirement account,” IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said.
Workers will be enrolled at a starting contribution rate of 3% of their pay, with that rate going up by at least 1% each year until it hits at least 10%, but no more than 15%.
Employees can still opt out or change how much they contribute to their retirement plans.
The new rules will take effect for plan years beginning after Dec. 31, 2027.
The Treasury Department estimated the expanded automatic enrollment could boost retirement savings by an average of $4.2 billion a year through 2032.
“A financially secure retirement is a cornerstone of the American Dream, and every worker deserves the opportunity to achieve it,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
Small and new businesses, government plans, church plans and SIMPLE 401(k) plans are exempt from mandatory automatic enrollment requirements.

title: Longtime Bangor landlord group sells all 55 of its rental units for $3.5M
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
The company that for years has managed 55 rental units around Bangor now owns them, after buying the entire portfolio for $3.5 million in late August.
The new owner, C & M Investment Group, is based in Bangor and has managed the properties since 2013.
The seller, Richway Associates LLC, is a company founded in 1992 and owned by nine shareholders. Some of them wanted to retire, while others had moved out of state or were in poor health, said Brent Hartley, the company’s treasurer.
“Everything was going well other than one-third of our shareholders wanting to move on and enjoy retirement,” Hartley said. “The company that managed the properties for us was interested in buying and made a nice offer, so we sold it right to them.”
The sale was one of the most expensive residential deals in Maine that month, and it moved a large share of long-standing Bangor rental housing to a new owner at a time when apartments the average renter can afford are hard to find. C & M Investment Group hasn’t said what it plans to do with the properties.
The properties included in the sale range from large apartment buildings near downtown Bangor to a mobile home park in Eddington. At the time of the sale, nearly all of the 55 units were occupied, according to Hartley.
The units have been consistently full since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, a sign of how much demand there is for housing, Hartley said.
Four of the buildings sit together on Main Street between the I-395 on-ramp and the Cool Girl Collective consignment shop. Three hold apartments while the fourth, at 585 Main St., is a three-bedroom, two-bathroom single-family house.
Two more apartment buildings sit across the street from John Bapst High School, with one positioned on Broadway while the other is on Pine Street. The remaining properties included in the sale are a cluster of seven mobile homes on Hill Street in Eddington.
A sale involving more than 50 units isn’t “very common at all,” Hartley said, though large swaths of real estate might change hands through private sales without ever being advertised.
C & M shares an address with Maine Real Estate Management, which oversees residential and commercial rentals across the state. The company did not respond to multiple emailed requests for comment about its plans for the properties.
Hartley said he didn’t know what the buyer planned, other than the 585 Main St. house was vacant and needed renovations. He expects little to change for tenants.
“[The buyer has] been the point of contact for 13 years, so I don’t think anything would really change,” Hartley said. “[Tenants] are still paying the same people and they’re still having the same maintenance people. It’s probably about as seamless as you can get for a transaction like this.”
The sellers did not send tenants a notice about the sale, Hartley said. Two tenants at 591 Main St., who declined to be named, said earlier this month that they had not been told their building had sold.
The city has issued permits only for interior work at 585 Main St., said David Warren, a city spokesperson. It issued an electrical permit in September and an HVAC permit for a new boiler in October. The house had not received an occupancy permit as of late last month, meaning no one can live there yet.
“From a commercial standpoint, it’s in a great location for a commercial project with the interstate right there,” said Anne Krieg, Bangor’s community and economic development director. “But the use is residential.”
The owner would need city approval to turn the property into something other than housing, and no such request had been filed as of last month, Krieg said.

title: Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world’s largest religion
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released Wednesday by the Pew Research Center.
Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity are growing, but Islam is growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, is that Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups.
“It’s the babies,” said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity are much smaller factors than fertility rates.
During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that’s considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.
According to Pew’s latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew’s new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.
The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration.
Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62% of U.S. adults, according to Pew, and will fall below 50% by 2065.
In neighboring Canada, Christians are expected to drop below 50% by 2030, Pew said.
In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41% of the U.S. population and to outnumber Christians in Canada.
Muslims and Christians are expected to keep pace with population growth
The world’s population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070, Pew said. Of the religious groups it analyzed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%.
Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew said. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan.
Over the coming decades, Pew said, most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted.
By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world’s Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing more than threefold to 299 million.
The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline.
For example, the number of people living in Europe will shrink by 17% by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there will drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe’s population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6% to 13%.
In the U.S., Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070.
Several mainline Protestant denominations in the U.S. have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations.
Fertility rates are a driving factor
By Pew’s estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020-2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers.
Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline.
If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia — which currently has the most Muslims.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations are “extremely important” in light of the evolving trends.
“The ‘clash of civilization’ theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides,” she said via email. “Many Christians are not happy to see that Islam will be the world’s largest religion and it’s causing even more angst.”
“I hope people seek opportunities for greater interreligious education,” she added. “Personal contact is important — when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanizes’ the ‘other’ in fruitful ways.”
Alan Cooperman, Pew’s director of religion research, noted that most of the projected proliferation of Muslims and Christians was occurring in countries where they already are the majority — with conversion playing only a minor role.
“I don’t think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians,” he added. “I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims.”
The ‘nones’ are growing in some areas
Many countries have seen a steady proliferation of the “nones” — people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of “nones” but faces a sharp decline in overall population, the ranks of “nones” elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070, Pew said.
The “nones” already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.
___

title: Red Cross urges cooking safety ahead of Thanksgiving
text:
Thanksgiving is the busiest day of the year for home cooking fires, with more than three times the daily average of cooking-related incidents nationwide. Ahead of the holiday, the American Red Cross of Northern New England is urging families to take simple precautions to prevent fires and ensure their smoke alarms are working.
According to the National Fire Protection Association, cooking causes about 80% of home fires reported on Thanksgiving and nearly 40% of civilian fire injuries that day. Home fires remain the nation’s most frequent disaster, and Red Cross volunteers in Maine respond regularly to help families affected by local fire emergencies. So far this year, the Red Cross has responded to nearly 220 home fires in Maine, assisting 730 people.
“Thanksgiving is a time to gather with loved ones, but it’s also one of the busiest days of the year for home cooking,” Caroline King, executive director of the Red Cross Northern and Eastern Maine Chapter, said. “A moment of distraction in the kitchen can have serious consequences. By staying attentive while cooking and making sure smoke alarms are working, families can help protect what matters most and enjoy a safe holiday together.”
Follow these safety tips and visit redcross.org/fire for more information, including a sample fire escape plan to practice with your family:
Never leave cooking food unattended.
Keep anything that can burn away from heat sources, like loose clothing or dangling sleeves, potholders, oven mitts, wooden utensils, paper or plastic bags, food packaging and towels.
Keep kids and pets at least three feet away from cooking areas.
Keep a fire extinguisher in your kitchen.
Make sure smoke alarms are working.
If using a turkey fryer, fully thaw and dry the turkey before frying and keep the fryer at least 10 feet from structures.
Specific to deep frying Turkeys:
Deep frying of turkeys should occur outside and at least 10 feet from any structure, vehicles, or anything that can burn. Never in a garage, on a porch or under any structure.
Thaw the turkey completely and pat it dry before frying. Ice or water reacting with hot oil can cause violent boiling and splattering.
Do not overfill the fryer with oil. Check the correct oil level by first placing the turkey in the pot with water to measure displacement, then remove and dry the pot completely before adding oil.
Turn off the burner before lowering the turkey into the oil to prevent flare-ups.
Lower the turkey slowly and carefully to avoid splashing.
Monitor the oil temperature with a fryer thermometer. Never allow it to exceed 350°F (177°C).
Never leave the fryer unattended while it is in use.
Always wear heat-resistant gloves, long sleeves, and eye protection.
Keep children and pets at least three feet away from the cooking area.
In case of fire, do not use water to extinguish a grease fire — it will make it worse. Use a Class K or ABC-rated fire extinguisher and call 911 immediately if a fire occurs.
After cooking, allow the oil to cool completely before moving or disposing of it.
Check your smoke alarms before Thanksgiving. Working smoke alarms can cut your risk of dying in a home fire by half.
Place smoke alarms on each level of your home, including inside and outside bedrooms and sleeping areas.
In addition to testing your alarms once a month, change the batteries at least once a year, if your model requires it.
Check the manufacturer’s date of your smoke alarms. If they’re 10 years or older, they need to be replaced because the sensor becomes less sensitive over time. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions.
Identify two exits from every room.
Teach children what smoke alarms sound like and what to do when they hear one.
The American Red Cross shelters, feeds and provides comfort to victims of disasters; supplies about 40% of the nation’s blood; teaches skills that save lives; distributes international humanitarian aid; and supports veterans, military members and their families. The Red Cross is a nonprofit organization that depends on volunteers and the generosity of the American public to deliver its mission. For more information, please visit redcross.org or CruzRojaAmericana.org, or follow us on social media.

title: Aging Untold: How to treat psoriasis flare-ups later in life
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down what triggers psoriasis later in life and share practical strategies to manage uncomfortable flare-ups.
Plus, we discuss why choosing less medical intervention can sometimes be the most compassionate care decision for an aging loved one.
Then, we meet an 81-year-old retired psychology professor turning everyday household items into whimsical, one-of-a-kind music.
For older adults, psoriasis can develop or flare later in life.
It’s not just a skin condition. It’s an immune-mediated inflammatory disease, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. And it also increases the risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
She said traditional and functional medicine play an important role in treating autoimmune disorders.
Sometimes understanding a person’s goals, weighing the burden of treatment and accepting what cannot be fixed might be the best choice when caring for an aging loved one, according to the Aging Untold experts.
“We don’t like to talk about death. We don’t like to talk about dying,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
Some yoga classes are bringing in puppies, and the classes blend calm movement with play, rest and cuddle time. Some puppies even meet future families in class.
“Give me a yoga mat and a bunch of puppies and I don’t care if I stretch. I just want the puppies,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
First-time puppy yoga participant Taylor Manley said the class left her calm. She said a puppy just wanted to sit in her lap the whole time.
“I was trying to relax with him, and he was gonna make me go to sleep with him,” Manley said.
Herb Leff’s condo is filled with music studios, including one that used to be the master bedroom.
The 81-year-old retired University of Vermont psychology professor uses traditional instruments along with pots, pans and even a rubber chicken to make experimental music in the Burlington home he shares with his wife, Ellen.
The basement musical menagerie includes an electronic keyboard, wind chimes, frying pans suspended from the ceiling and more.
On the second floor, you’ll find a room he used to call the metal percussion paradise. The third studio is what Leff calls his cockpit.
