title: Taking action early can make a lasting difference in diabetes prevention and management
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Matthew Toohey, MD, is Plan Performance Medical Director at Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield in Maine.
Diabetes affects millions of Americans, including many of our neighbors here in Maine. In 2024, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 9% of adults aged 20 and older in Maine were diagnosed with diabetes.
November is Diabetes Awareness Month, but the importance of prevention and proactive chronic condition management extends well beyond a single month. Taking action early and addressing the everyday challenges of managing a chronic condition can make a meaningful difference in long-term health.
Early detection is an important first step.
Type 2 diabetes can develop gradually, sometimes without noticeable symptoms. Many people may be unaware they have diabetes or prediabetes, making preventive care and conversations with healthcare providers especially important.
Risk factors such as family history, age, physical inactivity and a history of gestational diabetes can increase the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes. Understanding these risks and discussing appropriate screening with a healthcare provider can help identify concerns before complications develop.
Prevention and management go hand in hand.
For those at risk of developing type 2 diabetes, small, sustainable lifestyle changes can have a meaningful impact. Regular physical activity, balanced nutrition and routine preventive visits can help reduce risk.
For those already living with diabetes, managing the condition involves more than monitoring blood sugar. Taking medications as prescribed, keeping up with recommended screenings and maintaining regular communication with healthcare providers are important components of ongoing care.
Yet managing diabetes isn’t always straightforward. Access to nutritious food, reliable transportation, medications and timely appointments can all influence a person’s ability to follow a care plan.
Connected care can make managing diabetes easier and help lower healthcare costs.
Diabetes management often involves multiple healthcare professionals, including primary care providers, specialists, pharmacists and care managers. When these professionals communicate and coordinate care, people can receive more consistent guidance, better understand their treatment plans and identify potential gaps in care.
Pharmacists, for example, can help people understand their medications and address concerns that may interfere with taking them as prescribed. Care teams can also help navigate appointments, and access education and resources that support their health needs.
Beyond improving health outcomes, diabetes also carries a significant financial impact, extending beyond individuals and families to employers and the broader healthcare system. The CDC reported that estimated annual diabetes-related costs incurred by employers in Maine reached nearly $28,000 per employee, compared with approximately $13,000 nationally, underscoring the importance of prevention and effective chronic condition management. By identifying health concerns earlier and helping people stay connected to care, we can reduce the risk of serious complications, avoidable hospitalizations and more costly treatments down the road.
Consider these five steps to reduce your risk or manage your condition:
Know your risk. Understand your family history and other factors that may increase your risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
Ask about screening. Talk with your healthcare provider about whether blood sugar or A1C testing is appropriate for you.
Build healthy habits. Look for realistic ways to incorporate physical activity and balanced nutrition into your daily routine.
Stay current on care. If you have diabetes, follow your treatment plan, take medications as prescribed and keep up with recommended screenings and appointments.
Stay connected. Communicate with your healthcare team about questions, challenges or barriers that may affect your ability to manage your health.
Diabetes prevention and management are not about making one big change. They’re about understanding your health, taking manageable steps and having the right support along the way.
As we recognize Diabetes Awareness Month, let’s use the opportunity to encourage more conversations about early detection, prevention and the importance of coordinated care. Together, these steps can help Mainers build healthier futures year-round.

title: Here’s how much Medicare Part B premiums are increasing in 2027
text:
(Gray News) - Medicare Part B premiums are increasing next year.
The standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B enrollees will be $209.40 for 2027, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
That is a $6.50 increase from $202.90 this year.
The annual deductible for Medicare Part B beneficiaries will be $292 in 2027. The current deductible is $283.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said the increases in the 2027 Part B standard premium and deductible are because of projected increases in health care spending.

title: Driver charged after striking, killing youth and fleeing in Waldoboro
text:
WALDOBORO, Maine — A 16-year-old died Wednesday afternoon Nov. 18 when a vehicle struck him and fled the scene.
The Waldoboro Police Department responded at about 3:15 p.m. to a report of a hit-and-run motor vehicle/pedestrian accident on Friendship Road in Waldoboro. As a result of the accident, a juvenile pedestrian was killed, according to Waldoboro Police Chief John Lash.
The Waldoboro Police Department later arrested Gifford Campbell, 53, of Waldoboro in connection to the death, the chief said.
Campbell was taken to the Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset, charged with Class A manslaughter, Class C leaving the scene of a personal injury accident, and operating under the influence of drugs resulting in death.
He is being held without bail until he makes his initial court appearance Friday, Nov. 20.
Departments who responded to the scene or helped with the investigation include Waldoboro Police, Fire, Emergency Medical Services, the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, Damariscotta Police, and the Maine State Police.

Three people have died from a respiratory virus outbreak in Washington County, according to the Maine CDC.
Three dead amid respiratory virus outbreak in Washington County
Three people have died from a respiratory virus outbreak in Washington County, according to the Maine CDC.
A CDC spokesperson says higher than expected cases of the flu and COVID-19 are ongoing in Washington County, and they are also monitoring an instance of meningococcal disease, though they say that case is isolated and the risk to the general public contracting that disease is low.
A spokesperson for Worcester Wreath, the Harrington-based farm that works as a supplier to Wreaths Across America, says one employee and two others that worked for their contractors have died.

title: Oxygen And A Lit Cigarette: Burns Send Auburn Mother And Son To Hospital
text:
While the use of home oxygen systems can help people with breathing problems live full lives away from hospital settings, there is a reason why public safety officials always issue warnings against smoking near those oxygen tanks.
Read More: Maine Teen Charged With Attempted Murder In Leeds House Fire
The Oxygen that comes in those tanks is pure, and when a flame is introduced near it, it can be very dangerous.
In fact, the City of Bangor has an entire section on its website that explains the dangers of such behavior.
"When exposed to an open flame or spark, pure oxygen can ignite, and if a fire is already burning around home oxygen, a bottle can suddenly and violently explode or release O2, giving the fire more fuel and making the fire far larger and more dangerous....When more oxygen is in the air, the fire will burn hotter and faster. Smoking should not be allowed in a home where oxygen is used. Even if oxygen is not being used, it may have saturated the home, including clothing, curtains, furniture, bedding, hair, and anything in the area."
That's exactly what Investigators with the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office think happened in a case in Auburn Tuesday, leaving a woman and her son badly burned.
According to officials with the Maine Department of Public Safety, the Auburn Fire Department was called to the Reed Street apartment where 74-year-old Deborah Luna and her 51-year-old son, Roger Bouchard, had been badly burned.
That's when the Fire Marshals were called in to find out what happened.
"The investigation determined that Luna had been seated on a couch while using supplemental oxygen and smoking. According to information provided during the investigation, Bouchard was inside the residence when he heard a sudden noise and saw his mother’s clothing catch fire.
Bouchard immediately attempted to extinguish the flames by assisting his mother with a stop, drop, and roll maneuver. During his efforts to extinguish the flames, Bouchard sustained significant burns to his left thigh and hands, requiring medical treatment."
Authorities believe the fire was accidental, but the investigation is still active.
Read More: Proper Ash Disposal Urged After Oxford Friday The 13th Fire
Both Luna and Bouchard suffered severe burns that required hospitalization and medical treatment. Luna was taken to Maine Medical Center's burn unit because her injuries required specialized treatment, and her son suffered severe burns on his hands and thigh.

title: Donald Trump’s name is on Susan Collins’ final appropriations table
text:
In one of the final spending bills released by the Sen. Susan Collins-led Senate Appropriations Committee this week, there’s a striking new provision that targets President Donald Trump’s name.
Section 195 of the spending bill for the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development reads as follows: “None of the funds made available by this Act may be used to require a recipient of Federal funds to display signage containing the name of the President, Vice President, or any member of the President’s Cabinet as a condition of the receipt of such funds.”
In other words, the departments would not be allowed to withhold money if a state or project recipient doesn’t want to plaster the names of administration officials on signs near construction sites.
It is unclear how the new language was added to the bill — it wasn’t in last year’s DOT and HUD spending proposal and it is not included in any of the committee’s other 11 appropriations bills released this month. Collins’ office did not respond to questions about the provision.
But it is an interesting, if relatively insubstantial, addition to Collins’ final round of spending proposals as chair of one of the Senate’s most powerful committees.
Trump has long had a penchant for naming things after himself — from his hotel chain to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C. — but both he and his predecessor, Joe Biden, have put their names on signs near prominent federally funded infrastructure projects in recent years. Barack Obama did something similar before them, but erected signs with just a bill title, rather than his own name.
Many of the projects with Trump’s name nearby were funded by the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law championed by Biden, with Trump claiming credit for them once assuming office.
Collins, who has been on the appropriations committee since 2009, was one of 10 Senators who negotiated that law, and often pointed out that fact in preelection news releases celebrating federal money coming to Maine.
Her final round of appropriations bills, including this one, are expected to be voted on in the coming weeks.
Collins will be replaced in early January by Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who defeated her by about 6 percentage points earlier this month. It’s not clear whether Jackson will also serve on the appropriations committee.

title: 15 years of building community in Brunswick, told in my daughters’ voices
text:
Fifteen years ago, I was hired as the executive director at People Plus — a job that would change my life and the lives of my family — especially my daughters. And way back then in October 2011, the girls were ages 6, 9, and 11.
I asked my daughters how my job has impacted their lives and this is what they said. (And yes, it made me cry!)
Daphne: age 26 (11 in 2011)
Being raised by a total powerhouse of a mom, it can be easy to forget that not everyone understands just how hard she works and just how impressive she is. That high level of functioning just feels like the default — because when you’re a kid, you don’t think about how your parents exist as members of your evolving community … you just view them in their role in your family.
When my mom started her job at People Plus 15 years ago, that’s when I really got to see how her superpowers as a parent translated into skills within a world outside of our home. I was old enough to notice just how much changed around the center within her first couple years there and just how deeply she cared about continuing that upward trend. Having been there with her while she found her way in the world as a single mom, it was clear to me when she landed at People Plus that she had found her “other” home.
Fast-forward to now, I often refer to my mom’s years at the center as her “life’s work.” With how much the People Plus community has grown and flourished under her leadership, it truly feels like the grand finale to a lifetime of building all the skills she’s best at. While you could say my sisters and I are truly the products of her lifetime of hard work, People Plus is like another child in this way. She was just the kind of power-mom the center needed!
Violet: age 23 (8 in 2011)
I remember when my mom started her job at People Plus like it was yesterday. I was 8 and had the priorities of an 8-year-old, too. Curious, and maybe a bit intimidated, I would explore the center and all it had to offer. While my mom focused on integrating into a brand-new job and community, I was focused on helping to build puzzles in the café. One puzzle I still remember was called Farm Stand.
While my mom was writing grant applications and helping with the various events at the Center, I was looking at Jack Gable’s painting of the Topsham Fair in the lobby, or coloring in her office. Certain staff and longtime members began to become familiar faces: Frank Connors, Jill Ellis, Jeanne Mayo, Betty Bavor, Jordan Cardone, and Jenn Felkay, to name a few.
Before I knew it, I was entangled in the People Plus community, and it fast became more than just my mom’s place of work. It was a place to relax and hang out with friends at the Teen Center, a place to come to on a summer’s day to eat lunch from Big Top Deli, and a place to do homework after a long school day.
Now I am 23 and I have the priorities of a 23-year-old, too. But as an adult I can now see for her, the priority was always our community. The countless nights she sat awake on the couch writing emails or grants or heartfelt columns for the paper. The mornings she would drop us at school with hot cocoa and waffles — which she made all while she was getting ready to speak on the radio minutes later. The weeks (and months) she spent getting ready for Music in April, the Scoop-a-thon, and many other fundraising events, all while she was raising us girls with kindness and grace. And I remember the countless times members and friends alike would come into her office, just to say hello.
Through it all, she was larger than life, fostering a working environment that felt more like a family. So often members would approach my sisters and me and ask us about our lives, how school was going, how that choir concert went or what colleges we were thinking about. They would bring us gifts, baked goods, art supplies, you name it. The love my mom pours into the organization became love that was reciprocated tenfold by everyone in the center, past and present, and I could not be more appreciative of how this has impacted my life and the lives of my sisters. To everyone in the People Plus family, thank you for accepting us with open arms, your constant support and generosity are never lost on us. And to my mom, thank you for everything.
Juliet, age 21 (6 in 2011)
When I think about my mom’s 15 years at People Plus, one of the things that stands out most to me is watching her go from simply being my mom — the person who, in my little-kid world, felt like she belonged entirely to me — to someone who seemed to belong to an entire community (I swear it happened overnight). I was 6 years old when my mom joined the People Plus family, and suddenly, everywhere we went in Brunswick, someone knew her, stopped to say hello, knew about me or my sisters, or had a story about something she had done at People Plus. I got to watch her take the Brunswick community by storm.
I remember being a little kid, running and laughing and causing chaos through the hall. Perhaps you could find me bothering Frank Connors in his office or stealing potato chips from the kitchen pantry. People Plus was like a second home to me, and it is so special to look back now and realize that while I was running around the halls, I was also watching my mom build something meaningful. Seeing her thrive in a role that allowed her to connect with, and make a difference for, so many people has been one of the most inspiring things to witness as her daughter, and I could not be prouder of the woman she has become through it.
While there are endless things I could say about witnessing my mother’s journey throughout these 15 years, I will end with this: Thank you, Mom, for your 15 years of care and light you have brought to this organization, and for teaching your daughters that hard work and commitment can make waves in a community. You truly leave every place you touch a little better than you found it. We love you.
Stacy Frizzle-Edgerton is executive director of People Plus.

title: Cincinnati Zoo gives update on Fiona’s condition
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - The Cincinnati Zoo gave an update on Fiona’s condition after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat.
The zoo said Fiona, the zoo’s miracle hippo, will have to pass the hat on her own since surgery is not an option. She has undergone tests and been given medicine to ensure she stays hydrated and can pass it safely.
An ultrasound found that there was some bunching of her intestines, indicating she could be passing something through her small intestine, according to the zoo.
The Columbus Zoo assisted with a colonoscopy, but nothing was seen through the nine-foot-long scope, the zoo said in Monday’s update.
At this point, Fiona is receiving 24-hour supportive care and attention until she passes the object.
Her care team said Wednesday they used a vibration plate borrowed from a local horse farm and encouraged Fiona to stand on it several times during the day.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo said in its post.
According to a zoo spokesperson, the hat was tossed into the air in front of Fiona’s habitat and was caught by a ceiling fan. The fan then “catapulted” the hat into the 1-foot opening above the viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident,” the spokesperson told FOX19 NOW.
The zoo’s veterinary team and hippo care staff are watching Fiona around the clock to help her pass the hat safely.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said in a Facebook post.
Until then, Fiona will not make an appearance at the popular Hippo Cove habitat.
“Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.
Officials said they will keep people updated on Fiona’s health.

title: Penobscot County commissioners approve $41.6 million budget in 2-1 vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot County commissioners voted 2-1 Wednesday to approve the 2027 budget as recommended by the county’s budget committee.
Commissioner Dan Tremble cast the lone vote against the $41.6 million budget, which is about $6 million higher than last year’s. Commissioner Dave Marshall voted in favor.
The amount the county needs to raise through taxation, after other revenues are accounted for, is expected to increase by approximately 23%. That does not necessarily mean every taxpayer’s bill will rise by 23%; the impact will vary among municipalities and properties.
The increase follows a 15.6% rise in the amount the county needed to raise through taxation for 2026, according to the county’s budget calculation sheet.
Public comment
The vote followed more than an hour of public comment during Wednesday morning’s meeting. Most speakers urged commissioners to reject the budget, citing concerns about potential tax increases.
Brewer Mayor Michele LaBree Daniels said the county’s increases are affecting municipal spending.
“We keep eating these funds and we keep losing things. We were supposed to buy a fire truck last year. We did not do that because of the severity of the county increase,” Daniels said. “So, it’s stopping municipalities from actually doing the things they need to do because we have to keep Penobscot County in their budget.”
Marshall said the approved budget would help stabilize county finances.
“The budget that we have done today, in my opinion, is adequate to keep the county to stop hemorrhaging funds, to stabilize it somewhat. Stabilize, allow us to regroup, refocus. We know what we have to do,” Marshall said.
Jail costs
County officials have identified the cost of operating the jail as a major driver of the increase.
Penobscot County voters rejected a referendum on Election Day that would have allowed a new jail to be built outside the county seat of Bangor.

title: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time that the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin as relations between the United States and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. official who confirmed the Trump-Putin meeting in China spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to share plans that were not yet public.
The exact timing of the meeting on Thursday was unclear. Trump already had public plans for a separate meeting with Xi and a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin.
Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin in their joint meeting about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia’s invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump’s aides told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
“I think it’s very close to getting it done,” the Republican president said. “We’re going to have a good meeting on that.”
Trump lands in China’s tech hub as outages cause concerns at home
Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the U.S. public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the U.S. worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
At the start of the second day of Trump’s trip, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump’s behalf. Rubio told reporters there was “zero” evidence that the outages were connected or were tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, reciprocating a gesture by the American leader during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
Trump and Xi greeted each other on Wednesday at the foot of the airplane’s stairs in a handshake that became a hug as a group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier in the day, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their long-standing friendship.
As leaders were introduced on Wednesday night before an APEC group photo, Putin approached Trump. They shook hands and traded greetings.
The White House said Trump was scheduled earlier Wednesday to have separate meetings with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and he complimented Trump for “working very hard.”
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the country’s former first lady who is the mother of the Philippines’ current president. Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene.
What’s on the agenda for Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America’s largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease because Trump has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
___

title: Obituary: Emma E. Thurlow
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Emma E. Thurlow, 87, of Scarborough, died at her home on Nov. 13, 2026, surrounded by her family after a beautiful life of homemaking, crafts, and quality time with family. She was born July 17, 1939, the only child of Ethel Emma Libby Gochie and Samuel Edward Gochie.
Emma attended Scarborough Schools and lived and worked all of her life in Scarborough. She was a beautician, worked for the family business, the Clam Bake and Fish Market in Pine Point, and supported her husband in all of his lobstering and fishing work for many years. She was a loyal contributor to the Libby legacy in the town of Scarborough and a member of the Daughters of the American Revolution. She loved different kinds of crafting – sewing, attending tat and chat, crocheting, knitting, and most importantly card making. Emma (Grammy) also loved a good holiday party or birthday celebration filled with delicious homemade treats, festive decorations, and her warm presence made it special.
Emma is survived by her beloved children, Edward Thurlow of Scarborough and Debra Arbo of Stratham, NH. She is also survived by her granddaughter, Helena Arbo, and grandson, Hunter Arbo, and many other relatives and friends. She adored her family and friends with all of her heart. She was predeceased by her beloved husband, Fred H. Thurlow.
A Graveside Service will be held on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, at 11 a.m. at Scarborough Memorial Cemetery, Old Blue Point Road, Scarborough.
Online condolences may be expressed at http://www.hobbsfuneralhome.com.

title: Hakeem Jeffries could become the first Black House speaker after Democratic nomination
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past most skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker with the gavel.
Jeffries secured the nod during closed-door voting, 251-11, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January. Among those opposing him on the secret ballot were a group of progressive newcomers, who said in a statement there is “still work to be done” to ensure their priorities.
Afterward, Jeffries vowed to work hard, through every corner of the Democratic caucus, and said each generation has the opportunity to “show up, speak up, stand up, and help the country march toward a more perfect union.”
“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” he said, “and to get big things done for the American people.”
Jeffries, of New York, ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change in Congress after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media campaigns have been flooding the offices of Democrats in both the House and the Senate, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.
Ahead of Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. Yet having led the Democrats to one of the biggest incoming House majorities in decades, he has room to maneuver.
Those opposing Jeffries, including some backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, signaled that conversations are ongoing as they push to deliver Medicare for All, stop harsh actions from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, get money out of politics and end Israel’s war in Gaza.
“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” they said in a joint statement.
Signing on as opposed were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York and Frederick Haynes of Texas, though he was one of two Democrats who did not vote. Reps-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres of California and Don Leonard of Ohio also said they voted against.
Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed and were elected, as was Rep. Ted Lieu of California, as chairman of the House Democratic caucus.
He will need a simple majority of 218 votes from the whole House to be elected speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. It would be a milestone in the nation’s struggles to create a representative democracy, since the first Black lawmaker was elected to the House more than 150 years ago.
Skeptics question whether leaders are up to the job
Wednesday’s vote was the first of their careers for dozens of members-elect, before they’re even sworn into office in January.
Jeffries was nominated for House speaker by five Democrats essentially representing all aspects of the caucus, including Rep. James Clyburn, the legendary lawmaker from South Carolina.
“This is a historic moment for our nation,” Clyburn told the room, according to his private remarks that invoked voters’ outpouring for a change in the country.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., discounted the naysayers and said: “It is a day in the history of this nation that cannot be diminished in any way. I could never be more proud to be a Democrat than I am today.”
Rep. Kweisi Mfume of Maryland, who first came to Congress in 1987 with the late Civil Rights leader Rep. John Lewis of Georgia, said: “It just means so much in terms of moving the ball forward. Somebody’s got to break the glass, and in this instance that’s exactly what has happened.”
The tally, with 262 votes cast, included those elected to the new Congress and the House delegates.
Returning Rep. Emily Randall of Washington said earlier that she fielded questions about House leadership during town halls in her district and on her Instagram feed. So she decided to start dialing people back.
“People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the House,” she said, referring to the Vermont independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. “Technically yes, and it would be probably difficult.”
(It’s true that the House can elect anyone speaker, but it’s unlikely to be Sanders because he already has his day job in the Senate.)
She said she was voting for Jeffries. Lawmakers pointed to the livestream from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York trying to explain the role of the speaker and her support.
“There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries,” Ocasio-Cortez said earlier at the Capitol.
First leaders of a post-Pelosi era
Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders after the Nancy Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.
When Pelosi, of California, stepped aside from leadership in 2022 after the party’s electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era.
A similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in elections next month.
Schumer insisted Wednesday he had the votes: “I will be reelected as majority leader.”
Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House “are quite different.”
She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others. “His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction,” Ansari said.
Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who pulled off a stunning victory in a redrawn district favoring the Republican candidate, said before the vote that he’d be supporting Jeffries.
“It’s not even like a complex question,” he said about Jeffries, who he said “led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation.”
“I’m not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

title: PHOTOS: Central Maine Veterans Day celebrations (2026)
text:
Madison American Legion
Members of the American Legion Tardiff-Belanger Post #39 conducted their annual Flag Retirement Ceremony on November 11, 2026, Veterans Day, with the help of the Girl Scouts of Troop #351. The American Legion’s flag retirement ceremony is a formal, dignified ritual for the respectful disposal of worn or unserviceable U.S. flags. The ceremony was adopted by Resolution No. 440 at the 19th National Convention of the American Legion, in New York (Sept. 20-23, 1937) to ensure proper respect for the U.S. Flag and to provide a dignified method for destroying unserviceable flags. In 1944 it was reaffirmed and became a standard part of the Legion’s Manual of Ceremonies.
The ceremony includes the Honor Guard, a reading of the presentation, two inspections of the flags to confirm the flags are unserviceable, and a prayer. Following the presentation, the Girl Scouts, Legion members, and members of the Sons of the American Legion (SAL) lined up to place the unserviceable flags in the fire one by one.

Lows will drop to near 30 for most with light winds.
Thursday: Near or above 60 for some
The warming trend will reach its peak Thursday into Friday with highs getting to near 60 on Thursday. Light winds.

The warmth will continue likely into the weekend as well before the next chance for rain which may show up in the early portion of next week. Thursday: Very warm with highs near 60. Winds light.

title: Mom accused of smothering baby during FaceTime call with child’s father out of spite, police say
text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A Georgia mother is accused of smothering her 9-month-old son with a blanket during a FaceTime call out of spite toward the child’s father, according to authorities.
Ja’Shay Jackson, 24, was charged with aggravated assault involving family violence and first-degree cruelty to children.
Savannah police said an Aug. 15 report described videos that allegedly showed Jackson hitting her son and using a blanket to smother him while he cried. The report said she acted out of spite toward the child’s father.
One video shows the inside of a vehicle. No people are visible, but a woman can be heard saying something about not feeding or changing the child, according to authorities.
A second video shows a FaceTime call that the child’s father recorded on another phone, authorities said. Jackson’s face can be seen in the recording.
“You see Miss Jackson primarily in the video,” Savannah police Detective Ian Kite testified. “And then you hear a baby cry multiple times throughout the video. You hear the child’s cry instantly get cut off, and then you hear muffled cries.”
Kite said it happened two or three times. He testified that Jackson could be heard telling the child to “shut up” in a mocking tone.
Jackson was arrested in September, and her case has been moving through the court system since.
The baby is alive and is now in the care of the mother of Jackson’s ex-boyfriend. Kite said he did not know whether the child was taken to a hospital beyond a routine checkup.
The court heard that a Division of Family and Children Services plan was in place before Jackson’s arrest, allowing her only supervised visits with the child. Jackson is also expected to enroll in GED classes and is receiving counseling and taking parenting classes, the court heard.

title: House Democrat targets Trump family and top officials in early steps toward promised investigations
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is laying the groundwork for long-promised investigations of the Trump administration that will launch with the new Congress in January.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control, sent letters directing members of President Donald Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. It’s an early step toward undertaking investigations of the Republican president and his administration.
The letters released Wednesday cover a wide range of potential investigations, including alleged financial conflicts involving Trump’s family, misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security and the administration’s handling of files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”
Targets of the letters include two of Trump’s sons, Vice President JD Vance, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law.
The White House has repeatedly pushed back at the investigative ambitions outlined by Democrats, with officials saying they are willing to engage on oversight inquiries that they see as legitimate but not ones assessed as politically motivated.
The president is “willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”
Later Wednesday, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote a letter addressed to Democratic lawmakers, effectively dismissing requests for information from them for the remainder of the year because Democrats are currently not in the majority.
Scharf said he was citing a position that the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden took in 2022, and that while “some of you may (or may not) become a chair in the 120th Congress, that does not mean that requests from the 119th Congress carry over.”
The letters that the White House has gotten from Democrats in recent days, Scharf wrote, “drip with an animus or pettiness revealing that the purpose of these letters is not legitimate oversight but to harass and aggrandize.” The latest White House letter was first reported by Politico.
Still, the letters from Democrats offer an early glimpse of how they plan to use their newly won congressional majority to scrutinize Trump and his administration. As favorable election results rolled in for Democrats on election night, Garcia posted a two-word warning on social media: “Lawyer up.”
The preservation notices do not compel recipients to turn over documents, but they signal the investigations that Democrats intend to pursue once they gain control of the committee and its subpoena power in January.
Before the midterms, Garcia outlined several areas Democrats would scrutinize, including the administration’s handling of the Epstein investigation, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and potential financial conflicts involving Trump’s family.
The letters to Kushner and Trump’s sons Eric and Donald Jr. seek to preserve documents related to alleged conflicts of interest and their business dealings. Garcia also sent notices to Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former U.S. ambassador to Greece, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over separate allegations of misconduct and financial conflicts.
The letters to Vance and Blanche focus on the administration’s handling of files related to Epstein, including allegations by Democrats that White House officials sought to conceal information and manage the political fallout from the investigation.
The White House has warned Garcia and other Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration may open them up to investigations from the Justice Department.
Last week, Scharf said in a letter to Garcia that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”
The investigative powers of Congress are well established, inherent in its constitutional authority as a check on the other branches of government. Modern U.S. history is filled with congressional investigations and their aftermath, from the Watergate investigation to the 9/11 attacks to Republicans’ more recent look into Biden’s family.

title: Psychiatrist shares strategies for supporting neurodivergent children on Thanksgiving
text:
Psychiatrist shares strategies for supporting neurodivergent children on Thanksgiving
Dr. Kevin Simon says parents should focus on connection instead of perfection
Psychiatrist shares strategies for supporting neurodivergent children on Thanksgiving
Dr. Kevin Simon says parents should focus on connection instead of perfection
Thanksgiving can be a meaningful family tradition, but for neurodivergent children, the sights, sounds and changes in routine can quickly become overwhelming.
Dr. Kevin Simon, a psychiatrist at Boston Children’s Hospital, says parents can take a few steps before and during a holiday gathering to make the experience more manageable.
Why the holidays can feel overwhelming
“What can feel festive for one can feel overwhelming for another,” Simon said.
There can be a lot coming at a child at once: football on the TV, overlapping conversations, unfamiliar foods or smells, and more noise than usual. Children may also be asked to sit longer, greet unfamiliar people or follow routines that are different from their normal day.
“It’s a lot,” Simon said.
Three ways to prepare
Simon recommends three strategies:
Preview the day. Explain where you are going, who will be there and what will happen.
Prepare the space. If you're visiting someone else's home, ask about a quiet room or other place where a child can take a break. Families can also consider bringing familiar food, headphones or a favorite activity.
Make breaks easy. Agree ahead of time on a way the child can signal that they need a break. Simon says children should not have to become overwhelmed before adults recognize that they need space.
The approach can be adapted to how each child communicates, whether through words, gestures, pictures or a communication device.
Focus on connection, not perfection
Simon recommends setting realistic goals rather than expecting the holiday to go perfectly.
A moment of connection can be enough — helping prepare food, sitting beside a cousin or joining the family for dessert.
He also encourages parents to prepare relatives ahead of time. That could mean asking family members to give a child extra time to respond or explaining that the family is choosing high-fives instead of hugs.
And staying flexible matters. A shorter visit can still be a good visit.

title: ‘Among Us’ game chat helps lead to FBI arrest in case of teen missing for more than a year
text:
(KSL) - A Colorado mother said an online game chat between her teenage son and a girl from Utah led to the FBI’s arrest of Adam Hunter Harmel in the case of a teen missing for nearly a year and a half.
Khristina Tresp called the way the case came together “miraculous.” She said it started when her son played an online game and met a girl who needed help.
Chat moved from game to Discord
The conversation began during the teenage boy’s session of “Among Us” and moved to Discord.
“She shared with him that she was a runaway and being held against her will by a man that was older than her and was hurting her,” Tresp said.
Tresp then began chatting with the girl herself.
“She only knew the county she was in and the city she was in,” Tresp said.
Mother used property search and Zillow
Tresp, who is based in Colorado, then did her own investigation.
“She found the name of someone inside of the house so I typed that in to reverse property search, and pulled up a few addresses in the area,” Tresp said.
Tresp then used Zillow.
“I started sending her photos of the pictures of the homes off of Zillow so that I could be sure that she knew where she was at for sure. Once she saw the second house that I sent her, she said, ‘Yes, that’s it. That’s where I’m at,’” Tresp said.
Tresp called the FBI, and agents arrested Harmel.
Court documents detail allegations
Court documents say Harmel met the girl from Garden City, Utah, online in May 2025 and drove her to Oregon, where he would not let her leave.
According to the documents, Harmel sexually assaulted the girl repeatedly over the next 17 months. When agents searched the house, they recovered several knives and a machete.
Investigators wrote that Harmel expressed a desire to kidnap other minors, bind them, have sex with them and then injure or kill them.
“It was just one of those moments where it takes your breath away to know that you’ve actually found someone that is in desperate need of help,” Tresp said.
Tresp said she is grateful she was able to intervene.
Federal charge
A federal grand jury has charged Harmel with transportation with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
Court documents say there is evidence he tried to abduct one other minor and that he was involved in the production and distribution of child pornography.

title: Grandmother, 3-year-old die in fire after she went back into home to try to save him
text:
POCAHONTAS, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) — A grandmother and her 3-year-old grandson died in an Iowa house fire on Nov. 13 after family said she went back inside the burning home in an attempt to save him.
Elizabeth “Lisa” George, 65, and Rowan George were discovered in the hallway to the left of the living room. George was found lying on top of Rowan to protect him, family members said.
Family members said officials told them Rowan had no serious burns and that George took the brunt of the fire.
Fire reported on 2nd Avenue Northwest
The fire was reported around 4:53 p.m. at a home in the 400 block of 2nd Avenue Northwest.
Authorities said people who were out walking saw George come out of the home yelling for help. She then went back inside as the witnesses noticed smoke coming from the eaves.
Police officers tried to enter the house, but the fire was too intense, authorities said.
Firefighters from Pocahontas and several nearby departments fought the blaze. Once it was extinguished, George and Rowan were found inside. Both were taken by ambulance to Pocahontas Community Hospital, where they were pronounced dead.
A preliminary investigation, with assistance from the Iowa State Fire Marshal’s Office, indicates the fire started in a baseboard heater in the living room and does not appear suspicious, authorities said.
Remembering George and Rowan
George was an Army veteran whose family remembers her as caring, funny, loving, smart and strong. She loved Pepsi, rocks, her cat Maggie and Eeyore, the family said, but nothing more than her children and grandchildren.
“She would give them anything, even her life. We’re proud to call her Mom and Nama,” the family said in a statement.
Rowan turned 3 in August. His family described him as “daddy’s little helper and mommy’s little boy” who loved Paw Patrol, tools and cars, as well as wrestling with his big brother.
“He brightened everyone’s day just by the joy he got from life. Our days are darker without him,” the family said.
Community support and injured responders
More than a dozen businesses and organizations are coming together to help the family following the fire.
The family has a message for Siouxland: “Hug your loved ones a little closer, for them.”
Mitch Harrison, Pocahontas fire captain, said it is hard for the responders because they have children about the same age. He said the responders are “like a brotherhood.”
Firefighter Eric Buckner was hospitalized following the fire. He is still recovering but is expected to make a full recovery.
A Pocahontas police officer, identified as Dalton Hogan, was also injured. Authorities said the officer’s injuries were not life-threatening and that the officer was released after observation.
The Pocahontas County Sheriff’s Office, along with fire, police and EMS departments from around the area, assisted with the crash investigation.
The community has also put together a GoFundMe for the George family.

title: Commissioners approve $5K gift to sheriff's department from anonymous donor
text:
It seems somebody out there approves of how Sheriff Todd Brackett runs the Lincoln County Sheriff's Department. On Nov. 17, the commissioners approved a "$5,000 anonymous donation" earmarked for the sheriff's department. Finance Director Michelle Kane told commissioners she had limited information about the donation. "I received a phone call last week from a gentlemen who reached out with an anonymous donation with one stipulation: it went to the sheriff's office. After that, all I know is I received a $5,000 check from Goldman Sachs," she said.
In other action, commissioners approved the 2027 county budget. The commissioners approved a $15,886,518 budget which reflects a 3.67% increase.
Commissioners approved a $17,906.26 purchase for equipping the sheriff's department's new Chevy Tahoe SUV. The payment for equipment and installation went to Island Tech Services in Wiscasset. The new equipment includes a cage, lights, siren and a compartment for storing items in the back.
Commissioners authorized the sheriff's department to seek out requests for proposals for a new 2027 Chevy Tahoe SUV. Brackett expects the department will purchase five or possibly six more vehicles in 2027. He expects the RFPs back by Jan. 5, 2027.
The sheriff’s department also received approval to replace the department's 10-year-old handguns arsenal. Brackett told commissioners the department exchanges weapons every 10 years. Commissioners approved $7,360 for the purchase. Brackett expects resale of the old handguns will offset the purchase price.
The Lincoln County Regional Planning Commission received approval for two contract renewals. Commissioners approved renewing the Municipal Planning Assistance Program Coastal TA contract. The renewal runs through the rest of the fiscal year. Executive Director Emily Rabbe said the program is funded through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The program assists with land use planning, technical assistance and guidance to coastal municipalities. LCRPC received $10,539 in financial assistance.
The LCRPC is in year three of a contract for reslience coordinator funding through the Maine Office of Community Affairs. In the first two years, LCRPC used the funding to hire Gabe McPhail of Resilient Communties L3C in Vinalhaven for assisting with coordinating on a regional scale. Rabbe said McPhail would continue in the position for year three. "In cooperation with the Midcoast Council of Governments, Greater Portland Council of Governments, and Southern Maine Planning and Development Commission, she will provide some trainings," she said. "She is also doing a grid resiliency series. She also planned our Twin Villages site visit in Newcastle and Damariscotta."
The grant is for $12,000 as it was for the first two years, said Rabbe.
Commissioners approved hiring Stephanie Buzzell as the new county human resources director. Her first day is Dec. 1. The commissioners agreed to hear a tax abatement request between Pentaleri Trust v. Town of Alna. No hearing date was set.
Commissioners meet next at 9 a.m. on Tuesday, Dec. 1 in the courthouse.

title: Appeals court blocks Pentagon from expelling several transgender troops from US military
text:
Appeals court blocks Pentagon from expelling several transgender troops from US military
A federal appeals court on Tuesday blocked the Pentagon from forcing more than two dozen transgender troops out of the military, several months after it found that President Donald Trump’s administration unlawfully imposed the ban.
Related video above: Pentagon to offer troops testosterone therapy
The decision — implementing an earlier ruling by the same appeals court panel — could set the stage for the issue to return to the Supreme Court, which previously allowed the ban to go forward for now in a different case.
Trump's administration had asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to delay the June 1 ruling's implementation while it petitions the Supreme Court to take up the case. A three-judge panel voted 2-1 on Tuesday to reject the administration's request for a stay of the circuit's decision.
The Supreme Court had ruled in the administration’s favor last year, allowing the Pentagon to start enforcing the ban while the litigation proceeded.
Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, partially joined by Judge Judith Rogers, ruled in June that the Pentagon's policy was designed to exclude people from the military based on their gender identity. Their majority decision would bar the military from kicking out current service members named in the lawsuit, but it wouldn't allow new transgender recruits to join.
Plaintiffs’ attorneys challenging the Pentagon ban say 27 service members are covered by Tuesday’s order. Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said the plaintiffs are all “decorated troops who have met every standard the military sets.”
“The Trump administration asked the court to let it keep pushing these service members toward the door while it tries to get a different answer from the Supreme Court. Today, the D.C. Circuit said no,” Minter said in a statement.
On Tuesday, Wilkins said the administration hasn’t shown how retaining the plaintiffs currently serving in the military would cause any irreparable harm to the government or endanger national security. Wilkins also noted that the scope of the June 1 majority opinion was narrower than the injunction that the Supreme Court stayed last year.
“To the extent the government suggests that any injunction against the Executive Branch imposes irreparable harm, I am also unpersuaded,” Wilkins wrote.
The panel's June 1 majority opinion partially upheld a March 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who concluded that Trump’s executive order to exclude transgender troops from military service likely violates their constitutional rights.
A spokesperson for Hegseth’s office declined to comment on the court’s ruling.
In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order that claims the sexual identity of transgender service members “conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life” and is harmful to military readiness.
In response, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a policy that presumptively disqualifies people with gender dysphoria from military service. Gender dysphoria is the distress that a person feels because their assigned gender and gender identity don’t match. The medical condition has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
Wilkins was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Rogers was nominated by President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.
Circuit Judge Justin Walker, who was nominated by Trump, a Republican, wrote a dissenting opinion in June that said judges lack the power to second-guess the decision to exclude transgender troops. Walker also voted to grant the government's request to suspend the decision.

title: Jean Dempster cited for dedication to South China Library
text:
On Saturday, November 14, Jean Dempster’s contributions to the South China Public Library were celebrated. Past and present board members, friends, family, patrons of the library and those who benefited from Jean’s efforts – not only with sustaining the library, but with the China community as a whole – were present. As a young mother Jean became aware of the special place the South China Library was. We all were grateful for the welcoming atmosphere that Mrs. Evelyn Wicke had created.
As a young home schooling parent, Jean appreciated that perhaps more than most. Jean shared that passion and commitment – both to the enjoyment of books and learning, and, most of all, to maintaining a strong sense of community. Mrs. Wicke recognized Jean’s dedication and solicited her help in supporting the library.
Jean was soon volunteering and offered her services not only with her time but also with her talent. She served as treasurer and vice-president before becoming president in 2001. She finally passed the torch in 2025, after seeing the library through much growth and expansion, all while keeping that open and welcoming atmosphere. Over the years Jean assisted not only with manning the desk, cataloging books and leading story hour; but also, with making sound financial decisions, writing grants and obtaining funding, and organizing events to profit the library and the community.
Jean brought together several special guest speakers, oversaw and lent a hand with some profitable and fun events such as book and pie sales, plant sales, and an indoor “garage” sale.
Saturday’s gathering found all reminiscing about the many ways Jean’s contributions have touched our lives. She was presented with a beautiful plaque commemorating her service that will soon be placed in the library. We are all sure that Jean would love if everyone got the chance to experience the magic of the South China Library as it continues its tradition of building and growing through community.

title: Power blip causes systemwide water service interruptions for thousands in South Carolina
text:
SPARTANBURG, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - A South Carolina public water utility issued a systemwide boil water advisory Wednesday after a service interruption.
Spartanburg Water announced that service distribution problems began earlier in the day, affecting thousands of customers.
Officials said a power blip sent a surge through Spartanburg Water’s main distribution line and its backup line, causing substantial damage.
Crews have been working on the repairs, but officials said that the boil advisory would remain in effect until the issues were fixed, with customers to expect widespread water service interruptions.
Spartanburg Water shared that while there has been no confirmed contamination of the system, customers were advised to vigorously boil their water for at least one full minute before drinking or cooking as a precaution.
Any ice made from water that was not boiled should not be used for drinking purposes.
Spartanburg Water serves nearly 240,000 customers within Spartanburg County and other parts of the Upstate.
A spokesperson for Spartanburg Water said a “perfect storm” of problems created the service disruption.
Spartanburg Regional announced that the service interruptions also affected several of its hospitals in the area.
Several Spartanburg County School Districts additionally dismissed classes early as a result of Spartanburg Water’s announcement.
First responders said fire hydrants throughout Spartanburg County may not work during the water service interruption.

title: 1975 missing person case in Maine now officially considered a homicide
text:
50-year-old missing person case in Washington, Maine, now considered a homicide
The investigation into a man who disappeared in 1975 in the Knox County town of Washington, Maine, is now considered a homicide.
The Maine State Police Major Crimes Unsolved Unit and the Attorney General’s Office announced on Wednesday that the missing-person investigation involving Ludger Belanger has now been recategorized as a homicide. However, police say the person who killed him has since died, so they cannot prosecute his alleged killer. Police did not release the name of the suspect.
Belanger's body has never been found.
On Nov. 25, 1975, Belanger, who was 25 at the time, was dropped off in a field along Route 105 in Washington by his brother and wife.
Belanger's wife, Linda Perkins, said he was going hunting for about an hour or two, but he never returned home.
Belanger was 25 and Perkins was 20, and they had three young daughters together.
In 2025, Perkins told Maine's Total Coverage she still cannot drive down the road where investigators believe Belanger met foul play.
"I believe he shot the deer, dressed it and dragged it to the nearest (spot along the road). He knew this road was here, and he thought he could probably get a ride," Perkins said.
Investigators believe Belanger had done just that when two men in an old Buick stopped to offer him a ride. Belanger is believed to have placed his deer in the trunk before getting into the back of the vehicle, which is believed to have turned left off Creamer Lot Road instead of right — which would have been the way back to Belanger's home.
Perkins said investigators have pieced together a theory, and she believes her husband was murdered over the deer meat.
Police say they identified the person who killed Belanger after an intensive effort by the Unsolved Homicide Unit throughout 2025 and 2026, along with new technology, collaboration with experts, scene reconstruction, and interviews.
During the investigation, detectives went to multiple towns and states to conduct interviews and search wooded areas, bodies of water, and wells. Despite these efforts, Ludger’s body has not been found.
Police say the case remains open in hopes that a new lead will help find Belanger's body.

title: Student trades paper clip up to a BMW in social media challenge
text:
GREENVILLE, N.C. (WCTI) - At a university in North Carolina, students were challenged to use their negotiation skills to see what they could gain from a single paper clip.
One student took the challenge to the extreme and negotiated his way into owning a BMW.
“I thought this was the coolest class I’ve ever taken and such a great opportunity to take a paper clip and turn it into something great,” Christian Henry, a senior at East Carolina University, said.
That’s what Henry did in the purple paper clip challenge.
He documented on social media his skills trading a paper clip for something ultimately worth roughly 40,000 times its value.
Henry spent a semester negotiating for different items, such as an extra Roku remote and a drill, and even traded a fishing pole for a guitar. And in the end, he landed on a BMW 328i, putting his total revenue gain at $2,000.
“I’m like, I need one final really big thing to make this project a success, and I knew of this car back in Hickory, this old BMW that’s just sitting collecting dust. After a long, strenuous negotiation, I was able to secure that trade,” Henry said.
Assistant Professor of Management Leah Grubb said she was impressed at her students’ perseverance.
“Started emailing people, I started texting people, my husband was sitting next to me, I’m like, ‘A car! We got a car!’” Grubb said.
Other students also had impressive trades, starting with a paper clip and working their way to items such as Beats headphones, Yeti coolers, an Apple TV, and even an e-bike.
Grubb said it’s rewarding to see her vision for the project come to reality.
“Makes me so proud and so happy and my little professor heart is just thrilled,” she said.
As for the students, they learned valuable skills such as confidence, networking, perseverance, and the importance of taking risks.
“One of the most interactive, fun things I’ve ever been able to do at ECU and I’ll never regret taking it,” Henry said.
No word yet on whether Grubb will offer the challenge in future classes.

title: Democratic congressman pushing for $1,700 Iran war refund checks for all US families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (Gray News) - Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna has proposed refund checks for every family in the country to help reimburse them for the economic impact of the Iran war.
The California congressman took to social media this week to share his message.
“I want to give every American family a $1,700 check to make them whole for the war in Iran,” Khanna said. “This is to cover higher gas prices, food prices, electricity bills.”
Khanna’s video message continued, saying this is a chance for Democrats to deliver.
“The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a $1,700 refund check to Americans,” Khanna said. “Let’s put it on Trump’s desk.”
Earlier this year, Khanna also proposed legislation for an Illegal War Refund Act that would require the federal government to refund Americans for the economic costs they have dealt with as a result of “the Trump Administration’s illegal and unauthorized war in Iran.”
The rising cost of living has been a major talking point this year since the conflict in Iran started and especially during this year’s midterm elections.
According to the Labor Department, the consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months.
Gas prices have also jumped since the conflict started in February, rising above $4 a gallon nationally since July before finally dropping this month to a national average of $3.78 a gallon, AAA reports.
The representative has additionally called for Congress to eliminate funding for the Iran war. The cost of the conflict was said to be more than $47 billion in the latest report in October.

title: Let’s make the future of AI, not fall to it
text:
Jack Kartez is emeritus professor at the Edmund S. Muskie School of Public Service at the University of Southern Maine, co-founder and former director of the New England Environmental Finance Center and board secretary of the Environmental Mediation Center of Vermont, New Hampshire, California and Hawaii. He was also a founding board member of GrowSmart Maine.
A massive two-page ad in the Nov. 8 Sunday New York Times argued that data centers pose a threat unlike the one George Orwell portrayed in “1984.”
It’s refreshing to see that some remember the warnings that great literature gives us, in the face of otherwise collective amnesia or at least deadened sensibilities .
Today, concerns about surviving the present couldn’t be more vivid. Great speculative science fiction illustrates just how blind we have become to these impending dangers. Consider the “Matrix” movies. For 25 years, this phenomenally popular franchise has shown a future where human bodies generate electricity to fuel a digital world, while humanity vegetates on racks in towering warehouses, trapped in a simulated reality.
Is that really so far-fetched? That is precisely what data centers at scale mean today, with their voracious demands for electricity, water and arable land. This issue transcends particular debates over inflation or noise — it is about human extinction.
Like the clueless characters in a typical horror film, we continue to walk blindly into the dark cellar without a strategy. Conventional band-aids — like temporary moratoriums on data centers or parental controls on AI — are no longer enough. We need a new compact to protect humanity’s future, anchored by a fundamental principle: the primacy of everyday people for the future. The monsters are already here.
Readers may be unfamiliar with the extensive “Darkover” books by the late and beloved Marion Zimmer Bradley. Far in the future, Earth colonists to Darkover develop planet-induced psychokinetic abilities with devastating destructive potential. After a catastrophic war driven by a few elites utilizing these weapons of mass destruction, the planet establishes a compact: a strict ban on distance weapons, requiring all conflict to be face-to-face.
It requires no great leap of imagination to see that our online world of doxing, trolling and algorithmic warfare is a weapon of mass destruction — one that benefits a small elite of diabolical influencers and oligarchs. After decades of research on digital life’s effects, MIT’s Sherry Turkle sounds a similar alarm in her latest book, “Artificial Humanity.”
We must protect humanity at a human scale — the only scale that matters. We cannot let ideological bloviation about “socialists and communists” obscure it. Generations of American labor leaders and environmental justice advocates have long understood that humanity must seize its future beyond the confines of traditional political platforms.
The real question is whether your body is simply being thrown into the hopper to fuel a relentless machine, while its masters build bunkers or plot escapes to Mars. Where is our modern compact for humanity? In the traumatic wake of World War II, nations created the U.N. Declaration of Human Rights. Today, that document is too untethered from the forces we face.
Speculative fiction has always acted as a skunkworks for future planning, outthinking a dozen think tanks. In fact, institutions regularly pick the brains of these authors. Consider Kim Stanley Robinson. His 2020 novel, “The Ministry for the Future,” explores a coordinated global response after a catastrophic heatwave kills millions. It reads like a blueprint for survival, controversially spanning everything from geo-engineering to eco-anarchism.
Here in Maine, we just elected a true labor champion to Congress in Troy Jackson, alongside a governor-elect who deeply understands this forward-looking ethos: Hannah Pingree. Back in 2019 (coincidentally and by chance, just as I published an op-ed suggesting the concept), Hannah was tapped to head the newly formed Maine Office of Policy Innovation and the Future.
Though that office has since transitioned, Governor-elect Pingree has a unique opportunity to repurpose a bold approach to the future — one dictated by human welfare. As the old adage goes, “As goes Maine, so goes the nation.”

title: Mother charged with murder after 2 kids left home alone die in fire, police say
text:
VALDOSTA, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) - A Georgia mother is facing multiple felony charges after two of her children, who had allegedly been left home alone with a third sibling, died in a fire.
Taneika Lashae Sirmans, 37, was arrested last Monday in connection with an October house fire that left two of her children dead and a third injured, according to the Valdosta Police Department.
Police say firefighters, officers and emergency medical personnel responded to a Valdosta home around 8:20 a.m. Oct. 25 after receiving reports of a fire. Upon arrival, first responders saw flames coming from the home’s roof.
Firefighters removed three children, all under the age of 10, from inside the home. All three were unresponsive, and first responders attempted lifesaving measures before taking them to the hospital.
Police say two of the children later died from suspected smoke inhalation, while the third was flown to an Atlanta hospital.
Investigators determined Sirmans, the children’s mother, had left them home alone during the early morning hours to go to work. A fire started in the kitchen several hours after she left, according to police.
Following an investigation and consultation with the district attorney’s office, detectives obtained arrest warrants for Sirmans.
Sirmans is facing two counts of second-degree murder and three counts of second-degree cruelty to children, according to Lowndes County Sheriff’s Office booking records.
Police say the surviving child remains hospitalized in stable condition in Atlanta.
Valdosta Police Chief Leslie Manahan called the incident a heartbreaking tragedy that could have been prevented.
“This tragedy has not only had a devastating impact on the families involved and our community, but it also affects our first responders and medical personnel who responded to the scene or were working in the hospital that morning,” Manahan said.
She added that her thoughts remain with the families affected and the surviving child, whose life has been forever changed.
