title: Road salt is polluting Maine’s waters. Can it be curbed?
text:
Maine has spent decades hunting for a cure for its addiction to winter road salt.
The mixture that Maine spreads by the ton to keep drivers safe ends up seeping into the ground, where it can contaminate streams and drinking water, hurt wildlife and corrode pipes.
The state tried sand, only to find it choked nearby streams. Crushed seashells provided traction on parking lots but destroyed indoor carpets. Storm drain tanks trapped salty snowmelt but made chloride pollution worse.
The experimentation continues. Communities are blending sweet molasses into liquid brine to bind salt to the road, outfitting plows with adjustable blades that scrape down to the bare pavement, and mounting optical artificial intelligence sensors onto plow cabs to scan road ice in real time.
Will these new salt reduction methods succeed where others have fallen short? We’ll soon find out. Maine’s first measurable snowfall usually arrives in late October in the north and late November along the southern coast, according to the National Weather Service.
SALTING STATISTICS
Each winter, the Maine Department of Transportation buys about 150,000 tons of salt to maintain 8,800 miles of travel lanes. Last year, it spent about $12.3 million — almost a quarter of its snow budget — on salt, according to agency records.
Weather conditions vary from year to year, but the agency plans for an average snowfall of 60 to 110 inches from November to early April.
Decades of heavy salt use are taking a toll. The crystals, which are made of sodium chloride, dissolve upon contact with snow or ice, creating meltwater that runs into roadside ditches, unpaved ground or streams. Even moderate salt levels can stifle the growth, diversity and survival of bugs, frogs and fish, according to the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
In 2004, state environmental regulators identified five water bodies with unsafe chloride levels: an average of 230 milligrams per liter spread out over four days, or 860 milligrams per liter during a one-hour spike, according to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards.
Now, Maine has identified 20 streams impaired by chloride, ranging from Bangor to Saco, with another eight at risk. In Long Creek in South Portland, sensitive aquatic bugs like dragonflies and even fish are struggling to survive, according to Peter Carney, executive director of the Long Creek Watershed Management District.
Because it can’t be filtered out or absorbed by soil, roots or standard drainage systems, the salt can seep deep down through layers of rock into the underwater aquifers that supply local drinking wells.
Between 2001 and 2020, the state Department of Transportation found 182 wells that exceeded federal drinking water standards, or 250 milligrams per liter. The federal limit is about taste, not toxicology; salty water can drive people to stop drinking it or switch to better-tasting unsafe sources. Drinking salty water can also contribute to high blood pressure over time, which increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
High chloride levels have a dangerous secondary effect, too. As highly corrosive water travels through plumbing, it strips away protective pipe coatings and leaches lead and copper, which can cause other severe health issues.
MaineDOT estimates it replaces about 15 drinking water wells a year due to winter salt runoff.
Dissolved salt also accelerates asphalt breakdown, corrodes bridge decks and worsens seasonal road damage. In Ontario, researchers concluded that road salting was to blame for the crumbling infrastructure of the Gardiner Expressway in Toronto.
Climate change is compounding the salt problem. Shifting winter patterns are bringing warmer temperatures, rapid freeze-thaw cycles and more sleet and freezing rain instead of snowstorms. These conditions force trucks back onto the asphalt to spread salt over and over again.
THE BEHAVIORAL ADDICTION
Reducing salt isn’t just a technical challenge. The public has come to expect bare, black asphalt in the middle of a snowstorm. At shopping centers, pedestrians listen for the crunch of salt crystals underfoot as proof that a parking lot is safe, said Carney, Long Creek’s director.
That’s why private business owners are reluctant to cut back even when presented with scientific evidence that they are using more than is necessary, Carney said. It is not enough for a customer to be safe, he said. They must also feel safe enough to shop.
Terrified of costly slip-and-fall lawsuits from pedestrians, private contractors routinely dump excess salt onto pavement as an informal insurance policy, according to Aubrey Voelker, a salt specialist with the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services. Without legal protection against liability, contractors tell Carney that they will likely continue oversalting.
Private parking lots and strip malls account for about half of Maine’s salt runoff in urban areas.
FINDING SOLUTIONS
Realizing that salty runoff cannot be treated after it hits the ground, some Maine communities are finding success by experimenting with alternative methods to limit the snow that must be managed.
In Lewiston, highway manager Reggie Poussard has embraced that proactive approach.
Instead of dumping dry rock salt that bounces off the road, Lewiston mixes a liquid brine that has a freezing point of minus 6 Fahrenheit. It pretreats the road up to a day before a storm to create an anti-icing barrier that prevents snow from bonding to the asphalt.
To boost mechanical efficiency, Lewiston equipped its plow fleet with segmented blades that flex to scrape roads completely clean. That, plus the liquid treatments have combined to cut Lewiston’s salt usage in half.
It has also eliminated the city’s use of sand, protecting its streams and reducing the cost and time spent on spring street sweeping (saving $180,000 and 65 days), Poussard said.
Building on European successes, Maine is bringing high-tech tools into plow cabs statewide. Last winter, the transpoortation department partnered with a Swedish climate-tech firm, Klimator, to pilot artificial intelligence systems that calculate how much salt to use based on road and weather conditions.
It equipped a truck and a plow serving the Bangor area with optical sensors to scan road friction, temperature and moisture every quarter-mile. Integrated with in-cab weather stations, the system creates real-time dosing recommendations. The pilot cost about $60,000, according to MaineDOT.
Delays getting the imported equipment through customs cut last winter’s trial short, but state engineers hope to find out this winter whether the AI-assisted plows can achieve the 30% reduction in salt usage logged in Scandinavian countries, said Cindy Dionne, DOT’s stormwater manager.
Off the road, the agency is inspecting state salt storage lots, prioritizing structural upgrades such as reflective coating on salt and brine tanks, valve repairs and catch basins near sensitive drinking water aquifers in towns like Alfred, Bridgton, and Waldoboro.
Yet technology alone cannot solve a crisis driven by legal fear and regulatory gaps.
POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS
A commission established to reform Maine’s unmanaged stormwater policies has finalized a comprehensive roadmap for lawmakers to consider. The group includes state and local officials and experts representing development, engineering and environmental interests.
Its flagship recommendation would create a voluntary certification program administered by Maine Department of Environmental Protection that is modeled after New Hampshire’s successful program, which was adopted into law in 2013.
Commercial plow operators who undergo precision-salting training and keep salt logs would receive limited liability protection against slip-and-fall lawsuits, helping to minimize the main legal threat that drives commercial parking lots to over-salt.
Because chloride is a pollutant that never breaks down, the commission also calls for amending state law to explicitly add chloride to Maine’s list of regulated pollutants. This would empower DEP to set enforceable watershed chloride targets for commercial land developments.
Modeled after programs in Minnesota and Washington, the commission recommends creating an ongoing technical panel to track climate-driven runoff changes, synthesize fragmented water quality data and close regulatory loopholes, like Maine’s 1-acre soil disturbance permit threshold.
The commission said unmanaged runoff shouldn’t become an unfunded local taxpayer burden, and urged state lawmakers to create municipal stormwater toolkits, help small towns capture federal grants and create a stormwater fund within the state’s clean water revolving fund.

title: Alna’s McKenzie Named To KVAC Class B All-Conference Soccer Team
text:
Alna resident Thomas McKenzie, who attends Morse High School in Bath, was named to the boys soccer KVAC Class B All-Conference First Team. McKenzie, a junior, is a strong defender for the Shipbuilders.

title: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated.
They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them.
Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence.
“The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said.
McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers.
“These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said.
Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant.
“The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said.
Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction.
Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government.
“We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said.
It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence.

title: Foster family seeks answers after US-born baby taken into custody in Guatemala
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray) — A baby born in Kentucky is now in the custody of Guatemalan authorities after being deported, according to her former foster family.
On Aug. 2, 2025, police were called to Norton Women’s and Children’s Hospital. According to a police report, Baby “T” was brought in just hours after her birth with her biological mother, Marlena, who had recently arrived in Kentucky from Guatemala.
“T” had cuts all over her body, according to police.
The birth mother told nurses she tried to kill the baby because she did not want her, according to the police report. The mother’s attorney later challenged that narrative in court.
The mother was initially charged with criminal abuse, but a grand jury later indicted her on charges of attempted murder and assault.
In July, she pleaded guilty to the amended charge of wanton endangerment. She was sentenced to 340 days and received credit for time served.
Caleb Yeske, the baby’s foster parent, was ordered to turn the baby over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement by Sept. 7, so she could be deported and transferred to the care of her birth mother. The baby had not been with her mother since the hours after her birth.
The reunification happened over the objection of the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, and Yeske said there is no record of a hearing that found the mother was set up to take care of the baby successfully, which he said is typical for foster cases.
Yeske said he has stayed in touch with the birth mother, providing her with whatever she needed about the baby’s life over the last year, including medical history and the baby’s likes and dislikes. In a matter of weeks, those conversations changed from information to a request from the mom.
“We basically just told her, ‘Look, we cared for your child for the last year and some change. We want her to be set up for success. We want you to be set up for success,’” Yeske said. “We told her that we love this child and want the best for her. What can we do to support you? Do you want me to come down and visit? What does that look like? And basically, she said, ‘If you come down here and help me get a passport for my daughter, you can bring her back to the United States.’”
On the cusp of a custody exchange
Yeske showed WDRB+WAVE notarized documents signed by Marlena, allowing Yeske to take over guardianship and travel with the baby back to the U.S.
However, Yeske said Guatemalan authorities took “T” into custody while they were waiting for her passport from the embassy. He said the baby was reported missing, though Yeske said it remains unclear who made that report.
The foster family said they do not know where “T” is now. Even with the notarized custody papers, he is still working to sort out who can rule on where “T” should live.
“It’s very difficult to understand how a U.S. citizen is returned to another country when the cabinet, foster care here in Kentucky, agreed that reunification, at least at that time, should not occur,” Yeske said. “And then, less than two months later, to be getting calls saying, ‘Please, if you come and get this baby, you can bring her back to the U.S.’”
Yeske said he has been working with members of Congress and the embassy. Kentucky courts found he had no right to intervene in the mother and baby’s reunification.
“Because she is not in the U.S., the argument is that trying to figure out really who has jurisdiction to rule over where the child should remain, whether that be Guatemala or the United States,” Yeske said. “So, that’s kind of the position that we’re left in right now, is who should be advocating for this child? Who has the authority to make decisions for the best interest of this baby?”
As a foster parent, this is a situation Yeske never expected to be in, but he is doing what he can to make sure “T” is safe.
“What I can tell you, as well as anybody who’s a parent knows, is that when you love a child, that love never ends,” Yeske said. “And that care and that expectation to protect and find justice and support that child is unwavering. And ultimately, that’s the place that I come from as I try to advocate this baby.”
Kentucky’s attorney general files to unseal the confidential record
The case has had a complex history in court. The foster family attempted to intervene with an emergency motion to the Kentucky Court of Appeals, but the effort was rejected.
According to court records, the court essentially found they had not met the burden to prove irreparable harm, the reunification had already been ordered and the foster parents had never had custodial rights to begin with. Their emergency motion for a stay on reunification was also rejected on similar grounds.
The foster parents additionally filed a writ, challenging the reunification proceedings. They eventually withdrew the writ, after CHFS, the birth mom’s attorney and the Jefferson County Attorney’s Office submitted responses arguing they had no right to make such a challenge.
Now, Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman and the Kentucky Press Association have filed motions of their own, asking the court to unseal the confidential court record. They both argue that releasing information is in the public’s interest, considering the traction it has gained in the media.
KAP specifically cites an order by the courts for the foster parents to not speak about the case publicly, threatening jail time if they did so. This argument speaks to the AG’s motion, which cites allegations the foster parents were spreading misinformation.
The AG added that there are several questions the public deserves to have answered, laying them out in the motion, including:
- “Why was this case treated as a dependency case, Order at 4 (Sept. 9, 2026), rather than as an abuse or neglect case, given that the mother ultimately pleaded guilty to wantonly endangering the child?
- What was the factual and legal basis for the Jefferson Family Court to order immediate reunification of the child with the mother without any reunification process or plan, given the requirements in Kentucky law?
- What role did the mother’s committing a crime against the child play in the Jefferson Family Court’s reunification decision?”
The birth mom’s attorney and the JCAO have both filed responses, objecting to the state’s motion to unseal the record.

title: Bangor Christian boys basketball establishing culture ahead of upcoming season
text:
Just two practices into Rich Lowell’s tenure as Bangor Christian boys basketball coach, a bond is already forming.
The mood is light, players are building each other up despite mistakes, and the team is beginning to gel. That’s despite the Patriots having only a handful of practice hours under their belt.
It’s exactly what Lowell envisioned.
“This is about building a culture and growing as a family,” Lowell said. “So far, we’re already seeing a lot of that early. It’s great to witness.”
This season’s Patriots look fairly new, with three seniors departing from last year’s 16-3 squad. Lowell, also the school’s new athletic director, took the role knowing much of last year’s scoring was gone.
Right now, however, the scoreboard is the smallest of Lowell’s concerns.
“I want to get these kids buying into not worrying about the score or stats, at least for right now,” Lowell said. “What I want them to remember is that what matters is their development, more so as young men than as players.”
Lowell provides a practical example of what that looks like. He has his varsity and JV players stand near the sidelines during Bangor Christian’s middle school basketball games. He wants to see his players cheer on those younger players and invest in their growth.
But it doesn’t stop there.
“Obviously, it’s good to see those players cheering on the middle schoolers. But then, we want them to take it a step further,” Lowell said. “After we see them do that, then, we tell them to pick out one player from the middle school team and find them after the game.”
Lowell’s players then find their middle schooler and praise them, telling them one thing they were impressed with on the court.
“That’s the culture we want to build here,” Lowell said.
On the court, the Patriots hope to build on an impressive 2025-2026 season, even though it ended earlier than expected.
Bangor Christian finished 16-3 last season, but fell in the Class D playoffs to Hodgdon — a team the Patriots had defeated twice during the regular season.
This year’s returners are determined to make amends.
“I’d say that game left a really sour taste in our mouth,” sophomore guard William Godley said. “We all have to stay mentally tough this season and prove ourselves when it comes tournament time.”
Godley and senior forward Alden Stutheit will be two of the team’s leaders and key contributors this year as the Patriots look to replace last year’s graduates.
“We’ve got a lot of really good younger players this year and guys who are stepping into bigger roles,” said Stutheit, who pulled off several dunks and tough finishes at Tuesday night’s practice. “I’m just excited to be able to step into a leadership role for some of those guys as a senior.”
The Patriots are expected to contend in a wide-open Class D this season, but the first steps in building this year’s team don’t revolve around early results. It’s bigger than basketball, Godley said.
“This season, we definitely want to come out and be competitive,” Godley said. “And we believe we can do that. But also, we’re out here to lead and change as boys into men. That’s what we’re really looking forward to this year.”
Bangor Christian boys will begin the preseason with a matchup at Searsport on Nov. 28. The Patriots will play their first home game on Dec. 4 against Stearns.

title: Man breached security and destroyed $60 million US military plane, prosecutors say
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said.
The man’s supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States’ involvement in Middle East conflicts.
An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O’Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.
O’Corrain isn’t in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn’t been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.
Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.
The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won’t fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.
O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles (97 kilometers) southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated.”
An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport’s grounds, prosecutors said.
He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said in a statement.
O’Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport’s perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.
He used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.
O’Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O’Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would’ve risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O’Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.
Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane’s exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O’Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.
Shannon Airport, which was used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: China and Canada expand tariff relief while Ottawa-Washington relations are strained
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
China and Canada expand tariff relief while Ottawa-Washington relations are strained
The leaders of China and Canada agreed Tuesday on additional tariff cuts as they pledged for deeper ties and Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.
Carney’s office said in a statement that the new measures extend and expand an earlier agreement between the countries.
Related video above: How are President Trump's tariff policies affecting businesses?
Under the agreement, China will provide additional tariff relief on Canadian exports worth around 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million), including frozen pork cuts, fish and seafood.
In return, Canada will extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
The meeting between the leaders came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry.
“Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.”
Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised the fact that there is now “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” he said.
Carney added that his country is ahead of schedule in its plan to increase exports to China by 50% by the end of the decade.
Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

title: Man rents 15-foot U-Haul truck to drive nearly 500 miles home after ground stop caused flight to cancel
text:
MOVILLE, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) - When thousands of flights were delayed or canceled on Friday after a nationwide ground stop, one man had a pretty unique way of getting back home.
Kevin Lake traveled 477 miles from Chicago to Moville, Iowa, in a 15-foot U-Haul.
“My wife was telling me all the stories that they were watching on the news. And they had Chicago O’Hare, and she was trying to explain to the kids that that’s where daddy is, that’s where he’s stuck,” Lake said.
Lake was on his way back home from a work trip to Indianapolis and had a layover in Chicago.
“Chicago Airport’s one of the busiest airports in the world and we just got to get out of here,” said Lake.
His flight in Chicago was originally supposed to leave at 4:30 p.m. on Friday night.
“I think we got the initial text at about 12:45. That’s about what time I landed in Chicago. It was only a 25-minute delay. I didn’t think anything of it. I mean, it’s not that bad at all,” Lake said. “But sure enough, just kept on getting text messages from United that my flight got delayed again and then again and then again. And then it’s like, well, I don’t know if we’re even gonna get out of here today.”
As flights came to a stop, the terminals began to get crowded.
“And I even made a comment that I could feel the temperature it’s getting warm inside. There’s just so many people,” Lake said.
Even finding a bite to eat was a challenge, according to Lake.
“Because the lines were too long just get something to eat,” he said.
It started to sink in that maybe Lake wasn’t getting on his flight back home.
“We heard it might take days; it could take weeks. We didn’t know,” Lake said. “We took a tram all the way to all the rental cars and by the time we got there, every single rental car place was sold out. So we’re like, ‘Oh great, now what do we do?’”
At that point, the goal was trying to make anything work.
“We were joking around, saying we’re just grab one of those electric scooters they have all around the cities and we’ll just take one of those all the way there,” he said.
However, those batteries weren’t going to cut it.
“We’re thinking, I mean, it’s like ‘Planes, Trains and Automobiles.’ There’s definitely not going to be any boats going that way. So somehow we thought of going on a U-Haul,” Lake said.
After striking out with five different U-Haul locations, luck finally struck when Lake tried the sixth location that had one last 15-foot U-Haul.
“We just wanted just a van or a car or even a truck,” said Lake. “Well, of course, a 10-foot box was sold out.”
He finally secured a U-Haul at 7 p.m. An hour later, he was on the road.
“I got memes and messages from my friends and coworkers about the movie ‘Home Alone.’ We were in Chicago, we’re just trying to get home and the mom ended up going into a box truck and they’re playing in the band in the back. So we were trying to make the best that we could out of it,” Lake said.
Lake knew that the trip ahead wasn’t going to be much fun, but he made the best of it.
“We just had to stay awake, drink some caffeine and watch out for animals,” said Lake.
Eight hours later, Lake arrived back home at 5 a.m. Saturday.
“And I slept on the couch that morning when I got home,” said Lake. “I knew eventually the kids would wake up and come wake me up and give me a big hug.”
He said it was all worth it to be back with his family.
“I’ve got two young girls and wife that mean a lot to me. So I had to get home somehow, some way,” Lake said.

title: South Portland city services remain closed after cyberattack
text:
Residents trickled in and out of the South Portland post office on a surprisingly warm Wednesday morning. But no one entered or exited city hall next door.
A sheet of paper taped to the front door said the building was closed to the public. “We apologize for the inconvenience,” the sign read.
Four days after a suspected cyberattack triggered a network disruption to the city’s operations, South Portland’s city offices and library still remain closed, and officials have not given details on how the city’s systems might have been compromised or what data might have been stolen.
The suspected cyberattack has affected city services since Monday, and because of the city’s four-day workweek, city hall and the assessing department won’t reopen until next Monday at the earliest.
The city discovered the cybersecurity issue late Saturday night. A preliminary assessment “indicates cybercriminal activity” and that “the majority of city data is unaffected by this cyberattack,” according to releases from the city.
City officials did not answer questions about what city data might have been affected, who the “bad actors” might have been, or how the city’s systems were attacked.
Staff members said they’ve been coordinating with multiple state and federal agencies, and an independent forensic examiner has been hired to resolve the issue.
“It’s all hands on deck,” Mike Dery, the city’s IT director, said in a Monday statement.
City officials said a preliminary assessment indicated “the majority of city data is unaffected by this cyberattack.” An investigation is ongoing, Shara Dee, the city’s communications person, said Wednesday afternoon. Professionals are still working to verify what data might have been accessed in the outage, she said.
South Portland resident Patrick Smith said he’s worried his personal information might have been compromised in the leak.
“Is it going to be opened up to people with unsavory ideas?” he wondered, as he waited with his bike outside the post office.
Some residents have wondered why South Portland in particular was attacked.
“What’s in South Portland?” said Mae Healy, a customer service representative for Barber Brothers Meat & Provisions. “Why here?”
She wondered if the cyberattack in South Portland might be connected to the grounding of thousands of flights on Friday, or the Microsoft global outage last week. City officials did not answer questions on whether the attack on the city might be related.
“It all just seems weird,” Healy said. “It’s snowballing. It’s crazy that it’s been more than a couple of days without any meaningful updates.”
As of Wednesday afternoon, city officials did not have an estimate for when the city would resume normal operations, Dee said.
“We are committed to learning from this event, further protecting our systems where necessary, and safeguarding the information and services entrusted to us by the public,” Dee said.
Phil Butchart, 67, who has lived in South Portland since childhood, said he thinks people are blowing the situation out of proportion.
He thinks the city is “playing stupid” because they don’t want those behind the attack to know any details of how the city is working to fix the issue.
The city’s computer and phone systems, as well as some online administrative portals and mapping services, remain unavailable. In-person credit card payments and receipts at some city facilities also may be affected by the outage.
At the community center, a posted notice on the glass front door said the building had no internet or phone service, and patrons were instructed to use only cash or checks.
A resident stopped by around noon to swim. She only had her phone. “We’re so automated these days,” she told the cashier.
Healy said some of her neighbors were complaining about having trouble paying their taxes, which were due this week. The city has postponed tax collection to Nov. 23 because of the issues.
She said she feels bad about library programs that have been canceled and the lack of access to that public space. The network outage impacted the library’s access to collection, circulation, acquisitions and cataloging systems, according to the library’s Facebook post on Tuesday, as well as internet and telephone access.
A monthly event scheduled for Tuesday afternoon with Ferris the therapy cat for shy learners to practice reading out loud was canceled, as was a Tuesday evening knitting group.
Fire and EMS service have not been impacted, per the city’s Monday statement, and some services, such as vehicle registration renewal, can be completed online.
Mayor Elyse Tipton, at the City Council meeting Tuesday evening, said that the city is grateful for municipal staff who have been working through the shortage.
“They are both working to do their regular jobs and to repair the outage,” she said.
Dee said that the city will post updates on its social media accounts.

title: Two injured in Auburn fire involving supplemental oxygen
text:
Woman and son injured in Auburn, Maine, fire involving supplemental oxygen
Investigators say a woman suffered significant burns while smoking and using supplemental oxygen
Woman and son injured in Auburn, Maine, fire involving supplemental oxygen
Investigators say a woman suffered significant burns while smoking and using supplemental oxygen
Two people were injured Tuesday evening following a fire involving supplemental oxygen at a home in Auburn.
The Auburn Fire Department responded to 20 Reed Street at 6:51 p.m. for a report of woman who suffered burn injuries while smoking and using supplemental oxygen, according to the Maine Office of State Fire Marshal.
Investigators said 74-year-old Deborah Luna suffered significant burns. Her son, 51-year-old Roger Bouchard, was also injured while trying to put out the fire.
Both were taken to Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston. Luna was later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland because of the severity of her injuries.
Luna had been sitting on a couch while using supplemental oxygen and smoking when her clothing caught fire.
Bouchard was inside the home when he heard a sudden noise and saw his mother's clothing on fire. He suffered significant burns to his left thigh and hand during the rescue effort.
The State Fire Marshal's Office said preliminary findings indicate the fire was accidental and involved smoking materials in the presence of supplemental oxygen.
The investigation remains ongoing.

title: LeBron James sues makers of AI sports-betting app, saying they used his likeness and nickname
text:
LeBron James sues makers of AI sports-betting app, saying they used his likeness and nickname
NBA superstar LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app Tuesday, saying they have deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it “Bron” and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing.
In a lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court in New York, James' attorneys called it “a willful, bad-faith tactic” to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote “a new and unknown product.”
The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using the Philadelphia 76ers star's name, to give up any money it's already made, and to award damages — including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages.
Related video above: LeBron James at practice
"Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app," the lawsuit states. "They intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions."
The Associated Press sent messages through the app’s website and to its founders’ email addresses seeking comment, but did not immediately receive a response Tuesday.
The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc., is based in California. The app was launched by Chief Executive Anish Gupta and Chief Technology Officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans.
This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services like bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James — down to his tattoos, voice and number 23 jersey — sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.
James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said.
Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James' legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.
The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players.
“The integrity of NBA competition — and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play — is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

title: 2 Americans drown while swimming in the Bahamas, officials say
text:
(Gray News) - Two Americans died after being pulled from the water in the Bahamas, authorities said.
According to the Royal Bahamas Police Force, police on the island of Bimini responded to a reported drowning near the entrance to Bimini Harbour around 3 p.m. on Nov. 13.
Officials were told that a group of people were swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign for strong currents.
Several people were reportedly swept away by the currents while swimming. A nearby ferry boat assisted in rescuing some of the swimmers.
Two Americans, a 38-year-old man and a 40-year-old woman, were found unresponsive and pulled from the water, officials said. First responders administered CPR, and the pair were taken to a local hospital, where they were pronounced dead shortly before 4 p.m.
Officials are continuing to investigate and determine the exact cause of death.

title: Spicy situation: Over 11,000 pounds of peppers coat road after slipping from semitruck
text:
Spicy situation: Over 11,000 pounds of peppers coat road after slipping from semitruck
A semitruck left officials in a spicy situation after the load it was carrying spilled out onto a Florida roadway.
The Lee County Sheriff's Office said two lanes along Palm Beach Boulevard near Interstate 75 in Southwest Florida were closed for hours Tuesday evening after 19 pallets broke free from a semitruck.
The pallets, weighing 600 pounds, were filled with hundreds of green peppers.
"Peter Piper picked a peck of peppers on Palm Beach Boulevard," the Lee County Sheriff's Office said in a post on Facebook. "And then dropped the whole dang peck!"
Watch video from the department in the playfinder above
Authorities said 11,400 pounds of peppers were scattered across the roadway, with officials saying no injuries were reported.
"Peppers have lived to see another day. A few degrees cooler and SWFL will be beggin' for some fresh chili," the office said.

title: Man accused of kidnapping teen and her dog before abandoning her nearly 200 miles from home
text:
DARLINGTON COUNTY, SC (WMBF/Gray News) - An Ohio man is accused of kidnapping a teenage girl and abandoning her about 200 miles away, authorities said.
Matthew Morris Hawkins, 41, was charged with kidnapping, grand larceny and contributing to the delinquency of a minor, authorities said.
Deputies responded to the 17-year-old’s home on Aug. 6 after she was reported missing.
Hawkins allegedly took the teen and her labradoodle to Martinsville, Virginia where he abandoned her.
The Henry County Sheriff’s Office found the teen on Aug. 7.
The next day, Kentucky State Police arrested Hawkins in Winchester, Kentucky, where he had the dog with him.
Hawkins was initially held at the Clark County Detention Center before being extradited to Henry County, Virginia.

title: Power blip causes systemwide water service interruptions for thousands in South Carolina
text:
SPARTANBURG, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - A South Carolina public water utility issued a systemwide boil water advisory Wednesday after a service interruption.
Spartanburg Water announced that service distribution problems began earlier in the day, affecting thousands of customers.
Officials said a power blip sent a surge through Spartanburg Water’s main distribution line and its backup line, causing substantial damage.
Crews have been working on the repairs, but officials said that the boil advisory would remain in effect until the issues were fixed, with customers to expect widespread water service interruptions.
Spartanburg Water shared that while there has been no confirmed contamination of the system, customers were advised to vigorously boil their water for at least one full minute before drinking or cooking as a precaution.
Any ice made from water that was not boiled should not be used for drinking purposes.
Spartanburg Water serves nearly 240,000 customers within Spartanburg County and other parts of the Upstate.
A spokesperson for Spartanburg Water said a “perfect storm” of problems created the service disruption.
Spartanburg Regional announced that the service interruptions also affected several of its hospitals in the area.
Several Spartanburg County School Districts additionally dismissed classes early as a result of Spartanburg Water’s announcement.
First responders said fire hydrants throughout Spartanburg County may not work during the water service interruption.

title: Marshwood football: Strength in (small) numbers
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH BERWICK — Marshwood High’s football team is putting a new spin on the phrase “strength in numbers.”
The Hawks have 35 players in their program, but they’ll tell you the small roster has heightened each player’s strengths. As a result, the whole unit is stronger and ready to meet its biggest challenge in the Class B state championship game Saturday against Cony.
“We get a lot more reps in practice. All the guys are engaged, especially the guys who don’t get to see the field a lot on Fridays and Saturdays,” said senior fullback/linebacker Greg Castoras, one of the top backs in the state.
Ethan Reichert, a two-way lineman, said that because the younger players have had to adapt quicker, he’s getting better preparation with each passing week.
Quarterback Michael Sbrizza said Marshwood knows how to maximize its attributes.
“We try to take advantage of what we have, and I think we do a pretty good job of that,” Sbrizza said.
First-year head coach Andrew Elwell put it this way: “Everyone’s level of importance and their role in a team this small is magnified.”
Marshwood (9-1) will take on North champion Cony (9-1) at 2:30 p.m. Saturday at Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland. It is believed to be the first football matchup between the two schools.
Cony winning a second straight North crown after graduating a star-studded senior class led by Varsity Maine All-State quarterback Parker Morin is impressive.
Considering where the Hawks were this summer, their season borders on the incredible.
Elwell was named Marshwood’s interim coach in late June, a day after Alex Rotsko announced he was retiring. Rotsko led the Hawks to six Class B titles in seven seasons between 2014-21 and an overall record of 107-37 in 13 seasons, but made it clear he was retiring after 49 years as a football coach because Marshwood was again hovering around 30 players.
Elwell embraced the reality. He told the Press Herald on the day he was hired that Marshwood football was in a “vulnerable position,” and that he was “the correct person for the job and I look forward to the challenge.”
Elwell’s calm voice and sideline demeanor contrasts with his imposing 6-foot-3 frame and mountain man beard. A 2004 graduate of Marshwood and a three-year offensive line starter at the University of New Hampshire, Elwell had a one-year stint as a head coach at nearby Noble in 2013. He joined Rotsko’s staff in 2015.
Elwell knew that to build Marshwood’s program back up, he needed kids straddling the football fence to make the jump and join the team. And current players needed to help, a message he delivered on the first practice day.
Elwell told them they had to be good teammates. The ripple effects of their actions, positive or negative, would be greater with such a small team.
That day, 27 players were on the field. Now there are 35 Hawks.
“We didn’t have a single kid quit and we gained eight guys from that first day,” Elwell said.
All the newcomers have helped. Senior Jon Buttrick stepped in admirably when Castoras was hurt in the regular-season finale. Juniors Zeff Leera and Foster Merrill are playing regularly.
The players say Elwell deserves credit, too.
Reichert admits he was initially discouraged that he wouldn’t be coached by Rotsko for a fourth season, “but at the same time, Elwell coming in here was refreshing.”
Sbrizza said Elwell “was ready for the opportunity.”
Now, the players have their biggest opportunity against a Cony squad that Elwell firmly stated is the best team Marshwood has seen this season.
Cony’s players would be wise to be saying the same about Marshwood.
The Hawks beat two Class A teams, including Noble in a wild 52-51 shootout when they had only 33 players and Sbrizza proclaimed, “Thirty-three guys. Thirty-three strong.” The Hawks play with poise and purpose, rarely hurt themselves with mistakes and play hard the whole game, as they showed in beating top rival Kennebunk twice, dominating the fourth quarter in the regular season and winning 14-8 in overtime in the regional final.
“I know we’re playing a great team, but I think we’ll do what we need to do to get prepared and be ready to go on Saturday,” Sbrizza said. “I think we’re going to bring our best game. It’s going to be fun.”

title: Maine goaltender Albin Boija is in the midst of a bounce-back season
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Albin Boija is 5-3-1 so far this season for Maine with a 1.51 goals-against average and three shutouts.
“I’m happy just trying to play my game. Nothing too crazy, just trying to be calm and the rock that the team needs. I just (try to) do my best out there,” said Albin Boija, senior goaltender.
The Black Bears are coming off a 1-0-1 road trip to No. 20 Vermont.
Boija gave up one goal across two starts.
“I think we were just battling it out there. Everyone’s doing what they can, the best they can, obviously. Just playing methodical (is important), especially for me, just having the patience out there. You never know where the next pass is going to go, so you’ve just got to take it step by step,” said Boija.
Boija was a second team All-American two years ago, but saw his save percentage drop to .899 last season while giving up 2.59 goals per game.
He explained how he’s been able to bounce back.
“(It’s) just trusting the process and in my mind not putting pressure on anything. (It’s) just go out there and do what you do. I know I’ve had the capacity always and I just didn’t really get it out last year. I don’t really need to think about that at this point anyway still. I just keep going, and (I’m) not really comparing to anything,” said Boija.
“He’s obviously in a better place mentally, I think, right now. He’s more composed and poised than he was last year. He’s making saves, and he’s holding on to the puck. He’s a little more patient in the net. He’s competing,” said Ben Barr, head coach.
No. 20 Maine hosts the unranked Boston College Eagles on Friday and Saturday at 7 p.m.
Friday’s first intermission will feature a Teddy Bear Toss for donations to Toys for Tots.

Saco firefighters train for gas emergencies; here’s what people should know
If you suspect a natural gas leak, leave immediately and get at least 300 feet away. Call 911 from a safe location, then contact Unitil.
Firefighters in Saco are getting hands-on training for natural gas and propane emergencies, including how gas behaves and how to coordinate with utility responders.
Unitil says signs of a natural gas leak can include a rotten-egg smell, a hissing sound or dead or discolored vegetation near a gas line.
If you suspect a natural gas leak, leave immediately and get at least 300 feet away. Call 911 from a safe location, then contact Unitil.
Don’t operate lights, appliances or a garage door opener, or use a phone near the suspected leak; those actions could create a spark.
“The message is to evacuate the premises and call 911,” said Joseph Renda, Unitil’s manager of gas operations.
Officials said ruptured gas lines are the most common cause of natural gas emergencies, followed by aging infrastructure. They also advise residents to keep snow and ice clear of gas meters.

title: Paris Hilton urges House to pass AI deepfake bill
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Paris Hilton returned to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to urge the House to pass a bill aimed at combating nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfake images.
“Bring the DEFIANCE Act to the House floor. Let Congress vote,” Hilton said at a press conference, alongside Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Laurel Lee, R-Fla, the bill’s sponsors.
Hilton calls for a House vote
The legislation would allow victims to sue people who create or distribute sexually explicit images of them.
“DEFIANCE returns power to the hands of survivors by allowing them to hold their abusers accountable and seek financial and reputational recourse for the harm they caused in court,” Ocasio-Cortez said.
Hilton has advocating for the legislation for months. She made an initial appeal to House lawmakers in January, after it passed in the Senate by unanimous consent. But the bill still has yet to be voted on in the lower chamber.
“The Senate understood the urgency and passed this legislation unanimously in January. Now the House must act, too,” she said. “Why wait another day if they don’t pass this bill before the end of the year? All of our progress will be lost and we’ll have to start all over again. Speaker Johnson, Leader Scalise, and Chairman Jordan, I am speaking directly to you.”
During her January appearance on the Hill, Hilton spoke about her personal experience of having nonconsensual intimate images of her shared when she was 19-years-old.
“Ten months ago, I stood here at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent. And I asked Congress to do something about it,” Hilton said.
She also said that her team had done research about how AI deepfakes are affecting women in Congress.
“In preparation for today, my team studied how United States Congress women are appearing in adult deepfake content online. And what we found was shocking, but hardly surprising,” she said. “Of the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress. 83 have sexual deepfakes online right now. That’s more than half of the women in Congress.”
Lee also said the bill sends a message about the use of artificial intelligence.
“It gives victims the ability to fight back, to seek accountability, and to pursue justice. And importantly, it sends a clear message that using artificial intelligence to sexually exploit another person will have consequences,” she said.

title: 81-year-old creates music with anything from keyboards to a rubber chicken
text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Throughout Herb Leff’s condo you will find music studios, including one that used to be the master bedroom.
The 81-year-old retired University of Vermont psychology professor uses traditional instruments along with pots, pans and a rubber chicken to make experimental music in the Burlington home he shares with his wife, Ellen.
“I tend to make music just about every night,” Leff said.
Studios inside the condo
Leff calls the basement studio in his condo his “cave studio.”
“I play everything in this room,” he said.
Well, not everything: The washing machine does not double as a musical instrument.
The basement musical menagerie includes an electronic keyboard, wind chimes, frying pans suspended from the ceiling, a rubber chicken and more.
“I don’t use too many chicken sounds in my music,” he said.
One room Leff has not transformed into a music studio is the living room.
“I have to be very careful,” Leff said. “She’s very much devoted to having this room stay pretty much a living room.”
On the second floor, Leff records in a room he used to call the metal percussion paradise.
The third studio is in the condo’s former master bedroom. Leff calls it his cockpit.
Instruments and household items
“I really just like playing the piano itself,” Leff said in the former master bedroom.
Sharing the music
He records every day, in one studio or another.
“It really is a great way to approach life, and it helps you stay in the present, which is all we ever have,” he said.
Leff posts his recordings on Bandcamp, a website where people can listen to and buy music.
“I’m not after making money,” Leff said. “What I’m after is creating things that people can enjoy. If I know that somebody else likes it and has listened to it, enjoyed it, that’s the payment.”

The fire remains under investigation.

title: Portland residents cite concerns about safety, drug use in survey
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A survey of Portland residents conducted by a local grassroots group found widespread concern about public drug use, street safety and the City Council’s response to public safety.
Out of the more than 500 people surveyed, 70% said the Portland City Council has not done enough to address public safety, citing drug use as the top concern. Close to a third (32%) identified a lack of affordable housing as the biggest obstacle to addressing homelessness.
Despite those concerns, 66% said they feel somewhat or very safe in Portland. The survey was conducted by Together Portland, formed to enhance quality of life in Maine’s biggest city through collaboration with local government and residents, according to the group’s website.
“We view these results as an invitation to listen and learn, not as a final verdict or a prescription for any specific policy,” said Jill Moses, a local business owner who serves on Together Portland’s board.
“Portland residents care about their city. Our responsibility is to understand their concerns, bring people into the conversation, and examine which approaches can improve daily life,” added Moses, who owns Three Dollar Deweys in the city’s Old Port and the Saltwater Grille in South Portland.

title: Respiratory diseases kill 3 people in Washington County
text:
Three people have died in Washington County from respiratory viruses this fall, according to the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
Lindsay Hammes, spokesperson for the Maine CDC, said there are higher-than-expected cases of influenza and COVID-19 circulating in that county, and a Maine CDC advisory to clinicians on Tuesday warned that the area is experiencing “outbreaks of influenza A, influenza B and COVID-19.”
Hammes said it’s not yet known whether the deaths were caused by flu, COVID-19 or a combination. During a typical Maine respiratory virus season, there are over 100 deaths caused by influenza or COVID-19, and thousands of cases.
While Hammes said the Maine CDC couldn’t confirm where the outbreak occurred, Amber Caron, a spokesperson for Columbia Falls-based Wreaths Across America, said the nonprofit was “made aware of recent medical emergencies by our wreath vendor.”
“While the individuals were not employees of Wreaths Across America, we have been informed that the incidents were unrelated to workplace activities,” Caron said.
Wreaths Across America places wreaths at the graves of veterans.
Amelia Lyons Rukema, CEO of the Maine Mobile Health Program nonprofit, which serves agricultural workers, said in a statement that they are working with the Maine CDC to respond to the Washington County outbreak.
Rukema said they are “bringing testing, vaccination, treatment, health education, and follow-up care directly to affected workers.”
The Maine CDC is also reporting one case of meningococcal disease in Washington County, but because it’s an isolated case, the “risk to the public is low,” Hammes said.
Public health experts had warned that Maine was expecting an early flu season, with cases perhaps peaking in November.
But statewide, the Maine CDC is reporting low levels of flu and COVID-19 activity for the week ending Nov. 7, with a total of 205 cases of influenza. COVID-19 case counts for that week have not yet been updated.
“Fall marks the beginning of peak circulation of several major seasonal viruses, and getting vaccinated is the best way to protect yourself and your community from the flu, COVID-19 and RSV, as well as meningococcal disease,” Hammes said in a statement.

title: We crossed Katahdin for a surprising scientific mission. It involved collecting mud.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Not all adventures in the Maine outdoors are strictly for fun. Here’s one I experienced as part of a scientific research project. But first, I need to explain how it came about.
In the late 1970s and 1980s, as a professor at the University of Maine, I carried out research on the history of lake acidification in northern New England and southern Norway. My research team and I obtained the data we needed from the muddy sediment that accumulates year after year in the deepest parts of lakes.
This sediment contains the shells of microorganisms that indicate past acidity of the water. It also contains a chemical record of air pollutants. From cores of this sediment, we were able to compile histories of changes in lake acidity and the air pollutants associated with acid rain.
We chose to study lakes with watersheds that had experienced little human disturbance so we could isolate the effects of air pollutants on the lakes. These remote lakes had to be accessed by hiking.
Of our 12 New England study lakes, the northernmost and farthest from a road was Klondike Pond, possibly the most remote lake in the eastern United States. Klondike Pond has a large, pristine watershed where the only human influence is air pollution.
The small lake is at an elevation of about 3,360 feet at the base of a steep slope on the western side of Katahdin in Baxter State Park. The easiest route to the lake was to climb over Katahdin. There is no trail to the lake from the summit or anywhere else.
We could not hike to the lake, collect cores of lake sediment, section the cores into 1-centimeter slices at the lakeshore and hike out in one day. We had to spend a night, but camping there would require special permission from the park.
We gave our assurances to chief ranger Chris Drew that we would leave no trace of our presence at the lake, and he granted us permission. He wanted to accompany us to the lake, and we welcomed him as the sixth member of our crew because we needed more help carrying scientific equipment and the additional weight of sediment samples.
Heavily laden with gear, in early October 1979 we started the long haul from Roaring Brook Campground at an elevation of about 1,480 feet up to Hamlin Peak at about 4,755 feet, across the Tableland and down the steep other side of the mountain to the lake. The hiking distance was about 6 miles.
At the lake, we set up our tents where the land was flattest, least rocky and best drained near the inlet. I shared my little tent with Chris.
We barely had time before dark to inflate our dinghy and do soundings to find the deepest part of the lake and mark it with a small, anchored float.
During the night, it poured rain, and despite our careful choice of campsite, water entered our tents. When the rain ended in the wee hours of morning, the temperature dropped below freezing, covering most surfaces with ice.
Nevertheless, we were successful that morning in obtaining two good cores and sectioning them at the lakeshore. Then we prepared to hike back over the mountain.
The steep, largely bare granite slope we had descended was now ice-covered and hazardous. In ascending, we had to carefully place our feet in small, vegetated pockets of gravel to avoid losing our footing.
Roger Sweets, one of my graduate students (now a professor elsewhere), was well-liked and had a colorful personality. Struggling with a heavy load up the steep, icy bedrock slope, he dropped one of our expensive coring rods.
As he watched it bounce downslope beyond view, he let out an impressive verbal fusillade. Although the rest of us found humor in the situation, he did not. He grudgingly descended to search for the rod and successfully retrieved it.
Thanks to Roger and the other members of this crew, field crews at other lakes and laboratory personnel, we were able to publish a scientific history of lake acidification and air pollution in northern New England.
The fieldwork for this research included some great experiences in the beautiful wildlands of northern New England. As an old retired professor, I longingly look back at those exciting times.

title: Girl, 11, sentenced for rape, assault of 5-year-old
text:
CLEVELAND (WOIO/Gray News) - An 11-year-old Cleveland girl has been ordered to spend at least seven years in the juvenile system for her role in the attack on a 5-year-old girl.
Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court Judge Kristin Sweeney found the 11-year-old, identified in court as M.H., delinquent on nine charges that included attempted murder, rape and felonious assault.
Sweeney said the 11-year-old girl could remain in the juvenile system until she turns 21.
Attack and trial
Cleveland police said the 5-year-old was attacked Sept. 13, 2025, in a field near East 148th Street and St. Clair Avenue. Her mother found her injured, and she spent several weeks in the hospital.
During the trial, the judge heard testimony that the girl had been strangled with her own shirt. The girl’s mother testified about the effect of the attack on her daughter.
“When we left the hospital, she went through severe behavioral changes. She kept saying she’s not pretty anymore. She kept saying earth is a bad place,” the mother said.
Second child’s case
A second child, a 10-year-old boy, pleaded guilty to attempted rape and felonious assault on Sept. 28. He testified during the trial, with his disposition hearing scheduled for Dec. 3.
Case background
The Cleveland Division of Police Sex Crimes and Child Abuse Unit investigated the case.
In October 2025, prosecutors charged the 11-year-old girl and then 9-year-old boy with attempted murder, rape, felonious assault, kidnapping and strangulation.
On April 1, Sweeney ordered the two children to undergo competency restoration before they could stand trial.
According to court records, a change in the 11-year-old’s placement was necessary to get a true assessment of her competency.
When a placement was not found, prosecutors requested she be held in the detention center during the restoration process.
The court said returning to her home was not in her best interest, and the Court Diagnostics Clinic provided competency restoration services at the detention center.
Both children were previously held on home detention.
After a period of court-ordered rehabilitation, the children were later found competent to stand trial.

title: Now is the time to prioritize sustainability
text:
The truth is that our world is warming quite rapidly. The average global temperature has risen over 2.15 degrees Fahrenheit during the last 150 years and the rate of warming has accelerated significantly since the late 1970s.
Throughout Earth’s history, previous increases of 2°F have taken more than 5,000 years. Although 2.15°F may not seem like much, it is currently disrupting global weather patterns, leading to the severe droughts, rising sea levels and intense storms we all observe today.
This rapid increase is due to humanity’s burning of planet warming fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and methane (often referred to as “natural” gas), since the start of the Industrial Revolution. These polluting gases act like the glass on a greenhouse, allowing sunlight and heat to reach the Earth’s surface while trapping excess heat that would typically be released back into the space.
In the 1880s, the concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 280 parts per million. Today, it is over 428 ppm, an increase of 53% in just 150 years.
To combat this crisis, we citizens must use our voices and votes to lead a rapid transition to using clean, renewable energy sources and stop burning Earth-killing fossil fuels.
Global warming is a massive challenge, but solutions are readily available. By prioritizing sustainability in our policy choices and daily lives, we can, must and will secure a stable climate for future generations.
Ron Sadler
Portland

title: Man rents 15-foot U-Haul truck to drive nearly 500 miles home after ground stop caused flight to cancel
text:
MOVILLE, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) - When thousands of flights were delayed or canceled on Friday after a nationwide ground stop, one man had a pretty unique way of getting back home.
Kevin Lake traveled 477 miles from Chicago to Moville, Iowa, in a 15-foot U-Haul.
“My wife was telling me all the stories that they were watching on the news. And they had Chicago O’Hare, and she was trying to explain to the kids that that’s where daddy is, that’s where he’s stuck,” Lake said.
Lake was on his way back home from a work trip to Indianapolis and had a layover in Chicago.
“Chicago Airport’s one of the busiest airports in the world and we just got to get out of here,” said Lake.
His flight in Chicago was originally supposed to leave at 4:30 p.m. on Friday night.
“I think we got the initial text at about 12:45. That’s about what time I landed in Chicago. It was only a 25-minute delay. I didn’t think anything of it. I mean, it’s not that bad at all,” Lake said. “But sure enough, just kept on getting text messages from United that my flight got delayed again and then again and then again. And then it’s like, well, I don’t know if we’re even gonna get out of here today.”
As flights came to a stop, the terminals began to get crowded.
“And I even made a comment that I could feel the temperature it’s getting warm inside. There’s just so many people,” Lake said.
Even finding a bite to eat was a challenge, according to Lake.
“Because the lines were too long just get something to eat,” he said.
It started to sink in that maybe Lake wasn’t getting on his flight back home.
“We heard it might take days; it could take weeks. We didn’t know,” Lake said. “We took a tram all the way to all the rental cars and by the time we got there, every single rental car place was sold out. So we’re like, ‘Oh great, now what do we do?’”
At that point, the goal was trying to make anything work.
“We were joking around, saying we’re just grab one of those electric scooters they have all around the cities and we’ll just take one of those all the way there,” he said.
However, those batteries weren’t going to cut it.
“We’re thinking, I mean, it’s like ‘Planes, Trains and Automobiles.’ There’s definitely not going to be any boats going that way. So somehow we thought of going on a U-Haul,” Lake said.
After striking out with five different U-Haul locations, luck finally struck when Lake tried the sixth location that had one last 15-foot U-Haul.
“We just wanted just a van or a car or even a truck,” said Lake. “Well, of course, a 10-foot box was sold out.”
He finally secured a U-Haul at 7 p.m. An hour later, he was on the road.
“I got memes and messages from my friends and coworkers about the movie ‘Home Alone.’ We were in Chicago, we’re just trying to get home and the mom ended up going into a box truck and they’re playing in the band in the back. So we were trying to make the best that we could out of it,” Lake said.
Lake knew that the trip ahead wasn’t going to be much fun, but he made the best of it.
“We just had to stay awake, drink some caffeine and watch out for animals,” said Lake.
Eight hours later, Lake arrived back home at 5 a.m. Saturday.
“And I slept on the couch that morning when I got home,” said Lake. “I knew eventually the kids would wake up and come wake me up and give me a big hug.”
He said it was all worth it to be back with his family.
“I’ve got two young girls and wife that mean a lot to me. So I had to get home somehow, some way,” Lake said.
