title: Searsmont EMS chief returns home 6 months after being injured in mill explosion
text:
Searsmont EMS chief returns home 6 months after being injured in Robbins Lumber explosion
Sarah Tompkins was released from Spaulding Rehab on Wednesday
Searsmont EMS chief returns home 6 months after being injured in Robbins Lumber explosion
Sarah Tompkins was released from Spaulding Rehab on Wednesday
Searsmont residents and people from surrounding Maine communities gathered on Wednesday to deliver a warm welcome to Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins, who returned home for the first time since she was injured in the May 15 fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber.
Tompkins was hospitalized at Maine Medical Center in Portland for more than four months and spent another seven weeks at Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Boston.
After Tompkins was released from Spaulding Rehab, dozens of emergency vehicles escorted her from the Augusta Civic Center to the Searsmont Fire and Rescue Station Wednesday afternoon.
Tompkins declined to partake in any interviews on Wednesday, but she did share a thank-you letter before her homecoming.
"As a paramedic, I am used to being the one responding to other people’s worst day. First responders are pros at caring for the patient and their family during a crisis. I have worked in EMS for eight years, but for the last six months, I have been the one being cared for after my worst day. Thank you," Tompkins said in her letter. "To the EMTs, paramedics, firefighters, and LifeFlight crews that saved my life, to the CNAs, nurses, doctors and therapists who cared for me and took the time to learn who I am as a person, thank you. You took the time to console me as I cried and celebrate my successes. You made me feel like a person, not just a diagnosis."
Tompkins is also the deputy EMS chief for the town of Stockton Springs and runs Fine Line Farm in Searsmont with her partner, Hubert McCabe.
"She's a very giving person. She's running a farm and she still took time to come and help our town, and fill in when in need in an emergency," said Searsmont resident David Marceau, one of the many who welcomed Tompkins back. "I'm awfully glad to see her home."
The May 15 fire and explosion at the Robbins Lumber mill in Searsmont caused the deaths of three people: Morrill Firefighter Andrew Cross, Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and Robbins Lumber co-owner Alden Robbins. Tompkins and the following nine people were injured in the explosion:
- Searsmont Fire Chief James Ames
- Lincolnville Firefighter Aaron Heald
- Appleton Fire Chief Clifton Marriner
- Belmont Firefighter Katie Paige
- Robbins Lumber co-owner James A. Robbins, Alden's brother
- Searsmont EMS volunteer Lily Robbins, Alden's daughter
- Montville Firefighter Jacob Spaulding
- Lincolnville Firefighter John Ward
- Waldo Firefighter Thomas Wolf, who is also a Robbins Lumber employee

title: Eastport’s only grocery store is close to changing hands
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A pending sale of Eastport’s shuttered R&M IGA grocery store is close to completion, according to owner Merilyn Mills.
“I don’t want to identify the buyer on the record yet, but I can say that I am negotiating strongly and hope to have a signed agreement by the end of this week or the first of next week,” Mills said on Nov. 10. Mills said the deal is still “going back and forth” but “we’re close.”
She would not confirm on the record who the buyer is but wants the community to know that she is working diligently to get a signed agreement so that there is a grocery store in Eastport again.
Mills did confirm that the prospective buyer has already signed off on the deal and that the store will not be an IGA‑labeled grocery store. She added that she doesn’t know when the new grocery will open to the community.
“I know the buyer wants to do this, as do I, as soon as possible,” Mills said.
“It will be a grocery store and it will be great. It will be better than IGA. I’m excited,” she said with a laugh.
The R&M IGA on Washington Street in Eastport closed its doors permanently on Sept. 3, when Mills retired and no buyer stepped forward to keep it open. Prospective buyers were rumored to include the Passamaquoddy Tribe, as well as the small, Maine-owned Edwards Brothers Supermarkets, based in Winterport. No potential buyers have confirmed Mills’ account on the record so far.

title: How to contend with the violence all around us?
text:
The elections are over in Maine. Those Mainers who have just won government positions will face threats of violence that many public officials live under daily.
For others, there will be frequent beatings by ICE. For prisoners sentenced to death, the possibility of livestreamed executions. This is supposed to frighten those in the general public who might be tempted to commit crimes.
The poor will continue to bear lesser kinds of violence, like forcing them to defend themselves in court without lawyers. They will face evictions, credit card debt suits and terminations of driver’s licenses.
Andrew Mead of the Maine Supreme Judicial Court once described their suffering: “I have witnessed, time and again, the heart rending scenario, played over and over again, where people come to court — people from the absolute bottom rungs of the economic ladder, or otherwise rendered powerless by disability or circumstances — who try to navigate the complex waters of law. They are frightened, bewildered and sometimes distrusting of this institution that doesn’t seem to be designed for justice for them. They make mistakes, or sometimes just clam up, unable to speak for themselves. The results can range from unfortunate to downright tragic. ”
We can pray. Nothing else seems to work.
Donald Fontaine
Falmouth

title: Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center earns national ‘A’ grade for patient safety
text:
BANGOR — Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center has been awarded an “A” Hospital Safety Grade from The Leapfrog Group, a nationally recognized independent nonprofit organization dedicated to improving health care quality and safety. The distinction places the medical center among the nation’s leading hospitals for protecting patients from preventable harm and delivering safe, high-quality care.
The latest recognition adds to a growing list of national accolades earned by Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in 2026, including:
• CMS Five-Star Quality Rating from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
• Forbes Top Hospitals – Five-Star recognition – the only hospital in Maine to achieve this distinction
• U.S. News & World Report – Ranked as one of the nation’s best hospitals
Together, these honors reinforce the organization’s longstanding commitment to clinical excellence, patient experience, quality outcomes and patient safety.
“Providing safe, exceptional care to every patient, every day is at the heart of everything we do,” Ava Collins, MHA, FACHE, chief executive, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center, said. “Receiving an ‘A’ grade from The Leapfrog Group, alongside other nationally recognized quality distinctions, reflects the dedication of our physicians, nurses, clinical teams, and support staff who are committed to delivering the very best care for the communities we serve.”
The Leapfrog Hospital Safety Grade is the nation’s only hospital rating focused exclusively on patient safety. Hospitals receive letter grades from A to F based on their ability to prevent medical errors, injuries, accidents, and infections. Leapfrog’s program is peer-reviewed, fully transparent, and free to the public. The grades are designed to help patients and families make informed decisions about where to seek care. Grades are updated twice annually, in the fall and spring.
The CMS Five-Star Quality Rating evaluates overall quality outcomes, patient experience, and operational performance. Recognition from Forbes and U.S. News & World Report further highlights excellence in clinical care, reputation, and patient outcomes.
“These recognitions reflect more than awards and rankings,” Collins added. “They represent the trust our patients place in us every day and our unwavering commitment to delivering safe, compassionate, high-quality care close to home.”
To explore Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center’s full Leapfrog grade “A” details and to find valuable tips for staying safe in the hospital, visit hospitalsafetygrade.org. To learn more about Eastern Maine Medical Center’s safety honors as well as its available services, visit northernlighthealth.org/EMMC.

title: Historic Maine midterm results are only the beginning
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I know what it feels like to grow up loving a place and wondering whether you’ll be able to afford to stay.
I feel incredibly fortunate to have grown up in Brunswick, gone to school here, and built a small business here. When I first ran for office, it was because I wanted myself, my classmates, and neighbors to have a fair shot at building a life here, too. That feeling has stayed with me through every campaign, every bill idea, and every late night at the Statehouse.
First, thank you. Representing our communities is an extraordinary privilege, and I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to continue serving you. Whether you voted for me or someone else, I want to hear from you. Your concerns, ideas, and lived experiences belong in the work that we do in Augusta.
This election brought historic results. Maine Senate Democrats won 24 seats, securing our first supermajority since 1985. We protected every Democratic incumbent and flipped four districts. Our returning, all-women leadership team will lead a caucus in which women make up two-thirds of the membership.
I cannot express enough how proud I am of the people behind those results. Our newly elected Democratic senators are at the heart of their communities. They are teachers, veterans, emergency responders, small business owners, and working parents who stepped forward to serve their neighbors. They spent months knocking on doors and listening to Mainers, proving that you cannot buy the trust of Maine people. You have to earn it, conversation by conversation.
But I also want to acknowledge what a strange and difficult moment this is. I know many people are exhausted, worried about their families, and wondering whether anyone in government understands what their lives actually feel like. One election doesn’t fill a gas tank. One election doesn’t give someone a job. One election doesn’t make an increasingly unfair economy work for a family struggling to get by. And one election doesn’t immediately restore someone’s belief in our government. That is work we have to do every day.
For me, this next term is about a commitment to govern and a commitment to inspire. We could all use a little inspiration in these dark times: a reason to believe that our voices matter, that our neighbors will show up for us, and that we can still accomplish something together.
Those of us entrusted with public office have a responsibility to give people reasons for that belief. People should be able to see the difference our work makes when they pay their bills, look for a home, or try to get a medical appointment. An election result means very little to a parent who still cannot find childcare or an older neighbor worried about heating their home. Those are the concerns we will carry into the 133rd Legislature when we are sworn in on Dec. 2.
As a rural state, we know how closely these challenges are connected. When workers cannot find housing near their jobs, local businesses struggle. When childcare is unavailable, parents face impossible choices about work and family. When healthcare moves farther away, getting to an appointment can mean lost wages, a long drive, and another burden on an already stretched household.
We have made meaningful progress by investing in housing, expanding access to childcare, strengthening public education, and delivering property tax relief. Now we need to build on that work and make sure those investments are reaching the people who rely on them.
We will need to approach the state budget with care and honesty. The needs are significant, and the choices ahead will be difficult. Maine families deserve to understand those choices and have a voice in how we make them. They plan carefully with the resources they have, and they expect us to take that same responsibility seriously.
A commitment to governing means staying at the table when the conversations get hard. It means helping to find a solution and taking responsibility for whether it works. It is easier to say the government is failing when you have stepped away from the work of making it succeed. Mainers deserve leaders willing to stay involved, work through disagreements, and follow through.
That is the commitment I bring to working with my Democratic, Republican, and independent colleagues. A larger majority makes our responsibility to listen widely even greater. Good ideas come from every corner of Maine, and the people we serve expect us to work together to solve problems.
As I prepare for my final consecutive term in the Senate, I feel both grateful and impatient. Grateful for the trust you have placed in me. Impatient to get to work on the things that will help people put down roots and build a good life in the communities they love. I love this state and the people who call it home, and I will spend every day of this final term working to honor the trust you have placed in me.
Mattie Daughtry represents State Senate District 23, Brunswick, Chebeague Island, Freeport, Harpswell, Pownal, and part of Yarmouth in the Maine Senate. She also serves as Maine’s Senate President. She can be reached at Mattie.Daughtry@legislature.maine.gov or 207-287-1500.

title: Florida pastor convicted of US charges related to assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted Wednesday of U.S. charges arising from the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on all charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges, the most serious being conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
Sanon showed little reaction as the verdict was announced in a federal courtroom in Miami. He faces up to life in prison at sentencing, which is set for Feb. 10. He remains in federal custody and was taken back to a detention center after the trial concluded.
Prosecutors declined comment afterward. But Sanon’s attorney, Zeljka Bozanic, said the defense team was disappointed with the jury’s decision and would file an appeal at the appropriate time.
Federal prosecutors said at trial that South Florida was a hub for planning and financing a plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The prosecutors said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. They also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon had acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but said the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the U.S. as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the Midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a nighttime raid at their home on July 7, 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from U.S. government programs that were intended to help businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to court records. U.S. prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in South Florida with a former Haitian senator and several U.S. businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies — Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU — for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian Supreme Court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

title: Packers fan ejected from stadium after spreading loved one's ashes on the field
text:
Packers fan ejected from stadium after spreading loved one's ashes on the field
A Green Bay Packers fan was ejected from Lambeau Field for attempting to spread their loved one's ashes, according to police.
Green Bay police were called to the stadium Sunday after someone in the stands was seen releasing what appeared to be ashes onto the field after the game ended.
Officers confirmed the person had spread the cremated remains of a loved one onto the field.
"While we understand the desire of some fans to have their ashes, or those of friends or family, spread at Lambeau Field, it is against the law and prohibited at the stadium," the Packers said in a statement. "To honor a loved one’s legacy appropriately at Lambeau Field, we refer fans to the commemorative brick program. We also suggest they can coordinate tributes in other appropriate ways with their funeral home."
Police said the person could have received an $890 citation in addition to the ejection. It is not clear whether that person was fined.

title: Task force proposes plan to expand Wabanaki Nations’ access to federal laws
text:
A state task force recommended Tuesday that the next Legislature ensure that federal laws that benefit other tribes also benefit the Wabanaki Nations.
While essentially reiterating an earlier suggestion from a 2019 task force, the proposal addresses concerns about potential legal challenges that have stymied adoption since.
Earlier this year, lawmakers created the latest task force after a far more ambitious aim to fully restore sovereignty to the Wabanaki Nations was walked back following opposition from Gov. Janet Mills.
The Penobscot Nation, Passamaquoddy Tribe, Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and Mi’kmaq Nation — collectively known as the Wabanaki Nations — are treated differently than other federally recognized tribes, more akin to municipalities than sovereign nations because of a 1980 land settlement agreement.
Among several implications, the settlement agreement, known as the Maine Implementing Act, has prevented the Wabanaki Nations from benefitting from federal laws passed after 1980 that interfere with state law, unless they are specifically mentioned in the law.
During her two terms, Mills blocked sweeping overhauls of the settlement agreement and legislation to provide Wabanaki access to all federal beneficial laws, instead opting to usher through piecemeal reforms. But the Democratic governor terms out this year, and Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree, also a Democrat, has vowed to support the full restoration of tribal sovereignty.
Ahead of a new administration and Legislature in January, the task force made up of lawmakers and tribal leaders met to specifically address how the state should tackle changing the part of the agreement involving federal laws, gathering public feedback and discussing various approaches throughout the fall.
Sen. Rachel Talbot Ross, D-Cumberland, one of the chairs of the working group, said the process has left her “very excited about the possibilities for government-to-government relations that are built on mutual respect and, I will say, human dignity.”
The task force unanimously voted to recommend that the 133rd Legislature ensure all federal beneficial laws apply to each of the Wabanaki Nations, regardless of when they were enacted. Its recommendation is also that state laws that interfere with the implementation of existing or future beneficial federal laws not apply to the Wabanaki Nations and their citizens.
Back in 2019, the Human Rights and Indigenous Peoples Clinic at Suffolk Law School identified 151 federal laws enacted since 1980 that may not be applicable to the Wabanaki Nations.
Nicole Friederichs, who directs the clinic and teaches federal Indian law, expanded that research with her students for the latest task force. Friederichs said they found 23 more federal laws enacted since 2019 that may not be applicable, bringing the total to 174.
Additionally, the group recommended that the state establish a conflict resolution mechanism to resolve any potential legal disputes that could arise with the enactment of such laws, which was a key concern raised by Mills when she vetoed legislation to restore the Tribes’ access to federal laws in 2023.
“I fear it would result in years, if not decades, of new, painful litigation that would exacerbate our government-to-government relationship and only further divide the state,” Mills wrote in her veto message at the time.
Per the task force’s recommendation, when a federal law could have a disruptive and harmful effect on the state outside of Wabanaki Nation lands, the tribes and the state would be required to confer on implementation to avoid or minimize such potential effects. For example, the group agreed the state and its departments should be authorized to enter into cooperative agreements with the Wabanaki Nations to deliver government services and to avoid disputes on issues of mutual interest.
“The intention is for this to be a sovereign-to-sovereign relationship and discussion between the state and the Wabanaki nations,” said Corey Hinton, attorney for the Passamaquoddy Tribe.
This mechanism would expand upon the existing framework in the Tribal-State Collaboration Act of 2022, which established a consultation process between state agencies and tribes regarding agency programs, rules and services that uniquely affect the tribes. Maine also has the inter-governmental Maine Indian Tribal-State Commission, which was created by the 1980 settlement act.
Task force discussions underscored several concerns with the current framework.
“It’s the state’s language,” Talbot Ross said of the collaboration act. “If you read it, it does have, my word, a fairly inequitable agreement. Moving forward, it’s not as comprehensive, as strong as some of the other states that have dedicated offices.”
As part of the task force’s work, members reviewed the collaboration entities used in other states. They range from none, to commissions that act as liaisons, to specific departments and offices. Talbot Ross proposed a separate office in 2024. While the plan initially passed the legislature, it was placed on the appropriations table and lawmakers opted not to fund it.
“Perhaps in the 133rd, a whole new collaboration vehicle will be developed,” said Rep. Amy Kuhn, D-Falmouth, the task force’s other chair.
In addition to the suggestions for legislative action, the task force also recommended that should the state pass a law giving the Wabanaki Nations access to federal beneficial laws, a joint communication would be sent to Congress informing the federal body of the change.

title: Maine family gets national support in fight with town over rooster statues
text:
An Ogunquit family that’s in an ongoing dispute with the town over tin roosters they display in their front yard, now has the support of a national legal group.
The nonprofit Institute for Justice has filed a civil rights lawsuit against the town of Ogunquit, challenging fines charged to Sara and Dave LeBlanc.
The town said the 6-foot-tall roosters promote the couple’s restaurant next door and violate the municipal sign ordinance.
But the LeBlancs have said they serve as comfort animals for their daughter who has autism.
“The town government is trying to take away Pyper’s roosters, her friends and her security,” Sara LeBlanc said.
“We had two options: stand up and show Pyper what’s right or get walked on. This is the course we chose,” Dave LeBlanc added.
The Institute for Justice said the town is violating the LeBlancs’ First Amendment rights and is seeking more than $1,500 in fines already paid.
During a press conference Tuesday, Sara LeBlanc draped a blanket over one rooster as attorney Daniel Woislaw explained the symbolism.
“It will stand here as a testament to our clients’ will, their constitutional rights and the town’s campaign against them,” Woislaw said.
The town was served with the suit Tuesday.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: FOR YOUR HEALTH: What parents should know about vaccines this school year
text:
by Dr. Jerome Adams
Every school year brings the same routine: New shoes and backpacks. Shopping for new supplies. Nerves the night before the first day of school.
This year it also brings noise around vaccines, and a lot of parents asking some version of the same question: What am I supposed to do?
I get it. I’m a father of three. I’m a doctor. And I’ve spent my career working at the intersection of public health and daily reality – as Indiana’s State Health Commissioner, as the nation’s 20th Surgeon General, and now as someone who still regularly talks to parents, pediatricians, and pharmacists. I understand how confusing this moment feels.
This August, right as families were preparing for meet-the-teacher days and school forms, the president signed an executive order targeting childhood vaccines. The order instructs children to receive fewer vaccines, urges states to reconsider school requirements, directs the Justice Department to sue states that don’t provide religious and medical exemptions, and calls for the measles, mumps, and rubella shot to be split into three separate injections.
In practice, three shots instead of one would mean three visits instead of one. More copays. More time off work. More confusion. More chances a child never finishes the series and gains the protection that has kept infectious disease at bay for decades.
The good news?
The order does not actually remove the MMR vaccine from the U.S. market. It does not immediately override what your pediatrician recommends. It does not, by itself, change what vaccines your child’s doctor can administer. And it does not end free vaccination through the Vaccines for Children program, which by law follows the CDC’s advisory committee.
That’s critical because the CDC has confirmed more than 3,471 measles cases this year across 47 jurisdictions, the highest single-year count since 1991. Roughly 7 in 10 cases are children and teenagers – and we’ve only just begun the school year.
Where does that leave parents navigating annual check-ups and volatile news cycles at the start of this new school year?
Talk to your doctor. Talk to your pharmacist. These are your most trusted resources. Your child’s pediatrician knows your kid’s health history, your family’s needs, and the medical evidence. Your pharmacist is trained, accessible on the weekends, and right in your community. If you have questions, ask them.
To be very clear: You’re not failing as a parent if you’re uncertain, and we should never blame or shame any parent who has doubts or wants to understand what they’re giving their child. Questions are healthy. Confusion – especially in our current climate – is understandable. A good doctor will welcome the conversation, and ground their answers in decades of safety data, peer review, and clinical expertise.
Just bring those questions to the people who know the science and your family best.
That’s not political. That’s parenting.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Maine birders just got 2 new species. But there’s a catch.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Two bird species that nest in Maine have just been split into four. I’m not sure whether I should be gleeful or petulant.
I envy birders who enjoy a casual relationship with Maine’s avian world, and fully appreciate a bird’s beauty without the need to identify and categorize it. For instance, purple finches and house finches resemble each other, and both visit backyard bird feeders. Casual birders don’t care which species is eating their sunflower seeds. They’re just happy to observe them.
Hardcore birders are obsessed with knowing the differences between the two species. Bird identification is a skill honed by experience. Many birders keep lists of all the birds they’ve identified in the world. Imagine how they feel when scientists shake up that world.
Willets are medium-sized shorebirds that nest primarily in southern and coastal salt marshes. Scarborough Marsh near Portland is probably the best place to look for them, but they can pop up anywhere along the Maine coast before winter sends them south.
Willets are relatively easy to identify, standing nearly a foot tall. They are a uniform gray with no obvious field marks until they spread their wings, revealing a striking W pattern in flight.
That should have been the end of it. However, there is a race of inland-nesting willets in the prairie states. In October, after long consideration, scientists declared the two different races to be two distinct species. Maine’s willet has been renamed the saltmarsh willet. The western species is now the prairie willet.
I should be happy. Without raising my binoculars, I have added another species to my life list. I’ve observed many willets in the west, so I can confirm identifying a prairie willet. According to my eBird account — my official list counter — I’ve now seen 677 species in North America.
Those same scientists just split the marsh wren into two species. Marsh wrens breed coast-to-coast. They nest in many places in Maine, wherever cattails abound. They nest in Bangor’s Penjajawoc Marsh, for instance.
For years, researchers have noticed a vocal difference between marsh wrens in the east and west. There is a narrow overlap zone in the Great Plains, where they tend not to hybridize with each other. Hence, the two races are now two distinct species — the eastern marsh wren and the western marsh wren.
Confused yet? Blame the American Ornithological Society. This group of bird-focused biologists is responsible for deciding what constitutes a species, and how to name it.
Here’s the part that can drive a birder crazy. If you’ve ever posted a marsh wren in the eastern US on your personal eBird list, eBird credits you with an eastern marsh wren. If you’ve posted a marsh wren in the western US, you get credit for a western marsh wren. If you saw or heard a marsh wren in the middle third of the country — no credit whatsoever. Your original record disappears.
I know, that’s a picky complaint that only bothers obsessive birders who keep lists. But here’s the thing. I’ve encountered marsh wrens in many places. It never mattered before, but now it does. I must head farther west to get credit, even if I’ve seen that species before. How long is this renaming thing going to go on?
A year ago, the AOS split warbling vireos into eastern and western species. They also decided to split the yellow warbler, an abundant species that breeds throughout North America, into the northern yellow warbler and the mangrove yellow warbler. The mangrove yellow warbler is a Caribbean species that barely reaches the southern US coast. Although I’ve observed yellow warblers in the Florida mangroves for about 50 years, only last March could I document the newly anointed mangrove yellow warbler for my life list — number 660 at the time.
But here’s the other thing. That warbler I watched on the edge of Florida Bay did, indeed, behave differently than the yellow warblers I’ve seen in Maine. It deserved to be its own species. For those who still believe in science, this is how evolution and natural selection work.
As birds, or any creatures, expand into new regions, they must adapt to different habitats or die. Over time, these adaptations accumulate to the point where they’re a whole new species.
The bird and the scientists aren’t the problem. I am. Listing is such a crazy compulsion. I need to get a life.
And it gets worse. Every field guide on the bookshelf just went out of date. Again.

title: 81-year-old creates music with anything from keyboards to a rubber chicken
text:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Throughout Herb Leff’s condo you will find music studios, including one that used to be the master bedroom.
The 81-year-old retired University of Vermont psychology professor uses traditional instruments along with pots, pans and a rubber chicken to make experimental music in the Burlington home he shares with his wife, Ellen.
“I tend to make music just about every night,” Leff said.
Studios inside the condo
Leff calls the basement studio in his condo his “cave studio.”
“I play everything in this room,” he said.
Well, not everything: The washing machine does not double as a musical instrument.
The basement musical menagerie includes an electronic keyboard, wind chimes, frying pans suspended from the ceiling, a rubber chicken and more.
“I don’t use too many chicken sounds in my music,” he said.
One room Leff has not transformed into a music studio is the living room.
“I have to be very careful,” Leff said. “She’s very much devoted to having this room stay pretty much a living room.”
On the second floor, Leff records in a room he used to call the metal percussion paradise.
The third studio is in the condo’s former master bedroom. Leff calls it his cockpit.
Instruments and household items
“I really just like playing the piano itself,” Leff said in the former master bedroom.
Sharing the music
He records every day, in one studio or another.
“It really is a great way to approach life, and it helps you stay in the present, which is all we ever have,” he said.
Leff posts his recordings on Bandcamp, a website where people can listen to and buy music.
“I’m not after making money,” Leff said. “What I’m after is creating things that people can enjoy. If I know that somebody else likes it and has listened to it, enjoyed it, that’s the payment.”

title: Vassalboro school board to add two students to roster
text:
Vassalboro School Board members plan to add two students, one each from grades seven and eight, to their roster.
At the Nov. 10 board meeting, Vassalboro Consolidated School (VCS) Principal Tabitha Brewer said she is soliciting applications from interested students.
The two students chosen as 2026-27 board members will need their parents’ approval. They will commit to attend the monthly board meetings and, Brewer said, pre-meetings with her so she can explain unfamiliar agenda items.
Brewer reported on recent events, including a fire drill with town firefighters present; the firefighters were pleased, she said. Because she learned that not all of them are familiar with VCS, she plans to schedule a building tour soon.
The school is still short of personnel, especially substitute teachers and educational technicians, Brewer said; and the problem is still state-wide (see the Oct. 22 issue of The Town Line, p. 2). One reason is that private-sector jobs pay more. Some VCS positions are being filled by outside contractors.
One important position has been filled: board members approved hiring Whitney Guy as VCS dean of students. Brewer said Guy, currently teaching at Nokomis High School, in Newport, is finishing a master’s degree at the University of Maine. She is scheduled to start at VCS Monday, Nov. 16.
Brewer reversed an October plan to eliminate the boys’ junior varsity basketball team if no coach were found. To keep the varsity team competitive, she said, there needs to be JV players coming up behind them; so, for the benefit of VCS students, she will help coach the team, as she did last year.
Board members plan to talk again with Tom Seekins, head of Energy Management Consultants, Inc., of Portland, about remaining work needed to update the VCS building. At their next meeting, they intend to discuss the proposed expansion of the parking lot, to get parents’ cars off Bog and Webber Pond roads during afternoon pick-up time.
The next Vassalboro school board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m., Tuesday, Dec. 8, in the school library. Interested residents are welcome at all meetings.

title: Paramedic mom unknowingly responds to scene where son was crushed to death while working on car
text:
(Gray News) - A paramedic in Utah unknowingly responded to an emergency involving her son after a car he was working on fell on him, authorities said.
The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said Logan Mumford, a father of two from Sigurd, was helping a woman repair her car on Nov. 16 when it fell from the jack supporting it, trapping him underneath.
A neighbor who had been helping had briefly gone across the street to get additional lighting and a floor jack when he heard the car fall.
He tried to pull Mumford out and lift the car but couldn’t.
The neighbor returned with a floor jack as deputies arrived. Together, they raised the car enough to remove Mumford, who was unresponsive and had suffered significant head trauma. First responders immediately began lifesaving efforts.
One of the paramedics sent to the scene was Mumford’s mother, who did not know her son was the patient until she heard his name.
“Behind every emergency call is a family, a story, and a community forever changed,” the sheriff’s office said. “Last night, this tragedy became far too personal for one of our own.”
Mumford was taken to a hospital where he was pronounced dead. He leaves behind a 3-year-old son and a 1-year-old daughter.
Authorities described Mumford as “someone who was always willing to lend a hand and help others.”

title: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be next Speaker
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - House Democrats chose Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Wednesday to be their next leader, setting him on track to become the first Black Speaker of the House of Representatives. No one ran against him.
Current and incoming Democratic members of the House chose Jeffries by acclamation.
Jeffries represents Brooklyn and has served seven terms in the House. He previously became the first Black Minority Leader in the House, a position he’s held since 2023.
If elected Speaker, he would follow Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), who was the first woman to serve as speaker.
Jeffries is pledging to address an affordability crisis, reestablish government oversight and unite the nearly 260 members of his caucus.
“We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator to make life better for the American people,” Jeffries said.
He continued, “We hear you, see you, feel you,” and pledged to fight to make the country affordable.
“Failure is not an option, and I’m excited to deliver the bold change Americans deserve,” Jeffries said.
The first job of the 120th Congress is to select a speaker, before all members are sworn in.
Jeffries must secure 218 votes from the chamber to become speaker. The new Congress will have at least an 80-seat Democratic majority.

title: ‘Worst nightmare’: Paramedic responding to deadly accident discovers son is the victim
text:
‘Worst nightmare’: Paramedic responding to deadly accident discovers son is the victim
A paramedic responding to the scene of a deadly accident experienced “every parent's worst nightmare,” discovering the victim was in fact her son.
Logan Mumford was helping a neighbor with her car Monday evening in a small Utah town when a scissor jack gave way, trapping him beneath the vehicle, according to the Sevier County Sheriff’s Office.
A neighbor who witnessed the accident tried to free Mumford but was unable to lift the car, authorities said.
Someone called 911, summoning paramedics – including Mumford’s mother, a Sevier County paramedic – to the scene.
Paramedics used a floor jack to pull him out, and emergency crews began lifesaving efforts.
Deputies say Mumford’s mother was among those working to save his life. She did not learn it was her son until after hearing his name, officials said.
Mumford was flown to Utah Valley Medical Center, where he died from his injuries.
In the wake of Monday’s tragedy, a fellow Sevier County paramedic issued a statement via the local sheriff’s office, saying in part, "Last night, one of my fellow paramedics, a friend, and a fellow first responder, experienced every parent's worst nightmare. She was dispatched to an accident involving her own son.”
Mumford was a husband and father of two young children, a 3-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl, the paramedic said.
The unnamed paramedic described Mumford as someone who was always willing to help others, including when he was working on his neighbor’s car.
“As first responders, we prepare ourselves to respond to some of life's most devastating situations. We train for the unthinkable, and we answer the call when others need us most. But no amount of training can prepare a mother to respond to an emergency involving her own child, or a wife to watch as the person she loves fights for his life,” the statement reads. “Behind every emergency call is a family, a story, and a community forever changed. Last night, this tragedy became far too personal for one of our own."

title: Midcoast Maine Earns Seven First Place Ribbons on Way to Fourth Straight Win
text:
The Midcoast Maine IEA team won its fourth straight show of the season on Sunday, Nov. 15 at Evenstride in Byfield, Mass.
The team, based out of Nobleboro, won seven events to be crowned show champion for the fourth straight week.
Six of the best teams in Midcoast Maine’s region competed in the show, including Seahorse Stables, of Belfast, Dove Hill, of Amesbury, Mass., Cornerstone Farm from Haverhill, Mass., Whishmaker Stables from Rollinsford, N.H., and Team Evenstride.
Despite strong competition, the high school team rode to the top all day, amassing four first place finishes, two seconds, and a fifth in team competition to earn champion status with 38 points. Seahorse was reserve champion with 21.
Ava Genthner won in the varsity open flat and took second over fences. Isabel Bathe Oyer won in varsity intermediate over fences and placed third on the flat. Maddie Gundel took second over fences and fifth in the flat.
In JV novice, Gabriella Curtis was second in both over fences and flat, and Hannah Fougner won the flat section. Midcoast Maine earns seven first place ribbons on way to fourth straight win
“Our middle school riders showed real horsemanship and swept their classes,” team spokesman Kristen Mugnai said.
In the JV beginner flat class, Olivia Roberts took the win. Adeline Turgeon and Maizie Erskine both won their walk/trot/canter classes, and Emerson Curtis won the walk/ trot class.
Individuals who qualified for the regional semifinals at the show were Genthner in varsity open flat, Fougner in JV novice flat, and Curtis in future walk/trot.
Next week is the team’s last regular season show at Whishmaker Stables. Following this, the next competition will be regionals at Whishmaker on Saturday, Jan. 9.
The team will hold its annual Christmas fundraiser on Sunday, Dec. 13 with fun activities including pony rides, pictures with Santa, face painting, cookie decorating, and more.
In addition, the team will host the “12 days of Christmas” raffle, which will give anyone who purchases a ticket 12 chances to win gift cards from local businesses and a fabulous grand prize.
All the proceeds go to support the team, which is completely self financed.

title: Vassalboro select board ready to fill vacant positions
text:
By the end of their Nov. 10 meeting, Vassalboro select board members were optimistic about having two new town employees soon.
Interim Town Manager Michael Roy said the top choice for the bookkeeper’s job was “pondering.”
Select Board Chairman Chris French said two top candidates to become Vassalboro’s new town manager were to be interviewed Nov. 18.
Board members agreed to establish two new committees. Volunteers are welcome for the Spirit of America committee, whose task will be to suggest residents deserving of that award for volunteerism.
The public safety committee has been discussed before, Board Chairman Chris French said. It is to include representatives from the fire department, the rescue unit, the police department and the budget committee and a sheriff’s deputy who is a Vassalboro resident.
In the only public comment, Dana Meier read a statement and distributed a hand-out from Small Town Accountability (STA), the LLC (Limited Liability Company) resident William Paquet registered in June. Paquet had sent the board other documents, included with the meeting agenda.
Paquet had four requests concerning the town’s foreclosure on the property at 159 Lombard Dam Road, for unpaid taxes. He asked:
— French and board member Frederick “Rick” Denico to abstain on a Nov. 10 agenda item concerning the property, citing what he said were examples of conflict of interest;
— The select board to refer the issue to the Kennebec County District Attorney by Dec. 10;
— For his request letter and “STA’s Grounds for Referral to the District Attorney” to be part of the record of the board meeting; and
— That board members “reconsider” the town’s taking of the property and return it to the prior owners “by quitclaim deed and abating past taxes as a good-faith gesture.”
He added: “STA understands the family is represented. Any resolution reached with the family should take precedence over this request.”
If within 30 days town officials had neither referred the matter to the district attorney nor rebutted STA’s findings, STA reserved the right to act itself.
The select board’s first item under new business was an “Authorization for the Town Attorney to negotiate a Purchase and Sale Agreement for the foreclosed property at 159 Lombard Dam Road.” Roy recommended approval, and board members approved the authorization unanimously, without discussion.
Because the company that owns the solar development in Oakland from which Vassalboro gets some of its power has been sold, board members were asked to sign an “estoppal certificate” that Roy explained consents to the new ownership. Board members had enough questions to postpone action to their next meeting.
Roy commented that participating in the solar development seemed to have brought the town “pretty good savings” over the past six years.
On the town attorney’s advice, board members unanimously approved refunding a resident $5,100 for unnecessary expenses incurred because Codes Officer Eric Currie provided incorrect advice. Currie explained that he had misinterpreted the shoreland zoning ordinance.
From the audience, resident Douglas Phillips asked if the town has insurance to cover errors and omissions. Roy said yes, through the Maine Municipal Association.
Currie recommended upgrading the recently acquired ceo software program. French and board member Dan Bradstreet thought an upgrade worth considering as they plan next year’s budget.
The next regular Vassalboro select board meeting is scheduled for 6:30 p.m., Tuesday, Nov. 24, moved from the usual Wednesday evening to avoid the night before Thanksgiving.

title: Democratic congressman pushing for $1,700 Iran war refund checks for all US families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (Gray News) - Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna has proposed refund checks for every family in the country to help reimburse them for the economic impact of the Iran war.
The California congressman took to social media this week to share his message.
“I want to give every American family a $1,700 check to make them whole for the war in Iran,” Khanna said. “This is to cover higher gas prices, food prices, electricity bills.”
Khanna’s video message continued, saying this is a chance for Democrats to deliver.
“The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a $1,700 refund check to Americans,” Khanna said. “Let’s put it on Trump’s desk.”
Earlier this year, Khanna also proposed legislation for an Illegal War Refund Act that would require the federal government to refund Americans for the economic costs they have dealt with as a result of “the Trump Administration’s illegal and unauthorized war in Iran.”
The rising cost of living has been a major talking point this year since the conflict in Iran started and especially during this year’s midterm elections.
According to the Labor Department, the consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months.
Gas prices have also jumped since the conflict started in February, rising above $4 a gallon nationally since July before finally dropping this month to a national average of $3.78 a gallon, AAA reports.
The representative has additionally called for Congress to eliminate funding for the Iran war. The cost of the conflict was said to be more than $47 billion in the latest report in October.

title: Man accused of threatening ethanol plant with bomb worked as a trainee at the site, report says
text:
PEORIA, Ill. (25News Now/Gray News) - A man has pleaded not guilty after being accused of threatening an Illinois ethanol plant with an explosive.
Andrew K. Kozak, 41, was indicted Tuesday by a grand jury on charges involving threats regarding explosives and interstate communication threats.
Kozak is accused of using email to threaten to damage and destroy a building by means of fire and explosives and to threaten people at the BioUrja facility, according to the indictment and online records.
At a news conference Tuesday afternoon, U.S. Attorney Gregory Gilmore said the charge of threats regarding explosives carries up to 10 years while interstate communications threats carries up to five years.
The Associated Press reported Kozak has been a trainee at the ethanol plant for 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page.
Officials said over the weekend that an explosive device was found at the plant. The threat forced an evacuation order of a mile radius around the plant, on the Peoria and East Peoria sides of the Illinois River, shortly after 7 p.m. Friday. That order was lifted Saturday after no other devices were found at the plant.
During a weekend press conference, Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon declined to reveal the type of device discovered, only to say the package that was “rendered safe” was a “credible threat.” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told reporters late Friday that the device was a bomb.
The evacuation order forced the cancellation or postponement of numerous events in Peoria.
Kozak has a detention hearing set for Friday. Prosecutors are seeking to keep him detained. He is scheduled to appear in court again in December, with a jury trial is set for Jan. 11.

title: Maine compost site tainted with PFAS is months overdue for closure
text:
A compost facility in Unity Township heavily contaminated with forever chemicals has missed its target date to formally close, with state regulators saying they are still waiting on information from its owner.
Casella Waste Systems’ closure plan called for its Hawk Ridge Compost Facility to be cleared of compost, cleaned and closed by June 30, as first reported by the Bangor Daily News. The regulatory Maine Department of Environmental Protection said it has not yet issued the orders that would formally close the site and govern its monitoring afterward.
The delay leaves open how far Casella will have to go to clean up what was once the state’s largest composting operation, where contamination has spread to wetlands miles downstream. Maine is shutting down Hawk Ridge with little precedent and under a three-sentence closure rule that does not cover cleanup of surrounding land and water.
The facility is no longer operating, DEP spokesperson David Madore said, but it is not considered closed until the department issues those orders. He did not specify what information the DEP still expects from Casella. A Casella spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
Casella decided to close Hawk Ridge last year after regulators found high levels of forever chemicals on the site and signs that the contamination had spread beyond it. The DEP asked the company in February 2024 to test more and clean up. Casella declined, citing uncertain future regulations and high cleanup costs in letters later obtained by the BDN.
The state licensed Hawk Ridge in 1989 to turn sludge, a slushy byproduct of wastewater treatment, into compost. Maine became the first state to ban spreading sludge and sludge-based compost on land in 2022, so Casella kept making compost there from sludge trucked in mostly from Massachusetts and sold it out of state.
The last of that compost left this year. Casella shipped its remaining stock to buyers in New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Rhode Island in 2025 and the first three months of 2026, according to Madore and the company’s reports to the state.
“It is our understanding that this constituted the last of the remaining on-site materials as sludge acceptance and active compost production ceased at the facility during the third quarter of 2025,” Madore said.
Hawk Ridge produced more than 2 million cubic yards of compost over three decades, but routine testing of the site and its products did not begin until 2019. Results from a processing pond and the finished compost came in far above the limits the state set before the sludge ban.
A 2023 investigation by testing firm St. Germain found that Hawk Ridge was the primary source of the chemicals in the site’s soils and ponds and a significant source of groundwater pollution that is migrating off the property.
Casella’s plan calls for pumping out two contaminated ponds, scraping away soil from the most polluted areas, power washing buildings and sampling the site for 29 years. The company estimated the cost at just over $1 million.
Environmental advocates argued in January that the plan and the rule behind it fall short for a site this polluted, and that it should be treated more like a Superfund cleanup.
Madore said the DEP is working with Casella to make sure its closure plans meet the state’s solid waste rules. Casella is responsible for the cleanup costs, but it is not yet clear whether it will have to pay more for the contamination around the site.
“It is premature to discuss assessing fines,” Madore said.
Lori Valigra reports on the environment for the BDN’s Maine Focus investigative team. Reach her at lvaligra@bangordailynews.com. Support for this reporting is provided by the Unity Foundation, a fund at the Maine Community Foundation and donations by BDN readers.

title: Army to detonate large amount of lead azide in Iowa, risking toxic exposure to those in the area
text:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (KWQC/Gray News) - The U.S. Army is detonating a large quantity of lead azide on Friday in Middletown, raising health concerns among residents.
Lead azide is a highly sensitive explosive and a lead compound, meaning the blast could create environmental and public health risks.
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa and expert in environmental health, said the potential lead-carrying plume is among some of the top concerns.
The explosion could send lead-containing particles into the air, traveling with the wind before settling onto soil, buildings, vehicles and other surfaces.
This type of situation would create potential exposure risks for people who breathe in the particles or come into contact with contaminated dust.
“We inhale things that may get into our bodies; we ingest things, get into our gut. And we have the ability to have a dermal absorption of things that we touch,” O’Shaughnessy said.
Health effects of lead
Lead is a neurotoxin. Exposure can damage the brain and nervous system, kidneys and cardiovascular system.
Health experts said there’s no safe amount of lead. Young children are especially vulnerable.
“Maybe the most concerning thing is, say, 2-year-olds that just have this habit of, right, of touching everything and then everything goes right into their mouth, right,” O’Shaughnessy said.
The Army has shared the potential plume’s path. Officials said residents should hose down exterior surfaces, wipe down children’s play equipment and wash cars where dust may have settled following the planned detonation.

text:
The Best New Movies You Can Watch at Home This Weekend
New movies are coming to streaming this week and every week, at a faster pace than ever before. As always, ScreenCrush has your back, with a weekly guide to the latest releases on streaming (and digital rental or purchse) that deserve your attention. Sit back, relax, and check out what’s coming to a TV or computer (or, sigh, a phone) near you.
Then you’ve got all weekend to watch up with these titles. The theater is still the best, of course, but some weekends you just can’t muster the energy to get off the couch and haul yourself to the multiplex.
New Movies Streaming This Week and Weekend
This week you can watch Christopher Nolan’s epic retelling of a classic of ancient literature, Nicolas Cage play one of the most famous sports broadcasters in history, or a biopic about the beloved chef and TV host Anthony Bourdain. There’s also a new animated movie on Netflix, and a new Eli Roth horror film.
If these titles don’t do it for you, you can also check out some other recent streaming releases here. Or just keep scrolling, and see the new movies you can stream or rent on digital at home this weekend.

Russell’s biography of the football great that covers not only his time as an NFL coach and broadcaster, but also his involvement in the development of the ongoing series of video games that bear his name. Tony

Steps
Animation always does well on Netflix, and while the company mostly acquires or distributes titles from other studios (KPop Demon Hunters was by Sony; the upcoming Ray Gunn is from Skydance) this one is a product of Netflix’s own animation studio, and presents a twist on the old Cinderella story, this time with the stepsisters less wicked and more misunderstood.

Hostel and Thanksgiving director Eli Roth’s latest horror film is Ice Cream Man, about a vendor of frosty treats who arrives in a small town and sends his customers into a murderous rage. Good Humor? More like the worst...

title: Why doing less can be the most compassionate choice for someone you love
text:
(Aging Untold) — Our culture often pushes us to fix, treat or change every problem. But in health care and caregiving, the better path can be understanding a person’s goals, weighing the burden of treatment and accepting what cannot be fixed.
“We are a mortal being”
Sometimes doing less can be the most compassionate choice.
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, pointed to how people think about death.
“We are a mortal being, and we have an issue with that, especially in our culture,” Cradduck said. “We don’t like to talk about death. We don’t like to talk about dying.”
She said that leads people to want to treat everything.
She gave the example of paramedics doing chest compressions on a 98-year-old with advanced Alzheimer’s.
“To what value? Why are we bringing somebody back?” Cradduck said.
Accepting mortality as a gift
Accepting mortality can change what families give each other at the end of life, Cradduck said.
“Accepting the mortality of humanity and helping someone pass through their final sunset with grace and respect and dignity can oftentimes be the best gift you can give them and yourself,” Cradduck said.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said doing more is not always the same as helping more.
“Sometimes the goal should really be to recognize, know what the person wants as well and kind of abide by that,” Rogers said. “Sometimes doing nothing is the treatment.”
Acceptance is not giving up
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she sees people resist acceptance because they take it as giving up.
But she described acceptance differently.
“Well, you might be mad about it, but you’re still accepting it,” O’Rourke said. “You’re still going to go through the grief of why isn’t there one more thing I can do for mom. But you can process all of that and still be in an emotionally accepting place.”
Cradduck said accepting does not mean celebrating.
“Nobody’s asking you to throw a party because somebody you love is passing away, or you yourself are,” she said. “Nobody’s saying that this is something to be excited over, but it is something to accept. And accepting and understanding it can help everybody in the process.”
Adding life to the days
Rogers said advances in medicine have “tremendous power to add days to people’s lives,” but sometimes people want to add more life to the days they have.
O’Rourke said she was not happy when her mother decided against treatment for cancer, but later realized what her mom actually wanted.
“It was a hard pill to swallow, but the more I look back and I look at the quality time that we had in the months that she was alive, I’m so grateful that she had the courage to make that decision,” she said. “In her heart of hearts, she knew that she wanted to have really good, connected times with us as long as she could.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said looking back can bring regret when families learn a hard lesson.
“We’re not trying to torture people, you know, we’re trying to make good decisions,” Ambrose said. “Sometimes the patient might not always be thinking through everything, too. And we can really influence the answers that they give us.”
Cradduck added that treatment sometimes happens for the family rather than the patient.

title: Standish woman will help decorate the White House for Christmas: ‘It’s the people’s house’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Heidi Watson is used to a busy holiday season.
The Standish resident runs Watson Farm Christmas Trees with her family, teaches wreath-making classes and serves as the secretary-treasurer for the Maine Christmas Tree Association. For the past few years, she has presented Gov. Janet Mills with decorated wreaths after winning top accolades for her seasonal designs at the Fryeburg Fair. That’s all outside of her day job as an elementary school teacher at Standish Baptist Academy.
This year, she’s taking on yet another task: helping decorate the White House for Christmas.
After submitting an application detailing her experience decorating for Christmas, she was one of 150 chosen from an estimated 15,000 hopefuls to travel to Washington, D.C., next week and spend several long days working with other volunteers from all over the U.S. to transform the landmark’s interior for the holidays.
“I’m looking forward to the memories, and hopefully some new decorating ideas, learning from others, and making the season more meaningful and bright for the people that get to view the White House,” Watson said. “It’s not just about the White House. It’s the people’s house.”
The first lady decides a theme for the decorations each year. Melania Trump last year chose “Home Is Where the Heart Is,” and decorations included 51 Christmas trees, 75 wreaths, about 25,000 feet of ribbon, 2,000 strands of light, 700 feet of garland and 10,000 blue butterflies, according to the White House website. The official tree in the Blue Room was a 25-foot concolor fir. This year’s theme has yet to be announced.
Watson said she heard she will be assigned a team to decorate specific parts of the house. Like last year, decoration plans will deviate from history after President Donald Trump demolished the East Wing to make way for a new $600 million ballroom in 2025.
This was Watson’s first time applying to decorate the White House, and will be her first visit there. She said she prefers to focus on meeting new people and decorating rather than politics.
Watson’s personal style features natural-looking adornments that can stay up beyond the holidays, she said, allowing her wreaths to serve as a resting place for birds’ nests come spring. But after crafting Christmas decorations with balsam fir for over 20 years, she knows she will thrive with any theme and materials set before her next week.
“Creativity is kind of something that’s from within,” Watson said. “You can display it with whatever you’re given.”

title: MAINE-LY GARDENING: Thanksgiving
text:
As Americans prepare for Thanksgiving the media is full of images of tables laden with huge roast turkeys surrounded by platters of vegetables and pies. Magazines and TV cooking shows have been full of old and new recipes for weeks. Plans to host family and friends have been made, and the logistics of seating a large number of people are being worked out. Who will cook the meal, where and when, requires forethought. Which football game will be watched?
Many people travel, braving the roads and skies, for the modern version of what was once simply a large yet festive meal to celebrate harvest and family. Like so many things about our country, bigger is better.
Those who choose to enjoy the day, or long weekend, quietly can find it a little difficult as their local grocery store is crowded with shoppers and the aisles filled with all of the fixings for Thanksgiving plus reminders of the Christmas and New Year holidays to come. Sales lure even people who won’t be preparing a feast to buy a bird to cook in order to have leftovers to freeze for the weeks ahead. Turkey sandwiches which stuffing and cranberry sauce for lunches – what a treat!
Historians are asked to weigh in on the arguments about just where and when the American version of a harvest celebration began. Despite records of an annual thanksgiving observance in St. Augustine, Florida, the center of Spanish America in the mid 1500s, and a harvest celebration in Jamestown, Virginia, in 1619, it’s the Pilgrims in Plymouth that dominate the story.
Over the years, this holiday has become a favorite, less religious and political than others. Anyone can enjoy a good meal with good folks. People new to the U.S. from around the world have been adding their own traditions to Thanksgiving meals for centuries which has made the meal itself take on regional as well as family flavors.
The turkey is still the center piece for many, but we know that the first settlers in the U.S. were coastal people, so fish and shellfish were included, as well as wild ducks, deer and other game. Oysters remained popular for decades especially when the railroads made it possible for them to be packed in barrels and shipped from the East to new settlements across the country.
Farmed, gardened, or foraged, the side dishes of the meal are important. For some folks a “Sides giving” – all the vegetables, condiments, and, of course, pies – has become foundation for the feast. Who will miss turkey when there are so many other delicious things to enjoy? Meaty, or meatless, the Thanksgiving meal is centered on foods from the Western Hemisphere.
The potatoes and squashes, including pumpkin, have become popular with people in English speaking countries and elsewhere who have adopted the American Thanksgiving. Cranberry sauce, pecan pie, cornbread, and more all descend from our native plants.
After voicing our thanks, and before the big game, let’s have a game of “where did this food come from?”
 © Judith Chute Hsiang
Jude Hsiang is a retires University Extension Master Gardener instructor and a member of the China Community Garden.

title: Solidarity Harvest returns to support Maine farms and families
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - A local staple in solidarity is back to support Maine farms and families across the state.
This year marks the 24th Solidarity Harvest, put on by Food AND Medicine. Each year, the organization partners with local farms to purchase organic vegetables and works with other organizations to provide bread, stuffing and sweets.
With the help of about 200 volunteers, the food is packed into baskets and given to unions, churches and other agencies to distribute across the state.
The effort began with 134 baskets 24 years ago. Now, Food AND Medicine assembles close to 1,700.
As the need rises, organizers say their mission is to support local food producers and provide solidarity, not charity, to Mainers in need.
“Over 20% of children in the state of Maine live in food insecure households. And our goal really here is to try and strengthen the network and the supports for everybody, but especially children, to get access to food,” said Jack McKay, director of Food AND Medicine.
Volunteer Liam Parent said the quality of locally sourced food makes a difference.
“And these are honestly better than what you get at the store. And it’s fresher too, because these come right from the farmers,” Parent said. “You don’t have to deal with any middle man. You don’t have to worry about any of the real, like, bad stuff. ‘Oh, what hands does it touch before it gets to your plate?’ Here, your farmers and local volunteers.”
Food AND Medicine is still looking for volunteers as it continues to pack baskets, specifically on Thursday, Friday and Monday.
The organization is also accepting financial donations and is $29,000 away from reaching its fundraising goal.
For more information on how to help, visit their website.

title: ‘Very good at what they do’: Former Pentagon official and Husson professor weighs in on NSA outage
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency experienced an outage during scheduled maintenance Tuesday, a U.S. official said.
Michael Kamorski, interim dean of Husson University’s College of Business, spent 24 years on active duty in the Air Force, including four years at the Pentagon. He said the NSA collects electronic signals, including foreign communications, to help identify threats to the United States. Kamorski calls it one of the most secretive U.S. intelligence agencies.
“You look at what Microsoft, the FAA, the ground stop, the banks yesterday (Monday), now the NSA, very capable people at all those agencies but the NSA in particular, they’re very good at what they do and part of that ‘very good at what they do’ is protecting the information that they have so we actually refer to that as counterintelligence so the intelligence that they collect through signal intelligence puts us all in a safe place here and abroad as Americans.”
Kamorski says the outage is worth paying attention to, but he doesn’t believe it’s a reason to panic.
