title: House Democrat targets Trump family and top officials in early steps toward promised investigations
text:
House Democrat targets Trump family and top officials in early steps toward promised investigations
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is laying the groundwork for long-promised investigations of the Trump administration that will launch with the new Congress in January.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control, sent letters directing members of President Donald Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. It's an early step toward undertaking investigations of the Republican president and his administration.
The letters released Wednesday cover a wide range of potential investigations, including alleged financial conflicts involving Trump’s family, misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security and the administration’s handling of files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”
Targets of the letters include two of Trump’s sons, Vice President JD Vance, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law.
The White House has repeatedly pushed back at the investigative ambitions outlined by Democrats, with officials saying they are willing to engage on oversight inquiries that they see as legitimate but not ones assessed as politically motivated.
The president is "willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”
The letters offer an early glimpse of how Democrats plan to use their newly won congressional majority to scrutinize Trump and his administration. As favorable election results rolled in for Democrats on election night, Garcia posted a two-word warning on social media: “Lawyer up.”
The preservation notices do not compel recipients to turn over documents, but they signal the investigations that Democrats intend to pursue once they gain control of the committee and its subpoena power in January.
Before the midterms, Garcia outlined several areas Democrats would scrutinize, including the administration’s handling of the Epstein investigation, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and potential financial conflicts involving Trump’s family.
The letters to Kushner and Trump's sons Eric and Donald Jr. seek to preserve documents related to alleged conflicts of interest and their business dealings. Garcia also sent notices to Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former U.S. ambassador to Greece, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over separate allegations of misconduct and financial conflicts.
The letters to Vance and Blanche focus on the administration’s handling of files related to Epstein, including allegations by Democrats that White House officials sought to conceal information and manage the political fallout from the investigation.
The White House has warned Garcia and other Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration may open them up to investigations from the Justice Department.
Last week, White House counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to Garcia that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”
The investigative powers of Congress are well established, inherent in its constitutional authority as a check on the other branches of government. Modern U.S. history is filled with congressional investigations and their aftermath, from the Watergate investigation to the 9/11 attacks to Republicans’ more recent look into Democratic President Joe Biden’s family.

title: Ogunquit couple sues town over $1,700 in fines for rooster statues
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OGUNQUIT, Maine (WMTW) - An Ogunquit couple that has been fined $1,700 by the town over rooster statues displayed outside of their home has filed a federal lawsuit, claiming that their First Amendment rights have been violated.
Dave and Sara LeBlanc first displayed a 6-foot-tall tin rooster in front of their Main Street home in May 2025 as a show of love and support for their daughter, Pyper, who has autism. The couple said Pyper, who is now 6 years old, loves roosters and that the statue helped her find comfort while she waited for the school bus and when she came home from school each day.
Since their daughter loved the rooster statue so much, Dave and Sara LeBlanc said they acquired about two dozen tin roosters over time but never displayed more than eight at once on their property with the exception of the Christmas holiday season, when they arrange roosters to appear as if they are pulling Santa’s sleigh.
The LeBlancs also own The Omelette Factory, a breakfast restaurant that is attached to the family’s home. After the roosters on their front lawn became a popular landmark in town, the couple decided to add a rooster to the logo on The Omelette Factory’s merchandise, which is sold inside the restaurant. In the lawsuit, Dave and Sara LeBlanc said the rooster became like “a family crest,” and that the restaurant’s merchandise does not depict the roosters displayed on their lawn.
On or about April 3, 2026, the town sent a letter to the LeBlancs, notifying them that they were in violation of the Zoning Code for “unpermitted signage” and “overage of allowable square footage of signage.” In the letter, the town ordered the LeBlancs to immediately remove the unpermitted signage, including but not limited to the rooster statues.
“It’s a range of emotions for her because she’s like, ‘Why can’t the town be nice? Like, we’re taught to be nice,’” Sara LeBlanc said.
According to the lawsuit, Ogunquit Code Enforcement Officer Tyler McOsker told the couple that the town viewed the tin roosters as signs because the statues are believed to be advertisements for The Omelette Factory.
“Never imagined it getting to the point where it is. But it had to. We had no choice,” Dave LeBlanc said. “It’s just where it brought us. We have beliefs and we have a job to do to raise her. Do we go along and just get steamrolled, or stand up for what you believe in life?”
The town sent another letter to the LeBlancs on April 6, imposing a $150 fine for illegal signage because of the rooster statues. Ten days later, the town sent another letter imposing an additional $300 fine for failing to remove the decorative roosters.
The LeBlancs appealed their fines to the Zoning Board of Appeals, arguing that the rooster statues are not signs or advertisements but instead “are art, a comfort for their daughter, and a symbol of their love for her,” according to the couple’s lawsuit. The Zoning Board of Appeals heard the couple’s appeal on June 11 and affirmed McOsker’s determination that the rooster statues are signs. The board, however, did grant a disability variance, under which the couple could keep two roosters on the residential side of their home on the condition that the roosters be incorporated into a railing affixed to the residence.
In the lawsuit, the LeBlancs said they did not wish to add a railing to their home and instead chained two roosters to the decorative pillars flanking the front door of their house. The couple then gave their remaining rooster statues to friends and neighbors, who have displayed the roosters in front of their homes and businesses as a show of support for Pyper and as a symbol of neurodiversity awareness and acceptance.
On June 24, the town fined the LeBlancs an additional $500 for failing to build a railing for the two roosters. The couple was then fined an additional $750 on Sept. 17 for failing to remove the roosters or affix them to a railing.
The LeBlancs have paid all the fines assessed against them to date, totaling $1,700, under protest. The couple has also removed their decorative roosters from public sight.
The couple’s lawsuit states that in July, the LeBlancs filed a public records request under Maine’s Freedom of Access Act (FOAA) in an effort to obtain town records showing previous enforcement actions involving artwork, sculptures, lawn ornaments, public art or similar displays that were deemed to be signs under the Ogunquit Zoning Code.
The LeBlancs received all records related to the FOAA request from the town on Sept. 22. According to the couple’s lawsuit, the records the LeBlancs received contained no records relating to prior enforcement actions, whether historical or in relation to rooster statues.
In their lawsuit, the couple said that the rooster statues displayed in front of other Ogunquit homes and businesses — some of which belonged to the LeBlancs — have not resulted in any citations or fines against those residents and business owners. The LeBlancs also said in their lawsuit that the records they received from the town indicate Ogunquit does not apply its sign regulations to other decorative objects displayed on residential or commercial properties, such as lobster buoys, nautical art, antique farm equipment or large tiki statues.
The LeBlancs also take issue with the Ogunquit Zoning Code’s language. In their lawsuit, the couple said the Zoning Code defines an advertising sign as “a sign which identifies the goods or services available at a business or provides information about those goods and services.” The LeBlancs argue that under that definition, whether a display is a regulated advertising sign depends entirely on what the town perceives to be its expressive content.
“Here, the town has decided that the LeBlancs’ roosters are signs because the LeBlancs own The Omelette Factory, and town officials have therefore imagined the roosters to say ‘eat at The Omelette Factory.’ In reality, the roosters mean different things to different people,” the lawsuit states. “When the very same roosters stand in front of a neighbor’s home, the town treats them as decorations, not signs. The LeBlancs would own and display these roosters regardless of whether they owned a restaurant. Yet, merely because the LeBlancs happen to own an eatery, the town considers their roosters a sign for it.”
The couple argues that the town’s sign code and policies and practices regarding the enforcement of that code violate their right to free speech as guaranteed by the First Amendment.
“Plaintiffs want to display their tin roosters in front of their home without the threat of fines and code enforcement hanging over their heads,” the lawsuit states.
The LeBlancs seek a judgment declaring that the Ogunquit Zoning Code is “unconstitutionally vague,” as well as a permanent injunction prohibiting the town from enforcing the code against the decorative roosters. The couple also seeks damages in compensation for the town’s enforcement against them, including the $1,700 in fines they paid.
Attorneys from the Institute for Justice, a national nonprofit, public interest law firm, are representing the LeBlancs. Last month, Institute for Justice attorney Daniel Woislaw sent a letter to McOsker and Ogunquit Town Manager Matthew Buttrick, in which he called on the town to rescind the fines it levied against the LeBlancs.
“It is not something that towns have a monopoly on deciding what art is or what art means. These roosters mean a lot of things to a lot of people. To the LeBlancs, they are a comfort for Pyper and a symbol of their life,” Woislaw said. “It’s not neutral. It’s not evenhanded, it’s uneven, it’s unfair and it’s arbitrary. So that’s why this is unconstitutional.”
Ogunquit town officials did not provide a comment on the lawsuit filed by the LeBlancs.

title: Maine Eviction Prevention Program to stop accepting applications
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Eviction Prevention Program to stop accepting applications
After more than two years of helping people in Maine avoid eviction, the Maine Eviction Prevention Program, run by MaineHousing and Project Home, will stop accepting new applications at 5 p.m. on Nov. 30, 2026.
The organizations anticipate that the people already on the waitlist for help will exhaust available funding.
The program launched in October of 2024, thanks to an $18 million one-time appropriation in the state supplemental budget bill passed into law in June of 2024.
Video in the media player above is from when the program launched.
At the time, MaineHousing and Quality Housing Coalition said the program could help protect about 1,000 Maine tenants from losing their housing.
On Wednesday, in announcing the deadline for applications, Project Home said the program has helped 1,439 Maine households avoid eviction.
“MaineHousing greatly appreciates the focused work Project Home has done to manage this limited program and help thousands of Maine people avoid eviction and homelessness this year,” said MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan.
MaineHousing and Project Home said they will try to help eligible applicants who submit a completed application by the end of November, but there is no guarantee that assistance will be available.
“Eviction prevention is one of the most effective ways to address homelessness because it keeps people in the homes they already have,” said Victoria Morales, Executive Director of Project Home. “Since the program launched in 2024, our partnership with MaineHousing has helped 1,439 Maine households avoid eviction and the devastating ripple effects it can have on employment, education, and family stability. We’re grateful for the state’s investment in this program and committed to helping as many households as we can.”
The program provides rental assistance to eligible Maine households that have fallen behind on rent and are at risk of eviction. MaineHousing administers the program and provides funding and oversight. Project Home, formerly known as the Quality Housing Coalition, manages daily operations statewide as MaineHousing’s contracted agent, including reviewing applications and communicating with applicants and landlords.
To qualify, households must rent their primary residence in Maine, be behind on rent and at risk of eviction, owe no more than $9,600 in past-due rent, and have household income at or below 60 percent of area median income. Other requirements include rent limits and restrictions involving certain forms of subsidized housing.
Eligible households may receive assistance with rent owed to their current landlord and, after past-due rent is resolved, up to 12 months of rental assistance. Total assistance may not exceed $9,600 per eligible household. Payments are made directly to participating landlords, and landlord participation is required.
Full eligibility requirements, income limits, rent limits, required documents, and application information are available on the Eviction Prevention Program page on MaineHousing’s website.

title: Uber passenger charged with attempted murder allegedly told driver he didn’t like his name
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — An Uber passenger was charged Tuesday with attempted murder in a weekend attack near Minneapolis on a Somali American driver who was strangled with a seatbelt, run over by his own car and left in a ditch, authorities said.
Mohamed Yusuf, 51, is fighting for his life, has broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding from the attack, which occurred after the passenger allegedly told Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, according to court documents.
Samit Apurva Patel, 25, was charged with attempted second-degree murder and carjacking, but there wasn’t enough evidence to prove the attack was motivated by bias, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty. She said that decision “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now.”
An attorney representing Patel at his first court appearance Tuesday declined comment. A person who answered a phone number associated with Patel’s address said, “No comment,” before hanging up.
Dave Risk, a defense attorney in Minneapolis not connected to the case, said that to prove bias, prosecutors would have had to show that Patel intentionally targeted Yusuf because of a protected characteristic like race or religion.
In this situation, the pair likely met randomly, Risk said, adding that would make it tough for prosecutors to show Patel was motivated by bias.
Yusuf’s son Mustafa Osman said his father has been through five surgeries and is not doing well. He said Yusuf has driven taxis and Ubers for years and is known for his empathy and skill at de-escalating tense situations, making the attack especially shocking.
“We don’t have words to describe how bad it’s been. We haven’t really processed everything yet. It’s an emotional roller coaster,” he told The Associated Press.
The violence early Saturday in the Minneapolis suburb of Hopkins has increased fear among the Somali community after years of targeted rhetoric, including from President Donald Trump. Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S., with many concentrated in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The overwhelming majority are American citizens.
Yusuf’s brother says he heard him scream
According to court documents, Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger near a Minneapolis bar just before 1 a.m. Saturday. The drop-off location was in the nearby suburb of Hopkins.
Yusuf’s brother says he heard the passenger tell Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, the court documents say. He later heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and run over by the car, according to the filings.
Moriarty said the motive remains unknown but said, “There were some serious issues going on with this gentleman at the time he went home that so alarmed his parents that they called 911.”
She said she did not believe there was a recording of the call between Yusuf and his brother, and there was a camera in Yusuf’s car but it was not on.
Call for a wellness check led authorities to Patel
Patel’s parents called for a wellness check after Patel arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior,” according to the court filings. When officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged, according to the filings. Dirt, burs and a shoe were found in the driver’s side interior, and the phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was,” the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Yusuf is known for his empathy and ability to de-escalate
Osman, 27, said he was shocked when he got a frantic call from his uncle saying something had happened to his dad.
Osman, the oldest of Yusuf’s five children, described his father as empathetic and good at de-escalation. He said his father has dealt with aggravated or aggressive passengers during his many years driving.
“Anytime he’s in trouble, he’s the one that will calm things down, whether it’s between the family or if it’s while he’s at work,” he said.
Yusuf came to the U.S. in 1993 and spent some time working as a taxi driver in Chicago, said Osman. The family lived in Minnesota, which was where Osman was raised, and had moved back in 2018.
Dozens of community members visit hospital
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, said dozens of community members have been stopping by the hospital to show support for Yusuf.
“We feel as a community we’re under threat, constantly,” Hussein said. “Our community has, unfortunately, been feeling the brunt end of a disinformation and demonization campaign that has been going on now, and it’s coming from every corner.”
The Trump administration’s largest immigration enforcement effort, Operation Metro Surge, targeted the Twin Cities. Leading up to that operation, Trump said immigrants from the war-torn East African country have “caused a lot of trouble,” and he wants them to leave. He also referred to Somali immigrants in the U.S. as “garbage.”
Muhiyadin Yusuf, who knows Mohamed Yusuf but is not related to him, has been driving for ride-hailing apps in the Twin Cities for more than a decade. He said he’s felt unsafe in general because of comments from Trump and other politicians targeting Somalis. But since Saturday, he’s reduced his nighttime driving hours and added a third camera to his car. Some friends of his have stopped driving altogether.
“As a Muslim, as an immigrant, as a driver and as a Somali community, it affects me,” he said. “I’m scared now, more than before.”
___
Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press/Report for America reporter Laura Turbay contributed from Little Rock, Arkansas.

title: Eight County Teams Turn Regional Week Into Something Special
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 3: Eight Teams, Seven Finals, Five Titles
There are some weeks during a season when it feels like everything is happening at once.
Regional championship week was definitely one of those.
For two straight days, Aroostook County teams seemed to be everywhere. By the time it was over, eight different County teams had played in seven regional championship games, five had won, and five were still playing when state championship Saturday arrived.
That’s a pretty good reason for this one to land at No. 3 in my five stories that defined the fall.
It started Tuesday with Fort Kent and Wisdom.
Both schools sent their boys and girls teams into regional finals, and all four came home as Northern Maine champions.
Fort Kent’s girls beat Orono 3-0 to win their fourth straight Class C North title. The Fort Kent boys needed overtime against top-seeded Orono, with Dominic Cyr scoring the tying goal and then converting the game-winner just 36 seconds into overtime.
Wisdom had its own championship double.
The girls beat Dexter 3-1 behind three goals from Ellie Cyr, while the boys somehow found a way through one of the craziest games of the fall.
Cayden Hargrove scored four times in the second half against Piscataquis, Wisdom built a 4-1 lead, watched it disappear, and then Zeek Cyr scored with 13 seconds left to win it 5-4.
So by the end of Tuesday, Fort Kent and Wisdom had gone four-for-four in regional championship games.
And there was still another full day to go.
Wednesday brought three more regional finals involving four County teams.
Presque Isle’s girls reached the Class B North championship before falling to John Bapst. Fort Fairfield’s girls made it to the Class D North final before their run ended against Penobscot Valley.
Then Madawaska and Fort Fairfield met for the Class D North boys title, which meant the County was guaranteed one more regional champion either way.
Madawaska won that one 2-0, giving Aroostook County its fifth Northern Maine soccer championship in two days.
That’s when the numbers really started to stand out.
Eight County teams had reached regional championship games. Seven regional finals had at least one County team involved. Five championships came home, and five teams were headed to state championship games on the same Saturday.
Fort Kent sent both its boys and girls.
Wisdom sent both its boys and girls.
Madawaska sent its boys.
For one Saturday, five Aroostook County teams had a chance to bring home a Gold Ball.
Four finished as state runners-up, and one finished the job.
We’ll get to that one later in the countdown.
But what I’ll remember most about that week is just how much County soccer was represented when the season got down to its biggest games.
Presque Isle was there. Fort Fairfield was there. Madawaska was there. Fort Kent and Wisdom each had both teams still alive deep into the tournament.
For a couple of days, it really did feel like almost every regional championship had an Aroostook County team in the middle of it.
Eight teams. Seven regional finals. Five Northern Maine championships. Five chances at a Gold Ball.
That’s why this week of County soccer is No. 3 in my five moments that defined the fall of 2026.

title: Wilton board set to vote on proposed code of conduct
Mayor Sheline Talks to Bates Students Ahead of Runoff
text:
Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline spoke with Bates students outside of Commons on Monday, trying to educate students about the ongoing Lewiston mayoral runoff election for which he is campaigning.
Sheline promoted the Lewiston Community Policing Initiative, which he said promotes relationships between police officers and the Lewiston community.
He also mentioned his plan to develop Lewiston economically by attracting new businesses and supporting existing ones. He rejected his Republican adversary Rick LaChapelle’s plan to freeze property taxes, saying that it would force the city to fire employees and would disrupt public services.
He says that he opposes ICE presence in Lewiston. “They [ICE] came here claiming that they would take the worst of the worst, and instead what we find out is that the vast majority do not have a criminal record, they’ve taken our neighbors, our employees, and friends and family.” Sheline said.
He added, “Myself, along with the city council, acted immediately, enacting a city-wide ordinance that prevented city departments, including the police, from cooperating with ICE. Our residents can feel safe using city services and that when they call the police their information will not be immediately handed over to ICE.”
Alice Lamb ‘28 told The Bates Student that she supports mayor Sheline. “I’ve worked with him on different community engaged projects and I just see how much he cares about the community,” Lamb said.
Ella Caron ‘27, a volunteer for the Sheline campaign, said that a lot of Bates students don’t know the stakes of the election; “I think it’s really important to get the word out now because a lot of people are going home before the actual election day, so early voting is really important if you’re registered to vote,” Caron said.
Elle Gates ‘30, a Bates Fellow for the Community Organizing Alliance, said that students are not very aware of the election campaign, “but it is very important if we want to protect our immigrant community and make sure our government is doing all we can to resist ICE.”
She added that Sheline being mayor doesn’t guarantee safety for immigrants, but that LaChapelle’s support for ICE makes the race “a very clear choice for Bates voters.”
Sheline asked students to vote for him, saying, “I need everyone’s support to get across the finish line. Having a mayor supportive of the community and all of its residents is extremely important.”
Thursday, Nov. 19 is the last day of in person early voting. Registered voters can vote at City Hall from 7:45 a.m. to 4 p.m. There is also absentee voting, which can be found at www.lewistonmaine.gov/117/elections. Ballots must be requested by 4 p.m. on Dec. 10.

title: This state banned Waymo autonomous vehicles from its freeways
text:
(AP) - California banned Waymo’s autonomous vehicles from state freeways, saying they pose an “imminent hazard” after recent traffic incidents, including one where three of the driverless cars drove into a construction zone.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles issued the ban last Wednesday after two incidents on California freeways, Jonathan Groveman, a department spokesperson, said in a statement.
A Waymo spokesperson said in a statement that the company has “temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance.” The company did not provide more detail. Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have expanded onto freeways in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, according to the company.
The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions.”
Waymo continues to operate the vehicles as normal on California surface streets, according to the company.
California’s restrictions bar Waymo from both operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.”
___
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Center for Maine Contemporary Art’s new curator has big plans
text:
Museums plan exhibitions two or three years in advance as a general rule. This means that with every curatorial transition, it takes some time for the new curator’s vision to become apparent. So it is with the Center for Maine Contemporary Art in Rockland, where former Portland gallery owner Grant Wahlquist was appointed to the post last July (in September he also became the institution’s new director).
“In my interviews,” he says, speaking of the CMCA’s search for a new curator last summer, “I talked about wanting to do a conceptual painting show.” This wish has come to fruition in “Because the Sky Is Blue” (through Jan. 17). The exhibition essentially represents a new statement of purpose for the CMCA under his leadership, one aspect of which is to broaden its artistic scope.
While still committed to exhibiting artists active in the contemporary Maine art scene, “Because the Sky Is Blue” opens the aperture of this lens to include the larger international art world by putting Maine-based artists in conversation with other artists across the globe. Some of the artists in “Blue” have connections to Maine. Julie Poitras Santos lives in Portland and teaches at the Maine College of Art & Design. Selena Kimball grew up Down East. Ryosuke Kumakura lives in Rockport. There is Sharon Lockhart, five generations of whose family were raised in Bath, and Bo Bartlett, who paints on Wheaton Island every summer.
Other artists, however, have no specific relation to Maine, including Clémentine Adou, Wilfrid Almendra, Vija Celmins (though Wahlquist was told she has visited the state), Glenn Ligon, Matthew Metzger and Miao Wang. What connects the works is a complexity of form, technique, emotion and message that reveals itself with prolonged contemplation as we move past what looks seemingly simple and apparent on the surface. I recently visited Wahlquist at the CMCA to tour the show. Here he talks about the works and their meaning within the context of the show.
Bo Bartlett’s ‘Blue Sky’ paintings
The pivotal center of the show are four paintings of clear blue skies. Barlett himself talked about the impetus for these works on his Instagram feed: He began making them, he wrote, after the events of 9/11 in 2001, which he noted took place on “one of those crystal clear blue days … It dawned on me … that even with the horrific events, the world kept spinning, the sun kept shining, the tides kept ebbing and flowing, that what America was experiencing were ‘human problems,’ and that nature didn’t really seem to care.”
One of those original paintings — made with oil on paper — is in the show, along with several executed in 2011, 2012 and 2014. In these, Wahlquist observes, “There’s a formal complexity that relates to an emotional complexity. They refuse to be one thing. They look monochromatic from a distance, but more trompe l’oeil closer up. But they are also emotional. They grow out of grief, but grief is connected to love, to beauty … I thought I knew Bo’s work. But Bo would say these are the only original idea he has ever had.” Each title records the date they were painted, which also aligns them with conceptual art, specifically, Wahlquist points out, the “Today” series of date paintings of Japanese artist On Kawara. Bartlett continues to paint the sky, says Wahlquist, having done another this summer.
Selena Kimball’s ‘Atlas of Air’ installation
For this grid of 30 framed collaged works, Kimball first reproduced New York Times images that accompanied front-page stories onto Hahnemühle rice paper, cut away everything but the sky in each, then used the sky images as “strokes” or “marks” that comprise each collage “painting.” Most are assembled in a way that feels like an invitation to enter into a vortex or opening and travel deeper and deeper into the work.
“We assume that if it was a story that landed on the front page of the newspaper, it was an image that was not always a happy one,” says Wahlquist. Within that context, we could look at them as a sky that is fracturing and falling. “But when I look at these I get Georgia O’Keeffe’s ice cave paintings, which are so peaceful,” he says. “They also sometimes look like a camera aperture, which points up the slipperiness of the photographic medium itself. One thing I hope this show is trying to do is to think of painting not as a way of making, but as a way of seeing. These are not technically paintings, but spiritually they are in some way.”
Wilfrid Almendra’s site-specific ‘Dirt Under the Fingernails’ sculptures
Neither would we normally say that sculpture is painting. Almendra is a Portuguese-French artist who often juxtaposes man-made materials with natural objects to comment upon the futile attempts of humanity to impose control on nature. At the CMCA, textured cathedral glass — shipped from France thanks to a grant from that country, where Almendra lives and works — was assembled onsite and paired with what look like oranges, poppies and a pair of boots.
However, notes Wahlquist, “All of the things that look like found objects are cast aluminum and hand-painted, so they’re a kind of trompe l’oeil painting. The oranges allude orange and olive trees his family grew on their land in Portugal, which the family had to leave during the dictatorship [1933-1974]. So, they are a reference to the diaspora of Portuguese communities. The red poppies are basically weeds. But because they thrived in a landscape that was the site of trench warfare during World War I” — the reason poppies became symbols of Memorial Day — “that kind of association is the way they work powerfully with other works in the show.” Because the glass of the sculptures was cut onsite, Wahlquist says, they will likely be destroyed after the exhibition, adding another layer of complex emotion to them.
Sharon Lockhart’s ‘Untitled (Night Sky)’ works
These six works express the idea of painting without actually being solely painting since they also incorporate photography. “They were made in Gotland, a place in Sweden that reminds Sharon of Maine,” says Wahlquist. “She was thinking about the experience of extreme darkness. They are portraits of the night sky made with daylight, and they have this sort of Rothko and Ad Reinhardt thing going on.”
To make them, he explains, Lockhart used “pigmented fiber-reactive dyes in very bright colors that she washed into canvas. Then she applied cyanotype fluid [ferric ferrocyanide] and laid the canvases faceup in the sun, exposing them for anywhere from 59 to 110 hours. The more sunlight you put on them, the darker they get.” What appear at first to be enormous all-black canvases, then, actually reveal layers of color and gesture underneath the longer we gaze at them. “They change all the time,” says Wahlquist. “They are living, breathing things.” Painting and photography are both integral to the works, which evoke a velvety sensuality and light within a dark void.
Miao Wang’s ‘Place Yourself Into a Readymade Position‘
These 15 abutting red panels affixed to the wall with custom-sized artist’s tape are ostensibly paintings, but not in our usual conceptualization of the medium. Wang applies thin watercolor washes onto synthetic water-repelling paper in an array of red hues. “The water evaporates off and deposits the pigment directly onto the paper,” explains Wahlquist. Each hue submerses us in a color that is both pervasive and immensely symbolic in Wang’s culture. “Growing up in China, Miao was thinking about all the associations with red. It is a color that represents good luck, but also the color of the Communist Party, so it is both lucky and mandatory.”
This emotional and technical complexity conjures a simultaneity of good fortune and coercion, centuries-long cultural belief alongside temporal political ideology. Wang also includes “readymade wall” as one of the materials in descriptions of the work, complicating our reading further by alluding to the Duchampian idea of ordinary industrial objects that artists recontextualize by stripping them of their function and, so, elevating them. But read purely visually, notes Wahlquist, they are “so subtle and so beautiful.”
Glenn Ligon ‘Blue (for JB) #16‘
This work came straight to the CMCA from Ligon’s studio. It deals, at least in part, with a subject dear to Wahlquist’s heart, which is how the burden of the public’s need for legibility in art falls disproportionately on marginalized artists. Ligon is known for paintings that explore gay African-American experience, often incorporating text from literary works, in this case James Baldwin’s “Stranger in the Village,” an essay Baldwin wrote while recuperating from burnout in the Swiss Alps. His sense of being an “outsider” became evident when he realized many of the town’s people had never before seen a Black man.
Ligon uses carbon ink to apply letter stencils, which through reuse naturally smudge and blur the type. “Glenn’s work has always been about the relation between text and abstraction,” observes Wahlquist. Here Ligon also practices “frottage,” a technique of rubbing paper with the ink over a texture, “breaking down text even further to make it almost illegible. Text is a stand-in for how people approach Glenn’s work, and it pushes against them.” More layers of meaning become apparent when we realize that frottage happens also to refer to male-on-male non-penetrative sex. Additionally for Wahlquist, the painting invokes another Black gay artist, Beauford Delaney, through its use of the blue Delaney used in his painting “Paris Window.”
Vija Celmin’s ‘Untitled (Dark Sky)’ mezzotints
Mezzotints are, explains Wahlquist, “the inverse of etchings, where you abrade the copper plate everywhere then burnish images into them, producing really intense velvety blacks. She calls them redescriptions of photographs.” For the Latvian-American Celmins, this means both translating an image from one medium to another (a photo, say, onto a copper plate), as well as “paraphrasing the world.”
Images of a black starry sky “have a vastness that is the prototypical experience of the sublime because it can feel overwhelming.” In this way they relate to Bartlett’s paintings because they also illustrate that “in the grand scheme of things, these human feelings are small.” But the slow, deliberate process of mark-making is also a way for Celmins to process memory. Celmins has said that she has “lived” through her imagery, which, she adds, is “like an album of a certain time.”
Matthew Metzger’s ‘No Title (On Holiday)‘
This pair of paintings of gardenia plants are “paintings acting like photographs” says Wahlquist. “Matthew tends to cycle back to bodies of work. These were made two years apart. His work often also relates to coverings in music.” Here, the two works look like a black-and-white photo (in its monochrome also relating to Renaissance grisaille painting) and a blue cyanotype photo.
These paintings specifically allude to Billie Holiday’s “Strange Fruit,” the controversial protest song that compared lynched Black bodies to “strange fruit” dangling from trees. Metzger’s work is often focused on critiquing systems of power, and these certainly are congruent with his interest, says Wahlquist, of “people in solidarity with other, different kinds of marginalized people.”
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.
“Because the Sky Is Blue” Center for Maine Contemporary Art, 21 Winter St., Rockland. Through Jan. 17. Wed.-Sat. 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., Sun. noon to 5 p.m. For more, 207-701-5005, cmcanow.org

title: Ground stop puts needed spotlight on air traffic control modernization
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
Flying, for most of us, is a leap of faith.
We have faith that the physics of flight will keep the plane in the air. We have faith that the pilots are competent. We have faith that our fellow passengers will be mostly well behaved as we are crowded together in a metal tube hurtling across the sky miles above Earth.
We also have faith that the overworked air traffic controllers and the antiquated system they use will manage the thousands of planes in the air every day.
That faith was badly shaken last week when all flights in the U.S. were grounded Friday afternoon “out of an abundance of caution,” in the words of the Federal Aviation Administration.
Yes, the flight disruptions, delays and cancellations were inconvenient for travelers. That was acknowledged by the head of the Department of Transportation. But, what DOT Secretary Sean Duffy seems to downplay is that the unexpected suspension of all air traffic operations is more than an inconvenience. It has shaken the faith that many Americans have in our system of commercial air traffic, just days before the busiest travel days of the year.
That is why Congress must step in and do its oversight responsibility. Committees must quickly hold hearings to determine what went wrong, and more importantly, how it can be fully fixed, and when.
This isn’t so much about assigning blame, as it is about putting the U.S. on a better — and faster — track of modernizing its air traffic control system.
Friday’s shutdown was reportedly prompted by problems with the installation of new wiring at facilities in Arkansas and Texas. Problems that began at those facilities spread nationwide as communications flooded the air traffic control systems across the country.
By all accounts, America’s air traffic control system is severely outdated and the work to upgrade it has proceeded at a snail’s pace.
That is unacceptable.
It appears that the FAA has badly managed this work. This mismanagement stretches back through many presidential administrations.
While Congress has appropriated significant sums to pay for this work, the money may yet be insufficient for the huge scale of updating that is necessary.
There are also questions of who should oversee the system. While there are certainly concerns about privatizing such vital work — such as who the contractors share proprietary information with, including countries hostile to American interests — other countries, such as Canada and members of the European Union, have successfully moved to a private model.
These questions demand careful consideration. In the shorter term, Congress must get fuller answers about what prompted last Friday’s ground stop, which lasted about four hours, and what steps are being taken to avert such a situation in the future.
“The pilots and controllers faced an emergency and did their jobs. They brought thousands of passengers safely to the ground without needing to tell anyone how great their president was. The people running the system owe Americans the same seriousness,” Adam Kinzinger, a former Republican U.S. representative from Illinois and a former Air Force pilot, wrote on Facebook on Monday. “Tell us what went wrong, explain how you’re going to fix it and show us you can follow through.”
That is precisely what Congress — the nation’s oversight body — must do, despite assurances from House Speaker Mike Johnson it isn’t necessary.
Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have met with lawmakers and White House officials. That’s a good start, but more detailed, public oversight hearings must be held so the American people can know what happened and how both short-and long-term problems will be fixed — and how much it will cost.
These questions need to be answered as soon as possible to reassure the American people that boarding a plane is safe.

title: How scammers use ‘number cycling’ to get around spam filters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Five years after federal requirements to fight spoofed robocalls began taking effect, unwanted calls are still getting through, according to a new report from U.S. PIRG Education Fund.
Teresa Murray, a consumer watchdog with U.S. PIRG, said the problem is far from solved.
“I still get them. I’m sure you still get them. And in many ways, it’s as bad as ever,” Murray said.
In its “Ringing in Our Fears” report, U.S. PIRG Education Fund analyzed FCC records from more than 11,000 registered phone providers. Of those, 42% reported fully implementing technology designed to verify the number displayed on caller ID.
The report also found some progress. Unwanted robocalls have declined to an average of about 2.1 billion a month this year, down from nearly 2.5 billion last year.
One tactic is known as “number cycling,” according to the report. Some scammers buy or rent large blocks of phone numbers and use each one sparingly to avoid being flagged by spam filters. Once they have gone through the numbers, they start the cycle again.
Murray described where regulators are turning next.
“So now, what a lot of the regulators are focusing on, is trying to go after the companies that sell and lease phone numbers to bad guys. So they’re going to keep on going trying to go after the phone companies who aren’t doing a good job of filtering calls. And they’re going to continue going after guys who are scamming people,” Murray said.
The FCC is also considering stricter “know your customer” rules that would require phone companies to more closely vet who they provide phone numbers to. State attorneys general are also pushing for greater oversight of companies that buy and resell phone numbers, to help law enforcement track down illegal robocalls.
Murray recommends letting unrecognized calls go to voicemail and never providing personal or payment information to an unexpected caller, regardless of what the caller ID says.

title: Family fined nearly $2,000 over tin rooster statues in front yard sues town
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OGUNQUIT, Maine (WMTW) - A Maine family that has been fined $1,700 over tin rooster statues in their lawn has filed a federal lawsuit, claiming their right to free speech has been violated.
Dave and Sara LeBlanc first put a 6-foot-tall tin rooster in front of their Ogunquit home in May 2025. The couple say it’s a show of love and support for their daughter, Pyper, who has autism. The 6-year-old loves roosters, and her parents say the statue helped her find comfort on her way to and from school.
Over time, the couple acquired about two dozen tin roosters, but they say they never displayed more than eight at once – with the exception of the Christmas holiday season.
However, the LeBlancs also own The Omelette Factory, a breakfast restaurant that is attached to the family’s home, and the town of Oguinquit considers their rooster statues to be advertisement for the business.
In April 2026, the town sent the LeBlancs a letter, telling them they had to remove all “unpermitted signage,” including the rooster statues. Since then, the couple have been fined $1,700, which they say they paid under protest.
The couple now have just one rooster in their yard, which has been covered up. The remaining statues were given to friends and neighbors, who have displayed them outside their homes and businesses as a show of support for Pyper.
“Never imagined it getting to the point where it is, but it had to. We had no choice,” Dave LeBlanc said.
The LeBlancs are suing the town, arguing their right to free speech as guaranteed by the First Amendment has been violated.
“It’s not neutral. It’s not even-handed. It’s uneven, unfair and arbitrary. So, that’s why this is unconstitutional,” said attorney Daniel Woislaw from the Institute for Justice, a national nonprofit that is representing the LeBlancs. “It is not something that towns have a monopoly on deciding what art is or what art means.”
Pyper’s parents say the situation has brought up a mix of emotions for their daughter; though she’s happy other people are sharing in what she loves.
“It’s a range of emotions for her because she’s like, ‘Why can’t the town be nice? We’re taught to be nice,’” Sara LeBlanc said.
The LeBlancs’ lawsuit requests damages, including money to cover the paid fines.
Town officials did not provide a comment on the lawsuit.

title: Community Thanksgiving Dinner at St Joseph Parish Hall
MDI soccer star shines in China
text:
JIANGSU, China — It’s incredibly difficult for an athlete to make it into the professional ranks of any sport. The competition level nationwide is staggering, with the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) estimating that only about 7% to 8% of high school athletes go on to play at any NCAA level, with fewer than 2% of those student-athletes eventually earning a roster spot on a pro team in this country.
The odds of making it in the National Women’s Soccer League are even slimmer, with the consensus being that it’s a fiercely competitive process to earn a roster spot. The NCAA again estimates that only about .4% of female Division I college soccer players are signed to an American professional league.
Former MDI High School standout Daisy Granholm seemed to be on the right track to defy those odds, however, after making it a goal to go pro at an early age. Granholm began her soccer journey playing on the boys team at Acadia Fire, since the organization didn’t have a program for girls at the time, and fell in love with the sport, so much so that she and her family committed to driving four hours regularly in order for Granholm to play on the girls Seacoast United team, which required traveling for practice one day a week, first in Portland and then in Epping, N.H., and even longer weekend trips for games.
But Granholm always made this early commitment seem like a worthwhile investment as she continually excelled at every level of the game. In high school, Granholm made every All-Star and All-Conference team and set a new single-season scoring record for the program after netting 41 goals in her senior season. The previous record of 36 goals had stood for 32 years, and was set by none other than Granholm’s mother, Whitney Granholm née Williams, in 1987.
In her fifth season at Dartmouth — her freshman season was lost due to the Covid-19 pandemic — Granholm was a Second Team All-Ivy League selection after scoring 7 goals and adding 2 assists across 16 games. She had increased her statistical output each and every year at one of the top programs in the country and was seemingly checking off all the boxes one would need in order to even have a shot at signing an NWSL contract.
But the path to achieving one’s goals is rarely linear, especially when it comes to top-level sports in the competitive American market. For Granholm, it was injuries that threw a wrench into the machinery that she had worked so hard over the years to build. An ACL tear in her sophomore season set her back somewhat, but stress fractures in both of her feet in her fifth year necessitated a six- to nine-month recovery period right when she was getting ready to graduate early and begin the next phase of her career.
“I’ve struggled with injuries to a degree that I don’t think many other players do,” Granholm told the Islander. “And to come back from all of those, I think really just persevering for my goal is a general theme. Three major surgeries, three major recoveries, and I’m still the fastest, strongest I’ve ever been. It’s kind of just a story I would say of perseverance and kind of going against the odds a little bit from our small island in Maine to across the whole world.”
Yes, her injuries may have closed some doors locally as she became less attractive to NWSL clubs, having to rehab right out of college. But the setback forced her to take a different path available to American athletes hoping to break into the professional ranks, one that led her to a place she never thought she would end up — Jiangsu, China.
“I knew I didn’t want to go and sit on a bench. So, I was just looking for somewhere where I could play a lot and make a big impact, and where the soccer was good. I really wanted high-quality soccer. So, that’s what kind of led me to the Chinese Super League,” Granholm explained. “They have a great level. Their FIFA ranking is really good right now. And it was honestly just a perfect fit. It was a lot of luck and timing.”
Granholm signed a six-month contract with the top club, Jiangsu Suning W, during the summer transfer window in June and has been training and playing with the team ever since. She lives on a training campus along with members of two other professional teams, a men’s club and a U20 side. There, Granholm and her teammates eat meals together, rehab and prehab injuries, workout and lift weights, attend meetings and film sessions, and practice for a couple of hours seven days a week.
“ It always takes a minute to adjust every time you move up a level. So, in general, every step from high school to college, you get more comfortable, and then you start excelling at the end of your time. This is the first professional situation for me, so I’m just kind of learning all that I can and being okay with giving myself an adjustment period. I did score my first pro goal though, which was exciting — in my first game, which was amazing. So, just kind of working hard every day. It’s just a lot. It’s a lot of physical and mental load.”
While trying to focus on taking her game to the next level, Granholm has also had to adjust to some cultural differences and overcome language barriers. But she says the club and her teammates have been incredibly supportive during her transition. And the team’s away games on the schedule have presented her with the opportunity to travel to locales all around China, like Shanghai, Hong Kong, and Beijing.
Granholm’s contract is up once the season culminates with the FA National Cup tournament in December, and from there, the next phase of her journey is still unknown. While she has enjoyed her time so far in the Chinese Super League, Granholm’s ultimate goal remains the same, and she is prepared to attack the process with her trademark dedication. The former high school standout is perhaps even more motivated to play her way back to the States, where those she is closest to can more easily support her as they’ve done throughout her career.
“I think probably the hardest thing is just being so far away from my family,” Granholm said of her experience in Jiangsu. “But it’s always a dream for you to play in front of your family, so I think you kind of have to earn it. And I’m very young, so my goal is to move a little bit closer with each contract.”

title: '98% confident': Mullin doesn't suspect cyberattacks are behind recent tech outages
text:
'98% confident': Mullin doesn't suspect cyberattacks are behind recent tech outages
Trump administration officials took questions on Capitol Hill on the heels of a cascade of tech failures that have rattled Americans and raised questions about cybersecurity.
'98% confident': Mullin doesn't suspect cyberattacks are behind recent tech outages
Trump administration officials took questions on Capitol Hill on the heels of a cascade of tech failures that have rattled Americans and raised questions about cybersecurity.
A trio of Trump administration officials was in the hot seat on Capitol Hill on Wednesday on the heels of tech failures that have rattled Americans and raised questions about cybersecurity.
A routine hearing on a range of worldwide threats largely turned into a grilling session about a string of recent outages. The disruptions have impacted Microsoft and major banks, as well as the nation's air traffic control system and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency. 
"Is it your testimony today that the American people should believe that the series and sequence of events over the last week is purely coincidental?" asked Rep. Dan Goldman (D-NY).
"We have no indication that these events are related," responded Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
Clayton reiterated that, so far, these incidents appear to be separate service outages stemming from maintenance and technical changes. He stressed that the rate of system upgrades in public and private sectors is increasing to keep up with rapid advancements. 
FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia said their cyber experts are working with private sector partners out of "an abundance of caution."
"Again, to foot stomp it, we have seen no malicious activity as of today," Raia said.
"I'm 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems," echoed Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin.
Officials also warned that, in general, artificial intelligence is sharply increasing the speed, scale, and sophistication of cyberattacks.
In light of that threat, some lawmakers raised concerns about steep staff cuts under the Trump administration at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
"They fired and pushed out more than 1,000 cyber defenders at precisely the moment the cyber threat was exploding," said Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-VA).
Mullin said that CISA has continued to meet its mission, but didn't provide specifics when asked about the status of the agency's hiring efforts. He told lawmakers earlier this year that CISA was working to bring in hundreds of additional employees.
Asked if last year's firings were a mistake, Mullin said, "I wasn't there when that was made. I don't know the reasoning behind it, so I'm not going to talk about why someone was let go if I wasn't involved in it."
Immigration enforcement training update
Mullin was also pressed about immigration enforcement decisions made under former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem, including abbreviated training that was implemented during an Immigration and Customs Enforcement hiring surge.
"Unfortunately, Congressman, there was some decisions that were made before I was secretary that we're having to undo," Mullin said.
Mullin said every ICE agent currently serving on the street has now gone through the restored thirteen-week training schedule and passed a background check. Agents who have yet to complete those steps have been put on administrative leave, according to Mullin.
Iranian plot concerns
Officials also got several questions about a CNN report that Iran may be developing plans to potentially detonate a so-called "dirty bomb" or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C.
Clayton didn't comment on that report specifically, but told lawmakers that "lethal plotting" by Iran — both inside and outside the United States — has substantially increased.
"I will tell you a lot of the reporting is largely aspirational, but that does not mean that we do not take it seriously," Raia said. "We have revamped our Iranian threat mission center to help combat that threat."
Republican chairman calls out FBI director's absence
FBI Director Kash Patel was notably absent from Wednesday's hearing, a fact that Republican Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino called out in his opening remarks.
“There was no surprise or last-minute request, and despite repeated attempts over the span of several months between then and now to find any date when he could testify, the director made clear that he had no intention of appearing," Garbarino said.
Asked about those comments on Wednesday, an FBI spokesperson said that Patel is working in the field this week "doing five different law enforcement engagements."
The spokesperson also noted that the FBI designated Deputy Director Raia for the hearing and notified the committee several weeks ago.

title: Giant catsup bottle draws travelers to a landmark with history
text:
COLLINSVILLE, Ill. (InvestigateTV) - Route 66 turns 100 this year, and along the historic highway in Collinsville stands a landmark that is hard to miss: a 70-foot catsup bottle perched on a 100-foot stand.
The structure was built in 1949 as a water tower for a catsup factory — the original home of Brooks Catsup. It holds 100,000 gallons of water.
By the early 1960s, the bottling operation had moved to Indiana. In 1993, Brooks Foods decided to sell the property, and the bottle had fallen into disrepair.
“Major, major disrepair. So they were talking about tearing it down. The Catsup Bottle Preservation Group was formed, they raised a whole bunch of money, and in 1995 had it restored,” said Mike Gassmann of the World’s Largest Catsup Bottle Inc.
In 2002, the structure was placed on the National Register of Historic Places. It has since been inducted into the Illinois Route 66 Hall of Fame.
Gassmann, who holds the title of “Big Tomato” within the bottle’s fan club, said the landmark draws a steady stream of visitors.
“Doesn’t surprise me any day to come by here and see people taking photos,” he said.
As for what’s inside, Gassmann offered no definitive answer.
“I can neither confirm nor deny the reports that it is filled with catsup,” he said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Speeding up the life-saving process
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at the effort to bring blood transfusions on board ambulances to speed up the life-saving process.
Plus, as more people choose screen time over storybooks, how one museum hopes to change that narrative.
Then, we introduce you to an equestrian whose terminal diagnosis inspired her biggest adventure yet.
Push for prehospital blood
A national effort to stock ambulances with blood for transfusions in the field is expanding.
It’s a movement driven in part by two single but staggering statistics: Severe blood loss can lead to death in less than five minutes and about 40% of trauma-related deaths worldwide are due to uncontrolled bleeding.
Getting approval and funding for EMS crews to transfuse blood in the field has been difficult, but several updates in recent years are helping increase access across the U.S.
Down the Rabbit Hole
Reading is crucial for young children, helping them to build their vocabulary and their imaginations. But the joy and love of reading among kids is slipping away. Federal data shows fewer children are reading for fun today compared to years past. That’s also true for adults.
But The Rabbit hOle, a Kansas City museum based on children’s literature, aims to bring that love for literature back, by bringing your favorite stories to life.
A giant catsup bottle
Route 66 turns 100 this year, and along the historic highway in Collinsville stands a landmark that is hard to miss: a 70-foot catsup bottle perched on a 100-foot stand.
The structure was built in 1949 as a water tower for a catsup factory — the original home of Brooks Catsup. It holds 100,000 gallons of water.
Unbridled joy
Tricia Jackson has competed in endurance races, appeared on ‘Survivor’ and has chased a lifelong dream.
After being diagnosed with ALS, Jackson made it a mission to ride a horse in all 50 states.
“Everything goes away when I’m horse riding,” she said. “I feel good, my speech is better. It’s therapy. But I tell them my ALS journey so far and it’s not going to keep me down. As long as I can go, I go.”

title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska, beating incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan
text:
Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska, beating incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan
Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.
Related video above: "A change from status quo": Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen announces bid for Senate Majority Leader
The Alaska race is the last U.S. Senate contest to be resolved in this year's midterm elections, and Peltola’s victory expands the Democrats’ majority after they retook control of the chamber. The party already won campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and, most recently, Mississippi.
With Peltola’s victory, Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most since 1958. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, while Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin.
Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, after former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by Trump. The Associated Press has not yet called the U.S. House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich.
Flipping Alaska's seat was pivotal to Democrats' plans to retake the Senate
Peltola previously held the state's lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.
In the campaign’s final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent.
Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the Nov. 3 election. Peltola denied any involvement.
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats' behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since The Times’ article was published.
Candidacy of second Dan Sullivan roiled the race
The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year’s open primary and later sought to recant her statements. But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump’s mind. He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October.
Later, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered. It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit “flagrant corruption.”
The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed. Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election “without unwarranted interference by the United States.” They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska’s ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them.
The Justice Department also confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska’s U.S. attorney would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into.
Peltola finished first in the primary with 49.5% of the vote, followed by the incumbent with 41.4%.
Dan J. Sullivan finished a distant third with about 2.5%, but he advanced to the general election as one of the top four finishers. He was listed on both ballots as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation, while the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Peltola distanced herself from national Democrats
During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are often only accessible by air or water.
Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of “Alaska first.”
“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”
The race attracted a flood of spending by outside groups and at times turned negative, with the campaigns accusing each other of spreading lies. Trump and Vice President JD Vance made separate trips to the state in the month before the election in support of the incumbent.
“Lower 48” became something of an insult bandied by both sides. Sullivan and his supporters tried to align Peltola with “Lower 48 liberals” who want to restrict oil and gas drilling, mining and other resource development in the state. Peltola said that while she would work with Trump to get things done for Alaska, “I will never put any Lower 48 politician before Alaskans. That’s the difference between Dan and me.”
When Sullivan took issue with Peltola reading off note cards during a debate — “You can’t cue-card your way to the Senate,” he told reporters — Peltola said she simply was prepared. She also pushed back against Sullivan’s assertion that she was ineffective during her time in the House, saying she worked well with him as part of the state’s three-person delegation in Washington.
Peltola postponed two days of campaign events in late October after her campaign said she suffered minor injuries in a car accident in Anchorage.
Peltola emphasized affordability issues
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, emphasized her Alaska roots and resurrected the “fish, family and freedom” tagline from her prior campaigns. She spoke about growing up in western Alaska and fishing for salmon on the Kuskokwim River with her father and spending parts of the summer at fish camp with her children and late husband, who died in September 2023.
She said the fish and wildlife that Alaskans long relied on to fill their freezers for the winter were becoming harder to find. The changes were forcing people to buy more food and other staples at the store — supplies that must be barged or flown in — and deal with “crushing prices,” she said.
Peltola also said she saw members of Congress who were “more focused on their stock portfolios” than helping ease those costs and vowed to push back against the billionaire class.
Peltola will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014.

title: Algeria treats Kansans to free trip as thank-you for World Cup welcome
text:
Algeria treats Kansans to free trip as thank-you for World Cup welcome
A group of more than 30 people from Lawrence, Kansas, just returned from a weeklong, all-expenses-paid trip to Algeria.
The trip was a thank-you from the Algerian government to the people in Lawrence who went out of their way to welcome the country's national team during the FIFA World Cup.
The Algerian team spent more than a month living in a Lawrence hotel while playing World Cup group-stage matches.
"Never would have imagined that a relationship like this would have come out of the World Cup," said Lawrence Mayor Brad Finkeldei.
Finkeldei spoke to KMBC 9 just days after returning from the trip. On his shirt, he proudly wore a pin. One half of the pin featured a sunflower representing Lawrence, Kansas, while the other half featured a fennec fox, the national animal of Algeria.
The Lawrence group took river cruises, listened to live music, saw the Sahara Desert, attended a packed soccer match and saw as much of the country as they could in seven days.
It led to unforgettable memories.
"They had their band and our band members played together," Finkeldei said. "First they played the National Anthem of the United States together, and then they played the anthem of Algiers together. And then they went and played a couple more songs together. It was a very emotional experience to see that and to see those band people playing together."
This wasn't just a trip for dignitaries like the mayor. Algerian leaders invited people they wanted to thank personally for helping welcome their national team during the World Cup.
"They sent emails directly to people," Finkeldei said. "They sent a list of individual names of people they wanted to invite."
The list included more than 50 people. Just under 40 business owners, local artists and community members, including some who went viral for supporting Algeria, made the trip.
One of the most popular visitors appeared to be Lawrence police Detective Meghan Bardwell. Bardwell went viral during the World Cup for videos of her dancing and celebrating with Algerian fans.
"We felt like celebrities there," Finkeldei said. "In particular, Megan, our dancing police officer, she was very famous. People stopping her in the street. Even when we got to Montreal, I had two or three people stop me in the Montreal airport to take a picture with me. Even before we went, they knew who we were."
Another Lawrence resident who went viral is Tommee Sherwood. You may recognize him from a video of an interview with Algerian media.
Sherwood was outside the Algerian team's hotel in Lawrence when the players first arrived. He told the interviewer, "I want to say thank you to Algeria for choosing Lawrence, Kansas," and welcomed the team to town.
Looking back on the clip, now seen by millions around the world, Sherwood said he wanted to emphasize that Algerians were welcome in Lawrence.
"It just made sense to me to to say that and to say it over and over again," Sherwood said.
Sherwood said the people of Algeria were so grateful for the hospitality Lawrence showed them that they wanted to return the favor.
"That's exactly how they put it, 'Welcome to your second home,'" Sherwood said. "And then by the end of the trip, people were like, 'No, no, no, it's not your second home,' you know, 'welcome to your home.'"
Sherwood said he'll never stop being grateful to the people of Algeria, and he and his wife will certainly return.
"A portion of my heart is in that country and always will be," Sherwood said.
The Lawrence group didn't come home empty-handed. Finkeldei said they received so many gifts in Algeria that each person was given an extra suitcase to bring everything home.

title: High surf washes couple’s engagement ring away minutes after dream proposal
text:
SAN CLEMENTE, Calif. (KCAL/KCBS) - A dream beach proposal in California took an unexpected turn when high surf washed away the couple’s engagement ring.
Jace Harrick proposed to his girlfriend Sunday with a beautiful diamond engagement ring. The picturesque proposal, with the sunset blanketing Calafia State Beach in San Clemente, seemed perfect – until the surf washed onto the shore around the couple.
“Initially, I’m like, ‘OK, this is fine. Let’s lift her up,’” Harrick said. “I didn’t want her to get swept away because we have El Niño. We know that can be a bit aggressive.”
As he picked up his fiancée, Harrick lost his grip on the ring box. The 4-carat ring fell into the knee-high water, and the couple hasn’t seen it since.
Jessica Licon and her family were on the beach that day and said the surf was rough. Her husband heard all the commotion a few feet away, thinking that everyone was celebrating the proposal.
“That’s when I told him, ‘No, the ring is gone. Everyone’s looking for it,’” Licon said. “Everyone was looking for the ring… but nobody found anything.”
A few treasure hunters with metal detectors searched the sand but had no luck.
Harrick plans to replace the ring. He said the silver lining in all of this is the proposal was perfect up to that last moment and that his soon-to-be wife is safe.
“Let’s control what we can control right now, and that’s our attitude,” Harrick said. “I’m just grateful she’s OK. That’s what’s important.”
A diver has offered to come out and search for the lost ring. Harrick plans to offer a reward to anyone who can find it.
