title: From pop stars to poets to politicians, hundreds gathering for joyful tribute to Gloria Steinem
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Luminaries from political figures to pop stars to poets were gathering Wednesday in Manhattan for a joyful and music-filled tribute to Gloria Steinem, the trailblazing activist, prolific author and most visible symbol of American feminism.
“It’s Steinemite!” declared the invitation received by about 1,000 guests, an indication of the buoyant mood that organizers say Steinem, who died in September at 92, had wanted for her memorial.
In a way, the late afternoon celebration promised to mirror the spirit of Steinem’s famed talking circles, which she hosted at her Upper East Side home for more than 50 years: a vibrant mix of people from near and far, reflecting Steinem’s extensive travels and eclectic tastes in art and music.
Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton was expected to be one of the main speakers. There were performances planned from pop star Cyndi Lauper and actor-singer Cynthia Erivo, as well as poetry and choral presentations. Organizers requested that the location not be disclosed ahead of time for security reasons.
“Gloria wanted a true celebration filled with laughter and friends across generations,” said Jill Heller, director of programs at Gloria’s Foundation, which is working to preserve Steinem’s home as a center to further her work. The presenters “reflect how expansive a life Gloria lived but also just the spirit of community, celebration and hopefulness that she wanted for this moment,” Heller said.
Close friend Amy Richards, a chief organizer of the event, said Steinem “definitely wanted people to have a good time. She hoped that new people will meet each other, and there will be laughter.”
Steinem became an activist after an early career as a journalist. She has said she might have remained a journalist had editors been willing to let her write about social issues of importance, like the nascent women’s movement — but they weren’t interested. It was at a meeting where women spoke out about illegal abortions that she decided to change paths.
“That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me,” Steinem told The Associated Press in 2022. “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.”
Steinem went on to co-found Ms. Magazine and the National Women’s Political Caucus. She traveled constantly, to campuses and rallies and protests, despite an early fear of public speaking. And when she was at home in New York, her living room was a constant gathering place, where groups and movements were born as women gathered from across the country and around the globe.
Steinem, a prolific author, died just weeks before the release of her final memoir, “An Unexpected Life.”
“As I write this, I’m both older than I ever imagined I would become and happier than I ever imagined I could be,” she wrote in the introduction. “I’ve been rewarded with friends who are my chosen family. I have trusted friends in other countries, and we strive to be safe and free, and share hopes for a peaceful democracy in the world.”
Steinem added that she planned to live to 100.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first trilateral summit
text:
SHENZHEN, China (Gray DC) - The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China will meet for a trilateral summit for the first time.
President Donald Trump was greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Shenzhen Airport on Wednesday. Trump and Xi will be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for the trilateral summit.
Nuclear arms control is Trump’s top priority for the summit. He wants to secure a deal that would lead the U.S., Russia and China to reduce their nuclear stockpiles.
Russia’s war in Ukraine, which will soon mark its five-year anniversary, could also be on the agenda. Trump has not been able to end the conflict despite repeated efforts.
The U.S.-led war in Iran, which began in late February, could also be discussed. Russia and China are Iran’s closest allies.
Trump confirmed Wednesday that he will hold a separate bilateral meeting with Putin. He has also teased a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un

title: Ann Marie Quinnam Sparks
text:
Ann Marie Quinnam Sparks, 93, passed away on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026 at MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta.
She was born in Damariscotta on Nov. 10, 1932, a daughter of Murray Bradford and Alice Rosalie (Yarborough) Quinnam. Ann graduated from Wiscasset Academy in 1950 and enjoyed seeing classmates every year at the alumni banquet. She was employed at Brown Engine and National Semiconductor, as well as Eagle Pencil in Danbury, Conn.
In 1957, she married Allen W. Gagnon. In 1964, they moved back to Wiscasset with their three children, David, Debbie and Cindy. They welcomed their fourth child, Joe, in Damariscotta in 1965. They owned and operated Gagnon’s Trailer Court for many years. She was employed at Eaton Shoe Co. in Richmond and ran a home daycare. She was employed as a clerk in the Lincoln County Courthouse’s registry of deeds office for 20 years.
In 1983, Ann was diagnosed with Stage 4 non-Hodgkin lymphoma and given six months to live. One year after that diagnosis, she single-handedly purchased a property and created a popular dance hall, Tuxedo Junction, which was her pride and joy for over 25 years. She told her brother Jimmy that Tuxedo Junction was the highlight of her life.
She was a member of St. Philip’s Episcopal Church in Wiscasset, serving on the Altar Guild. She was a ballot clerk for the town of Wiscasset and was an active member of the Wiscasset Female Charitable Society as well as belonging to the Rebekahs.
Ann had a big, generous heart and donated to many charitable organizations. She was a woman of deep faith and quietly supported others who were diagnosed with cancer.
Ann enjoyed dancing, music (especially Elvis Presley), fishing, boating, digging clams, going to the beach, knitting, quilting, and cooking. She especially loved spending time with her family, creating wonderful gatherings with her beloved children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and her brother Jimmy.
She is survived by her son, David Gagnon and his wife Debbie, of Wiscasset; daughter Deborah Gagnon and her partner, Dan Gurney, of Dresden; daughter Cynthia Gagnon-Young and her husband, Barry, of Wiscasset; and son, Joseph Gagnon and his fiance, Catherine Pendergast, of Wiscasset; and one brother, Jimmy Quinnam.
She is also survived by five grandchildren, Cassandra, P.J., and Christopher Fairfield, Ashley Gagnon, and Sara Harvey; and seven great-grandchildren, Bryan Gagnon, Charlotte Bickford, Anthony Monfiletto, Isla Bickford, Wren Fairfield, Emmett Harvey, and Rayelle Fairfield.
She is survived by many cousins, including Pat Lewis, her special cousin, who was like a sister.
She was predeceased by her husbands, Allen W. Gagnon, Elwood Willette, and Michael Sparks.
The family extends heartfelt thanks to the staff and friends at Hodgdon Green Assisted Living in Damariscotta for the compassionate care and love they showed her.
Visiting hours will be from 4-7 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026 at Daigle Funeral Home, at 819 High St. in Bath. A funeral service will be held on Saturday, Nov. 21 at 1 p.m. at St. Andrew’s Episcopal Church, at 11 Glidden St. in Newcastle. Burial will follow at Greenlawn Cemetery in Wiscasset. A gathering of family and friends will be at the Montsweag Restaurant in Woolwich following services.
Memorial contributions may be made to the American Cancer Association, P.O. Box 6704, Hagerstown, MD 21741. Condolences may be made online at daiglefuneralhome.com.

title: DOT Secretary Sean Duffy keeps blaming L3Harris after FAA ground stop, even as cause remains unknown
text:
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy continues to blame a contractor for the events that prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to order a ground stop last week, even though investigators haven’t determined the root cause.
Since aviation was disrupted for more than four hours on Friday, Duffy has been sharply critical of L3Harris, which owns and maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network. A section of old copper wire in Arkansas was being replaced with fiber optic lines before the incident.
Duffy said on “The Morning Meeting” show Wednesday that a contractor failed to identify and isolate the router issue that caused the weekend ground stop quickly enough.
“The monitoring of the network matters,” he said, adding that officials were working on remedying that problem. In the meantime, any new installations of these same routers have been paused, and technicians have disabled the function that was linked to Friday’s outage.
The FAA did not offer any updates Wednesday on the investigation into what happened.
Computer router blamed
This was only the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Officials have said that a Juniper router that was installed as part of the upgrade in El Dorado, Arkansas, suddenly started sending thousands of inquiries out every few seconds and that overwhelmed the older parts of the network.
That led to inconsistent radar and communications signals at 17 of the 22 key air traffic control centers across the country, so the FAA grounded planes.
But FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a different event hosted by The Hill that he understands that his agency is ultimately responsible for what happened even if L3Harris was the one doing the work.
“I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it,” Bedford said. “I wish people would lay off the secretary. He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So, blame me.”
L3Harris hasn’t commented on the ground stop since issuing a statement Saturday pledging to support the FAA’s investigation into what happened, and the company declined to say more on Wednesday.
It remains a mystery why the device that was installed Friday seemed to behave differently from any of the others that have been installed during 68 previous copper-to-fiber optic upgrade projects that have been completed across the FAA’s network.
Congress unlikely to approve funding request
Officials have suggested the router may have been configured incorrectly. But Bedford has said the technician who performed the work was a highly trained Air Force veteran who had completed the same work dozens of times before.
The FAA nearly doubled its funding request to Congress to $50 billion after Friday’s ground stop to pay for the rest of the overhaul of the nation’s air traffic control system. Last year, the agency received $12.5 billion to get started on the project. Bedford said he understands why members of Congress might be having “some indigestion associated with that.”
Several key lawmakers said Tuesday that Congress is unlikely to approve that full amount right now — especially when the FAA hasn’t spent all the money that was approved last year. Only about $10 billion of the $50 billion request would go to air traffic control technology. The rest of the money would go to other projects, including upgrades to runways, airport towers and aging air traffic control centers that were built in the 1960s.
Chris Sununu, who is president of the Airlines for America trade group, praised Bedford for keeping the airlines informed during the ground stop. Sununu said Bedford asked to set up a conference call with all the airline CEOs and operations leaders within about half an hour of the ground stop starting and briefed them on what he knew so far. Several additional calls were held throughout the ground stop.
“To be honest, he stayed on the phone effectively with all the CEOs all night long,” Sununu said. “We did, I think, three or four calls over the period of the next few hours, brought in those operational folks. And so as they learned more, as they understood more of what was happening.”
Sununu said the FAA has a difficult job in trying to overhaul “what is really the most robust telecom system on the planet while you’re using it 24 hours a day and ensuring the safety of everyone who is part of it.” And he said this might not be the last technical problem that happens during the project because the work the FAA is doing is akin to trying to get your iPhone to talk to your flip phone.
“Can we say, ‘oh, you know, this is really the last time we’re going to have a bump like this?’, No, no. Because the technologies we’re replacing and that we’re asking to talk to each other are literally multigenerational,” he said.
____
Associated Press writers David Collins and Sudhin Thanawala contributed to this report.

title: Husband-and-wife coaching duo leads Woodland Dragons teams
text:
BAILEYVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Woodland’s got a husband-and-wife duo as Dragons head coaches.
Carl and Michelle Ripley have been coaching at the school since 2012.
They spoke about being a part of the Baileyville sports community and becoming coaches of sports they played during their high school careers with the Dragons.
“There is about a half hour where by the time he gets home, I’ve already made dinner. I wave, ‘see you later,’ and then I leave. Then, I get home in time for bedtime. It’s lots of communication, scheduling, help with babysitters, late nights, and talking about all our games,” said Michelle Ripley, Woodland volleyball, club boys volleyball, rec K-2 basketball coach.
“When you have someone reaching out and saying, ‘hey, look, these people are doing a lot for the community,’ it’s kind of reassuring that you are making a difference,” said Carl Ripley, Woodland boys soccer, e-sports coach.
Carl just retired as boys soccer coach.
In the past, he has also coached wrestling and Michelle has coached girls basketball.
They have two daughters, Sophia and Avery, and they’re Dragons superfans.

title: ‘I just wanted to challenge myself’: High school junior earns perfect scores on ACT and SAT
text:
KIRKWOOD, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - A high school student in Missouri earned perfect scores while taking the American College Testing and Scholastic Aptitude Test.
Luka Artomov, a Kirkwood High School junior, took the ACT in 2025 and the SAT in 2026, earning perfect scores on both while taking the tests for the first time.
“I was pretty surprised and definitely kind of elated because, you know, it’s something that happens so rarely,” Artomov said.
Artomov said he took both tests to maximize scholarship opportunities.
“Also I just wanted to challenge myself,” he said.
Artomov did the practice tests. He also attributed his success to building on what he learned in the classroom, with the support from teachers and family.
When asked if any questions left him unsure of the answer, Artomov said there were some.
“But I just went with my gut and saw what worked best, and it, you know, turned out to work,” he said.
Outside the classroom, Artomov is involved in the math team and mock trial. He also said history and growing his knowledge are some of his top interests.
School leaders note his impact goes beyond academics.
“He’s always a pleasure to be around. He always has a smile on his face. He’s a great person to engage with,” Kirkwood High School Principal Seth Harrell said. “He’ll always ask how your day is going, and I just think that positive interaction says a lot about his character and who he is as a person.”
Artomov said he plans to major in math and possibly attend law school. He also offered advice to students who would be taking the same tests.
“The number one way to not stress out about something is to come prepared. So definitely study. Review your past mistakes ... but at the same time, be confident in yourself ... trust in yourself and trust that you know what you’re doing,” Artomov said.

title: Cincinnati Zoo gives update on Fiona’s condition
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) - The Cincinnati Zoo gave an update on Fiona’s condition after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat.
The zoo said Fiona, the zoo’s miracle hippo, will have to pass the hat on her own since surgery is not an option. She has undergone tests and been given medicine to ensure she stays hydrated and can pass it safely.
An ultrasound found that there was some bunching of her intestines, indicating she could be passing something through her small intestine, according to the zoo.
The Columbus Zoo assisted with a colonoscopy, but nothing was seen through the nine-foot-long scope, the zoo said in Monday’s update.
At this point, Fiona is receiving 24-hour supportive care and attention until she passes the object.
Her care team said Wednesday they used a vibration plate borrowed from a local horse farm and encouraged Fiona to stand on it several times during the day.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo said in its post.
According to a zoo spokesperson, the hat was tossed into the air in front of Fiona’s habitat and was caught by a ceiling fan. The fan then “catapulted” the hat into the 1-foot opening above the viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident,” the spokesperson told FOX19 NOW.
The zoo’s veterinary team and hippo care staff are watching Fiona around the clock to help her pass the hat safely.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said in a Facebook post.
Until then, Fiona will not make an appearance at the popular Hippo Cove habitat.
“Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.
Officials said they will keep people updated on Fiona’s health.

title: World's largest wildlife crossing lets animals pass over 8 lanes of traffic
text:
World's largest wildlife crossing lets animals pass over 8 lanes of traffic
Touring the world's largest wildlife crossing, Beth Pratt stepped carefully through freshly planted native vegetation and held up her hand for silence.
“Hear that? We're listening to birdsong right now, on top of one of the busiest freeways in the U.S.!” a beaming Pratt, one of the project’s leaders, said excitedly. “That makes my heart glad.”
The warbling was the latest sign that the bridge, spanning U.S. 101 and a feeder road about 35 miles northwest of downtown Los Angeles, is already in use by animals ahead of the official Dec. 2 opening ceremony.
Just two weeks earlier, motion-sensor cameras captured a lone coyote believed to be the first mammal to make the trek safely across. Days after that momentous crossing, three juvenile coyotes were seen on camera playing in the brush beneath the 10-foot sound-dampening walls that line the span.
“They don't care about ribbon cuttings,” laughed Pratt, president of the nonprofit Wildlife Crossing Fund.
About 300,000 cars a day travel that stretch of the 101 in Agoura Hills, a small city surrounded by a patchwork of protected wild land that the new crossing will connect. Fencing along the freeway funnels animals to the crossing.
The bridge, with a landscape that's indistinguishable from surrounding hillsides, stretches 1,250 feet in two sections over the roadways to give animals hemmed in by urban sprawl a safe path to the nearby Santa Monica Mountains and beyond.
It is named the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing for the late philanthropist whose foundation donated $25 million toward the $114 million total budget. The cost ballooned from an initial $92 million, and the money came from donations from 6,000 members of the public, as well as grants from nonprofits and state funds set aside for conservation purposes. Leonardo DiCaprio was one of the earliest donors after a funding drive was launched a decade ago.
Waiting for the cougars
Pratt said for her the real official opening will be when a mountain lion, a species listed as threatened in California, finds its way to the overpass.
The star of the campaign to build the bridge was the cougar — known as P-22 — an LA celebrity in its own right who traveled across freeways and made a home in a huge Los Angeles park. P-22, who was euthanized in 2022 after likely being hit by a car, became a symbol of the shrinking genetic diversity of wild animals that must remain all but trapped by sprawling development or risk becoming roadkill. Thousands attended a memorial service for him.
Scientists tracking mountain lions fitted with GPS collars found over decades that roadways were largely confining animals in mountains that run along the Malibu coast and across the middle of Los Angeles to Griffith Park, where P-22 settled.
During the tour last week, Pratt wore a shirt emblazoned with an image of the beloved cougar. She hopes to eventually erect a statue of P-22 on the side of the new bridge.
Caged by concrete, killed by cars and sickened by rat poison, the isolated pumas risk inbreeding themselves into extinction, scientists and state wildlife officials say. A report just last week from the University of California, Davis, found that at least 780 mountain lions — or 18% of the state’s population — are killed by vehicles each year.
“The story of P-22 was just so compelling,” said Mari Galloway, California program director for the nonprofit Wildlands Network. “We saw the peril in what happened to that particular cat. It was demonstrative of what these mountain lions are facing in this part of the landscape.”
Galloway's group, which was not involved in the Annenberg crossing, hopes the new bridge will spur the construction of many others across California and the nation. The Wildlands Network is working with state transportation officials in the early stages of planning a wildlife bridge for a stretch of highway in the Mojave Desert east of Los Angeles where bighorn sheep roam.
Wildlife crossings — bridges and tunnels — are common in western Europe and Canada. A famous one in Banff National Park in Alberta spans the Trans-Canada Highway and is frequently used by bears, moose and elk.
A large overpass in Colorado over Interstate 25, along with other mitigation efforts including underpasses and fencing, has contributed to a 91% decrease in wildlife collisions, that state's parks and wildlife department announced in September.
Hummingbirds, bees and spiders too
Atop the Annenberg crossing, Anthony Deascentis, a field inspector for the California Department of Transportation, waved Pratt over to some scrub brush. He pointed out an orb-weaver spider, as big as a silver dollar, building an elaborate circular web.
“There's also a good amount of bees enjoying the native plants,” said Deascentis. In addition, he's spotted an oak titmouse, sparrows and hummingbirds — further evidence that wildlife is taking to the new terrain even as crews using heavy machinery continued to fill in the landscape on the bridge's south side.
Jeff Sikich, a biologist for the National Park Service who collars and tracks cougars and other wild animals, said the next step will be to implant “biologgers” that will allow scientists to also monitor physiological data like heart rate, body temperature and activity levels. With that information, they'll be able to tell if the animals are stressed while using the wildlife bridge, or “if they're relaxed up there.”
Sikich said in recent weeks scientists have detected multiple mammals in the hills near the new span, including bobcats, deer, gray foxes and a female mountain lion with two kittens.
He said they're “sniffing around,” hopefully getting ready to make the crossing.

title: Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
text:
Cambridge Dictionary chooses 'human' as word of the year in response to AI fears
Fears of artificial intelligence inspired the Cambridge Dictionary to flip back to the 15th century for the word that best captures the 2026 cultural zeitgeist.
Video above: “Tremendous self-policing”: Trump unveils voluntary AI safety accord with tech leaders
“Human,” the dictionary's word of the year, is not just a throwback but also a backlash of sorts that reflects the debate over how AI has blurred the lines between machines and people.
“AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children."
The adjective derived from the Latin “humanus” and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as “having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines.”
Dictionaries typically choose a novel word — sometimes slang that has crossed into the mainstream — or an existing word that has taken on a new meaning.
Artificial intelligence has factored heavily in Word of the Year distinctions across several dictionaries in recent years.
“AI” itself was chosen by Collins Dictionary in 2023 — a year when Cambridge picked “hallucinate,” in reference to the tendency of AI to fabricate information. Merriam-Webster last year named “slop” its word of the year for low quality content produced by AI while Collins went with “vibe coding” for the AI-assisted software development method.
“AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has promoted the smart use of AI, said in a comment on the Cambridge Dictionary selection. "The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”
Other word contenders for 2026 included “agent,” for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and “analogue” for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology.

title: Xi says Asia-Pacific needs open trade and Putin condemns sanctions as Trump arrives in China
text:
Xi says Asia-Pacific needs open trade and Putin condemns sanctions as Trump arrives in China
The Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic, Chinese President Xi Jinping told business executives gathered Wednesday in the southern Chinese technology and financial hub of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
U.S. President Donald Trump arrived Wednesday for the APEC leaders’ summit, traveling from the Philippines, where he attended an annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
Trump's “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone. U.S. limits on Chinese access to leading-edge American technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.
Related video:
Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticizing the U.S. shift toward protecting its own markets.
APEC summit venue showcases China's central role in trade
The summit is showcasing Shenzhen, which China has transformed in the past four decades from a fishing village into a skyscraper-studded center for export manufacturing and technology. China's ascent as the second-largest economy hinged on global investments and access to world markets as global manufacturers shifted factories overseas to tap into cheaper labor and faster-growing markets.
“China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further. We will carry out reform in challenging areas such as rules, regulation, and standards,” Xi told the CEO summit, reiterating Beijing's pledges to improve conditions for global investors.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
Xi's speech highlighted China's aim to lead global industrial transformation, said George Chen, partner and chair of Digital Practice at The Asia Group.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia or the U.S. directly.
Pressures lie behind the pomp and positivity over open trade
Xi faces pressure at home from slowing growth as retail spending and investment have dragged as China endures a prolonged property market slump. The economy is still growing at a rate of more than 4%, but that's mainly due to surging exports that are provoking a backlash among many of China's trading partners. China's trade surplus for this year is on track to exceed $1 trillion for a second year in a row.
Still, Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may lead to an extension of the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.
Friction with Washington over higher U.S. tariffs and other trade barriers is leading to realignments among other trading partners. On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Xi and they agreed to cut tariffs on each other’s goods. Carney has cultivated tighter economic ties with China and the European Union in response to strains in Canada’s relationship with Trump.
“Canada is undergoing a transformation of our own. We are turning global uncertainty into national opportunity in a more dangerous and divided world,” Carney told the CEO summit. "Canada is choosing a path towards a stronger, more prosperous, more resilient future.”
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told the executives of top Chinese and multinational companies that bigger economies should recognize that fair and dynamic growth benefits all.
“Countries cannot impose their position, their own peculiar circumstances, to countries to decide," Anwar said. "They must accept that countries must emerge, focus on trade and investments, because that would ultimately benefit their people.”
Putin takes aim at sanctions, says Asia-Pacific is vital for Russia
Russian President Vladimir Putin took aim at “instruments of economic dominance,” such as the sanctions imposed following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
“Sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions” have “outlived their usefulness and have largely lost their intimidating effect," Putin told the CEO summit in his first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders meeting since 2017.
He highlighted his country's desire to cultivate closer economic ties with the Asia-Pacific, saying the region accounts for more than half of its total trade.
Russia has submitted a bid to chair APEC in 2035, Putin said.
The 21 APEC economies account for 60% of global economic activity, half of global trade and 40% of humanity. The leaders will meet behind closed doors on Thursday, while holding other meetings on the event's sidelines. That will include a “trilateral” encounter between Trump, Putin and Xi, the first such summit between those three global powers.
APEC does not take binding decisions, but over 37 years it has served as a forum for building a consensus on cooperation and more open trade.
“The decisions we, and particularly you take today, individually and collectively, will determine whether the APEC region and the international community continue to be a source of dynamism, stability and opportunity in an increasingly uncertain world," Anwar said.
___
Associated Press writer Kanis Leung in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

title: Mom accused of smothering baby during FaceTime call with child’s father out of spite, police say
text:
SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC/Gray News) - A Georgia mother is accused of smothering her 9-month-old son with a blanket during a FaceTime call out of spite toward the child’s father, according to authorities.
Ja’Shay Jackson, 24, was charged with aggravated assault involving family violence and first-degree cruelty to children.
Savannah police said an Aug. 15 report described videos that allegedly showed Jackson hitting her son and using a blanket to smother him while he cried. The report said she acted out of spite toward the child’s father.
One video shows the inside of a vehicle. No people are visible, but a woman can be heard saying something about not feeding or changing the child, according to authorities.
A second video shows a FaceTime call that the child’s father recorded on another phone, authorities said. Jackson’s face can be seen in the recording.
“You see Miss Jackson primarily in the video,” Savannah police Detective Ian Kite testified. “And then you hear a baby cry multiple times throughout the video. You hear the child’s cry instantly get cut off, and then you hear muffled cries.”
Kite said it happened two or three times. He testified that Jackson could be heard telling the child to “shut up” in a mocking tone.
Jackson was arrested in September, and her case has been moving through the court system since.
The baby is alive and is now in the care of the mother of Jackson’s ex-boyfriend. Kite said he did not know whether the child was taken to a hospital beyond a routine checkup.
The court heard that a Division of Family and Children Services plan was in place before Jackson’s arrest, allowing her only supervised visits with the child. Jackson is also expected to enroll in GED classes and is receiving counseling and taking parenting classes, the court heard.

title: Democrats flipped 9 US Senate seats — the most in almost 70 years
text:
Democrats flipped 9 US Senate seats — the most in almost 70 years
Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s competitive U.S. Senate race has flipped a ninth Republican-held seat to the Democrats, giving Peltola’s party its biggest midterm gain in nearly 70 years.
Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term. That year, Democrats wrested away 13 Republican-held seats and also won both of Alaska’s newly created seats, for a total gain of 15 seats.
Peltola’s victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the Senate in 16 years. Democrats held 58 Senate seats in the waning days of the 111th Congress, which concluded on Jan. 3, 2011.
Related video: Republicans, Democrats select next leaders for new Congress
“Fifty-six seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in statement posted on social media. "Most people didn’t think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle.”
Even without Alaska, Democrats would have secured their largest majority since January 2015, when Republicans took control after flipping nine Democratic seats in the 2014 midterms during President Barack Obama’s second term.
Democrat Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate victory Wednesday in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race gave his party its eighth Republican-held seat. That win delivered Democrats their most midterm pickups since President Ronald Reagan’s second midterm election 40 years ago.
Democrats also reclaimed the House, picking up 42 seats as of Tuesday. The gains continued a historical trend of midterm losses for the president’s party.
The Senate has tended to be less susceptible to the midterm effect than the House. In seven of the last 16 midterms prior to 2026, the president’s party either held its ground or gained seats in the Senate, though all but one of those midterms occurred in the president’s first term. A president’s second midterm tends to be more punishing.
By comparison, the president’s party had gained House seats in only two midterms since the end of World War II.

title: Uber passenger charged with attempted murder allegedly told driver he didn’t like his name
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — An Uber passenger was charged Tuesday with attempted murder in a weekend attack near Minneapolis on a Somali American driver who was strangled with a seatbelt, run over by his own car and left in a ditch, authorities said.
Mohamed Yusuf, 51, is fighting for his life, has broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding from the attack, which occurred after the passenger allegedly told Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, according to court documents.
Samit Apurva Patel, 25, was charged with attempted second-degree murder and carjacking, but there wasn’t enough evidence to prove the attack was motivated by bias, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty. She said that decision “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now.”
An attorney representing Patel at his first court appearance Tuesday declined comment. A person who answered a phone number associated with Patel’s address said, “No comment,” before hanging up.
Dave Risk, a defense attorney in Minneapolis not connected to the case, said that to prove bias, prosecutors would have had to show that Patel intentionally targeted Yusuf because of a protected characteristic like race or religion.
In this situation, the pair likely met randomly, Risk said, adding that would make it tough for prosecutors to show Patel was motivated by bias.
Yusuf’s son Mustafa Osman said his father has been through five surgeries and is not doing well. He said Yusuf has driven taxis and Ubers for years and is known for his empathy and skill at de-escalating tense situations, making the attack especially shocking.
“We don’t have words to describe how bad it’s been. We haven’t really processed everything yet. It’s an emotional roller coaster,” he told The Associated Press.
The violence early Saturday in the Minneapolis suburb of Hopkins has increased fear among the Somali community after years of targeted rhetoric, including from President Donald Trump. Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S., with many concentrated in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The overwhelming majority are American citizens.
Yusuf’s brother says he heard him scream
According to court documents, Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger near a Minneapolis bar just before 1 a.m. Saturday. The drop-off location was in the nearby suburb of Hopkins.
Yusuf’s brother says he heard the passenger tell Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, the court documents say. He later heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and run over by the car, according to the filings.
Moriarty said the motive remains unknown but said, “There were some serious issues going on with this gentleman at the time he went home that so alarmed his parents that they called 911.”
She said she did not believe there was a recording of the call between Yusuf and his brother, and there was a camera in Yusuf’s car but it was not on.
Call for a wellness check led authorities to Patel
Patel’s parents called for a wellness check after Patel arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior,” according to the court filings. When officers arrived, they found Yusuf’s car in the driveway with the exterior and driver’s seatbelt damaged, according to the filings. Dirt, burs and a shoe were found in the driver’s side interior, and the phone call with Yusuf’s brother was still active through the car’s system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was,” the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Yusuf is known for his empathy and ability to de-escalate
Osman, 27, said he was shocked when he got a frantic call from his uncle saying something had happened to his dad.
Osman, the oldest of Yusuf’s five children, described his father as empathetic and good at de-escalation. He said his father has dealt with aggravated or aggressive passengers during his many years driving.
“Anytime he’s in trouble, he’s the one that will calm things down, whether it’s between the family or if it’s while he’s at work,” he said.
Yusuf came to the U.S. in 1993 and spent some time working as a taxi driver in Chicago, said Osman. The family lived in Minnesota, which was where Osman was raised, and had moved back in 2018.
Dozens of community members visit hospital
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.
Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, said dozens of community members have been stopping by the hospital to show support for Yusuf.
“We feel as a community we’re under threat, constantly,” Hussein said. “Our community has, unfortunately, been feeling the brunt end of a disinformation and demonization campaign that has been going on now, and it’s coming from every corner.”
The Trump administration’s largest immigration enforcement effort, Operation Metro Surge, targeted the Twin Cities. Leading up to that operation, Trump said immigrants from the war-torn East African country have “caused a lot of trouble,” and he wants them to leave. He also referred to Somali immigrants in the U.S. as “garbage.”
Muhiyadin Yusuf, who knows Mohamed Yusuf but is not related to him, has been driving for ride-hailing apps in the Twin Cities for more than a decade. He said he’s felt unsafe in general because of comments from Trump and other politicians targeting Somalis. But since Saturday, he’s reduced his nighttime driving hours and added a third camera to his car. Some friends of his have stopped driving altogether.
“As a Muslim, as an immigrant, as a driver and as a Somali community, it affects me,” he said. “I’m scared now, more than before.”
___
Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press/Report for America reporter Laura Turbay contributed from Little Rock, Arkansas.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: Want to discuss 'Grand Theft Auto VI' with gaming friends? Here's a primer as the new version drops
text:
Have a gamer in your life or work? Wave goodbye for awhile — and get literate on “GTA VI.”
That’s “Grand Theft Auto VI,” the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world gaming world that’s skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York, Los Angeles and is returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City.
The first new “GTA” game in 13 years — so long that the interval became a punchline — has the power to make millions of people vanish from their real lives ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States. With a massive rollout that includes huge billboards, a takeover of an NBA game and a soundtrack stacked with Grammy winners, “GTA VI” will affect the lives of tens of millions, including many nongamers.
Even for those who never pick up a controller, YouTube, memes and viral clips will extend the game’s reach, its edgy content and its viral catchphrases — the ever-present “wasted,” for one — far beyond those planning midnight playing sessions or time off work.
“It’s not just relationships on the line,” notes a mock boilerplate for a leave agreement to present to HR. “Every console generation has one game that erases its players from normal life for a while, and Grand Theft Auto VI is shaping up to do it at a scale nobody has really tested.”
Now version VI is arriving, and here we go again: The game started its march across the globe Thursday at midnight local time, kicking off in New Zealand and leaving North American gamers panting in anticipation.
It’s an immersive narrative that carries players away
These days it’s part of the culture, but the arrival of a “Grand Theft Auto” game didn’t always capture such mainstream attention and adulation. Earlier editions drew pointed criticism for their violence — against police, women and innocent bystanders — and emphasis on casual sex, including with prostitutes.
Take-Two Interactive, the studio behind the “GTA” juggernaut, has layered its fictional worlds with social satire. One character in “GTA V,” for instance, prompted a lawsuit from actor Lindsay Lohan over perceived similarities. A New York court tossed the case.
Experts note that “GTA” games tend to have a long life span, with the 13-year hiatus this time giving plenty of time for “GTA” to seep into culture through social videos and memes. Expect an explosion of “GTA VI” videos in the days ahead as people discover new aspects of it.
The story of “GTA VI” is centered on a couple, and early reviews for the game have noted that it has a depth of relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups and bank robberies.
“It’s an amazing piece of entertainment, but also culturally, just the way it brings a simulated world to life. And how they use music, and just the world that they build is really incredible. Again, it’s made by 4,700 people who worked for a decade to build this thing, so it is a monumental game in terms of the scale and scope of what it is,” said gaming journalist Geoff Keighley.
The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. It will be awhile before “GTA VI” sales are available.
It focuses on a couple trying to succeed at crime
The main characters of the open-world game are a couple, Lucia and Jason, who are trying to improve their circumstances through crime.
Lucia has recently been released from prison while Jason, a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the game’s “Leonida Keys,” is looking for a different path. The game feels especially personal to Florida residents.
Early reviews of “GTA VI” praise its level of detail and choices that allow players to resolve certain some interactions without violence and for the way players have to carefully approach Jason and Lucia’s relationship.
Also, some players think it’s fun just to “drive” around the game’s virtual world. (Just more carefully in this edition, the New York Times notes in its review.)
You can view the trailers for the new version of “GTA VI” here.
It got to New Zealanders first — and the reviews are good
Adam Simmons, 50, fired up the game at midnight in New Zealand. He kept it on low volume to avoid waking his wife and daughters. Simmons, a director of photography who moved to New Zealand just five months ago from Portland, Oregon, was impressed.
“You really feel like you are in a world,” he said. “The places and how they’re put together feel right.”
He played for about an hour before heading to bed. Work is a priority, though he jokingly expects to be distracted by Vice City in the days ahead. “I have my own company that I have to run,” he said. “So I’m the boss, but also I’m just going to lose sales because a video game came out.”
It has gamers rearranging their lives to play, and some employers are OK with that
Some organizations have been planning for months how to accommodate the intense interest to play the game on launch day.
At least one U.S. Army unit offered a reenlistment bonus that included four days to play “GTA VI” at launch. Logitech, the maker of keyboards, mice and gaming peripherals, announced it was giving its 7,000 employees a paid day off to play games — “GTA” or any one of their choosing.
One German educational institution is offering a paid three-day course for people to play the game and apply what they’ve learned to community-building, collaboration and storytelling lessons.
Its music will probably reach your ears even if you don’t play
One of the many ways the new “Grand Theft Auto” is permeating culture is through music.
Music has long been woven into the game’s experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.
For “GTA VI,” Rockstar Games commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing.
A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
A music festival featuring “GTA VI” artists is planned for Miami this weekend, and some of the music is being played on SiriusXM stations.
That means the game’s music could soon be a part of people’s real-world drives around town. Sometimes, it seems, life does imitate art.
___
Kellman reported from London. Associated Press Entertainment Writer Jonathan Landrum Jr. contributed to this report from Los Angeles.

title: CMP customers to pay more for supply after regulators set 2027 rates

Central Maine Power customers to pay more for supply after regulators set 2027 rates
For an average residential customer using about 550 kilowatt-hours a month, that will add about $5 to the monthly bill.
Central Maine Power customers to pay more for supply after regulators set 2027 rates
For an average residential customer using about 550 kilowatt-hours a month, that will add about $5 to the monthly bill.
Central Maine Power customers who receive the default Standard Offer electricity supply will pay more beginning Jan. 1, 2027, the Maine Public Utilities Commission announced Tuesday.
The rate for residential and small business customers will rise from 12.72 cents to 13.63 cents per kilowatt-hour.
For an average residential customer using about 550 kilowatt-hours a month, that will add about $5 to the monthly bill.
The Standard Offer is the default supply option for customers who have not chosen a competitive electricity supplier.
CMP bills customers for the supply but does not set its rate; the commission sets it through a competitive bidding process.
Supply is separate from delivery, which covers the system that brings electricity to homes and businesses.
In a separate case, CMP is seeking a $189 million increase in distribution rates.
The commission estimates the proposed increase could add $11.06 a month to the average residential customer’s bill if approved.
The case remains under review, and the proposed change would affect delivery charges.

title: The 2026 Country Music Association Awards are here with Taylor Swift performing: How to watch
text:
(AP) - It didn’t take a crystal ball to see: The 2026 Country Music Association Awards were always going to be all about Ella Langley.
The Alabama-born-and-raised singer was named entertainer of the year during Wednesday’s event — beating the host of the evening and last year’s winner Lainey Wilson, as well as Cody Johnson, Luke Combs and Chris Stapleton, for the top prize.
“At this point, I’m sick of me,” she started her acceptance speech with a joke, after having spent so much of the show on stage. “I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life.” Wilson emerged with a bedazzled broom because, “I told you, you was going to sweep, girl!” she said as she embraced Langley.
It really was Langley’s night from the jump. The 60th annual CMA Awards, broadcast live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, started and ended with her. Langley accepted the first award of the night, single of the year, for her history-making “Choosin’ Texas.”
Competition was fierce: Taylor Swift’s song for the “Toy Story 5” film, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” was also nominated in the category, as were Langley’s own “Be Her,” Wilson’s “Somewhere Over Laredo” and Johnson’s “The Fall.”
And then Langley was back on stage almost immediately afterward — to perform her joyous “Loving Life Again” with a string quartet and to pick up another award, when “Choosin’ Texas” was named song of the year.
“This song is the gift that keeps on giving,” she said in her speech.
She also won female vocalist as well as album of the year, the latter for her thrilling, old-soul country “Dandelion.”
“My lip is already quivering,” she said. “I’m at a loss for words.”
The return of Taylor Swift and a tribute to Dolly Parton
Swift was in the building. The pop powerhouse lit up the CMA Awards by performing “I Knew It, I Knew You” with a bit of her 2006 country hit “Our Song” mixed in for good measure.
She began her set in the back halls of the arena before hitting the stage — joined by Keith Urban on banjo, no less — as if no time had passed.
But it’s been 13 years since Swift last performed at the CMA Awards, a decade after her last appearance there and 17 years after being named the youngest entertainer of the year in the show’s history.
Consider it a treat in a night full of them. The show began with a powerful tribute to the larger-than-life Dolly Parton. The American icon died in August at age 80, and her legacy will be felt for many decades to come.
Host Wilson got the celebration started, duetting Parton’s “I Will Always Love You” with the legendary singer-songwriter Vince Gill.
Then she was joined by singer Brad Paisley in a funny opening monologue where the pair sang modern parodies of famous country songs: Loretta Lynn’s “Coal Miner’s Daughter” became “Data Miner’s Daughter,” and Willie Nelson’s “Always On My Mind” was transformed into “Always On My Phone.”
No shortage of awards and performances here
A standout set arrived early: Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert duetted “Horses & Divorces” — a song from Musgraves’ latest album, “Middle of Nowhere,” that doubles as a delicious resolution from the pair of former frenemies — with its norteño accordion and shout-along lyrics. The stage was set to look like an ’80s beauty parlor, recalling one of Parton’s most famous acting roles: the 1989 film “Steel Magnolias.”
Tim McGraw brought it back to the ’90s, singing “Don’t Take the Girl.” Megan Moroney slowed things down with her big-hearted ballad “Beautiful Things.” Tucker Wetmore was joined by a brass band for a bit of his single “Who Told You That” before launching into some of Hank Williams Jr.’s 1984 hit “All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight.”
Combs tackled his song “Miss You Here.” Lambert and Langley brought some country-disco with “Snakeskin Boots.” Mumford & Sons teamed up with Stapleton for “Here.”
Later, Stapleton would hop back on stage to join Stephen Wilson Jr. — and to be awarded male vocalist of the year, for a ninth time in his career.
Lainey Wilson performed a brand new one, the full-throated “Just A Woman.”
It was a bit of a theme: The modern traditionalist Zach Top also debuted a new track, the bluegrass-y “Moonshine.” Before he left the stage, Dierks Bentley joined in for a tribute to the late John Anderson. They sang his 1983 single “Swingin’.”
Best new artist went to Stephen Wilson Jr.; vocal group went for a second year in a row to the Red Clay Strays, who also performed their song “Revival.”
Brooks & Dunn took home vocal duo for the 17th time.
“I love to hear myself talk, and I’ve actually run out of things to say,” Kix Brooks said in his acceptance speech. “Thanks for making us famous.”
“Follow the yellow brick road,” added Ronnie Dunn.
Later in the night, they received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award. Halestorm, Marcus King, Brothers Osborne, Hardy and Luke Bryan paid tribute to the legendary country music duo, covering some of their biggest hits: “Boot Scootin’ Boogie,” “Rock My World (Little Country Girl),” “Hard Workin’ Man,” “Hillbilly Deluxe” and “Play Something Country.”
Prizes are nominated and voted on by members of the Country Music Association, which includes music executives, artists, publicists, songwriters and other industry professionals.

title: Penobscot County commissioners approve $41.6M budget
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Penobscot County commissioners approved a 2027 budget Wednesday that will raise the county tax by 23.36%, over objections from town officials and residents who said their communities can’t absorb another big hike.
Commissioners David Marshall and Andre Cushing voted for the budget, ending a contentious monthlong process in which commissioners, residents and local leaders sparred over what to keep and what to cut.
The budget fully funds the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor, which has drained roughly $11 million from the county’s reserve accounts since 2021, and adds three employees. The hit will vary by community, with some towns’ share of the county tax rising by as much as roughly 60%, as in Clifton.
Commissioner Dan Tremble voted against the budget, as he did at the commissioners’ first budget vote on Oct. 23. The budget was always going to grow because most costs have risen, he said, but commissioners could have cut more to keep tax rates down.
“There’s no pain felt in this budget. The only pain is felt by [taxpayers],” Tremble said.
Several speakers from around the county echoed his concerns. Town managers from Veazie, Carmel and Bradley, along with elected officials from Bangor, Brewer, Hampden and Bradley, said county spending needs closer scrutiny next year so taxpayers don’t face a double-digit hike for a third straight year. Residents will struggle to pay their taxes, and some towns will have to cut their budgets to stay affordable, they said.
“There are limits to what our taxpayers can afford,” Veazie Town Manager Mark Leonard said.
While affordability dominated the hearing, eight speakers asked commissioners to put money back into the budget: $100,000 for the University of Maine Cooperative Extension in Penobscot County. The program brings UMaine research and education to residents and has used county money to teach gardening and get fresh produce to food pantries across the county, said Kerry Chasteen, executive director of extension operations.
Tremble moved to restore the funding, but the motion died for lack of a second from Marshall or Cushing.
Before voting on the budget, Marshall and Cushing said the county provides important services but can do more to be fiscally responsible. County officials need to secure more state money for jail operations, switch from a calendar year to a fiscal year, and push for a new jail, they said. If those changes are made, tax rates should go down, they said.
On Nov. 3, Penobscot County voters narrowly rejected moving the county jail out of Bangor.
Commissioners did not comment Wednesday on the referendum results or the jail’s future, but Marshall said the county has mapped out a five-year plan he is confident in.
“The budget we have today, in my opinion, is adequate to stop the county from hemorrhaging its funds to stabilize it and allow us to regroup,” Marshall said. “We know what we have to do.”

title: Missing midcoast Maine hunter was a homicide victim, police say
text:
A midcoast Maine man who disappeared 51 years ago was killed.
Ludger Belanger, 25, was last seen on the morning of Nov. 25, 1975, when his brother and wife dropped him off to go hunting in the woods near his home on Route 105 in the Knox County town of Washington, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Belanger, who had three daughters, told his wife he’d be home in an hour, but he was never seen alive again. He had a .30-30 rifle with him.
Police believe Belanger shot a deer and hauled it out to the road, where he was picked up, according to his missing person profile.
Turcotte said Wednesday morning that investigators determined Belanger wasn’t merely a missing person but a homicide victim.
Detectives identified a suspect in Belanger’s death but that person also is dead, meaning prosecution isn’t possible.
His case remains open as authorities continue to look for his body.

title: Sen. Grohoski, Sen.-elect Warren announce plan for regulating data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ELLSWORTH — On Nov. 12, Sen. Nicole Grohoski (D-Ellsworth) and Rep. Sophie Warren (D-Scarborough) announced a plan to regulate data centers that they will put forward in the 133rd Maine Legislature, which will be sworn in on Dec. 2.
In the 132nd Legislature, both Grohoski and Warren supported LD 307, which would have implemented a temporary statewide moratorium on the development of data centers with electricity loads larger than 20 megawatts and created the Maine Data Center Coordination Council. That bill was vetoed by Gov. Janet Mills. Without a statewide moratorium in place, many municipalities — including Wells, North Berwick, Brownfield, Eliot, Peru, Freedom, Sabattus and Wiscasset this month — have enacted their own protections.

title: Philippine president has Jollibee fried chicken delivered to Trump for a late-night snack
text:
Philippine president has Jollibee fried chicken delivered to Trump for a late-night snack
Call it Jollibee diplomacy.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. told President Donald Trump on Wednesday that he arranged a delivery of Jollibee fried chicken as a late-night snack for the American president and his delegation so he could have a “taste of Manila” during his short stay in the capital city.
Jollibee is the Philippines’ biggest homegrown fast-food chain and it has emerged as one of the country’s strongest global brands, a cultural touchstone and a feature of regional diplomacy.
Related video:
The American president arrived in Manila on Tuesday evening for talks with Asia-Pacific allies. By Wednesday afternoon, after a meeting and lunch with Marcos at the presidential palace, Trump had landed in Shenzhen, China, to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and participate in a historic three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Marcos said his gift of fried chicken was intended as a pick-me-up of sorts for a hard-working president. And he sounded like Trump by boasting that Jollibee was more popular than one of the most recognized fast-food fried chicken chains in the United States.
“Jollibee … is a very, very popular chain. And one of their main products is fried chicken. And we are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity,” Marcos said.
Upon hearing the claim, Trump said, “Oh wow. Fantastic.”
“So we thought that will give you a taste of Manila,” Marcos continued. "And, I think, I hope some of your staff was also able to partake.
“You have been working very hard, Mr. President, so just think of it as providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do that you have done and continue to do, and that is in front of you,” he added.
Trump, who is widely known to enjoy McDonald's hamburger fare, did not say if he had tried the Filipino fried chicken. The White House did not respond to an emailed request for comment.
Jollibee is the largest Filipino hamburger chain in the island nation, becoming one of the fastest-growing restaurant chains in the world with outlets across Asia and the United States after starting as a small snack house in the 1970s.
Many of its offerings, like burgers, fries and “Chickenjoy” fried chicken drumsticks, are familiar to fast-food lovers the world over. Other menu items have a distinctly Filipino flavor. The sweet-sauce spaghetti is a beloved restaurant item for fans — and an acquired taste for many others.
The chain, famous for its red, white and yellow bee logo, traces its origins to a Manila ice cream business in the 1970s that quickly pivoted to serving hot food.
It now boasts more than 1,600 branches in 17 countries. Many of its international stores can be found in places with large populations of Filipino migrant workers, such as Hong Kong, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The company has expanded rapidly in North America. It says it now has more than 85 stores open or coming soon in the United States, many of them in California.
The Trump meal wasn’t the first time Jollibee fare was used for diplomacy.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visited a Jollibee restaurant on Sunday in Manila, where he was attending the annual summit of leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Jollibee is opening dozens of restaurants in Australia.
“Jollibee will be a source of pride for Australians of Filipino backgrounds,” Albanese said during the visit. More than 400,000 Australians trace their heritage to the Philippines.
In July, Marcos and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney posed with the crew and bee mascot at a Jollibee branch in Vancouver.
Marcos’ comment about Jollibee's popularity surpassing that of KFC appeared to refer to Jollibee’s claim that it has the No. 1 fried chicken in America. That seems to be a reference to a series of USA Today “readers’ choice” awards rather than Jollibee sales, which are dwarfed by larger American fast-food chains.
—-
Superville reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Adam Schreck in Bangkok contributed to this report.
