title: Thanksgiving travelers could face highest gas prices on record, according to AAA
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Thanksgiving travelers could face highest gas prices on record, according to AAA
Thanksgiving travel is expected to decrease by 200,000 travelers nationwide this year as drivers in New England could face the highest gas prices on record, AAA reports.
Thanksgiving travelers could face highest gas prices on record, according to AAA
Thanksgiving travel is expected to decrease by 200,000 travelers nationwide this year as drivers in New England could face the highest gas prices on record, AAA reports.
Thanksgiving travel is expected to dip slightly compared with last year, as drivers in New England could face the highest gas prices on record.
According to AAA, more than 3.6 million New England residents are expected to travel 50 miles or more from home during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period, a .1% decline from last year.
Nationally, 81.5 million Americans will travel for Thanksgiving this year, just below last year's record-setting total of 81.6 million travelers.
Driving remains the most common way to travel: AAA expects 3.1 million New Englanders and 72.9 million people nationwide to go by car.
AAA forecasts 403,000 New England residents will fly, while 63,000 will travel by bus, train or cruise. Nationally, 5.9 million people are expected to fly and 2.6 million to use other forms of transportation.
"Thanksgiving is one of the busiest travel periods of the year because spending time with family and friends is a priority for so many people," said Dan Goodman, manager of public affairs and traffic safety for AAA Northern New England. "Whether you're heading across town or across the region, motorists should be prepared for heavier traffic, allow extra travel time, and make sure their vehicles are ready before leaving home."
AAA predicts traffic is likely to be heaviest Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons before Thanksgiving, and Sunday and Monday as travelers return. Travel experts recommend leaving earlier in the day when possible and checking tire pressure, battery condition, fluid levels and windshield wipers before driving.
Last year, AAA responded to more than 500,000 roadside assistance calls nationwide during the holiday period, including calls for dead batteries, flat tires, lockouts, fuel delivery and towing.
Potentially record-setting gas prices for Thanksgiving
As of Nov. 18, the average price for regular gas was $3.97 in Maine, $3.92 in New Hampshire and $4.06 in Vermont, according to figures provided by AAA. Those prices were lower than a week earlier but higher than a year ago. Maine's average price for a gallon of regular gas a year ago was $3.03.
AAA says Thanksgiving Day gas prices could reach a record and that this year's projected decrease of 200,000 travelers is due in part to higher travel costs.
The national average on Thanksgiving Day has never been above $4 per gallon.
The Thanksgiving travel period runs from Nov. 24 through Nov. 30.

title: Off-duty firefighter saves boy from drowning is honored for heroism in Florida
text:
Off-duty firefighter saves boy from drowning is honored for heroism in Florida
Firefighter Brandon Catron was recognized for saving a young boy from drowning while off duty, forming a lasting bond with the family he helped.
Off-duty firefighter saves boy from drowning is honored for heroism in Florida
Firefighter Brandon Catron was recognized for saving a young boy from drowning while off duty, forming a lasting bond with the family he helped.
For firefighter Brandon Catron, the call to save a life came unexpectedly while he was off duty last November.
Nathan Goulart’s mother and sister vividly recall the terrifying day when Nathan, now 21 months old, was found unconscious in their pool.
"I just remember running out and, like, being so nervous and being so scared, seeing Nathan unconscious in the pool ... having to, like, dive headfirst," said Sophia Gulya, Nathan’s sister.
Nathan had slipped into the pool on the morning of Nov. 24, 2025. Sophia jumped into the pool to save Nathan, but Catron, who was next door cleaning a neighbor’s pool, heard the frantic cries for help and rushed over to provide critical, life-saving care.
"I have a 10-year-old, an 8-year-old, a 6-year-old, and a 2-year-old. And so knowing that they had children and knowing that this little boy was the exact same age as our youngest really hit home," said Catron, who works for the North Collier Fire Control and Rescue District.
Today, Catron is seeing the impact of his actions firsthand. He reunited with Nathan and his family, bringing the story full circle. The firefighter who ran toward a family’s worst nightmare now stands face-to-face with the boy he helped save.
Catron was honored as one of five recipients of the Greater Naples Chamber’s 2026 Distinguished Public Service Awards. The annual awards recognize first responders who go above and beyond to protect and serve Collier County.
The chamber emphasized that these awards are about recognizing individuals whose actions make a lasting difference in the community.
Now, the Goulart and Catron families share a brighter way to remember the month of November. Nathan and Catron’s son have become friends, and Brandon is now considered part of the Goulart family.
"It was a gift for us to have Brandon, you know, a firefighter, right there for us, with us," said Maiza Goulart, Nathan’s mother.
"They have a beautiful, awesome family. They're doing a great job. Their kids are very well-behaved. I love them dearly and hope they feel the same way," Catron said.
For Catron, the recognition is about more than an award. It’s a chance to reunite with a family whose lives he helped change forever and a toddler who is here today because he didn’t hesitate to help.
"I would just encourage everybody to act immediately. Don't sit there and wait for somebody else to do it, because somebody else may not step in," Catron said.

title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
text:
After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
After a 13-year wait, “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun its global rollout, sending players back to Vice City and kicking off one of the most anticipated entertainment launches in years.
Players in New Zealand were among the first to enter Rockstar Games’ sprawling Florida-inspired world as midnight Thursday arrived, hours before the game becomes available across the United States.
Video above: Miami prepares for new GTA release
Internet providers there had prepared for a massive surge in downloads. Chorus New Zealand expected about 35 petabytes — 35 million gigabytes — of additional traffic across its network as players downloaded the massive game.
“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, the company’s network strategy manager. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”
In Wellington, Adam Simmons launched the game from his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low so he wouldn’t wake his wife and daughters.
“The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep,” he said after about half an hour of play.
Shares of Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, rose more than 8% Wednesday as the rollout continued.
In the Dallas area, Bryan Banuelos, a mobile auto detailer, told customers he wouldn't be taking calls Thursday so he could focus on “GTA VI.” His social media post actually drove some business beforehand, with customers trying to get their cars detailed before he disappeared into Vice City.
“Tomorrow will be the beginning of a new era for the gamers that like GTA,” Banuelos said.
Game returns to Vice City after 13 years
The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.
Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.
At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.
Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.
Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.
Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.
Miami embraces its fictional alter ego
Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.
Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.
The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.
Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.
In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.
Years of hype arrive at launch day
Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.
The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.
“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.
The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.
Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.
“Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album,” a 34-track collection of original songs tied to the game, is scheduled for release Friday.
A separate 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” by Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice is scheduled for release Dec. 11. The adaptive score is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
What players will find next
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.
The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.
___
Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

title: Mother charged with murder after 2 kids left home alone die in fire, police say
text:
VALDOSTA, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) - A Georgia mother is facing multiple felony charges after two of her children, who had allegedly been left home alone with a third sibling, died in a fire.
Taneika Lashae Sirmans, 37, was arrested last Monday in connection with an October house fire that left two of her children dead and a third injured, according to the Valdosta Police Department.
Police say firefighters, officers and emergency medical personnel responded to a Valdosta home around 8:20 a.m. Oct. 25 after receiving reports of a fire. Upon arrival, first responders saw flames coming from the home’s roof.
Firefighters removed three children, all under the age of 10, from inside the home. All three were unresponsive, and first responders attempted lifesaving measures before taking them to the hospital.
Police say two of the children later died from suspected smoke inhalation, while the third was flown to an Atlanta hospital.
Investigators determined Sirmans, the children’s mother, had left them home alone during the early morning hours to go to work. A fire started in the kitchen several hours after she left, according to police.
Following an investigation and consultation with the district attorney’s office, detectives obtained arrest warrants for Sirmans.
Sirmans is facing two counts of second-degree murder and three counts of second-degree cruelty to children, according to Lowndes County Sheriff’s Office booking records.
Police say the surviving child remains hospitalized in stable condition in Atlanta.
Valdosta Police Chief Leslie Manahan called the incident a heartbreaking tragedy that could have been prevented.
“This tragedy has not only had a devastating impact on the families involved and our community, but it also affects our first responders and medical personnel who responded to the scene or were working in the hospital that morning,” Manahan said.
She added that her thoughts remain with the families affected and the surviving child, whose life has been forever changed.

title: 2 Americans drown while swimming in the Bahamas, officials say
text:
(Gray News) - Two Americans died after being pulled from the water in the Bahamas, authorities said.
According to the Royal Bahamas Police Force, police on the island of Bimini responded to a reported drowning near the entrance to Bimini Harbour around 3 p.m. on Nov. 13.
Officials were told that a group of people were swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign for strong currents.
Several people were reportedly swept away by the currents while swimming. A nearby ferry boat assisted in rescuing some of the swimmers.
Two Americans, a 38-year-old man and a 40-year-old woman, were found unresponsive and pulled from the water, officials said. First responders administered CPR, and the pair were taken to a local hospital, where they were pronounced dead shortly before 4 p.m.

title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to LSU-Texas game after ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop that caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the game a day after all planes were grounded. Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as flights were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
Mullin’s flight comes as the ground stop is garnering increasing scrutiny, with Democrats in the Senate demanding that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it was pausing the installation of the routers that were linked to the ground stop.
Asked on CNBC whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
Mullin took over as DHS secretary earlier this year from Kristi Noem, whose tenure was rocked by scandal over spending at the department, as well as an aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. Mullin vowed to serve as a steady hand for the department and keep it out of the headlines.
The Department of Homeland Security said Mullin was required by law to travel on a government plane. It said in a statement that he pays personally for any flight unrelated to government work.
“Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements,” it said.
The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports. The stoppage resulted in thousands of canceled flights and massive disruptions at airports across the nation ahead of the busy Thanksgiving holiday.
President Donald Trump’s administration has said the air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.
“I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said.
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.
___
Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pennsylvania.

Explore mortgage rates
Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in October 2026 was $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.42% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,313 amounts to about 26% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 0.4% over the past year, and the median of $416,700 was an all-time high for the month of October. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late October showed national home prices grew 2.1% in the year ending in August, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have retreated a bit after spiking amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, and 10-year Treasury yields remain above 5%.
“Recent elections may have changed expectations for additional federal spending, but persistent inflation, relatively strong economic activity and the likelihood of another Federal Reserve rate increase should continue to put upward pressure on rates,” says Sean Salter, a finance professor at Middle Tennessee State University.
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Driver hits 3 pedestrians in midcoast Walmart parking lot
text:
THOMASTON, Maine — A driver hit three pedestrians Wednesday afternoon in the Walmart parking lot.
The vehicle that struck the pedestrians had significant front end damage. The car had Maine handicapped plates. An elderly woman was in the driver’s seat of the vehicle.

title: Paris Hilton urges House to pass AI deepfake porn bill
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Paris Hilton returned to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to urge the House to pass a bill aimed at combating nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfake images.
“Bring the DEFIANCE Act to the House floor. Let Congress vote,” Hilton said at a press conference, alongside Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Laurel Lee, R-Fla, the bill’s sponsors.
Hilton calls for a House vote
The legislation would allow victims to sue people who create or distribute sexually explicit images of them.
“DEFIANCE returns power to the hands of survivors by allowing them to hold their abusers accountable and seek financial and reputational recourse for the harm they caused in court,” Ocasio-Cortez said.
Hilton has advocating for the legislation for months. She made an initial appeal to House lawmakers in January, after it passed in the Senate by unanimous consent. But the bill still has yet to be voted on in the lower chamber.
“The Senate understood the urgency and passed this legislation unanimously in January. Now the House must act, too,” she said. “Why wait another day if they don’t pass this bill before the end of the year? All of our progress will be lost and we’ll have to start all over again. Speaker Johnson, Leader Scalise, and Chairman Jordan, I am speaking directly to you.”
During her January appearance on the Hill, Hilton spoke about her personal experience of having nonconsensual intimate images of her shared when she was 19-years-old.
“Ten months ago, I stood here at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent. And I asked Congress to do something about it,” Hilton said.
She also said that her team had done research about how AI deepfakes are affecting women in Congress.
“In preparation for today, my team studied how United States Congress women are appearing in adult deepfake content online. And what we found was shocking, but hardly surprising,” she said. “Of the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress. 83 have sexual deepfakes online right now. That’s more than half of the women in Congress.”
Lee also said the bill sends a message about the use of artificial intelligence.
“It gives victims the ability to fight back, to seek accountability, and to pursue justice. And importantly, it sends a clear message that using artificial intelligence to sexually exploit another person will have consequences,” she said.

title: Battle for top positions: Who will lead the Democrats in the next session of Congress?
text:
Battle for top positions: Who will lead Democrats in the next session of Congress?
Democrats are selecting new leaders in the House and Senate, with key votes shaping the party's direction for the next two years.
Battle for top positions: Who will lead Democrats in the next session of Congress?
Democrats are selecting new leaders in the House and Senate, with key votes shaping the party's direction for the next two years.
Democrats are choosing new leaders in the House and Senate to guide the party's agenda as the new session of Congress approaches.
Overnight, Democrats expanded their majority in the Senate with Democrat Mary Peltola winning the Senate seat in Alaska over the Republican incumbent. This victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate when the new Congress begins in January.
A closely watched race in the Senate is the contest for the next majority leader. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen has announced he will run against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
"This is not about one person or any one individual. This really is a response to the call of the voters who clearly rejected Donald Trump and his awful policies, but they haven't fully hired the Democrats. They've given us a chance, and I think we need to earn their trust, and I think that begins by not going back to business as usual, not going back to the status quo," Van Hollen said.
Despite the challenge, Schumer insists he will gain enough support to secure the title. The vote for this position is scheduled for next month.
"I'm confident I'll be the next leader. I have the votes, and we're all going to roll up our sleeves, and we're going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption. Those are the things we're focused on," Schumer said.
In the House, Democrats are holding a private vote today and tomorrow to select the next speaker of the House. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is running for the position, and political analysts have indicated he is likely to secure the role. If elected, Jeffries would make history as the first Black Speaker of the House.
"He's extraordinarily popular. He led them to the majority, and there will be debate. Maybe somebody will run against him, but even if that happens, it will be perfunctory," said Thomas Kahn, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University.
The lawmakers chosen to lead both parties will have significant influence over policy, congressional actions, and the overall direction of the country.
Keep watching for the latest from the Washington News Bureau:

title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska, beating incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.
The Alaska race was the last U.S. Senate contest to be resolved in this year’s midterm elections and gave Democrats a 56-44 majority after they flipped nine GOP-held seats to retake the chamber. The party also won campaigns in other conservative states, including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi.
In a statement, Peltola said voters sent a clear message that “the status quo in D.C. is not working for Alaska.”
“Over the course of this campaign I’ve spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table,” she said. “Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first.”
Sullivan spokesperson Nate Adams did not respond to a request for comment. Adams had said Monday that the campaign would let the process “run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.” A spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee also did not respond.
As part of the Nov. 3 general election, Alaskans also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, as former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by Trump. The Associated Press has not yet called the U.S. House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich.
Flipping Alaska’s seat was pivotal to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate
Peltola previously held the state’s lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.
In the campaign’s final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent. Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the Nov. 3 election. Peltola denied any involvement.
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats’ behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since The Times’ article was published.
Candidacy of second Dan Sullivan roiled the race
The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with a former Peltola campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year’s open primary and later sought to recant her statements. But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump’s mind. He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October.
The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered. It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit “flagrant corruption.”
The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed. Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election “without unwarranted interference by the United States.” They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska’s ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them.
The Justice Department also confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska’s U.S. attorney would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into.
Peltola finished first in the primary with 49.5% of the vote, followed by the incumbent with 41.4%.
Dan J. Sullivan finished a distant third with about 2.5%, but he advanced to the general election as one of the top four finishers. He was listed on both ballots as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation, while the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Peltola played up her rural roots during the campaign
During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are generally only accessible by air or water.
Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of “Alaska first.”
“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”
The strategy resonated with voters who felt they could relate to Peltola, who is Yup’ik and often spoke about growing up in western Alaska.
“People across the country don’t understand what it means to grow up in a place where there isn’t running water, where there’s only one store, where gas costs $17 a gallon, where heating fuel is not a guaranteed thing, which means that your house isn’t necessarily going to be warm when it’s 50 below zero,” Sam Schimmel, who is Alaska Native, said in Anchorage after Peltola’s win.
“Having somebody who really understands what that means in D.C., representing us in the Senate, is an enormous achievement,” he added and also noted the significance of Peltola’s election as the first Alaska Native in the Senate.
Michael Dunn, also in Anchorage, said he voted for Sullivan but hopes Peltola does well.
“She put in the effort,” he said of her campaign. “So hopefully she puts in the effort in D.C. for us.”
Peltola emphasized affordability issues
“Lower 48” became something of an insult bandied by both sides. Sullivan tried to align Peltola with “Lower 48 liberals” who want to restrict oil and gas drilling, mining and other resource development in the state. Peltola said that while she would work with Trump to get things done for Alaska, “I will never put any Lower 48 politician before Alaskans. That’s the difference between Dan and me.”
Emphasizing her Alaska roots, she spoke about fishing for salmon on the Kuskokwim River with her father and spending parts of the summer at fish camp with her children and late husband, who died in September 2023.
She said the fish and wildlife Alaskans long relied on to fill their freezers for the winter were becoming harder to find. The changes were forcing people to buy more food and other staples at the store — supplies that must be barged or flown in — and deal with “crushing prices,” she said.
Peltola also said she saw members of Congress who were “more focused on their stock portfolios” than helping ease those costs and vowed to push back against the billionaire class.
She will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014.
___
Associated Press journalist Mark Thiessen in Anchorage contributed to this report.

title: Bruins top Red Wings, halt 3-game skid
text:
DETROIT — David Pastrnak had a goal and an assist as the Boston Bruins beat Detroit 4-1 on Wednesday night, spoiling the Red Wings’ Centennial celebration game.
The contest was played on the 100th anniversary of Detroit’s first NHL game — a 2-0 loss for the then-Cougars to the Bruins. Pregame ceremonies on Wednesday included a video introduction from Scotty Bowman.
The centennial celebration resulted in a rare color-on-color game, with Detroit wearing red and the Bruins in black.
JJ Peterka and Pavel Zacha also scored for the Bruins, who snapped a three-game skid. Mason Lohrei and Morgan Geekie each had two assists.
Daniil Tarasov, coming off a shutout of the Tampa Bay Lightning, made 27 saves but couldn’t prevent Detroit’s sixth loss in seven games.
Detroit’s Lucas Raymond made it 1-0 at 16:58 of the first period. Keegan Kolesar knocked the puck loose in the neutral zone to set up a 2-on-1 break, and Raymond blasted Andrew Copp’s pass inside the left post for his ninth goal.
Peterka tied the game at 2:47 of the second, cutting in from the left wing and beating Tarasov on the glove side.
Zacha then gave the Bruins a 2-1 lead with a power-play goal at 11:48, putting in a rebound for his sixth of the season.
Pastrnak made it 3-1 at 5:11 of the third, beating Tarasov from the slot after a pass from Lohrei.
Casey Middelstadt finished the scoring into an empty net at 19:05.
Up next
Bruins: Host the Washington Capitals on Saturday
Red Wings: Host the New York Islanders on Saturday

title: This state banned Waymo autonomous vehicles from its freeways
text:
(AP) - California banned Waymo’s autonomous vehicles from state freeways, saying they pose an “imminent hazard” after recent traffic incidents, including one where three of the driverless cars drove into a construction zone.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles issued the ban last Wednesday after two incidents on California freeways, Jonathan Groveman, a department spokesperson, said in a statement.
A Waymo spokesperson said in a statement that the company has “temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance.” The company did not provide more detail. Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have expanded onto freeways in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, according to the company.
The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions.”
Waymo continues to operate the vehicles as normal on California surface streets, according to the company.
California’s restrictions bar Waymo from both operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.”
___
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Pizza restaurant to open in former Stonington pharmacy building
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A roving wood-fired pizza maker on Deer Isle has bought the island’s former pharmacy and plans to turn it into a restaurant selling her local, farm-fresh pizza.
Janet Marciniec, who started Hearth and Soul Oven in 2020 soon after leaving the corporate world for culinary school, and her husband are adding a “second act to their second act” with the purchase of the former Seaside Pharmacy in neighboring Stonington.
After spending most of the last six summers traveling across the Blue Hill peninsula and beyond with an 8,000-pound copper oven in tow, the sit-down eatery will give them their first permanent location. It would also add a new year-round establishment to the island, which quiets down considerably in the winter.
“It’s really the giving back to the community,” she said. “We have had so, so much fun doing this, and people think that we’re absolutely crazy at our ages to even be taking things on … [but] this is just fun to us.”
An artisan bread class in culinary school led Marciniec to the Maine Grain Alliance’s annual conference in Skowhegan, where she encountered wood-fired pizza ovens for the first time. She was impressed with the simplicity of creating sourdough from just flour and water, and captivated by the fires.
“I just recognized that fire draws people in,” Marciniec said, adding that people connect to seeing their pizza being made in front of them. “There is something just very deep in terms of that almost prehistoric connection with fire, and it’s that ability to make something very simply…You can taste the difference.”
Soon, she was making a business plan for her own mobile wood-fired pizza business, which her husband, Phil LoBianco, joined as the pizza chef. Hearth and Soul has made regular weekday stops at businesses around the peninsula and appeared at pop-ups and private events from Belfast to Sullivan.
Marciniec prioritizes Maine-grown ingredients and the menu changes with the season, highlighting local vegetables with unique sauces. She keeps it simple and doesn’t add too much cheese so each flavor stands out, she said.
They were looking for a permanent location to reduce the physical wear and tear of traveling with the oven, and the pharmacy is close to their home in Deer Isle.
Seaside Pharmacy shuttered last year after the sudden death of its owner, 70-year-old Doug Edinger, who had been a pharmacist on the island for more than two decades and ran the 59 School St. location — a former restaurant — for 11 years.
When Hearth and Soul moves in, its name and menu will stay mostly the same, with the possible addition of Italian sandwiches inspired by those Marciniec makes for staff using extra pizza dough.
She hopes to open by May, depending on renovation needs, with some indoor seating and picnic tables. After that, the couple aims to operate year-round with limited winter hours.
The couple will still provide mobile pizzas for public and private events, but won’t keep the same regular weekly schedule of local stops.
They also prioritize giving back through charitable events and hiring locals. For Marciniec, pizza serves a community function, too.
“It’s our passion, it’s our purpose,” she said. “It allows us to give back and connect in a way that is just very meaningful for people.”
Making pizza is the “last thing” she ever thought she’d do back in culinary school, but it’s drawn her in like nothing else has.
It’s always changing, even with the weather as conditions affect the dough behavior, providing a rewarding challenge. And, especially, compared to the long timelines of corporate life, it’s rewarding to see people smile in response to something that took five minutes to make.
“This is something that really touches my heart,” she said.

title: Bernie Sanders unveils his plan to push Medicare for All when Democrats take power
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation’s healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities.
Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, is currently the ranking member on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and is expected to become its chairman when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. His agenda, first provided to The Associated Press, lays out the legislative implementation for proposals that he and progressive candidates championed on the campaign trail this cycle.
At the center is Sanders’ longstanding push for Medicare for All, a universal healthcare system that would be implemented over four years. The first year would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guarantee healthcare to children through age 18.
“This is no longer a utopian vision. This is where the American people are,” Sanders said in an interview with the AP.
The proposals offer an early glimpse of how progressives hope to shape the Democratic Party’s priorities after an election that delivered the party control of Congress but also exposed competing visions for its future. With the 2028 presidential election already looming, Sanders is seeking to push Democrats toward a populist economic agenda that he argues has gained broader support.
“I think the election, in my opinion, was a crying out for fundamental change in the way the government does business and the absolute need to protect a struggling working class,” Sanders said. “I think this is a time to bring about very significant changes in policies so that we can actually improve the lives of working families.”
Sanders keeps pushing for Medicare for All
Sanders has long championed a single-payer national health insurance program that would replace most private insurance with a federally administered system providing universal coverage.
His proposal for the new Congress lays out a four-year transition to that system, beginning with expanding Medicare eligibility and benefits. In the second year, the eligibility age would fall to 45, followed by 35 in the third year, before extending coverage to everyone in the fourth year.
“Transforming a system which is 18% of the GDP of America, you don’t do that overnight,” Sanders said of the transitional period.
But the costs of lowering Medicare eligibility are likely to lead to massive debate between the two major political parties as the national deficit stands at $2 trillion, or 6.2% of gross domestic product. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that lowering the age of Medicare eligibility to 60 would increase federal budget deficits by $155 billion over the 2026–2031 period.
Sanders’ prior proposals to pay for the program shift healthcare financing away from private insurance premiums and toward payroll contributions — including a combination of employer and household premiums, higher taxes on the rich and new taxes on Wall Street and large firms.
Sanders also argued that Democrats could pass the first stage of the transition through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain tax and spending legislation to advance through the 100-member Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically required to overcome a filibuster. Democrats will have a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the chamber in 16 years.
Along with pushing for greater access to primary care, Sanders says Democrats will push for lower prescription drug costs.
A changing political landscape
Sanders has previously balanced his progressive ambitions with the realities of governing. During his first stint chairing the HELP Committee from 2023 to 2025, he worked with Republicans on legislation to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to primary care. He also chaired the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, helping advance major Democratic spending priorities.
But now, just weeks after the midterms, Sanders is laying out an ambitious agenda that he argues reflects a shift not in his own positions but in voters’ demands for sweeping changes to the healthcare system.
He sees signs of that shift among Democratic leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has pledged to get to work “right out of the gate” to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republicans.
Jeffries said Tuesday that Democrats know that simply returning to the status quo “is not acceptable” and they are preparing ways to further expand healthcare access by lowering the Medicare eligibility age, adding access to vision, hearing and dental coverage, and ensuring all kids are covered.
“Jeffries basically supported the first year of Medicare for All,” Sanders said.
But anything that passes Congress the next two years will still need to be signed by President Donald Trump to take effect. Sanders rejected the notion that Trump, a Republican, wouldn’t sign something like Medicare for All into law.
“Donald Trump may be crazy, but he is not stupid. He’s a smart guy, and he’s a very good politician,” Sanders said.
An agenda beyond healthcare
Sanders is also preparing to use the committee to advance a broader economic agenda that includes raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $20 an hour and promoting the PRO Act, which would strengthen workers’ rights to unionize.
The proposed wage increase would nearly triple the federal minimum, which has remained unchanged since 2009, and could face resistance from lawmakers concerned about the impact on small businesses and employment. Sanders proposes to implement it over a four-year transition period.
Sanders’ agenda also calls for sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence, including a moratorium on new AI data centers, a pause in advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.
___

title: Student trades paper clip up to a BMW in social media challenge
text:
GREENVILLE, N.C. (WCTI) - At a university in North Carolina, students were challenged to use their negotiation skills to see what they could gain from a single paper clip.
One student took the challenge to the extreme and negotiated his way into owning a BMW.
“I thought this was the coolest class I’ve ever taken and such a great opportunity to take a paper clip and turn it into something great,” Christian Henry, a senior at East Carolina University, said.
That’s what Henry did in the purple paper clip challenge.
He documented on social media his skills trading a paper clip for something ultimately worth roughly 40,000 times its value.
Henry spent a semester negotiating for different items, such as an extra Roku remote and a drill, and even traded a fishing pole for a guitar. And in the end, he landed on a BMW 328i, putting his total revenue gain at $2,000.
“I’m like, I need one final really big thing to make this project a success, and I knew of this car back in Hickory, this old BMW that’s just sitting collecting dust. After a long, strenuous negotiation, I was able to secure that trade,” Henry said.
Assistant Professor of Management Leah Grubb said she was impressed at her students’ perseverance.
“Started emailing people, I started texting people, my husband was sitting next to me, I’m like, ‘A car! We got a car!’” Grubb said.
Other students also had impressive trades, starting with a paper clip and working their way to items such as Beats headphones, Yeti coolers, an Apple TV, and even an e-bike.
Grubb said it’s rewarding to see her vision for the project come to reality.
“Makes me so proud and so happy and my little professor heart is just thrilled,” she said.
As for the students, they learned valuable skills such as confidence, networking, perseverance, and the importance of taking risks.
“One of the most interactive, fun things I’ve ever been able to do at ECU and I’ll never regret taking it,” Henry said.
No word yet on whether Grubb will offer the challenge in future classes.

title: Acting Navy secretary questioned about $65M shortfall at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Acting Navy secretary questioned about $65 million shortfall at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard
Outgoing U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat from New Hampshire, questioned the acting Secretary of the Navy about the future of Portsmouth Naval Shipyard on Tuesday.
Shaheen pressed Hung Cao, who is poised to take the Secretary of the Navy role permanently, at his confirmation hearing about how to deal with the $65 million budget shortfall at the shipyard, which is located in Kittery, Maine.
Shaheen cited two Department of the Navy actions as causes of the deficit, including federal funding not being provided to supplement civilian employee salaries and the department improperly pulling millions during a hiring freeze, according to WMTW sister station WMUR.
The senator said federal funding to provide required bonuses to top-performing civilian employees was not provided, forcing the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard to pull $32 million from its operations and maintenance budget.
The department reportedly pulled back another $33 million for "under-execution of hiring" during a federally instated 2025 civilian hiring freeze, which was only remedied through congressional intervention.
Cao admitted he failed to provide answers after being previously questioned on the topic at a hearing in May. He committed to providing answers within one week of the hearing, and if confirmed, pledged to work with Shaheen to free up the $33 million.
"We're also increasing the wage grade in order to pay our shipyard workers more. We need to be able to pay more for them instead of giving them only $2 more per hour than what they would make for minimum wage," Cao said. "So you have my pledge that I will work with you in order to properly compensate our shipyard workers."
Shaheen also questioned Cao about the department's level of transparency and said members from both parties are frustrated with the lack of information. Cao denied ever being directed not to be open with Congress.

title: Democrats flipped 9 US Senate seats in the midterms — the most in almost 70 years
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) - Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s competitive U.S. Senate race has flipped a ninth Republican-held seat to the Democrats, giving Peltola’s party its biggest midterm gain in nearly 70 years.
Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower’s second term. That year, Democrats wrested away 13 Republican-held seats and also won both of Alaska’s newly created seats, for a total gain of 15 seats.
Peltola’s victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the Senate in 16 years. Democrats held 58 Senate seats in the waning days of the 111th Congress, which concluded on Jan. 3, 2011.
“56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in statement posted on social media. “Most people didn’t think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle.”
Even without Alaska, Democrats would have secured their largest majority since January 2015, when Republicans took control after flipping nine Democratic seats in the 2014 midterms during President Barack Obama’s second term.
Democrat Scott Colom’s U.S. Senate victory Wednesday in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race gave his party its eighth Republican-held seat. That win delivered Democrats their most midterm pickups since President Ronald Reagan’s second midterm election 40 years ago.
Democrats also reclaimed the House, picking up 42 seats as of Tuesday. The gains continued a historical trend of midterm losses for the president’s party.
The Senate has tended to be less susceptible to the midterm effect than the House. In seven of the last 16 midterms prior to 2026, the president’s party either held its ground or gained seats in the Senate, though all but one of those midterms occurred in the president’s first term. A president’s second midterm tends to be more punishing.
By comparison, the president’s party had gained House seats in only two midterms since the end of World War II.

title: Gardens Aglow light show switches on
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Each winter, the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens are brightened by an ethereal light show. Colorful sculptures representing Maine’s wildlife and quintessential symbols — moose, lobster and lighthouses — dot the gardens. Towering trees and wooden trolls are illuminated by kaleidoscopic spotlights.
Gardens Aglow is open from Nov. 14 to Jan 2. The theme of the show changes each year — this winter’s is titled “Gathered in Maine,” and it depicts the many ways that human and animal residents gather the things they need to survive, and gather together, this time of year.
A Nov. 12 preview walk through the light show began in a display depicting a marsh with lighted lily pads and a moose in a pond. Recorded cello music drifted through the gardens. A wooden troll statue called Roskva, created by Thomas Dambo, overlooked the scene.
Visitors can follow the map through the gardens, or just get lost among the lights. Many displays are also educational. For instance, beaver sculptures were placed next to a realistic depiction of a beaver dam, with a sign explaining how beavers create habitats.
The gardens now display over 300 lighted sculptures of bees, mushrooms, birds, and more. The display uses more than 750,000 LED lights — if connected, the strands would stretch from Boothbay to South Portland.
Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens CEO Gretchen Ostherr said that most of the light show changes year to year. Many of the statues are reused , but they are set up differently. Noteworthy additions this year include a maple tapping forest, complete with sap buckets and glowing sap lines, and a display featuring an ant colony — including an ant statue on the roof of the cafe.
“It’s still a really fun thing to do for the holidays, but it’s not about any particular holiday. It’s about getting people outside, and light in the dark times,” Ostherr said. “You’re not going to see any Santas here.”
The team at the botanical gardens worked with Maine artists, including visual artist Hannah Holt and cellist Robin Lane, while designing the show.
Now in its 12th year, Gardens Aglow has drawn over 1 million visitors since its debut. In 2025, the light show drew over 100,000 people. This included visitors from all 50 states, but 95% were from New England.
Ostherr said that Gardens Aglow was started in part to provide staff with year-round employment. She said the influx of visitors also helps out local businesses.
On weeknights, tickets are $20 for adults, $18 seniors and veterans, and $10 for children. On Fridays and Sundays, prices increase slightly— $24 for adults, $22 for seniors and veterans, and $14 for kids. They are most expensive on Saturdays — $28 for adults, $26 for seniors and veterans, and $18 for kids. Tickets can be purchased on the Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens website, or over the phone at (207) 633-8000. Shuttles are available from the Boothbay Town Office on Friday, Saturday and Sunday nights, ending at 9 p.m.

title: Republican Nick Begich wins reelection to Alaska's US House seat, a rare bright spot for the GOP
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich has won reelection to Alaska’s lone U.S. House seat, hanging on during a year that saw Democrats regain control in both houses of Congress.
His win Wednesday through the state’s ranked vote tabulations process was a rare bright spot for Republicans, whose ranks in the House were decimated in the midterms. It came a day after Democrat Mary Peltola flipped one of Alaska’s U.S. Senate seats by defeating Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Begich was endorsed by President Donald Trump in his run for a second term and pitched himself as an effective leader who was in lockstep with the president’s efforts to expand oil and gas drilling and other resource development in the state.
His main challenger was independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher who was endorsed by the state Democratic Party. He sought to focus on affordability issues, limiting the influence of big money in elections and pushing back against the billionaire class in the U.S.
The race also included Democrat Eric Hafner, who is incarcerated in a federal prison in New York after being convicted in 2022 of threatening to kill judges, police officers and others.
Hill’s campaign and state Democrats cried foul after voters were sent text messages from an undisclosed source supporting Hafner. Hill’s campaign manager, Kevin Groh, and the Democratic Party’s executive director, Jenny-Marie Stryker, said they never learned who sponsored the texts.
Stryker said the party spent “thousands of dollars to send texts clarifying that the real Alaska Democratic Party endorsed Bill Hill.”
Hill’s campaign expressed concerns over Hafner’s candidacy, particularly in the final weeks of the race, distributing stickers and yard signs labeling him a “fake ‘Democrat.’” Hafner, who received nearly 8% of the vote, submitted a candidate biography that appeared in state election materials that made no reference to his incarceration.
Hafner’s mother, Carol “Kitty” Hafner, responded to an email from The Associated Press that was sent to her son. She said it would seem “next to impossible” for voters not to know he was in prison, given the coverage of his candidacy for Alaska’s House seat in 2024. She also said the “media has gone well overboard identifying his incarceration status.”
“Absolutely no one encouraged” Hafner to run, his mother wrote, adding that his campaigns have been “entirely independent of any influencers.”
“Tell President Trump to Pardon Eric Hafner!” she wrote.
Both she and her son lack ties to the state. Carol Hafner ran in Alaska’s Senate primary in August, finishing sixth with 0.6% of the vote. The major candidates in the U.S. Senate race were Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. But the race also included a second Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan. Peltola faced allegations that members of her team helped recruit the second Sullivan, but she denied involvement in any such effort.
Both Hafners have run in Alaska and other states before.

title: How to do your job as a board member
text:
Given the shakeup at tech giant Nvidia, many boards are quietly wondering whether they have transparency into the organizations they theoretically oversee. If you’re on such a board, take heart: very few leaders are targeted by Chinese spies, and even fewer blithely take the bait.
That said, serving on a board involves a a clearly defined obligation to handle the policy and strategy, not the day-to-day operations. That distinction is necessary for a functional organization. Within your role, you have key fiduciary duties (in almost all circumstances). They include the following:
- Duty of care. Act as an ordinary, prudent person would in managing the organization. Skipping meetings and being a rubber stamp usually doesn’t cut it;
- Duty of loyalty. Put the organization’s interests first, above your own and above the interests of other individuals; and
- Duty of obedience. Make sure the organization complies with laws and its internal governance documents. Have a working familiarity with regulations, audit reports or financials and bylaws.
It can feel hard to strike the balance between prudent oversight and operational meddling. Current events show that even very experienced board leaders get this wrong, and most err on the side of being too conservative.
If you want to polish up your board participation, here are some simple, policy-driven questions that can help you understand whether you’re living up to your mandate:
Does the board fully understand the staff structure?
You only oversee the top executive, but there should be personnel policies that require updated job descriptions, goal setting and periodic reviews for staff. These requirements only help if they’re being followed. Are they? Have you reviewed the policies this year? Have you seen an organizational chart? Do you have a map of decision-making authority? The board’s role isn’t to answer these questions, but its oversight of the executive includes understanding how — and how well — they do their job.
What would happen if a senior leader won the lottery and left?
Managing risk is a normal board function, and key-person risk is surely top of mind for most boards this week. Beyond a file of passwords and a phone tree for emergencies, what is the plan for keeping each facet of your organization running? How long could you run on that continuity plan? Would it be prudent to test the plan by insisting that each of your important leaders take a two-week vacation annually (and fully disconnect for that time)? This is a normal provision in certain regulated industries to ensure that no one is cooking the books or otherwise running amok.
Does the board insist on accountability and outcomes?
When you have a rock star leader who delivers fantastic outcomes, it’s easy to shift from oversight to gratitude. That can creep into deference, creating a board that doesn’t want to rock the boat. Ask yourself and your fellow members, “Do we have a strategic plan? Do we benchmark outcomes against that plan? When we ask for changes and how does the interaction feel? Have we asked any hard questions in the last few meetings? Did dissent feel comfortable and productive, or did people get defensive?”
Do we have an independent HR function to protect the organization?
Many small organizations have small, tight-knit teams and no dedicated human resources function. In that environment, it can feel impossible to tell a hard truth about someone who is well liked. Ensuring that your whole staff is trained to call an external, third-party HR consultant to report anything unusual means that you hear about trouble sooner. This service is inexpensive and beneficial, no matter what gets reported.
Do we have directors and officers liability insurance?
It won’t protect board members from their intentional or knowing misdeeds, but if you’re trying your best and the worst happens anyway, this insurance can be worth its weight in gold.

title: Unbridled joy: Woman with ALS races rides a horse in all 50 states
text:
LUGOFF, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Tricia Jackson has been riding horses since she was 3 years old. Seventy-one years later, she’s still in the saddle — and she has no plans to stop.
Jackson, an award-winning competitive equestrian, lives on a farm in South Carolina that she calls her place of peace.
Over the years, she has owned as many as 12 horses at once, riding and racing them all. These days, most of her time is spent with her favorite horse, Luke, competing in endurance rides that span anywhere from 25 to 100 miles in a single day.
“That’s a lot of miles,” Jackson said. “We’ve done 50 miles in 3 hours and 50 minutes — way too fast. We riders have to be tough.”
Earlier this year, Jackson was diagnosed with ALS, a rare disease that attacks the brain and spinal cord and gradually steals a person’s ability to speak, move and eventually breathe. There is no cure.
“Statistics say 3 to 5 years, but the kind I have is bulbar ALS, which starts up here and not weakness and loss of limbs, which is coming,” Jackson said. “That’s why I decided I’m not sitting on the front porch and wait to die.”
Riding through all 50 states
Instead of slowing down, Jackson is chasing a lifelong dream — riding a horse in all 50 states.
“Everything goes away when I’m horse riding,” she said. “I feel good, my speech is better. It’s therapy. But I tell them my ALS journey so far and it’s not going to keep me down. As long as I can go, I go. And even if I lose my speech first, which I’m going to do, I can write. I ain’t stopping. That ain’t me.”
In September, she completed her goal with her final ride in Arkansas.
A life already full of adventure
Jackson’s 74 years have been marked by a series of pursuits. In 2001, she competed on Season 4 of “Survivor” after her son dared her to audition. She has traveled on mission trips.
And now she is passing her love of horses, hard work and life to 11-year-old Cooper, a young rider she mentors on her farm.
“I love this boy. He’s my heart,” Jackson said.
For Cooper, the lessons are already taking hold.
“I’ve learned you always have to help people,” he said.
‘Never give up’
Jackson said her faith and the people around her are carrying her through.
“Never give up. Use what God gave you, don’t sit on it,” she said. “This is a terminal disease. I’m going to die from it, but that’s okay because I’m right with God. He’s blessed me, and I’m so blessed to have so many people in my life supporting me.”

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: From Anne Lindbergh to John Ford
text:
Anne Lindbergh
In 1955, Anne Morrow Lindbergh (1906-2001), wife of the politically controversial aviator Charles Lindbergh (1902-1974), published Gift from the Sea, a series of meditations on the constant search for meaning that were inspired by her visits to the Maine seacoast and the peace she experienced examining seashells, beach combing and taking long walks.
One timely passage refers to the unwarranted dismissal of life after 40 by those younger folks who think they know everything:
“We Americans, with our terrific emphasis on youth, action, and material success, certainly tend to belittle the afternoon of life and even to pretend it never comes. We push the clock back and try to prolong the morning, overreaching and overstraining ourselves in the unnatural effort. We do not succeed, of course. We cannot compete with our sons and daughters. And what a struggle it is to race with these overactive and under-wise adults! In our breathless attempts we often miss the flowering that waits for afternoon.”
A slim book of just under 150 pages with insights into the madness of modern life still pertinent these days.
Count Basie
A ten-inch Decca blue label 78-#2355, recorded November 9, 1938, features pianist Count Basie (1904-1984), guitarist Freddie Green (1911-1987), double bassist Walter Page (1900-1957) and drummer Jo Jones (1911-1985) on two selections – Boogie Woogie; and How Long How Long Blues.
The Count came out of the Kansas City early 1930s honing his musicianship with the jazz band of Bennie Moten (1893-1935), an important influence on Basie but who unfortunately died very young during a routine tonsillectomy.
In the 1943 film Stage Door Canteen, Basie can be seen using his small stubby fingers to tap a few notes on his piano with exquisite results, and surrounded by his jazz band colleagues. Whether with the band or with the above three colleagues, Basie could be depended on to deliver top quality work.
The pianist and his orchestra also made a cameo appearance in the 1974 Mel Brooks movie Blazing Saddles.
In 1975, the Sunday New York Times arts section ran a full page ad announcing an upcoming Carnegie Hall concert presenting the Basie Orchestra with Frank Sinatra (1915-1998) and Ella Fitzgerald (1917-1996) with supposedly no leaks anywhere. Within an hour, the event was sold out.
John Ford
Cape Elizabeth native John Ford directed Sergeant Rutledge, one of his lesser known films, which was released to the theaters May 1960, with quotations of warm critical approval on its poster as follows:
Ward Bond – “If ever there was a picture to thrill an audience, this is it.”
Spencer Tracy – “Terrific! The kind of excitement motion pictures were invented for!”
John Wayne – “I knew it had to be great – but who could have expected it to be this great!”
Anybody could rightfully argue that the above good reviews might be a conflict of interest since Bond, Tracy and Wayne appeared in movies directed by Ford and were personal friends, thus negating any objectivity.
A greater item of interest is that the subject of the movie is an African American Cavalry Sergeant being court-martialed for murder and rape and the movie was one of the first from a major Hollywood studio – Warner Brothers – to address racism with the main character being an African American, very eloquently portrayed by Woody Strode.
The film was rightfully praised by Bond, Tracy and Wayne, it has a very suspenseful plot using flashbacks during the trial, the on-location Technicolor cinematography of Utah’s Monument Valley is a feast for the eyes and the ensemble fellow cast members – Jeffrey Hunter as Rutledge’s commanding officer/defense lawyer Lt. Cantrell, Constance Towers as a key witness Miss Beecher, Willis Bouchey as the Judge, Billie Burke as the judge’s wife (She was most memorable as the good witch Glenda in 1939’s The Wizard of Oz), and Juano Hernandez as the African American Sergeant Skidmore – each did memorable work.
Just about everyone in the film were part of Ford’s stable of performers, the seniors having been in films directed by him all the way back to the silent film era.
Both Bond and Wayne were members of the Motion Picture Alliance for the Preservation of American Ideals, a group that actively supported the Hollywood blacklist which denied employment to anyone even suspected of being a Communist and even believed that the Civil Rights Movement was a Communist plot whereas their friend John Ford, although a Goldwater/Reagan Republican, held the blacklist in contempt.
Sixty-six years ago yesterday (I am writing this on November 6), Ward Bond died from a massive heart attack at a Dallas hotel where he and his wife were staying for the weekend after flying into Marvin D. Love Airport from Los Angeles to attend a football game at Southern Methodist University. He was 57.
His widow perished in a house fire in 1988 at the age of 83.

title: Why doing less can be the most compassionate choice for someone you love
text:
(Aging Untold) — Our culture often pushes us to fix, treat or change every problem. But in health care and caregiving, the better path can be understanding a person’s goals, weighing the burden of treatment and accepting what cannot be fixed.
“We are a mortal being”
Sometimes doing less can be the most compassionate choice.
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, pointed to how people think about death.
“We are a mortal being, and we have an issue with that, especially in our culture,” Cradduck said. “We don’t like to talk about death. We don’t like to talk about dying.”
She said that leads people to want to treat everything.
She gave the example of paramedics doing chest compressions on a 98-year-old with advanced Alzheimer’s.
“To what value? Why are we bringing somebody back?” Cradduck said.
Accepting mortality as a gift
Accepting mortality can change what families give each other at the end of life, Cradduck said.
“Accepting the mortality of humanity and helping someone pass through their final sunset with grace and respect and dignity can oftentimes be the best gift you can give them and yourself,” Cradduck said.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said doing more is not always the same as helping more.
“Sometimes the goal should really be to recognize, know what the person wants as well and kind of abide by that,” Rogers said. “Sometimes doing nothing is the treatment.”
Acceptance is not giving up
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she sees people resist acceptance because they take it as giving up.
But she described acceptance differently.
“Well, you might be mad about it, but you’re still accepting it,” O’Rourke said. “You’re still going to go through the grief of why isn’t there one more thing I can do for mom. But you can process all of that and still be in an emotionally accepting place.”
Cradduck said accepting does not mean celebrating.
“Nobody’s asking you to throw a party because somebody you love is passing away, or you yourself are,” she said. “Nobody’s saying that this is something to be excited over, but it is something to accept. And accepting and understanding it can help everybody in the process.”
Adding life to the days
Rogers said advances in medicine have “tremendous power to add days to people’s lives,” but sometimes people want to add more life to the days they have.
O’Rourke said she was not happy when her mother decided against treatment for cancer, but later realized what her mom actually wanted.
“It was a hard pill to swallow, but the more I look back and I look at the quality time that we had in the months that she was alive, I’m so grateful that she had the courage to make that decision,” she said. “In her heart of hearts, she knew that she wanted to have really good, connected times with us as long as she could.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said looking back can bring regret when families learn a hard lesson.
“We’re not trying to torture people, you know, we’re trying to make good decisions,” Ambrose said. “Sometimes the patient might not always be thinking through everything, too. And we can really influence the answers that they give us.”
Cradduck added that treatment sometimes happens for the family rather than the patient.

title: Police: Mother called 911 to report shooting her 2 children, who died
text:
SAVAGE, Minn. (KARE) — Two young children are dead after their mother reported shooting them Wednesday near Minneapolis, according to authorities.
What police say happened
Police in Savage said the mother called 911 around 6:30 a.m. Wednesday after allegedly firing at her 3- and 5-year-old children at a scene on 126th Street.
Police said one child died at the scene. The other child died after being taken for medical care.
“It’s a tragedy. It’s a tragedy to this family. It’s a tragedy to this community,” Chief Brady Juell of the Savage Police Department said.
Neighbor reacts
“Gut-wrenching kind of thing to hear. You hear about crazy things like that, but you just think it’s not going to happen in your neighborhood,” Joe Carleton, a neighbor, said.
Mother in custody
Officers took the mother into custody. The police chief said she was being interviewed by detectives.
“Most importantly, please pray for this family. There’s extended family that showed up on the scene,” Juell added.

title: Celebrating a local artist
text:
Submitted by L. Marie Meagher, of Starks
Allow me to introduce to you an unsung Maine Wildlife Artist, who’s amazing talent deserves recognition. Janet Foster, born, raised and residing in Maine all her life, will soon be 85 years young! She is producing more of her art than ever before! Her rural Maine wildlife on mediums such as smooth rocks, wooden plaques, canvases, and various other items, have been loved by people far and wide, being given as birthday and Christmas gifts for over 40 years.
Janet’s artistic life was influenced by the family hunting trips in the great Maine outdoors. Each hunting trip up to “Camp Micky” gave her many opportunities to observe and appreciate the woods and wildlife in down-east Maine. Growing up with one older and one younger brother also played a part in shaping her artistic talent. At the young age of 10, Janet recalls sketching a battle ship on a large piece of cardboard with just a regular pencil, for her older brother.
She continued her sketching in high school, on her own, as there were no art classes available in those days. As a young adult, her first formal education in art, was a semester of drawing at UMO. Using a gift of fifty dollars from her dad and her own hard work to scrape-together the other fifty dollars, she paid for the class. Janet also remembers, when her children were young, she completed her first Adult Education class in Tole Painting.
Janet’s talent grew as she watched Bob Ross and Donna Dewberry painting classes on TV programs. She practiced her techniques, teaching herself all along the way. Her love for nature and the animals of the Maine woods have always caught her attention. She produces her renditions of these creatures and scenes with great detail in their natural Maine environment.
In the early 1980s, Janet started painting on stones, giving them to family and friends as gifts. Then she began participating in Local Craft Fairs from Orono’s Sportsmen’s Craft Fair, The Bangor and Brewer Craft Fairs, to Ellsworth, Waterville, Augusta and Lewiston. During this season of her life she also began painting on saw blades of various shapes and sizes. Most of them she obtained at yard sales, which required another layer of work to properly prepare them by de-rusting, sanding and priming, before she could paint on them. However, her main focus has been painting on stones of all sizes. Some the size of a thumbnail up to football size. These make excellent doorstops!
Currently, she displays and sells her art on stones, canvases and wooden items, at a local country-style-family-restaurant called, “OUR “FAMB”ily” Restaurant, in Dexter, Maine.
“People from far and wide” purchase Janet Foster’s artistic creations! She is sharing her love for nature in Maine through her talented work! Janet Foster is my wonderful mother! I’m so proud of her! Perhaps you have a painted stone that you use as a paper-weight on your desk or a Maine scene on canvas on your wall, painted by my mom, Janet Foster.
