title: Hot Radio Maine announces 14th Annual Free Thanksgiving Turkey Give-Away
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WELLS — Hot Radio Maine has announced details for its 14th Annual Free Thanksgiving Turkey Give-Away. The station will distribute 200 free turkeys, along with Thanksgiving sides, to members of the community on Tuesday, Nov. 24 beginning at 11 a.m. at Wells IGA, located at 1517 Post Road.
The event is held in conjunction with the Maine Credit Unions’ Campaign for Ending Hunger and the Law Office of Joe Bornstein. Additional turkeys are being brought to the event by The Place in Ogunquit, with Thanksgiving sides for everyone provided by MC Perkins Cove in Ogunquit.
Turkeys will be distributed on a first come, first served basis while supplies last.
As in years past, this is a no-cost, no-strings-attached event. Community members simply need to arrive at Wells IGA at 11 a.m. Hot Radio Maine respectfully asks that those most in need of assistance be allowed to go first.
Hot Radio Maine’s Program Director and morning host Ryan Deelon announced the giveaway on the station’s statewide signal and web broadcast, saying, “Annually, this is one of those events that reminds us why being part of the Maine community means so much to us. With food prices still so high, we know how challenging it can be for families to put food on the table, especially around the holidays. For 14 years, we’ve been able to help local families with Thanksgiving dinner, and, together with our great partners, we’re proud to keep that tradition going. Hopefully, this helps take a little pressure off families this Thanksgiving. We can’t wait to see everyone on Nov. 24th.”
Hot Radio Maine is an award-winning station with a statewide reach. It is heard on 104.7 FM in Portland and southern Maine, on 100.3 FM in Lewiston/Auburn and Brunswick, and 102.9 FM in Bangor/Brewer, Old Town and Orono. Hot Radio Maine has given out tens of thousands of dollars to local Maine listeners, as well as other prizes, concert tickets, free back-to-school haircuts for kids and even thousands of turkeys at Thanksgiving. Hot Radio Maine is the most streamed music format in Maine and New Hampshire and has a sizable social footprint that can be found at @hotradiomaine across all platforms.

title: Cincinnati Zoo shares update on Fiona the hippo after she ingested knit cap
text:
Cincinnati Zoo shares update on Fiona the hippo after she ingested knit cap
The Cincinnati Zoo says it is continuing to provide extensive care to Fiona the hippo after she ingested an object that was thrown into her habitat.
The zoo made the announcement on Monday, saying Fiona "ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat" over a week ago.
According to zoo officials, the object was a knit cap tossed by a child who was in front of the habitat. The cap was caught by a fan and "catapulted through a 1-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window."
Fiona will be off the habitat until the situation is resolved, and the zoo said she’s being monitored all day.
The zoo is optimistic that Fiona will be able to pass the hat on her own and return to her normal self.
The zoo said Fiona’s appetite has decreased and she has received rectal fluids as they consult with specialists to help Fiona pass the hat.
They said surgery isn’t an option to remove the hat, and said a colonoscopy determined that zoo officials won’t be able to reach further than nine feet.
"The scope's about nine feet long, and we weren't able to reach any farther than that," director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger said. "Ultrasound today did show that there is some bunching of intestines, so we do think she's passing something through her small intestine. And at this point, what we can do is supportive care and hope to help support her through passing it. So, for now, we're giving (her) some pain meds, some antiemetics so that she doesn't feel nauseous."

title: White House pulls FDA nominee Heidi Overton after wavering support from Senate Republicans
text:
White House pulls FDA nominee Heidi Overton after wavering support from Senate Republicans
The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn't have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation.
Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultous year under Trump's first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his unsupported claims about the risks of childhood vaccines.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday.
Cassidy had previously called Overton's support for Trump's plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot— "almost disqualifying." And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to push back against Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on chamber floor.
Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump's nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January.
It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee.
Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees
Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee. With only a matter of weeks left in his term, Cassidy faced little downside in withholding support from the latest nominee. He lost a primary race in June to run for a third term.
Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton's approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children.
Opposition to Overton's nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy's top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides.
Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists.
"There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for," Means said.
Trump has pulled back several other health nominations
Trump's first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump's surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means' sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats.
The FDA is currently being led on acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency's top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency.
The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office.

title: Rubio says 'zero' information that US outages are linked or caused by a malign actor
text:
Rubio says 'zero' information that US outages are linked or caused by a malign actor
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's 'zero' information that a series of outages and technical failures across the U.S. are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio looked to calm Americans as he was traveling with President Donald Trump as they prepared to leave Manila for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.
President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.
Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.
Each outage has been blamed on internal technical problems, with the companies and government agencies involved denying that they were the result of cyberattacks or rogue artificial intelligence systems. Trump was nonchalant after arriving in Asia on Tuesday, declaring that "things like that happen," a response that did little to calm the country.
Karoline Leavitt, Trump's former press secretary, offered advice for her old colleagues in the administration.
"What I would say to the White House is transparency is key," Leavitt said on Fox News. She said the president or someone else at the White House should explain what they know after Trump returns from Asia "to really calm the temperature."
She later praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network. "Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident," Clayton said in a clip that Leavitt shared on X. He said the U.S. government believes the incidents are caused by organizations making security upgrades that are taking longer than planned and encountering unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump's Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical about the lack of information coming out of the federal government.
"Americans aren't stupid," she posted on social media. "We want and deserve to know what's really going on."
Meghan McCain, who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, had similar advice.
"Someone high in the administration needs to get on tv and tell the American people NOW what is going on," McCain wrote on X. "No one who lived through Covid is believing this is all a coincidence."
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Some prominent figures in Trump's Make America Great Again movement expressed alarm.
"Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyber attack," Laura Loomer wrote on social media. "President Trump should come back to the United States." She did not present any evidence of an attack.
The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to "an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by "a software bug" and was "not cyber-related."
The same day, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as "routine maintenance."
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage.
"It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine," Trump said in Manila, Philippines, where he began a three-day Asian trip on Tuesday.
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages is an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
"Where is the transparency? Where is the accountability?" conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer wrote on X. "And why does it feel like we're being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?"

title: Built to break? Why newer appliances may not last like they used to
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Built to break? Why newer appliances may not last like they used to
The Hernandez family in Lehigh Acres, Florida, has spent thousands of dollars replacing refrigerators over the past five years, highlighting concerns about the lifespan of modern appliances.
The family purchased a new refrigerator in 2020, only to have it fail after less than three years.
They then bought another refrigerator, switching to a different brand. But they had the same issue.
"This one has lasted about two years and a half," Ghislaine Hernandez said.
In total, the family has purchased two refrigerators in five years, spending thousands of dollars.
"A little over $3,000 to $4,000 on the refrigerators," Hernandez said.
Technicians have suggested environmental factors may be to blame, but one hinted at a bigger issue.
"One of the technicians did let us know that it might be due to the coils not being full copper. So non-full-copper coils mixed with cheaper metals can cause the corrosion quickly," Hernandez said.
The family’s original refrigerator lasted much longer, raising questions about whether newer appliances are being cheaply made.
Alex Radov, a technician with OHM Appliance Repair, works on refrigerators of all ages. He explained that as more technology is added to refrigerators, more issues arise.
"This is a simple refrigerator. It doesn't have any inverter boards. They have the simple control board and the simple, static relay on the compressor," Radov said.
He said the biggest problems stem from the materials used in newer appliances.
"Old appliances, they will make all of the coils out of copper. The new ones, unfortunately, are made of aluminum in some cases. And it can make it cheaper for the manufacturer not to spend a lot of money," Radov said.
This shift has reduced the lifespan of refrigerators from 20 years to just a fraction of that.
"The lifetime is around four or five years," Radov said.
Even for those who know what to look for, Radov said companies don’t make it easy to identify potential issues.
"Nobody tells about the compressor, about the inverter boards. Nowadays, this information, they try to hide it," Radov said.
Radov advises customers to hold onto older refrigerators whenever possible.
"I advise every customer to save the old refrigerators, because they will spend less money," Radov said.

title: School committee seeks further resolution of transportation issue
text:
BAR HARBOR — The school committee began its latest meeting on Monday with a toast to a successful transition into the new Conners Emerson school building the week prior, a process that has been in the works for over a decade. But after a brief pause to acknowledge all the work that went into making that dream a reality, the committee turned its attention to issues new and old facing the broader school community.
According to CES Principal Dr. Heather Webster, about 800 people attended the school’s community open house following the move on Nov. 12, and the feedback from those who visited was overwhelmingly positive. And week two in the new building has seen things begin to return to a new normal for the school population.
“ Last week, we had a lot of scavenger hunts so the kids could figure out where they were in the school and where everything is. And so it’s almost like we’ve started with the first day of school again,” said Dr. Webster. “So, this week you can tell that the classes are more settled, and we’re really getting back to academics, which is great.”
Dr. Webster did caution, however, that the process is not over yet and that there would still be impacts from the construction for some time. The move is about 90% complete, and the demolition of the original buildings is slated to begin shortly. The school is anticipating the grounds to remain an active construction site through this upcoming summer, with the project still slated to wrap up fully in 2028. There are also small issues that are still being worked out in the new building that come with having new systems and processes to master.
One issue that has persisted for some time, though, is the need for a reliable transportation plan to move students from CES to the Mount Desert Island YMCA for after-school activities. Theoretically, that question was solved with the approval of the latest Memorandum of Understanding between the town and the Y, approved by the Town Council on Oct. 20. That agreement requires, among other things, the community organization to “… provide or arrange transportation when reasonably able to do so,” in exchange for the funding it receives from the municipality.
But committee members, including committee chair Marie Yarborough, were frustrated with the lack of public discussion during the negotiation of the MOU and during the meeting when the document was approved unanimously by the council.
“ I am continuously pretty frustrated with that process,” Yarborough said when introducing the discussion topic.
“I’m frustrated with the fact that there was zero public comment about the draft MOU. Right before the meeting, I did send an email to councilors saying I was looking forward to the public discussion. This is something that has been on our agenda and an important piece of our discussions for the last year, and I was looking forward to a public discussion. There was no public discussion.”
“ I’m a little troubled by the fact that the school is having to play this role that we thought we didn’t need them to play and having to be adaptable because in the end, we’re all trying to do the same thing, which is get the kids safely from this amazing school to this amazing after-school program,” added vice chair Misha Mytar. “It makes sense to me that they have challenges meeting that part of the MOU and that we have challenges trying to step up to be the fallback … But I just can’t seem to understand how we all have this common interest in safe transportation between these two incredible, wonderful, safe institutions for our kids, and we can’t seem to get together.”
According to committee members and school officials, under the previous MOU the YMCA was responsible for transporting students from CES to the YMCA, and additional funding was distributed from the town to aid the organization in that mission. That practice ceased during the Covid-19 pandemic, as best as school officials could remember, and in the years since it has fallen on the CES administration to find additional seats and divert bus routes to make it work. Dr. Webster said that there are 41 students currently who require busing from Conners Emerson to after-school programming and that the Y currently serves nine of them.
“We said we had 24 slots on the bus,” Dr. Webster said she told the Y at the beginning of the year. “Since then, they have increased the number of slots [in afterschool programs] at the Y but didn’t decrease the number of kids on our bus.”
And while the disruption has not been felt acutely by parents in previous years, school officials warned that “there will be no room at the inn” with the introduction of pre-K students to bus routes next fall.
“ We are putting an incredible burden on our staff, on our buses, on the transportation system, on the transportation plan, on our bus drivers. We’re putting an incredible burden on us trying to negotiate this and follow the way that we’ve been given to have these communications and express our needs — way more work than other entities are on this,” said Yarborough.
“And your decision is going to be made for you next year. There’s not going to be any negotiating. ‘I can give you two seats. I can give you five seats.’ There’s going to be absolutely no seats that they can be given. And what I don’t want to see is parents not understanding this in advance or being upset about it and thinking that we don’t care, but it’s just the reality of the situation.”
According to Superintendent Michael Zboray, who was present at the meeting, the district is responsible for transporting students to and from school or to and from school-sanctioned events, none of which includes after-school programming offered by the Y. But committee members said that they were willing to sit down and discuss the issue further with the town and the Y to come up with an acceptable solution for all parties.
“The MDI YMCA is appreciative of the Town Manager’s coordination of developing an MOU with the Y so that the community clearly sees and experiences our impact in service to everyone,” YMCA CEO and Executive Director Ann Tikkanen said in a statement to the Islander.
Town Manager James Smith was also approached for comment.

title: ‘I just wanted to challenge myself’: High school junior earns perfect scores on ACT and SAT
text:
KIRKWOOD, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - A high school student in Missouri earned perfect scores while taking the American College Testing and Scholastic Aptitude Test.
Luka Artomov, a Kirkwood High School junior, took the ACT in 2025 and the SAT in 2026, earning perfect scores on both while taking the tests for the first time.
“I was pretty surprised and definitely kind of elated because, you know, it’s something that happens so rarely,” Artomov said.
Artomov said he took both tests to maximize scholarship opportunities.
“Also I just wanted to challenge myself,” he said.
Artomov did the practice tests. He also attributed his success to building on what he learned in the classroom, with the support from teachers and family.
When asked if any questions left him unsure of the answer, Artomov said there were some.
“But I just went with my gut and saw what worked best, and it, you know, turned out to work,” he said.
Outside the classroom, Artomov is involved in the math team and mock trial. He also said history and growing his knowledge are some of his top interests.
School leaders note his impact goes beyond academics.
“He’s always a pleasure to be around. He always has a smile on his face. He’s a great person to engage with,” Kirkwood High School Principal Seth Harrell said. “He’ll always ask how your day is going, and I just think that positive interaction says a lot about his character and who he is as a person.”
Artomov said he plans to major in math and possibly attend law school. He also offered advice to students who would be taking the same tests.
“The number one way to not stress out about something is to come prepared. So definitely study. Review your past mistakes ... but at the same time, be confident in yourself ... trust in yourself and trust that you know what you’re doing,” Artomov said.

title: Paris Hilton urges House to pass AI deepfake bill
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Paris Hilton returned to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to urge the House to pass a bill aimed at combating nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfake images.
“Bring the DEFIANCE Act to the House floor. Let Congress vote,” Hilton said at a press conference, alongside Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Laurel Lee, R-Fla, the bill’s sponsors.
Hilton calls for a House vote
The legislation would allow victims to sue people who create or distribute sexually explicit images of them.
“DEFIANCE returns power to the hands of survivors by allowing them to hold their abusers accountable and seek financial and reputational recourse for the harm they caused in court,” Ocasio-Cortez said.
Hilton has advocating for the legislation for months. She made an initial appeal to House lawmakers in January, after it passed in the Senate by unanimous consent. But the bill still has yet to be voted on in the lower chamber.
“The Senate understood the urgency and passed this legislation unanimously in January. Now the House must act, too,” she said. “Why wait another day if they don’t pass this bill before the end of the year? All of our progress will be lost and we’ll have to start all over again. Speaker Johnson, Leader Scalise, and Chairman Jordan, I am speaking directly to you.”
During her January appearance on the Hill, Hilton spoke about her personal experience of having nonconsensual intimate images of her shared when she was 19-years-old.
“Ten months ago, I stood here at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent. And I asked Congress to do something about it,” Hilton said.
She also said that her team had done research about how AI deepfakes are affecting women in Congress.
“In preparation for today, my team studied how United States Congress women are appearing in adult deepfake content online. And what we found was shocking, but hardly surprising,” she said. “Of the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress. 83 have sexual deepfakes online right now. That’s more than half of the women in Congress.”
Lee also said the bill sends a message about the use of artificial intelligence.
“It gives victims the ability to fight back, to seek accountability, and to pursue justice. And importantly, it sends a clear message that using artificial intelligence to sexually exploit another person will have consequences,” she said.

title: Mother accused of faking 2-year-old’s illnesses; child had 175 doctor visits, underwent invasive surgery
text:
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. (WDTV/Gray News) — Three people in West Virginia are accused of faking a 2-year-old’s medical diagnoses, which led to the child receiving medical treatments they did not need.
Munchausen syndrome by proxy is a serious mental health condition and a form of abuse in which a caregiver, most often a parent, falsely claims another person has medical problems, according to the Mayo Clinic.
On Oct. 7, the Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office began an investigation into allegations of child neglect involving a 2-year-old and a 9-year-old.
Detectives said they determined that the 2-year-old had about 175 doctor visits in just over two years after reviewing extensive medical records and speaking with numerous medical professionals.
Emilee Guzman, the child’s mother, repeatedly told doctors that the 2-year-old had an inability or refusal to eat food and that the child had a fear of food (ARFID), officials said.
The information provided by Guzman led to the child undergoing surgical placement of a gastrostomy tube (G-tube) on Oct. 1. Guzman also allegedly told friends and family that the child had rare diagnoses such as microgastria, an extremely rare birth defect where the stomach fails to grow and rotate normally during pregnancy.
During an interview on Oct. 13, Guzman admitted that she knowingly withheld information from doctors concerning the child’s actual food intake. Guzman told officials she misrepresented the child’s eating habits because she feared medical providers would believe she was not properly caring for the child and contact CPS, according to official documents.
On Oct. 27, the detective spoke with the pediatric surgeon who performed the G-tube placement, who said he would not have performed the surgery and instead would have pursued less invasive treatment options if he had the proper information. The doctor said the procedure could be very painful for a child during placement and removal and could also expose the child to serious potential harm, documents said.
After the child was removed from Guzman’s custody, the child was seen eating plenty of food without issue. Foster caregivers also said that the child did not want to let anyone near the G-tube to clean it and was uncomfortable with its placement, according to officials.
Throughout the investigation, officials executed a search warrant at Guzman’s home in Morgantown. Officials said her husband, Milton Guzman Cisneros, and another woman, Caitlin Meredith, were also living in the home.
During the search, officials found deplorable and unsanitary living conditions. The home contained garbage, scattered food, dried feces believed to be from cats and possibly humans, cockroaches and a substantial infestation of flies and gnats, according to official reports.
Officials were particularly concerned about the 2-year-old who had undergone abdominal surgery and required appropriate care and hygiene of the surgical site.
Throughout the investigation, officials also found communications between Emilee Guzman and Meredith that documented “troubling treatment” of the 9-year-old, including ridicule concerning incontinence, threats and descriptions of physical punishment and expectations that the child clean the home.
Emilee Guzman is charged with one felony count of child neglect resulting in serious bodily injury. Meredith and Guzman Cisneros are each charged with two counts of child neglect creating risk of bodily injury.
All three adults are being held in the North Central Regional Jail.

title: Pres. Trump flies to Philippines, China
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump kicked off a three-day Asia trip on Tuesday - with a visit to Manila in the Philippines. There the President met with Asia-Pacific leaders and signed a new trade deal.
The President arrived in Asia touting America’s strong relationships with countries in the Asia-Pacific and also announced a new trade agreement with Thailand.
Upon landing in the Philippines, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. welcomed President Trump with a ceremony on the airport tarmac.
Following that, President Trump met with his counterparts from the Quad, Australia, Japan and India, to discuss artificial intelligence collaboration, maritime security in the Asia-Pacific, and joint military exercises.
President Donald Trump promoted friendship, “So from right here in the Philippines to nations across Southeast Asia and throughout the Indo-Pacific, this is one of the world’s most vibrant and productive regions, filled with the tremendous potential great friends of the United States.”
The President also signed a preliminary trade deal with Thailand that the President said lays the foundation for a much stronger trading relationship.
“Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports, which is something that we’ve been after for a long time, and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry. Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products.”
Following the ASEAN Summit, President Trump flew to Shenzhen, China for the APEC Summit and a separate trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. That meeting is expected to focus on nuclear non-proliferation.
The President’s Asia trip coincides with new rules issued from the Commerce Department that will now require a U.S. government license for advanced AI chip sales to data centers in much of Asia. The new rules are aimed at preventing China from acquiring indirectly advanced American technology.

title: Changes to Trundy Farm subdivision delayed by split Planning Board
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — After an hour-long debate and a split Planning Board decision of 3-3, Lee Worcester’s request to switch from public sewer to private septic in his Trundy Farm development is on hold.
The meeting, which lasted approximately 1 hour and 25 minutes, raised questions about the sewer options in the subdivision, lots splitting and merging, and two new fire hydrants.
Planning Board member Charlotte Gill, who has been critical of the development, asked Worcester why he wanted to implement the changes. “Is it because of the cost of hooking into the town sewer system that you’re looking to put individual ones in?” she asked.
Worcester said that it was one of the reasons and noted that the cost “outweighed the benefit from private septic tanks” and stated that they knew it would be expensive from the start but didn’t realize it would be as expensive. “In aggregate, we thought it would be less,” he said. “Well, as it turned out, no. In aggregate, the private septic tanks are predicted to cost less than the sewer.”
Gill responded, “But that means we’re disturbing the ground on those lots?” Gill never received an answer to this question but was drawn into multiple debates questioning the Planning Board’s responsibility to safeguard groundwater in the areas around the Trundy Farm and adjacent uncontrolled landfill.
A lengthy conversation about how septic and leach fields are developed continued until resident Jim Vallette spoke during the public comment portion of the meeting.
Vallette presented recent test results from the Department of Environmental Protection showing elevated levels of PFAS and other forever chemicals found adjacent to the uncontrolled landfill.
Vallette, along with the voters who approved a citizen’s petition requiring soil testing for any land use within a half-mile radius of the uncontrolled site in an overwhelming 554-187 vote in November 2025, believes that any new significant excavation or construction on the site could potentially disturb contaminated soils, therefore potentially harming residents in Southwest Harbor.
Vallette reported that recent DEP sampling along Marshall Brook showed elevated per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) levels compared to sampling 10 years ago. He said Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) increased from no detection to 42.8 parts per trillion, perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) increased from 3.5 to 43.7 parts per trillion, and the total of six measured PFAS increased from 17 to 110.
“They found high levels of both of those and many other PFAS. Well, 10 years later, they took more tests, and guess what? We have some of the highest levels of PFAS in Marshall Brook of any surface testing that the state’s doing in the state of Maine.”
He compared the total with a state drinking-water limit of 20, noting the result was “More than five times that limit.”
He also said PFAS had been detected in soil samples from the subdivision and argued that the patterns could be connected.
“So in the course of 10 years, there’s a seepage area of the landfill that faces the subdivision and drains into that leachate ditch that forms the western boundary of the subdivision. That’s been moving with all this inaction from the state and the town. Honestly, during that time, we’ve had that plume of contamination intensify considerably,” explained Vallette.
During Vallette’s time speaking, he was stopped multiple times by the board and asked about the connection between Trundy Farm and the amendment on the agenda.
“We are reviewing the changes. We’re not reviewing the entire plan. So it has to be a subject that’s pertinent to these particular changes,” said Planning Board Chair Eric Davis.
Vallette explained the connection in detail, noting that current abutters were notified of the potential amendments, but “the Town of Southwest Harbor did not receive notices back in August 2025, and because at that time the applicant changed the configuration of the lots in the middle of the application and the Planning Board agreed, there were no abutters other than the family members of the applicant and its related entities.”
According to Vallette, the current notices to abutters reopen the original application and the lack of notice given then. “So that part is relevant, and the abutters were denied their status in the original application. The sending of the notices to abutters now brings to light that fundamental issue with the original application, which should render it null and void,” said Vallette.
Craig Kesselheim, chair of the Sustainability Committee, was attending via Zoom and said, “I have a couple thoughts about the process tonight. From the conversation that’s happened at the Planning Board level, it has felt to me, my impression from your discourse about the proposal, proposed changes, has been that two or maybe three of you have been talking in a way that sounds like you’re giving allowance and giving rationale for the applicant as opposed to asking him critical questions.”
Kesselheim also said he felt like members of the board were giving leeway to what to him looked like “friends” as opposed to their job as Planning Board members and asking critical questions related to the proposed changes. He suggested the board consult the CEO about concerns and potential monitoring in the future based on the current findings, noting that the elevated findings of PFAS were a significant concern.
“There is PFAS in the soil, so I’m asking you to do your job. This feels like money over public safety and public health. Mr. Worcester has explained to you several times tonight that this is a financial decision, not an environmental decision, not a public health and safety decision and I take issue with that. On behalf of my townspeople and the folks who have to live with the soil and water quality. So that’s a big concern for me about your action as a board that represents the townspeople, not the developers, but the townspeople of Southwest Harbor. So I’d ask you to do your job.”
Kesselheim was met with silence before Davis closed the public speaking part of the meeting and moved on.
At this point, the board had no objections to the lot adjustments or the hydrants, but the proposed wastewater switch did spark debate among board members, Worcester, and residents concerned about PFAS and leachate.
Gill referred to the original plan, stating concerns that if the 12 lots have leaching water with potential contaminants, it would now be an issue, unlike before, when the subdivision was planned to be on a closed system handled by the town.
Planning Board member Priscilla Ksionzyk also shared concerns with Gill about the amendments.
Gill referred to the town’s soil standard, which requires proposed uses to be established and maintained without adverse environmental impacts, including water pollution and stated this multiple times throughout the meeting.
Eventually stating, “What I’m looking for is, ‘is this going to be safe?’” The question revolved around disturbing the soils while adding septic and leach fields for the 12 lots, and whether the applicant has met the performance standards of the land use ordinance.
Davis explained that the original approval had already been reviewed by two engineers and said that if the board has a split vote, they would then have a dialogue on what to do next, which would require finding another engineer to look over the site and determine if installing 12 septic systems and leach fields would be safe.
“I’m almost tempted to vote, see how it goes. If we have a split, then maybe have a dialogue about whatever. I’m not trying to twist anybody’s arm. I’m almost thinking we’re kind of coming at an impasse,” said Davis. He paused for a moment and then said, “I’ll make a motion that the applicant has is complete and is met to performance standards of the land use ordinance as presented.”
The motion was seconded by Wolak, with Gill, Williams, and Ksionzyk giving votes of nay, and Davis, Wolak, and Lloyd votes of approval, splitting the decision 3-3.
Williams, in a turn of events, voted nay on the amendment and stated that he wanted to see more about the proposed changes before giving his approval.
The split board will now seek an engineer’s advice on whether a leach field and septic were placed on these properties and to determine if it will conflict with potential underlying contamination, and will return to the item at the Dec. 1 meeting, which will also include the application for 72 Clark Point Road. That meeting will take place at the Southwest Harbor Fire Station at 6 p.m.

title: US and Venezuela sign a deal to reestablish military ties, Hegseth says
text:
US and Venezuela sign a deal to reestablish military ties, Hegseth says
The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties, from training to intelligence sharing, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday on a visit with the South American nation's interim leaders.
Hegseth said that following the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro by the U.S. military, the country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.”
He also praised the “close cooperation” with interim President Delcy Rodriguez that allowed officials “to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all.”
The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.
Rodríguez separately lauded the opportunity to strengthen the military partnership. “I hope that this technical-military cooperation … can be brought to its highest possible level, so that ... we may address common threats,” she said.
Hegseth's visit underscores efforts by President Donald Trump's administration to deepen its influence in the South American country since U.S. forces ousted Maduro in January.
Hegseth is the latest member of Trump’s Cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap its oil reserves and critical minerals. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.
The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.
The U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump returned to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.
To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs.
Hegseth’s visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years. Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture. Rodríguez’s court-allowed term expired in July, but she continues to function as Venezuela’s head of state.
Opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by his country, which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.
The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.
The Trump administration says it has returned more than $12 billion, or almost 99%, of the revenue obtained from the sales of Venezuelan oil back to the country under the terms of the energy deal reached with Rodríguez’s government, according to a report released this month.

title: Letter: Senators should reject permitting reform bill
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I’m happy to see that Attorney General Aaron Frey recently signed a letter in opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), but I was frustrated to learn that Sen. Angus King voted to advance the legislation to a full vote before the U.S. Senate that could come any day.
I think this bill is an affront to longstanding environmental protections and yet poses as “pro-environment.” In promoting new energy development, the bill weakens protections for endangered species, puts limits on scientific review, and creates formidable roadblocks for communities who oppose incoming projects that could harm their coastlines.
Worse, it would lock in unpopular proposals in the works by the Trump administration to expand offshore oil drilling and deep-sea mining.
Although the bill includes transmission improvements to help bring about more clean energy projects, it does so at the expense of the same environment those projects are supposed to protect.
America’s core environmental laws have safeguarded our environment and public health for more than 50 years, and they shouldn’t be dismantled so that unpopular dirty and dangerous proposals can be approved more quickly.
Sens. King and Susan Collins should vote “no” on BAAJA when it comes to a floor vote. There is simply too much at stake.
Lucy Baker
Waterville

title: Man accused of kidnapping teen and her dog before abandoning her nearly 200 miles from home
text:
DARLINGTON COUNTY, SC (WMBF/Gray News) - An Ohio man is accused of kidnapping a teenage girl and abandoning her about 200 miles away, authorities said.
Matthew Morris Hawkins, 41, was charged with kidnapping, grand larceny and contributing to the delinquency of a minor, authorities said.
Deputies responded to the 17-year-old’s home on Aug. 6 after she was reported missing.
Hawkins allegedly took the teen and her labradoodle to Martinsville, Virginia where he abandoned her.
The Henry County Sheriff’s Office found the teen on Aug. 7.
The next day, Kentucky State Police arrested Hawkins in Winchester, Kentucky, where he had the dog with him.
Hawkins was initially held at the Clark County Detention Center before being extradited to Henry County, Virginia.
The investigation remains active.

title: Grandmother, 3-year-old die in fire after she went back into home to try to save him
text:
POCAHONTAS, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) — A grandmother and her 3-year-old grandson died in an Iowa house fire on Nov. 13 after family said she went back inside the burning home in an attempt to save him.
Elizabeth “Lisa” George, 65, and Rowan George were discovered in the hallway to the left of the living room. George was found lying on top of Rowan to protect him, family members said.
Family members said officials told them Rowan had no serious burns and that George took the brunt of the fire.
Fire reported on 2nd Avenue Northwest
The fire was reported around 4:53 p.m. at a home in the 400 block of 2nd Avenue Northwest.
Authorities said people who were out walking saw George come out of the home yelling for help. She then went back inside as the witnesses noticed smoke coming from the eaves.
Police officers tried to enter the house, but the fire was too intense, authorities said.
Firefighters from Pocahontas and several nearby departments fought the blaze. Once it was extinguished, George and Rowan were found inside. Both were taken by ambulance to Pocahontas Community Hospital, where they were pronounced dead.
A preliminary investigation, with assistance from the Iowa State Fire Marshal’s Office, indicates the fire started in a baseboard heater in the living room and does not appear suspicious, authorities said.
Remembering George and Rowan
George was an Army veteran whose family remembers her as caring, funny, loving, smart and strong. She loved Pepsi, rocks, her cat Maggie and Eeyore, the family said, but nothing more than her children and grandchildren.
“She would give them anything, even her life. We’re proud to call her Mom and Nama,” the family said in a statement.
Rowan turned 3 in August. His family described him as “daddy’s little helper and mommy’s little boy” who loved Paw Patrol, tools and cars, as well as wrestling with his big brother.
“He brightened everyone’s day just by the joy he got from life. Our days are darker without him,” the family said.
Community support and injured responders
More than a dozen businesses and organizations are coming together to help the family following the fire.
The family has a message for Siouxland: “Hug your loved ones a little closer, for them.”
Mitch Harrison, Pocahontas fire captain, said it is hard for the responders because they have children about the same age. He said the responders are “like a brotherhood.”
Firefighter Eric Buckner was hospitalized following the fire. He is still recovering but is expected to make a full recovery.
A Pocahontas police officer, identified as Dalton Hogan, was also injured. Authorities said the officer’s injuries were not life-threatening and that the officer was released after observation.
The Pocahontas County Sheriff’s Office, along with fire, police and EMS departments from around the area, assisted with the crash investigation.
The community has also put together a GoFundMe for the George family.

title: Maine's eviction prevention program will close to new applications Nov. 30
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An eviction prevention program for Maine residents will stop taking new applications at the end of the month.
MaineHousing and the nonprofit Project HOME, which operates the program, announced Wednesday that funding will be exhausted soon. The eviction prevention program provides assistance to households that have fallen behind on rent and may face eviction.
Maine lawmakers set aside $11 million for the program this year. Applications have been open for about two months.
MaineHousing is encouraging those who believe they qualify to submit an application by Nov. 30. But the agency cautioned that applying does not guarantee assistance will be available.
Households are eligible if they are behind on rent and earn less than 60% of the area median income.
The program will make a one-time payment to eligible households to catch up on rent and up to 12 months of rental assistance, not to exceed $9,600. The payments go directly to the eligible household’s landlord.
MaineHousing is encouraging people looking for more information about the eviction prevention program to visit the agency’s website.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

WATERVILLE — Alfond Youth & Community Center and Mid-Maine Chamber of Commerce, through the Central Maine Community Betterment Collaborative, are presenting the Festival of Trees this weekend.
Participation in this year’s event continues a fabulous holiday tradition. At the same time, money raised supports families in the community experiencing food insecurity through the services of Alfond Youth & Community Center and funds workforce development services and assistance through the Mid-Maine Chamber of Commerce, meeting a need existing throughout our region.

This year’s wonderful family event will be held at Kennebec Valley Community College, Kennebec Room – Carter Hall, 92 Western Ave. Fairfield, Nov. 20-22 and Nov. 27-29. Hours on both Fridays and Saturdays are 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. On Sunday, Nov. 22, hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on the final day, Nov. 29, hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m..

Children are also given a free book upon arrival. This year, Santa will be joining us from 1 to 4 p.m. on Saturday, Nov. 21 and Sunday, Nov. 22.
Purchase and drop your individual tree tickets (just 50 cents each) into the bucket of your favorite tree, and you could go home with a beautifully decorated tree complete with all trimmings, gift cards, and merchandise displayed. Tree winners will be drawn after 5 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 29 and notified that evening. Trees will be available for pickup on the following Monday and Tuesday.
This year’s 50/50 experience has also been enhanced by increased prize amounts, with a maximum payout of $10,000 daily. Tickets are just 50 cents each. Winners will be drawn each day, and you do not need to be present to win.
