title: Wiscasset remembers Judy Flanagan
text:
Wiscasset Selectboard Chair Alissa Eason rose and made the following statement at the start of the board’s Nov. 17 meeting:
“Our town has recently learned that a dear and valued citizen has passed away: Judy Flanagan … She had a really rich and meaningful life that was important to our town in so many ways. She was, as her last job, the children's librarian at (Wiscasset) Public Library. And she really believed in education, books, literature, children, reading, etc.
“For the town, she was the first woman selectboard member that our town has ever had. That was in 1984. So we’d like to recognize all of the many things that she did for Wiscasset.”
Eason then noted Flanagan’s obituary was in the Wiscasset Newspaper, and she said a remembrance is planned for Dec. 5 at Wiscasset Community Center from 10 a.m. to noon. “Everybody is welcome to come by and pay your respects, last thoughts about Judy, etc., and in lieu of flowers, if anybody wants to make a contribution, make it to the school district, for the libraries; and she would appreciate that.”
A moment of silence followed.

title: America’s Affordability Crisis: Excess mortgage costs are holding down borrowers who can least afford it. Here’s what you can do
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
America’s Affordability Crisis: Excess mortgage costs are holding down borrowers who can least afford it. Here’s what you can do
When Chad Cupp was buying a home in 2022, he couldn’t afford to be picky.
Cupp’s $58,000 income and fair credit were no match for a frenzied housing market that wasn’t kind to anyone with limited financial resources. With the help of his co-signing mother and the FHA loan program, he was fortunate to lock in a 4.75% interest rate on a $280,000 home.
And yet, what looks affordable on paper doesn’t always feel affordable in practice. Cupp is now married. But even with dual incomes, his monthly housing payment, which has risen to almost $2,376, remains a significant financial strain.
“You walk this tightrope all the time,” says Cupp, 47, an electrician in Butte, Montana. “Every month there’s something that is not paid or paid late. There’s just not enough [money] to go around.”
Cupp’s struggle is more than a story about one man who’s stretched too thin. It reflects the broader affordability crisis where buying a home is only half the battle. Even if you can break into the high-rate, high-cost housing market and successfully achieve homeownership, you face another uphill climb: affording your mortgage payments at a time when every other expense in your budget might be rising too.
Housing is the largest burden in American budgets — 34% of the average person’s costs go to it, according to October 2026 BLS data. That leaves less money available for anything else. In fact, 27% of adults say they can’t afford all of their bills, according to recent Pew Research Center data that highlights the affordability challenge millions of Americans faced in 2026.
America's Affordability Crisis
Millions of people are struggling with affordability challenges, and Bankrate is committed to highlighting the causes and the best solutions available.
Read more of our work
Adding to that pressure is the Hidden Homeownership Tax, which Bankrate research shows is contributing to 87% of American borrowers overpaying on their mortgages. This surcharge makes homeownership even less affordable, especially for people with lower incomes who are facing a higher-rate environment than Cupp encountered.
For borrowers earning less than $49,000 before taxes, their average overpayment in 2025 was six times higher relative to their income than for borrowers earning $500,000 or more, according to our analysis. And for the largest share of American homeowners — people like Cupp who earn closer to $50,000 or under $199,000 — their overpayment is almost triple that of their highest-earning counterparts.
Cupp, who’s also facing rising property taxes and homeowners insurance premiums, is not alone. Research from the Urban Institute highlights how housing costs have outpaced income growth.
The reality is, the burden of housing affordability isn’t distributed equally: While wealthier Americans have more resources to weather rising homeownership costs, lower- and middle-income homeowners are being crushed by the very asset meant to provide financial security and grow their wealth. Every dollar spent on their mortgages means less money for savings, investments, and just about everything else.
Data: The burden of mortgage overpayment rises as a homebuyer’s income falls
Mortgage overpayment can make homeownership harder to afford for anyone, but the financial burden isn’t just about how much extra borrowers pay in real dollars.
On average, low-, moderate-, and middle-low-income borrowers overpay by $12,580, $18,816, and $30,712, respectively, over eight years, the median period most Americans keep their mortgages. This is much less than the $61,805 paid by high-income borrowers.
Although lower-income families pay less in dollar terms and carry smaller loans on average, these costs take up a larger share of their income.
Source: Bankrate analysis of 2025 HMDA data 
*Figures don’t sum to 100 because of an unknown percentage in the data
Cupp feels the impact of the overpayment burden every day as his income and high mortgage costs constantly collide. He entered mortgage mitigation twice with his lender to catch up on payments. This includes help from the federal government’s Homeowner Assistance Fund, which saved him from foreclosure twice. His experience comes as more homeowners are facing similar financial pressures. Property data firm ATTOM Data Solutions says foreclosure filings in the first six months of 2026 rose 21% compared to the same time last year.
Despite his regrets about buying his home, Cupp vows to do “anything” he can to keep it. The electrician has taken a side job delivering packages for Amazon Flex and fears his wife may soon be forced to do the same. Cupp also enrolled in a payment plan after falling behind on his power bills. The pressure of juggling the mounting obligations also took a toll on his well-being. He says he developed an ulcer because of all the stress.
“I worry about the mortgage every month,” he says. “I worry about being able to pay it.”
Bankrate findings are consistent with…
The U.S. Census Bureau’s 2025 American Community Survey highlights the widening gap between household incomes, rising housing costs, and families’ ability to afford homeownership. The median percentage of monthly household income spent by people with a mortgage rose 21.9% in 2025. Rising mortgage payments are a major driver of that burden, with the median monthly cost rising to $1,598.
Mortgage repayment hits lower-income borrowers harder in these ways, too
Income is a defining factor in how difficult it is for families to manage housing costs and mortgage overpayment in particular. It’s a simple numbers game: a family with earnings in the low six figures — let alone one earning $49,000 — has considerably less room to absorb an additional housing expense than a family earning more.
The sting of closing costs, down payments
Cupp had second thoughts about buying his home well before the ink dried on his signed mortgage documents. The $280,000 purchase required him to dip into his entire $18,000 in savings, and he still hasn’t recovered financially.
His experience reflects a broader problem. The Pew Research survey shows that more than half (53%) of Americans don’t have rainy-day funds and can’t cover three months of expenses in an emergency. For lower-income families — which Pew defines as having adjusted incomes of less than $50,700 — the percentage rises to 77%. This is at odds with the common-sense advice that we should all have three to six months of expenses tucked away for emergencies. For many homeowners, limited savings can make it even harder to keep up with mortgage payments and unexpected expenses that may crop up.
“I always like to have a $2,000 or $3,000 buffer in my checking account,” Cupp says. “Buying a home really took that away.”
Of all income groups, low-income buyers are stretched the most by upfront mortgage costs. Bankrate’s research found a buyer earning $49,000 or less has to come up with about $5,503 in closing costs when buying a home. This is roughly equal to 14.8% of their annual income, the highest burden of any income group.
Source: Bankrate analysis of HMDA data
On top of closing costs, there’s the standard 3% to 3.5% down payment ($5,400 to $6,300) on the average $181,255 purchase loan for low-income buyers in 2025, as reported by HMDA. That means a low-income buyer would need to bring roughly $11,000 to $12,000 to closing, equivalent to 30% to 32% of their annual pre-tax income.
“If 30% to 40% of your income is going toward paying your monthly mortgage costs for a lower-income family, that’s the difference between having an emergency amount of money or wherever else they need to put it,” says the Urban Institute’s Walsh.
This problem isn’t exclusive to low-income Americans. Moderate-income buyers ($50,000 to $99,000) surrender a fifth of their pre-tax annual income to obtain the keys to their home, while middle-income buyers ($100,000 to $199,000) must give up about 14% to 15% of their earnings.
The long-term cost of not being able to buy down an interest rate
Lower-income buyers often face a one-two punch when trying to afford a home. Not only may they have a harder time coming up with the down payment and closing costs, but their limited cash can also leave them paying more on their mortgage once they finally get one.
Lower-income buyers who have exhausted their liquid savings to meet closing requirements may have to forgo discount points that could lower their mortgage rate and save them money.
The same buyers may also be forced to accept lender credits to keep their application from being rejected. Lender credits cover some closing costs in exchange for a higher rate. In 2025, nearly 790,000 low-, moderate-, and middle-income borrowers took lender credits, according to Bankrate’s analysis of HMDA data. Although some higher-income homebuyers accept lender credits to preserve cash, for buyers with limited savings, the trade-off can make purchasing a house today possible but increase costs over time.
Our research also found that over the first eight years of homeownership, mortgage interest and fees consume 31.6% of low-income homeowners’ annual gross income, the highest of all income groups. While the percentage drops as incomes rise, the overpayment still eats up a significant portion of the budget for moderate- and middle-income folks.
For Cupp, the reality of those costs became clear only after he moved into his home.
“You’re just so pumped about being a homeowner,” he says. “Then you have the first mortgage payment, and you don’t really know the gravity of the situation.”
The mortgage insurance penalty behind FHA loans
For lower-income buyers, a FHA loan can be a lifeline in an increasingly expensive housing market. With a 620 credit score that might qualify him for a conventional loan, Cupp believed an FHA loan would give him an even better chance of getting approved for a mortgage. But the same loan program that helped make homeownership possible is the main source of his angst.
According to HMDA data, low- and moderate-income borrowers made up more than half of FHA loan borrowers in 2025. FHA loans are a go-to option for lower-income buyers because of their competitive interest rates, less stringent credit score requirements, and low down payments.
But even with all their perks, FHA loans can make homeownership more expensive over time. It all comes down to two FHA mortgage insurance premiums (MIPs): annual and upfront. Both are designed to protect the lender if you default on the loan.
Annual MIPs are typically paid monthly. If you put down more than 10%, the MIP will automatically drop off after 11 years. But if you put down less than 10%, you can’t get rid of MIP unless you refinance your mortgage or sell your home. An executive order from the Trump Administration in October 2026 directed federal agencies to start a pilot program to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on future loans once borrowers meet the requirements, but no go-live date was announced.
Cupp is constantly reminded of his $180 monthly MIP payment that will stay with him for the life of the loan.
“I should have asked more questions, but it was my first time buying a home, and frankly, I was a fish out of water,” he says.
How much are annual FHA MIPs?
FHA annual premiums typically range from 0.15% to 0.75% of the loan balance, depending on your loan term, loan amount, and loan-to-value ratio. For a loan of $321,475 — the average FHA purchase loan in 2025 as reported by HMDA — the monthly cost could range from $40.18 to $200.86.
On top of the annual MIP is the FHA loan’s mandatory upfront MIP, which is 1.75% of the loan amount. For that same $321,475 loan, that adds an additional $5,626 charge at closing.
Mortgage insurance premiums are the reason FHA loans cost nearly twice as much at closing as conventional loans ($11,954 vs. $6,264, a $5,690 difference), according to Bankrate’s analysis. While you can pay the full amount at closing, nearly all FHA borrowers roll upfront MIPs into their loan balance. This not only increases the amount they owe but also the interest they pay over time.
“A lot of people wrongly think that at least it gets rolled into the loan most times, so ‘it doesn’t really affect me,’” says Alan Silber, a longtime mortgage broker in South Carolina. Silber points out that for someone putting down 3.5%, the cost of MIP could add up to nearly as much as the down payment, depending on the purchase price of the home.
The result? FHA loan or not, homeowners who already earn less may be forced to make financial sacrifices in areas like saving for retirement, building an emergency fund, or paying down debt.
“If you max out a mortgage, even though you are qualified, all these other things are going to take a hit over time,” adds Silber.
The equity drain happening behind the scenes
How to keep your mortgage from eating up a burdensome share of your income
While 87% of homeowners overpay on their mortgage, the stakes are simply higher for lower-income borrowers. There are steps you can take to lessen the blow, and your options depend on where you find yourself in the process.
If you are thinking about buying a home
Don’t let FOMO drive a six-figure decision: If you are concerned that mortgage rates may keep rising as they have in 2026, that shouldn’t be the reason you rush to buy a home now. Before buying, plug in your information into a home affordability calculator. Make sure you can still afford your home even if you lose your income or if property taxes, homeowners insurance, or other expenses rise. If your circumstances are shaky, it might make sense to pause your search and commit to shoring up your finances.
Shop around for your mortgage: When money is tight, your mortgage takes up a large share of your monthly income, and it also impacts what you can afford. Avoid overpaying by shopping around and comparing multiple lender offers. Get at least three quotes from a mix of banks, credit unions, and online lenders. Compare the loan estimates side by side, and ideally on the same day, to help you make an informed decision.
Ask lenders to lay out your options: Don’t assume a specific loan type might be better for you. A loan officer won’t necessarily compare the total costs of a conventional, FHA, or VA loan (if eligible) unless you ask. For example, Fannie Mae HomeReady and Freddie Mac Home Possible loans only require 3% down and $0 in upfront mortgage insurance fees. The biggest purchase you will likely ever make deserves more than a quick “yes.”
Look at the short- and long-term costs: Don’t get roped in by a lower monthly payment, which can sometimes mean paying more over the life of the loan. Look beyond the advertised rate and compare the APR (total cost of the loan), plus closing costs and other fees. How much you will pay over time in interest and other costs should factor into your decision-making. Don’t forget to factor in property taxes, homeowners insurance, and contributions to your emergency fund. Use a mortgage calculator to figure out how much you can comfortably afford.
A rule of thumb is that you shouldn’t spend more than 28% of your gross monthly household income on housing costs. If you have additional debt, your housing costs and debt can be bumped up to 36% of your gross income. But don’t let a rule dictate your finances. Only you know if you can handle all of your expenses, even if your costs fall below the threshold.
Utilize state & local housing assistance: State housing finance agencies are located in every state. They offer down payment assistance, including grants, forgivable loans, and zero- or low-interest second mortgages specifically designated for low-income homeowners. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) can connect you with a HUD-approved housing counselor for free or little cost, who can help you review your mortgage and explain your options.
If you have already bought your home
Contact your lender to discuss mortgage mitigation options: If you are struggling with your payments, don’t be afraid to reach out to your servicer. Depending on your financial circumstances, you may have options, including a mortgage forbearance or loan modification.
Refinance only if it makes sense: Refinancing your mortgage replaces your current mortgage with a new one and could help you lower your rate, make your monthly payments more affordable, remove private mortgage insurance, or change your loan terms. Make sure you run the numbers through a refinance calculator to figure out if the benefits outweigh the costs. Be cautious to avoid forfeiting a low, COVID-19-era interest rate, for example, unless absolutely necessary, as it can significantly increase your monthly payment and overall cost of repayment.
Look into mortgage assistance programs: Seek help early if your payments become difficult. Depending on where you live, non-profits and government agencies may offer free help with property taxes or other housing-related costs. A HUD-approved housing counselor can help you review your budget and identify potential assistance programs.
Even with options available to make mortgage payments more manageable, keeping up with the cost of homeownership can still be challenging. Cupp has benefited from mortgage mitigation but hasn’t pursued other options that might help ease the strain of his expensive mortgage. While he’s grown to love his three-bed, one-bath home, he wishes he’d understood the full costs of homeownership before buying.
“I absolutely would not do it again,” he says. “It’s difficult, and I know I’m not the only one out here struggling.”
-  Methodology To measure how mortgage overpayment affects borrowers across different income levels, Bankrate analyzed 30-year mortgage loan originations from public government records and compared them with matched, competitive offers on Bankrate’s mortgage marketplace as of 2025. Overpayment is the difference in total cost between each loan and its matched offer over the first eight years, the average duration of a mortgage. It accounts for interest payments, upfront lender fees, discount points, and lender credits. From the dataset, Bankrate focused on purchase mortgage applicants in five income groups: low-income (<$49K), moderate-income ($50K to $99K), middle-income ($100K to $199K), upper-income ($200K to $499K), and high-income (>$500K). The objective was to measure the annual burden of mortgage overpayment relative to income across income groups. For each loan, we divided the 8-year expected overpayment by 8 to get the annual dollar overpayment, then divided that by the applicant’s exact reported annual income. The final measure for each income group is the mean of those loan-level percentages. We drew on four sources: Bankrate’s proprietary mortgage marketplace data, the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) loan-level dataset, the Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) and loan-level disclosure data from Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae. Together, these sources allowed us to account for competitive pricing, loan originations, borrower credit profiles and household wealth. To keep the comparison fair, our statistical model controlled for 17 different factors that can influence a mortgage rate.
© 2026 Bankrate.com

title: Trump gets a personal tarmac welcome from Xi after landing in China
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump’s trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump’s behalf. He told reporters there was “zero” evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
“Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you’ve identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption,” said Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It’s a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
The White House said that Trump would have two separate meetings on Wednesday with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.
As leaders were introduced on Wednesday night ahead of an APEC group photo, Putin approached Trump. They shook hands and traded greetings.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia’s invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump’s aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
“I think it’s very close to getting it done,” Trump said. “We’re going to have a good meeting on that.”
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. But neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for “working very hard.”
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
“Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes,” Trump said. “I love what you’ve done here.”
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines’ current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 “People Power” uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines’ strongman leader.
Trump called her “always the most beautiful” and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
What’s on the agenda for Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America’s largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China’s trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump’s close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China’s access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that “We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
___
Price reported from Manila, Philippines. AP writers Darlene Superville in Washington and Jim Gomez in Manila contributed to this report.

title: Waymo suspends all driverless taxi rides on freeways after ban in California
text:
Waymo suspends all driverless taxi rides on freeways after ban in California
Waymo has temporarily stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways after California banned the vehicles from state freeways following recent traffic incidents.
The company had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver.
A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service,” though it’s “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel.” The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn't say how long it would last.
Related video: Why are gas prices dropping and how low will they go?
The suspension came after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned the company's robotaxis from freeways that same day. The ban followed two incidents including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman said in a statement.
The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
“The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said.
Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18.
The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions.”
California's restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.”
Kelety reported from Phoenix.

title: Piscataquis Regional Food Center helps 350 families prepare for Thanksgiving
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DOVER-FOXCROFT, Maine (WABI) - With Thanksgiving just around the corner, one food center in Piscataquis County is helping hundreds of families prepare for the holiday.
Since 2022, the Piscataquis Regional Food Center has been organizing annual Thanksgiving food distributions for families. Distribution took place Wednesday morning at the Dover-Foxcroft Food Cupboard.
“We’re finding a huge increase in need regardless of the holiday. Thanksgiving is often very expensive. It’s more expensive this year,” said PRFC executive director Kelly Sirimoglu.
People who booked appointments received Thanksgiving packages through a drive-thru system, with ingredients donated by community members and funds for turkeys collected throughout the year.
“It’s a long project. We have someone that collects funds for the turkeys all year long,” said Sirimoglu. “The turkeys come here and we have volunteers on Monday who went through and packed all the bags.”
In total, the distribution helped provide Thanksgiving items to around 350 households, with around 20 volunteers helping load cars.
One volunteer, board member Dolly Perkins, says her family once relied on a food cupboard where they used to live. Perkins and two of her sons helped to bring bags of Thanksgiving food, helping to support those in need.
“It is very humbling when you’re a recipient, and to be on the other side of it is such a blessing,” said Perkins. “If we can pay that forward, then that is an absolute honor and a blessing to me.”
Sirimoglu says the need has increased for food assistance in order to help families through rough financial periods.
“It’s been a really difficult year for a lot of families. The cost of heating oil and fuel and everything else going up. To be able to help people ensure they get a Thanksgiving dinner on the table is really what this is all about.”

MAINE (WABI) - A program that assists low-income Mainers who are facing eviction from their homes is set to close to new applicants.
The deadline to apply for the Maine Eviction Prevention Program is Monday, November 30 at 5 p.m.
Those who apply by the deadline may not receive funding, however officials with MaineHousing and Project Home said they will make every effort to help all those that sent in their applications on time.

The Maine Eviction Program has been around since 2024 and has already helped more than 1,400 households.

title: Cat lovers can live on a beautiful island for free – if they help care for cats
text:
Cat lovers can live on a beautiful island for free – if they help care for cats
Cat lovers can live on a beautiful Greek island for free – and all they have to do is help care for the furry locals.
Syros is a small island in the Cyclades, a cluster of Greek islands scattered across the Aegean Sea, and the quiet heart of the region.
One of Greece’s most under-the-radar islands, Syros is home to a large population of stray cats, with estimates often cited in the thousands across the small island.
Related video above | Abandoned kitten has surgery to repair deformed legs
With no formal safety net for animals on the island, care for the strays is largely supported by rescues, volunteers and trap-neuter-return programs.
That’s where the nonprofit Syros Cats comes in.
Syros Cats is a rescue and welfare nonprofit for the island’s cats.
It provides care for dozens of long-term residents and runs sterilization, feeding and medical programs for stray cats across the island.
The organization will soon be looking for volunteers to help with its mission in 2027, seeking individuals for July through December. Applications open on Nov. 30.
The best part? Room and board will be provided.
“We welcome volunteers – singles or couples, who are fit, mature, healthy and independent and would like to come for a minimum of a month to help with all aspects of cat care,” the organization wrote on its website. “We offer bed, brunch and utilities, in exchange for about six hours of work a day five days a week. If you have training or experience as a veterinary nurse, or feral cat experience, you’d be particularly welcome, but we’re happy to take any cat lovers, so long as you are prepared to get your hands dirty, be reliable, self-sufficient and can turn up on time.”
The organization said it typically has about four volunteers at any given time – all of whom come from different backgrounds and locations across the globe.
Volunteers would be given their own bedroom, but would share a kitchen and a communal living space with two or three other volunteers.

title: Former Rockland lawyer has been disbarred
text:
A former Rockland lawyer has been disbarred six months after an interim suspension was imposed.
On Oct. 13, Maine Superior Court Justice Michaela Murphy issued an order accepting the surrender of the license to practice law of David Zirschky. Then, U.S. District Court Chief Justice Lance Walker ordered on Nov. 13 that Zirschky be disbarred.
In her order, Murphy noted there is presently a pending investigation into allegations of misconduct. The details of those allegations are in an impounded affidavit.
Murphy had ruled May 18 that Zirschky be suspended until a further order of the court. The court order stated that the decision was based on a confidential affidavit filed by the Maine Board of Overseers of the Bar.
“The Court concludes that the evidence supports the existence of exigent circumstances and that Zirschky appears to be a disabled attorney, currently posing an imminent threat to clients, the public and the administration of justice,” the May order stated.
Attorney Julian Richter was appointed as the receiver of Zirschky’s law practice, Midcoast Law LLC.
Zirschky was admitted to the Maine Bar in 2015.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Biddeford Regional Center of Technology to acquire The Landing School
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Biddeford Regional Center of Technology to acquire The Landing School in Arundel
The Landing School of Boatbuilding and Design, which was set to be auctioned off, will instead be sold to the Biddeford Regional Center of Technology.
In August, The Landing School suspended its academic programs for the 2026-27 school year due to declining enrollment and ongoing funding challenges. School leaders said in August that the closure was not permanent, but the Board of Trustees ultimately could not find a viable way to keep the school open, and announced last month that the school would be closing for good.
The Landing School planned to auction off its real estate property in Arundel, as well as the contents of the school building, but the Biddeford Regional Center of Technology (BRCOT) was able to secure a deal to acquire the building and equipment with support from the Maine Department of Education and private donors.
School officials said the deal will help support future careers in technical education for students across York County.
"This school will not only offer programs to students who attend Biddeford Regional, but also students that attend Sanford tech school," said BRCOT Director Paulette Bonneau.
"It's an opportunity to have a brand-new partnership with Biddeford COT and an opportunity to expand our opportunities for our kids," said Matt Petermann, director of the Sanford Regional Technical Center.
Officials are planning to reopen The Landing School next fall.

title: Allagash Brewing taps national branding expert to lead marketing
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland-based Allagash Brewing Co. has named national branding expert Emily B. Keeney as marketing director.
Keeney joins Maine’s largest brewer after nearly a decade at Oatly, a Swedish maker of oat milk and other dairy-based alternatives. Most recently served as Oatly’s vice president of brand for North America, overseeing the company’s creative strategy.
Previously at 360i, a digital and social marketing agency headquartered in New York City, Keeney developed brand strategies for food, beverage and lifestyle clients. She brings more than 15 years of industry experience.
“Emily understands how to build on what makes a brand special, while finding new ways to bring it to new audiences,” said Allagash founder Rob Tod.
‘Exciting time’
Founded in 1994, Allagash was ranked Maine’s largest brewer in the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists, based on 2024 production.
Today, Allagash distributes its beer in 22 states, Washington, D.C., and select international markets. Its flagship Allagash White, a Belgian-style wheat beer, was recently inducted into the American Craft Beer Hall of Fame.
Keeney is the latest addition to Allagash’s leadership team. Matt Place was recently named national sales director after working at Athletic Brewing Co.
“It is an exciting time for the brewery,” Tod said. “We’re continuing to double down on Allagash White … while bringing in fresh ideas and perspectives to keep our innovation in the craft space going strong.”
Tod was honored as a Mainebiz Business Leader of the Year in 2025.

title: ‘Among Us’ game chat helps lead to FBI arrest in case of teen missing for more than a year
text:
(KSL) - A Colorado mother said an online game chat between her teenage son and a girl from Utah led to the FBI’s arrest of Adam Hunter Harmel in the case of a teen missing for nearly a year and a half.
Khristina Tresp called the way the case came together “miraculous.” She said it started when her son played an online game and met a girl who needed help.
Chat moved from game to Discord
The conversation began during the teenage boy’s session of “Among Us” and moved to Discord.
“She shared with him that she was a runaway and being held against her will by a man that was older than her and was hurting her,” Tresp said.
Tresp then began chatting with the girl herself.
“She only knew the county she was in and the city she was in,” Tresp said.
Mother used property search and Zillow
Tresp, who is based in Colorado, then did her own investigation.
“She found the name of someone inside of the house so I typed that in to reverse property search, and pulled up a few addresses in the area,” Tresp said.
Tresp then used Zillow.
“I started sending her photos of the pictures of the homes off of Zillow so that I could be sure that she knew where she was at for sure. Once she saw the second house that I sent her, she said, ‘Yes, that’s it. That’s where I’m at,’” Tresp said.
Tresp called the FBI, and agents arrested Harmel.
Court documents detail allegations
Court documents say Harmel met the girl from Garden City, Utah, online in May 2025 and drove her to Oregon, where he would not let her leave.
According to the documents, Harmel sexually assaulted the girl repeatedly over the next 17 months. When agents searched the house, they recovered several knives and a machete.
Investigators wrote that Harmel expressed a desire to kidnap other minors, bind them, have sex with them and then injure or kill them.
“It was just one of those moments where it takes your breath away to know that you’ve actually found someone that is in desperate need of help,” Tresp said.
Tresp said she is grateful she was able to intervene.
Federal charge
A federal grand jury has charged Harmel with transportation with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
Court documents say there is evidence he tried to abduct one other minor and that he was involved in the production and distribution of child pornography.

title: Man, 50, allegedly stabs another man to death at party celebrating his release from prison
text:
HOPKINS, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - Authorities in South Carolina say a 50-year-old man is facing charges after he allegedly stabbed another man to death at a party celebrating his release from federal prison.
Cedrick Cunningham, 50, was charged Monday with murder and possession of a weapon during a violent crime, according to the Richland County Sheriff’s Office.
Cunningham is accused of killing 42-year-old Andre Smith, who was found dead in a car Saturday in Hopkins. Deputies say Smith had a large laceration on his chest.
According to authorities, Cunningham was at a celebration held after his release from federal prison when he and Smith got into an altercation. That allegedly led to Cunningham stabbing Smith.
Deputies say Smith then got in his car and fled the area.
Cunningham was being held at the Alvin S. Glenn Detention Center, as of Tuesday.
Suspect’s criminal history
Details of Cunningham’s reported release from prison were not immediately clear, but federal records show he was sentenced to 10 years in 2019 after pleading guilty to a weapons charge.
Other documents from his case note that prior drug convictions qualified Cunningham for status as an armed career criminal under the federal Armed Career Criminal Act.
Documents also show that a judge denied a request for compassionate release made by Cunningham in 2023.
A search of the Federal Bureau of Prisons website shows that Cunningham was located at the Residential Reentry Management office in Raleigh, North Carolina.
WIS has reached out to the bureau for more details about Cunningham’s status.

title: Oxygen And A Lit Cigarette: Burns Send Auburn Mother And Son To Hospital
text:
While the use of home oxygen systems can help people with breathing problems live full lives away from hospital settings, there is a reason why public safety officials always issue warnings against smoking near those oxygen tanks.
Read More: Maine Teen Charged With Attempted Murder In Leeds House Fire
The Oxygen that comes in those tanks is pure, and when a flame is introduced near it, it can be very dangerous.
In fact, the City of Bangor has an entire section on its website that explains the dangers of such behavior.
"When exposed to an open flame or spark, pure oxygen can ignite, and if a fire is already burning around home oxygen, a bottle can suddenly and violently explode or release O2, giving the fire more fuel and making the fire far larger and more dangerous....When more oxygen is in the air, the fire will burn hotter and faster. Smoking should not be allowed in a home where oxygen is used. Even if oxygen is not being used, it may have saturated the home, including clothing, curtains, furniture, bedding, hair, and anything in the area."
That's exactly what Investigators with the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office think happened in a case in Auburn Tuesday, leaving a woman and her son badly burned.
According to officials with the Maine Department of Public Safety, the Auburn Fire Department was called to the Reed Street apartment where 74-year-old Deborah Luna and her 51-year-old son, Roger Bouchard, had been badly burned.
That's when the Fire Marshals were called in to find out what happened.
"The investigation determined that Luna had been seated on a couch while using supplemental oxygen and smoking. According to information provided during the investigation, Bouchard was inside the residence when he heard a sudden noise and saw his mother’s clothing catch fire.
Bouchard immediately attempted to extinguish the flames by assisting his mother with a stop, drop, and roll maneuver. During his efforts to extinguish the flames, Bouchard sustained significant burns to his left thigh and hands, requiring medical treatment."
Authorities believe the fire was accidental, but the investigation is still active.
Read More: Proper Ash Disposal Urged After Oxford Friday The 13th Fire
Both Luna and Bouchard suffered severe burns that required hospitalization and medical treatment. Luna was taken to Maine Medical Center's burn unit because her injuries required specialized treatment, and her son suffered severe burns on his hands and thigh.

title: With measles spreading, do you need a booster shot?
text:
Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot?
Generally, experts say, the answer is no.
“Most people are protected without getting a booster shot” because they’ve either been vaccinated or had measles as kids, said Dr. Richard Martinello at Yale School of Medicine.
The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress. Last year, Canada lost its measles-elimination designation.
Doctors say getting two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is the best way to protect against one of the most contagious viruses in the world. The vaccine usually protects people for life, as does having had the disease. Americans born before 1957 are considered to have “presumptive evidence” of immunity because almost everyone back then got measles during childhood.
For some people, boosters may be a good idea
But doctors say certain people should consider getting boosters.
One group is healthcare workers born before 1957 without proof of immunity. They’re more likely than the general public to come in contact with people who have measles, so they may get it or even spread it to vulnerable patients.
Adults vaccinated between 1963 and 1967 also might want to think about boosters. During those years, some children received an inactivated vaccine that uses a killed version of the virus, which was less effective than the current vaccine containing live, weakened virus. Doctors said people who know they got the inactivated vaccine or aren’t sure should get at least one dose of the live MMR vaccine. One dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, while two doses are 97% protective.
Until 1989, only a single dose was standard. Now the recommendation is for adults to have at least one documented dose of MMR. Two doses are recommended for certain people in high-risk groups who don’t have other evidence of immunity.
“People who have had no shots should go get vaccinated, if they weren’t born before 1957,” said Dr. Joshua Sharfstein at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “If they have had only one shot, they may want to consider whether they’re in a risk group for a second shot.”
That risk group, he said, includes people in school, healthcare workers, international travelers or people living with family members who have compromised immune systems. In places with active measles outbreaks, health officials sometimes recommend that everyone have two shots, Sharfstein said.
For people who have only had one shot, especially in an area where measles is circulating, “it’s always a good idea to talk with your physician about whether another shot is needed,” Martinello said.
Tracking down your vaccination status
But what if you don’t know how many shots you received or even if you’ve been vaccinated?
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests asking your parents or doctor, checking with your high school or college health services or reaching out to previous employers that required immunizations. You can also try contacting your state’s health department; some states have registries that include adult vaccines.
If you’re still unsure about your vaccination status, you can talk with your doctor about an MMR immunity blood test that can show whether you have antibodies against measles. But Martinello said this isn’t an ideal measure of how safe you are from the virus. Though the test is accurate, he said, scientists don’t know how to link the result perfectly with the level of protection someone might have.
Regardless, doctors said getting a booster just to be safe won’t harm you unless you’re in a group that is not supposed to get the vaccine at all, such as pregnant women.
Now that measles is circulating in the U.S., doctors said it’s crucial to take measures to protect yourself.
“This is a moment to not just check for yourself, but also encourage others to make sure that they are adequately vaccinated,” Sharfstein said. “Too many people took measles for granted … or just didn’t think about measles. But now it’s something to think about.”

title: Mariners shut out by Steelheads
text:
Ty Pelton-Byce recorded a hat trick, Arno Tiefensee made 28 saves, and the Idaho Steelheads opened a three-game series against the Maine Mariners with a 5-0 victory in an ECHL game Wednesday night in Boise, Idaho.
The Steelheads were 3 for 7 on the power play, including a first-period goal by Mason Nevers. Pelton-Byce made it 2-0 midway through the second period, then added two power-play goals in the third, one of which came with a 5-on-3 advantage.
Liam Malmquist assisted on all three goals by Pelton-Byce.
Caleb Price capped the scoring with 1:20 remaining.
The series continues with games Friday and Saturday night.

title: Downtown Bangor gets a ‘micro public market’ just in time for the holidays
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangin’ Whoopie is opening a market for local vendors in downtown Bangor on Wednesday, just in time for holiday shopping.
The new space at 76 Main St. will give shoppers a chance to browse a variety of vendors under one roof and give local craftspeople, chefs and other entrepreneurs a low-cost way to try selling their products. It will also add 30 seats, four public bathrooms and a deli to a stretch of downtown that’s about to get busy with holiday events.
James Gallagher, who owns Bangin’ Whoopie, said he envisions it as a “micro public market,” a “really cool space that’s been missing” from downtown.
The market will be open 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday. On Sunday, it’ll be open 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Customers can enter through a shared entryway with the Maine Discovery Museum and browse rows of vendor kiosks around the edges of the room. They can order food through a window that connects the market to Bangin’ Whoopie next door.
The menu includes coffee, ice cream, whoopie pies and deli items Gallagher used to offer when Bangin’ Whoopie was on Hammond Street and is now bringing back. Customers can also fill a plate at Bangin’ Whoopie’s hot bar or salad bar and bring it next door to eat.
The market has tables and 30 seats, more than the Bangin’ Whoopie storefront, so visitors can shop, grab lunch, bring takeout from a neighboring business or just sit and read. The patio seating outside his store has been popular, a sign people want more places to sit, Gallagher said.
He’s especially looking ahead to Bangor’s annual Festival of Lights parade Dec. 5, when crowds descend on downtown. The market will add bathrooms and a place where festival-goers can step inside for a hot chocolate, he said.
He also expects the market to be busy on Plaid Friday and Small Business Saturday next week and said he’s had “quite a bit of interest” from sellers for those days. Vendors signed up so far sell skin care products, custom ornaments, toys and baked goods.
Vendors will pay $25 a day Sunday through Wednesday and $45 a day Thursday through Saturday. They can choose which days to sell, Gallagher said.
Gallagher has had the space for about four years and mostly used it for storage. He wanted to turn it into a marketplace inspired by larger venues like Boston’s Faneuil Hall, he said.
Eventually, he plans to revamp the large commercial kitchen in the back of the market, move his whoopie pie production there and rent the kitchen to local chefs and bakers who need a place to get started.
Having everything set up so vendors can just bring their products will “give people a chance to test the market,” Gallagher said. He wants to build a “community of entrepreneurs.”

title: Taking a Closer Look at Bates’ 56,000-Acre 1864 Land Grant
text:
How much land does Bates College own? Today, the college’s main campus is roughly 130 acres, with Bates-Morse Mountain Conservation Area and Shortridge Coastal Center taking up another 700 or so acres combined. But at one point in its history, the college owned roughly 56,000 acres, more than 75 times the size of its current holdings, thanks to a grant from the Maine government.
During the 19th century, the U.S. government funded colleges and universities in an attempt to make them more accessible to the working class. The endowments were not in cash, however, but in land. The idea was that universities could sell this land, or extract resources from it, and make money instead of being given it directly. This was known as a land grant, and the revenue it created was foundational to these institutions’ early success.
But what of the history of the land itself, and the people who call it home? In a Short Term class on Wabanaki History in Maine last spring, students discussed the legacy of the land grant system. Before it could be granted, land had to be expropriated from Indigenous communities. Land grants and the money they generated are not just transactions: they are a crucial part of an institution’s legacy, and a practice firmly rooted in a history of dispossession and colonialism.
All told, over 100 universities across the U.S. received land grants, including several institutions in Maine. The University of Maine received 210,000 acres, while Colby and Bowdoin received some 234,000 collective acres between them. Bates College, however, was listed as having only received cash.
In the fall of 2025, through his work at the Muskie Archives, librarian Sam Howes discovered striking new information about Bates’ history with land grants. For the Short Term course’s final project, Sarah McOsker ‘28, Sofia Schaffer ‘28 and I spoke with Howes, conducting our own research in order to build a clearer picture of what this information means for the college.
Howes had originally been researching the institution’s transition from the Maine State Seminary to Bates College when he made his discovery. Bates received its current name in 1864, and along with it an endowment of $15,000. But that wasn’t all: Howes also came across a document from the Maine State legislature which also granted the college roughly 56,000 acres of land, distributed between the unincorporated townships of T8 and T10 R17 WELS on the northwestern border of the state.
Bates owned the land for one year, after which they sold all of it to a Bangor-based logging enterprise. While 56,000 acres might seem insignificant in comparison to UMaine, Bowdoin and Colby’s grants, Bates made $23,000 in this transaction, equivalent to more than $500,000 in today’s money. Though it is not yet clear how exactly this money was spent, such a sizable endowment undoubtedly played a role in Bates’s early development.
Associate Professor of History Joseph Hall, who studies Native American interactions with Europeans prior to the 1850s, noted that “given the obvious material benefits that have come from Bates’s access to Wabanaki land, it’s worth asking what the material reparations might be.”
Kazumi Haag ‘28 developed a proposal for a tuition waiver, similar to the one offered by the University of Maine, as her final project in the Wabanaki History in Maine Short Term course. “Once you find out that you’re a land grant institution, there are certain responsibilities that come with that,” she said. Haag emphasized the importance of concrete action, comparing the tuition waiver to a written statement like a land acknowledgement: “Having a land acknowledgement is not something you just get… Even if you acknowledge and teach [Wabanaki history] in your classes, the lack of purposeful action towards a goal makes that acknowledgement not meaningful to anybody.”
May Fastaia ‘27, Anthropology and Classical and Medieval Studies double major, is writing her thesis on Bates-Wabanaki relations. Like Haag, Fastaia said she has been reflecting on “what kinds of policies [Bates College] has the right to apply,” noting that “there are certain [actions] that colleges have done that they can do only because of their specific situation.”
Fastaia praised Hamilton College’s land acknowledgement. According to the college’s website, Hamilton views its relationship with the Oneida Indian Nation as a partnership that stretches back more than 230 years. Their land acknowledgement was written in direct conversation with the Oneida and was preceded by strong support of Indigenous rights. Fastaia argued that this history gives Hamilton the right to publish such a land acknowledgement.
Fastaia also pointed out that Bates’s own history of Indigenous relations has been complicated and, at times, problematic. As part of her thesis, she has been studying Bruce Bourque, former lecturer in Anthropology at Bates College. In a lawsuit lobbied by the Penobscot Nation against the State of Maine, Bourque, then actively working at Bates, testified against the Penobscot’s right to steward their namesake river. Bourque’s testimony as expert witness in the case eroded Penobscot sovereignty in Maine, contributing to the ruling that the nation’s reservation includes islands in the Penobscot river, but not the waters themselves, despite the latter’s longstanding significance in Penobscot culture and subsistence. Although Bourque no longer lectures at Bates, his arguments were deeply offensive to the Wabanaki community. According to lectures from Hall in the course Wabanaki History in Maine, some Wabanaki have since expressed hesitancy to collaborate with Bates, citing the fact that the college has done little to address or take accountability for Bourque’s actions and their consequences.
In this context, Fastaia said, a land acknowledgement risks feeling performative and hollow. Part of Fastaia’s thesis involves exploring “the [specific actions] we can [take] that actually address what we’ve done as an institution.” For example, like Haag, she hopes that the financial nature of the land grant inspires economic reparations. Fastaia notes that tangible actions such as these can help a college work towards building new and better relationships with Indigenous people.
Fastaia, Haag and Hall each stressed that any reparative action should be taken in concert and conversation with Wabanaki people. Additionally, all three emphasized the importance of educating students, faculty, and staff about the issue.
Over the past few years, Bates College has begun to more openly acknowledge its complicated history with the slave trade in the United States. Though the college was founded by abolitionists, Benjamin Bates owned and profited heavily from several cotton mills. The man, and the college named for him, therefore still profited from slave labor.
Fastaia envisions a similarly nuanced portrayal of the college’s relations with Wabanaki people. “Bates can’t be selective in the history it chooses to portray,” she said.
Similarly, Professor Hall affirmed that the first step towards improving Bates-Wabanaki relations is creating and sharing a clearer picture of the history of those relations. “Really, I think that’s true with any kind of change. You need to learn about it… and you then have to decide what you want to do about it.”
Additional contributions made by Sarah McOsker ‘28 and Sofia Schaffer ‘28.

title: Standish-area school district will receive state funding for new building
text:
The Maine State Board of Education voted last week to place a Standish school on the state’s Approved Projects List for major school construction, MSAD 6 Superintendent Brian Campbell said Monday.
George E. Jack School, one of the district’s six elementary schools, was built in the 1950s and is in need of several renovations and repairs. It ranked fourth of 95 schools on the state’s priority list to receive funding for major construction.
Former Superintendent Clay Gleason said last year that the school is made of wood but lacks sprinklers, is out of compliance with the Americans With Disabilities Act and its heating and cooling system leaks, among other issues. It has portable classrooms that have long exceeded their intended lifespans.
Campbell said the concept for a new building is due in 2029, and SAD 6, which spans Standish, Buxton, Hollis, Limington and Frye Island, will begin the planning process immediately. A new site will also allow the district to consider consolidation — the state has identified six of its other schools as needing overhauls.
One plan Bonny Eagle floated in recent years called for combining five of its six elementary schools at the current middle school, building a new high school and relocating the present middle school at the old high school.
In a message to families, Campbell wrote that the district is “focused on creating a clean, safe facility that supports our students’ academic needs and provides modern resources for the future of education,” adding that there will be opportunities for public input on consolidation and building design.
Major renovation projects are often difficult for Maine school districts to fund on their own. Voters in June approved a referendum question allowing the district to borrow $554,575 through Maine’s zero interest rate School Revolving Renovation Fund program to fund indoor air quality renovations at George E. Jack, and to borrow up to $8.2 million for districtwide repairs and renovations.
SAD 6 is one of the state’s largest school districts by geography and student enrollment. It has more than 3,200 students and 700 employees.

title: Mullin heads to Congress to face questions over flight disruptions, football trip and immigration
text:
Mullin, appearing before Congress, defends his flight to LSU-Texas game after nationwide ground stop
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended before a House committee Wednesday his flight to a weekend LSU-Texas football game as travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights, saying canceling it could have caused confusion.
Mullin spoke at a congressional hearing about threats facing the country at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the college football game.
The hearing in front of the House Homeland Security Committee is a standard yearly opportunity for members of Congress to grill top administration officials over national security threats. But it comes as the U.S. has faced a series of cyber and technology problems that have left Americans feeling vulnerable.
The hearing is also the first opportunity for Democrats after their midterm drubbing of Republicans to grill the Cabinet official who is key to President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. Two others facing questioning are FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and the Trump administration's national intelligence director, Jay Clayton.
Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling
The secretary has faced scrutiny over his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday to watch the LSU-Texas game.
Mullin's flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.
Mullin said the trip had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and that there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.
"If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we're not even willing to fly," Mullin said.
Mullin had said Tuesday and reiterated Wednesday that he is required to fly on government planes and that he personally paid for the trip.
Mullin defends ground stop response
Mullin, whose department includes the agency tasked with protecting the country's cyber infrastructure, was front and center in the Republican administration's response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.
The Trump administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration's telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.
At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn't giving the American public clear answers.
"We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn't have one single incident. That in itself is a great success," Mullin said.
During a news conference Friday with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at the White House, he pushed for more funding for the aging air traffic control system while also assuring the public that the government was not seeing any signs of a deliberate cyberattack.
The Trump administration has been attempting to offer reassurances about a spate of outages over the last week that have affected everything from Microsoft and the Federal Aviation Administration to the banking industry, United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration national security officials have said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.
Clayton told the committee Wednesday that the outages are "not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." Instead, they appear to be "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes."
Mullin's sprawling Department of Homeland Security also includes an agency designed to play a central role in the federal government's response to cyber incidents. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.
But CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump's original pick to lead the agency withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it languished for months in the Senate.
CISA also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the federal government.
Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny
Mullin, whose department includes Customs and Border Protection and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, faced questions over the Republican president's immigration agenda at a time when Democrats are vowing rigorous oversight of everything from immigration detention contracts to the use of force by ICE officers.
Trump has indicated he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff, raising questions over how easily compromise could be reached on the issue.
Mullin took over from ousted Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March after the killing of two American citizen protesters in Minneapolis at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.
Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies across the country.
___
Associated Press writers Eric Tucker in Washington, Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pennsylvania and Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, contributed to this report.

title: Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world’s largest religion
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released Wednesday by the Pew Research Center.
Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity are growing, but Islam is growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, is that Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups.
“It’s the babies,” said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity are much smaller factors than fertility rates.
During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that’s considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.
According to Pew’s latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew’s new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.
The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration.
Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62% of U.S. adults, according to Pew, and will fall below 50% by 2065.
In neighboring Canada, Christians are expected to drop below 50% by 2030, Pew said.
In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41% of the U.S. population and to outnumber Christians in Canada.
Muslims and Christians are expected to keep pace with population growth
The world’s population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070, Pew said. Of the religious groups it analyzed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%.
Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew said. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan.
Over the coming decades, Pew said, most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted.
By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world’s Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing more than threefold to 299 million.
The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline.
For example, the number of people living in Europe will shrink by 17% by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there will drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe’s population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6% to 13%.
In the U.S., Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070.
Several mainline Protestant denominations in the U.S. have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations.
Fertility rates are a driving factor
By Pew’s estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020-2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers.
Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline.
If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia — which currently has the most Muslims.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations are “extremely important” in light of the evolving trends.
“The ‘clash of civilization’ theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides,” she said via email. “Many Christians are not happy to see that Islam will be the world’s largest religion and it’s causing even more angst.”
“I hope people seek opportunities for greater interreligious education,” she added. “Personal contact is important — when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanizes’ the ‘other’ in fruitful ways.”
Alan Cooperman, Pew’s director of religion research, noted that most of the projected proliferation of Muslims and Christians was occurring in countries where they already are the majority — with conversion playing only a minor role.
“I don’t think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians,” he added. “I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims.”
The ‘nones’ are growing in some areas
Many countries have seen a steady proliferation of the “nones” — people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of “nones” but faces a sharp decline in overall population, the ranks of “nones” elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070, Pew said.
The “nones” already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.
___
This version corrects the number of projected Christians in Congo by 2070 to 299 million, instead of 270 million.
___

title: Sarah Tompkins welcomed home to Searsmont after months-long hospitalization
text:
SEARSMONT, Maine (WABI) -Sarah Tompkins, a first responder injured in a mill fire and explosion in Searsmont, was welcomed home Wednesday, just over six months after the incident.
Crews escort Tompkins home
Community EMS and fire crews escorted Tompkins. The route started at the Augusta Civic Center and ended at Searsmont Fire and Rescue.
Interim EMS Chief Amy Drinkwater helped organize the homecoming, which brought together crews from across the state.
“It has been a long six months for everybody, but especially for the people that have been healing. And it’s just amazing to see the support for everybody here, and we’re ready for her to come home,” Drinkwater said.
Tompkins releases letter
Tompkins was treated at Maine Medical Center and Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Massachusetts.
She declined to speak to the media Wednesday but released a letter Monday. In part, she wrote:
“I have worked in EMS for eight years, but for the last 6 months I have been the one being cared for after my worst day.”
She also wrote: “I still have wounds and scars, but I am also filled with so much hope for all of us.”
Town official comments
Searsmont selectman and firefighter Christopher Staples said Tompkins has made a lasting impact on the community.
“She’s got a big heart and she’s been a big part of our community for several years. So, getting her back is a big, big thing for the town,” Staples said.
