title: 'I thank God': After 19 years behind bars, man credits Innocence Project with his release
text:
'I thank God': After 19 years behind bars, man credits Innocence Project with his release
After spending 19 years in prison for a murder he says he didn’t commit, an Oklahoma man is finally home, thanks to the Innocence Project.
'I thank God': After 19 years behind bars, man credits Innocence Project with his release
After spending 19 years in prison for a murder he says he didn’t commit, an Oklahoma man is finally home, thanks to the Innocence Project.
After spending 19 years in prison for a murder he maintains he didn't commit, an Oklahoma man is finally home.
The Oklahoma Innocence Project has been fighting to get Joshua Christon out of prison. Last week, the group made that happen.
Christon was about to graduate high school when he was arrested. Now, he and his legal team hope to raise awareness of the Innocence Project and help reunite more families.
He served 19 years behind bars for a 2007 murder he said he was not responsible for.
"I thank God for the Oklahoma Innocence Project," Christon said. "I was trying to get out of that prison yard as fast as possible, just in case they made a mistake. I’m like, 'Let’s go! Put your foot on the gas!'"
Christon describes first taste of freedom in nearly 2 decades
Christon recalled the night in 2007 when he was arrested for murder.
"I open the door. Literally, they had lasers pointing at my chest, and they grabbed me, and I start asking a question like, 'Why are y’all here?' They said, 'You’ve been charged with first-degree murder,'" Christon said.
He would spend nearly 20 years behind bars.
"Coming in at 18 years old, they sent me to a place called McAlester, the Walls, that’s the worst of the worst. Being a young man not in gangs and trying to be a Christian — that’s something that is unheard of," Christon said.
He spent the years missing out on family milestones and holidays at home.
"You start to doubt yourself, like, 'Man, will you ever be free?'" he said.
In 2023, he connected with the Oklahoma Innocence Project at Oklahoma City University's School of Law.
"I was very ... a skeptic. I was like, can they really do it? Because when you’ve been incarcerated so long, you know, anybody can sell you anything," he said.
The group had multiple meetings with the Oklahoma County District Attorney's Office and came to a resolution, reducing his murder conviction to second-degree murder. He was sentenced to time served.
After a celebratory dinner, he rushed to be reunited with his mother and family.
"When she seen me, she said,' Joshua. Joshua,' and she was crying and so happy to see the joy in her face. That was worth it," Christon said.
He is now enjoying the little things.
"I took like five baths and four showers. Thank God for a good bath. Do not take it for granted, a bath. Let it soak and let the water hit your skin," Christon said. 
But a lot can change in 19 years, even indoor plumbing.
"I use the restroom, and the thing just started flushing. I said, 'Hold on. What’s going on?' I was like, you know, is it demons in his restroom or something? Because I know I ain’t flush the toilet," Christon said.
Christon plans to graduate from Oklahoma Baptist University next spring with a bachelor's degree in Christian studies. He said he hopes to share his story with students and work towards improving nutrition for inmates.
"I have this business proposal, like greenhouses. I believe in fresh produce, and inside incarceration, sometimes you don’t get fresh produce," Christon said. "We think about gut health, A1Cs when people come out because we eat so much processed food, and it’s not good for the body."
Oklahoma Innocence Project helps free those wrongfully imprisoned
Andrea Miller, director of the Oklahoma Innocence Project at OCU School of Law, said the Innocence Project found evidence his defense attorney had never seen.
"Evidence of statements by the co-defendant to an inmate who, where he basically confessed on multiple occasions to being the shooter, but that they didn’t have evidence against him because both the co-defendants were pointing the finger at Joshua since he was the youngest person present at the time," Miller said. "It was clear, though, from the circumstance, the actual physical circumstances of the crime, that he could not have committed the crime."
The Oklahoma Watch reported that the newly discovered materials included the fact that a .45-caliber handgun was found under a co-defendant's bed months after the arrests. Prosecutors also allowed one co-defendant to testify against Christon despite knowing that the other had confessed to the murder in prison.
Miller said she is grateful to reunite Christon with his loved ones.
"To watch him walk out and to have such a belief in his future and all the things that I think that he is capable of doing, it’s an honor to be just part of that process," Miller said.
Now, Miller said she hopes to see the program grow so there can be more success stories.
"The project opened in 2011. So, we’ve just celebrated our 15th anniversary here at the law school, and I believe that we have five releases to date, which on average, it takes 10 years from beginning to exoneration. So, we’re doing OK. But we are limited by our size. So, the more, you know, hands we had on deck, the more work we could do to get more people out," Miller said.

title: Anthropic set to begin trading after pricing its stock at $83 per share in biggest IPO on record
text:
OAKLAND, Calif. (AP) — Anthropic is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday after pricing its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion and surpassing SpaceX as the largest initial public offering on record.
The higher-than-anticipated pricing signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some market uncertainty stemming from the ouster of Nvidia’s CEO and worries about an AI bubble. But the bigger test will be how Anthropic fares on the stock market.
Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totaling $81 billion put Anthropic’s IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June. SpaceX, however, holds a higher valuation, about $1.9 trillion as of Wednesday afternoon.
The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut on Wall Street sometime after the stock market opens at 9:30 a.m. EST under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The company had earlier set a price range of $70 to $78 per share.
Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there’s the spectacular downfall of one of the industry’s biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
The company’s rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year.
IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt
Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.
While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.
Anthropic’s IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.
The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock, 956,351,354 of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 of which are being sold by certain selling stockholders.
AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.
Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.
Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.
Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.
Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.
“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”
___
Associated Press business writers Bernard Condon, Kaitlyn Huamani and Michelle Chapman contributed.

title: Family calls for sedation law changes after father’s death during dental procedure
text:
Family calls for sedation law changes after father’s death during dental procedure
A year after her husband died following a dental implant procedure, Sarah DiMatteo says the loss remains difficult to comprehend.
Anthony DiMatteo, a father of five, died on Sept. 17, 2024, after undergoing a full-mouth dental implant procedure at a Florida dental office.
Now, his family and attorney are advocating for changes to Florida law governing sedation in dental procedures, arguing additional safeguards could help prevent similar tragedies.
"His absence has left us with an emptiness that's really hard to describe with words," Sarah DiMatteo said.
According to Sarah, her husband sought the procedure after years of dental problems.
"Unfortunately, no matter how well he took care of them, he had cracked teeth, teeth that had fallen out and were loose, and he was in a lot of discomfort and pain," she said. "He was embarrassed. He loved to smile and laugh and he felt very self-conscious."
The procedure was expected to be completed in a single day.
Sarah DiMatteo said she dropped her husband off shortly before 7 a.m. on the day of the surgery. About three hours later, she received a call from police informing her he was being rushed to a hospital.
"I've never felt so much panic in my life," she said. "That phone call was terrible."
Doctors later determined Anthony DiMatteo was brain dead.
"I never knew I would not see him awake again when I dropped him off," she said.
According to the St. Lucie County Medical Examiner's Office, Anthony DiMatteo's death was caused by complications from the administration of fentanyl, midazolam and dexmedetomidine during the procedure. The manner of death was ruled accidental.
The medical examiner's report also listed cardiovascular disease, hypertension and diabetes as contributing factors.
Sarah DiMatteo said her husband had a complex medical history, but she believes more scrutiny should have been given to whether he was an appropriate candidate for sedation.
"We trusted without asking those questions," she said. "Now we know."
Under Florida law, dentists who meet training requirements may obtain permits to administer moderate intravenous sedation. State records show Anthony DiMatteo's dentist holds an active Florida Department of Health permit for moderate sedation.
Sarah DiMatteo and her attorney, Mike Grife, are now pushing for legislation that would require a dedicated anesthesia professional or other qualified provider to monitor patients receiving IV sedation during dental procedures, rather than allowing the operating dentist to oversee both the procedure and sedation.
"Wouldn't it make sense to have a physician, anesthesiologist or a certified registered nurse anesthetist who has gone through years of specialized training there to make sure the patient is protected?" Grife said.
Grife argues that asking one person to perform a procedure while simultaneously monitoring sedation and responding to complications creates unnecessary risk.
"Imagine trying to juggle all those things at once," he said. "You're handling the sedation, the dental procedure and, if complications arise, you're supposed to be handling that."
He said the family believes Anthony DiMatteo's death could have been prevented.
"We feel that Anthony's death was preventable, that if the proper safeguards were in place, he would still be here today," Grife said.
For Sarah DiMatteo, the legislative effort is about ensuring other families do not suffer a similar loss.
"It's been devastating," she said. "He was everyone's best friend, but he was really our best friend. And we really miss him."

title: Lawmakers call for national data center construction pause
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Members of Congress are calling for a national moratorium on data center construction until the artificial intelligence field can be regulated.
They said data centers are not helping local communities and, in many cases, are actively harming them.
Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) said the White House is not doing enough on artificial intelligence.
“The alarm bells are flashing. And the president and the White House are asleep at the switch when it comes to AI,” he said.
McGovern said big tech leaders are becoming oligarchs and are enriching themselves at the expense of local communities with data centers.
“These billionaires want to come into our communities, tell us what to do, and make a profit by driving up our utility prices, and wrecking our environment,” he said.
Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Mich.) said data centers do not provide the same community value as an automotive plant.
“The value, the billions of dollars that is being raised to build these data centers, is built on the promise that it’s going to put people out of work,” he said.
Lawmakers said pausing new construction would give Congress time to pass regulations and protect communities from future construction.
Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) said she wants transparency in dealings between big tech and the government.
“We don’t want back door deals and secret handshakes between big tech and the government. We want transparency, community engagement, and strong regulations that protect our air, water, climate and communities,” she said.
It is not yet clear whether the plan has enough support to pass in the next Congress. The Trump administration has attempted to rename AI - artificial intelligence - as SI - super intelligence.

title: Bernie Sanders unveils his plan to push Medicare for All when Democrats take power
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation’s healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities.
Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, is currently the ranking member on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and is expected to become its chairman when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. His agenda, first provided to The Associated Press, lays out the legislative implementation for proposals that he and progressive candidates championed on the campaign trail this cycle.
At the center is Sanders’ longstanding push for Medicare for All, a universal healthcare system that would be implemented over four years. The first year would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guarantee healthcare to children through age 18.
“This is no longer a utopian vision. This is where the American people are,” Sanders said in an interview with the AP.
The proposals offer an early glimpse of how progressives hope to shape the Democratic Party’s priorities after an election that delivered the party control of Congress but also exposed competing visions for its future. With the 2028 presidential election already looming, Sanders is seeking to push Democrats toward a populist economic agenda that he argues has gained broader support.
“I think the election, in my opinion, was a crying out for fundamental change in the way the government does business and the absolute need to protect a struggling working class,” Sanders said. “I think this is a time to bring about very significant changes in policies so that we can actually improve the lives of working families.”
Sanders keeps pushing for Medicare for All
Sanders has long championed a single-payer national health insurance program that would replace most private insurance with a federally administered system providing universal coverage.
His proposal for the new Congress lays out a four-year transition to that system, beginning with expanding Medicare eligibility and benefits. In the second year, the eligibility age would fall to 45, followed by 35 in the third year, before extending coverage to everyone in the fourth year.
“Transforming a system which is 18% of the GDP of America, you don’t do that overnight,” Sanders said of the transitional period.
But the costs of lowering Medicare eligibility are likely to lead to massive debate between the two major political parties as the national deficit stands at $2 trillion, or 6.2% of gross domestic product. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that lowering the age of Medicare eligibility to 60 would increase federal budget deficits by $155 billion over the 2026–2031 period.
Sanders’ prior proposals to pay for the program shift healthcare financing away from private insurance premiums and toward payroll contributions — including a combination of employer and household premiums, higher taxes on the rich and new taxes on Wall Street and large firms.
Sanders also argued that Democrats could pass the first stage of the transition through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain tax and spending legislation to advance through the 100-member Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically required to overcome a filibuster. Democrats will have a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party’s largest advantage in the chamber in 16 years.
Along with pushing for greater access to primary care, Sanders says Democrats will push for lower prescription drug costs.
A changing political landscape
Sanders has previously balanced his progressive ambitions with the realities of governing. During his first stint chairing the HELP Committee from 2023 to 2025, he worked with Republicans on legislation to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to primary care. He also chaired the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, helping advance major Democratic spending priorities.
But now, just weeks after the midterms, Sanders is laying out an ambitious agenda that he argues reflects a shift not in his own positions but in voters’ demands for sweeping changes to the healthcare system.
He sees signs of that shift among Democratic leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has pledged to get to work “right out of the gate” to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republicans.
Jeffries said Tuesday that Democrats know that simply returning to the status quo “is not acceptable” and they are preparing ways to further expand healthcare access by lowering the Medicare eligibility age, adding access to vision, hearing and dental coverage, and ensuring all kids are covered.
“Jeffries basically supported the first year of Medicare for All,” Sanders said.
But anything that passes Congress the next two years will still need to be signed by President Donald Trump to take effect. Sanders rejected the notion that Trump, a Republican, wouldn’t sign something like Medicare for All into law.
“Donald Trump may be crazy, but he is not stupid. He’s a smart guy, and he’s a very good politician,” Sanders said.
An agenda beyond healthcare
Sanders is also preparing to use the committee to advance a broader economic agenda that includes raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $20 an hour and promoting the PRO Act, which would strengthen workers’ rights to unionize.
The proposed wage increase would nearly triple the federal minimum, which has remained unchanged since 2009, and could face resistance from lawmakers concerned about the impact on small businesses and employment. Sanders proposes to implement it over a four-year transition period.
Sanders’ agenda also calls for sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence, including a moratorium on new AI data centers, a pause in advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.

title: Here’s how much more Americans are expected to pay for Thanksgiving dinners this year
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday.
The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.
The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it’s the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a record of $64.05 in 2022.
High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said. Diesel prices have surged since the start of the Iran war and hit a record average of $6.53 per gallon in the U.S. in September, according to AAA.
On Wednesday diesel averaged $5.96 per gallon, up 58% from a year ago, AAA said.
Turkey prices have also risen sharply over the past year. The Farm Bureau said the 16-pound turkey in its survey cost an average of $23.68 this year, up from $21.50 last year.
Bird flu has been decimating U.S. turkey flocks since an outbreak began in 2022. But cases have been waning, and turkey production increased substantially this year, said Mark Jordan, the executive director of Leap Market Analytics.
At the same time, turkey demand has been rising, as more Americans seek out lean protein and U.S. turkey exports rise. That strong demand has limited U.S. turkey inventories and raised prices. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average a record $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year.
“Over the last few years there’s been a lot of doom and gloom for the turkey industry,” Jordan said. “This is one of those years that turkey producers are feeling a little bit better about their lot in life.”
Jordan said diesel costs likely didn’t impact turkey prices this year, since so much of the decision-making and timing related to the turkeys that will be consumed this Thanksgiving happened before diesel prices spiraled. But diesel costs could have a notable impact on turkey prices next year, he said.
A few of the items on the Thanksgiving menu are cheaper than last year, the Farm Bureau said. A 1-pound vegetable tray featuring carrots and celery is 5 cents cheaper, while a 16-ounce bag of frozen peas is 4 cents cheaper. Frozen pie crusts are also slightly cheaper, although a can of pumpkin pie filling is more expensive.
And in some cases, stores will price turkey and other Thanksgiving staples lower in order to draw shoppers. Aldi said its feast for 10, which mirrors the Farm Bureau’s menu, costs $39 this year. Walmart, which adds items like corn muffin mix and marshmallows but doesn’t include carrots and celery, said its feast for 10 is $35.
Persistently high grocery prices have been frustrating Americans since the pandemic and played a role in Republicans’ recent losses in the midterm elections. Prices for food eaten at home jumped 22% between October 2021 and October 2026, according to U.S. government data. That’s almost double the usual pace of food price inflation.
This year, the USDA predicts prices for food eaten at home to rise 2.3%. That would be lower than the recent annual average of 2.6%.

title: White House pulls FDA nominee Heidi Overton after wavering support from Republicans
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation.
Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for President Donald Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his administration’s approach to vaccines.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday morning.
Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot — “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to disagree with Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.
But late Tuesday night, Cassidy suggested he had been prepared to back Overton and suggested her nomination was derailed by disagreements over abortion, not vaccines.
“I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy stated in a posting on X.
He went on to say that anti-abortion Republicans had sought commitments on “life issues” from the White House, but “the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.”
Currently, the FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone — at the request of Trump — that could reinstate restrictions on the drug’s use, including a requirement for in-person prescribing. FDA has promised a report on its safety findings by March.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on the chamber floor.
Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January.
It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee.
Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees
Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee.
Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton’s approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children.
Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides.
Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists.
“There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said.
Trump has pulled back several other health nominations
Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats.
The FDA is currently being led on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency.
The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office.

title: New ‘Doomsday’ Posters Debut Nightcrawler’s New Look
text:
New ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Posters Debut Nightcrawler’s New Look
We had Old Man Logan, now I guess we have Old Man Nightcrawler.
It’s no secret that Alan Cumming will appear as Nightcrawler in Avengers: Doomsday, marking his return as the teleporting mutant he originated onscreen in 2003’s X2. But so far Cumming’s character has been suspiciously absent from all of the movie’s posters and trailers. Mein Gott! Where is he?!
Finally, Nightcrawler is front and center on one of the 11 (!) new posters for Doomsday Marvel released today, marking the final month before the blockbuster sequel’s release. Ten of the 11 posters feature two of the Marvel heroes starring in the movie; the final one contains just Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom.
Arranged in order they form a massive widescreen image, a la Jim Lee’s multiple covers for X-Men #1 from 1991. Cumming appears on the last poster in the sequence, alongside Winston Duke’s M’Baku.
The other posters show Paul Rudd’s Ant-Man and David Harbour’s Red Guardian, Vanessa Kirby’s Invisible Woman and Tenoch Huerta’s Namor, Channing Tatum’s Gambit and Florence Pugh’s Black Widow, Chris Hemsworth’s Thor and Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers, Anthony Mackie’s Captain America and James Marsden’s Cyclops, Rebecca Romijn’s Mystique and Tom Hiddleston’s Loki, Ian McKellen’s Magneto and Letitia Wright’s Black Panther, the late Patrick Stewart’s Professor X and Oscar Isaac’s Mr. Fantastic, and Sebastian Stan’s Bucky Barnes and Simu Liu’s Shang-Chi.

Cumming’s look evokes his costume from X2, where he bamfed around the White House in a long duster. The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in October 2026 was $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.42% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,313 amounts to about 26% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 0.4% over the past year, and the median of $416,700 was an all-time high for the month of October. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late October showed national home prices grew 2.1% in the year ending in August, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have retreated a bit after spiking amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, and 10-year Treasury yields remain above 5%.
“Recent elections may have changed expectations for additional federal spending, but persistent inflation, relatively strong economic activity and the likelihood of another Federal Reserve rate increase should continue to put upward pressure on rates,” says Sean Salter, a finance professor at Middle Tennessee State University.
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Tracking the scent: How a bloodhound named Zoe tracks down missing people
text:
Tracking the scent: How a bloodhound named Zoe tracks down missing people
Michael Louis, a 12-year-old from Fort Myers, Florida, finds peace in his calming room, away from a world that can often be overstimulating for him.
"Michael's on the spectrum. He was diagnosed when he was 4 years old," said his mother, Marie Jean-Louis.
About 50% of children on the autism spectrum are prone to wandering, a behavior that can be dangerous. Marie recalled a terrifying moment when Michael bolted from their home.
"Oh, that was the worst day of my life," she said.
Marie immediately called 911, fearing for her son’s safety.
"That's scary, because the back of the house is a lake. There's a lake in the front. And if he's gone? Either way, traffic has come in, cars come in. He has no safety awareness. He just goes," she said.
After that frightening experience, the family decided to put safeguards in place, including a scent kit that could help law enforcement track Michael if he goes missing.
"It's just something you just wipe under his arm, and you store it," Marie explained.
The scent kit works in conjunction with a trained bloodhound, like Zoe from the Charlotte County Sheriff's Office.
"Canine Zoe is a discriminant bloodhound. What that means is she can help locate missing endangered persons," said Corporal Steven Sella, Zoe's handler.
Corporal Sella explained the importance of Zoe’s tracking abilities.
"Without her, without her nose putting it on the ground or having some type of camera system, we're in the unknown, so we're going every which way, and we don't know where to start looking," he said.
Bloodhounds are uniquely suited for this work, Sella said.
"So bloodhounds are known for their sense of smell. Reason being is it's 40 times stronger than a German shepherd is. They're actually the only dog that's recognized in law that you can use in a court case," he said.
To demonstrate Zoe’s skills, her tracking abilities were put to the test. After being given a scent from the kit, Zoe followed a trail that included pavement, mulch, grass, and even a turn into the woods. Within minutes, she successfully located the hidden person.
"We've had a lot of successful cases, and we've been able to reunite families with their loved ones because of her nose," Sella said.
For families like Michael's, tools like the scent kit and Zoe provide much-needed peace of mind.
"Most of these stories do not end well for these kids. So any extra step we can take to keep them safe, it's worth it," Marie said.

A clinical assistant at a youth and teen residential treatment facility in New Hampshire is charged with indecent exposure and lewdness and certain uses of computer services prohibited in connection with an investigation involving a child under the age of 13.

title: Foster family seeks answers after US-born baby taken into custody in Guatemala
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray) — A baby born in Kentucky is now in the custody of Guatemalan authorities after being deported, according to her former foster family.
On Aug. 2, 2025, police were called to Norton Women’s and Children’s Hospital. According to a police report, Baby “T” was brought in just hours after her birth with her biological mother, Marlena, who had recently arrived in Kentucky from Guatemala.
“T” had cuts all over her body, according to police.
The birth mother told nurses she tried to kill the baby because she did not want her, according to the police report. The mother’s attorney later challenged that narrative in court.
The mother was initially charged with criminal abuse, but a grand jury later indicted her on charges of attempted murder and assault.
In July, she pleaded guilty to the amended charge of wanton endangerment. She was sentenced to 340 days and received credit for time served.
Caleb Yeske, the baby’s foster parent, was ordered to turn the baby over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement by Sept. 7, so she could be deported and transferred to the care of her birth mother. The baby had not been with her mother since the hours after her birth.
The reunification happened over the objection of the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services, and Yeske said there is no record of a hearing that found the mother was set up to take care of the baby successfully, which he said is typical for foster cases.
Yeske said he has stayed in touch with the birth mother, providing her with whatever she needed about the baby’s life over the last year, including medical history and the baby’s likes and dislikes. In a matter of weeks, those conversations changed from information to a request from the mom.
“We basically just told her, ‘Look, we cared for your child for the last year and some change. We want her to be set up for success. We want you to be set up for success,’” Yeske said. “We told her that we love this child and want the best for her. What can we do to support you? Do you want me to come down and visit? What does that look like? And basically, she said, ‘If you come down here and help me get a passport for my daughter, you can bring her back to the United States.’”
On the cusp of a custody exchange
Yeske showed WDRB+WAVE notarized documents signed by Marlena, allowing Yeske to take over guardianship and travel with the baby back to the U.S.
However, Yeske said Guatemalan authorities took “T” into custody while they were waiting for her passport from the embassy. He said the baby was reported missing, though Yeske said it remains unclear who made that report.
The foster family said they do not know where “T” is now. Even with the notarized custody papers, he is still working to sort out who can rule on where “T” should live.
“It’s very difficult to understand how a U.S. citizen is returned to another country when the cabinet, foster care here in Kentucky, agreed that reunification, at least at that time, should not occur,” Yeske said. “And then, less than two months later, to be getting calls saying, ‘Please, if you come and get this baby, you can bring her back to the U.S.’”
Yeske said he has been working with members of Congress and the embassy. Kentucky courts found he had no right to intervene in the mother and baby’s reunification.
“Because she is not in the U.S., the argument is that trying to figure out really who has jurisdiction to rule over where the child should remain, whether that be Guatemala or the United States,” Yeske said. “So, that’s kind of the position that we’re left in right now, is who should be advocating for this child? Who has the authority to make decisions for the best interest of this baby?”
As a foster parent, this is a situation Yeske never expected to be in, but he is doing what he can to make sure “T” is safe.
“What I can tell you, as well as anybody who’s a parent knows, is that when you love a child, that love never ends,” Yeske said. “And that care and that expectation to protect and find justice and support that child is unwavering. And ultimately, that’s the place that I come from as I try to advocate this baby.”
Kentucky’s attorney general files to unseal the confidential record
The case has had a complex history in court. The foster family attempted to intervene with an emergency motion to the Kentucky Court of Appeals, but the effort was rejected.
According to court records, the court essentially found they had not met the burden to prove irreparable harm, the reunification had already been ordered and the foster parents had never had custodial rights to begin with. Their emergency motion for a stay on reunification was also rejected on similar grounds.
The foster parents additionally filed a writ, challenging the reunification proceedings. They eventually withdrew the writ, after CHFS, the birth mom’s attorney and the Jefferson County Attorney’s Office submitted responses arguing they had no right to make such a challenge.
Now, Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman and the Kentucky Press Association have filed motions of their own, asking the court to unseal the confidential court record. They both argue that releasing information is in the public’s interest, considering the traction it has gained in the media.
KAP specifically cites an order by the courts for the foster parents to not speak about the case publicly, threatening jail time if they did so. This argument speaks to the AG’s motion, which cites allegations the foster parents were spreading misinformation.
The AG added that there are several questions the public deserves to have answered, laying them out in the motion, including:
- “Why was this case treated as a dependency case, Order at 4 (Sept. 9, 2026), rather than as an abuse or neglect case, given that the mother ultimately pleaded guilty to wantonly endangering the child?
- What was the factual and legal basis for the Jefferson Family Court to order immediate reunification of the child with the mother without any reunification process or plan, given the requirements in Kentucky law?
- What role did the mother’s committing a crime against the child play in the Jefferson Family Court’s reunification decision?”
The birth mom’s attorney and the JCAO have both filed responses, objecting to the state’s motion to unseal the record.

title: Paris Hilton urges House to pass AI deepfake porn bill
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Paris Hilton returned to Capitol Hill on Tuesday to urge the House to pass a bill aimed at combating nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfake images.
“Bring the DEFIANCE Act to the House floor. Let Congress vote,” Hilton said at a press conference, alongside Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Laurel Lee, R-Fla, the bill’s sponsors.
Hilton calls for a House vote
The legislation would allow victims to sue people who create or distribute sexually explicit images of them.
“DEFIANCE returns power to the hands of survivors by allowing them to hold their abusers accountable and seek financial and reputational recourse for the harm they caused in court,” Ocasio-Cortez said.
Hilton has advocating for the legislation for months. She made an initial appeal to House lawmakers in January, after it passed in the Senate by unanimous consent. But the bill still has yet to be voted on in the lower chamber.
“The Senate understood the urgency and passed this legislation unanimously in January. Now the House must act, too,” she said. “Why wait another day if they don’t pass this bill before the end of the year? All of our progress will be lost and we’ll have to start all over again. Speaker Johnson, Leader Scalise, and Chairman Jordan, I am speaking directly to you.”
During her January appearance on the Hill, Hilton spoke about her personal experience of having nonconsensual intimate images of her shared when she was 19-years-old.
“Ten months ago, I stood here at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent. And I asked Congress to do something about it,” Hilton said.
She also said that her team had done research about how AI deepfakes are affecting women in Congress.
“In preparation for today, my team studied how United States Congress women are appearing in adult deepfake content online. And what we found was shocking, but hardly surprising,” she said. “Of the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress. 83 have sexual deepfakes online right now. That’s more than half of the women in Congress.”
Lee also said the bill sends a message about the use of artificial intelligence.
“It gives victims the ability to fight back, to seek accountability, and to pursue justice. And importantly, it sends a clear message that using artificial intelligence to sexually exploit another person will have consequences,” she said.

title: Central Maine Medical Center nurses discuss possible strike two months after unionizing
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Medical Center nurses discuss possible strike two months after unionizing
Nurses at Central Maine Medical Center voted to unionize in September and said hospital ownership has not met any demands, such as lowering the patient-to-nurse ratio.
Central Maine Medical Center nurses discuss possible strike two months after unionizing
Nurses at Central Maine Medical Center voted to unionize in September and said hospital ownership has not met any demands, such as lowering the patient-to-nurse ratio.
Nearly two months after nurses at Central Maine Medical Center voted to unionize, dozens of nurses held a town hall on Tuesday to rally support from Androscoggin County residents. Twenty nurses were fired or suspended for what the hospital said were "violations of longstanding policy," but nurses are accusing ownership of retaliating against them for organizing. Prime Healthcare owns Central Maine Medical Center, Bridgton Hospital, and Rumford Hospital.
"A majority of them would like to have their positions back, and I lost three nurses. We are a small team to begin with," said April Potvin, who works in a vascular unit.
Potvin said her unit is under stress with fewer staff members, and it is creating an even higher nurse-to-patient ratio than what nurses are fighting.
"Heating oil is expensive, there are car payments and bills that just do not go away. So I have cut back on what I could," said Katie Grinnel, a nurse who was fired in September.
Grinnel said she was suspended and then, two days later, fired for "solicitation" and hopes to return to work as soon as possible.
"Just because I am not there does not mean that nurses don't go to work or that patients deserve good care," said Grinnel.

title: New Adult Soccer League Kicks Off at CLC YMCA
text:
The Central Lincoln County YMCA has started a new adult soccer league, holding its inaugural games on Oct. 27. The CLC YMCA Futsal League hosts a pair of games between 6-9 p.m. on Tuesday nights.
According to Ben Popken, the league co-organizer and captain of the Wild Oysters team, the league was started as a way to add more consistent adult soccer offerings in Lincoln County.
“The league grew out of the roving adult pickup game called Damariscotta Co-Ed Adult Soccer that I started in the summer of 2025 at the Lincoln Academy grass field, and it has been going on a weekly basis ever since,” said Popken. “After seeing the continued success of our pickup and capitalizing on rising soccer interest generated by the new Portland Hearts of Pine pro team and the World Cup tournament in June, the YMCA wanted to grow their soccer program.”
Popken collaborated with CLC YMCA Senior Program Director Sarah Glenn and Program Coordinator Kaleb Davis to add a league night on Tuesdays.
CLC YMCA’s Futsal League matches are played on the basketball court at the YMCA, which has handball sized nets ideal for the indoor-style of game. The league also features a scoreboard, a referee, and the scores and standings maintained at leagues.teamlinkt.com/ clcymcafutsalleague.
“Futsal is a really cool style of soccer that has a long association with YMCAs,” said Popken. “It was invented in Uruguay in the 1930s as a way to adapt soccer for YMCA indoor basketball courts and has spread worldwide. Famous international soccer players like Messi, Ronaldo, Neymar, and Ronaldinho credit it for their success.”
Each CLC YMCA Futsal League match is 50 minutes long with a brief warm-up, two 25-minute halves, and a five-minute halftime. Five players compete on the pitch for each team, including a goalie.
There are four teams in the CLC YMCA Futsal League: Wild Oysters, Sam’s Team, Outta Shape, and the Free Agents. The cost to play in the league’s eight-game season is $100 for individuals or $500 for each team.
The CLC YMCA League plays an adapted version of futsal, with “kick-ins” instead of throw-ins after a ball goes out of bounds.
“The play is fast and fun with lots of quick, intelligent passes, fancy footwork, and sneaky and hard shots,” said Popken. “It’s a great workout and a fun way to connect with others, especially during the winter when everyone seems to hunker down.”
The first regular season, consisting of eight weekly games, will conclude on Tuesday, Dec. 15. Based on the early success of the program, the league plans to add another session in January, and hopes to expand the number of teams from the current four to six.
“I’m definitely planning on keeping the futsal momentum going and carrying it into the spring,” said Davis. According to Popken, players in the league are from Damariscotta, Rockland, Bath, Wiscasset, South Bristol, Bremen, and more. “There’s a pretty wide age range in the league,” said Davis. “We have a few Lincoln Academy soccer players, a few parents of soccer players, and some older folks that just want to stay active and play soccer. More people have been joining each week as word spreads.”
In addition to the League offering, CLC YMCA also hosts adult soccer (futsal) skills clinics on Wednesday nights from 6-6:30 p.m., followed by adult soccer (futsal) pickup from 6:30-8 p.m. Ryan Hamilton, the soccer specialist at the YMCA who played the sport at the NCAA Division I level in college, runs the adult clinics, pickup games, and league nights.
Glenn thinks the league is another way to stay active and social to help beat the winter blues.
“People love the adult soccer programs not just for the workout but also the community,” said Glenn. “The players are meeting new people and forming friendships. Ben (Popken) has done a lot to grow our local soccer community. It has been wonderful to see this league come together.”
Davis agrees that the league is foremost a friendly community. “My favorite thing about the league would be the social aspect of it all,” said Davis. “I’ve been a part of many leagues, and I haven’t been around a community as friendly and fun loving as the Futsal League.”
For more information about Damariscotta Co-Ed Adult Soccer, find the group page on Facebook.

title: Russian national accused of spying on employees of Silicon Valley defense and technology company
text:
Russian national accused of spying on employees of Silicon Valley defense and technology company
A Russian man who prosecutors say was recruited by his government has been charged with stalking employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in order to gather intelligence, the Justice Department said Wednesday.
Igor D'iu was tasked with collecting information about the company's activities because it was supplying Ukraine with weapons for its war with Russia, according to an FBI affidavit outlining the allegations. Officials say D'iu was directed by his handlers to visit a coffee shop near the company's northern California office, identify employees and take photographs of their laptop screens while they worked. They also say he collected home addresses and personal information about company employees and at times followed them from the office in his car.
The company was not identified in charging documents. It was also not immediately clear from whom D'iu received his taskings, but his contacts on the encrypted communications platform Telegram told him he was working for "the Motherland," the affidavit says. The document also says the alleged scheme follows the pattern of a clandestine operation of a Russian intelligence service, which typically relies on proxies to carry out intelligence collection of targets.
The spying is alleged to have occurred soon after D'iu, a Russian national believed to have been recruited by contacts on Telegram, illegally arrived in the United States last summer without any active or approved visas, the Justice Department said. Prosecutors say he traveled from Turkey to Mexico last June and posted on a Facebook group page in Russian asking for help getting across the border and into the United States.
D'iu was arrested Oct. 30 and agents who searched his East Palo Alto home found $18,000 in cash, two Russian passports, laptops, iPhones and wireless networking equipment, and a notebook containing addresses of residences of some of the company employees and detailed profiles about them and their employment histories, the authorities said.
He is due in court Nov. 24. It was not immediately clear from court records if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
A grand jury indictment announced Wednesday and filed in the Northern District of California contains charges including conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, interstate stalking and fraud in connection with fake identity documents that he used to conceal his true name.
Prosecutors say his surveillance of company employees included an incident in September when an employee contacted police to report having been followed for nearly 30 miles upon leaving the office by a driver who ran a red light and made illegal turns.
The Justice Department says that after being contacted by police about that episode, D'iu changed cars, got a new phone number and temporarily traveled out of state.

title: Ogunquit couple sues town over $1,700 in fines for rooster statues
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OGUNQUIT, Maine (WMTW) - An Ogunquit couple that has been fined $1,700 by the town over rooster statues displayed outside of their home has filed a federal lawsuit, claiming that their First Amendment rights have been violated.
Dave and Sara LeBlanc first displayed a 6-foot-tall tin rooster in front of their Main Street home in May 2025 as a show of love and support for their daughter, Pyper, who has autism. The couple said Pyper, who is now 6 years old, loves roosters and that the statue helped her find comfort while she waited for the school bus and when she came home from school each day.
Since their daughter loved the rooster statue so much, Dave and Sara LeBlanc said they acquired about two dozen tin roosters over time but never displayed more than eight at once on their property with the exception of the Christmas holiday season, when they arrange roosters to appear as if they are pulling Santa’s sleigh.
The LeBlancs also own The Omelette Factory, a breakfast restaurant that is attached to the family’s home. After the roosters on their front lawn became a popular landmark in town, the couple decided to add a rooster to the logo on The Omelette Factory’s merchandise, which is sold inside the restaurant. In the lawsuit, Dave and Sara LeBlanc said the rooster became like “a family crest,” and that the restaurant’s merchandise does not depict the roosters displayed on their lawn.
On or about April 3, 2026, the town sent a letter to the LeBlancs, notifying them that they were in violation of the Zoning Code for “unpermitted signage” and “overage of allowable square footage of signage.” In the letter, the town ordered the LeBlancs to immediately remove the unpermitted signage, including but not limited to the rooster statues.
“It’s a range of emotions for her because she’s like, ‘Why can’t the town be nice? Like, we’re taught to be nice,’” Sara LeBlanc said.
According to the lawsuit, Ogunquit Code Enforcement Officer Tyler McOsker told the couple that the town viewed the tin roosters as signs because the statues are believed to be advertisements for The Omelette Factory.
“Never imagined it getting to the point where it is. But it had to. We had no choice,” Dave LeBlanc said. “It’s just where it brought us. We have beliefs and we have a job to do to raise her. Do we go along and just get steamrolled, or stand up for what you believe in life?”
The town sent another letter to the LeBlancs on April 6, imposing a $150 fine for illegal signage because of the rooster statues. Ten days later, the town sent another letter imposing an additional $300 fine for failing to remove the decorative roosters.
The LeBlancs appealed their fines to the Zoning Board of Appeals, arguing that the rooster statues are not signs or advertisements but instead “are art, a comfort for their daughter, and a symbol of their love for her,” according to the couple’s lawsuit. The Zoning Board of Appeals heard the couple’s appeal on June 11 and affirmed McOsker’s determination that the rooster statues are signs. The board, however, did grant a disability variance, under which the couple could keep two roosters on the residential side of their home on the condition that the roosters be incorporated into a railing affixed to the residence.
In the lawsuit, the LeBlancs said they did not wish to add a railing to their home and instead chained two roosters to the decorative pillars flanking the front door of their house. The couple then gave their remaining rooster statues to friends and neighbors, who have displayed the roosters in front of their homes and businesses as a show of support for Pyper and as a symbol of neurodiversity awareness and acceptance.
On June 24, the town fined the LeBlancs an additional $500 for failing to build a railing for the two roosters. The couple was then fined an additional $750 on Sept. 17 for failing to remove the roosters or affix them to a railing.
The LeBlancs have paid all the fines assessed against them to date, totaling $1,700, under protest. The couple has also removed their decorative roosters from public sight.
The couple’s lawsuit states that in July, the LeBlancs filed a public records request under Maine’s Freedom of Access Act (FOAA) in an effort to obtain town records showing previous enforcement actions involving artwork, sculptures, lawn ornaments, public art or similar displays that were deemed to be signs under the Ogunquit Zoning Code.
The LeBlancs received all records related to the FOAA request from the town on Sept. 22. According to the couple’s lawsuit, the records the LeBlancs received contained no records relating to prior enforcement actions, whether historical or in relation to rooster statues.
In their lawsuit, the couple said that the rooster statues displayed in front of other Ogunquit homes and businesses — some of which belonged to the LeBlancs — have not resulted in any citations or fines against those residents and business owners. The LeBlancs also said in their lawsuit that the records they received from the town indicate Ogunquit does not apply its sign regulations to other decorative objects displayed on residential or commercial properties, such as lobster buoys, nautical art, antique farm equipment or large tiki statues.
The LeBlancs also take issue with the Ogunquit Zoning Code’s language. In their lawsuit, the couple said the Zoning Code defines an advertising sign as “a sign which identifies the goods or services available at a business or provides information about those goods and services.” The LeBlancs argue that under that definition, whether a display is a regulated advertising sign depends entirely on what the town perceives to be its expressive content.
“Here, the town has decided that the LeBlancs’ roosters are signs because the LeBlancs own The Omelette Factory, and town officials have therefore imagined the roosters to say ‘eat at The Omelette Factory.’ In reality, the roosters mean different things to different people,” the lawsuit states. “When the very same roosters stand in front of a neighbor’s home, the town treats them as decorations, not signs. The LeBlancs would own and display these roosters regardless of whether they owned a restaurant. Yet, merely because the LeBlancs happen to own an eatery, the town considers their roosters a sign for it.”
The couple argues that the town’s sign code and policies and practices regarding the enforcement of that code violate their right to free speech as guaranteed by the First Amendment.
“Plaintiffs want to display their tin roosters in front of their home without the threat of fines and code enforcement hanging over their heads,” the lawsuit states.
The LeBlancs seek a judgment declaring that the Ogunquit Zoning Code is “unconstitutionally vague,” as well as a permanent injunction prohibiting the town from enforcing the code against the decorative roosters. The couple also seeks damages in compensation for the town’s enforcement against them, including the $1,700 in fines they paid.
Attorneys from the Institute for Justice, a national nonprofit, public interest law firm, are representing the LeBlancs. Last month, Institute for Justice attorney Daniel Woislaw sent a letter to McOsker and Ogunquit Town Manager Matthew Buttrick, in which he called on the town to rescind the fines it levied against the LeBlancs.
“It is not something that towns have a monopoly on deciding what art is or what art means. These roosters mean a lot of things to a lot of people. To the LeBlancs, they are a comfort for Pyper and a symbol of their life,” Woislaw said. “It’s not neutral. It’s not evenhanded, it’s uneven, it’s unfair and it’s arbitrary. So that’s why this is unconstitutional.”
Ogunquit town officials did not provide a comment on the lawsuit filed by the LeBlancs.

title: Psoriasis later in life is more than a dry patch — how to treat flare-ups
text:
(Aging Untold) — Psoriasis can develop or flare later in life, and it can show up as more than dry or irritated skin.
Some people notice scaly patches, redness, itching or nail changes such as pitting, discoloration or lifting.
It’s an immune condition, not just a skin condition
“Psoriasis can occur at any age, and it really is not a skin condition. It really is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Swollen or tender joints alongside a rash are a signal to look further.
“Then you have to start thinking further, because it is a clue that you have some systemic inflammation going on underneath, and it is systemic,” Rogers said.
What can trigger a flare
Rogers said genetics play a role.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck has lupus and shared that two of her children have psoriasis. One also has psoriatic arthritis.
“When you have autoimmune diseases already in your genetic history, you have a predisposition, and then something triggers it. Then the inflammatory response takes off, and there you go,” Cradduck said.
Rogers listed stress, infection, skin injury and certain medications as triggers, including beta blockers, lithium and antimalarial drugs.
Cradduck compared stress-related flares to breakouts before a big event.
“That same kind of stress that was causing that can cause these kind of flares in someone with autoimmune,” she said.
Getting sick can also cause a flare because the immune system is already not regulating properly.
Rogers said psoriasis also increases the risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
“So it’s a serious thing that’s telling your body you’re susceptible to some other things,” Rogers said.
Looking at the whole picture
Rogers said traditional and functional medicine play an important role in treating autoimmune disorders.
“I like to say it’s not traditional or functional. It really is integrative,” Rogers said. “If you can understand treating autoimmune disorders, you want to look at nutritional deficiencies and hormonal imbalances and GI infections and cortisol and stress and toxins. All those things play a role.”
She said the goal is not simply to suppress the immune system.
Treatment and when to get help
For daily skin care, aging expert Amy O’Rourke offered direct advice.
“The long, hot shower? Not so much. Use the moisturizer. If you get an infection, get to the doctor right away,” she said.
O’Rourke suggested the National Psoriasis Foundation as a resource.
“I would want people to go there and read up to really enhance their strategy to approach this issue,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck said her daughter has had good results with a cream from her doctor and has not had a flare in some time.
An active flare needs treatment, Cradduck said.
“When you have a flare and you’re active in it, you do have to get that treated and taken care of, because it’s not going to just go away on its own,” she said.
Rogers also cautioned against assuming that skin changes later in life are psoriasis.
“Don’t just think, ‘Oh, it’s psoriasis.’ Now you have to look at other things, like maybe a fungal infection, or are you having a reaction to medicines?” Rogers said.
If joints are involved, Rogers said the search should go beyond a dermatologist.
“Once it becomes no longer a skin disorder, this is a systemic disorder,” Rogers said. “If you have one autoimmune disorder, you have others. Go to someone who knows how to look for it.”
Know your triggers and your treatment
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose encouraged viewers to stay curious about what their bodies are signaling.
“Don’t just stay in judgment thinking you know what it is, or it’s only this or it’s only that, because it’s definitely feedback that your body’s giving you,” Ambrose said.
Rogers urges people with psoriasis to pay attention to things that trigger or worsen it, because those will be different for everyone.
Cradduck said approaches that may help include meditation, de-stressing, medications and oatmeal baths.
Resource
The National Psoriasis Foundation is a nonprofit psoriatic disease research organization.
The website has resources on causes and triggers, treatments, diet and lifestyle information and more.
Key takeaways
- Psoriasis is more than skin deep. It is a sign of immune system inflammation that appears through the skin and nail beds.
- Don’t self-treat or assume. Later-in-life skin changes can have other causes, such as a fungal infection or a reaction to medication. Monitor unexplained nail changes and consult a dermatologist.

title: Congress skeptical as Trump officials seek $50B for air travel system
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy urged a skeptical Congress on Tuesday to make a massive $50 billion investment in the nation’s air transportation system even as the Federal Aviation Administration took steps to prevent a repeat of last week’s ground stop that caused chaos for travelers.
President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for last week’s upheaval at the nation’s airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration. The agency said Tuesday it had paused installing routers linked to the ground stop.
Duffy met with Republican senators about the administration’s efforts to enhance air travel and safety, which were detailed in a letter to lawmakers earlier in the day. The $50.1 billion in funding would be divided into five distinct categories, each category getting about the same amount, including $10 billion for modernizing the air traffic control system.
“I hope they don’t piecemeal it. There’s been too much piecemeal happening over the course of 20 and 30 years. I hope we get the full investment,” Duffy told reporters before the meeting started.
But several Republican senators took issue with the request, and Democrats are even more skeptical. Lawmakers said they are for funding safety, but they voiced some concern about other aspects of the administration’s request, including billions for airport infrastructure and the replacement of aging terminals at key airports.
“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air travel issues.
“We’re not going to give them $50 billion,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. “But I think that we are willing to provide the money to replace the copper wires with fiber optics, and to try to stop the bleeding.”
Another senator, Republican Rick Scott of Florida, said the airline industry should pay for many of the upgrades being sought, not the federal government.
Duffy, meanwhile, said he’s open to other options that could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.
FAA’s focus turns to routers
As lawmakers debated the funding request, the Federal Aviation Administration took more immediate action.
FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.
The FAA said the Juniper routers linked to the ground stop serve as translators to allow the older analog part of the network to communicate with the newer digital parts of the network as upgrades are completed. So they serve a different role than the Wi-Fi routers that most people have at home.
The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
Duffy said the ground stop was needed after the installation of a new router by L3Harris in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been installed three weeks earlier, also contributed to the trouble.
The FAA said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
Duffy seeks ‘root cause of what happened’
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s trouble.
The routers at issue last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the company believes its “device functioned as it was configured by the installer” when the ground stop occurred. “The FAA is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause,” the statement said.
Duffy said Tuesday that 68 previous installations involving the same routers worked well before this latest problem.
“We’ve been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado,” he said. “But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet.”
Democrats in the Senate have called for halting the replacement of thousands of routers across the nation’s air traffic control system. They also demanded that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” said the letter sent to Duffy.
Ground stop cost big airlines over $300 million
Equity research and brokerage firm Bernstein estimated the ground stop and the weekend work needed to recover from it cost the four biggest U.S. airlines $345 million combined.
The airlines had to offer cash refunds, credits or rebooking options to customers who decided to cancel their trips, Bernstein analysts said.
The lost revenue and additional costs from the ground stop still are enough to have a measurable effect on the quarterly earnings for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines, the analysts wrote in a Monday research note.
“A booking slowdown before Thanksgiving, or a second outage, would cost more than the weekend’s cancellations did,” the analysts said, adding they did not see any signs of waning ticket demand.
___
Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails domestically made weapons
text:
Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails domestically made weapons
Ukraine struck two oil refineries in southern Russia, Ukrainian officials said Wednesday, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the effectiveness of domestically produced weapons used to damage the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Both sides have continued their attacks as delegations await word on another round of U.S.-mediated talks. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to discuss the nearly five-year war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during a visit to China.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the strikes hit storage tanks at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, also targeted Sunday night, can together process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the front lines in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.
Related video: Who's meeting with President Trump for this week's historic nuclear summit in Asia?
Russian officials reported attacks on two industrial facilities in the region but gave no details.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted refineries as it seeks to hurt Russia’s oil sector, a mainstay of its economy, and Moscow presses on with its all-out invasion of its neighbor.
“Our technologies and companies are developing very well,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.
Ukraine's cutting-edge long-range drones and missiles were deployed against the Kerch Bridge in a large-scale attack on Monday night that was prepared over weeks, he said.
“Right now, we’re in the top three in the world for tech development. In Europe, I think we’re number one,” Zelenskyy said.
The Pentagon has argued that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive, but Ukraine’s European backers disagree.
Zelenskyy said the strike on the Kerch Bridge, which could disrupt supplies to Russian troops on the front lines, was justified by Russia’s relentless bombardment of Ukraine.
Russian forces have focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before the winter, aiming to erode the morale of civilians.
Attacks last month killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians and wounded 1,981 others — a number 95% higher than in October 2025, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on social media Wednesday.
This year, the war has brought “significantly higher” civilian casualties than in previous years, the agency said.
“The first 10 months of this year have seen more civilian deaths than all of 2025, which in turn was worse than the year before,” said Danielle Bell, who heads the U.N. agency in Kyiv. “The world should not become numb to the deadly toll the war exacts on Ukraine’s civilians.”
Russian drones attacked energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings in five regions overnight and Wednesday morning, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
A Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa killed four people Wednesday, local officials said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces used drones overnight to strike the port of Izmail in the Odesa region.
A Russian drone attack on a market in the Kharkiv region wounded 12 people, including an 11-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Services said.
___
Barry Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.
