title: 'Just uppercut or kick': Professional mermaid fights off attacker after requesting Lyft
text:
'Just uppercut or kick': Professional mermaid fights off attacker after requesting Lyft
Authorities said an investigation is underway after a professional mermaid was attacked while waiting for a Lyft ride in New Orleans earlier this month.
Hearst sister station WDSU said the attack occurred on Nov. 6 around 5:40 p.m.
Luma, the professional mermaid who only wanted to be identified by her first name, said she was visiting the area to attend a diving conference when the incident happened.
Luma said she had gone out with friends and later called a Lyft to take her back to her hotel. She said the driver canceled, so she began to walk. That's when she said a car matching the description of her Lyft driver pulled up next to her.
Thinking it may be her ride, she walked around to check the license plate. She said that's when a man jumped out of the vehicle.
"He goes for my bag, he takes it from me. So I grab the bag, shoulder roll, kick back, kick the assailant away from me towards the fence of a parking lot," she said. "I jumped into his car and grabbed his key fob and threw it out the passenger side window."
What seemingly started as a robbery then turned into a brutal attack, but Luma decided she wasn't going down without a fight.
In addition to being a professional mermaid, she is a former professional Muay Thai boxer.
"He pulled me out of the car and grabbed me by the back of the hair and from standing he just slammed me into the pavement face first. I heard a crunch. It broke my nose and he just kept doing that," she said. "And then he stomped on my head."
Luma said the man attempted to take her bag, wedding band and shoes.
"Every time he took something from me I would take it back, and just uppercut or kick," she said.
The attacker eventually found his keys and fled the scene.
Bloody, concussed, and unable to walk, Luma crawled several blocks down the street before calling her brother, husband, and 911.
"When EMS arrived, they were horrified," she said. "They were like, 'Are you sure he didn't run you over?' Like I looked that bad."
She was unconscious in the hospital for the next day and a half and is now recovering at home in California.
It'll be at least a month before she is able to dive again.
Her story went viral on social media, and now she's encouraging other women to stay vigilant and learn how to defend themselves.
"I had a voice in my head saying, 'If he's hitting you this hard, what's he going to do to the next girl?' And I don't want to sit here in silence and let that happen to anybody else," she said.
Despite the traumatic incident, Luma said she still loves New Orleans.
"I one thousand percent want to go back to New Orleans. I received nothing but love from the citizens," she said. "They have all apologized. It's not your fault. I don't blame New Orleans, and I can't wait to come back. And I'm dying to swim in that aquarium."
No arrests have been made in connection with the assault. According to the New Orleans Police Department, the investigation is ongoing.

title: New land purchase opens door to Coastal Rivers’ Wild Lily Preserve
text:
Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust has purchased approximately 12 acres along Turner Road in Bremen from Matthew and Gigi Ravenhall. Adjacent to Coastal Rivers’ existing 120-acre Wild Lily Preserve, the newly conserved land will make it possible to open the preserve to the public for the first time.
Although Coastal Rivers conserved Wild Lily Preserve in 2022, the property lacked a location for parking.Acquiring the Ravenhall parcel provides direct frontage along Turner Road, allowing the organization to build a small parking area, a trailhead, and a new trail leading into the woods and down to the shoreline of Pemaquid Pond. Once complete, the preserve will welcome residents and visitors for walking, fishing, and nature observation.
"Since acquiring Wild Lily Preserve in 2022, we’ve been looking for a way to invite the community into this beautiful place," said Katie Beaver, Deputy Director of Coastal Rivers. "The Ravenhall property gives us the chance to create a welcoming trailhead where people can explore the forest and enjoy the shoreline of Pemaquid Pond. We are deeply grateful to Matthew and Gigi Ravenhall for working with us to conserve this land for future generations."
Made up primarily of woods and wetlands, this 12-acre addition protects important wildlife habitat and contributes to water quality in Pemaquid Pond. It also expands an existing block of conserved land between Pemaquid, McCurdy, and Muscongus ponds.
While the land purchase is complete, additional work is needed before the preserve can open. Coastal Rivers is now seeking community support to fund and build the new parking area and trail, with a final opening timeline dependent on fundraising and project planning.
Community members interested in supporting the parking area and trail improvements are encouraged to contact Executive Director Steven Hufnagel at shufnagel@coastalrivers.org.
For more information, email info@coastalrivers.org or visit coastalrivers.org.

title: York Ambulance Association says voted funding will be 'more than enough' to cover services
text:
York Ambulance Association says voted funding will be 'more than enough' to cover services
On Election Day, the York Ambulance Association asked residents to vote for $350,000 in additional funding.
That was approved, but less than a week later, organization leaders said they might need more in a Selectboard meeting. They added claims they could face closure if further funding wasn't received.
"I'm concerned that we're going to be here months from now, and 'Oh, no, it's not $480,000. It's $600,000," said Selectboard member Robert Palmer. "I mean, it just seems like the numbers change."
However, YAA leaders are now claiming the funds voters approved will be enough.
The organization's treasurer, Matt McTighe, said the numbers needed a deeper dive when projecting for a budget.
Originally, they were looking at last year's numbers, which included reimbursement from two other towns and an ambulance, which they don't run anymore.
"Everything has gone up. Everything has become more expensive," McTighe said. "But the rates, which were reimbursed through Medicare, which is our primary source of revenue, have stayed flat or, in many cases, gone down."
McTighe said additional funding from the taxpayers was needed. He claims the rate received from the town per the contract and Medicare's reimbursement are antiquated.
He also added that about one-third of all calls that come in, the YAA knows immediately they won't be compensated.
"Unless we transport somebody to the hospital, we generally don't get paid for a call," McTighe said.
He said that even further down the road, they also come back without payment. But, through conversations with town leaders, that will now change.
For things like car accidents, they are now allowed to charge through auto insurance. For calls like lift assists, they will now abide by the rule of "first three are free," then they will be charged.
McTighe believes that with these changes, along with private donations, the YAA can continue running until its contract ends with the town in June.
"There are no other options I'm aware of that are a better deal for the taxpayers of York than to continue the coverage that we have through the York Ambulance Association," McTighe said.

title: Army to detonate large amount of lead azide in Iowa, risking toxic exposure to those in the area
text:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa (KWQC/Gray News) - The U.S. Army is detonating a large quantity of lead azide on Friday in Middletown, raising health concerns among residents.
Lead azide is a highly sensitive explosive and a lead compound, meaning the blast could create environmental and public health risks.
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa and expert in environmental health, said the potential lead-carrying plume is among some of the top concerns.
The explosion could send lead-containing particles into the air, traveling with the wind before settling onto soil, buildings, vehicles and other surfaces.
This type of situation would create potential exposure risks for people who breathe in the particles or come into contact with contaminated dust.
“We inhale things that may get into our bodies; we ingest things, get into our gut. And we have the ability to have a dermal absorption of things that we touch,” O’Shaughnessy said.
Health effects of lead
Lead is a neurotoxin. Exposure can damage the brain and nervous system, kidneys and cardiovascular system.
Health experts said there’s no safe amount of lead. Young children are especially vulnerable.
“Maybe the most concerning thing is, say, 2-year-olds that just have this habit of, right, of touching everything and then everything goes right into their mouth, right,” O’Shaughnessy said.
The Army has shared the potential plume’s path. Officials said residents should hose down exterior surfaces, wipe down children’s play equipment and wash cars where dust may have settled following the planned detonation.

title: Arts funding cuts also hurting news outlets covering the arts, study finds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As arts and cultural organizations struggle to adapt to changing funding models, the news outlets that cover the arts are also challenged, according to a report by a Portland-based foundation.
The Rabkin Foundation, working with the Detroit nonprofit Critical Minded, surveyed 141 independent arts and culture publications across 34 states and the District of Columbia, producing hard evidence of the situation. (In Maine, seven publications completed the survey.) Just over half of the publications that responded, 51.1%, are nonprofits.
The report, “Support for Arts and Culture Journalism,” argues that arts journalism is not a niche concern but essential civic infrastructure deserving far greater investment.
“The findings reveal a striking contradiction,” the Rabkin Foundation said. “The publications are themselves punching above their weight, serving expanding audiences with remarkably small staffs and budgets. But they struggle to secure the kind of consistent support prioritized for other sectors of journalism. This deepening precarity is further compounded by escalating free-speech pressures and shifting funding priorities.”
The findings
Researchers found that, of the publications that responded to the survey, the editorial staff averaged just four people and the average operating budget was $181,000.
Most of the publications cover a range of arts and cultural “scenes,” filling gaps in local coverage after larger publications scaled back. The demand for arts and culture news and reviews — in areas like visual art, film, books, music, food and theater — has grown even as coverage has waned at larger outlets.
Despite the funding decline, nearly four out of five organizations surveyed said their audience has grown.
Yet the sector of the news media that covers the arts “has largely been left out of existing nonprofit funding networks” and “need[s] increased philanthropic support,” the report said.
News organizations have increasingly relied on philanthropy to address funding shortfalls, with more than half of respondents citing foundation and philanthropic grants as sources of funding — a percentage exceeded only by gifts from individual donors.
Advertising revenue, subscriptions or memberships, sponsorships and events are also sources of funding. State and local funding are also part of the mix.
Third-party point of view
Unrelated to the Rabkin findings, a media expert recently weighed in on the topic in Editor & Publisher magazine, a newspaper trade publication.
“The most immediate impact of a shrinking newsroom is the severing of the local arts visibility pipeline. Over the past two decades, we have watched thousands of newspapers vanish or hollow out, leaving millions of Americans with limited access to local reporting,” writes Stuart N. Brotman, digital media laureate at the McLean, Va.-based Media Institute, adding that “the first desks to be cleared out are almost always the arts and culture beats.”
Echoing the findings in the Rabkin report, Brotman notes that foundations and other sources of funding are often called on for rescue.
“Philanthropy is increasingly stepping into the breach to subsidize local news, treating it as a public trust much like a municipal museum or regional theater. But isolated, parallel grants are only a stopgap,” Brotman writes.

title: Iran widens Gulf attacks, firing on a US air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain
text:
Iran widens Gulf attacks, firing on a US air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain
Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before.
After about two months without such attacks, Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain in recent days. The small Persian Gulf island kingdom hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet.
The early morning attacks came after a U.S. fighter jet struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site Tuesday on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. strike was in retaliation for an Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain earlier Tuesday.
Related video: Who's meeting with President Trump for this week's historic nuclear summit in Asia?
Iran said that its recent attacks — including those on other U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday — were in response to U.S. drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
The uptick in fighting with the tit-for-tat attacks raises the risk of further escalation toward the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
The U.S. military didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest attacks.
Blockade puts pressure on Tehran
With its economy suffering under a U.S. naval blockade and American military escorts helping restore the passage of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say that the recent attacks suggest Tehran may be growing weary of the status quo.
“Even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation and escalation beyond what either side originally intended,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X following the initial reports of the attack on Kuwait.
U.S. President Donald Trump has sent mixed messages on his next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely, but also sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East.
Though U.S. military protection has helped restore oil shipments from the Gulf, Iran has continued to attack tankers as they attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
United Arab Emirates state-owned oil company ADNOC said Wednesday that one of its tanker crew members was missing after an attack in the strait on Tuesday, while 11 others were injured and were receiving medical care.
Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, described an “increasingly clear” pattern of attacks by Iran on shipping and U.S. facilities in the Gulf region.
“Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of deliberate, calibrated escalation,” he wrote in an analysis on X. “The objective is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade.”
He said that Washington is faced with the dilemma that a limited response may encourage Iran to push further, while a stronger response risks accelerating the escalation that the U.S. is trying to avoid.
“As long as the U.S. naval blockade remains in place and no agreement is reached, further escalation will become increasingly difficult to avoid,” he said. “There are two clear paths to de-escalation: a negotiated agreement or a U.S. decision to lift the blockade.”
Iran renews attacks on American bases
After Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 to launch the war, Iran regularly fired on American facilities and interests in neighboring Gulf countries, as well as energy infrastructure and other targets.
In the attack early Wednesday on the Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait, the Iranian military fired at air defense systems and drone and missile launch platforms, according to a report on Iran's state broadcaster.
Kuwait's military said that its air defenses had intercepted drone attacks and didn't immediately report any damage. The Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the repeated Iranian attacks as “criminal,” saying that they threatened the country's security and stability.
During the war, Ali Al Salem Air Base has been struck at least 30 times by Iran, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to a report by The Associated Press.
Meanwhile, Bahrain's Interior Ministry issued two alerts early Wednesday urging people to take shelter, followed by the “all clear” a short time later. The country's military later said that it had intercepted a number of attacks from Iran, but gave no information on any damage or casualties.
Houthis target Riyadh after deadly coalition strikes
Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles fired toward the capital, Riyadh, by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. Alerts also sounded in three other Saudi cities. Civil defense authorities later said that the danger had passed, but provided no further details.
The previous day, coalition forces launched a major air attack across rebel-held areas of Yemen that the Houthis said killed at least 17 people.
Al-Malki said that Tuesday’s strikes destroyed “60 legitimate military targets” and aimed to weaken the Houthis’ missile and drone capabilities.
The strikes followed the withdrawal of Saudi-backed forces from areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a setback for the anti-Houthi camp. The withdrawal consolidated the Houthis' grip on the strategic waterway, which is crucial to international trade and global oil shipments.
___
Rising reported from Bangkok.

Amazon return settlement: Could you get a payment?
Amazon agreed to a $309.5 million settlement over return and refund claims. See who may qualify and how to file before the Dec. 1 deadline.
Amazon return settlement: Could you get a payment?
Amazon agreed to a $309.5 million settlement over return and refund claims. See who may qualify and how to file before the Dec. 1 deadline.
Go check your Spam folder. Notices are going out that you could be eligible for money from an Amazon settlement, but you'll need to move fast.
Amazon agreed to pay $309.5 million into a settlement fund to resolve a class-action lawsuit over its return and refund practices. The lawsuit alleges Amazon failed to issue some refunds, issued them late or incorrectly, or charged customers again after they returned products. Amazon denies wrongdoing in the case.
Consumers may qualify if they initiated a return or requested a refund for a physical product sold through Amazon.com and recorded as received in the U.S. from Sept. 5, 2017, through Feb. 12, 2026, and then did not receive a refund, received an untimely or incorrect refund, or were later charged for the returned product.
The settlement does not promise a set payment for each person. The $309.5 million fund also covers administration costs and court-approved attorneys' fees and other expenses. Payments will depend on the eligible transactions and whether a person’s claims fall into Subclass A or Subclass B.
Subclass A members do not need to file a claim form. They will receive payments automatically but should visit the settlement website to select a payment method.
Subclass B members must submit a claim online or mail a completed form by Dec. 1, 2026. Forms can be submitted through the settlement website or mailed to:
Amazon Return Policy Litigation
Attn: Claim Forms
P.O. Box 10
East Brunswick, NJ 08816-9998
People unsure whether they qualify or which subclass they are in can call the settlement administrator at 1-888-553-4246 or email info@ReturnSettlement.com. The settlement notice also says consumers can check "Your Transactions" on Amazon.com for information about their returns and refunds.

title: Rainfall supercharged by El Niño causes road flooding, collapsed synagogue roof in south Florida
text:
PLANTATION, Fla. (AP) — A slow-moving storm system dumped heavy rains that prompted an emergency declaration Wednesday in South Florida where the roof of a synagogue collapsed and cars were submerged along roads, authorities said.
On the West Coast, heavy rain and high winds grounded planes at San Francisco’s airport, disrupted ferry service and flooded roads in Napa County and other wine country areas north of the city.
Preliminary figures for Florida showed 15.3 inches (39 centimeters) of rain fell in a 24-hour period ending Wednesday in parts of Broward County, the National Weather Service said.
The threat was expected to last through Friday along Florida’s Atlantic Coast with additional rainfall amounts of 12 inches (30 centimeters) possible, the weather service said.
The Florida Division of Emergency Management said in an advisory Tuesday night that “potentially catastrophic” amounts of rainfall could cause flash flooding, life-threatening rip tides and expected minor beach erosion due to high surf.
On top of all that, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday, a low-pressure system is expected to form near the northern Bahamas. It could become a subtropical or tropical storm over parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts into early next week, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami.
The natural warming cycle called El Niño has disrupted Florida’s typical dry season that runs from October to May, said Alejandra Garcia, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Miami. El Niño is “helping bring these low pressure systems down toward the southeastern United States, which in turn is causing these heavy precipitation events,” she said.
Florida mayor calls the deluge ‘historically significant’
In Florida, the city of Hollywood declared a state of emergency Wednesday and Mayor Josh Levy urged motorists to stay off roads and avoid unnecessary travel. Portions of the Florida Turnpike and Interstate 95 in Hollywood were closed due to high water and stalled vehicles.
The city said it received more than 300 calls for service overnight.
“It’s a historically significant rainfall event in the city,” Levy said.
Some residents complained that motorists who were driving too fast caused a wake that pushed floodwaters into their homes, he said.
Heavy rains caused the roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood to collapse. No injuries were reported.
The highest rainfall amount was recorded in Plantation, where resident Jade Jaime said the storm just kept going all day “and then by the time we went to sleep at night, still just pouring down like it was never going to end.”
In Fort Lauderdale, the 5.72 inches (14.5 centimeters) of rain that fell in a downpour ending early Wednesday broke the daily record of 1.8 inches (4.5 centimeters) set in 1959, Garcia said.
In northern Florida, a warning was issued for minor flooding along the St. Johns River.
California is loaded with weather concerns
The Los Angeles County Fire Department issued an evacuation warning Wednesday for the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn scar areas, saying there was a risk of debris flows as a storm approaches. The warning is in effect from Wednesday evening through Friday morning.
In San Francisco, areas along the Embarcadero were flooded Wednesday morning as waves crashed over barricades recently installed to prevent flooding near the Ferry Building, a waterfront landmark. Officials canceled several ferries leading from the city due to the storm.
Several highways were blocked by flooding or debris in Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties, according to the California Department of Transportation and the California Highway Patrol.
Heavy rain that began falling north of San Francisco was expected to spread south to the Central Coast later Wednesday, the weather service said.
Wind gusts of up to 50 mph (80 kph) were forecast for San Francisco’s East Bay and up to 70 mph (113 kph) for the Altamont Pass, which connects Bay Area highways to I-5 in the Central Valley.
Snow accumulations of up to 4 feet (1.2 meters) were forecast through Friday in the highest portions of the Sierra Nevada Mountains.
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. Associated Press reporter Olga R. Rodriguez in San Francisco contributed to this report.

title: Pearl Harbor survivor Gebhard 'Geb' Galle dies at 105. He's remembered for saving 4 shipmates
text:
Pearl Harbor survivor Gebhard 'Geb' Galle dies at 105. He's remembered for saving 4 shipmates
Gebhard “Geb” Galle, one of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors who later saved four shipmates from a sinking vessel in battle, has died.
Galle died Saturday at his home in Moses Lake, Washington, his daughter, Lynda Palmer, said. He was 105.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
“Your humility, quick thinking and selfless actions remain a shining example of Navy valor,” then-Acting Chief of Naval Operations Adm. James Kilby wrote in a letter to Galle for his 104th birthday in 2025.
Galle died the same day as the oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor, Freeman Johnson, of Centerville, Massachusetts, who was 106. Galle and Johnson were among the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941.
The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
Galle was waiting to leave the USS Nevada for church the day of the attack
Galle was born in Germany. He came to North Dakota with his family in 1928 at age 7. He joined the U.S. Navy in 1939 at age 18.
On Dec. 7, 1941, Galle, then 20, was a machinist's mate aboard the USS Nevada, waiting below deck to be taken ashore for church services. He looked out of a porthole and saw planes approaching.
Galle went down to his battle station two decks below in the engineering section.
A torpedo hit the Nevada, allowing water to enter the ship, but officers were able to get it moving, the Navy said. The ship was attacked again, causing more leaks in the hull and fires. The Nevada ran aground.
Galle could not see what was happening.
“Of course, we felt a couple jolts, and that’s when we got hit with the torpedo, and we had a few bomb hits,” he told the Columbia Basin Herald, a newspaper based in Moses Lake, in 2020.
“After we were beached and everything, and we got up to topside, then we saw all the mess that took place,” including the capsized USS Oklahoma and the partially submerged USS Arizona, he said.
“A pretty sad lookout,” Galle said.
Palmer, the oldest of his five children, told The Associated Press in an interview Tuesday that her dad didn't talk much about the war until after he saw “Tora! Tora! Tora!,” the 1970 film that examines events leading up to the 1941 attack.
“I said, ‘Dad, go see this movie and tell me how much of it is true,’ and he said, ‘Most of it was.’ It was really something. And then he started to elaborate a little bit,” she said.
Galle rescued shipmates from sinking ship during battle in 1942
Galle was reassigned to the USS Northampton after the Pearl Harbor attack. That ship came under fire on Nov. 30, 1942, by Japanese torpedoes during the Battle of Tassafaronga.
Galle told the Basin Herald he was ordered to leave a hatch closed behind four sailors who would've been trapped when the ship was sinking. The officer left, but Galle defied the order, opening the hatch. He closed and secured it after the sailors escaped.
“He heard those guys pounding on the roof of the hatch,” Palmer said. “He went to open it up, and the senior officer walked by and said, ‘No, leave it closed, because we don’t want water to get in there because the ship might go down.”
Her dad told her, “'I was in that. It's called an after-steering compartment,'” Palmer recalled. “'It's very scary, because you are enclosed and you cannot get out from down there. You have to be let out from the top.'”
The Northampton sank, and Galle and other sailors spent more than a day adrift in life rafts before they were rescued.
“From the decks of the USS Nevada to the battles of the Pacific aboard the USS Northampton and USS Mobile, your courage under fire and steadfast dedication were extraordinary,” Kilby wrote in his letter to Galle. “You helped save shipmates from a sinking vessel, witnessed the launch of the Doolittle Raid, and fought in 19 of 20 Pacific naval engagements.”
He attended the 75th anniversary Pearl Harbor service honoring the USS Nevada
In December 2016, Galle attended a 75th anniversary service at Pearl Harbor to honor and commemorate the USS Nevada and those who served on it. A total of 76 sailors and Marines lost their lives as a result of that attack, the Navy said.
“You can carry your hatred all of your life,” Galle said of the attack at the event. “You have to remember, they had a leader who led them astray. We’re at peace now, and I feel comfortable. I have no qualm. We’re all good people.”
After the war, Galle got married and opened a refrigeration and air-conditioning business in Grafton, North Dakota. He then served as a civil engineer with the U.S. Air Force and then later worked for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. He retired in the 1980s.

title: Family fined nearly $2,000 over tin rooster statues in front yard sues town
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OGUNQUIT, Maine (WMTW) - A Maine family that has been fined $1,700 over tin rooster statues in their lawn has filed a federal lawsuit, claiming their right to free speech has been violated.
Dave and Sara LeBlanc first put a 6-foot-tall tin rooster in front of their Ogunquit home in May 2025. The couple say it’s a show of love and support for their daughter, Pyper, who has autism. The 6-year-old loves roosters, and her parents say the statue helped her find comfort on her way to and from school.
Over time, the couple acquired about two dozen tin roosters, but they say they never displayed more than eight at once – with the exception of the Christmas holiday season.
However, the LeBlancs also own The Omelette Factory, a breakfast restaurant that is attached to the family’s home, and the town of Oguinquit considers their rooster statues to be advertisement for the business.
In April 2026, the town sent the LeBlancs a letter, telling them they had to remove all “unpermitted signage,” including the rooster statues. Since then, the couple have been fined $1,700, which they say they paid under protest.
The couple now have just one rooster in their yard, which has been covered up. The remaining statues were given to friends and neighbors, who have displayed them outside their homes and businesses as a show of support for Pyper.
“Never imagined it getting to the point where it is, but it had to. We had no choice,” Dave LeBlanc said.
The LeBlancs are suing the town, arguing their right to free speech as guaranteed by the First Amendment has been violated.
“It’s not neutral. It’s not even-handed. It’s uneven, unfair and arbitrary. So, that’s why this is unconstitutional,” said attorney Daniel Woislaw from the Institute for Justice, a national nonprofit that is representing the LeBlancs. “It is not something that towns have a monopoly on deciding what art is or what art means.”
Pyper’s parents say the situation has brought up a mix of emotions for their daughter; though she’s happy other people are sharing in what she loves.
“It’s a range of emotions for her because she’s like, ‘Why can’t the town be nice? We’re taught to be nice,’” Sara LeBlanc said.
The LeBlancs’ lawsuit requests damages, including money to cover the paid fines.
Town officials did not provide a comment on the lawsuit.

title: US and Venezuela sign a deal to reestablish military ties, Hegseth says on visit to interim leaders
text:
CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties that will range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday in Caracas while visiting the South American nation’s interim leaders.
Hegseth touted how U.S. forces in January captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, telling an audience of diplomats and military officials from both countries that now Venezuela “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.”
He also praised the “close cooperation” with acting President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials “to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all,” in a reference to drug traffickers.
Hegseth’s visit, the latest in a series of stops in Venezuela by members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet, underscores efforts by the U.S. administration to deepen its influence in the South American country. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.
Hegseth praises Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
The Pentagon chief praised the energy deal by referencing another major military action by the Trump administration this year — the Iran war. The conflict has disrupted global energy supplies through a critical waterway in the Persian Gulf, raising gasoline prices and contributing to the Republican Party’s severe losses in this month’s midterm elections.
The Venezuela oil deal “makes the Strait of Hormuz a nonfactor for the Western Hemisphere,” Hegseth said at the U.S. Embassy in Caracas.
In the meeting with Hegseth, Rodríguez asserted that the deal enables “the energy development of our nations” and “benefits both the people of the United States and the people of Venezuela.”
Among those in attendance for Hegseth’s speech was Alejandro Betancourt, the owner of North American Blue Energy Partners, the second-largest oil operator in Venezuela. The U.S. government and Betancourt’s company entered into the ambitious agreement to tap Venezuela’s vast oil reserves.
Both the Interior and Energy secretaries also visited Venezuela earlier this year and focused their efforts on tapping its oil reserves and critical minerals. The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.
Hegseth later stopped in Bogota, Colombia, where he was greeted at a military base by the country’s defense and foreign ministers.
Few details provided on the US-Venezuela military agreement
Hegseth offered few specifics on what the military agreement would entail, beyond saying that the two countries’ militaries would be “training together, partnering together, sharing intelligence, more defense equipment and capabilities together.”
Speaking separately, Rodríguez said she hoped the countries’ military cooperation “can be brought to its highest possible level” to allow them to “address common threats.”
Hegseth pointed to Venezuela partnering with the U.S. “to recover its territory from narco-terrorist networks.” The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.
The development comes as the U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump’s return to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.
To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narco-terrorists” in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs or that they have made an impact on the availability of drugs in the country.
Hegseth also used his speech to boast about the military operation that seized Maduro, calling it “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America” that “lasted just 48 minutes.”
“America’s best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours,” he added.
But Venezuela’s ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.
Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader “predicted,” the operation ended with “no war, yes, peace.”
Uncertainty about Venezuela’s political future
Hegseth’s visit also comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.
Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela’s head of state.
Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for “working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela.”
Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by the U.S., which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.
The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.
___
Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Mainers can write household energy plans to reduce usage, combat climate change
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Nov. 9, negotiators from nearly 200 countries met in Antalya, Türkiye, for the 31st United Nations climate conference (COP31) to review one another’s climate plans. Strip away the diplomatic language and each plan says this: Here’s what we emit now, here’s how much less we intend to emit, and here’s how we’ll get there. You can do your part by writing a household energy plan: Review 12 months of utility bills and decide how to save energy (and money) at home.
It may feel like homework. But it’s the kind of homework that pays you back every month. It also sets you on the path to becoming a Sustainable Practitioner.
This step sits on the energy pathway (wasting less, electrifying, choosing cleaner sources) and leans into community, because a plan you share is a plan you’re more likely to keep. We usually suggest energy steps that are single moves: flipping the ceiling fan, resetting your thermostat, choosing green power. This one is the ledger behind all of them, showing which moves matter most in your house and whether they’re working.
WHAT ANTALYA IS CHECKING
COP31 ran through this week, ending Nov. 20, hosted by Türkiye with Australia presiding over negotiations. A central question is whether countries’ newest climate plans add up to enough. Every one starts from a measured baseline.
National energy data reflect decisions made at kitchen tables. Most of us know roughly what we pay for heat and power, but few know how much fuel and electricity we consume each year, and fewer still have a number to aim for.
A GOAL PLUS A SCOREBOARD
Behavioral scientists have tested this pairing for decades. In a 1978 field study, psychologist Lawrence Becker asked families to set goals for cutting summer electricity use. Some picked an easy 2% target, others a hard 20%, and half of each group got feedback three times a week. Only one group significantly outperformed households with no intervention: families with the hard goal and regular feedback, who cut use 13-15%.
Nearly three decades later, researchers in the Netherlands gave households a 5% savings goal, information tailored to their homes, and periodic feedback. After five months, those households used 5.1% less energy, while a comparison group used 0.7% more.
Neither the target nor the scoreboard does the job alone. Together, they reliably move the gauge.
DRAFTING YOUR PLAN
Start by gathering 12 months of energy use. You want quantities, not dollars: kilowatt-hours from your electric bill, therms or hundreds of cubic feet (CCF) from your gas bill, gallons from oil or propane delivery receipts. Many utilities offer the whole year in one file; log in and look for a “Green Button” or “Download My Data” link. Add it all up. That’s your baseline.
Now write three lines on a single sheet of paper:
• Baseline: how much energy your household used over the past 12 months.
• Target: what you’ll aim for in 2027. Becker’s work suggests a goal that makes you stretch beats a comfortable one, so aim for 10-20% less.
• Practices: two or three specific actions that will get you there. Last week’s thermostat and timer schedules are a natural first entry.
Post the sheet wherever you open bills. Each month, compare the bill with the same month a year earlier. Note “very cold month” to explain a jump. Most people who set a goal never check progress. This two-minute monthly glance is your feedback.
YOUR 1 STEP THIS WEEK
• Set a deadline to pull 12 months of energy use, including both fuel and electricity.
• Add it up, and put your baseline, your 2027 target, and your practices on one page.
• Show it to one other person: whoever shares your utility bill, or a neighbor or friend who’d enjoy comparing notes.
Delegates in Antalya will have argued over gigatons. You can finish your own energy plan before the end of the day, and a year from now you’ll know exactly how far you’ve come.

You can pick up their new 2026 edition of “Your Earth Share: Seven Pathways to Sustainable Living” or any of their other publications at SustainablePractice.Life. title: How scammers use ‘number cycling’ to get around spam filters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Five years after federal requirements to fight spoofed robocalls began taking effect, unwanted calls are still getting through, according to a new report from U.S. PIRG Education Fund.
Teresa Murray, a consumer watchdog with U.S. PIRG, said the problem is far from solved.
“I still get them. I’m sure you still get them. And in many ways, it’s as bad as ever,” Murray said.
In its “Ringing in Our Fears” report, U.S. PIRG Education Fund analyzed FCC records from more than 11,000 registered phone providers. Of those, 42% reported fully implementing technology designed to verify the number displayed on caller ID.
The report also found some progress. Unwanted robocalls have declined to an average of about 2.1 billion a month this year, down from nearly 2.5 billion last year.
One tactic is known as “number cycling,” according to the report. Some scammers buy or rent large blocks of phone numbers and use each one sparingly to avoid being flagged by spam filters. Once they have gone through the numbers, they start the cycle again.
Murray described where regulators are turning next.
“So now, what a lot of the regulators are focusing on, is trying to go after the companies that sell and lease phone numbers to bad guys. So they’re going to keep on going trying to go after the phone companies who aren’t doing a good job of filtering calls. And they’re going to continue going after guys who are scamming people,” Murray said.
The FCC is also considering stricter “know your customer” rules that would require phone companies to more closely vet who they provide phone numbers to. State attorneys general are also pushing for greater oversight of companies that buy and resell phone numbers, to help law enforcement track down illegal robocalls.
Murray recommends letting unrecognized calls go to voicemail and never providing personal or payment information to an unexpected caller, regardless of what the caller ID says.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: November Warmth Continues Across Northern Maine Before a Colder Pattern Returns Next Week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Tuesday. We’re continuing to enjoy a rather quiet stretch of weather across Northern Maine and Western New Brunswick, and it looks like that trend will stick around for much of the remainder of the week. Temperatures are running well above average for the middle of November, and we could even see a few communities climbing into the mid 50s before the weekend arrives. While the sunshine and warmer temperatures are certainly nice, the extended stretch of dry weather isn’t helping our ongoing drought conditions. Looking further ahead, we’re keeping an eye on a potential weather system early next week that could bring some rain to the region before a much colder air mass moves in.
Heading into the overnight hours tonight, we’ll see a few more clouds beginning to work their way into the region. Skies will start off partly cloudy before becoming mostly cloudy as we head toward Wednesday morning. These clouds, combined with a continued westerly breeze, will help keep temperatures a little milder than what we experienced last night. Most locations will see overnight lows falling into the lower to mid 30s. I’m forecasting a low of 35 degrees in Presque Isle, 34 in Caribou, and 34 degrees in Houlton. Winds will remain out of the west at around 5 to 10 mph, although some of our northern communities could see gusts around 20 to 30 mph during the evening hours.
As we head into Wednesday, we’ll be looking at a fairly cloudy day across much of the region, but that won’t stop temperatures from climbing well above average. An upper-level ridge of high pressure continues to build across the Northeast, helping to keep our weather quiet while allowing warmer air to move into the region. Despite seeing more clouds than sunshine throughout the day, temperatures should still manage to reach the upper 40s and lower 50s. I’m forecasting a high of 53 degrees in Presque Isle, around 50 in Caribou, and 53 degrees in Houlton. For reference, the average high temperature in Caribou for this time of year is only 39 degrees! One thing you’ll certainly notice Wednesday is the wind. We’re expecting west winds around 10 to 15 mph, with occasional gusts up to 25 mph. While it won’t be an exceptionally windy day, that breeze will be noticeable, especially if you’re spending time outdoors. The good news is that we’re not anticipating any precipitation, so despite the clouds, it should remain a dry day across the region.
Looking ahead to Thursday, we’ll start to see more sunshine returning to Northern Maine and Western New Brunswick. We’ll likely begin the day with a few clouds around, but those should gradually give way to increasing sunshine as we head through the afternoon. Temperatures will continue to run well above average, with most locations climbing into the lower to mid 50s. I’m forecasting a high of 53 degrees in Presque Isle, 53 in Caribou, and 55 degrees in Houlton. Some of our southern communities, including Millinocket, could also reach the mid 50s. Winds will be relatively light out of the southwest at around 5 mph, making Thursday a fairly pleasant day for the middle of November.
Taking a look at our cloud cover forecast, you’ll notice that Wednesday will likely feature the greatest amount of cloud coverage over the next several days. From there, we’ll see improving conditions heading into Thursday and Friday, with plenty of opportunities for sunshine. Saturday may bring a few more clouds into the region, but we’re still expecting a decent amount of sunshine before heading into Sunday. The reason for all of this quiet weather is a strong ridge of high pressure that continues to dominate much of the eastern United States. This ridge is helping to suppress the development of any significant precipitation across our region, while also allowing temperatures to remain considerably warmer than what we’d normally expect this time of year. Even a weak upper-level disturbance moving through on Friday is unlikely to produce any precipitation, thanks to the influence of high pressure closer to the surface.
As we look at our temperature trend for Caribou, you’ll notice that we’re expecting an extended stretch of above-average temperatures. Highs should remain in the lower 50s through Thursday, before potentially climbing into the mid 50s on Friday. That’s roughly 15 degrees warmer than what we’d typically expect for the middle of November. Temperatures will cool off a little on Saturday, with highs dropping back into the upper 40s, but we’ll see another rebound heading into Sunday as temperatures once again climb into the lower 50s. That’s certainly not a bad way to spend a November weekend across The County!
Unfortunately, all of this dry weather is continuing to take a toll on our ongoing drought conditions. While we did receive some beneficial rainfall earlier this month, it wasn’t nearly enough to eliminate the significant moisture deficits that have developed across Northern and Eastern Maine. Groundwater levels and streamflows remain well below normal in many locations, and the continued lack of precipitation will only make it more difficult for those levels to recover. With little to no meaningful rainfall expected through the weekend, we’re likely to see drought conditions persist or potentially worsen.
For now, we’ve got several more days of relatively quiet and warmer-than-average November weather ahead of us! I’ll continue to keep an eye on that potential system early next week, especially as we get a better idea of its track and what it could mean for precipitation across our region. For a closer look at the forecast, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening everyone!

title: Historical Society fall art raffle drawing Dec. 12
text:
The Boothbay Region Historical Society is holding a fundraising raffle of a Douglas Remley painting and the drawing will be held Saturday, Dec. 12. Tickets are $10 each or three for $25.
The framed painting, “Damariscove,” is 32” x 43” or 23” x 35” unframed.
Born in Indiana, Remley (1946-2004) came to East Boothbay in 1984. He experimented in different media, creating maritime and coastal images, often in almost photographic detail. His art can be seen in museums, private collections and online auctions. This wonderful oil painting is on display at the historical society, 72 Oak Street, Boothbay Harbor.
Proceeds from this fundraiser will support our mission to collect and preserve the history of the Boothbay Region and promote public interest through research, exhibits, and programs offered at the Society.
For more information, call 207-633-0820 or email Connie at chart@boothbayhistorical.org.

title: Official said ground stop might have been shorter if L3Harris had spotted the problem sooner
text:
Official said ground stop might have been shorter if L3Harris had spotted the problem sooner
The nationwide ground stop on Friday could have ended sooner if the contractor that did the work linked to the disruptions at key air traffic control facilities had located the problem sooner, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Investigators are still working to determine exactly why the newly installed router at the center of everything started blasting out thousands of connection attempts not long after it was turned on as part of a project to replace a section of old copper wires with fiber optic lines in Arkansas.
Duffy appeared on the 2WAY streaming platform's “The Morning Meeting” show Wednesday and said that L3Harris failed to identify and isolate the router issue that caused the ground stop quickly enough. That contributed to this being the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks because it lasted more than four hours.
Related video above: Transportation leaders give update after rare FAA nationwide ground stop
“The monitoring of the network matters,” he said, adding that officials were working on remedying that problem. In the meantime, any new installations of these same routers have been paused, and technicians have disabled the function that was linked to Friday’s outage.
Experts continue testing the equipment linked to the problem to determine why this Juniper router behaved differently from any of the ones installed in 68 previous projects across the FAA network. The investigators are focused on whether the router was configured incorrectly by the experienced technician who did the work or whether it was faulty. The company that made the router has said it believes the “device functioned as it was configured by the installer.”
Friday's problems are reminiscent of a 2009 outage
The circumstances of the technical problems that led to last week's nationwide ground stop appear eerily similar to a 2009 outage caused by a technician doing the same kind of work installing new fiber optic lines.
The Transportation Department's Inspector General said the 2009 disruption that led to 820 delayed flights was caused by a Harris technician setting up a router incorrectly. Harris later became L3Harris as part of a merger, but that company has been operating and maintaining the FAA network for decades.
Matthew Hampton, who was the former assistant inspector general for aviation at that time, said that the FAA has long had weak oversight of the contractors it relies on.
“Poor contractor oversight has been a problem at the FAA in both developing systems and deploying them; there’s a whole history of that,” Hampton said.
L3Harris hasn’t commented on the ground stop since issuing a statement Saturday pledging to support the FAA’s investigation into what happened. The company declined to say more on Wednesday.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a different event hosted by The Hill on Wednesday morning that he understands that his agency is ultimately responsible for what happened even if L3Harris was the one doing the work.
“I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it,” Bedford said. “I wish people would lay off the secretary. He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So, blame me.”
It's not clear how much more money Congress will approve for the overhaul
The FAA nearly doubled its funding request to Congress to $50 billion after Friday's ground stop to pay for the rest of the overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. Last year, the agency received $12.5 billion to get started on the project. Bedford said he understands why members of Congress might be having “some indigestion associated with that.”
Several key lawmakers said Tuesday that Congress is unlikely to approve that full amount right now — especially when the FAA hasn't spent all the money that was approved last year. Duffy has said that a big part of why some of the money hasn't been spent yet is that the new radars and other systems that will be installed are still being built, so he hasn't been able to buy them yet.
Only about $10 billion of the $50 billion request would go to air traffic control technology. The rest of the money would go to other projects, including upgrades to runways, airport towers and aging air traffic control centers that were built in the 1960s.
More problems are possible while upgrading the outdated FAA system
Chris Sununu, who is president of the Airlines for America trade group, praised Bedford for keeping the airlines informed during the ground stop. Sununu said Bedford asked to set up a conference call with all the airline CEOs and operations leaders within about half an hour of the ground stop starting and briefed them on what he knew so far. Several additional calls were held throughout the ground stop.
“To be honest, he stayed on the phone effectively with all the CEOs all night long,” Sununu said. “We did, I think, three or four calls over the period of the next few hours, brought in those operational folks. And so as they learned more, as they understood more of what was happening.”
Sununu said the FAA has a difficult job in trying to overhaul “what is really the most robust telecom system on the planet while you’re using it 24 hours a day and ensuring the safety of everyone who is part of it.” And he said this might not be the last technical problem that happens during the project because the work the FAA is doing is akin to trying to get your iPhone to talk to your flip phone.
“Can we say, ‘oh, you know, this is really the last time we’re going to have a bump like this?’ No, no. Because the technologies we’re replacing and that we’re asking to talk to each other are literally multigenerational,” he said.

title: Commissioners approve $5K gift to sheriff's department from anonymous donor
text:
It seems somebody out there approves of how Sheriff Todd Brackett runs the Lincoln County Sheriff's Department. On Nov. 17, the commissioners approved a "$5,000 anonymous donation" earmarked for the sheriff's department. Finance Director Michelle Kane told commissioners she had limited information about the donation. "I received a phone call last week from a gentlemen who reached out with an anonymous donation with one stipulation: it went to the sheriff's office. After that, all I know is I received a $5,000 check from Goldman Sachs," she said.
In other action, commissioners approved the 2027 county budget. The commissioners approved a $15,886,518 budget which reflects a 3.67% increase.
Commissioners approved a $17,906.26 purchase for equipping the sheriff's department's new Chevy Tahoe SUV. The payment for equipment and installation went to Island Tech Services in Wiscasset. The new equipment includes a cage, lights, siren and a compartment for storing items in the back.
Commissioners authorized the sheriff's department to seek out requests for proposals for a new 2027 Chevy Tahoe SUV. Brackett expects the department will purchase five or possibly six more vehicles in 2027. He expects the RFPs back by Jan. 5, 2027.
The sheriff’s department also received approval to replace the department's 10-year-old handguns arsenal. Brackett told commissioners the department exchanges weapons every 10 years. Commissioners approved $7,360 for the purchase. Brackett expects resale of the old handguns will offset the purchase price.
The Lincoln County Regional Planning Commission received approval for two contract renewals. Commissioners approved renewing the Municipal Planning Assistance Program Coastal TA contract. The renewal runs through the rest of the fiscal year. Executive Director Emily Rabbe said the program is funded through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The program assists with land use planning, technical assistance and guidance to coastal municipalities. LCRPC received $10,539 in financial assistance.
The LCRPC is in year three of a contract for reslience coordinator funding through the Maine Office of Community Affairs. In the first two years, LCRPC used the funding to hire Gabe McPhail of Resilient Communties L3C in Vinalhaven for assisting with coordinating on a regional scale. Rabbe said McPhail would continue in the position for year three. "In cooperation with the Midcoast Council of Governments, Greater Portland Council of Governments, and Southern Maine Planning and Development Commission, she will provide some trainings," she said. "She is also doing a grid resiliency series. She also planned our Twin Villages site visit in Newcastle and Damariscotta."
The grant is for $12,000 as it was for the first two years, said Rabbe.
Commissioners approved hiring Stephanie Buzzell as the new county human resources director. Her first day is Dec. 1. The commissioners agreed to hear a tax abatement request between Pentaleri Trust v. Town of Alna. No hearing date was set.
Commissioners meet next at 9 a.m. on Tuesday, Dec. 1 in the courthouse.

title: White House pulls FDA nominee Heidi Overton after wavering support from Republicans
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation.
Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for President Donald Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultuous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary.
But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his administration’s approach to vaccines.
Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday morning.
Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot — “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to disagree with Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.
But late Tuesday night, Cassidy suggested he had been prepared to back Overton and suggested her nomination was derailed by disagreements over abortion, not vaccines.
“I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy stated in a posting on X.
He went on to say that anti-abortion Republicans had sought commitments on “life issues” from the White House, but “the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.”
Currently, the FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone — at the request of Trump — that could reinstate restrictions on the drug’s use, including a requirement for in-person prescribing. FDA has promised a report on its safety findings by March.
To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on the chamber floor.
Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January.
It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee.
Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees
Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee.
Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton’s approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children.
Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides.
Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists.
“There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said.
Trump has pulled back several other health nominations
Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats.
The FDA is currently being led on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency.
The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. The FDA has lost about 20% of its employees to layoffs, buyouts, retirements or resignations since Trump took office.

title: House Democrat targets Trump family and top officials in early steps toward promised investigations
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is laying the groundwork for long-promised investigations of the Trump administration that will launch with the new Congress in January.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control, sent letters directing members of President Donald Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. It’s an early step toward undertaking investigations of the Republican president and his administration.
The letters released Wednesday cover a wide range of potential investigations, including alleged financial conflicts involving Trump’s family, misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security and the administration’s handling of files related to Jeffrey Epstein.
“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”
Targets of the letters include two of Trump’s sons, Vice President JD Vance, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law.
The White House has repeatedly pushed back at the investigative ambitions outlined by Democrats, with officials saying they are willing to engage on oversight inquiries that they see as legitimate but not ones assessed as politically motivated.
The president is “willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”
Later Wednesday, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote a letter addressed to Democratic lawmakers, effectively dismissing requests for information from them for the remainder of the year because Democrats are currently not in the majority.
Scharf said he was citing a position that the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden took in 2022, and that while “some of you may (or may not) become a chair in the 120th Congress, that does not mean that requests from the 119th Congress carry over.”
The letters that the White House has gotten from Democrats in recent days, Scharf wrote, “drip with an animus or pettiness revealing that the purpose of these letters is not legitimate oversight but to harass and aggrandize.” The latest White House letter was first reported by Politico.
Still, the letters from Democrats offer an early glimpse of how they plan to use their newly won congressional majority to scrutinize Trump and his administration. As favorable election results rolled in for Democrats on election night, Garcia posted a two-word warning on social media: “Lawyer up.”
The preservation notices do not compel recipients to turn over documents, but they signal the investigations that Democrats intend to pursue once they gain control of the committee and its subpoena power in January.
Before the midterms, Garcia outlined several areas Democrats would scrutinize, including the administration’s handling of the Epstein investigation, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and potential financial conflicts involving Trump’s family.
The letters to Kushner and Trump’s sons Eric and Donald Jr. seek to preserve documents related to alleged conflicts of interest and their business dealings. Garcia also sent notices to Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former U.S. ambassador to Greece, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over separate allegations of misconduct and financial conflicts.
The letters to Vance and Blanche focus on the administration’s handling of files related to Epstein, including allegations by Democrats that White House officials sought to conceal information and manage the political fallout from the investigation.
The White House has warned Garcia and other Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration may open them up to investigations from the Justice Department.
Last week, Scharf said in a letter to Garcia that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”
The investigative powers of Congress are well established, inherent in its constitutional authority as a check on the other branches of government. Modern U.S. history is filled with congressional investigations and their aftermath, from the Watergate investigation to the 9/11 attacks to Republicans’ more recent look into Biden’s family.
