title: New 'toxic hall of shame' includes Publix, Trader Joe’s and McDonald’s
text:
New 'toxic hall of shame' includes Publix, Trader Joe’s and McDonald’s
Released just in time for this season’s flurry of holiday shopping, the 2026 Toxic Hall of Shame gives 16 major retailers an F for their failure to prioritize reducing hazardous chemicals and plastics in the products they sell.
Recent research has found that nearly 93% of studied plastic chemicals used to wrap food and make clothes, toys, and other common household and personal care products may pose a high risk to human health. Human and animal studies link these synthetic compounds to cancer, genetic changes, and endocrine, reproductive and organ toxicity.
Well-known brands such as Trader Joe’s, Wayfair, Publix, Albertsons, McDonald’s, Williams-Sonoma and Sherwin-Williams earned an F for their lack of action in reducing toxins, according to the 2026 Retailer Report Card.
Williams-Sonoma owns West Elm and Rejuvenation; Wayfair owns Birch Lane, Joss & Main, AllModern and Perigold; and Albertsons owns Safeway and a number of other grocery store chains.
The report has been published since 2016 by Toxic-Free Future, a nonprofit consumer safety organization, as part of its Mind the Store campaign. Investigators mine publicly available corporate data on 50 of the largest retailers in the United States and Canada — encompassing more than 140 businesses when subsidiaries are included. Collectively, those businesses generate more than $4 trillion in annual revenue.
The 2026 report also gave failing grades to Chipotle; Five Below; Subway; Lumber Liquidators; 7-Eleven; Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc., which owns Circle K; Ahold Delhaize, which owns Food Lion and Stop & Shop; Inspire Brands, which owns Arby’s, Baskin-Robbins, Jimmy John’s, Sonic, Dunkin’ and Buffalo Wild Wings; and Yum! Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill.
There were top performers: Apple earned an A and Ikea, Target and Sephora received an A- for their actions to reduce dangerous chemicals. For example, each company has invested in hazard assessments that could identify new concerning chemicals or in identifying safer alternatives to existing toxins.
Dollar Tree was named as the most improved retailer, moving from a D to a C grade, partly by becoming one of the first retailers to require private-label suppliers use safer alternatives to toxic chemicals.
“Still, there are too many companies that try to get away with prioritizing short-term profits over consumer health,” said Jane Muncke, managing director and chief scientific officer at the Food Packaging Forum, a nonprofit foundation based in Zurich, Switzerland, that focuses on science communication and research.
“This report contributes to making such business models become something of the past, because people do care about hazardous chemicals and will vote with their dollars to protect their health,” said Muncke, who was not involved in the analysis.
Overall D+ grade in consumer protection
Consumers are increasingly worried about chemicals in products they buy. A 2025 survey by The Pew Charitable Trusts found more than 70% of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about harmful chemicals, while some 5 out of 6 adults in the United States want government and industry to “do more to ensure chemical safety and increase transparency around the use of chemicals.”
Yet the average grade for all major retailers in the report was a D+, and nearly half of previously scored major retailers slid backward by at least 2 percentage points. Only 10% of retailers reported measurable goals to reduce or eliminate toxic chemicals and plastics, compared with 44% of the companies analyzed in 2024, according to the 2026 report.
Walmart received an A- and Whole Foods Market got a B in 2024, but both companies dropped to a C in 2026 and saw the largest score declines. Walmart dropped by 32 percentage points while Whole Foods lost 20 percentage points since the prior analysis. Walgreens, Dick’s Sporting Goods and Amazon, which owns Whole Foods, each dropped by 11 or more percentage points.
To earn points, companies are rated in four areas: corporate responsibility, such as adopting a companywide safer chemical policy; transparency, including accurately disclosing ingredients to consumers; banning the worst toxic chemicals and plastics in products within a set timetable; and implementing safer solutions, including investments to develop cleaner, less toxic options.
“These retailers have considerable influence over the chemicals and materials used in products and packaging across their supply chains,” said report author Cheri Peele, the director of government and market policy for Toxic-Free Future.
“When they demand change, it can encourage manufacturers everywhere to provide consumers safer options,” Peele said.
Toxic Hall of Shame industry response
CNN reached out several times to the 16 companies in the 2026 Toxic Hall of Shame. Only Ahold Delhaize and McDonald’s replied before publication.
Christy Phillips-Brown, vice president of communications for Ahold Delhaize, told CNN in an email the company plans to reach out to Mind the Store to discuss its “progress related to sustainable chemistry.”
“Each of our brands complies with all federal requirements and state regulations pertaining to chemicals of concern,” she said. “We remain committed to partnering within our industry and with other stakeholders to address this and other health and sustainability topics.”
McDonald’s sent CNN its 2025 Purpose & Impact report, released in recent weeks, well past the July deadline required by Mind the Store. The report showed the company has met more than 99% of its 2025 goal to reduce added fluorinated compounds, which are a marker of cancer-causing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
However, the company did not set new goals for reductions in other problematic plastic chemicals such as bisphenols and phthalates, said Mike Schade, senior director of programs and strategy for Toxic-Free Future.
“We’re thrilled they accomplished their goal, but PFAS is really just the tip of the toxic iceberg,” Schade said. “There are hundreds, if not thousands, of chemicals of concern that can migrate out of food packaging into food.”
McDonald’s received an F in 2018, 2019 and 2024 and a D in 2021, Schade said. “They’ve had opportunities to improve, and unfortunately, they just do not seem to take these issues as seriously as they should.”
The report’s findings are surprising and troubling, said David Andrews, chief science officer for the Environmental Working Group, or EWG, a nonprofit health and environmental advocacy group.
“At a time when our government oversight cannot be counted on to prioritize public health over corporate profits, retailers also seem to be stepping away from strong public health commitments to safer products,” said Andrews, who was not involved in the report.
Former top performers respond
A spokesperson for Walmart, which declined 32 points and dropped from an A- to a C in the 2026 report, told CNN in an email that “until we have the full results and information from Toxic-Free Future, we won’t be able to provide a public statement.”
Amazon told CNN in an email that it requires products sold in its stores to “comply with applicable laws and regulations, and we maintain policies that restrict products containing certain chemicals from sale in our store.”
“For Amazon Private Brands, we have additional chemical requirements and work directly with our suppliers to verify compliance through measures including product testing. We regularly review and update our policies to help ensure customers can shop with confidence,” a spokesperson said.
Amazon dropped by 11 points despite receiving acknowledgement in the report for its Climate Pledge Friendly Program, which puts a green leaf on products on its website that meet environmentally friendly and safer chemicals standards.
The drop from a C+ to a C- occurred for numerous reasons, according to the report: Amazon removed a preference for safer alternatives from public documents; did not report additional progress on “ban the bad” — eliminating chemicals or plastics of concern — and did not announce any new goals to eliminate worrisome chemicals.
“We have been encouraging companies to put their money where their mouths are,” Schade said. “In 2024, Amazon earned points for investing financial resources in chemical hazard assessments, but we’ve seen no reports of progress since then. Amazon is one of the wealthiest corporations in the world, and we think that they can help invest financial resources to evaluate the hazards of alternatives to chemicals of concern.”
Whole Foods Market, which is owned by Amazon, told CNN in an email that its 20-point decline and reduction in score from B to C was “based on incomplete information.”
“Because of an internal error, we didn’t submit some of our information by Toxic-Free Future’s deadline, and we’re asking them to update our score and grade,” said Whole Foods Market spokesperson Kristen Orsborn.
“We ban more than 350 ingredients across body care, beauty and household cleaning products. Our Quality Standards team continually reviews ingredients as the science evolves, so our customers don’t have to,” Orsborn said.
To assure the report has the latest information, retailers were given a chance to attend a December 2025 webinar and work with Mind the Store researchers until July to update corporate data before the report was finalized, Schade said.
“Whole Foods attended the webinar. We later granted them an extension in July on their response. So it’s unfortunate that they did not disclose this new information until four months past the deadline,” he said. “We are pleased they have expanded the list of chemicals it restricts in beauty and household cleaning products. We especially appreciate the new progress on petroleum ingredients and fragrance chemicals.”
However, Whole Foods already received credit in the report for restricting bisphenols, PFAS and heavy metals, as well as banning various types of plastics from its private-label and food-service packaging, according to the report. Without more data from Whole Foods, it’s unclear if the new actions would have improved its grade, Toxic-Free Future’s Peele said.
“In contrast to 2024, Whole Foods did not respond to the Chemical Footprint Project Survey or disclose its chemical footprint. It also no longer has an active chemical reduction goal. Unlike 2024, it did not report progress in reducing chemicals of high concern during the evaluation period,” Peele said.

title: Man accused of threatening ethanol plant with bomb worked as a trainee at the site, report says
text:
PEORIA, Ill. (25News Now/Gray News) - A man has pleaded not guilty after being accused of threatening an Illinois ethanol plant with an explosive.
Andrew K. Kozak, 41, was indicted Tuesday by a grand jury on charges involving threats regarding explosives and interstate communication threats.
Kozak is accused of using email to threaten to damage and destroy a building by means of fire and explosives and to threaten people at the BioUrja facility, according to the indictment and online records.
At a news conference Tuesday afternoon, U.S. Attorney Gregory Gilmore said the charge of threats regarding explosives carries up to 10 years while interstate communications threats carries up to five years.
The Associated Press reported Kozak has been a trainee at the ethanol plant for 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page.
Officials said over the weekend that an explosive device was found at the plant. The threat forced an evacuation order of a mile radius around the plant, on the Peoria and East Peoria sides of the Illinois River, shortly after 7 p.m. Friday. That order was lifted Saturday after no other devices were found at the plant.
During a weekend press conference, Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon declined to reveal the type of device discovered, only to say the package that was “rendered safe” was a “credible threat.” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told reporters late Friday that the device was a bomb.
The evacuation order forced the cancellation or postponement of numerous events in Peoria.
Kozak has a detention hearing set for Friday. Prosecutors are seeking to keep him detained. He is scheduled to appear in court again in December, with a jury trial is set for Jan. 11.

title: High school valedictorians to get custom kicks after senator-elect Colom asks Nike to 'Just Do It'
text:
Nike is gifting high school valedictorians across the country with a pair of custom sneakers after Mississippi’s incoming senator appealed to the company on social media.
Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, called on the sneaker giant to honor his historic election by giving every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of custom Air Force 1s — his favorite style. The sneakers cost between $90 and $180 on the company’s web site.
“It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit,” the Democrat suggested Monday on X, referencing Nike’s famous slogan.
The company accepted the challenge and took it one step further.
“The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea,” Oregon-based Nike responded Tuesday on X. “@scott_colom, we’ll do you one better… For this year, 2026/2027 high school valedictorians from across the U.S., let’s go!”
Nike said more details would be forthcoming, but Colom has already suggested the custom sneaker should give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippian who was the first African American to serve in Congress when he took office in 1870.
“I’m so proud of @Nike for stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment. This is the #justdoit mentality that makes your company great,” he wrote on X on Tuesday. “Please consider honoring Hiram Revels in the design.”
Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in this month’s midterm elections.
When he takes office in January, he’ll become the state’s third Black senator, following Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce, who was the only formerly enslaved person to serve in the U.S. Senate when he took office in 1875.
Colom’s victory marked a major shift in the Magnolia State, which has the nation’s largest proportional share of Black people but for decades has largely been controlled by white conservatives. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist.

title: National push grows to stock ambulances with blood for use in the field
text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (InvestigateTV) — A national effort to stock ambulances with blood for transfusions in the field is expanding.
It’s a movement driven in part by two single but staggering statistics: Severe blood loss can lead to death in less than five minutes and about 40% of trauma-related deaths worldwide are due to uncontrolled bleeding.
Getting approval and funding for EMS crews to transfuse blood in the field has been difficult, but several updates in recent years are helping increase access across the U.S.
Trapped under a tree
Katie McClanahan, who lives in Arkansas, recalls it had been raining a lot in the weeks before the April 2025 incident that nearly took her life. She said the ground was saturated, and she was home alone when it happened.
“I heard this thud and I ran from the kitchen to our bedroom where there was a bay window,” McClanahan said. “And then the next thing I know, it’s just boom, I’m knocked to the ground, just complete darkness surrounding me. I had no idea what happened.”
McClanahan was pinned beneath a fallen tree that she said was four feet in diameter. She was trapped, alone and severely injured.
“I screamed as loud as I could, someone help me, please help me, just screaming, breaking down into tears,” McClanahan said.
A neighbor’s 911 call brought first responders to her home. Crews determined it would take hours to cut through the debris and get her out.
Dr. Ben Davis, a trauma surgeon, said he was on call at UAMS Medical Center in Little Rock when he got a call from the scene. The hospital was less than a mile away, but Davis said time was not on McClanahan’s side.
“An adult human has about five liters of blood in their body, and you can lose enough of that to die in just a few minutes,” Davis said.
Davis said the tree initially acted as a tourniquet around McClanahan’s crushed pelvis.
“It just compresses the blood vessels,” Davis said.
Davis knew that once the tree was removed, McClanahan would begin bleeding uncontrollably.
“I had that in mind, and I talked to my ER nurses and I said I need to go out to the field with some blood,” Davis said.
The decision went beyond standard protocols and made it possible for McClanahan to receive a blood transfusion in the field, known as prehospital blood.
McClanahan was under the tree for three and a half hours. Asked whether she would be alive today without prehospital blood, she answered, “Absolutely not. No.”
“I have no doubt that she would not be here today if we hadn’t gotten her that blood,” Davis said.
McClanahan underwent 13 surgeries and rehabilitation after her rescue.
“When your life is saved like that, I just have to make sure this can happen for everyone else,” McClanahan said, adding that she believes every patient who needs it should have access to prehospital blood.
Research and military roots
The practice has roots in military medicine, where prehospital blood has long been shown to improve survival of injuries in combat settings.
A 2025 study noted that blood transfusion at a trauma scene or in an ambulance has “not been widely implemented across the U.S.” The researchers called it a “life-saving intervention” and found that expanding access nationwide “offers the potential to save thousands of injured patients’ lives” every year.
Cost and coverage
The Prehospital Blood Transfusion Coalition is working toward expanding access. Jon Krohmer, the coalition’s board chair, said the number of states that allow paramedics to initiate blood transfusions has grown.
“When we started the coalition several years ago, there were 24 states that allowed paramedics to initiate blood transfusions. Now it’s up to 46,” Krohmer said.
Krohmer said the biggest barrier to scaling up prehospital blood programs is cost. Expenses include upfront costs for training and specialized equipment. Blood must be stored cold and warmed before it is given to a patient.
“It takes about $20,000 to $25,000 to set up the infrastructure for a program, and then $1,200 to $1,500 per transfusion,” Krohmer said.
Krohmer said Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance typically do not pay for blood transfusions in the field.
He pointed to a recent update to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reimbursement criteria as a step in the right direction. CMS now classifies blood transfusions during prehospital transport as Advanced Life Support Level 2, which in some cases will help increase payment to EMS agencies.
“It’s helpful, but agencies are still not recouping the cost of providing the transfusion,” Krohmer said.
Federal funding
Krohmer, who previously served as director of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of EMS, said recent investments from NHTSA are also helping to expand access to prehospital blood.
Current NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said he views prehospital blood as a way to try to reduce traffic fatalities.
He pointed to NHTSA data that shows 43% of people killed in vehicle crashes between 2019 and 2023 were still alive when first responders arrived.
“What we’ve seen with research is with traumatic blood loss situations, pre-hospital blood transfusions can improve mortality rates by 37%,” Morrison said.
In the spring of 2026, the agency announced $80 million in funding for prehospital blood programs. The grant money is intended to help local jurisdictions that cannot afford to operate programs on their own. “I can tell you, we’ve had record numbers of applicants for these programs,” Morrison said.
And in November 2026, NHTSA announced an additional $202.4 million investment “to establish new or expanded prehospital blood transfusion capabilities”.
Experts say even more financial support is needed for prehospital blood to become the national standard of care.
Advocacy in Washington
In April 2026, McClanahan and Davis traveled from Arkansas to Washington, D.C., for the first-ever Economics of Prehospital Blood Conference.
“I think the way to get it done for all Americans is ultimately going to be federal involvement, federal legislation,” Davis said.
McClanahan said she wants lawmakers and others to hear her story.
“I’m just trying to raise the awareness of the absolute lifesaving potential, because truly every second mattered. I would have died without it,” McClanahan said.
Blood supply
Meanwhile, blood shortages have become more frequent in the U.S., raising the question of whether stocking more ambulances with blood could affect the nation’s supply.
Dr. Emily Coberly, a chief medical officer at the American Red Cross, works closely with EMS agencies looking to launch prehospital blood programs. She recommends several steps to ensure no blood goes to waste.
“The blood supply can absolutely support the needs of patients in the hospital and the needs of pre-hospital patients,” Coberly said. “What we want to do is be strategic, look at the data, which vehicles are most likely to encounter patients who are bleeding, that’s where we want to prioritize blood products. Also, in some cases EMS programs may be able to partner with a local hospital to move units that are approaching the end of their shelf life, move them to a location where they’re more likely to be used.”
Coberly said it is also crucial for EMS agencies with prehospital blood programs to encourage blood donation. She said agencies could also sponsor their own community blood drives to help maintain supply.
A local blood donation center or drive can be found online at redcross.org/give-blood by entering a ZIP code.

title: SCORES OUTDOORS: NFL’s most annoying fans
text:
We’re going to shift gears this week. We haven’t talked sports in quite a while, and I came across this little tidbit the other day. Since a lot of our readers are probably fans of some of the teams, we are going to go over the top 10 most annoying fans of NFL teams.
This is from Bovado, a Las Vegas outfit.
Let’s start with some positives. Most of the time, when you visit a city to watch the NFL, you’ll see tailgates, families, cool fans who may throw a couple of jabs your way if you root for the opposing team. But like any sport, some NFL fan bases have a higher percentage of annoying fans amongst the good-natured ones.
They can be anything from annoyingly righteous to annoyingly overconfident, or, in some cases, annoyingly violent.
Take these with a grain of salt.
Here we go:
10. Las Vegas Raiders – From Black Hole to Blackjack
The Raiders used to be scary. Their old Oakland Stadium was called the “Black Hole,” where its fans were a mix of Halloween and UFC Fight Night. Now, it’s a pit stop for sports bettors, bachelor parties, or middle-aged moms in town for the latest residency.
9. Pittsburgh Steelers – We’re Bored, So We Travel
What is there to do in Pittsburgh? We assume besides building Minecraft cities it’s watching the Steelers. That’s why the fan base grabs their yellow towels and follows the team on the road. While a passionate fan base is commendable, the droves of Steelers fans that show up in opposing stadiums have us concerned for their social life.
8. Los Angeles Chargers – One Battle After Another
Which fan base had the most stadium fights in 2025? Somehow, the Los Angeles Chargers – a surprise considering nobody knows where their fans come from. San Diego holdovers? Raiders fans who skipped Vegas? L.A. fans avoiding Rams prices?
7. New York Giants – It’s New York
Have you seen Knicks fans? Have you seen Yankees fans?
As great as it was to see the Knicks finally get over the hump, taking your family to a New York game still means risking an unsolicited vocabulary lesson – especially if you’re rooting for the other team.
6. Houston Texans – The Bitter Ex
In the J.J. Watt era, Houston had all but forgotten the “Luv Ya Blue” brand that moved to Music City. But then, the Tennessee Titans did the unthinkable: they wore their Oilers throwbacks on a Sunday afternoon.
The Texans started looking at the Titans like an ex who suddenly got a summer bod.
5. Dallas Cowboys – Remember America’s Team?
The Cowboys used to be No. 1 most annoying, and we’re sure they wore that as a badge of honor. But it’s not just that they haven’t made the NFC championship game since the Clinton era; it’s that they lack … flavor. Their confidence isn’t nearly as loud as it once was.
4. Buffalo Bills – Breaking Tables; Making Excuses
The “Bills Mafia” table-breaking stuff was cute for a minute, but then it started to feel a little try-hard. Then the Josh Allen discourse heated up, and that’s how they ended up in the top five.
While Allen has been great at times, he’s had his share of mistakes, too. But don’t tell that to the Bills Mafia.
3. New England Patriots – The Patriot Way = Blind Loyalty
Pats fans climb into the top three not just because of the arrogance and band wagoners that come with sustained success, but because they defend the Pats’ long list of transgressions like Ty Law in press coverage:
Spygate, Deflategate, the owner soliciting prostitutes, or their head coach sleeping with reporters. The list is long and ever-growing, and these issues are either minimized or ignored completely.
2. Kansas City Chiefs – The Swiftie Circus
The Chiefs used to be known for their fiercely loyal fan base, innovative offense, and humble success.
But since Taylor Swift arrived, the fan base has increasingly gone … Hollywood. And it’s not just the Swift camera cuts or the influx of Swifties, but the growing number of celebs who seem to pop up beside her. .
It’s hard to remember what an “old” Chiefs fan looks like.
1. Philadelphia Eagles – They Love Misery and Rocky
Did you know that in the last four seasons, the Eagles have had at least 11 wins under head coach Nick Sirianni? Talk to an Eagles fan in 2026, and you’d think they’re the worst-coached franchise in the league. Eagles fans are annoyingly miserable and seem to have no appreciation for the contender Sirianni and the front office have built.
It’s as if they began to enjoy the 50-year mantra of being miserable and ringless yet passionate. Now that the Eagles are yearly contenders, they’ve never been more unhappy. Poll some old-timers from the Eagles Nation and they probably appreciate the Dick Vermeil years more than Sirianni’s Super Bowl run.
Roland’s trivia question of the week:
What is the Boston Celtics record for most wins in a single season?

title: Higgins Becomes First LA Cross Country Runner to Earn All-New England Honors
text:
Lincoln Academy senior Karen Higgins became the first Lincoln Academy athlete to achieve All-New England status after placing 19th in the girls race at the 91st annual New England Interscholastic Cross Country Championships on Saturday, Nov. 14 at the Troy Howard Middle School course in Belfast.

title: Aging Untold: How to treat psoriasis flare-ups later in life
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down what triggers psoriasis later in life and share practical strategies to manage uncomfortable flare-ups.
Plus, we discuss why choosing less medical intervention can sometimes be the most compassionate care decision for an aging loved one.
Then, we meet an 81-year-old retired psychology professor turning everyday household items into whimsical, one-of-a-kind music.
For older adults, psoriasis can develop or flare later in life.
It’s not just a skin condition. It’s an immune-mediated inflammatory disease, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. And it also increases the risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
She said traditional and functional medicine play an important role in treating autoimmune disorders.
Sometimes understanding a person’s goals, weighing the burden of treatment and accepting what cannot be fixed might be the best choice when caring for an aging loved one, according to the Aging Untold experts.
“We don’t like to talk about death. We don’t like to talk about dying,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
Some yoga classes are bringing in puppies, and the classes blend calm movement with play, rest and cuddle time. Some puppies even meet future families in class.
“Give me a yoga mat and a bunch of puppies and I don’t care if I stretch. I just want the puppies,” gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said.
First-time puppy yoga participant Taylor Manley said the class left her calm. She said a puppy just wanted to sit in her lap the whole time.
“I was trying to relax with him, and he was gonna make me go to sleep with him,” Manley said.
Herb Leff’s condo is filled with music studios, including one that used to be the master bedroom.
The 81-year-old retired University of Vermont psychology professor uses traditional instruments along with pots, pans and even a rubber chicken to make experimental music in the Burlington home he shares with his wife, Ellen.
The basement musical menagerie includes an electronic keyboard, wind chimes, frying pans suspended from the ceiling and more.
On the second floor, you’ll find a room he used to call the metal percussion paradise. The third studio is what Leff calls his cockpit.

title: CMP reducing vegetation trimming for rest of year due to financial pressures
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Central Maine Power says it is reducing its vegetation trimming maintenance for the rest of this year due to financial pressures.
A CMP spokesperson said the company will reduce tree maintenance by 20%.
The spokesperson said trees are the leading cause of outages for CMP customers.
The reduction will not affect hazard tree maintenance. It will delay the six-year cycle for regular tree maintenance along CMP’s lines.
Despite the reduction, Dustin Wlodkowski, a CMP spokesperson, said CMP works year-round to prepare for outages and will still ensure service is restored if a customer loses power.
“We prepare for extreme weather year round. We have line worker training. We have all kinds of resources to deploy in the event that a customer experiences an outage. So we want to make sure that our customers understand that for those emergent issues that our crews will still be responding to them,” Wlodkowski said.
Wlodkowski said CMP has also paused all hiring in response to the financial struggles.
WABI has reached out to the Public Utilities Commission but has not received a response.

title: Recount affirms Democratic win over incumbent in southern Maine House race
text:
Democrat Bradley Youngs was confirmed as the winner in House District 106, defeating incumbent Republican Barbara Bagshaw, following a Wednesday recount.
Youngs picked up one vote in the recount bringing the totals to 2,648 votes for Youngs and 2,500 for Bagshaw, a 148-vote margin.
House District 106 covers part of the town of Windham in Cumberland County.
Of the three legislative recounts this week, Bagshaw had the widest margin to overcome to win. All three recounts confirmed the initial election results, with small changes to the final vote tallies.
Bagshaw told Maine Morning Star last week that she was encouraged by local residents to request the recount, and took issue with same-day voter registration and the role newly registered voters may have played in the election.
The results won’t have a large impact on the balance of power in the Maine Legislature, as Democrats already secured a strong majority in the Maine House of Representatives and a supermajority in the Maine Senate.
This was the third of four recounts this week. The secretary’s office already confirmed Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth as the winner in Senate District 18 and Republican Kerryl Lee Clement as the winner in House District 96.
There will be one more recount tomorrow for the District 2 seat on the Kennebec County Commission. The recount is open to the public at the Maine Public Safety Building in Augusta and live-streamed on the secretary’s office Youtube page.

title: Here’s how much Medicare Part B premiums are increasing in 2027
text:
(Gray News) - Medicare Part B premiums are increasing next year.
The standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B enrollees will be $209.40 for 2027, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
That is a $6.50 increase from $202.90 this year.
The annual deductible for Medicare Part B beneficiaries will be $292 in 2027. The current deductible is $283.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said the increases in the 2027 Part B standard premium and deductible are because of projected increases in health care spending.

title: 'The safeguards did not work': Four major AI chatbots helped plan terror attacks in hours
text:
'The safeguards did not work': Four major AI chatbots helped plan terror attacks in hours
Federal investigators bypassed safeguards on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to develop viable terrorist attack plans, raising questions about whether AI companies can adequately police their own technology.
'The safeguards did not work': Four major AI chatbots helped plan terror attacks in hours
Federal investigators bypassed safeguards on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to develop viable terrorist attack plans, raising questions about whether AI companies can adequately police their own technology.
Four of the world's most popular artificial intelligence chatbots helped federal investigators develop viable plans for terrorist attacks in the United States, each in less than 12 hours, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Wednesday.
Investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. All four platforms had safeguards designed to prevent misuse, but investigators were able to get around them every time.
"We were four for four. The safeguards did not work," Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO, told Hearst Television.
Two chatbots helped plan bombings intended to kill large numbers of people, while the other two helped plan attacks on electrical substations. One even suggested using a drone.
The chatbots provided detailed information that could be used to carry out the attacks, with one producing a 15-step plan.
Investigators consulted with experts, including a bomb squad commander who confirmed that the AI-generated instructions could produce explosions. Investigators did not actually build a bomb.
"We assess that these were viable attack plans. And even if, you know, we didn't go through with it, we felt that these could have helped someone who set out to do evil," Walsh said.
Weeks of planning reduced to hours
Walsh said much of the information investigators obtained was already available on the internet. What stood out to him was how quickly AI could bring it all together.
"Rather than taking weeks or months to plan, this came together in a matter of hours," Walsh said.
He said the investigation also exposed a dangerous consequence of a technology designed to make people's lives easier.
“These products are built to be helpful. And that can be amazing. It can decrease, you know, task times. It can help the productivity of American workers. But damn it if it doesn't have a dark side,” Walsh said.
Have the companies fixed the problem?
The companies behind the chatbots say they are continuing to improve their safety measures. Google noted that investigators conducted their tests in April using older versions of its AI.
Walsh cautioned that the investigation was not exhaustive and that its findings do not necessarily mean someone conducting the same tests today would get identical results.
Congress weighs new restrictions
New Hampshire Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who requested the investigation, plans to hold hearings on AI safety in January when she takes over as chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee.
"At the very least we need to have rules that prevent the release of models that don't have adequate safety safeguards," Hassan said.
Last week, Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., and Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., introduced the American AI Security Act, which would require developers of certain advanced AI models to give the National Security Agency access to their technology for cybersecurity and national security evaluations before deployment.
The legislation would also authorize penalties of $500,000 per day for certain violations.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in June directing federal agencies to develop a voluntary framework for developers to share advanced AI models with the government before release. He has resisted calls to slow AI development, citing the importance of maintaining America's technological advantage over China.
AI is already being weaponized
While the GAO investigation involved hypothetical attacks, federal authorities and cybersecurity researchers say hackers are already using AI to carry out real-world cyberattacks.
The FBI's Dallas field office on Tuesday highlighted a federal advisory issued Friday warning that cybercriminals and state-aligned hackers are using AI-powered technology to automate attacks against businesses and organizations worldwide.
Google separately revealed Monday that it had identified hackers using AI to fully automate the discovery and exploitation of security vulnerabilities without human intervention.
Both findings underscore a concern raised by GAO investigators: Artificial intelligence can significantly reduce the time and expertise needed to cause harm.

title: RSU 63 board accepts superintendent’s resignation at first meeting since Eddington Elementary closure vote
text:
HOLDEN, Maine (WABI) - The RSU 63 School Board voted Tuesday night to accept Superintendent Sheila Caldwell’s resignation at a special meeting in Holden. It was the board’s first meeting since the vote in favor of the closure of Eddington Elementary School.
The board also welcomed new Special Education Director Kimberly Bennett.
Vote on resignation
The meeting comes amid concerns about a disconnect between the superintendent and the board over what is happening in the schools.
All but one board member present at last night’s meeting, voted to accept the resignation.
Board Chair Rachel Downs voted no.
Public comment
Parents and advocates also spoke at the meeting.
“I hope this board recognizes that our next superintendent will inherit more than a leadership position. They’ll inherit the responsibility of restoring trust, ensuring legal compliance, and addressing systemic concerns that have persisted through multiple administrations. That responsibility must be taken seriously from day one,” one parent said.
“I hope that parents in our district who are angry about the school closure recognize that this decision came after many years of discussion, consideration, and study. I also hope that we can move away from framing this as an Eddington vs. Holden issue. That division is not healthy for our community, nor is it a message we should be sending to our students,” another speaker said.
Interim superintendent task force
The board also appointed four people to a task force to appoint an interim superintendent.
Shelia Caldwell served about a year as superintendent at RSU 63.
The MSAD 17 school district announcing on their website that Caldwell will become the new interim superintendent in Oxford Hills.

title: VETERANS CORNER: Happy with VA doctors and support team
text:
Well, here we are again. I will give you a little of my personal news and other veteran stuff. First, I would like to share my week with you. I went to Boston this week for a pre-op appointment for a urological surgery. The reason I am giving you my intimate details is not so much that it is medical, but I am sharing my experience to both the male and female veterans of the Maine VA System. I accidentally was assigned to a female doctor. That is not what I asked for but I believe there was some possible divine intervention as it was too late to back out and my need was urgent.
Anyway, Julie and I were placed in a small procedure’s room when in came my doctor whose name is “Lori Lerner”. It turns out that the VA has in its midst a world reknown surgeon who was the first one who perfected the “HoLEP Procedure and was given the pathway to fame in the whole world. Look it up on your computer. She is a very prestigious and world reknown surgeon who has performed at Beth Israel, Brigham & Women’s and throughout the Mass General Network. Everyone knows her and she is fantastic.
She allowed my wife to stay in the room while she scoped the inside of my body. She showed and explained everything as she went along. It was painless and very impressive as she showed us the things noticeably wrong and the possible negatives if certain things were not done.
Everything was shown and explained in a meaningful and logical manner. She knew that Julie and I were preparing to go to S.E. Asia to work with widows and orphans as well as veterans. She told us surgery was necessary, the how and what of it and what the outcome looked like. It turned out to be a wonderful medical experience and well worth the three hour drive. Ask your PCP for a referral to Dr. Lerner if you are having serious problems in this area. You can request this now as part of the new administration’s pathway to better health possibilities. Don’t remain with those you don’t feel comfortable is my point and advise.
Next comes my Endoscopy of just yesterday. I have to mention this as we do have some fantastic medical personnel here at Togus. There aren’t many remaining and I think we all know why but my experience again yesterday was also fantastic, so I will say thank you to some who assisted with my procedure. Unfortunately, I didn’t get many last names but they will know who they are by what I do remember.
I had two of the most well versed nursing staff one could have. One was Jeff and the other was Dallas. There was also one intern watching on the procedure as a learning process. She probably was a student. My anesthetist was Dr. Carl Saba and my surgeon was the none other Dr. Barry Raskin. They had a long talk with me explaining what was going to happen, what they would do and the outcome. Before I forget, the lovely nurse who put the painless I.V. into my arm was Alley. I have been on operating tables many times throughout my life but this one took the cake for professionalism and patient comfort in all aspects of the word. In other words, you couldn’t have had a finer team put together if you tried. It is with great pride I speak of this team headed up by Dr. Barry Raskin. I was very comfortable and before I knew it I was waking up to my Julie with a smile. There were snacks and then Julie took me home. I had “O” pain even though I was alerted to the fact that I might feel a little discomfort post surgery. None. The best part, that evening Dr. Raskin called to see how we were doing. Great experience. Now you know and I have shared my week with you. There is very little negative I can say.
Now another late but good event that should please some of you is, after Togus Administration put a fence all around the “Community Living Center” so that we journalists with cameras couldn’t take any more pictures we snuck in to see lights on in all the new buildings with actual people inside working. That was a smiley face, wow moment for me. I’ve been fighting the fight for that to happen for the past five years.
Now we need to see something done about the “Fisher House of Togus”. If you’ve been to the Fisher House of Roxbury then you will know how important that is to veterans and their families. Veterans who are inpatient are very happy knowing that their loved ones are just outside the door and during the day those loved ones lend support to their significant other by being there for them, as it could and should be. Things such as this, aid in healing.
They, the administration, were warned formally that something like this might happen. I hear vets and volunteers talk about this often. The Fisher House parking lot was turned from private to public over night. And, of course, it is always an accident area looking for the realized accident. Also the emergency room bottle neck and ambulance hazard zone. I hear that insurance may pay to resurrect the building and then public parking will revert back to the Fisher House. Of course, administration will wait until more vets die to finish the job. After all, most of them are not vets themselves. Oh well, let’s pray for the best and a change in administrative policy. That will be the day they allow we veterans to become part of the process, we’re willing.
Last but not least the little million dollar bridge. How long will we wait for that bottle neck to be repaired? Even the ducks were upset. I personally think we should give the bridge a name, any suggestions? I am all ears, make it good. There is a lot of construction happening in the rear of the hospital. You can’t see it but they are doing something. Somebody is motivating something. We should watch and bear witness.
My greatest concern is the stress and strain on our veterans and the doctors who are over taxed and very tired. Administration has said, we are advertising but no takers. This has never been the case since 1886. What does that tell you? We have hundreds, if not thousands, of Philippine medical professionals waiting to immigrate and have applied and even paid, yet they, for the most part, wait. Where does the fault lie there?
These professionals are very well trained and don’t demand large salaries, just a fair living to help support their families, yet we procrastinate and our veterans suffer. I can use myself as an example. I tried to get an appointment with Orthopedics recently which entailed some serious medical problems and a Nexus Letter request. I have been a patient of orthopedics for over 40 years and use to know all the doctors on a friendly basis, not anymore. I was told in September that appointments were going out to the end of February. I think they just wanted to avoid. All other departments were willing to see me. There is no real over sight. I spoke to one particular doctor who said, I wouldn’t know Tracye Davis if I passed her in the hall and, as a matter of fact, I don’t even know most of the other doctors. We have never been introduced.
That my friend, is the voice calling out, poor management. Let’s see what happens next week. God bless and keep all of good heart.

It is also expensive!

title: AAA projects Thanksgiving travel will fall from 2025 record

BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Fewer people are expected to hit the roads for Thanksgiving this year.
AAA projects 81.5 million people will travel for Thanksgiving, down 100,000 from 2025’s record total.
Nearly 73 million people will be driving to their destination.
It comes as gas prices continue to drop under the $4 mark.
The national average cost for a gallon of gas was $3.75 as of Wednesday, Nov. 18. In Maine, the average price was $3.97.
More than 3.6 million people who live in New England will be traveling at least 50 miles from home for the holiday, AAA officials said.
More than 3 million of those people will be driving. Another 403,000 will be flying to their destination.
Travel officials said people will face the most traffic congestion before Thanksgiving on Tuesday, Nov. 24 and Wednesday, Nov. 25. Travelers will also face congestion after the holiday with Sunday, Nov. 29 and Monday, Nov. 30 being the busiest days.

title: Pearl Harbor survivor Gebhard 'Geb' Galle dies at 105, remembered for saving 4 shipmates
text:
Gebhard “Geb” Galle, one of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors who later saved four shipmates from a sinking vessel in battle, has died.
Galle died Saturday at his home in Moses Lake, Washington. He was 105, according to the Pacific Historic Parks, an organization that helps preserve Pearl Harbor’s history.
“Your humility, quick thinking and selfless actions remain a shining example of Navy valor,” then-Acting Chief of Naval Operations Adm. James Kilby wrote in a letter to Galle for his 104th birthday in 2025.
Galle died the same day as the oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor, Freeman Johnson, of Centerville, Massachusetts, who was 106.
Galle and Johnson were among the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941.
The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
Galle was waiting to leave the USS Nevada for church the day of the attack
Galle was born in Germany. He came to North Dakota with his family in 1928 at age 7. He joined the U.S. Navy in 1939 at age 18.
On Dec. 7, 1941, Galle, then 20, was a machinist’s mate aboard the USS Nevada, waiting below deck to be taken ashore for church services. He looked out of a porthole and saw planes approaching.
Galle went down to his battle station two decks below in the engineering section.
A torpedo hit the Nevada, allowing water to enter the ship, but officers were able to get it moving, the Navy said. The ship was attacked again, causing more leaks in the hull and fires. The Nevada ran aground.
Galle could not see what was happening.
“Of course, we felt a couple jolts, and that’s when we got hit with the torpedo, and we had a few bomb hits,” he told the Columbia Basin Herald in 2020.
“After we were beached and everything, and we got up to topside, then we saw all the mess that took place,” including the capsized USS Oklahoma and the partially submerged USS Arizona, he said.
“A pretty sad lookout,” Galle said.
Galle rescued shipmates from sinking ship during battle in 1942
Galle was reassigned to the USS Northampton after the Pearl Harbor attack. That ship came under fire on Nov. 30, 1942, by Japanese torpedoes during the Battle of Tassafaronga.
Galle told the Columbia Basin Herald, a newspaper based in Moses Lake, that he was ordered to close the hatch behind four sailors who would’ve been trapped when the ship was sinking. The officer left, but Galle defied the order, opening the hatch. He closed and secured it after the sailors escaped.
The Northampton sank, and Galle and other sailors spent more than a day adrift in life rafts before they were rescued.
“From the decks of the USS Nevada to the battles of the Pacific aboard the USS Northampton and USS Mobile, your courage under fire and steadfast dedication were extraordinary,” Kilby wrote in his letter to Galle. “You helped save shipmates from a sinking vessel, witnessed the launch of the Doolittle Raid, and fought in 19 of 20 Pacific naval engagements.”
He attended 75th anniversary Pearl Harbor service honoring the USS Nevada
In December 2016, Galle attended a 75th anniversary service at Pearl Harbor to honor and commemorate the USS Nevada and those who served on it. A total of 76 sailors and Marines lost their lives as a result of that attack, the Navy said.
“You can carry your hatred all of your life,” Galle said of the attack at the event. “You have to remember, they had a leader who led them astray. We’re at peace now and I feel comfortable. I have no qualm. We’re all good people.”
After the war, Galle got married and opened a refrigeration and air-conditioning business in North Dakota. He then served as a civil engineer with the Air Force and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. He retired in the 1980s.

title: Searsmont EMS chief returns home 6 months after lumber mill explosion
text:
SEARSMONT — Her head wrapped in a green and yellow scarf, smiling widely and crying, Sarah Tompkins returned to Searsmont for the first time in six months.
Tompkins was EMS chief when she responded to the Robbins Lumber Mill fire and explosion in May that killed three people and injured more than a dozen others. Tompkins was one of the last to come home after spending four and a half months in Maine Medical Center, followed by seven weeks in Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital.
Dozens gathered outside Searsmont Fire and Rescue Wednesday to welcome her.
Tompkins left the Augusta Civic Center with an emergency vehicle escort around 2 p.m., and by 2:45 p.m. greeters were on their tip toes, waiting to hear sirens and see a silver Toyota. Holding signs, they cheered for Tompkins, and while many shed tears, they said the event was a hopeful point in a long journey.
Tompkins hugged loved ones in the fire station upon her return, and the emotional moment yielded plenty of laughter.
“We love you, Sarah,” the crowd surrounding her cheered.
Tompkins has remained private while healing, and in a letter she asked town officials to share Monday she thanked everyone who sent cards and letters.
Former selectman and planning board member David Marceau was one of those people. He wrote Tompkins a long letter and included some photos to let her know what was going on in Searsmont. A group of five friends from Deer Isle said they sent cards, too.
“Sarah has made a point to be involved in this community,” Marceau said. “We need those people … that’s why we support her so much.”
Marceau said for Searsmont, the wound left by the explosion is still raw.
“We’re not done healing,” Marceau said through tears. “People who came home from the fire, we see them almost daily … we really haven’t moved on.”
In her letter, Tompkins wrote that when she began treatment she couldn’t see or walk and everything was bandaged.
“After fighting to survive, after all the pain of surgeries and the bandage changes, after hearing the exhaustion and grief in my loved ones voices, the relearning how to do tasks that were once routine, and then slowly get stronger to heal,” Tompkins wrote, “I am finally coming home.”
Ben Jackson was putting down flooring from Robbins Lumber Mill when he heard about the explosion. Even where he lives on Deer Isle, it shook the whole community.
Jackson said he and Tompkins used to sell their products at the same farmers markets and that she inspired him to earn more EMS certifications. Ellen Wieske, another friend from Deer Isle, said Jackson is not alone in being inspired by Tompkins.
“Sarah is a force to be reckoned with, which is obvious in her ability to recover,” Wieske said. “Sarah and Hubert … they’re just go-getters.”
Tompkins and her partner Hubert McCabe run Fine Line Farm in Searsmont, and one sign at Tompkins’ homecoming read simply “Sarah + Hubert.” Wieske said the couple has touched so many lives.
Supporters who don’t know Tompkins also came out to welcome her home. Emily Gruchow, of Belfast, spoke to Tompkins only once, when she gave her advice on leading a training about lifesaving skills, but Gruchow has been to as many homecomings as she could.
“Even if you know other first responders around here, you see the impact on them,” Gruchow said. “You want to be there for the other people in your community.”
The May 15 explosion killed 27-year-old Andrew Cross, of Morrill, who died at the scene, Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury, 76, who died in June and Alden Robbins, co-owner of the lumber mill, who died in July.
Lily Robbins, a volunteer with Searsmont EMS returned home most recently on Oct. 30.
The Maine Department of Labor announced last week that it cited seven emergency departments for safety violations but suspended almost all of the penalties so the towns can pay for training and new equipment.
As Tompkins continues to recover, community members said they’ll be there to support her, and will take their cues from her.
“I still have wounds and scars, but I am also filled with so much hope for all of us. People are good and kind,” Tompkins wrote. “I can only hope that when everyone has to go through their worst day, when they have to call for help, they are treated with the same level of love and care that I have been.”

title: South Portland gets $500k to expand community schools model
text:
South Portland schools received nearly $500,000 in grant funding to support expanding the community schools model, a strategy that treats schools as community hubs for academic, health and social services in partnership with local organizations.
The school district will start by expanding the model to the high school and focusing on engaging students who are receiving special education services and students from low-income households, the district said in a news release. The grant is funded through the Nellie Mae Education Foundation – an organization that supports local education agencies battling inequities.
The grant was also given to 30 other recipients in New England, including organizations working with Portland schools.
South Portland Middle School became the district’s first community school when it opened in 2023, forming partnerships with local organizations to help students and families through homelessness, food insecurity and lack of healthcare access.
The Locker Project, a local food pantry, delivered 7,000 pounds of food and 6,000 pounds of snacks to students and their families through their location on site in the 2024-25 school year. Nearly a thousand students visited the school-based health center, which offers medical, dental, behavioral health and vision care, during the 2024-25 school year. And students participated in afterschool activities led by local groups like The Telling Room, Girls on the Run and Maine Youth Circus.
Middle school Principal Rebecca Stern said the model has had a positive impact on her students.
Chronic absenteeism was halved and there was an increase in parent-teacher conference participation, both of which are indicators of higher graduation rates and life outcomes. Students’ math and reading scores have increased each year.
Earlier this year, South Portland voted to become a community schools district, committing to expanding the model to the city’s elementary and high schools. The rate of the expansion relies upon funding, and this grant, awarded over three years, will help speed the rollout.
“This grant is an incredible investment in our school community, giving us the opportunity to build on the meaningful work already happening here, strengthen partnerships, and expand the resources and supports available to our students and families,” said Claire Lindquist, the city’s new community school director. Formerly a social worker in the district, she was hired for the school year to support the expansion of this programming.
“Ultimately, we want every student and family to feel that they belong at South Portland High School and know they are valued,” she said.

title: Recount confirms Bradley Youngs as victor in Windham House race
text:
A recount confirmed Bradley Youngs’ narrow victory over incumbent Republican Rep. Barbara Bagshaw in the race for Maine House District 106, which covers part of Windham.
The recount, during which volunteers hand-counted ballots, confirmed that Youngs, a Democrat, won by 148 votes, receiving 2,648 to Bagshaw’s 2,500. The results were signed off on by representatives of both campaigns. The result differs slightly from the 2,637-2,498 count released on election night.
”The results from the recount today were expected,” Youngs said. “I have confidence that our clerks did a good job today at the time, and I wasn’t expecting anything different.”
As the recount started Wednesday morning, Bagshaw posted on social media a Freedom of Access Act request she sent to the Maine Department of the Secretary of State requesting records of everyone who cast a ballot in the election in order to verify that all voters were U.S. citizens. In the same social media request, Bagshaw said she had requested an “extended audit” of the election, which would take place after the recount.
Bagshaw previously said in radio interviews that lines for same-day registration on Election Day were filled with people who “looked foreign.”
Windham election officials said the number of same-day voter registrations weren’t out of the norm in this election.
Bagshaw said she had reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, asking the agency to run everyone who voted that day through the department’s SAVE database, which is intended to screen for noncitizen voters, and has been criticized for falsely flagging U.S. citizens.
Bagshaw, who has represented Windham in the Maine State House since 2022, previously drew scrutiny for her attendance at the “Stop the Steal” Rally in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 6, 2021.

title: After a 13-year wait, ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ arrives with enormous hype and expectations
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — After a 13-year wait, “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun its global rollout, sending players back to Vice City and kicking off one of the most anticipated entertainment launches in years.
Players in New Zealand were among the first to enter Rockstar Games’ sprawling Florida-inspired world as midnight Thursday arrived, hours before the game becomes available across the United States.
Internet providers there had prepared for a massive surge in downloads. Chorus New Zealand expected about 35 petabytes — 35 million gigabytes — of additional traffic across its network as players downloaded the massive game.
“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, the company’s network strategy manager. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”
In Wellington, Adam Simmons launched the game from his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low so he wouldn’t wake his wife and daughters.
“The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep,” he said after about half an hour of play.
Shares of Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, rose more than 8% Wednesday as the rollout continued.
In the Dallas area, Bryan Banuelos, a mobile auto detailer, told customers he wouldn’t be taking calls Thursday so he could focus on “GTA VI.” His social media post actually drove some business beforehand, with customers trying to get their cars detailed before he disappeared into Vice City.
“Tomorrow will be the beginning of a new era for the gamers that like GTA,” Banuelos said.
Game returns to Vice City after 13 years
The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.
Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.
At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.
Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.
Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.
Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.
Miami embraces its fictional alter ego
Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.
Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.
The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.
Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.
In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.
Years of hype arrive at launch day
Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.
The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.
“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.
The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.
Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.
“Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album,” a 34-track collection of original songs tied to the game, is scheduled for release Friday.
A separate 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” by Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice is scheduled for release Dec. 11. The adaptive score is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
What players will find next
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.
The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.
___
Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

title: Most city data safe after cyberattack; still unclear when South Portland offices will open
text:
Most city data not compromised, but no estimate for reopening South Portland offices after cyberattack
The City of South Portland said on Wednesday that officials have confirmed that most city data was not compromised in a recent cybersecurity incident. However, officials said they were still working to verify what specific city data may have been accessed in the systems.
The city's IT team shut down the network Saturday night after discovering a cybersecurity issue. Officials said earlier this week that the network outage that is disrupting some municipal services may involve cybercriminal activity.
City officials had already said that City Hall, the Assessor's Office and the public library would remain closed through Thursday, Nov. 19. City Hall and the Assessor's Office will also be closed on Friday per the regular city schedule.
On Wednesday, city officials said there was no estimated timeline for reopening those facilities.
While three city buildings remain closed to the public, city employees are working to maintain essential operations and safely restore affected services as quickly as possible.
South Portland is working with state and federal agencies to investigate what they believe was a cyberattack. The city has hired an independent forensic investigator to assess the incident.
The city said residents should expect continued disruptions to its phone system, in-person credit card payments, some online administrative portals and mapping services, printed receipts and materials, and online streaming of city meetings.
Some South Portland residents told Maine's Total Coverage that they are losing faith in these systems that are supposed to be "secure."
The city postponed the property tax payment deadline to Monday, Nov. 23. Residents can still leave payments in secure drop boxes outside City Hall. The city is working on a solution for new vehicle registrations; renewals are available through the state's Rapid Renewal website.
Police, fire and EMS services are not affected.
On Wednesday, city officials said the city has made significant investments in cybersecurity protections over the years, and that systems and security practices are regularly updated to address evolving threats.
"We are committed to learning from this event, further protecting our systems where necessary, and safeguarding the information and services entrusted to us by the public," the city said in a statement.

title: Coastal storm tracks toward Maine this weekend
text:
Coastal storm tracks toward Maine this weekend
Coastal storm tracks toward Maine this weekend
A long dry stretch continues in Maine, but that could end by Monday, as a storm rides up the East Coast. Rain, gusty winds, storm surge, and some mountain snow are all possible ahead of Thanksgiving.
An area of low pressure off Florida's east coast will strengthen as it tracks northward over the weekend. The storm likely passes to the southeast on Monday into Tuesday as it turns northeast.
Long-range weather models indicate a strong storm system near the Northeast coast early next week but disagree on timing and track. A closer-to-shore track would mean high winds, storm surge, and soaking rains. A track farther out to sea would mean a lower-impact storm. Those details will likely be ironed out as the storm develops at the end of this week.
Either way, expect a cold blast next week as the storm pulls away, with highs in the 30s and low 40s through Thanksgiving.
