title: Immigration officials ordered to explain warrantless arrest during Maine traffic stop
text:
Federal immigration agents detained a man during a traffic stop in Livermore Falls on Monday despite not having a warrant for his arrest and knowing the man has special immigrant status, according to court records.
The 18-year-old from Ecuador, who is using a pseudonym in court filings, entered the country in 2024 as an unaccompanied minor and was granted special immigrant juvenile status — a classification given to undocumented immigrants under 21 who have been abused, neglected or abandoned by a parent.
He was among eight people riding in a van that was stopped by a Border Patrol agent, according to court documents. Six of them were arrested.
As the agent questioned each of the van’s occupants about their citizenship, the man called his brother, whom he’d been living with in Rhode Island. A petition filed in federal court on his behalf says his brother informed the agents of his special status. The officer told the man’s brother that “it appeared (he) was not in removal proceedings,” according to court documents.
The agent “said that (he) would be detained nonetheless,” according to the petition.
The agent, whose name is redacted in court filings, said in an incident report that they pulled the van over because it had Massachusetts license plates, no markings and a ladder rack.
“Vans matching the description of this van often transport illegal aliens from where they live in Massachusetts to work sites in the state of Maine,” the agent wrote. After questioning the passengers about their citizenship, the agent “decided to make a warrantless arrest of the six illegal aliens,” according to the report.
Some of those arrested were taken to the U.S. Customs and Border Protection station in Rangeley, the report says. Others, including the 18-year-old, were brought to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Scarborough.
Court documents filed Tuesday indicate CBP drafted an administrative warrant, which is signed by immigration officials rather than a judge, after the traffic stop. Agents served the man with the warrant after he was detained at the ICE facility, according to the warrant return.
Spokespeople for ICE, CBP and the U.S. Department of Justice did not respond to questions about the incident.
Because both the initial traffic stop and subsequent detention were made without a warrant, U.S. District Judge Stacey Neumann ordered ICE on Monday not to remove the man from Maine and demanded the government provide a legal basis for his arrest.
After being served with the administrative warrant at ICE’s Scarborough facility, the man was transferred to a detention center in Rhode Island on Monday evening, the government said in court records filed on Tuesday. The man was already en route to the facility when agents were notified of the judge’s order, wrote Assistant U.S. Attorney Trevor Taniguchi, who is representing ICE and CBP in the case.
Taniguchi wrote that the man was arrested “under the authority of a valid arrest warrant” and argued the legality of the man’s initial arrest is irrelevant. The court, he said, must only focus “on the lawfulness of the current detention.”
“The detention is lawful because (the man) is now in removal proceedings, and those proceedings are not likely to be terminated due to the alleged arrest/processing violation,” Taniguchi wrote.
The Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition, which tracks and monitors ICE detentions in the state, said similar instances of warrantless arrests and “dragnet” enforcement have become increasingly common amid President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
“Unfortunately, this level of detail often doesn’t have a chance to surface in the public because the rush to deport coupled with the absence of universal representation means many similar cases don’t make it in front of judges,” said spokesperson Panagioti Tsolkas.
The 18-year-old’s attorney, Talia Rothstein, declined to comment on the case. Rothstein filed a habeas corpus petition on the man’s behalf shortly after he was detained on Monday, challenging the constitutionality of his arrest.
The man has no known criminal history in the U.S. or in Ecuador, according to the petition. He came to the U.S. at age 16 to escape his father, who “physically and psychologically abused him” in Ecuador, court documents state.
“As a child, he lived in a home without warm water, no shower and no heat,” the petition reads. “He fled to the United States in search of a respite from the abuse and for a better life.”
About six months after arriving in the U.S., a Massachusetts state court judge ruled he had suffered abuse and neglect at the hands of his father, according to the petition. Shortly after, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services granted him special immigrant juvenile status, which is intended to put at-risk youth on a path to citizenship.
“The U.S. government promised him that he would be given a meaningful path to (lawful permanent resident) status in this country,” the petition reads. “That came with the expectation that he could build a life here without risking arbitrary arrest, detention and removal.”
The man’s special juvenile status, Taniguchi wrote, is “not a lawful immigration status; it is a classification.”
Because the man is using a pseudonym in court, the Press Herald could not verify where he was being held Wednesday.
Staff Writer Emily Allen contributed to this report.

title: Meet 20 Maine girls hockey players to watch in 2026-27
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Izzy Brideau, John Bapst senior forward: The playmaking forward has been a consistent performer for the Penobscot Pioneers the past three seasons. She put up 14 goals and 15 assists last winter and has 86 career points.
Lia Collins, Gorham junior forward: Collins is a strong skater who, coach Dave Grant said, “gives everything she’s got.” Her 17 goals last season were a team high, and she also recorded 13 assists.
Lydia Costa, Yarmouth/Freeport junior goalie: Costa, who attends Freeport, became the Clippers’ starter last season and went 17-2-2 with a 1.04 goals-against average and .922 save percentage. She made 24 saves to notch a 1-0 shutout in the state championship game.
Logan Curry, Cheverus co-op sophomore forward: Curry made an immediate impact by leading the Stags in scoring last season. The Windham student’s 20 goals led all freshman in the state, and she also tallied 10 assists.
Ashley Davis, Biddeford co-op sophomore forward: Davis likes to drive to the net and pounce on the puck near the crease. In her first season, she produced six goals and seven assists. Expect her to have a bigger role in the offense.
Kalia Davis, Gorham co-op sophomore defense: Davis, who attends Bonny Eagle, is a defensive stalwart who can backcheck but also isn’t afraid to rush the puck into the offensive zone. She scored seven times and added 12 assists in 2025-26.
Kylie Dulac, Edward Little co-op senior forward: Dulac is a top candidate for the Becky Schaffer Award as the state’s best senior. The speedy forward averaged 2.50 points per game last season, with 29 goals and 21 assists. She has 73 goals and 33 assists in her career.
Maddie Durant, Lewiston co-op junior forward: Lewiston coach Sarah Pomerleau lauds Durant’s speed and high-scoring potential. The Mt. Ararat student scored nine times and added nine assists to lead the Blue Devils with 18 points last season.
Paige Fecteau, Edward Little co-op junior goalie: Fecteau, who attends Poland, knows how to shut the door on opponents. In 38 career starts, she has 17 shutouts. The Varsity Maine All-State selection allowed two or more goals only three times in her sophomore campaign.
Mikaela Furt, Cape Elizabeth co-op sophomore forward: Furt used her accurate, hard shot to produce 18 goals as a freshman, which led the Beacons. She also had 12 assists.
Azalea Grant, Gorham co-op senior defense: Grant, another potential Becky Schaffer Award candidate, is a two-way defender from Fryeburg Academy who eclipsed 100 career points last season, during which she tallied 14 goals and 27 assists. Coach David Grant said she’s a strong skater with a strong shot who isn’t afraid to block shots.
Avery Guyer, Yarmouth/Freeport sophomore defense: Guyer made a name for herself in the state championship game, when she scored the only goal in a 1-0 victory over the Cheverus co-op. She finished the season with four goals and seven assists — the second-most points by a Yarmouth/Freeport defender — and posted a plus-24.
Josephine Kelly, Winslow co-op junior forward: Black Tigers coach Elliot Emberley is high on Kelly’s potential . The Erskine Academy student scored nine times and notched two assists last winter. Her 11 points were tied for most on the team.
Leski Langevin, Edward Little co-op junior forward: Langevin has put a lot of pucks past opposing goalies in her first two seasons, and she could reach 100 career goals this winter. The Poland student has accumulated 67 goals and 38 assists.
Erica O’Connor, Yarmouth/Freeport senior defense: O’Connor is one of the top returning defenders in the state. She tallied six goals and 10 assists and had a plus-34 rating in 2025-26. Coach Dave Intraversato said O’Connor will be relied on to lead a young defense.
Maya Nasveschuck, Yarmouth/Freeport junior forward: Nasveschuck has been one of the team’s offensive catalysts over the past two seasons, and recorded 24 goals and 14 assists in 2025-26. She led the team with seven game-winning goals.
Gabryella Phelan, Biddeford co-op senior forward: Phelan is a puck-controlling playmaker adept at setting up her teammates. The Biddeford student scored 14 goals and added seven assists as a junior.
Grace Townsend, Cheverus co-op senior defense: Townsend was a Maine High School Hockey Girls Coaches Association All-State selection for her all-around play last winter, when she recorded five goals and 11 assists. The Medomak Valley student is the lone returning defender from a state runner-up team.
Tessa Woodbury, Falmouth/Scarborough senior goalie: Woodbury kept low-scoring Falmouth/Scarborough in games last season with a 2.65 goals-against average and an .897 save percentage. She finished with a 6-9-3 record that included a playoff victory over the Portland co-op.
Delia Vital, Brunswick senior forward: Vital provided scoring depth for Brunswick last season with five goals and eight assists. She should have a bigger role for a team that lost several players to graduation.

title: A Maine lawyer brought a gun to court months before judiciary axed screening exemption
text:
Nine months before Maine’s courts told lawyers they would have to start going through security like everyone else, one of them was charged with bringing a gun into a York County courthouse.
Daniel Feldman, a Kennebunk lawyer and former assistant district attorney in Kennebec and Sagadahoc counties, went through the public screening line on Feb. 5, not the attorney bypass that the Maine Judicial Branch has since ended.
Court officials say they aren’t sure how much the charge against Feldman shaped the decision and that changes were already under discussion. But some lawyers aren’t convinced, arguing the entire bar is being penalized for something the bypass program had nothing to do with. Starting Jan. 1, every attorney in the state, prosecutors included, will wait in the same security lines as jurors and the public, a change the state bar association worries could slow early-morning conferences and trial prep.
Feldman has been charged with unauthorized possession of a firearm in a courthouse, a Class D crime punishable by up to a year in jail and a $2,000 fine, according to court records. A July hearing on the case was continued, though online court records don’t show when he is next due to appear in court.
Feldman did not respond to a request for comment. His lawyer, William Bly, declined to comment on the charge or the policy change.
The Judicial Branch began letting approved lawyers bypass courthouse screening roughly a decade ago. By this past May, the courts had paused the program and denied all pending renewals, according to Barbara Cardone, a spokesperson for the courts.
“I am not sure how much this incident influenced the policy change,” Cardone said. “I certainly cannot say that the program would still be in place but for this incident. There were already recommendations for change being discussed internally.”
The program had been under scrutiny for some time, Cardone said, and the change will bring Maine’s court security in line with federal courts and neighboring states.
Darrick Banda, an Augusta criminal defense lawyer, criticized the decision, noting that the judiciary told lawyers the change was prompted by an uptick in violence in and around courthouses nationwide. Despite the change for lawyers, it’s his understanding that court staff will still get to skip the screening, Banda said.
“It is disheartening and insulting that members of the bar are getting the short end of the stick on this,” he said.
Rachel Okun, president of the Maine State Bar Association, said her group was disappointed by the decision because her members rely on the bypass program to enter courthouses efficiently.
Still, she acknowledged that the Judicial Branch is responsible for ensuring courthouse safety.
Augusta lawyer Walter McKee criticized the latest policy change, noting that having lawyers wait in a security line alongside potential jurors was a “terrible look.” McKee, who said he worked for years to get the program in place, said he was deeply disappointed to see it end “without specific details as to why.”
McKee said he was aware a lawyer brought a gun to court in Biddeford, which many attorneys had talked about.
“I suppose correlation is not causation, but the timing sure has raised eyebrows,” he said.

title: Wiscasset Speedway to Add ‘Battle for the Belt’ Pro Stock Triple Crown
text:
Wiscasset Speedway, in partnership with HF Motorsports and the Hutchinson family, will introduce the HF Motorsports Battle for the Belt Triple Crown Series for the 2027 racing season.
Created to provide meaningful opportunities for Pro Stock competitors of all experience levels and budgets, the new championship will unite three of the speedway’s premier events into one seasonlong battle for race wins, championship points, cash prizes, and ultimate bragging rights at Maine’s biggest and fastest track. The Triple Crown will begin on Saturday, June 19, 2027 with the BIW Shipbuilder 100. That will be followed by the HF Motorsports Triple 50’s on Saturday, July 31, 2027.

title: Searsmont mill faces $55K fine for fatal explosion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Federal work safety regulators have cited Robbins Lumber for five serious safety violations and proposed $54,691 in penalties after a monthslong investigation into a deadly explosion at the mill.
A U.S. Department of Labor spokeswoman said on Wednesday that she did not know what the specific violations were. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration will disclose that information within the next 30 days, she said.
The owners of Robbins Lumber did not immediately respond Wednesday to a request for comment.
The May 15 explosion killed three people, including mill owner Alden Robbins, and injured more than a dozen others, including two members of the Robbins family. According to investigators, sparks from machinery at the base of a silo ignited wood dust, triggering a massive blast.
Jim Robbins is still being treated. Alden Robbins’ daughter, Lily, is a volunteer with Searsmont EMS and returned home Oct. 30 after six months of treatment. The Robbins family has owned the lumber mill since the late 1800s.
Searsmont EMS chief Sarah Tompkins returned home Wednesday after six months of treatment.
OSHA classifies a violation as serious if there is substantial probability that death or serious injury could result and the employer should have known the risk. These are less severe than willful violations, which are levied when employers knowingly failed to comply with a law.
Willful violations carry the highest fines and potential criminal referrals if a death occurred.
The citations and fines are preliminary. Under federal law, Robbins Lumber has 15 business days to comply, to request to negotiate the findings or reduce the penalty amounts, or to contest the citations before the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission.
All case records — including inspector narratives, photos and physical evidence — are kept confidential until citations are either settled or adjudicated.
In August, the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health found the mill’s owners had inadequately planned for the risk of fighting a fire inside a sealed sawdust silo. Firefighters sprayed water on the blaze when they should have let it burn out.
Instead, according to NIOSH, the high-pressure stream likely acted as a mechanical pump, driving fresh oxygen into the sealed upper vault. The force blasted microscopic wood dust off the interior walls, churning it into a cloud. When oxygen hit the hot fuel, the mixture detonated.
The Maine Department of Labor cited seven emergency departments last week for safety violations related to the incident, but suspended almost all of the fines so the towns can pay for new equipment and training to address the problems.
The state cited the mostly volunteer fire and rescue crews for problems ranging from sloppy record keeping to staging a treatment area in a blast zone. The settlement requires the towns to overhaul safety protocols, buy new equipment and send members to mandatory state training.
The Maine Department of Labor has jurisdiction over workplace safety conditions of all public institutions, such as fire departments and schools. Privately owned workplace safety conditions are regulated by OSHA.
Staff Writer Rachel Estabrook contributed reporting.

title: A Maine woman is missing
text:
A Chelsea woman is missing.
Joanne Bolduc, 44, was last seen walking on Route 9 in Augusta on Thursday, according to J. Chris Read, the chief deputy of the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office.
Bolduc was wearing cranberry-colored pants and a long gray jacket. She is 5 feet tall, has long brown hair and brown eyes, Read said Wednesday morning.
He said that Bolduc’s family are “very worried” about her.
Anyone with information about Bolduc’s whereabouts can call the sheriff’s office at 207-624-7076, ext. 9.

title: National push grows to stock ambulances with blood for use in the field
text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (InvestigateTV) — A national effort to stock ambulances with blood for transfusions in the field is expanding.
It’s a movement driven in part by two single but staggering statistics: Severe blood loss can lead to death in less than five minutes and about 40% of trauma-related deaths worldwide are due to uncontrolled bleeding.
Getting approval and funding for EMS crews to transfuse blood in the field has been difficult, but several updates in recent years are helping increase access across the U.S.
Trapped under a tree
Katie McClanahan, who lives in Arkansas, recalls it had been raining a lot in the weeks before the April 2025 incident that nearly took her life. She said the ground was saturated, and she was home alone when it happened.
“I heard this thud and I ran from the kitchen to our bedroom where there was a bay window,” McClanahan said. “And then the next thing I know, it’s just boom, I’m knocked to the ground, just complete darkness surrounding me. I had no idea what happened.”
McClanahan was pinned beneath a fallen tree that she said was four feet in diameter. She was trapped, alone and severely injured.
“I screamed as loud as I could, someone help me, please help me, just screaming, breaking down into tears,” McClanahan said.
A neighbor’s 911 call brought first responders to her home. Crews determined it would take hours to cut through the debris and get her out.
Dr. Ben Davis, a trauma surgeon, said he was on call at UAMS Medical Center in Little Rock when he got a call from the scene. The hospital was less than a mile away, but Davis said time was not on McClanahan’s side.
“An adult human has about five liters of blood in their body, and you can lose enough of that to die in just a few minutes,” Davis said.
Davis said the tree initially acted as a tourniquet around McClanahan’s crushed pelvis.
“It just compresses the blood vessels,” Davis said.
Davis knew that once the tree was removed, McClanahan would begin bleeding uncontrollably.
“I had that in mind, and I talked to my ER nurses and I said I need to go out to the field with some blood,” Davis said.
The decision went beyond standard protocols and made it possible for McClanahan to receive a blood transfusion in the field, known as prehospital blood.
McClanahan was under the tree for three and a half hours. Asked whether she would be alive today without prehospital blood, she answered, “Absolutely not. No.”
“I have no doubt that she would not be here today if we hadn’t gotten her that blood,” Davis said.
McClanahan underwent 13 surgeries and rehabilitation after her rescue.
“When your life is saved like that, I just have to make sure this can happen for everyone else,” McClanahan said, adding that she believes every patient who needs it should have access to prehospital blood.
Research and military roots
The practice has roots in military medicine, where prehospital blood has long been shown to improve survival of injuries in combat settings.
A 2025 study noted that blood transfusion at a trauma scene or in an ambulance has “not been widely implemented across the U.S.” The researchers called it a “life-saving intervention” and found that expanding access nationwide “offers the potential to save thousands of injured patients’ lives” every year.
Cost and coverage
The Prehospital Blood Transfusion Coalition is working toward expanding access. Jon Krohmer, the coalition’s board chair, said the number of states that allow paramedics to initiate blood transfusions has grown.
“When we started the coalition several years ago, there were 24 states that allowed paramedics to initiate blood transfusions. Now it’s up to 46,” Krohmer said.
Krohmer said the biggest barrier to scaling up prehospital blood programs is cost. Expenses include upfront costs for training and specialized equipment. Blood must be stored cold and warmed before it is given to a patient.
“It takes about $20,000 to $25,000 to set up the infrastructure for a program, and then $1,200 to $1,500 per transfusion,” Krohmer said.
Krohmer said Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance typically do not pay for blood transfusions in the field.
He pointed to a recent update to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reimbursement criteria as a step in the right direction. CMS now classifies blood transfusions during prehospital transport as Advanced Life Support Level 2, which in some cases will help increase payment to EMS agencies.
“It’s helpful, but agencies are still not recouping the cost of providing the transfusion,” Krohmer said.
Federal funding
Krohmer, who previously served as director of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of EMS, said recent investments from NHTSA are also helping to expand access to prehospital blood.
Current NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said he views prehospital blood as a way to try to reduce traffic fatalities.
He pointed to NHTSA data that shows 43% of people killed in vehicle crashes between 2019 and 2023 were still alive when first responders arrived.
“What we’ve seen with research is with traumatic blood loss situations, pre-hospital blood transfusions can improve mortality rates by 37%,” Morrison said.
In the spring of 2026, the agency announced $80 million in funding for prehospital blood programs. The grant money is intended to help local jurisdictions that cannot afford to operate programs on their own. “I can tell you, we’ve had record numbers of applicants for these programs,” Morrison said.
And in November 2026, NHTSA announced an additional $202.4 million investment “to establish new or expanded prehospital blood transfusion capabilities”.
Experts say even more financial support is needed for prehospital blood to become the national standard of care.
Advocacy in Washington
In April 2026, McClanahan and Davis traveled from Arkansas to Washington, D.C., for the first-ever Economics of Prehospital Blood Conference.
“I think the way to get it done for all Americans is ultimately going to be federal involvement, federal legislation,” Davis said.
McClanahan said she wants lawmakers and others to hear her story.
“I’m just trying to raise the awareness of the absolute lifesaving potential, because truly every second mattered. I would have died without it,” McClanahan said.
Blood supply
Meanwhile, blood shortages have become more frequent in the U.S., raising the question of whether stocking more ambulances with blood could affect the nation’s supply.
Dr. Emily Coberly, a chief medical officer at the American Red Cross, works closely with EMS agencies looking to launch prehospital blood programs. She recommends several steps to ensure no blood goes to waste.
“The blood supply can absolutely support the needs of patients in the hospital and the needs of pre-hospital patients,” Coberly said. “What we want to do is be strategic, look at the data, which vehicles are most likely to encounter patients who are bleeding, that’s where we want to prioritize blood products. Also, in some cases EMS programs may be able to partner with a local hospital to move units that are approaching the end of their shelf life, move them to a location where they’re more likely to be used.”
Coberly said it is also crucial for EMS agencies with prehospital blood programs to encourage blood donation. She said agencies could also sponsor their own community blood drives to help maintain supply.
A local blood donation center or drive can be found online at redcross.org/give-blood by entering a ZIP code.

title: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries to be next Speaker
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - House Democrats chose Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Wednesday to be their next leader, setting him on track to become the first Black Speaker of the House of Representatives. No one ran against him.
Current and incoming Democratic members of the House chose Jeffries by acclamation.
Jeffries represents Brooklyn and has served seven terms in the House. He previously became the first Black Minority Leader in the House, a position he’s held since 2023.
If elected Speaker, he would follow Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), who was the first woman to serve as speaker.
Jeffries is pledging to address an affordability crisis, reestablish government oversight and unite the nearly 260 members of his caucus.
“We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator to make life better for the American people,” Jeffries said.
He continued, “We hear you, see you, feel you,” and pledged to fight to make the country affordable.
“Failure is not an option, and I’m excited to deliver the bold change Americans deserve,” Jeffries said.
The first job of the 120th Congress is to select a speaker, before all members are sworn in.
Jeffries must secure 218 votes from the chamber to become speaker. The new Congress will have at least an 80-seat Democratic majority.

title: The Latest: Trump arrives in China, seeking to reinforce US's status as world’s leading tech power
text:
President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the United States’ status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public. The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump on Wednesday reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, who is known for her vast shoe collection. The brief meeting took place in the Philippine capital, Manila, at the Malacañang Presidential Palace, where Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who received him with a red-carpet welcome and full military honors, said Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is set to appear Wednesday at a congressional hearing about threats facing the U.S. at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game as travelers across the country were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.
Here’s the latest:
Colleagues nominating Jeffries to be House speaker
Five Democrats essentially representing all corners of the caucus will nominate Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.
Among them is Rep. James Clyburn, the legendary lawmaker from South Carolina.
Democrats are meeting to elect their leaders for the new Congress in January.
House hearing on worldwide threats begins
A congressional hearing on worldwide threats is underway in Washington, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin set to testify.
The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee is aimed at assessing threats 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.
It also comes amid disruptive technological outages, including a rare nationwide ground stop of flights last week.
Also appearing are FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
Mullin, along with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, took the lead briefing the public after the outage, which the Trump administration has said likely is not the result of an attack.
Mullin has also been in the news because he took a government flight — which he said he personally paid for — to an LSU-Texas college football match Saturday, hours after the upheaval at airports.
House Democrats meet to elect leadership for new Congress
House Democrats are gathering behind closed doors to nominate the House speaker and choose other top leadership positions.
Leader Hakeem Jeffries faces a key test on his path to becoming House speaker, and is expected to easily clear the majority threshold from Democrats during the private caucus election. He and the other top leaders are running unopposed.
In first voting, Rep. Ted Lieu of California has been elected the caucus chairman.
The House elects its speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. Jeffries would make history as the nation’s first Black American to become speaker of the House.
Trump plans to meet separately with Russia’s Putin on his China trip
Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to his already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time the pair have sat down since they met in 2025 in Alaska, conducting talks that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The distressing series of technical outages back home has put the Trump administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with Xi and Putin.
Trump meets longtime friend Imelda Marcos while visiting her son, the Philippine president
Trump on Wednesday reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, who is known for her vast shoe collection.
The brief meeting took place in the Philippine capital, Manila, at the Malacañang presidential palace, where Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who received him with a red-carpet welcome and full military honors, Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez said.
Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday night to join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in their annual summit meetings with major Asian and Western counterparts. In a speech before ASEAN and other Asian leaders over dinner Tuesday, Trump praised Marcos and his parents.
“I just don’t wanna date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” Trump said, addressing the Philippine president. “They were great. I believe in genetics, and they did a good job.”
Trump and Putin shake hands at APEC as formal meeting seems like a long shot
Before leaders got into position for the traditional summit family photo, Russian President Vladimir Putin approached President Donald Trump, and they shook hands and exchanged greetings.
Trump had said before departing Washington that he was open to a formal one-on-one meeting with Putin, but it appeared that it might not come to pass while both are in China.
Instead, Trump, Putin and Xi will meet as a group on Thursday on the summit sidelines.
Marcos sends late-night snack of Filipino fried chicken to Trump and staff
Marcos said he sent Trump a Jollibee delivery so he could have a “taste of Manila” during his short stay in the capital.
Marcos said it was intended as a pick-me-up of sorts for a president who works hard.
“Jollibee … is a very, very popular chain. And one of their main products is fried chicken. And we are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity,” Marcos said at their palace meeting.
“Oh wow,” Trump said upon hearing the claim. “Fantastic.”
“You have been working very hard, Mr. President, so just think of it as providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do that you have done and continue to do, and that is in front of you,” Marcos said.
Trump, who enjoys McDonald’s, didn’t say whether he had tried the chicken. Neither did the White House.
In Manila, Trump arm dances and admires presidential palace
Trump was led by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on a rather lengthy red-carpet stroll around the lush grounds of the Malacañang presidential palace after they reviewed the troops.
They stopped at one point to listen as musicians using bamboo instruments played Elvis Presley’s “It’s Now or Never” and a Filipino folk song.
For a few seconds, Trump moved his forearms from side to side in a windshield-wiper-type motion.
Once seated inside the sprawling palace for their meeting, Trump told Marcos their countries’ people have a lot in common and stressed “architectural tastes.”
“I love what you’ve done here,” Trump said, referring to the palace. “You’ve done a fantastic job.”
Trump is a former real estate developer and builder who has been putting those skills to work on numerous renovations at the White House.
Carney says Canada’s growing trade ties with China are not a top concern for Trump
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday said that Canada ’s growing trade relations with China are not a top priority for Trump, pointing out that Canada primarily exports commodities to China rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“In my conversation with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen, ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Carney’s comments came amid criticism from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro over Canada’s willingness to pursue closer economic relations with Beijing, including potentially bringing Chinese automakers to Canada.
Canada and the U.S. have one of the world’s largest trading relationships, but Trump’s tariffs have strained ties and pushed Ottawa to seek other markets. After negotiations collapsed in August, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa.
Xi says Asia-Pacific needs open trade and Putin condemns sanctions as Trump arrives in China
The Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic, Chinese President Xi Jinping told business executives gathered Wednesday in the southern Chinese technology and financial hub of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Trump’s “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone. U.S. limits on Chinese access to leading-edge American technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.
Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticizing the U.S. shift toward protecting its own markets.
Xi faces pressure at home from slowing growth as retail spending and investment have dragged as China endures a prolonged property market slump.
Still, Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may lead to an extension of the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.
Xi meets Trump on the tarmac
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed Trump to Shenzhen at an airport, a rare courtesy for Xi that highlights the importance Beijing attaches to its relationship with Washington.
During Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Trump had also taken the unusual step of greeting Xi on the tarmac.
Chinese official news agency Xinhua reported that Xi recalled Trump’s gesture and said: “China is a nation of etiquette, with a tradition of reciprocating courtesy.”
Xi and Trump greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs and shared a brief hug as an ensemble of young people chanted, “Welcome! Welcome! Warmly welcome!”
Xi said he looked forward to talking with Trump on major issues concerning China-U.S. relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape to advance “strategic stability,” Xinhua said.
Trump seeks to show strength in China, but a series of technological snafus raises concerns at home
President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.

title: Man breached security and destroyed $60 million US military plane, prosecutors say
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said.
The man’s supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States’ involvement in Middle East conflicts.
An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O’Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.
O’Corrain isn’t in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn’t been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison.
Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.
The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won’t fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.
O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles (97 kilometers) southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated.”
An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport’s grounds, prosecutors said.
He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” James Barnacle, the head of the FBI’s New York office, said in a statement.
O’Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport’s perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.
He used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.
O’Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O’Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would’ve risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O’Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.
Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane’s exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O’Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.
Shannon Airport, which was used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: Haley Ward promotes COO with land development background
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor-based engineering, architecture, planning, environmental and surveying consulting firm Haley Ward, is promoting Shawn Tobey to the position of chief operating officer, effective Jan. 1, 2027.
Tobey’s appointment is part of several planned executive transitions at the firm.
Denis St. Peter, who has served as president and CEO, will retire from that role on Dec. 31, and will be succeeded by COO Travis Noyes, while Tobey assumes responsibility for company operations as COO.
Tobey joined Haley Ward in 2025 as a land development manager, working out of the company’s Portsmouth, N.H., office. In July of this year, he was named the company’s first Northeast operations director, a new position designed to strengthen regional leadership and support the firm’s expanding operations across New England.
Tobey will now oversee company operations across Haley Ward’s geographic footprint, working with regional and department leaders to support clients and employees, while advancing the firm’s strategic priorities.
With nearly two decades of experience prior to joining Haley Ward, Tobey brings an extensive background in client relations, project management, planning, design, permitting and construction for multidisciplinary engineering projects throughout New England, Florida and the U.S. Virgin Islands.
“Shawn has demonstrated strong leadership from the time he first joined Haley Ward, and his impact on our company has been clear,” said Noyes. “He understands our business, values the people who make this company successful, and brings the experience and perspective needed to lead our operations.”
“I’m honored to take on this role and continue working alongside the talented people who make Haley Ward what it is,” said Tobey. “I’m looking forward to building on that foundation, working with our leadership team and employee-owners, and being part of what comes next for Haley Ward.”
Haley Ward, whose roots go back to 1978, has offices in Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Florida and Tennessee. The firm has more than 300 employees and is licensed in 47 states.

title: Peltola says Alaska voters want relief from high prices and did not elect her to be partisan
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaska’s newly elected U.S. senator said Wednesday that the state’s voters sent a clear message that they want relief from the “crippling” prices for fuel, healthcare and other necessities and did not elect her to be partisan.
Both were “clear and resounding” directives, Democrat Mary Peltola said in an interview with The Associated Press.
Peltola defeated two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the last U.S. Senate race to be decided after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. She said she had not made a decision yet on whom she would support as majority leader, noting that her race had just been called Tuesday night. Democrats secured a 56-44 majority after flipping nine GOP-held seats.
Current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who is facing a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, told reporters in Washington, D.C., that Peltola’s victory was “an exclamation point on what has been a great election year.” He said he and Peltola spoke Tuesday night.
“The American people have given us their votes. Now we have to earn their trust,” Schumer said.
Democrats, he said, “have to produce,” lower costs and end the “corruption” and chaos in President Donald Trump’s administration.
Sullivan’s campaign did not respond to messages seeking comment Tuesday or Wednesday. Peltola said she had not yet heard from Sullivan but had “every confidence that we’ll be in communication in the next few weeks.”
Peltola said she would work across party lines on issues important to the state, including affordability and infrastructure needs. Spikes in fuel prices caused by the war in Iran have hit many communities hard, particularly in rural areas where fuel must be flown or barged in.
She said she was with family and close friends when the race was called.
“You know, for so many days we’ve wondered if today would be the day,” she said. Alaska accepts absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day and mailed within the U.S. up to 10 days after the election and up to 15 days for overseas voters.
From the start of the campaign, Peltola said she’s had “a good feeling about this race.”
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, previously held Alaska’s only House seat and was the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term in 2024, but became central to Democrats’ efforts to retake the Senate this year.
Late in the campaign, she faced allegations that members of her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to pull votes from the incumbent. Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times reported the allegations the week before the election. Peltola denied any involvement.
On Wednesday, she called the allegations and Trump’s comments “a very unfortunate distraction.”
“I personally know that I am innocent, so I don’t spend a lot of time handwringing” about it, she said. “I know my involvement has been zero, and I believe in the American justice system and I believe in the processes that we have. And I have had no involvement in any of the unfortunate distractions that Alaskan voters have been subjected to.”
The U.S. Justice Department last month confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska’s U.S. attorney did not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into. Peltola said she has not been contacted by the department.
The Alaska Bureau of Investigation, at the request of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, opened an investigation into the allegations. Austin McDaniel, deputy commissioner with the state Department of Public Safety, said by email Wednesday the investigation is ongoing and the agency could not provide additional details.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats’ behest. He was in fourth place with less than 2% of the vote and has not returned messages since the Times story was published.

title: Congress skeptical as Trump officials seek $50B for air travel system
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy urged a skeptical Congress on Tuesday to make a massive $50 billion investment in the nation’s air transportation system even as the Federal Aviation Administration took steps to prevent a repeat of last week’s ground stop that caused chaos for travelers.
President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for last week’s upheaval at the nation’s airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration. The agency said Tuesday it had paused installing routers linked to the ground stop.
Duffy met with Republican senators about the administration’s efforts to enhance air travel and safety, which were detailed in a letter to lawmakers earlier in the day. The $50.1 billion in funding would be divided into five distinct categories, each category getting about the same amount, including $10 billion for modernizing the air traffic control system.
“I hope they don’t piecemeal it. There’s been too much piecemeal happening over the course of 20 and 30 years. I hope we get the full investment,” Duffy told reporters before the meeting started.
But several Republican senators took issue with the request, and Democrats are even more skeptical. Lawmakers said they are for funding safety, but they voiced some concern about other aspects of the administration’s request, including billions for airport infrastructure and the replacement of aging terminals at key airports.
“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air travel issues.
“We’re not going to give them $50 billion,” said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. “But I think that we are willing to provide the money to replace the copper wires with fiber optics, and to try to stop the bleeding.”
Another senator, Republican Rick Scott of Florida, said the airline industry should pay for many of the upgrades being sought, not the federal government.
Duffy, meanwhile, said he’s open to other options that could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.
FAA’s focus turns to routers
As lawmakers debated the funding request, the Federal Aviation Administration took more immediate action.
FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.
The FAA said the Juniper routers linked to the ground stop serve as translators to allow the older analog part of the network to communicate with the newer digital parts of the network as upgrades are completed. So they serve a different role than the Wi-Fi routers that most people have at home.
The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
Duffy said the ground stop was needed after the installation of a new router by L3Harris in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been installed three weeks earlier, also contributed to the trouble.
The FAA said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
Duffy seeks ‘root cause of what happened’
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s trouble.
The routers at issue last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the company believes its “device functioned as it was configured by the installer” when the ground stop occurred. “The FAA is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause,” the statement said.
Duffy said Tuesday that 68 previous installations involving the same routers worked well before this latest problem.
“We’ve been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado,” he said. “But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet.”
Democrats in the Senate have called for halting the replacement of thousands of routers across the nation’s air traffic control system. They also demanded that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” said the letter sent to Duffy.
Ground stop cost big airlines over $300 million
Equity research and brokerage firm Bernstein estimated the ground stop and the weekend work needed to recover from it cost the four biggest U.S. airlines $345 million combined.
The airlines had to offer cash refunds, credits or rebooking options to customers who decided to cancel their trips, Bernstein analysts said.
The lost revenue and additional costs from the ground stop still are enough to have a measurable effect on the quarterly earnings for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines, the analysts wrote in a Monday research note.
“A booking slowdown before Thanksgiving, or a second outage, would cost more than the weekend’s cancellations did,” the analysts said, adding they did not see any signs of waning ticket demand.
___
Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed to this report.

title: Rubio says ‘zero’ information that recent outages in US are linked or related to each other
text:
MANILA, Philippines (AP) - Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the cascade of service outages, which snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications, are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Donald Trump and they prepared to leave the Philippines for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the tech hub of Shenzhen, China.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.
In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for disruptions — and even staunch Trump allies have accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage on Tuesday.
“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila, declaring that “things like that happen.”
But as concern mounted, Rubio appeared to publicly address American worries from the other side of the world.
There has been a steady stream of outages this week
Trump’s nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages was an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
The series of outages began Thursday, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade.”
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related.”
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
Trump’s nonchalance was not shared by some of his allies
Earlier Tuesday, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.
“What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. Later on social media, she praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.
“Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyberattack incident,” Clayton said, explaining that the U.S. government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump’s Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical of the lack of information from the federal government.
“Americans aren’t stupid,” she posted on social media. “We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”
Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, voiced similar concerns.
“Someone high in the administration needs to get on TV and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” McCain, who is also the daughter of late GOP Sen. John McCain, wrote on X. “No one who lived through COVID is believing this is all a coincidence.”
After Trump and other administration officials failed to offer reassurance on those cascading tech problems, Rubio seemed to take on the role of reassurer-in-chief when he appeared unexpectedly in Manila to take questions. The secretary of state is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, though he lately has declined to comment on whether he would consider a campaign to try to succeed Trump.
But Trump’s role in the immediate moment was a pressing concern, even for supporters in his Make America Great Again movement.
“Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack,” Laura Loomer, a right-wing personality known for her incendiary social media presence, wrote on X. “President Trump should come back to the United States.” She did not present any evidence of an attack.
Conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer, writing on X, demanded accountability. “And why does it feel like we’re being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?” she said.
___
AP writers Aamer Madhani in Washington, Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., and Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa contributed to this report.

title: What happened to Fiona the hippo? Latest on her condition
text:
What happened to Fiona the hippo? Latest on her condition
Fiona the hippo is under 24-hour care at the Cincinnati Zoo as staff work to help her recover after swallowing a child's hat.
Here's what we know about what happened and Fiona's condition.
What happened?
The incident occurred 10 days ago when a child tossed a knit cap, which got caught on a fan and was catapulted through a one-foot gap into Fiona's habitat, where she ate it.  
Latest treatment efforts
Zoo officials said Fiona is too large for surgery, so they are doing everything possible to help her pass the hat through her system. In a social media post, the zoo shared that Fiona was sedated again on Tuesday for diagnostic tests. While her blood work was normal, she was found to be slightly dehydrated.
The zoo brought in a nine-foot scope from the Columbus Zoo to attempt a colonoscopy, but staffers were unable to reach the hat. They believe Fiona is passing something through her small intestine and are providing supportive care in the meantime.
Care team providing updates
"So for now, we're giving some pain meds, some antiemetics so that she doesn't feel nauseous. We're trying to give her all of her favorite foods and try to get her to keep passing things through," said Dr. Mike Wenninger, director of animal health at the Cincinnati Zoo.
Wenninger said they are continuing to provide 24-hour care and attention, and they will reassess Wednesday, saying they may need another procedure in the future for further supportive care.
In a statement, the zoo said they are rooting for Fiona and hoping she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life.
Not Fiona's first health challenge
Born six weeks premature at the Cincinnati Zoo on Jan. 24, 2017, Fiona weighed only 29 pounds at birth – 25 pounds less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
She survived because of her animal care team's tireless efforts to save her and has inspired many to care about her species and wildlife.
Now, she's one of the most well-known animals not just in Cincinnati or the country, but around the world.
Community rallies support for beloved hippo
Many took to social media to share their support and love for Fiona as she undergoes treatment.
Timothy the hippo, otherwise known as Fiona's biggest admirer, shared a message via San Antonio Zoo for Fiona.
"We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!" a post from the zoo reads.
Plenty of other zoos shared messages of support in the comments of the Cincinnati Zoo's health update post.

title: Actress and author Victoria Rowell always finds her way back to Maine
text:
Actress, author and filmmaker Victoria Rowell is a Portland-born Renaissance woman. The Emmy-nominated, NAACP Image Award-winning actress, New York Times bestselling author, dancer, director, photographer, lecturer and advocate has built a multifaceted career spanning decades.
While her lengthy filmography includes two memorable television roles – Drucilla Barber on “The Young and the Restless” and Dr. Amanda Bentley on “Diagnosis Murder,” opposite Dick Van Dyke – Rowell, 67, said she’s most often recognized for her supporting role in the 2004 comedy “Dumb and Dumber,” where she played FBI agent Beth Jordan.
Now based in Los Angeles, Rowell returned to her home state for a few weeks earlier this month.
“There are touchstones in Maine for me. I’m a daughter of Maine,” said Rowell after leading a class at Portland Ballet.
Rowell’s latest visit home included an artist’s residency at the University of Southern Maine, reconnecting with people from her past and directing a new film in familiar Maine locations.
At USM, she taught memoir writing and ballet classes, gave the keynote address at the university’s Women in Leadership event and was one of three authors on a panel titled “The Women Who Raise Us: Stitching Together Stories of Motherhood” at Mechanics’ Hall.
During her time in Maine, she has also been directing “Merry Murder,” a suspense movie she also wrote. Filming locations included Ruski’s Tavern in Portland, Hanscome’s Christmas Tree Farm in North Yarmouth and Washburn-Norlands Living History Center in Livermore.
Rowell said returning home has always been meaningful for her because it gives her an opportunity to reconnect with people who have played important roles in her life.
Rowell was born at Mercy Hospital in Portland. Her mother, Dorothy Rowell, was unable to care for her, and shortly after her birth, Rowell was placed in the foster care system, where she remained until she turned 18.
Much of her childhood was spent with her foster mother, Agatha Armstead, who raised her on a farm in West Lebanon. Armstead played a pivotal role in Rowell’s development, helping her secure three scholarships to ballet school. She also introduced Rowell to photography and instilled in her a love of nature.
Those early experiences helped shape Rowell’s life in the arts and her advocacy for children in foster care. “We don’t want to warehouse children in group homes, we want to get them placed,” she said.
Rowell made a point of connecting with her former social worker, Linda Webb.
Webb and her husband Bruce met Rowell for a meal at Becky’s Diner, where they discovered an extraordinary coincidence.
Rowell was staying at the Docent’s Collection hotel on 178 Middle St., a place she described as “beautiful and very Zen” and a place where she felt safe. “I am vigilant, because of my foster care experience,” she said.
As they talked, Linda Webb realized the hotel was located where the Maine Department of Child Welfare used to be located, when she was involved in Rowell’s life. Both Rowell’s hotel room and Webb’s old office were on the fourth floor.
Rowell invited the Webbs to see her room. The spot where Rowell was sleeping turned out to be where Webb’s desk was once located.
“One miracle begat another miracle,” Rowell said.
Rowell called the connection magic and mysticism, and it led back to Webb.
“I know that more than ever, it’s so important to see, reach, call, hug and teach what you can,” she said. “It matters. So I always let Linda know how much she mattered, and she didn’t want any credit.”
One of Rowell’s biggest hopes is to see her 2007 memoir, “The Women Who Raised Me,” adapted into a film or television series.
“HBO has shown substantial interest in the book, and optioned it twice,” said Rowell. Her dream casting choice for the project is Australian actress Sarah Snook playing her birth mother, with the production filmed in Maine.

title: New land purchase opens door to Coastal Rivers’ Wild Lily Preserve
text:
Coastal Rivers Conservation Trust has purchased approximately 12 acres along Turner Road in Bremen from Matthew and Gigi Ravenhall. Adjacent to Coastal Rivers’ existing 120-acre Wild Lily Preserve, the newly conserved land will make it possible to open the preserve to the public for the first time.
Although Coastal Rivers conserved Wild Lily Preserve in 2022, the property lacked a location for parking.Acquiring the Ravenhall parcel provides direct frontage along Turner Road, allowing the organization to build a small parking area, a trailhead, and a new trail leading into the woods and down to the shoreline of Pemaquid Pond. Once complete, the preserve will welcome residents and visitors for walking, fishing, and nature observation.
"Since acquiring Wild Lily Preserve in 2022, we’ve been looking for a way to invite the community into this beautiful place," said Katie Beaver, Deputy Director of Coastal Rivers. "The Ravenhall property gives us the chance to create a welcoming trailhead where people can explore the forest and enjoy the shoreline of Pemaquid Pond. We are deeply grateful to Matthew and Gigi Ravenhall for working with us to conserve this land for future generations."
Made up primarily of woods and wetlands, this 12-acre addition protects important wildlife habitat and contributes to water quality in Pemaquid Pond. It also expands an existing block of conserved land between Pemaquid, McCurdy, and Muscongus ponds.
While the land purchase is complete, additional work is needed before the preserve can open. Coastal Rivers is now seeking community support to fund and build the new parking area and trail, with a final opening timeline dependent on fundraising and project planning.
Community members interested in supporting the parking area and trail improvements are encouraged to contact Executive Director Steven Hufnagel at shufnagel@coastalrivers.org.
For more information, email info@coastalrivers.org or visit coastalrivers.org.

title: Former UMaine football coach Jack Cosgrove reflects on career before Ring of Honor induction
text:
Jack Cosgrove isn’t sure exactly how he’ll feel on Saturday afternoon.
He hasn’t thought that far ahead yet.
“To be honest, I’m just honored,” Cosgrove said. “I like to consider myself a humble person, but this truly means a lot to me and my family.”
This Saturday, the longtime Maine football head coach will be inducted into the school’s Ring of Honor. The ceremony will take place during UMaine’s rivalry game against New Hampshire.
Cosgrove, who amassed 129 victories across 23 years coaching at UMaine, is the program’s all-time winningest coach. He led the Black Bears to three conference championships and five NCAA postseason appearances.
UMaine has dedicated this weekend to celebrating Cosgrove. He will be just the sixth inductee into the football program’s Ring of Honor — a distinction for the school’s athletic pillars created, interestingly, by Cosgrove himself.
“Back in 2003, there was a conversation within UMaine football about retiring numbers,” Cosgrove said. “I had never been a fan of that idea. In the game of football, what about the other players on the field with you? Why would your number get retired vs. the players on the field with you who helped you get it retired? So, we came up with the Ring of Honor.”
Cosgrove, who is now the head coach at Colby College in Waterville, stepped down from his position in 2015. He’s kept up with the Black Bears since then, from a farther distance. His children attended UMaine.
But being back on campus, in the stadium he helped rebuild will bring back memories, Cosgrove said.
“Our program represented our state really well,” Cosgrove said. “I always saw [UMaine] as underdogs who overachieved. It was really uplifting to see what we accomplished, even if we didn’t have as much as other schools did. We had our setbacks. We got punched in the face a few times. But there was so much to be proud of.”
Cosgrove graduated in 1978 from UMaine. He was a standout quarterback for the Black Bears, earning All-Yankee Conference honors twice. He served as a graduate assistant coach while working toward his master’s, which he earned from UMaine in 1984. In 1987, he became a full-time assistant coach. In 1993, he earned the head coaching job at his alma mater and never looked back.
Maine, both school and state, will always be home to Cosgrove.
“The sign that you see when you cross the border into Maine, that’s how I feel about this place,” Cosgrove said. “‘The way life should be.’ It’s been that for me, my wife, and my kids ever since we’ve been here … I can’t thank the fans, the school, and the community enough for everything they’ve meant to us.”

title: Here’s how much more Americans are expected to pay for Thanksgiving dinners this year
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday.
The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.
The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it’s the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a record of $64.05 in 2022.
High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said. Diesel prices have surged since the start of the Iran war and hit a record average of $6.53 per gallon in the U.S. in September, according to AAA.
On Wednesday diesel averaged $5.96 per gallon, up 58% from a year ago, AAA said.
Turkey prices have also risen sharply over the past year. The Farm Bureau said the 16-pound turkey in its survey cost an average of $23.68 this year, up from $21.50 last year.
Bird flu has been decimating U.S. turkey flocks since an outbreak began in 2022. But cases have been waning, and turkey production increased substantially this year, said Mark Jordan, the executive director of Leap Market Analytics.
At the same time, turkey demand has been rising, as more Americans seek out lean protein and U.S. turkey exports rise. That strong demand has limited U.S. turkey inventories and raised prices. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average a record $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year.
“Over the last few years there’s been a lot of doom and gloom for the turkey industry,” Jordan said. “This is one of those years that turkey producers are feeling a little bit better about their lot in life.”
Jordan said diesel costs likely didn’t impact turkey prices this year, since so much of the decision-making and timing related to the turkeys that will be consumed this Thanksgiving happened before diesel prices spiraled. But diesel costs could have a notable impact on turkey prices next year, he said.
A few of the items on the Thanksgiving menu are cheaper than last year, the Farm Bureau said. A 1-pound vegetable tray featuring carrots and celery is 5 cents cheaper, while a 16-ounce bag of frozen peas is 4 cents cheaper. Frozen pie crusts are also slightly cheaper, although a can of pumpkin pie filling is more expensive.
And in some cases, stores will price turkey and other Thanksgiving staples lower in order to draw shoppers. Aldi said its feast for 10, which mirrors the Farm Bureau’s menu, costs $39 this year. Walmart, which adds items like corn muffin mix and marshmallows but doesn’t include carrots and celery, said its feast for 10 is $35.
Persistently high grocery prices have been frustrating Americans since the pandemic and played a role in Republicans’ recent losses in the midterm elections. Prices for food eaten at home jumped 22% between October 2021 and October 2026, according to U.S. government data. That’s almost double the usual pace of food price inflation.
This year, the USDA predicts prices for food eaten at home to rise 2.3%. That would be lower than the recent annual average of 2.6%.
