title: An acclaimed architect revisits his Maine roots
text:
Over the course of his long career in architecture, Turner Brooks has designed buildings ranging from distinctive homes that harmonize with the landscape to a campus designed for residents with autism spectrum disorders. In his new book “Spatial Memories and Preoccupations of an Architect,” Brooks shares his thoughts on space and revisits some of the projects that helped clarify his aesthetics — all the while tracing the role Maine played in his artistic evolution.
Brooks’ childhood memories of visiting his grandparents in Maine provide one of the keys to his philosophy of space. Their home — and the bedroom where he slept, “suspended over the front porch of the house and centered directly above the front door” — left a formidable impression on him through its combination of indoors and outdoors, light and shadow. Elsewhere, he revisits a moment of traveling foggy waters around Seal Island and perceiving “a miraculous little circle of clarity” around the boat — another key to his conception of space.
We spoke with Brooks about the genesis of his book, his philosophy of architecture and design, and the importance of bats.
Was there any one specific impetus that led to you writing an overview of your career?
I don’t know if there was one incident. I’d say it was a series of incidents. One came from teaching and feeling that there wasn’t much discussion about what space actually was about. Mostly it was a description of form and things like that: Details and colors. The actual issue of how to talk about space, which to me is the most important part of architecture, was somewhat ignored.
I was given a project when I was a student that was very important to me. I keep invoking it, and as a teacher I’ve given this project to my own students for years and years. It’s called the dominant void, and it was given to us by the guy who the book is dedicated to, Kent Bloomer. It was really our first project in architecture school: To define a space that was more palpably present than whatever was around it. It sounds like an insane paradox. I’ve called it the quest for the Holy Grail, though there are very few Galahads — more sweating Lancelots struggling to do it.
For the student project, these spaces seemed to be very inhabitable to me, and they were designed around the movement of the body. You would feel happily encapsulated in these spaces, because they had an atmosphere of its own that was different from the landscape outside of it. The inspiration was about making spaces that contain the body in a comfortable way.
Another element that inspired the book was my memories of spaces I inhabited as a child, like that little bedroom in Maine. It had these wonderful windows that looked out at the road to the landscape and also down the stairs into the living room, so it was embedded in that cozy atmosphere of the larger landscape of the house, as well as the larger landscape.
There was not one moment when I thought, “I’m going to write a book.” But I’ve been working on it for 20-something years, off and on. I didn’t think of it as writing a book, but just writing memories of space. Then it became clear what I was doing. That’s also in part due to my friend Cynthia Zarin, who edited a lot of the initial writing.
For readers who aren’t familiar with your work, are there any spaces that you could point them toward to get a sense of how these spaces and absences work in practice?
In the book, I wrote about buildings in Rome designed by Francesco Borromini. Those spaces feel incredibly, wonderfully active, like there are overlapping vibrating ripples that are moving around. The funny thing is, I’ve always wanted to release a thousand bats into those spaces, because bats are the most amazing space definers. If you had a cloud of bats flying around, they would define the shape of the space and, in an amazing way, demonstrate that it’s full of some sort of atmosphere.
The Sant’Ivo alla Sapienza and San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane would be two spaces where I think you would get a really clear idea of what the whole book is about, in terms of palpable space.
Buildings aren’t the only thing you cite as an inspiration in your book. You also mention a few paintings, including work by René Magritte.
There are several paintings that are cited, like Edward Hopper’s “Rooms by the Sea.” That’s an amazing painting: You have the open door that looks out at the horizon of the ocean at a far distance and in the center two-thirds of the painting, which is so radical, is just a blank wall with a light coming down diagonally over it. The shaft of light leads you to a little open door on the left side of the painting which reveals a cozy domestic space with furniture. “It’s like the house in Maine, an interior space which relates to the vast space of where the horizon meets the ocean. It illustrates everything I’m trying to talk about in the book.”
Besides the house you spent time in while growing up, are there any other spaces in Maine that have had a significant influence on your aesthetic sensibility?
I love the streets of Kennebunkport, and the great houses all over the place. But in Maine, it’s about the landscape. In Biddeford Pool, you go from The Gut into the vast ocean, and that’s also part of what the book is about: The coziness of the pool and then that little transitional liminal zone of The Gut and then the ocean beyond it, which opens up to the rest of the hemisphere. The landscape there was very influential on me — the harbor in Biddeford Pool and the transition out into the ocean and the islands.
In writing about your work as an architect, you discuss a lot of community-oriented spaces and housing designed for working people. Given that affordability has been in the news a lot lately, do you feel vindicated about some of the stances you’ve taken over the years?
I’m actually quite proud of the fact that I’ve never done a house for a yuppie. When I started in Vermont, I was paid in pots for my design fee for the first house I designed, because it was for a potter. I made four dollars an hour as a carpenter; this was in 1972.
A few more recent clients have been fairly wealthy, but nobody’s been super wealthy — most of them have been not very wealthy. And then the other projects I’ve done frequently are schools, which is satisfying too because they’re places for learning. I believe in affordable, humble things that are not grand and expensive.
Having taught architecture, have you seen any of the concepts you’ve taught making their way into the world from your students in ways you would not have expected?
I’m 83. I’ve been retired for a couple of years. It’s an interesting question, because there have been so many fluctuations since I graduated. When I was a student, we did what’s called at Yale a building project. For the first building project, we were revolting against fancy sorts of corporate architecture. We had a wonderful dean named Charles Moore who also was revolting against those things and we designed and built a community center down in New Zion, Kentucky, in Appalachia.
There was an emphasis on smaller and affordable things, and then it all changed with the sort of fancy post-modernist material that erupted later. I’m not saying it has anything to do with my influence, but I feel now that students are much more involved in socially relevant projects and are not so interested in the corporate stuff. I find that very refreshing. There are more studios now at Yale that are devoted to affordable housing and socially relevant projects, which I think is a good change.
Fifteen years ago, there was a lecture by a developer. He showed this hill of beautiful vernacular villages that were falling apart. And then he showed how they were all destroyed by his company, which built all these fancy high-rises. There was no discussion of what happened to the people who lived in the original village. That would never happen now. There’s more awareness of social issues now, which is very much like the attitude of that period when I was in school.
New York City resident Tobias Carroll is the author of five books, most recently the novel “In the Sight.” He has reviewed books for The New York Times, Bookforum, the Star Tribune and elsewhere.

title: Business community pushes council to act on cruise ships
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — Members of the town’s business community were out in force at the town council meeting on Tuesday, urging members of the council to act on the uncertainty surrounding the status of cruise ship regulation. Business owners and employees rose during the public comment portion of the meeting to say that the town’s pledge not to accept any new reservations while it works out a response to the latest court ruling regarding passenger caps has put their livelihoods in jeopardy.
“The absence of cruise ship passengers is tangible lost income to local small businesses. My wife and I sell only domestic products, several of them from local artists on the island. To buy more from them, we need people to buy from us. That is Business 101,” said Darren Stavnesli, owner of The Maine Store. Stavnesli, a self-proclaimed “cruiser” and small business owner since 1997, was one of 13 residents who rose to speak on the issue.
“Cruise ship passengers are motivated; they are only in port for a short period of time. They do not contribute to the parking issues,” Stavnesli added. “They are more friendly and polite than your average August visitor; they spend way more money than the average August visitor, and way, way, way more than locals … If this council really cares about what’s best for Bar Harbor, please consider opening the cruise ship reservations immediately.”
Since Judge Lance Walker ruled in May that the current 1,000-passenger cap was “unenforceable” outside of the months of July and August, the town has been in a sort of limbo. Five days after the ruling, the council promised not to accept any new advance cruise ship reservations “until a regulatory tool to manage disembarkation is enacted and the ongoing litigation is resolved.” The council has met several times with the town’s legal team in executive sessions, with the stated purpose of those meetings described as discussions on whether or not to appeal the most recent ruling, and how any decision might impact other pending litigation involving cruise ships. But the business community says there has been too little in the way of public progress on the issue.
“The one thing that I’m really asking for is communication. There’s been silence for half a year since the most recent ruling, and I have staff, dozens of them, that want to know if they have a job next year and I can’t tell them,” said tour operator Duncan Holley, “and a plan to move forward is the only way I’m going to be able to answer that. Communicate on what the intention is so I can start to answer that question.”
Some business owners also claimed that the reduction in ships this summer season, with only around 12 larger ships having been grandfathered in due to preexisting reservations, has already begun to hurt their bottom line. Kristi Bond, owner of the FishMaine Restaurant Group, said that when she looked at the numbers for her restaurants during the 12 days that cruise ships called on Bar Harbor this summer, she found that between the hours of 11 a.m. and 4 p.m. the restaurants served 81% more people on a cruise ship day than on a non-cruise ship day.
“And I’m not talking weeks away from each other, I’m comparing Tuesday to Wednesday of the exact same week,” Bond explained. “We’re not just business owners, we’re residents. This is how we make our life and our livelihood. And to have an 81% difference in one day to the other is huge and makes a drastic difference in the way that we are able to run our business.”
Bond also referenced a potential “trickle-down” effect by pointing out that area nonprofits have been struggling as well, referencing the recent decision by the board of the Bar Harbor Historical Society to lay off its four full-time staff members, which the board claimed was due to significant revenue shortfalls. Bond said that cruise ship passengers had been a key part of the revenue base for the society in the past as they paid for tours at the museum.
Supporters of the cruise ship passenger cap have routinely pushed back against claims that the reduction in cruise ship passengers would represent a potential death blow for local businesses. To bolster their argument, critics of the cruise ship industry have pointed to state sales tax data for the Bar Harbor Economic Summary Area, which has shown either a steady flow or even a modest increase in the amount the state has collected from local businesses over the last few years that the cap has been in place. This fact, they argue, shows that local businesses continue to make money despite a drop in cruise ship passengers. But business owners have pushed back against using this as a metric for the overall health of the local economy, as there are other factors that influence the overall numbers.
“This is a very flawed notion to conflate gross sales with visitor volume or somehow business health,” said Tom Testa during the meeting. “Sales tax is a percentage of gross sales, and as prices rise due to inflation, so do tax revenues based on gross sales. It does every year.”
“We’ve seen general inflation nationally, on a larger scale, closer to home in the state, new taxes, higher electric rates, locally, higher property taxes, increased water rates, combined with increased payroll costs, insurance costs, costs of goods sold,” Testa added. “All of these costs need to be covered to remain viable, and they increase prices and gross revenues. This kind of misapplication of data would be like saying, ‘my grocery bill is higher this year, there must be more people grocery shopping.’”
Overall, the residents who spoke were asking for a plan, some kind of compromise between the years that saw unregulated cruise ship traffic and what they felt were draconian caps in recent years.
“I think you’re hearing that it’s time,” Ocean Properties’ Eben Salvatore told the council when summing up the testimony of his fellow business owners. “We’ve been waiting patiently, it’s been a long summer, and next summer looks terrifying, there’s not a ship booked, and I think you’re hearing how much that’s going to hurt people. We have a ruling, it’s clear: 10 months out of the year there’s no limits. Let’s set some limits, let’s make a schedule, and move forward. We’ve done this for decades … We just had eight days where a 4,000-passenger cruise ship came and went this fall, peacefully, and it was the best day by far for the majority of the people in this room. There’s more of those days that we deserve, and we should have.”
The members of the council generally agreed that there was a need to act on the issue, though some pushed back against the notion that they were dragging their feet.
“We’ve gotten the emails, we saw the room tonight. Whether you’re left, right, up, down, on your opinion on more boats, less boats, whatever, we as a group need to expedite this, we need to move this along, we need to provide guidance, and I look forward to doing that with the rest of you,” councilor Steve Boucher said at the conclusion of the meeting.
“I worry about the misinformation because when people can stand there and say … that 10 months out of the year we can’t regulate cruise ships, that’s not what the court decision said. If you read the court decision, it says we can’t cap it at 1,000 in those months. But we can regulate it because it didn’t overturn the 1,000 [passenger] cap, and so I think that’s a little facetious to say, ‘what’s the holdup?’” argued council member Earl Brechlin.
“And I want to find a compromise, I think we can … as far as council foot dragging, I can’t argue that we couldn’t have moved a little faster, but at the same time there’s other court cases related to this particular issue and the decisions of those particular court cases and the appeals periods that have to play out inform our decisions too, and it’s not being done in a vacuum. So, I think people need to understand that it’s not just us not taking reservations.”

title: Holden police hold jail and bail event for 25 Days of Kindness
text:
HOLDEN, Maine (WABI) - Holden police arrested more than 20 local business owners in the afternoon, but the business owners did not break the law. They turned themselves in.
The Holden Police Department held its second jail and bail event to raise money for 25 Days of Kindness.
Local business owners put themselves behind bars to raise money for their “bail.”
The money donated will go into the 25 Days of Kindness fund. The fund helps community members across the state with things like heating oil and food insecurity.
Holden Police Chief Eddie Benjamin said raising the money is a lot of work, but helping the community is always worth it.
“It’s a lot of work. But, you know, when you give like 100 gallons to somebody that needs, the hugs and the thank yous. And, you know, that warms your heart and just like energizes you to do even more. We are a community first, second, and third. And it’s just who we are as a police department,” Benjamin said.
Last year, the event raised $22,000. Donations can be made year-round.
Last we checked, none of the business owners have to spend the night behind bars.

title: Over a freeway near Los Angeles, animals can roam safely thanks to world's largest wildlife crossing
text:
AGOURA HILLS, Calif. (AP) — Touring the world’s largest wildlife crossing, Beth Pratt stepped carefully through freshly planted native vegetation and held up her hand for silence.
“Hear that? We’re listening to birdsong right now, on top of one of the busiest freeways in the U.S.!” a beaming Pratt, one of the project’s leaders, said excitedly. “That makes my heart glad.”
The warbling was the latest sign that the bridge, spanning U.S. 101 and a feeder road about 35 miles (56 kilometers) northwest of downtown Los Angeles, is already in use by animals ahead of the official Dec. 2 opening ceremony.
Just two weeks earlier, motion-sensor cameras captured a lone coyote believed to be the first mammal to make the trek safely across. Days after that momentous crossing, three juvenile coyotes were seen on camera playing in the brush beneath the 10-foot (3-meter) sound-dampening walls that line the span.
“They don’t care about ribbon cuttings,” laughed Pratt, president of the nonprofit Wildlife Crossing Fund.
About 300,000 cars a day travel that stretch of the 101 in Agoura Hills, a small city surrounded by a patchwork of protected wildland that the new crossing will connect. Fencing along the freeway funnels animals to the crossing.
The bridge, with a landscape that’s indistinguishable from surrounding hillsides, stretches 1,250 feet (380 meters) in two sections over the roadways to give animals hemmed in by urban sprawl a safe path to the nearby Santa Monica Mountains and beyond.
It is named the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing for the late philanthropist whose foundation donated $25 million toward the $114 million total budget. The cost ballooned from an initial $92 million, and the money came from donations from 6,000 members of the public, as well as grants from nonprofits and state funds set aside for conservation purposes. Leonardo DiCaprio was one of the earliest donors after a funding drive was launched a decade ago.
Waiting for the cougars
Pratt said for her the real official opening will be when a mountain lion, a species listed as threatened in California, finds its way to the overpass.
The star of the campaign to build the bridge was the cougar — known as P-22 — an LA celebrity in its own right who traveled across freeways and made a home in a huge Los Angeles park. P-22, who was euthanized in 2022 after likely being hit by a car, became a symbol of the shrinking genetic diversity of wild animals that must remain all but trapped by sprawling development or risk becoming roadkill. Thousands attended a memorial service for him.
Scientists tracking mountain lions fitted with GPS collars found over decades that roadways were largely confining animals in mountains that run along the Malibu coast and across the middle of Los Angeles to Griffith Park, where P-22 settled.
During the tour last week, Pratt wore a shirt emblazoned with an image of the beloved cougar. She hopes to eventually erect a statue of P-22 on the side of the new bridge.
Caged by concrete, killed by cars and sickened by rat poison, the isolated pumas risk inbreeding themselves into extinction, scientists and state wildlife officials say. A report just last week from the University of California, Davis, found that at least 780 mountain lions — or 18% of the state’s population — are killed by vehicles each year.
“The story of P-22 was just so compelling,” said Mari Galloway, California program director for the nonprofit Wildlands Network. “We saw the peril in what happened to that particular cat. It was demonstrative of what these mountain lions are facing in this part of the landscape.”
Galloway’s group, which was not involved in the Annenberg crossing, hopes the new bridge will spur the construction of many others across California and the nation. The Wildlands Network is working with state transportation officials in the early stages of planning a wildlife bridge for a stretch of highway in the Mojave Desert east of Los Angeles where bighorn sheep roam.
Wildlife crossings — bridges and tunnels — are common in western Europe and Canada. A famous one in Banff National Park in Alberta spans the Trans-Canada Highway and is frequently used by bears, moose and elk.
A large overpass in Colorado over Interstate 25, along with other mitigation efforts including underpasses and fencing, has contributed to a 91% decrease in wildlife collisions, that state’s parks and wildlife department announced in September.
Hummingbirds, bees and spiders too
Atop the Annenberg crossing, Anthony Deascentis, a field inspector for the California Department of Transportation, waved Pratt over to some scrub brush. He pointed out an orb-weaver spider, as big as a silver dollar, building an elaborate circular web.
“There’s also a good amount of bees enjoying the native plants,” said Deascentis. In addition, he’s spotted an oak titmouse, sparrows and hummingbirds — further evidence that wildlife are taking to the new terrain even as crews using heavy machinery continued to fill in the landscape on the bridge’s south side.
Jeff Sikich, a biologist for the National Park Service who collars and tracks cougars and other wild animals, said the next step will be to implant “biologgers” that will allow scientists to also monitor physiological data like heart rate, body temperature and activity levels. With that information, they’ll be able to tell if the animals are stressed while using the wildlife bridge, or “if they’re relaxed up there.”
Sikich said in recent weeks scientists have detected multiple mammals in the hills nearby the new span, including bobcats, deer, gray foxes and a female mountain lion with two kittens.
He said they’re “sniffing around,” hopefully getting ready to make the crossing.

title: Maine’s Amy Allen could win 3rd songwriter Grammy
text:
Maine’s Amy Allen has a chance to win the songwriter of the year Grammy for the third consecutive time.
Allen, who grew up in Windham and South Portland, was nominated for the award this week on the strength of songs she’s written or co-wrote for Noah Kahan, Olivia Rodrigo, Ed Sheeran, Megan Moroney, and others. She won her second consecutive songwriter of the year Grammy in February.
Allen has been nominated for the award four of the five years it has been given out. She would become the first person to win it three consecutive times. Other nominees for the songwriter Grammy this year include Edgar Barrera, RAYE, Joybeth Taylor and Theron Thomas. The Grammys will be presented Feb. 7 in Los Angeles.
Allen could win a Grammy for her work as a songwriter in the category of album of the year, for her work on “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So In Love” by Olivia Rodrigo.
Also nominated for a Grammy this week was recording engineer Wellington Gordon, who graduated from Skowhegan Area High School in 1993. Gordon was nominated along with five others in the category of best engineer Classical Album, for their work on “Forward Into Light” by Sarah Kirkland Snider. Gordon now lives in Virginia.
Allen graduated from Waynflete School in Portland in 2010. She performed with her band, Amy and The Engine, before moving to Los Angeles around 2017 and beginning her career as a songwriter.
By 2019, she had co-written the Selena Gomez hit “Back to You” and the Halsey hit “Without Me.” The latter song reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Hot 100 pop chart. Allen has become one of pop music’s most in-demand songwriters in the past half-dozen years, working with Sabrina Carpenter, Selena Gomez, Harry Styles and many others.
“This award belongs to every single songwriter out there,” Allen said, after accepting the songwriter Grammy in February. “To all the songwriters out there continuing to fight the good fight, thank you for teaching me and inspiring me.”
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Ray Routhier can be reached at rrouthier@pressherald.com.

title: Grand jury indicts Illinois man on terrorism and weapons charges in foiled Hindu temple shooting
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in a Chicago suburb faces new charges of terrorism and armed violence, police said Wednesday.
Authorities allege Alexandros Paporakis planned to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Oct. 11, the first day of the Hindu holiday of Navaratri. Paporakis’ co-workers at a Taco Bell reported to authorities that he told them he planned to “kill Indian people” and police arrested him that afternoon. He was initially charged with making a terrorist threat and illegally possessing a rifle.
Prosecutors have said Paporakis, of Palatine, Illinois, calls himself a white supremacist and neo-Nazi, and that he wrote a document detailing his fantasies about murdering non-white people. Police have said they recovered a rifle, ammunition, a tactical vest and a patch “displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism” from his house.
A grand jury indicted Paporakis on Nov. 5 on six counts of terrorism, two counts of armed violence and two counts of attempted terrorism, all felonies, according to police. The jury also added nine more counts of making a terrorist threat.
The indictment also included new weapons-related charges, including possession of a firearm without a serial number and not having a police-issued identification card, police said.
It is not clear why police delayed releasing information about the grand jury indictment.
A judge ordered Paporakis to be detained, declaring him a threat to the community. He is due to be arraigned in court on Thursday morning.
Fedor Kozlov, an attorney for Paporakis, told The Associated Press in a text message Wednesday that his client is still planning to plead not guilty to the charges.
The thwarted shooting sparked alarm among members of Chicago’s Hindu community and South Asian leaders, who said an uptick in racist rhetoric against their community had fueled the threat. U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was at the temple that was targeted on the day of the planned attack, urged authorities to charge Paporakis with a hate crime. Authorities have not announced any such charge.
The FBI’s Chicago field office said Wednesday there was no additional information about possible federal charges. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois has not responded to a request for comment.
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: US authorities interviewed Alice Huang in probe over possible diversion of chips
text:
US authorities interviewed Alice Huang in probe over possible diversion of chips
U.S. investigators conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang last summer, the U.S. Commerce and Justice Departments said, as part of an investigation into whether the Singapore-based company had been diverting highly coveted U.S. semiconductors.
The departments included that detail in a joint statement released late Monday, which laid out a timeline of their investigation into the cloud computing and data center provider. The Commerce Department launched an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations, the departments said.
The statement comes after days of mounting scrutiny of U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism for being too slow in taking action against Megaspeed. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added to the pressure on Friday, accusing the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling the Nvidia customer a possible national security threat.
The departments said Commerce investigators requested records in May 2025 from Nvidia concerning “direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed,” and that Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list the following month.
Following that, agents from agents from the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, “conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang,” the joint statement said.
U.S. government officials have identified Alice Huang as having had an affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and have raised concerns that she could be a potential Chinese intelligence asset. The U.S. intelligence community has been working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.
Megaspeed said in a statement Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and currently holds no role there. It also said that the company is “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence.”
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Monday’s statement offered few other details, but said that the Justice Department has since taken on the lead role in the criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
The statement follows similar details released last week by the Singaporean government, which also noted US authorities’ visit to Megaspeed last summer. It said the Bureau of Industry and Security conducted a check at Megaspeed, “with Huang present,” on June 24, 2025, which “was the first time Singapore came to know about the US’s interest in Megaspeed and Huang,” the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement.
That same day, Singaporean police also interviewed her as part of its ongoing investigations into Megaspeed, and her passport was impounded to secure her attendance for purposes of the ongoing investigations, since Alice Huang was not based in Singapore, the statement said.
Ultimately, the Singapore Police Force concluded there was “insufficient evidence” that Alice Huang had committed any offenses relating to the investigation, but she was barred from re-entering the country due to attempts to “downplay her role” at Megaspeed, the government said.

title: Edgecomb Fire & Rescue October report
text:
Edgecomb Fire and Rescue responded to 24 calls in October, compared with 10 calls in September. October calls included seven fires, 16 medical emergencies (ME), and two motor vehicle accidents (MVA). Year-to-date, we have responded to 201 calls, slightly fewer than 223 calls at the same time last year.
Training during October included training with our mutual aid departments for a “firefighter down.” We also trained in the use of thermal imaging with our thermal imaging camera. Other training included our monthly “truck check” of all apparatus and equipment. Ongoing training and proper equipment are critical in maintaining our readiness to respond to any call.

title: The 2026 Country Music Association Awards are here with Taylor Swift performing: How to watch
text:
(AP) - It didn’t take a crystal ball to see: The 2026 Country Music Association Awards were always going to be all about Ella Langley.
The Alabama-born-and-raised singer was named entertainer of the year during Wednesday’s event — beating the host of the evening and last year’s winner Lainey Wilson, as well as Cody Johnson, Luke Combs and Chris Stapleton, for the top prize.
“At this point, I’m sick of me,” she started her acceptance speech with a joke, after having spent so much of the show on stage. “I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life.” Wilson emerged with a bedazzled broom because, “I told you, you was going to sweep, girl!” she said as she embraced Langley.
It really was Langley’s night from the jump. The 60th annual CMA Awards, broadcast live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, started and ended with her. Langley accepted the first award of the night, single of the year, for her history-making “Choosin’ Texas.”
Competition was fierce: Taylor Swift’s song for the “Toy Story 5” film, “I Knew It, I Knew You,” was also nominated in the category, as were Langley’s own “Be Her,” Wilson’s “Somewhere Over Laredo” and Johnson’s “The Fall.”
And then Langley was back on stage almost immediately afterward — to perform her joyous “Loving Life Again” with a string quartet and to pick up another award, when “Choosin’ Texas” was named song of the year.
“This song is the gift that keeps on giving,” she said in her speech.
She also won female vocalist as well as album of the year, the latter for her thrilling, old-soul country “Dandelion.”
“My lip is already quivering,” she said. “I’m at a loss for words.”
The return of Taylor Swift and a tribute to Dolly Parton
Swift was in the building. The pop powerhouse lit up the CMA Awards by performing “I Knew It, I Knew You” with a bit of her 2006 country hit “Our Song” mixed in for good measure.
She began her set in the back halls of the arena before hitting the stage — joined by Keith Urban on banjo, no less — as if no time had passed.
But it’s been 13 years since Swift last performed at the CMA Awards, a decade after her last appearance there and 17 years after being named the youngest entertainer of the year in the show’s history.
Consider it a treat in a night full of them. The show began with a powerful tribute to the larger-than-life Dolly Parton. The American icon died in August at age 80, and her legacy will be felt for many decades to come.
Host Wilson got the celebration started, duetting Parton’s “I Will Always Love You” with the legendary singer-songwriter Vince Gill.
Then she was joined by singer Brad Paisley in a funny opening monologue where the pair sang modern parodies of famous country songs: Loretta Lynn’s “Coal Miner’s Daughter” became “Data Miner’s Daughter,” and Willie Nelson’s “Always On My Mind” was transformed into “Always On My Phone.”
No shortage of awards and performances here
A standout set arrived early: Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert duetted “Horses & Divorces” — a song from Musgraves’ latest album, “Middle of Nowhere,” that doubles as a delicious resolution from the pair of former frenemies — with its norteño accordion and shout-along lyrics. The stage was set to look like an ’80s beauty parlor, recalling one of Parton’s most famous acting roles: the 1989 film “Steel Magnolias.”
Tim McGraw brought it back to the ’90s, singing “Don’t Take the Girl.” Megan Moroney slowed things down with her big-hearted ballad “Beautiful Things.” Tucker Wetmore was joined by a brass band for a bit of his single “Who Told You That” before launching into some of Hank Williams Jr.’s 1984 hit “All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight.”
Combs tackled his song “Miss You Here.” Lambert and Langley brought some country-disco with “Snakeskin Boots.” Mumford & Sons teamed up with Stapleton for “Here.”
Later, Stapleton would hop back on stage to join Stephen Wilson Jr. — and to be awarded male vocalist of the year, for a ninth time in his career.
Lainey Wilson performed a brand new one, the full-throated “Just A Woman.”
It was a bit of a theme: The modern traditionalist Zach Top also debuted a new track, the bluegrass-y “Moonshine.” Before he left the stage, Dierks Bentley joined in for a tribute to the late John Anderson. They sang his 1983 single “Swingin’.”
Best new artist went to Stephen Wilson Jr.; vocal group went for a second year in a row to the Red Clay Strays, who also performed their song “Revival.”
Brooks & Dunn took home vocal duo for the 17th time.
“I love to hear myself talk, and I’ve actually run out of things to say,” Kix Brooks said in his acceptance speech. “Thanks for making us famous.”
“Follow the yellow brick road,” added Ronnie Dunn.
Later in the night, they received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award. Halestorm, Marcus King, Brothers Osborne, Hardy and Luke Bryan paid tribute to the legendary country music duo, covering some of their biggest hits: “Boot Scootin’ Boogie,” “Rock My World (Little Country Girl),” “Hard Workin’ Man,” “Hillbilly Deluxe” and “Play Something Country.”
Prizes are nominated and voted on by members of the Country Music Association, which includes music executives, artists, publicists, songwriters and other industry professionals.

title: Highway patrol to pay $70,000 to former Wild Orchid member in DUI arrest settlement
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — The Tennessee Highway Patrol will pay $70,000 to Stefanie Fair, a former member of the 1990s pop group Wild Orchid, in a settlement over her DUI arrest.
Blood work later showed Fair was sober at the time of her arrest.
The state Board of Claims approved the settlement, and a payout should result in the next few weeks, according to a spokesman for the attorney general’s office.
Court records show lawsuits by sober drivers are piling up against the state. The claims include reports that a single trooper arrested nine sober drivers for DUI.
Stefanie Fair’s arrest
Fair’s 2024 arrest was featured in WSMV4 Investigates’ “Sobering Problem” investigations.
The trooper who arrested her for DUI said he smelled alcohol.
“There’s a very distinct odor of alcohol that comes from either the person or inside the vehicle,” Trooper Keith Velez said.
“But on my life, I don’t drink alcohol,” Fair responded.
Video obtained by WSMV4 Investigates shows Fair eating ice cream before her arrest.
“I was more scared being with that cop alone than I actually was inside the jail,” Fair said.
Attorney’s comments on the settlement
Fair’s attorney, Ben Raybin, said the state has recognized problems with arrests like hers.
“I think that the state has recognized that a lot of these arrests are just completely legally unsupportable and that if they went to a jury trial, a jury would find against them,” Raybin said.
There is no recourse in Tennessee for sober drivers to recoup costs, even after their DUI charges are dismissed. Raybin said their only option is to sue.
Other lawsuits against the state
Fair is the second sober driver to sue the Tennessee Highway Patrol and settle.
Thomas Manis was paid $75,000 after state troopers arrested him for DUI in East Tennessee.
Other sober drivers who first told their stories to WSMV4 Investigates are also suing the state, including NASA employee Labreesha Batey and former U.S. attorney Jane Bondurant.
WSMV4 Investigates found Bondurant was the eighth sober driver arrested by state trooper James Zahn.
According to a lawsuit filed this year by a Thompson Station man, Zahn also arrested him for DUI while he was sober. That would make him the ninth sober driver arrested by Zahn.
Other agencies
The Tennessee Highway Patrol is not the only agency to settle lawsuits.
Court records show the Rutherford County Sheriff’s Office and La Vergne police have also settled lawsuits from sober drivers arrested for DUI.

title: Islander celebrates 25 years of community journalism
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — This week, the Mount Desert Islander celebrates its 25th year of publishing community news on Mount Desert Island.
What started as an idea by former publisher Alan Baker was taken to the next level by founding editor Earl Brechlin.
Baker, who had owned The Ellsworth American since 1991, said he wanted to start a paper on the island to compete with the Bar Harbor Times, which was beginning to show signs of financial distress.
At the time, said Baker, the Times was on its second or third round of hedge fund investor/operators and was losing ground in the community. “It was obvious during that time that [the Bar Harbor Times] didn’t have a local presence. They were not involved in the community, and it started to show,” he said.
Baker said he and Brechlin met the Tuesday before Labor Day 2001 to hash out their ideas. Brechlin began his first day as the Islander’s managing editor on Oct. 1. With no staff, no design concept, no name and no sales representative, the two got to work. In less than six weeks, the first issue rolled off the press.
For Baker, it was important that the newspaper serve not only the entire island, but also the outer islands such as the Cranberry Isles, Swan’s Island and Frenchboro. “I knew I didn’t want Bar Harbor in the name,” said Baker. “I wanted the other islands to feel like they were a part of this as well.”
Baker credits Brechlin for helping the paper get off the ground and earning the trust of the community. “Earl was already well known and respected,” said Baker.
Reporters, contributors and columnists have come and gone over the years, but there are some familiar faces that have appeared in the first issue and continue on today, including columnists V. Paul Reynolds and Tim Plouffe. Anne Kozak of Bar Harbor is also a name you will find in the first few issues. Kozak, who covered the science community, among others, is still part of the Islander family, reporting from time to time on organizations such as MDI Bio Lab and Friends of Acadia.
Three years into the new venture, said Baker, was when he realized the paper was going to be successful. It was at that time that the overall circulation of the Islander eclipsed that of the Bar Harbor Times. The Times would eventually close in 2012.
“When we passed the Bar Harbor Times in circulation, I knew we were locked in,” said Baker, adding, “To me, circulation numbers are a direct recognition by the people of the community, and that is when I knew we were real.”
Since Brechlin stepped down from his role in 2017, the Islander has remained in capable hands. First, Liz Graves assumed the role of managing editor, continuing to produce excellent, award-winning work. In 2020, Faith DeAmbrose joined the Islander after a nearly 20-year career leading the Penobscot Bay Press newspapers, bringing the papers through the Covid pandemic. Under all three editors, the paper continues its legacy of excellence, routinely recognized as newspaper of the year by the Maine and New England Press Associations.
Today, a new evolution is underway. The Islander, along with its sister publications The Ellsworth American and Bangor Historian, is working toward nonprofit ownership through Acadia Newspaper Trust. The move is aimed at preserving independent local journalism and ensuring community news remains a vital part of life on Mount Desert Island for generations to come. To learn more, visit acadianewspapertrust.org.
It’s hard to believe that 25 years have passed since we published the first issue of the Mount Desert Islander,” said Publisher Chris Crockett. “What started as an idea in 2001 has grown into an important part of the island community.”
That success, he said, “belongs to the talented journalists and staff who have poured their hearts into this newspaper over the years, and to the readers, advertisers and community members who have supported us from day one.
“I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve built together, and even more excited about what the next 25 years will bring.”

title: China planners OK lone applicant
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
With only the applicant, Ralph Howe, present for the China Planning Board’s Nov. 10 public hearing on Howe’s application to use a house at 15 Alder Park Road as an office, board chairman Milton Dudley declined to hold the hearing (see the Nov. 5 issue of The Town Line, p. 2).
Instead, Dudley led board members through the town’s ordinance requirements for the change of use. Finding requirements met, and minimal effects on the neighborhood, board members unanimously approved the application.
Howe, head of BioRenewable Fuels, said he intends to use the house and garage on the property as an office and to store office materials.
Dudley presided over the hearing as acting board chairman. Board members then elected him chairman. No one was willing to become co-chairman. Dudley said he plans a conversation with Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood about the shortage of volunteers for town committees.
He thanked board member Bruce Fitzgerald for interrupting his work schedule in California to zoom in to the meeting.
Codes Officer Nicholas French reported he has been busy with required inspections as residents hurry to finish projects before bad weather.
The subdivision application from Daniel Ouellette, on Two Ponds Road, that board members saw at their Oct. 27 meeting has been amended, French said. The applicant needs to provide more information before it is ready for review.
Fitzgerald reminded the rest that the board still needs a subdivision application form and matching criteria so members can properly review the application when it is presented.
With no urgent pending business, board members accepted Dudley’s proposal to cancel a second November meeting. Their next meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m., Tuesday, Dec. 8, in the China town office meeting room.

title: Youth Full Maine provides free Thanksgiving groceries to families in need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Youth Full Maine provides free Thanksgiving groceries to York County families in need
Ahead of Thanksgiving, Maine nonprofit organizations are working to ensure that everyone has what they need to feed their family.
On Wednesday, volunteers with Youth Full Maine handed out free groceries at Rotary Park in Biddeford.
Youth Full Maine hosts food distributions every month, but the Biddeford-based nonprofit notes the need for food climbs during the holiday season, especially when children are out of school.
Bear Geister, Youth Full Maine's food resource coordinator, said that what he described as an "uncertain political climate" has fewer people coming out to get the help they need.
"We have seen the cars that are coming through the lines, though, increase the number of families they're picking up for. So this does show us that people are picking up for other families that may be hesitant to come out and grab food for themselves right now," Geister said.
Youth Full Maine is the beneficiary of the MyMaine Winter Launch Party, which is being hosted by MyMaine Media and Evergreen Credit Union at Pepperell Mill in Biddeford from 6 to 8:30 p.m. Thursday. Guests are asked to bring child-friendly food such as cereal, macaroni and cheese, peanut butter, granola bars and soup, or Hannaford gift cards.

title: Tech outages are piling up, and AI is raising the stakes. Could this be the new normal?
text:
Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.
In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.
Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.
The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.
Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.
“To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.”
What’s gone offline recently
Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.
Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.
For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday.
Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.
And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.
Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.”
The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there’s no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.
Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents,” although it didn’t immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email.
AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks
AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.
For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.
President Donald Trump’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA’s outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month’s PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said.
Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it.
At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions.
“As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week.
He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.”
While recent outages haven’t been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.
“AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering.
In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them.
Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives
Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.
Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era.
“These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.
Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added.

title: 3 dead in Washington County from respiratory viruses
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Three people have died from respiratory viruses in Washington County.
The Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention warned Tuesday that Washington County is experiencing outbreaks of influenza A, influenza B and COVID.
That’s left three people dead, Maine CDC spokesperson Lindsay Hammes confirmed Wednesday morning.
Worcester Resources Co. said in a statement that one of its employees and two people who worked for a contractor died from illnesses unrelated to their factory work.
“We are saddened by the deaths of one of our employees and two individuals who worked for our contractors, and extend our sincere condolences to their families, friends and coworkers. Out of respect for the families’ privacy, we will refrain from commenting on individual medical circumstances,” a Worcester Resources spokesperson said.
The company is working with the Maine CDC to provide guidance and care to workers.
Hammes advised Mainers to get vaccinated as the state heads into the peak season for respiratory viruses and to take steps to minimize the risk of spreading illnesses to others, including staying home when sick, covering coughs and sneezes, and washing hands frequently.
Additionally, an adult in Washington County has contracted meningococcal disease, a bacterial infection that can spread to the brain and spinal cord or bloodstream.
Symptoms include confusion, fever and headache, while more serious cases can cause nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light, according to the Maine CDC.
People infected with the disease are contagious from seven days before the onset of symptoms to a day after beginning antibiotic treatment.
Hammes told the Bangor Daily News that the meningococcal case is isolated, meaning there’s a low risk to the general public.
It’s not the first time a member of the company’s mostly migrant seasonal workforce, who generally live in temporary housing that Worcester Resources provides, has died from such an illness.
A wreath maker died from COVID-19 in November 2021 amid an employee outbreak that sickened more than 80 workers, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. It fined Worcester Resources for violations that included not reporting her death to the agency.
The company did not do contact tracing to find out who she had been in contact with, according to OSHA, nor did it report 24 other “work-related” cases to the agency.
Worcester officials defended their COVID policies, saying at the time that the company wasn’t certain the death was work-related and thought state officials had reported it, the Maine Monitor previously reported.
The company has been cited numerous other times for recordkeeping and safety violations in recent years. The most recent was in 2024, according to an OSHA database, when the agency found three “serious” issues with the living quarters provided to workers.
Worcester Resources makes wreaths for Wreaths Across America, the nonprofit that places them on veterans’ graves. Members of the Worcester family head both the company and the nonprofit.
BDN writer Elizabeth Walztoni contributed reporting.

title: St. John’s Catholic School students spread Thanksgiving cheer through annual Community Turkey Walk
text:
BRUNSWICK – Students from St. John’s Catholic School will once again take to the streets of downtown Brunswick for one of the school’s favorite annual traditions: the Community Turkey Walk which will be held Thursday, Nov. 19 in the morning.
During this special Thanksgiving tradition, students visit local downtown businesses to deliver handmade paper turkeys decorated with heartfelt messages of gratitude. Each turkey is a small reminder of the importance of kindness, appreciation and the connections that make a community strong.
The Community Turkey Walk has become a beloved tradition for students and staff, as well as the local business owners who eagerly welcome the colorful creations each year. Many businesses proudly display the handmade turkeys in their storefront windows and on their doors throughout Thanksgiving and for weeks afterward, turning downtown Brunswick into a colorful celebration of gratitude.
As part of Discover Catholic Schools Week, the Community Turkey Walk offers a wonderful example of how Catholic education extends beyond the classroom. Through meaningful traditions like this, students put their faith into action by practicing gratitude, building relationships and making a positive difference in the community around them. The walk highlights the importance St. John’s places on service, compassion and helping students become thoughtful, engaged members of their community.
“At St. John’s, we believe that gratitude is something best demonstrated through action,” Principal J. P. Yorkey said. “The Community Turkey Walk is a wonderful way for our students to share a little joy, recognize the people around them and remind our neighbors how much they are appreciated.”
St. John’s Catholic School is grateful for the continued support and enthusiasm of Brunswick’s downtown business community. This annual tradition is a simple but meaningful way to celebrate the spirit of Thanksgiving while strengthening the connections between the school and the greater Brunswick community.
St. John’s Catholic School is devoted to providing students with an enriching classical education anchored by faith. Through academics, service and community engagement, St. John’s strives to nurture students who lead with kindness, compassion and purpose.

title: Presque Isle salon, Fort Fairfield church, and others collect gifts for foster, adoptive families
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Businesses and organizations are collecting gifts for children in foster, adoptive and kinship families through Adoptive and Foster Families of Maine, known as AFFM.
Each gift tag represents a child connected to AFFM. At Total Look in Presque Isle, customers and staff have been sponsoring children for the past few years.
Total Look expands sponsorships
Total Look owner Sheila Cunningham said the salon sponsored 40 tags last year and donated more than $1,000 on top of that.
This year, the group is covering more than 60 children. It partnered with Thrive Body Spa in Caribou, which took on an additional 15 tags. This is Thrive Body Spa’s second year supporting the program.
Cunningham said customers look forward to filling a bag year after year.
“We’ll have some that will start asking us in the summer, are you going to do that again? I want to be sure I get one,” Cunningham said. “I had a lady this year who was like, I didn’t get one last year. Can I be sure to have one this year?”
Celebration Center collects donations and toys
Other groups and businesses are also taking part. In Fort Fairfield, the Celebration Center has a tradition of collecting donations for AFFM’s gift program. That tradition started with one person.
Lacey Guiou, an attendee of Celebration Center Church, said the effort started about 5 years ago.
“I started sponsoring and then I realized like we have a great church family here, church body. And so I started, just making the connection, like getting [Sarah Hatt’s] information here for everybody and offering sponsorships for children, gift cards for teens, and then monetary donations,” Guiou said.
The effort grew to include a toy drive. The toy drive is another way to help without sponsoring a child. The program asks sponsors to spend around $75, but Guiou said people can give to the toy drive within their own budgets.
“There’s no set amount, so if they can afford to buy a puzzle or a package of blocks or a doll, that still goes to the program and can help somebody,” Guiou said.
The toy drive helps fill any last-minute requests AFFM receives.
Hatt, a resource family specialist at AFFM, said costs are higher and needs are greater this year. She said the support she has seen from the community has been big.
“There’s lots of local businesses, churches, individuals that are just really stepping up and want to give and love to help and they do it with a joyful heart,” Hatt said.
Other groups supporting the program
AFFM provided a list of other community support:
- The Kiwanis Club of Presque Isle has sponsored 10 children for two years in a row.
- Framework church provides space to store gifts and allows AFFM to distribute gifts from its building.
- The University of Maine at Presque Isle allows AFFM to use the Owls Nest in the Campus Center for its gift drop-off event in November.
- Neighborhood Books hosts a literacy tea each year. Proceeds go toward books added to each child’s Christmas gift.
- Northern Lighthouse provides space to store gifts and allows AFFM to use its offices in various locations to distribute gifts.
- Washburn District High School National Honor Society students volunteer their time to load and unload gifts and transport them to the Houlton area. They also help distribute the gifts.
- Community members volunteer to sponsor individual children.
How to donate
Sponsors can drop off gifts Saturday, November 21st at the University of Maine at Presque Isle Campus Center from 9 a.m. to noon. Hatt said anyone can also bring extra toys or gift cards during that time.
The Celebration Center’s toy drive runs through Dec. 6. The church can be contacted on Facebook.

title: 2 injured when driver hits stopped U-Haul on Maine Turnpike
text:
Two drivers were injured in an early morning crash Wednesday on Interstate 95 in Portland when a driver hit a stopped U-Haul truck.
The crash was reported at 4:40 a.m. near mile marker 51, according to state police.
John McCain, 63, of Hallowell had pulled a U-Haul van into the emergency lane because of a mechanical failure. The truck was initially reported to be partially in the travel lane, police said.
Jonathan Smith, 46, of Chelsea, was driving in the travel when his pickup truck hit the U-Haul, pushing it off the roadway into a ditch.
Smith’s pickup rolled over and came to rest on its roof in the passing lane.
Both drivers were taken by ambulance to local Portland hospitals with injuries that police said were not life-threatening.
One lane of the highway remained open after the crash. Normal traffic was restored just before 6 a.m., police said.
Troopers are still investigating the cause of the crash.

title: New owner of Brewer bar with illegal wrestling past promises ‘light entertainment’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The newest operator of a Brewer bar that once held illegal wrestling and burlesque events says there won’t be any of that when it reopens in a few weeks.
Frank Berenyi, the owner of the MarijuanaVille medical cannabis chain, plans to open Ubu’s Tavern in the North Brewer Shopping Center in early to mid December, according to kitchen manager Troy Ripley.
He got city licenses in October over a resident’s objection that pointed to his past bars, including an Augusta nightclub that police were called to 350 times. Berenyi’s other recent ventures have also stalled: a cannabis store in Ellsworth that was denied twice and a Portland sports bar.
“I’m not looking at bringing in midget wrestling, or bowling, or strippers, or anything like that,” he told the Brewer City Council on Oct. 13. “I’m looking to run a sports bar with light entertainment.”
Berenyi will be the third owner to try running a bar in the location in two years. The space, which has served alcohol for over a decade under different names, was most recently Mad Kat and Company. It was listed for sale in May.
The tavern will offer food, drinks and interactive entertainment. Berenyi told the council Ubu’s would be similar to a sports bar.
Berenyi has owned multiple bars in Maine in the past 25 years, including Shenanigans, a nightclub in Augusta. At the Oct. 13 meeting, Brewer resident Kathleen Kramer urged the Brewer City Council to review Berenyi’s history as a business owner before approving his liquor, restaurant and amusement license applications because of previous complaints about Shenanigans.
During the eight years that Berenyi owned it, Augusta police responded to 350 calls at the bar, more than any other similar business in the city, according to Augusta Police Chief Kevin Lully.
Berenyi told the council that police are called to many bars, and he never received a violation.
“I’ve owned some of the busiest places in Maine, and I’ve had no violations,” he said at the council meeting on Oct. 13.
Ubu’s is not the only new business Berenyi is trying to open. In April, Ellsworth twice denied a business license for a MarijuanaVille store after pesticides were found in products sold there.
In May, Berenyi announced on social media that he planned to open Ubu’s Sports Pub & Club in Portland. It was slated to open in October, according to the Portland Press Herald, but has not.
Berenyi did not respond to requests for comment about Ubu’s Tavern.

title: Meet Lara Croft, our Adoptable Pet of the Week
text:
Meet Lara Croft, our Adoptable Pet of the Week in Greater Portland
This week's featured adoptable pet from the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland is Lara Croft, a 2-month-old puppy who is ready to play.
Lara comes to Maine from a transport partner in Massachusetts and is part of a litter of five puppies that will become available for adoption starting Thursday, Nov. 19.
Matt Blanchard of the Animal Refuge League wanted to remind potential adopters that puppies require a lot of work and training, but he noted that Lara Croft is a sweetheart and that she already knows how to sit.
"She is super sweet. She's very friendly. She loves everyone she meets. She's very well behaved," Blanchard said of Lara. "But, you know what? It's going to be a long journey getting her into being a real adult dog. When she gets to that 6-month-old to 8-month-old phase, where she becomes a little teenager and doesn't want to listen anymore, maybe it's a different experience. We always want to prepare people. Talk amongst your family and make sure that you're dedicated to this commitment, you guys know how to coordinate it among the family and are ready for the responsibility of bringing home a little puppy."
More information about Lara Croft is available on the Animal Refuge League's website, as long as she is still looking for her forever home.
Anyone who is interested in meeting Lara Croft or other adoptable pets can visit the Animal Refuge League's shelter at 217 Landing Road in Westbrook between 11 a.m. and 4 p.m., except on Wednesdays, when the shelter is closed for adoptions.
The Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland does adoptions on a first-come, first-served basis. On the days the shelter is open, sign-in sheets will be placed on the front door at 9 a.m. to track the order of arrival of adopters who show up early. People who arrive early are asked to remain on the campus once they sign in.
Dog owners who are interested in adopting dogs that are older than 6 months are required to have their dogs meet the adoptable pet before a new pet can be brought home.

title: Unbridled joy: Woman with ALS races rides a horse in all 50 states
text:
LUGOFF, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Tricia Jackson has been riding horses since she was 3 years old. Seventy-one years later, she’s still in the saddle — and she has no plans to stop.
Jackson, an award-winning competitive equestrian, lives on a farm in South Carolina that she calls her place of peace.
Over the years, she has owned as many as 12 horses at once, riding and racing them all. These days, most of her time is spent with her favorite horse, Luke, competing in endurance rides that span anywhere from 25 to 100 miles in a single day.
“That’s a lot of miles,” Jackson said. “We’ve done 50 miles in 3 hours and 50 minutes — way too fast. We riders have to be tough.”
Earlier this year, Jackson was diagnosed with ALS, a rare disease that attacks the brain and spinal cord and gradually steals a person’s ability to speak, move and eventually breathe. There is no cure.
“Statistics say 3 to 5 years, but the kind I have is bulbar ALS, which starts up here and not weakness and loss of limbs, which is coming,” Jackson said. “That’s why I decided I’m not sitting on the front porch and wait to die.”
Riding through all 50 states
Instead of slowing down, Jackson is chasing a lifelong dream — riding a horse in all 50 states.
“Everything goes away when I’m horse riding,” she said. “I feel good, my speech is better. It’s therapy. But I tell them my ALS journey so far and it’s not going to keep me down. As long as I can go, I go. And even if I lose my speech first, which I’m going to do, I can write. I ain’t stopping. That ain’t me.”
In September, she completed her goal with her final ride in Arkansas.
A life already full of adventure
Jackson’s 74 years have been marked by a series of pursuits. In 2001, she competed on Season 4 of “Survivor” after her son dared her to audition. She has traveled on mission trips.
And now she is passing her love of horses, hard work and life to 11-year-old Cooper, a young rider she mentors on her farm.
“I love this boy. He’s my heart,” Jackson said.
For Cooper, the lessons are already taking hold.
“I’ve learned you always have to help people,” he said.
‘Never give up’
Jackson said her faith and the people around her are carrying her through.
“Never give up. Use what God gave you, don’t sit on it,” she said. “This is a terminal disease. I’m going to die from it, but that’s okay because I’m right with God. He’s blessed me, and I’m so blessed to have so many people in my life supporting me.”
Her only ask of the community: educate yourself about ALS. Click/tap here for more information and resources.

title: Pres. Trump flies to Philippines, China
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump kicked off a three-day Asia trip on Tuesday - with a visit to Manila in the Philippines. There the President met with Asia-Pacific leaders and signed a new trade deal.
The President arrived in Asia touting America’s strong relationships with countries in the Asia-Pacific and also announced a new trade agreement with Thailand.
Upon landing in the Philippines, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. welcomed President Trump with a ceremony on the airport tarmac.
Following that, President Trump met with his counterparts from the Quad, Australia, Japan and India, to discuss artificial intelligence collaboration, maritime security in the Asia-Pacific, and joint military exercises.
President Donald Trump promoted friendship, “So from right here in the Philippines to nations across Southeast Asia and throughout the Indo-Pacific, this is one of the world’s most vibrant and productive regions, filled with the tremendous potential great friends of the United States.”
The President also signed a preliminary trade deal with Thailand that the President said lays the foundation for a much stronger trading relationship.
“Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports, which is something that we’ve been after for a long time, and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry. Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products.”
Following the ASEAN Summit, President Trump flew to Shenzhen, China for the APEC Summit and a separate trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. That meeting is expected to focus on nuclear non-proliferation.
The President’s Asia trip coincides with new rules issued from the Commerce Department that will now require a U.S. government license for advanced AI chip sales to data centers in much of Asia. The new rules are aimed at preventing China from acquiring indirectly advanced American technology.
