title: Maine Public Advocate seeks records in CMP rate case following whistleblower allegations
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Public Advocate seeks records in CMP rate case following whistleblower allegations
Maine's Public Advocate is asking state regulators to review records related to allegations of misconduct involving Central Maine Power's parent company, Avangrid, as part of CMP's pending rate case.
The motion follows a whistleblower lawsuit filed by Andrew Jacobs, the former chief compliance officer at Avangrid.
In the complaint, Jacobs alleges he was directed to withhold information from federal auditors, downplay a 2025 bribery matter involving CMP and overstate the company's compliance with federal requirements.
The Office of the Public Advocate says the allegations could have implications for CMP's rate case and what customers ultimately pay. The office is seeking access to records related to the claims as regulators consider the utility's request to raise rates.
CMP says the incident involved approximately $39,000, including unauthorized credit card charges in 2025. The company maintains there will be no rate consequences for customers.
CMP also expressed disappointment that the Office of the Public Advocate did not contact the company before filing the motion.
"We investigated, we disclosed this to FERC, and we no longer work with this individual who was involved," said Jon Breed, speaking on behalf of CMP.
Breed said the company will review the motion carefully and respond through the appropriate process.

title: Country singer pulls out of CMA Awards: 'Going 100 mph all the time isn't healthy'
text:
Country star Cody Johnson won't attend CMA Awards: 'Going 100 mph all the time isn't healthy'
Country singer Cody Johnson says he will not be attending the 2026 CMA Awards.
In a social media post, Johnson said after getting sick at the end of his tour in the United Kingdom earlier this month, he "realized much of it stemmed from mental and physical exhaustion," further saying he needs to step back from the award show.
"At the end of the day, I'm a human being, no matter how much I tell myself and others I'm superman," Johnson said. "I have everything to be thankful for, but sometimes I put too much pressure on myself."
Related video: Carrot Top at the 2006 Billboard Music Awards
When talking about his career and the long wait it took to get to where he is today, he said although it was well worth it, "going 100 mph all the time isn't healthy."
Johnson says he is going to take time recouping at home with his family.
The announcement comes hours ahead of the 60th annual CMA Awards Wednesday night.

title: Government watchdogs asked chatbots to plan a terrorist attack. They did
text:
Government watchdogs asked chatbots to plan a terrorist attack. They complied
The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators.
Video above: Cyberattacks or system malfunctions: What's to blame for the recent technology outages?
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who will helm the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks.
According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation's electrical grid to create economic harm.
“We need to act now,” Hassan said on a conference call with reporters.
The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.
“The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical,” Hassan said in a statement. “If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack.”
The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — who largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security.
"The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors," the GAO wrote.
“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the GAO said. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”
Government watchdogs conduct covert AI tests
GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026.
In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said.
"Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods," the GAO found. “Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans.”
In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events were scheduled that meant large crowds.
While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said the platform were able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.
The other tests had similar outcomes.
For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images.
The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms.
In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.
Tech companies say AI models are evolving
In their responses to the GAO report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined.
Anthropic, in a letter to the GAO included in the report, said that it does not dispute that a determined tester can get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, “and we take the finding seriously.” But it said it's not able to verify the findings in the GAO's report.
Google said the GAO's testing occurred on earlier models, and “we continue to improve our models.”
OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to GAO's findings, “as well as the work that remains.”
SpaceXAI said it “continues to work diligently” to improve safety with each model release.

title: What new automatic enrollment rules mean for your retirement savings
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - The Treasury Department and the IRS have finalized new rules intended to make saving for retirement easier.
The final regulations implement a key part of the SECURE 2.0 Act, which required many new 401(k) and 403(b) workplace plans to automatically enroll eligible employees.
“With the SECURE 2.0 regulations in place, American families will be able to boost their savings and keep more of their hard-earned money through their automatic enrollment in a retirement account,” IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said.
Workers will be enrolled at a starting contribution rate of 3% of their pay, with that rate going up by at least 1% each year until it hits at least 10%, but no more than 15%.
Employees can still opt out or change how much they contribute to their retirement plans.
The new rules will take effect for plan years beginning after Dec. 31, 2027.
The Treasury Department estimated the expanded automatic enrollment could boost retirement savings by an average of $4.2 billion a year through 2032.
“A financially secure retirement is a cornerstone of the American Dream, and every worker deserves the opportunity to achieve it,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
Small and new businesses, government plans, church plans and SIMPLE 401(k) plans are exempt from mandatory automatic enrollment requirements.

title: America’s Affordability Crisis: Excess mortgage costs are holding down borrowers who can least afford it. Here’s what you can do
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
America’s Affordability Crisis: Excess mortgage costs are holding down borrowers who can least afford it. Here’s what you can do
When Chad Cupp was buying a home in 2022, he couldn’t afford to be picky.
Cupp’s $58,000 income and fair credit were no match for a frenzied housing market that wasn’t kind to anyone with limited financial resources. With the help of his co-signing mother and the FHA loan program, he was fortunate to lock in a 4.75% interest rate on a $280,000 home.
And yet, what looks affordable on paper doesn’t always feel affordable in practice. Cupp is now married. But even with dual incomes, his monthly housing payment, which has risen to almost $2,376, remains a significant financial strain.
“You walk this tightrope all the time,” says Cupp, 47, an electrician in Butte, Montana. “Every month there’s something that is not paid or paid late. There’s just not enough [money] to go around.”
Cupp’s struggle is more than a story about one man who’s stretched too thin. It reflects the broader affordability crisis where buying a home is only half the battle. Even if you can break into the high-rate, high-cost housing market and successfully achieve homeownership, you face another uphill climb: affording your mortgage payments at a time when every other expense in your budget might be rising too.
Housing is the largest burden in American budgets — 34% of the average person’s costs go to it, according to October 2026 BLS data. That leaves less money available for anything else. In fact, 27% of adults say they can’t afford all of their bills, according to recent Pew Research Center data that highlights the affordability challenge millions of Americans faced in 2026.
America's Affordability Crisis
Millions of people are struggling with affordability challenges, and Bankrate is committed to highlighting the causes and the best solutions available.
Read more of our work
Adding to that pressure is the Hidden Homeownership Tax, which Bankrate research shows is contributing to 87% of American borrowers overpaying on their mortgages. This surcharge makes homeownership even less affordable, especially for people with lower incomes who are facing a higher-rate environment than Cupp encountered.
For borrowers earning less than $49,000 before taxes, their average overpayment in 2025 was six times higher relative to their income than for borrowers earning $500,000 or more, according to our analysis. And for the largest share of American homeowners — people like Cupp who earn closer to $50,000 or under $199,000 — their overpayment is almost triple that of their highest-earning counterparts.
Cupp, who’s also facing rising property taxes and homeowners insurance premiums, is not alone. Research from the Urban Institute highlights how housing costs have outpaced income growth.
The reality is, the burden of housing affordability isn’t distributed equally: While wealthier Americans have more resources to weather rising homeownership costs, lower- and middle-income homeowners are being crushed by the very asset meant to provide financial security and grow their wealth. Every dollar spent on their mortgages means less money for savings, investments, and just about everything else.
Data: The burden of mortgage overpayment rises as a homebuyer’s income falls
Mortgage overpayment can make homeownership harder to afford for anyone, but the financial burden isn’t just about how much extra borrowers pay in real dollars.
On average, low-, moderate-, and middle-low-income borrowers overpay by $12,580, $18,816, and $30,712, respectively, over eight years, the median period most Americans keep their mortgages. This is much less than the $61,805 paid by high-income borrowers.
Although lower-income families pay less in dollar terms and carry smaller loans on average, these costs take up a larger share of their income.
Source: Bankrate analysis of 2025 HMDA data 
*Figures don’t sum to 100 because of an unknown percentage in the data
Cupp feels the impact of the overpayment burden every day as his income and high mortgage costs constantly collide. He entered mortgage mitigation twice with his lender to catch up on payments. This includes help from the federal government’s Homeowner Assistance Fund, which saved him from foreclosure twice. His experience comes as more homeowners are facing similar financial pressures. Property data firm ATTOM Data Solutions says foreclosure filings in the first six months of 2026 rose 21% compared to the same time last year.
Despite his regrets about buying his home, Cupp vows to do “anything” he can to keep it. The electrician has taken a side job delivering packages for Amazon Flex and fears his wife may soon be forced to do the same. Cupp also enrolled in a payment plan after falling behind on his power bills. The pressure of juggling the mounting obligations also took a toll on his well-being. He says he developed an ulcer because of all the stress.
“I worry about the mortgage every month,” he says. “I worry about being able to pay it.”
Bankrate findings are consistent with…
The U.S. Census Bureau’s 2025 American Community Survey highlights the widening gap between household incomes, rising housing costs, and families’ ability to afford homeownership. The median percentage of monthly household income spent by people with a mortgage rose 21.9% in 2025. Rising mortgage payments are a major driver of that burden, with the median monthly cost rising to $1,598.
Mortgage repayment hits lower-income borrowers harder in these ways, too
Income is a defining factor in how difficult it is for families to manage housing costs and mortgage overpayment in particular. It’s a simple numbers game: a family with earnings in the low six figures — let alone one earning $49,000 — has considerably less room to absorb an additional housing expense than a family earning more.
The sting of closing costs, down payments
Cupp had second thoughts about buying his home well before the ink dried on his signed mortgage documents. The $280,000 purchase required him to dip into his entire $18,000 in savings, and he still hasn’t recovered financially.
His experience reflects a broader problem. The Pew Research survey shows that more than half (53%) of Americans don’t have rainy-day funds and can’t cover three months of expenses in an emergency. For lower-income families — which Pew defines as having adjusted incomes of less than $50,700 — the percentage rises to 77%. This is at odds with the common-sense advice that we should all have three to six months of expenses tucked away for emergencies. For many homeowners, limited savings can make it even harder to keep up with mortgage payments and unexpected expenses that may crop up.
“I always like to have a $2,000 or $3,000 buffer in my checking account,” Cupp says. “Buying a home really took that away.”
Of all income groups, low-income buyers are stretched the most by upfront mortgage costs. Bankrate’s research found a buyer earning $49,000 or less has to come up with about $5,503 in closing costs when buying a home. This is roughly equal to 14.8% of their annual income, the highest burden of any income group.
Source: Bankrate analysis of HMDA data
On top of closing costs, there’s the standard 3% to 3.5% down payment ($5,400 to $6,300) on the average $181,255 purchase loan for low-income buyers in 2025, as reported by HMDA. That means a low-income buyer would need to bring roughly $11,000 to $12,000 to closing, equivalent to 30% to 32% of their annual pre-tax income.
“If 30% to 40% of your income is going toward paying your monthly mortgage costs for a lower-income family, that’s the difference between having an emergency amount of money or wherever else they need to put it,” says the Urban Institute’s Walsh.
This problem isn’t exclusive to low-income Americans. Moderate-income buyers ($50,000 to $99,000) surrender a fifth of their pre-tax annual income to obtain the keys to their home, while middle-income buyers ($100,000 to $199,000) must give up about 14% to 15% of their earnings.
The long-term cost of not being able to buy down an interest rate
Lower-income buyers often face a one-two punch when trying to afford a home. Not only may they have a harder time coming up with the down payment and closing costs, but their limited cash can also leave them paying more on their mortgage once they finally get one.
Lower-income buyers who have exhausted their liquid savings to meet closing requirements may have to forgo discount points that could lower their mortgage rate and save them money.
The same buyers may also be forced to accept lender credits to keep their application from being rejected. Lender credits cover some closing costs in exchange for a higher rate. In 2025, nearly 790,000 low-, moderate-, and middle-income borrowers took lender credits, according to Bankrate’s analysis of HMDA data. Although some higher-income homebuyers accept lender credits to preserve cash, for buyers with limited savings, the trade-off can make purchasing a house today possible but increase costs over time.
Our research also found that over the first eight years of homeownership, mortgage interest and fees consume 31.6% of low-income homeowners’ annual gross income, the highest of all income groups. While the percentage drops as incomes rise, the overpayment still eats up a significant portion of the budget for moderate- and middle-income folks.
For Cupp, the reality of those costs became clear only after he moved into his home.
“You’re just so pumped about being a homeowner,” he says. “Then you have the first mortgage payment, and you don’t really know the gravity of the situation.”
The mortgage insurance penalty behind FHA loans
For lower-income buyers, a FHA loan can be a lifeline in an increasingly expensive housing market. With a 620 credit score that might qualify him for a conventional loan, Cupp believed an FHA loan would give him an even better chance of getting approved for a mortgage. But the same loan program that helped make homeownership possible is the main source of his angst.
According to HMDA data, low- and moderate-income borrowers made up more than half of FHA loan borrowers in 2025. FHA loans are a go-to option for lower-income buyers because of their competitive interest rates, less stringent credit score requirements, and low down payments.
But even with all their perks, FHA loans can make homeownership more expensive over time. It all comes down to two FHA mortgage insurance premiums (MIPs): annual and upfront. Both are designed to protect the lender if you default on the loan.
Annual MIPs are typically paid monthly. If you put down more than 10%, the MIP will automatically drop off after 11 years. But if you put down less than 10%, you can’t get rid of MIP unless you refinance your mortgage or sell your home. An executive order from the Trump Administration in October 2026 directed federal agencies to start a pilot program to proactively cancel mortgage insurance on future loans once borrowers meet the requirements, but no go-live date was announced.
Cupp is constantly reminded of his $180 monthly MIP payment that will stay with him for the life of the loan.
“I should have asked more questions, but it was my first time buying a home, and frankly, I was a fish out of water,” he says.
How much are annual FHA MIPs?
FHA annual premiums typically range from 0.15% to 0.75% of the loan balance, depending on your loan term, loan amount, and loan-to-value ratio. For a loan of $321,475 — the average FHA purchase loan in 2025 as reported by HMDA — the monthly cost could range from $40.18 to $200.86.
On top of the annual MIP is the FHA loan’s mandatory upfront MIP, which is 1.75% of the loan amount. For that same $321,475 loan, that adds an additional $5,626 charge at closing.
Mortgage insurance premiums are the reason FHA loans cost nearly twice as much at closing as conventional loans ($11,954 vs. $6,264, a $5,690 difference), according to Bankrate’s analysis. While you can pay the full amount at closing, nearly all FHA borrowers roll upfront MIPs into their loan balance. This not only increases the amount they owe but also the interest they pay over time.
“A lot of people wrongly think that at least it gets rolled into the loan most times, so ‘it doesn’t really affect me,’” says Alan Silber, a longtime mortgage broker in South Carolina. Silber points out that for someone putting down 3.5%, the cost of MIP could add up to nearly as much as the down payment, depending on the purchase price of the home.
The result? FHA loan or not, homeowners who already earn less may be forced to make financial sacrifices in areas like saving for retirement, building an emergency fund, or paying down debt.
“If you max out a mortgage, even though you are qualified, all these other things are going to take a hit over time,” adds Silber.
The equity drain happening behind the scenes
How to keep your mortgage from eating up a burdensome share of your income
While 87% of homeowners overpay on their mortgage, the stakes are simply higher for lower-income borrowers. There are steps you can take to lessen the blow, and your options depend on where you find yourself in the process.
If you are thinking about buying a home
Don’t let FOMO drive a six-figure decision: If you are concerned that mortgage rates may keep rising as they have in 2026, that shouldn’t be the reason you rush to buy a home now. Before buying, plug in your information into a home affordability calculator. Make sure you can still afford your home even if you lose your income or if property taxes, homeowners insurance, or other expenses rise. If your circumstances are shaky, it might make sense to pause your search and commit to shoring up your finances.
Shop around for your mortgage: When money is tight, your mortgage takes up a large share of your monthly income, and it also impacts what you can afford. Avoid overpaying by shopping around and comparing multiple lender offers. Get at least three quotes from a mix of banks, credit unions, and online lenders. Compare the loan estimates side by side, and ideally on the same day, to help you make an informed decision.
Ask lenders to lay out your options: Don’t assume a specific loan type might be better for you. A loan officer won’t necessarily compare the total costs of a conventional, FHA, or VA loan (if eligible) unless you ask. For example, Fannie Mae HomeReady and Freddie Mac Home Possible loans only require 3% down and $0 in upfront mortgage insurance fees. The biggest purchase you will likely ever make deserves more than a quick “yes.”
Look at the short- and long-term costs: Don’t get roped in by a lower monthly payment, which can sometimes mean paying more over the life of the loan. Look beyond the advertised rate and compare the APR (total cost of the loan), plus closing costs and other fees. How much you will pay over time in interest and other costs should factor into your decision-making. Don’t forget to factor in property taxes, homeowners insurance, and contributions to your emergency fund. Use a mortgage calculator to figure out how much you can comfortably afford.
A rule of thumb is that you shouldn’t spend more than 28% of your gross monthly household income on housing costs. If you have additional debt, your housing costs and debt can be bumped up to 36% of your gross income. But don’t let a rule dictate your finances. Only you know if you can handle all of your expenses, even if your costs fall below the threshold.
Utilize state & local housing assistance: State housing finance agencies are located in every state. They offer down payment assistance, including grants, forgivable loans, and zero- or low-interest second mortgages specifically designated for low-income homeowners. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) can connect you with a HUD-approved housing counselor for free or little cost, who can help you review your mortgage and explain your options.
If you have already bought your home
Contact your lender to discuss mortgage mitigation options: If you are struggling with your payments, don’t be afraid to reach out to your servicer. Depending on your financial circumstances, you may have options, including a mortgage forbearance or loan modification.
Refinance only if it makes sense: Refinancing your mortgage replaces your current mortgage with a new one and could help you lower your rate, make your monthly payments more affordable, remove private mortgage insurance, or change your loan terms. Make sure you run the numbers through a refinance calculator to figure out if the benefits outweigh the costs. Be cautious to avoid forfeiting a low, COVID-19-era interest rate, for example, unless absolutely necessary, as it can significantly increase your monthly payment and overall cost of repayment.
Look into mortgage assistance programs: Seek help early if your payments become difficult. Depending on where you live, non-profits and government agencies may offer free help with property taxes or other housing-related costs. A HUD-approved housing counselor can help you review your budget and identify potential assistance programs.
Even with options available to make mortgage payments more manageable, keeping up with the cost of homeownership can still be challenging. Cupp has benefited from mortgage mitigation but hasn’t pursued other options that might help ease the strain of his expensive mortgage. While he’s grown to love his three-bed, one-bath home, he wishes he’d understood the full costs of homeownership before buying.
“I absolutely would not do it again,” he says. “It’s difficult, and I know I’m not the only one out here struggling.”
-  Methodology To measure how mortgage overpayment affects borrowers across different income levels, Bankrate analyzed 30-year mortgage loan originations from public government records and compared them with matched, competitive offers on Bankrate’s mortgage marketplace as of 2025. Overpayment is the difference in total cost between each loan and its matched offer over the first eight years, the average duration of a mortgage. It accounts for interest payments, upfront lender fees, discount points, and lender credits. From the dataset, Bankrate focused on purchase mortgage applicants in five income groups: low-income (<$49K), moderate-income ($50K to $99K), middle-income ($100K to $199K), upper-income ($200K to $499K), and high-income (>$500K). The objective was to measure the annual burden of mortgage overpayment relative to income across income groups. For each loan, we divided the 8-year expected overpayment by 8 to get the annual dollar overpayment, then divided that by the applicant’s exact reported annual income. The final measure for each income group is the mean of those loan-level percentages. We drew on four sources: Bankrate’s proprietary mortgage marketplace data, the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) loan-level dataset, the Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) and loan-level disclosure data from Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae. Together, these sources allowed us to account for competitive pricing, loan originations, borrower credit profiles and household wealth. To keep the comparison fair, our statistical model controlled for 17 different factors that can influence a mortgage rate.
© 2026 Bankrate.com

title: EVENTS: VUMC annual cookie walk set for Nov. 21, 2026
text:
Vassalboro United Methodist Church (VUMC), at 614 Main Street, is holding their annual Cookie Walk on Saturday, November 21, 9 a.m. – 2 p.m. This is an exciting time for all ages when for $5 folks can take home as many cookies as can be fit inside the container provided. There will be more than two dozen varieties of homemade cookies to choose from.
“Suppahs to GO” will available to purchase as well as homemade canned goods including relishes, jellies, salsa and pickles. Christmas decorations and crafts will be for sale – some made by the VUMC Sunday School children to benefit the John & Celeste McLean Youth Program.
There will also be a food drive during those hours when people can bring donations of food for the Vassalboro Food Pantry Station (VFPS). Cindy Ferland, VFSP director reports that boxed meals (i.e. hamburger helper), cereals, canned meats, tuna fish and soups, and pasta products are among the items needed at this time. A complete list is available for viewing on the VUMC and VFPS Facebook pages. VFPS volunteers will also be there selling crafts to help financially support the mission. “The generosity from the community is very much appreciated and goes a long way to support our neighbors during these tumultuous times of uncertainty,” said Ferland.
Another mission present at the event will be the Vassalboro Ministry Association Fuel Fund, a nonprofit organization that provides Vassalboro families who are in need of fuel assistance.
FMI about this event and other VUMC programs and services visit the VUMC Facebook page or contact vumc.info@gmail.com or (207) 873-5564 or pick up a copy of the Nov.-Dec. VUMC newsletter at the Vassalboro Library, Town Office or Historical Society.

title: WWE Hall of Famer 'Cowboy' Bill Watts dies at 87
text:
WWE Hall of Famer 'Cowboy' Bill Watts dies at 87
WWE Hall of Famer 'Cowboy' Bill Watts dies at 87
WWE Hall of Famer “Cowboy” Bill Watts died on Tuesday at age 87.
WWE announced his passing on X and its official website. Sports Illustrated also reports that Watts’ son, Erik, confirmed that the Hall of Famer died.
Watts attended the University of Oklahoma and played for the Houston Oilers of the American Football League.
His feud with WWE World Heavyweight Champion Bruno Sammartino was memorable.
“Watts was an incredible adversary and inflamed crowds across the country with his villainous persona,” according to the WWE official website.
Watts was well-known as the promoter of Mid-South Wrestling, which eventually became the Universal Wrestling Federation (UWF). Watts later became the executive vice president of WCW. He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2009.
WWE chief content officer Triple H said in a social media post, "Just learned of the passing of "Cowboy" Bill Watts. Bill performed across the United States and Japan, but is remembered for his contributions behind the scenes in various NWA promotions and eventually WCW. His Mid-South Wrestling featured future @WWE Hall of Famers every week, each character having a distinct voice and style ... and for those contributions, he was made a member of the WWE Hall of Fame class of 2009." 
“Watts helped standardize the idea of turning journeyman competitors into grappling mainstays, where fans could get to know their heroes on a more regular basis. He helped implement the idea of hosting televised wrestling on an episodic basis, rather than as rare special events,” the WWE website stated.

title: El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
text:
El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.
Video above: Five years after Haiti's president was killed, trials resume in Miami for dozens accused in the conspiracy
Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.
Gang leader flaunted pool visible by satellite
Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. His so-called Taliban gang, which has a couple hundred members, has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince.
“It is one of the most organized gangs, with the strictest territorial control,” said Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group.
Da Rin said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”
He noted that Jeff’s home was very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been extremely difficult.
Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years.
“In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said.
The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that.
While it has allowed forces to chase after gangs more efficiently, it also has multiplied the number of innocent victims and prompted gangs to retaliate against civilians.
“It is not surprising that gangs would seek to undermine enthusiasm for the arrival of new forces by targeting civilians who have expressed support for security operations,” said Sandra Pellegrini, a senior analyst with Armed Conflict Location and Event Data.
She and Da Rin warned that despite Bukele's attacks against Haitian gangs, one persistent challenge is forces retaining long-term control over territories recaptured from gangs, further placing civilians at risk.
Haitians cheer Bukele's latest hit
Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on Nov. 8, Salvadoran troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He wasn’t killed in the attack.
Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control.
He noted that Jeff and Lanmò San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue.
“He and Lanmò San Jou are arguably the most powerful warlords in Port-au-Prince,” Da Rin said.
Canaan was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there.
The attack comes a day after thousands of Haitians in Port-au-Prince and beyond marched in favor of Bukele, thanking him and his troops for fighting violent gangs.
On Wednesday, Haitians were again celebrating.
“Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesperson in Port-au-Prince. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.”
Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.

title: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
text:
SHENZHEN, China (AP) — President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time that the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin as relations between the United States and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
The U.S. official who confirmed the Trump-Putin meeting in China spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to share plans that were not yet public.
The exact timing of the meeting on Thursday was unclear. Trump already had public plans for a separate meeting with Xi and a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin.
Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin in their joint meeting about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia’s invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump’s aides told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
“I think it’s very close to getting it done,” the Republican president said. “We’re going to have a good meeting on that.”
Trump lands in China’s tech hub as outages cause concerns at home
Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the U.S. public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the U.S. worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
At the start of the second day of Trump’s trip, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump’s behalf. Rubio told reporters there was “zero” evidence that the outages were connected or were tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
“Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you’ve identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption,” said Rubio, who is also Trump’s national security adviser.
Trump is trying to project strength in Asia, but the outages challenge that image
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, reciprocating a gesture by the American leader during Xi’s state visit to Washington in September.
Trump and Xi greeted each other on Wednesday at the foot of the airplane’s stairs in a handshake that became a hug as a group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier in the day, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their long-standing friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It’s a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
As leaders were introduced on Wednesday night before an APEC group photo, Putin approached Trump. They shook hands and traded greetings.
The White House said Trump was scheduled earlier Wednesday to have separate meetings with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney before the official APEC greeting ceremony. Trump has previously voiced his disapproval of the U.S. trade pact with Canada and Mexico that was negotiated during his first term.
Trump has a reunion with old friend Imelda Marcos
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and he complimented Trump for “working very hard.”
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
“Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes,” Trump said. “I love what you’ve done here.”
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the country’s former first lady who is the mother of the Philippines’ current president. Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene.
What’s on the agenda for Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America’s largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease because Trump has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China’s trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world’s dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump’s close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
___
Associated Press writers Darlene Superville in Washington and Jim Gomez in Manila, Philippines, contributed to this report.

title: US and Venezuela sign a deal to reestablish military ties, Hegseth says on visit to interim leaders
text:
CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties that will range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday in Caracas while visiting the South American nation’s interim leaders.
Hegseth touted how U.S. forces in January captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, telling an audience of diplomats and military officials from both countries that now Venezuela “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.”
He also praised the “close cooperation” with acting President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials “to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all,” in a reference to drug traffickers.
Hegseth’s visit, the latest in a series of stops in Venezuela by members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet, underscores efforts by the U.S. administration to deepen its influence in the South American country. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.
Hegseth praises Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
The Pentagon chief praised the energy deal by referencing another major military action by the Trump administration this year — the Iran war. The conflict has disrupted global energy supplies through a critical waterway in the Persian Gulf, raising gasoline prices and contributing to the Republican Party’s severe losses in this month’s midterm elections.
The Venezuela oil deal “makes the Strait of Hormuz a nonfactor for the Western Hemisphere,” Hegseth said at the U.S. Embassy in Caracas.
In the meeting with Hegseth, Rodríguez asserted that the deal enables “the energy development of our nations” and “benefits both the people of the United States and the people of Venezuela.”
Among those in attendance for Hegseth’s speech was Alejandro Betancourt, the owner of North American Blue Energy Partners, the second-largest oil operator in Venezuela. The U.S. government and Betancourt’s company entered into the ambitious agreement to tap Venezuela’s vast oil reserves.
Both the Interior and Energy secretaries also visited Venezuela earlier this year and focused their efforts on tapping its oil reserves and critical minerals. The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.
Hegseth later stopped in Bogota, Colombia, where he was greeted at a military base by the country’s defense and foreign ministers.
Few details provided on the US-Venezuela military agreement
Hegseth offered few specifics on what the military agreement would entail, beyond saying that the two countries’ militaries would be “training together, partnering together, sharing intelligence, more defense equipment and capabilities together.”
Speaking separately, Rodríguez said she hoped the countries’ military cooperation “can be brought to its highest possible level” to allow them to “address common threats.”
Hegseth pointed to Venezuela partnering with the U.S. “to recover its territory from narco-terrorist networks.” The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.
The development comes as the U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump’s return to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.
To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narco-terrorists” in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs or that they have made an impact on the availability of drugs in the country.
Hegseth also used his speech to boast about the military operation that seized Maduro, calling it “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America” that “lasted just 48 minutes.”
“America’s best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours,” he added.
But Venezuela’s ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.
Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader “predicted,” the operation ended with “no war, yes, peace.”
Uncertainty about Venezuela’s political future
Hegseth’s visit also comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.
Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela’s head of state.
Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for “working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela.”
Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by the U.S., which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.
The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.
___
Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Lawmakers weigh where to draw the line as unaccompanied migrant children spend months in federal custody
text:
Lawmakers weigh where to draw the line as unaccompanied migrant children spend months in federal custody
Members of Congress are responding to a Hearst Television National Investigative Unit report that found unaccompanied migrant children are spending months longer in federal custody while officials work to find safe sponsors for them.
The National Investigative Unit and Hearst’s Get the Facts data team analyzed years of federal data. They found the average time children spent in custody rose from about one month to more than six months over the past two years.
The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) is part of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and is responsible for the children while they are in federal care. ORR says stricter sponsor screening is one factor in the increase.
Pediatric experts told the National Investigative Unit that prolonged uncertainty and separation from family can add to a child’s trauma.
Kansas Republican Rep. Derek Schmidt said the debate is whether sponsor vetting has reached the right balance.
"We’ve gone from, perhaps too little scrutiny, to a point where there are now people asking thoughtfully, have we gone to too much scrutiny? I don’t know the answer to that," Schmidt said. "I think it’s a healthy discussion to be having."
A proposed rule would formalize stricter sponsor checks
The debate is playing out as HHS considers a proposed rule that would put stricter sponsor-screening practices into federal regulation. The proposal would formalize standards for acceptable identification, proof of income verification and background checks for sponsors and adults in their households.
Examples of income documents include tax returns, pay stubs and employer verification letters.
ORR says its screening has identified sponsors with histories of child abuse or sex offenses. When the National Investigative Unit asked the agency how many sponsors had been flagged, the agency could not provide an exact count.
"I recognize the data collection in that area may be challenging," Schmidt said, "but I think it's helpful to the public debate about where that right balance is to have as much data as is possible."
Lawmakers disagree on how to speed placements
Maryland Democratic Rep. Johnny Olszewski said the increase in custody time is a concern to him.
"I think every day that we keep a child in custody and away from a responsible adult or loving family member is too long," he said. "And so certainly I'm alarmed by any increase."
The debate also raises the question of whether federal law should set a deadline for placing children with approved sponsors. Massachusetts Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch said he would be cautious about timelines.
"I’m a little bit cautious about asking for a default assignment just because of the clock running out," Lynch said. "That might put a child in peril."
Georgia Republican Rep. Buddy Carter said the process could be reviewed for ways to move faster.
"I'm sure that we can streamline the process and do a better job and cut those days down." Carter said, "Perhaps what we could do is look at some of the checks and balances that are in there, and if they could be tweaked, then we could tweak them to make it more efficient."
Regardless of party or politics, there was agreement that the system needs review — from the sponsor-screening process to the data on the delays we discovered.
"I think this is something I really want to take a close look at, because we should look at all the data," said New Hampshire Democratic Rep. Maggie Goodlander. "We should really look at what the state of play is."
"It's not something I've personally proposed legislation on," Schmidt said. "I have been in a position to convene hearings, but I'd certainly be open to that if the folks who are in those positions wanted to have that discussion."
However, for some, the center of the debate should keep the children’s journey in view.
"They were not brought here by a sponsoring agency, but they were brought here by some element of hope and determination," Massachusetts Democratic Rep. Richard Neal said. "And we should honor that path."
HHS published the proposal in June 2026, and the public comment period closed in late August. The agency has not published a final rule or announced when any final requirements might take effect.

title: A very constructive tsunami
text:
On Nov. 11, 2026, when Scott Colom’s U.S. senatorial victory in deep-red Mississippi was finally called, David Goodman, brother of the late desegregation activist slain in Mississippi by the Ku Klux Klan in 1964, had this to say: “This is not a blue tsunami. A tsunami is destruction for all. This is a spiritual change of heart, and it wasn’t easy and a long time coming. And the people of Mississippi have spoken.”
The people of America have spoken as well. In a state that last elected a black senator in reconstruction times, pre-Jim Crow and David’s martyred organizer brother’s murder, and other flipped Senate and House races, notably in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas and Kansas. Nov. 3 saw unexpected healing tsunamis in numerous state mansions and legislatures as well. Incredibly, Texas was a trifecta, now sporting a Democrat state house — both chambers — and governor. January is right around the corner.
Jon St. Laurent
North Windham

title: Maine Community Foundation testifies in front of the legislature regarding mass shooting funds
text:
Maine Community Foundation testifies in front of the legislature regarding Lewiston shooting funds
Maine Community Foundation said it was clear to people donating online that there were two funds but there was different communication sent to victims.
Maine Community Foundation testifies in front of the legislature regarding Lewiston shooting funds
Maine Community Foundation said it was clear to people donating online that there were two funds but there was different communication sent to victims.
Three years ago, the Maine Community Foundation held a press conference explaining its plans to raise money after the Lewiston mass shootings. Victims have been saying for months that the foundation's plan was not clear to them and they thought they would get 100% of the proceeds, instead of some of it going to nonprofits.
"We launched the Lewiston-Auburn response fund with two components. One to support victims and families and the other focused on broader community needs," Maine Community Foundation President Deborah Ellwood said during a November 2023 press conference launching the fund.
Victims of the Lewiston mass shooting have been pushing back against the Maine Community Foundation for months now, as they believed all the money raised was to be distributed to victims.
$4.7 million of it was, but $1.9 million was given to area nonprofits that were providing support for those impacted by the shooting.
Wednesday morning, at the Government Oversight Committee hearing, foundation officials said it was clearly spelled out that there were two separate funds on the website where someone would donate, but there was different communication sent directly to victims, including a document that said 100% of the money raised would go to the victims.
"Why there were instances on the victim and survivor side of the communications that it was imprecise, that it did not clarify between the existence of those two funds," Rep. Adam Lee, D-Auburn, asked Ellwood.
"What difference do you think that would make?" she responded, which caused scoffing in the room.
"What difference would it make? It makes a difference that people from a shooting were lied to. They were told 100% of this fund was for them, and that is not what happened," Amy Sussman said. Sussman is the aunt of Maxx Hathaway, who was killed in the shooting.
The foundation faced pointed questions and some criticism, for about an hour, before the victims got the apology that they have been asking for.
"This is an error, wouldn't you say?" Sen. Craig Hickman, D-Kennebec, asked Ellwood.
"Yes. I think it was confusing for victims for sure," she responded.
"Do you have anything else to say to them?" Hickman followed up.
"Yes. I'm sorry that they felt confused. And by this particular piece of documentation," Ellwood said.
The Government Oversight Committee invited the Maine Community Foundation to speak, but it doesn't actually have jurisdiction over the foundation because it's a nonprofit, not a government entity.

title: Maine woman burned while smoking and using oxygen tank
text:
An Auburn woman was severely burned Tuesday evening while smoking and using an oxygen tank.
The 74-year-old was sitting on a couch, smoking and using supplemental oxygen, at a Reed Street home about 6:51 p.m. when her clothes caught on fire, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Her 51-year-old son heard a sudden noise and rushed to her aid, helping his mother stop, drop and roll, Turcotte said Wednesday.
The son helped get the flames under control but suffered significant burns to his left thigh and hands.
The woman was taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland because of the severity of her injuries, while her son was treated at Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston.
Turcotte said that oxygen itself isn’t flammable, but it supports combustion, increasing the risk that clothes, bedding, furniture and other materials will burn more easily and intensely.
The Maine fire marshal’s office called smoking and supplemental oxygen a “deadly combination.”

title: LA Athletes and Coaches Receive Top KVAC Awards
text:
Lincoln Academy was well represented in the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference fall sports All Conference awards, with several athletes and coaches receiving top accolades.
The Eagles fall sports teams held their end-of-year banquets to celebrate their fall sports seasons and to name their team award winners.
Girls Cross Country
The Lincoln Academy girls won the KVAC Class B small school division cross country championships on Oct. 17 at Cony High School in Augusta. Cross country co-coaches Garrett Martin and Monique Boutin were named KVAC Class B girls cross country Coaches of the Year for the second year in a row.
Karen Higgins was recognized as the KVAC Class B Runner of the Year. Higgins won her second consecutive KVAC girls cross country championship race with a time of 18:56 at Cony High School in Augusta. Higgins followed that up by winning the Class B girls state championship race with a time of 18:58 at Cony on Oct. 31.
August Miller and Jillian Higgins were also named to the KVAC Class B girls cross country First Team. Annabel Garvan-Soto was named to the Second Team, and Fiona Duffy, Carmella Fraser, Zoe Hufnagel, and Ori Taylor were named to the All Academic team.
The Lincoln Academy girls cross country team awards were presented to Carla Almeida Pena (Breakthrough Award) and Karen Higgins (Grit & Grace Award).
Boys Cross Country
The Lincoln Academy boys won the KVAC Class B small school division cross country championships on Oct. 17 at Cony High School in Augusta. It was the third KVAC championship for the Eagles in the last five years.
Eagles co-coaches Garrett Martin and Monique Boutin were named the KVAC Class B boys cross country Coaches of the Year.
Holden Nehrboss was named to the KVAC Class B boys cross country First Team. Nehrboss placed third in the KVAC Class B championship race and placed 30th in the Class B state championship race.
Wilton Scott was named to the KVAC Class B boys Second Team, and Isaiah Felton and Sebastian Morey were named to the KVAC Class B boys cross country All Academic team.
The Lincoln Academy boys cross country team awards were presented to Thomas McKitrick (Breakthrough Award) and Isaiah Felton (Grit & Grace Award).
Golf
The Lincoln Academy golf team won its first-ever team Class B state championship on Oct. 10 at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro. The Eagles also won the KVAC Shootout championship tournament on Oct. 1 at Rockland Golf Club. Coach Todd Brackett was named the KVAC Class B Coach of the Year.
Colin Mitchell was named the KVAC Class B Player of the Year. Mitchell won the individual Class B state championship by shooting a two over-par 74 on Oct. 10 at Natanis Golf Course in Vassalboro.
Morgan McIvor and Dylan Lomas were each presented with a Coach’s Award at the golf team’s end-of season festivities.
Girls Soccer
Rowan Coffin was named the KVAC Class B South Player of the Year and made the All-Conference First Team. Coffin also earned accolades from the Maine Soccer Coaches Association, who named her to the Southern Class B regional all-star team.
Charlotte Abello, Flannery Brady, LeeAnne Lord, Kylee Parlin, and Lily Pinkham were named to the All-Academic team.
Head coach Lauren Ober presented girls soccer team awards to Rowan Coffin (Most Valuable Player, and Golden Boot Award for most goals scored); Samantha Kopp (Coach’s Award); Ava Larrabee Cotz (Rookie of the Year); Yzze Bhe (Offensive Player of the Year and Captains Award); Natalie Hanna (Most Improved); Dory Westhaver (Playmaker Award); and the defensive unit of Lee Anne Lord, Lily Pinkham, Flannery Brady and Jozie Levensaler shared the Defensive Player of the Year Award.
Field Hockey
Field hockey team awards were presented to James Neptune Benner (Most Valuable Player), Isabel Bathe Oyer (Most Improved Player), and Bella Collamore (Coach’s Award). Head coach Lindsey Herring announced Elise Lupien, Zea Arbuckle, Lily Coleman, and Neptune-Benner will be the captains for next season.
Boys Soccer
Head coach Jeffrey Burroughs was named the KVAC Class B Coach of the Year after leading the Eagles to the KVAC Class B championship.
George Siegel and Peter Norian were named to the KVAC All Conference South First Team. Koleman Chesebro, Siegel, Joseph Crooker, and James Hanley were named to the All-Academic team. Siegel was also named to the Maine Soccer Coaches Association Southern Class B regional all-star team and was selected to play in the Senior All Star game on Sunday, Nov. 15 at Thomas College in Waterville.
Winning the Eagles team awards for boys soccer were James Hanley (Most Improved Player) and Siegel (Register Cup). The Register Cup is given to the player that has had the biggest impact on the program throughout their time on the varsity team.

title: Read the poem ‘My Hundred-Year Flood’ by Abbie Kiefer
text:
This week’s poem, by Abbie Kiefer, recalls a childhood glimpse of an odd and unsettling vessel traveling along a Maine river during flood. I love how this poem’s phrases move across stanzas, river-like, and how it all flows toward an end not definite but liminal, precarious, ever-shifting—a child’s new sense of an unsure world.
Abbie Kiefer is the author of Certain Shelter (June Road Press, 2024), named a 2025 Julia Ward Howe Award Notable Book. Her work is forthcoming or has appeared in The Atlantic, Ploughshares, The Southern Review, and other places. Originally from Maine, she now lives in New Hampshire.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Submit your credits at mainewriters.org/deep-water
My Hundred-Year Flood
On a bridge newly risen
from the current’s rough cover,
we watched the river. Its continuing
urgency. I was just beginning
to feel bored when the Kennebec bore forward
a fridge—that strange craft cutting,
I know now,
toward Merrymeeting Bay. Then on
to the Atlantic, which must take so often
into its cold plenty
something like this—a person’s particular
and once-essential belonging. My parents offered
a name: hundred-year flood.
Not again while we’re alive they said
but at seven, lifetime flared itself
wide like the river carrying
a fridge carrying apples and a jar of mustard
and a wrapped square of cake,
small holes in the frosting
where the candles had been. I didn’t think
of it then—the food, or the forty miles
to Phippsburg, where the river’s mouth
always delivers its truth.
I didn’t know it would return
to me, that slow-sinking Whirlpool,
in my sometimes-
spells of indeterminate sadness.
A metal box in the chop—
it’s how I started to learn
uncertainty. My mother holding my hand
as it went under my feet.
– Abbie Kiefer
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland.
