title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, November 19, 2026
text:
DENNIS N. WITHAM
BENTON – Dennis N. Witham Sr., 80, passed away on Monday, November 2, 2026, following a courageous battle with kidney disease. Dennis was born on June 1, 1946, to the late Audrey and Irving Witham, of Fairfield,. Dennis attended Lawrence High School, in Fairfield, graduating in 1965.
Dennis married the love of his life, Laura Roy, on November 13, 1965. Shortly after his marriage to Laura, he was called to duty where he served in the U.S. Navy for two years. During his time in the Navy, he was on the USS Stickell as a boiler tender, and also becoming a shellback. On January 11,1969, Dennis was honorably discharged, followed by two years of Reserves.
Throughout his earlier years after discharge, Dennis worked various jobs including Sampson’s, in Fairfield. Dennis later followed his late father’s path and was employed for many years at Keyes Fibre, in Waterville. Dennis later went on to work at Statler Tissue, in Augusta. After the closing of Statler Tissue, Dennis went to school at UMA for substance abuse counseling. He was then employed at Seton Hospital, in Waterville, on the detox and rehab floor, before retiring.
Dennis was known by many for his words of wisdom, help and encouragement; helping numerous people along the way. He was also known for his wit, laughter, pranks and he loved to make people laugh.
Dennis was a proud friend of Bill W. and on October 17, 2026, proudly celebrated 50 years of sobriety.
Together Dennis and his wife, Laura, raised four children, Dennis Jr., Bryan, Angela and Jessica. He was a grand-pa to his three grandchildren, Taylor, Riley and Hunter.
Dennis enjoyed many outdoor activities and was an avid hunter, fisherman and trapper. He and Laura enjoyed many summers camping at seasonal sites throughout Maine. Together they enjoyed four-wheeling, driving on backroads and site seeing.
Dennis enjoyed family gatherings, spending time with his grandchildren and telling stories of the olden days.
Dennis had a great sense of humor that he carried with him right to the end; always making his family and wide circle of friends laugh.
He enjoyed going to many short track races and when he could no longer go, he avidly watched them on the television.
Dennis was predeceased by his father Irving, mother Audrey and his sister Priscila. .
Dennis is survived by his wife, Laura, of 61 years; his two sons Dennis, of Winslow, and Bryan, of Boston; his two daughters Angela and her husband Shawn, of Palmyra, and Jessica and her fiancé Max, of Winslow; his two granddaughters Taylor, of Winslow, and Riley, of Benton; his grandson Hunter, of Benton; several nieces, nephews and many cousins.
Visitation will take place at Veilleux Funeral Home, Silver St., on Thursday, November 19, 2026, from 5 – 7 p.m. The service will take place on Friday, November 20, 2026, at 10 a.m., at Veilleux Funeral Home, with the burial to follow at the Veterans Cemetery, in Augusta.
MARGARET S. VEILLEUX
WINSLOW – Margaret “Chick” Susi Veilleux, 81, passed away peacefully, on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Chick was born on October 16, 1945, in Los Angeles, California, the daughter of Guy and Bettijane “BJ” (Maloney) Susi.
In 1963, Chick attended the University of Maine at Orono, where she was one of only two women selected to attend the School of Engineering. Her intelligence was matched by her compassion and her natural desire to care for others. She later worked at The Hilltop School, where she helped support children with special needs.
Chick eventually left The Hilltop School to take on the role she cherished most: motherhood. She devoted herself wholeheartedly to her family and was always there for the moments that mattered. Whether it was a football game, basketball game, cheerleading competition, parent-teacher conference, or simply time spent together as a family, Chick was there.
Chick possessed all the qualities any husband, son, daughter, grandchild, or friend could ask for. She was intelligent, beautiful, kind, and simply a wonderful human being. Her dry wit and facial expressions were unmatched and often said more than words ever could and brought laughter to everyone around her. Anyone who had the privilege of knowing Chick was truly blessed to have had her in their life.
Chick was predeceased by her parents, Guy and BJ Susi; her father-in-law and mother-in-law, Lawrence B. and Adeline C. Veilleux; her brother, Dominic “Nick” F. Susi II; and many family pets.
She is survived by her husband of 57 years, Larry J. Veilleux; her son, Jason R. Veilleux (Natalie Veilleux); her daughter, Margaux V. Holcomb and her husband Robert M. Holcomb; and her grandchildren, Addyson and Lukas Holcomb (Owen West); her sister-in-law, Martha S. Anderson; niece, Abbi S. Beal; nephew, Nate Susi.
A Mass will be held at Notre Dame Church, 116 Silver St., in Waterville, at 11 a.m., on Saturday November 21, 2026. Following the Mass, family and friends are invited to gather for a reception to celebrate Chick’s life.
In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations in Chick’s memory be made to one of the following organizations:
Rheumatoid Arthritis Foundation – Help Fight RA, 8815 Conroy Windermere Rd., Suite 309; Orlando, FL 32835, the Humane Society Waterville Area, 100 Webb Rd., Waterville, ME 04901, or Mid-Maine Homeless Shelter, 19 Colby Street, Waterville, ME 04901
DOREEN M. LARLEE
WATERVILLE – Doreen M. (McCue) Larlee, 89, of Fairfield, Waterville and Millinocket, died peacefully on Friday, November 6, 2026, at Mount Joseph, in Waterville. Doreen was born on November 18, 1936, in Millinocket, to Michael J. and Ina L. (Howard) McCue.
She grew up in Millinocket and graduated from Stearns High School, where she met Bryant Preston Larlee, a boy from the same community who would become the love of her life. They were married in 1958 and in 1961 they made their home in Fairfield, where they raised their family.
Doreen began working at 16 years old at J.J. Newberry’s five-and-dime, in Millinocket, in the women’s apparel department. One of her favorite stories from those days involved her best friend’s father, who leaned on the counter and asked her to “show me your flufferstuffer.” She felt her cheeks glow bright red as she spun around to relay exactly what the customer had said. She went on to work at Belanger’s Market/Drive-In, Keyes Fibre, Mount St. Joseph’s, Thayer Hospital, Larlee’s Market, CMP, Home Phone Service, LaVerdiere’s Pharmacy, the Somerset Motor Lodge, and SAPPI Paper, her many roles included positions in customer service as well as switchboard operating. She officially retired from JC Penney, in Waterville. Still, being a homemaker was always her true joy. She also gave her time to others as a Brownie troop leader creating lasting memories for all.
Those who knew Doreen remember her exceptional heart, her infectious smile, and her love of people. She never did anything halfway and followed through on everything she began. Empathetic and courageous, she was always a fighter for what was right, and when she put her foot down, her Irish spirit shone brightest.
Doreen loved the outdoors. In 1952 she climbed Mt. Katahdin, finishing the climb the morning after roller skating in Brownville until 11 p.m. She treasured summer trips with her family, camping in their Nimrod camper and making many happy memories. When 10-pin bowling came to the area in the 1960s, she and Bryant joined a couples league and won six first-place awards, among many others. Later in life they joined another couples league, where they took on Wii bowling and kept on winning. Her favorite saying was, “Big things come in small packages.”
Doreen is survived by her husband, Bryant; her son, Stephen Bryant Larlee; her daughter, Deborah Ann Larlee.
She was predeceased by her parents; her daughter, Karen Belinda Larlee, who passed at the age of 25 from cystic fibrosis; and her brother-in-law and sister-in-law, David and Jeanie Larlee.
Above all, Doreen will be remembered for her comfort, her warmth, and the way she cared for everyone she met. “I’ll Meet You in the Morning” was a song she and Bryant shared. He often sang it to her, personalized just for her, and it continues to bring him comfort.
A graveside service was held at the Maine Veterans’ Memorial Cemetery in Augusta on November 18, 2026.
Condolences, photos, and special memories may be shared at https://www.svremembrancecenter.com/obituaries/doreen-larlee .
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made in Doreen’s memory to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.
MILDRED C. MUSHERO
OAKLAND – Mildred “Charlene” (Parker) Mushero, 82, died on Friday, November 6, 2026, at home, in Oakland. She was born March 29, 1944, in Waterville, the daughter of Charles and Madeline (Thomas) Parker.
She graduated from Williams High School, in Oakland, and attended Thomas College, in Waterville. For decades she was the office manager, bookkeeper and coordinator of the family construction company, William Mushero, Inc. She served on the board of, and volunteered with, the Humane Society Waterville Area, and later volunteered at Thayer Hospital and MaineGeneral Medical Center. She also opened her home as a foster parent to expectant teen mothers.
She is survived by her husband of 61 years, William “Bill”; her sons, Steve and his wife Yinan, and Adam and his wife Patty; her sister, Kim Parker; grandchildren Jeff, Scott, Cathy, Brittany, and Gregory; great-grandchildren Brock, Wyatt, Dresden and Emma; and her niece and nephew, Kathy and Robert Samuels.
She was predeceased by her daughter-in-law, Dawn.
A funeral service was held Saturday, November 14, at Wheeler Funeral Home, 26 Church St., Oakland. Burial followed at Lakeview Cemetery in Oakland.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Humane Society Waterville Area or Maine Children’s Home.
THOMAS BUCKLIN
WINSLOW – Thomas Bucklin, 61, passed away on Friday, November 6, 2026. He was born to Ralph and Ann Bucklin on November 24, 1964, and was raised in Belmont.
He graduated from Belfast High in 1983. He married Gail Corey in 1990 and they started their life together in Albion.
Tom was a graduate of Word of Life Bible Institute, and Columbia Bible College. He was an active member of Living Water Community Church and Central Maine Bible Conference.
Tom came to know Jesus as a teenager and spent many years at Camp Fair Haven serving the Lord. He loved drives to coastal spots and mountain views alike with his wife Gail, and their loyal dog, Tucker. Tom and Gail owned their own painting & carpentry business together for many years. In their later adventures together, they delivered picnic tables across the state for their daughter and son-in-law’s business, always finding a local diner to try on the way. Tom spent many hours working alongside his son, Will, happily sifting through their antique finds or discussing Camp. Tom and Jess shared a sense of humor and uncontrollable laughter when witnessing any physical comedy.
One of Tom’s greatest joys was his grandchildren, making model planes for their ceilings and endlessly reading books to them.
He is survived by his wife of 36 years, Gail Bucklin; his children Will Bucklin and wife Katie, Jess (Bucklin) Billington and husband Tony.; grandchildren, Thea and Callahan Bucklin, Weston, Avenly, and (coming soon) Conrad Billington; brother, Ben Bucklin and wife Jan; and sister, Marlene Bennett; brothers-in-law, Tim Corey and wife Carolyn, Scott Corey and wife Robin, and Ken Dudley; many nieces, nephews, cousins.
Tom was predeceased by his parents, Ralph and Ann; sister, Linda Bucklin; nephew, Donald Cushman; mother-in-law, Roberta Corey; and sister in law, Jill Dudley.
Visiting hours will be held at Faith Church, on Kennedy Memorial Drive, in Waterville from 5 – 7 p.m., on Friday, November 20. Tom’s celebration of life will be held at Faith Church, on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at 10:30 a.m., with a reception immediately following the service.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Veilleux Redington Lawry Brothers Funeral Home, www.vrlfuneralhome.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made in Tom’s name to Fair Haven Camps, 81 W Fairhaven Ln., Brooks, ME 04921.
JANICE J. ADAMS
WINSLOW – Janice “Jan” Joy Peterson Adams, 92, passed away from a brief illness on Monday, November 9, 2026, at MaineGeneral Medical Center, in Augusta, following a long battle with dementia, spending the last two years of her life in supportive memory care. She was born on April 25, 1934, in Akeley, Minnesota, the youngest of eight children, to Carl A. Peterson and Lilabelle J. Van Ornum.
Janice was a sweet, kind, creative, artistic soul with a deep abiding faith, whose most cherished role was as a loving mother to her five children and devoted wife to her husband. She was proud of her Swedish heritage from her father who emigrated from Sweden as a young man and built a new life in America. Janice spoke fondly of life on the farm where she learned that hard work, persistence and common sense, with a bit of humor thrown in, can lead to a fulfilling life.
Janice graduated from Akeley High School in 1952 and worked various jobs in Minnesota until she moved to Maine in 1954. There she lived with her sister-in-law Pauline while her brother Walter served in the military at a base in Greenland. She worked at the Presque Isle Recreation Center where she met Richard Adams and they married in August 1955. She moved to Maryland in 1956 with her husband when he was stationed at Aberdeen Proving Ground and she worked at the base as a secretary. The couple moved back to Presque Isle upon Richard’s honorable discharge from the military. Janice spent the next 16 years as a devoted homemaker and mother, and oversaw family moves to Augusta in 1968 and Weeks Mills in 1972, a home she loved dearly.
In 1976, Janice was hired as the first secretary to the Guidance Counselor at Erskine Academy, in South China, and was instrumental in developing the position. She was a steady, reliable support to the counselors and students and was recognized for her dedication upon her retirement in 1996.
In her early years she was a trophy winning bowler, and in retirement she enjoyed playing golf. Janice had many talents and was a master at nearly everything she did. She could build it, sew it, cook it, grow it, paint it, embroider it, knit it, create it, and fix it. Her apple pie was award winning and she even designed and built a barn with her daughter Mary Kay! She was a skilled crafter and a beautiful painter. She loved writing letters and designing greeting cards for family and friends. She created incredible scrapbooks for her children that included family ancestry history, which she delved into once she retired.
Janice was a devout Christian who found great comfort as a member of the Weeks Mills Baptist Church and regularly attended worship services. She enjoyed being involved with Sunday School, Bible school, church suppers, writing bulletins, and she could even be found reupholstering a pew or up on a ladder with a paint brush in her hand.
Until dementia made social interactions more difficult for her, Janice was fun loving and outgoing. She enjoyed crafting and having tea with friends and other social gatherings of any size. When her children were young, she thought nothing of piling her car full of kids and taking them all to the lake for the day, or hosting an impromptu pizza party for her children and all their friends. She was the “Kool-Aid mom” to many!
Janice was predeceased by her husband Richard; her parents Carl and Lilabelle Peterson; son Mitchell Adams; brothers Linus, Lewis, Walter “Pete”, Harry “Bud” and an infant brother Calvin, and sister, Ruth Sustad.
She is survived by her children Michele Prince and husband David, Michael Adams and husband Meynard Patascil, Marsha Adams and partner Bruce Wescott, Mary Kay Tisdale and husband Greg; her daughter-in-law Karen Adams; her brother, George “Bob” Peterson; her grandchildren Joel Allen, Benjamin Allen and wife Megan, Travis Adams and wife Tori, Curtis Adams and wife Kim, and Noah Tisdale; her great-grandchildren Ava, Josie, Angus, Hazel and Ethel; and many nieces, nephews and friends.
A memorial service will be held at China Regional Church of the Nazarene, on Route 3, on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at 11 a.m., followed by a luncheon. A private burial to be held in the spring in Chadwick Hill Cemetery, China.
Arrangements are under the care of Plummer Funeral Home, Windsor Chapel, 983 Ridge Rd., Route 32, Windsor. Condolences, photos and stories may be shared through the funeral home website at: http://www.plummerfh.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Weeks Mills Baptist Church, or to the Center for Dementia Research (CDR)
CHARLES E. PULLEN
OAKLAND – Charles Everett Pullen, 85, passed away on Monday, November 9, 2026. He was born April 30, 1941, the oldest of two sons born to Edward and Dorothy (Hutchinson) Pullen.
He attended schools in Oakland and graduated from Williams High School with the Class of 1959. One week after graduation, Charlie joined the U.S. Army and served in Korea with the 7th Infantry Division supporting the United Nations Peace Keeping Force at the DMZ. On his return to the States, he was sent to Fort Hood, Texas, and was assigned to the Second Armored Division as a tank mechanic.
After his discharge, he returned to Oakland to work for his Uncle Horace at the Greeley and Getchell Ford Dealership, later known as Pullen Ford. At the same time, he joined the Oakland Fire Department. He worked his way up through the ranks and was promoted to Chief of the department in 1982. From 1982 until 1992 he worked both jobs as the Fire Chief and at Pullen Ford. In 1992 the town voted to make the Fire Chief’s job a full-time position. So, Charlie left the Ford Garage, following his heart, and became Oakland’s first full-time Fire Chief serving in that position until 2017.
During his tenure as Chief, he was instrumental in having a smaller sub-station constructed on Oak Street so there would be some firefighting equipment on the other side of the railroad tracks, as it was common to have trains block both crossings for several minutes. He was also one of the organizers of the first automatic mutual aid systems between the towns of Belgrade, Oakland, Sidney, Smithfield, and Rome.
Charlie married the love of his life, Donna Lund, in 1970, and together they raised six children.
He is survived by his wife Donna; daughter Susan and son-in-law Flint, son Charles (Chuck) and daughter-in-law Tammy; 14 grandchildren; several great grandchildren;.
He was predeceased by both parents; brother Allen Pullen; daughter Prudi Merrill, daughter Robin Miller, daughter Karen Pullen, son Christopher Pullen; grandson Alex Charles Miller, and grandson Kodi Merrill.
A celebration of life was held at the United Methodist Church, in Oakland, on Saturday, November 14, 2026. A private graveside service will be held at a later date at Lakeview Cemetery, in Oakland.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Oakland Fire Fighters Association, c/o Chief David Coughlin, P.O. Box 187, Oakland, ME 04963.
PAUL E. REYNOLDS
WINSLOW – Paul Edward Reynolds, 79, passed away peacefully on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at his home, in Winslow. Born on December 3, 1946, to George and Leona Reynolds, Paul was a proud sixth generation farmer who spent his life close to the land and community that he loved.
In his youth, Paul was an accomplished athlete and an especially impressive basketball player. Leading his teams at Winslow High School, The University of Maine, and Thomas College, Paul is remembered for his dedication and fortitude on and off the court. He parlayed that love of sports into a love for supporting his children and grandchildren in all of their athletic and artistic endeavors. He was a regular at Winslow High School sports, Houlton football games, UMF basketball games, dance recitals, youth soccer matches, swim meets, and music recitals.
He always showed up. He was influential to not only his family but was a favorite teacher and coach at Winslow Junior High School for many years, remembered always for his wit, ability to connect and engage with students, and for his remarkable deep timbre voice.
Paul married his best friend, Sandra Lee Grenier, on September 14, 1974. Together they built a home full of warmth, music, laughter, and boisterous gatherings where “the more the merrier” was always their motto. Together they enjoyed sunsets, playing cards, sitting around a bonfire, listening to old records and cassette tapes, and being surrounded by family and friends. Though her passing in 2020 was incredibly difficult for Paul, he continued to find community, make new friends, and find joy in spending time with his loved ones. There is some comfort in knowing that the two of them are reunited.
Paul was predeceased by his parents and wife Sandra.
Paul is survived by children, Brian Reynolds, of Houlton, Eric Reynolds, of Winslow, Kris Reynolds and his wife Stephanie Reynolds, of Winslow, Casey Everett and her husband Michael Everett, of Rockport, and daughter-in-law Susan Reynolds, of Winslow; his grandchildren Damon, Noah, Kurtis, Jackson, Lexi, Jason, Matthew, Boden and Cyrus; his brothers Gary and wife Dianne and Timothy and wife Nancy; and his special friend, Barbara Lawe, who brought so much joy to his life in his final years.
The family will receive those who wish to pay tribute to Paul at the Winslow VFW, at 175 Veteran Drive, in Winslow, on Friday, November 20, at 2 p.m., for a Celebration of Life and reception to follow.
In lieu of flowers, the family suggests a donation to the Winslow Basketball Boosters. Checks may be made out to Winslow High School Basketball Boosters and sent to Winslow High School, 20 Danielson St., Winslow, ME 04901.
RODNEY A. BUCK
CLINTON – Rodney A. Buck, 73, of Clinton, passed away peacefully in Augusta, following a long and courageous journey with Lewy Body Dementia.
“Rocky” was born to parents Lloyd Buck and Hilda Nelson Buck, the youngest of their three children. He attended Fairfield schools and graduated from Lawrence High School in the class of 1971. As a child he could be found locking up Fairfield PAL with Mr. McGee most every night. In his neighborhood he was always organizing pick-up games. Rumor has it that he knew the best apple trees in town and swimming pools to cool off in after dark. He was mischievous and a jokester, and always in the middle of things. He was a three-sport athlete, captain of his high school football, basketball and baseball teams. After high school he attended UMA, and then in 1973 joined the U.S. Army Reserves serving for over six years.
He married his high school sweetheart, Marcia, on August 24, 1973. They moved to Clinton and started a family. He began working for Keyes Fibre, now Huhtamaki, that fall and remained employed there for 44 years. He served as a union representative for many years.
He loved raising his two sons and began coaching them and countless others in the Fairfield PAL program through the ‘80s into the ‘90s sharing his love of sports. He served on the PAL Board of Directors for decades and was president, following Dick McGee, until 2020. He was director of the PAL baseball program for 30 years. He was a member of the Waterville Board of Football Officials and IAABO Board 20 Basketball Officials Board for decades, holding offices including president of both and officiating countless tournament and state championship games.
In retirement he volunteered at the Fairfield Interfaith Food Pantry and learned to play Pickleball. He was very patriotic, loved patriotic music, and enjoyed listening to Christmas music. He was a member of the Fairfield United Methodist Church. He and Marcia enjoyed camping at Abenaki in early years and traveling to tropical resorts and several other trips in the U.S. as “empty nesters.” Rocky loved his climbs of Mt. Katahdin, and Schoodic Point and Ocean Point were some of his and Marcia’s favorite places in Maine.
Pinnacles of his life included the field dedication ceremony of the PAL baseball field, now the “Rocky Buck Field” in 2021, and his induction to the LHS Hall of Fame.
He was pre-deceased by his parents, half- brothers George Buck, David Buck and William Foster, and half-sisters Stella Austin, Muriel Flaherty, Shirley Williams and Nancy Hanson.
He is survived by his wife Marcia; sons Jason and wife Jennifer, Travis and wife Tania; grandchildren Jordyn, Sydney (AJ), Brady (Hailey), Luke, Ella and Ethan; and great-granddaughter Sofia; brother Lloyd “Peanut” (Kathy) Buck; and sister Linda (Bob) Gauthier; sisters-in-law Linda Sherrard, Cynthia (Michael) LeClair, and Melissa (Chris) Falcone; and many nieces and nephews.
Visitation will be held Friday, November 20, from 3 – 6 p.m., at VRL Funeral Home, 8 Elm St, Waterville. A fun and upbeat Celebration of Life will be held Saturday, November 21, 2026, from noon – 4 p.m., at the Waterville Elks Lodge, 76 Industrial Drive.
It was a longtime dream of Rocky’s to light up the field. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to PAL Cal Ripken Baseball Field Lighting Project, P.O. Box 334, Fairfield, ME 04937.

title: Survey participants want BRHS to stay in town
text:
Out of 400 people surveyed on Election Day, 82% of Boothbay-Boothbay Harbor residents want to keep the high school in Boothbay Harbor. About 16% (59 people) think consolidation should be explored, and about 2% (8 people) think the school needs to be closed.
Community School District (CSD) school committee members and trustees created this survey to gauge public opinion as they explore future school options. On Nov. 10, the school committee discussed findings and next steps.
Members found that survey participants wanted more information on what consolidation would look like practically and financially. Mike Bartles also noted that many people interested in consolidation gave the caveat that the school should remain on the peninsula. "A lot of people said, 'Yeah, keep the school, but if we can't keep the school, let's look at consolidation if it stays here.' There was sort of a disclaimer thrown on a lot of the time."
Overall, the board felt it was a good initial response and planned more opportunities to gather information.
The future of the Alternative Organization Structure (AOS) governance system was again on the table. As reported in the Register, there are four main options:
1) Stay in the AOS but make improvements.
2) All member schools go separate ways.
3) Reorganize into a Regional School District (RSU), which creates a single board, budget, contracts and policies, but gives up a level of town control.
4) Explore whether an Educational Service Center (ESC) can exist without an AOS. An ESC is a state-created system designed to promote central office efficiency where, in exchange for towns sharing services, schools receive reimbursement funding. Because the schools were already sharing services, AOS 98 added the ESC as an additional layer.
The discussion focused on the latter two options, with concerns raised about how an RSU affects school building ownership, and Kahler explained that an ESC vastly increases the workload for office staff.
"I think if we have the numbers for what a continued AOS structure, what an ESC structure, what an RSU structure looks like, I think that's going to help inform the town," said Chair Jenn Whitney. The committee discussed hosting public workshops.
In other business, Stephanie Hawke expressed concerns about the ongoing revisions of the board's public comment policy. She opposed time or topic constraints, believing that if citizens took time to attend a board meeting, their concerns should be heard.
Vice Chair Tory Paxson said parameters would be in place to handle a large influx of speakers, so everyone has a chance to be heard. "To be really clear, no changes in this policy are about avoiding difficult conversations … It's trying to create guardrails so we can move forward in a way that is productive with public comment. It is not meant to curtail public comment."
It was also clarified that the custom of confining the first public comment to agenda matters and the second to other topics is not in the current policy, but has been standard practice over the past few years.
Suggestions were made to provide a handout outlining policies for participants, such as stating name and town, no vulgar language, and not calling out specific employees or board members.
Discussion was tabled. During the second public comment at the end of the over 3-hour meeting, multiple attendees suggested moving the second higher on the agenda or having it no later than a certain time during long meetings.
During last month's meeting, Tom Perkins asked if his Sept. 8 "yes" vote allowing AOS98 Superintendent Robert Kahler to accept donations for the Boothbay Region Elementary School renovations on behalf of the board could be changed, explaining he felt "coerced" into making the decision unanimous. Otherwise, he'd vote "no" on accepting the Sept. 8 minutes.
At the Nov. 10 meeting, Kahler said a vote couldn't be changed after it was cast after consulting with a lawyer.
“I did feel some amount of pressure to vote unanimously. I went to the board chair workshop, and I didn't see any presentation saying that the board chair should be … exerting any pressure whatsoever on anybody during a vote,” Perkins said.
Chair Jenn Whitney then invited him to discuss her conduct as chair in executive session.
Before voting, Paxson emphasized the importance of approving accurate minutes. "The point is that we're trying to make sure that's an accurate account of what happened in the meeting. That is what we are approving, not whether or not we agree with where a vote went, because that is what this item is about."
The board approved the Sept. 8 minutes; Perkins opposed.
During discussion of the Oct. 13 minutes, Perkins expressed issue with how Whitney presented a Sept. 28 letter from CSD faculty and staff about health, sanitation and Maine Food Code violations caused by the lack of heat/hot water due to the fuel tank issue. He believed the information was unnecessarily delayed in reaching the rest of the board and presented in a deliberately unfavorable way to CSD trustees.
"In my opinion, the person who presented it (Whitney) did so to make the trustees look bad, and herself look good," he said.
"I'm going to take offense to that, Tom ... It was something that the board chair reviews, and I have discretion as to disseminating information," Whitney responded. She again invited Perkins to go into executive session.
The board approved the Oct. 13 minutes; Perkins opposed.
The board did a second read on Temperature Standards for Schools, which defines the optimal environment for teaching and learning between 68 and 82 degrees. This policy follows a new state law requiring districts to set temperature standards. Kahler clarified that the policy will not arbitrarily close the school; instead, it outlines steps the school should take to reduce effects if temperatures go outside the accepted range. The board also held a second policy reading on automated external defibrillators.
Athletic Director Alan Crocker presented a plan to dedicate the court in the high school's Porter Memorial Gymnasium to I.J. Pinkham, in honor of his years of basketball coaching. This would be a ceremonial gesture, with no plans for a plaque at this time. Since CSD trustees oversee the buildings, it would be their decision, but Crocker still wanted to introduce the idea to the school committee. They responded enthusiastically.
So far, Crocker has 14 girls interested in softball, so plans are moving forward for creating a club sport. The club would fill out a form to use the school's facilities, and the school would not be fiscally responsible for busing, uniforms or other expenses. This would be a two-year pilot program to see if the team is sustainable enough to be included as a school sport and added to the budget.
More information about the meeting’s second half, addressing the Dirigo proposal and fuel tank issue, is forthcoming.

title: Mullin faces questions from Congress over flight disruptions, football trip and immigration
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.
The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.
A look at some of the highlights:
Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions
Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.
“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”
Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.
“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.
Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin’s Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.
That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.
Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling
Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.
Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.
Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.
“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.
Mullin defends ground stop response
Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.
The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.
At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn’t giving the public clear answers.
“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success,” Mullin said.
Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny
Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring spree, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The hiring rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.
Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.
The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump’s immigration agenda.
Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths.
“You are killing people,” McIver replied.
“No ma’am. That’s your opinion,” Mullin said, ending the exchange.
Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.
Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.
Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff.
___
Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.

title: Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court over legal protections for Venezuelan migrants
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt an order that would restore deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants.
The emergency appeal comes after a California-based judge found it was unlawful to end their temporary protected status.
The Supreme Court allowed the administration to strip protections from Venezuelans when the case was at an earlier stage last year. If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.
The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorization.
It argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm.”
President Donald Trump has moved to withdraw protections that have allowed immigrants from multiple countries to remain in the United States and work legally, some for decades.
The Supreme Court also allowed the Trump administration to end temporary legal protections for people from Haiti and Syria in June. An appeals court subsequently paused the judge’s decision that kept the program in place for Venezuelans, but that pause is set to expire Friday.
The program known as TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It is granted in increments of up to 18 months.
The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9 and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan, in October.
About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections. After the administration ended TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also ceased to be valid. Thousands of people were subjected to removal proceedings, detained and deported. Many Venezuelans chose to leave the country voluntarily. It is not clear how many Venezuelans who had the protections are still living in the U.S.
——
Salomon reported from Miami.
___
This story has been corrected to remove an incorrect response deadline.

title: Less than one day away from the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, Mainers get an early look
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Less than one day away from the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, Mainers get an early look
Grand Theft Auto VI has a rolling launch Thursday at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S
Less than one day away from the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, Mainers get an early look
Grand Theft Auto VI has a rolling launch Thursday at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S
As the joke goes, we got Grand Theft Auto VI before we got Grand Theft Auto VI.
Fans have been waiting 13 years for the next game in the franchise, and some just couldn't wait until the midnight release.
It's not a new trick, but fans in Westbrook and Scarborough say they were able to play early by changing the time zone on their consoles to New Zealand to start playing on Wednesday.
"The anticipation building up has been crazy," said Asa Farley, a student at the University of Southern Maine. "I know there was a guy that rented a hotel room for a whole week just to play."
"I get videos on my For You Page all the time. Yeah, it looks really good. Graphics are amazing, the gameplay looks sick," said a student at the school.
The game is $79.99 at launch and will initially be out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. There will be no online mode at launch, which some fans say they are waiting for.
The game's ESRB rating is "M" for mature.
According to the sales tracking site Sensor Tower, 17 million copies had been sold as of Wednesday afternoon.
The release will also look different this year. There is no physical version of the game; instead, there is a download code that can be purchased in-store. Staff at the Bull Moose in Scarborough say that means no more returning copies and buying used, which is a large part of their stock.
"It's a little strange seeing a game that's this big have no option for a used market," said Tyler Lepak, who works at Bull Moose.
That also means no long lines for a midnight release.
"I think we lose some of that nerd hype for the new things coming out, when you can no longer show anybody," Lepak said.

title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins US Senate race in Alaska, beating incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.
The Alaska race was the last U.S. Senate contest to be resolved in this year’s midterm elections and gave Democrats a 56-44 majority after they flipped nine GOP-held seats to retake the chamber. The party also won campaigns in other conservative states, including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Mississippi.
In a statement, Peltola said voters sent a clear message that “the status quo in D.C. is not working for Alaska.”
“Over the course of this campaign I’ve spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table,” she said. “Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first.”
Sullivan spokesperson Nate Adams did not respond to a request for comment. Adams had said Monday that the campaign would let the process “run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.” A spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee also did not respond.
As part of the Nov. 3 general election, Alaskans also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, as former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by Trump. The Associated Press has not yet called the U.S. House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich.
Flipping Alaska’s seat was pivotal to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate
Peltola previously held the state’s lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.
In the campaign’s final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent. Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the Nov. 3 election. Peltola denied any involvement.
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats’ behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since The Times’ article was published.
Candidacy of second Dan Sullivan roiled the race
The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with a former Peltola campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year’s open primary and later sought to recant her statements. But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump’s mind. He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October.
The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered. It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit “flagrant corruption.”
The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed. Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election “without unwarranted interference by the United States.” They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska’s ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them.
The Justice Department also confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska’s U.S. attorney would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into.
Peltola finished first in the primary with 49.5% of the vote, followed by the incumbent with 41.4%.
Dan J. Sullivan finished a distant third with about 2.5%, but he advanced to the general election as one of the top four finishers. He was listed on both ballots as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation, while the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Peltola played up her rural roots during the campaign
During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are generally only accessible by air or water.
Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of “Alaska first.”
“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”
The strategy resonated with voters who felt they could relate to Peltola, who is Yup’ik and often spoke about growing up in western Alaska.
“People across the country don’t understand what it means to grow up in a place where there isn’t running water, where there’s only one store, where gas costs $17 a gallon, where heating fuel is not a guaranteed thing, which means that your house isn’t necessarily going to be warm when it’s 50 below zero,” Sam Schimmel, who is Alaska Native, said in Anchorage after Peltola’s win.
“Having somebody who really understands what that means in D.C., representing us in the Senate, is an enormous achievement,” he added and also noted the significance of Peltola’s election as the first Alaska Native in the Senate.
Michael Dunn, also in Anchorage, said he voted for Sullivan but hopes Peltola does well.
“She put in the effort,” he said of her campaign. “So hopefully she puts in the effort in D.C. for us.”
Peltola emphasized affordability issues
“Lower 48” became something of an insult bandied by both sides. Sullivan tried to align Peltola with “Lower 48 liberals” who want to restrict oil and gas drilling, mining and other resource development in the state. Peltola said that while she would work with Trump to get things done for Alaska, “I will never put any Lower 48 politician before Alaskans. That’s the difference between Dan and me.”
Emphasizing her Alaska roots, she spoke about fishing for salmon on the Kuskokwim River with her father and spending parts of the summer at fish camp with her children and late husband, who died in September 2023.
She said the fish and wildlife Alaskans long relied on to fill their freezers for the winter were becoming harder to find. The changes were forcing people to buy more food and other staples at the store — supplies that must be barged or flown in — and deal with “crushing prices,” she said.
Peltola also said she saw members of Congress who were “more focused on their stock portfolios” than helping ease those costs and vowed to push back against the billionaire class.
She will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014.
___
Associated Press journalist Mark Thiessen in Anchorage contributed to this report.

title: Habitat for Humanity’s newest Bangor home goes to single mom priced out of the market
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
Angie Works assumed she’d never be able to buy a home for herself and her 5-year-old daughter on her single income.
But on Thursday, Works, 27, will move into her new house on Grove Street, ending nearly five years of renting since she moved to the Bangor area.
“Nine months ago I never thought this would be possible,” Works said. “This means a future and life-changing stability.”
The three-bedroom, one-bathroom house is the 31st home built by Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor since its founding in 1988. Nonprofit leaders, volunteers and donors celebrated its completion Wednesday afternoon.
Works earns too much to qualify for subsidized housing but too little to buy in a market where prices have climbed nearly 80% since 2019. Her path to homeownership ran through a nonprofit, community college students and more than 135 volunteers, a sign of how few routes remain for buyers like her.
The median sale price of a single-family home in Bangor reached nearly $297,000 last month, according to Redfin, up from $166,000 in 2019.
“I’ve joked with people at work that I’d buy a home when I’m 60,” Works said.
Habitat’s work alone won’t close Maine’s housing gap. The state needs at least 76,400 new homes by 2030 to make up for historic underproduction and meet future demand, according to a MaineHousing study.
Melissa Huston, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Greater Bangor, did not know exactly what the home cost to build, but said it was likely close to its appraised value of $323,000.
“That’s staggering to me, and it’s not hard to understand why for-profit developers aren’t building small starter homes,” Huston said. “The cost of real estate and construction is beyond what they’re able to realize a profit for.”
The house is the 11th Habitat home built with students from Eastern Maine Community College’s Building Construction and Fine Woodworking program. Students built it on campus over the last academic year, including its custom interior cabinetry, Huston said.
After the spring semester, the modular house was moved to the Grove Street lot and set on its foundation in early July. More than 135 local volunteers and professional contractors finished it over the summer and early fall, according to Huston.
The home has 1,040 square feet of living space, plus a full unfinished basement. It’s nestled in Bangor’s Tree Streets neighborhood, a short walk from both Broadway and Chapin parks and several schools.
Habitat pairs homeowners with lenders so monthly mortgage payments don’t exceed 30% of their monthly income, according to the organization’s website. That’s the threshold the federal government uses to define affordable housing.
Bangor Savings Bank was the lender for Works’ home, Huston said.
Works estimated her mortgage payments will be about $200 a month less than the rent on her one-bedroom apartment in Old Town.
The house sits on a double lot that once held a home that was “beyond repair” and had to be demolished, Huston said. Eastern Maine Community College students are now building another single-family home that will go next door.
“We love the idea of infill housing,” Huston said. “We’re focusing on what other developers aren’t doing — affordable starter homes in Bangor.”

title: Video shows lifeguard charging into rough waves to save swimmer in act of bravery
text:
Video shows lifeguard charging into rough waves to save swimmer in act of bravery
A California lifeguard made an impressive rescue as waves reached several feet high over the weekend, and the moment was captured on video by a beachgoer on shore.
The unidentified man was saved from rough ocean waters at La Jolla Shores Beach in San Diego, California, on Saturday, after he was spotted swimming alongside a seal.
The lifeguard, Griffin Houldin, told NBC News that he dove in behind the man as the water became increasingly aggressive.
"We got pulled back 5 to 10 feet every wave, and they just kept coming," Houldin told the outlet. "All I was trying to do was stay in this current here and fend off the rocks for as long as possible."
The video shows Houldin swimming out to reach the man as both are repeatedly engulfed in waves. A second lifeguard arrived on a jet ski and pulled them both to safety.
Jamie Rea, who posted the video on social media, called the lifeguard's effort "an incredible act of courage," according to the San Diego Union-Tribune.
"What could have ended in tragedy became a story of hope, bravery, and a life saved," she told the newspaper through a text message.
CNN contributed to this report.

title: Video shows pregnant US citizen pepper-sprayed and detained by ICE agents
text:
Video shows pregnant US citizen pepper-sprayed and detained by ICE agents
A pregnant woman says she was pepper-sprayed and detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents during a protest outside a California jail on Sunday afternoon. The incident was captured on video.
See video of the incident in the player above.
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, seen in the video wearing a blue sweatshirt, said she went to the Stanislaus County Jail to protest ICE after hearing reports of its presence in the area. She said her husband recorded the video, which shows ICE agents attempting to remove a man from a minivan in the jail parking lot.
"My friend had parked in the parking lot, and she'd seen that there was someone walking from the jail, and she offered him a ride," Vargas Andrade said. "She was like, 'We can give you a ride if you want,' and she was driving off down the street, and that's when they all pulled her over. There were like five ICE cars."
At the beginning of the video, Vargas Andrade is seen in the background with two ICE agents. About a minute into the video, she is seen on the other side of the vehicle, yelling at one of the agents and following him closely around the vehicle. The video appears to show the agent turning around to detain her.
"Lizbeth was tackled by ICE, was forced to the ground on her belly, she was pregnant, she was pepper-sprayed in the face," said Patrick Kolasinski, Vargas Andrade's attorney.
The video also captures Vargas Andrade's husband yelling at the agents, telling them she is pregnant.
Vargas Andrade said she was taken to an ICE facility in Stockton, where she was held for several hours, denied a medical exam, and prevented from contacting her attorney. She said she was released around 8 p.m. on Sunday and later cleared by a hospital, where she confirmed her baby was unharmed.
"This was something I never expected, especially from ICE agents, and knowing that I'm a United States citizen," Vargas Andrade said. "I was using all my rights to protest and to record and show everybody in the world what was going on, but unfortunately this did happen. And being pregnant, my first thought was my baby, my kids, what was going to happen."
Kolasinski said it is too early to determine whether legal action can be pursued against ICE but expressed relief that Vargas Andrade is safe and back home.
ICE said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon that the incident happened during the arrest of a man from Mexico who had entered the country illegally at an unknown time. The man had been charged with multiple DUIs and accepted voluntary return, according to the agency.
"During the arrest, a female individual actively interfered with, obstructed, and attempted to prevent the arrest - a federal crime," ICE said. "Our ICE officer relied on his training to safely control the situation despite the combative, aggressive, and heinously vulgar conduct of the woman interfering with his lawful duties. The individual immediately received medical care and was transported to the San Joaquin General Hospital for medical evaluation."
"Obstructing law enforcement is a federal crime and assaulting law enforcement is a felony," the statement continued. "ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers. Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training, and they are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct."

title: Troy Jackson’s victory could transform rural healthcare in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kristina Smith, LMSW, is a senior policy analyst at Boston University School of Public Health. She lives in Portland.
Mainers have spoken and we have chosen Senator-elect Troy Jackson to lead the effort toward a better healthcare system here and across the country.
Whether you’re a first-time mother on the Midcoast or an older veteran in the High Peaks region seeking specialty care, access to healthcare affects us all. And as one of the most rural states in the country, with the oldest population, Maine faces growing healthcare demands that are putting greater strain on an already challenged system.
Now, Senator-elect Jackson has the opportunity to deliver the improvements rural Mainers have been waiting for — something his predecessor Sen. Susan Collins fell short on in her five terms in Congress.
Rural Maine communities have long struggled with a variety of healthcare challenges. Hospitals in Aroostook, Washington and Hancock counties have faced financial pressure from high operating costs and low insurance payments from Medicaid and Medicare, putting 25% of Maine hospitals at risk of closing.
Rural hospitals rely heavily on these reimbursements, which often don’t cover the full cost of care, making it difficult to keep essential services, like emergency care, running. At the same time, more than 50 nursing homes and residential care facilities have closed since 2014, and over 10 hospital-based labor and delivery units have shut down.
These closures mean longer drives for families seeking care and fewer home healthcare options for older adults and people with disabilities who depend on them to stay independent. Access to other basic services is also shrinking, with nearly half of Mainers living in areas with limited pharmacy services.
Workforce shortages further limit access to care, with 15 of 16 Maine’s counties lacking enough primary care, mental health and dental providers. As the older generation of providers retires, rural communities have difficulty finding qualified replacements, competing with larger and more urban areas like Portland.
Long travel distances, limited public transportation and poor roads also make it harder for rural Mainers to reach specialists and emergency services. This is especially tough for veterans, who make up roughly 10% of the state’s adult population. Those living far from the Togus Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Augusta may struggle to get regular and consistent follow-up care.
These longstanding issues highlight the need for urgent reform. The question now is, will Jackson deliver?
While Jackson doesn’t have the five-term record of Collins to provide a roadmap for his time in the Senate, he’s provided hints as to how he plans to continue to address the concerns of rural Mainers.
Throughout his campaign, Jackson emphasized that healthcare should be a basic right, not a privilege. His top priority is passing the Medicare for All Act, to expand coverage to medically necessary services and prescription drugs and eliminate out-of-pocket costs (e.g., copayments, deductibles, coinsurance) that prevent Mainers from getting the care they need.
Medicare for All or similar legislation would expand access to care for so many rural Mainers who currently struggle to pay for services and medicine. But even with Democratic majorities in both the House and the Senate come January, it would have a long and challenging path toward passage.
Jackson has also committed to signing on to the Keeping Obstetrics Local Act to help keep birthing centers like Miles Labor & Delivery open and adequately staffed. Additionally, he plans to fight to reverse nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts enacted through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (originally supported by his predecessor), to restore federal funding that rural hospitals depend on.
Jackson’s 20-year career in the state legislature, which includes six years as Senate president, gives him a solid foundation to continue improving rural healthcare for Mainers. During that time, he introduced legislation to lower prescription drug costs, expand access to generic medications and attract more healthcare providers to rural, underserved areas.
He also sponsored laws creating a Prescription Drug Affordability Board, allowing Maine to import lower-cost prescription drugs from Canada. Additionally, he helped secure funding for both rural hospitals and ambulance services.
That record points to a senator-elect who understands that Mainers and the broader American people are struggling to access, pay for and choose their healthcare.
Jackson’s victory represents hope and a chance to address longstanding gaps in the state’s current healthcare system. His success will depend on turning campaign priorities and a record of state-based action into measurable improvements in affordability, access and quality of care.
As Mainers, we should be optimistic about Jackson’s clean slate while continuing to make rural community needs heard. The election is over, but the work is just beginning.

title: Outkast rapper Big Boi reels in a big fish! A 200-pound striped marlin, to be exact
text:
(Gray News) - Rapper Big Boi reeled in a huge striped marlin while reportedly deep-sea fishing in Mexico.
The Grammy-winning rapper, whose real name is Antwan André Patton, took to social media over the weekend to share his enormous catch, a reported 200-pound striped marlin.
The rapper said he was able to reel in the fish after nearly an hour-long battle.
“Catch of the day ... striped marlin … 99 inches, 200 LBS!!!," Big Boi shared in the caption of his post. “Took me 50 minutes to get him in the boat!”
In a video shared by the rapper, the enormous fish can be seen launching itself out of the water as crews worked to bring it alongside the boat.
Big Boi’s catch came last Saturday during a reported deep-sea fishing excursion near Cabo San Lucas.
A second video also showed the 51-year-old Atlanta native standing next to the massive striped marlin at a marina, where the enormous fish could be seen hanging by its tail.
The rapper shared that he planned to have the marlin mounted and shipped back to Atlanta while also noting that the fish’s meat would be donated to help feed families.
Big Boi is best known for his work as being a part of Outkast with fellow rapper André 3000. The hip-hop duo launched the group in 1992 while attending high school in the Atlanta area.

title: Girl, 11, sentenced for rape, assault of 5-year-old
text:
CLEVELAND (WOIO/Gray News) - An 11-year-old Cleveland girl has been ordered to spend at least seven years in the juvenile system for her role in the attack on a 5-year-old girl.
Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court Judge Kristin Sweeney found the 11-year-old, identified in court as M.H., delinquent on nine charges that included attempted murder, rape and felonious assault.
Sweeney said the 11-year-old girl could remain in the juvenile system until she turns 21.
Attack and trial
Cleveland police said the 5-year-old was attacked Sept. 13, 2025, in a field near East 148th Street and St. Clair Avenue. Her mother found her injured, and she spent several weeks in the hospital.
During the trial, the judge heard testimony that the girl had been strangled with her own shirt. The girl’s mother testified about the effect of the attack on her daughter.
“When we left the hospital, she went through severe behavioral changes. She kept saying she’s not pretty anymore. She kept saying earth is a bad place,” the mother said.
Second child’s case
A second child, a 10-year-old boy, pleaded guilty to attempted rape and felonious assault on Sept. 28. He testified during the trial, with his disposition hearing scheduled for Dec. 3.
Case background
The Cleveland Division of Police Sex Crimes and Child Abuse Unit investigated the case.
In October 2025, prosecutors charged the 11-year-old girl and then 9-year-old boy with attempted murder, rape, felonious assault, kidnapping and strangulation.
On April 1, Sweeney ordered the two children to undergo competency restoration before they could stand trial.
According to court records, a change in the 11-year-old’s placement was necessary to get a true assessment of her competency.
When a placement was not found, prosecutors requested she be held in the detention center during the restoration process.
The court said returning to her home was not in her best interest, and the Court Diagnostics Clinic provided competency restoration services at the detention center.
Both children were previously held on home detention.
After a period of court-ordered rehabilitation, the children were later found competent to stand trial.

title: Man, 50, allegedly stabs another man to death at party celebrating his release from prison
text:
HOPKINS, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) - Authorities in South Carolina say a 50-year-old man is facing charges after he allegedly stabbed another man to death at a party celebrating his release from federal prison.
Cedrick Cunningham, 50, was charged Monday with murder and possession of a weapon during a violent crime, according to the Richland County Sheriff’s Office.
Cunningham is accused of killing 42-year-old Andre Smith, who was found dead in a car Saturday in Hopkins. Deputies say Smith had a large laceration on his chest.
According to authorities, Cunningham was at a celebration held after his release from federal prison when he and Smith got into an altercation. That allegedly led to Cunningham stabbing Smith.
Deputies say Smith then got in his car and fled the area.
Cunningham was being held at the Alvin S. Glenn Detention Center, as of Tuesday.
Suspect’s criminal history
Details of Cunningham’s reported release from prison were not immediately clear, but federal records show he was sentenced to 10 years in 2019 after pleading guilty to a weapons charge.
Other documents from his case note that prior drug convictions qualified Cunningham for status as an armed career criminal under the federal Armed Career Criminal Act.
Documents also show that a judge denied a request for compassionate release made by Cunningham in 2023.
A search of the Federal Bureau of Prisons website shows that Cunningham was located at the Residential Reentry Management office in Raleigh, North Carolina.

title: Investigators reclassify 1975 disappearance of Washington, Maine man as homicide

Disappeared after being dropped off
Belanger, then 25, disappeared after being dropped off to go deer hunting in the woods near his home on Route 105 in Washington.
His wife, Linda Perkins, said he was going out for an hour or two. He never returned home.
New technology and the investigation
Officials said new technology helped investigators uncover leads, evidence and a person of interest in the 51-year-old case.
During the investigation, detectives traveled to multiple towns and states to conduct interviews and search wooded areas, bodies of water and wells. Belanger’s body has not been found.
Case remains open

title: Family of Ecuadorian killed in New York building collapse receives his remains
text:
QUITO, Ecuador (AP) — The remains of one of two Ecuadorian construction workers killed when a building collapsed into an adjacent pit that was being excavated in New York were returned Wednesday to his home in Quisapincha, high in the country’s central Andean region.
Relatives received the body of José Caguana, 26, in the rural town’s Bahía neighborhood, where his friends and family cried together as mournful Andean melodies played from a speaker.
“So this is how it ends — to leave in search of a better life and come back as a corpse,” one of relatives, Segundo Caguana, told Quisapincha TV, his voice breaking with emotion.
Gabriel Sigüenza, 22, also died in the collapse in Brooklyn, and his remains were expected to arrive Wednesday night in the port city of Guayaquil before being returned to his family in Cañar, in Ecuador’s southern Andes region.
The Ecuadorian government paid for the repatriations, a foreign ministry statement said.
Tens of thousands of Ecuadorians have migrated to the United States without authorization in recent years, seeking work as their country struggles with recurring economic and employment crises and rising violence.
New York authorities said the collapse of the three-story building next to an excavation site killed eight people, including some from Ecuador, Mexico, Guatemala and Trinidad.
The collapse remains under investigation. City officials said authorities had determined that the demolition of the previous building lacked adequate safeguards, and court records show the construction company faced two lawsuits accusing it of damaging adjacent buildings in other projects. The building that collapsed also had a record of safety violations.

title: Decades-old Knox County missing person case deemed a homicide
text:
A 25-year-old hunter who went missing in the Knox County woods 51 years ago was killed by a person who is now dead, according to new information from Maine State Police’s Unsolved Homicide Unit.
The investigation into Ludger Belanger’s disappearance is still open, but police announced Wednesday that the person believed to be responsible for his death is deceased, “and therefore prosecution is not possible.” Maine State Police did not identify the suspect.
Belanger went missing in 1975 after he was dropped off to go deer hunting in snowy woods near his home along Route 105 in Washington. The father of three young daughters told his wife he’d be back by noon, the Kennebec Journal reported in 2015. He never made it home.
He was formally declared dead in 2001 by a Knox County probate court judge, at his wife’s request.
Police reports point to a few suspects and theories about how Belanger died, including a gunshot after a confrontation over a deer, according to the Kennebec Journal. His widow, Linda Perkins, told the paper that she knew the names of two suspects.
State police did not say how Belanger died and added Wednesday that they will not release more information about the case. Throughout the decadeslong investigation, police say they uncovered multiple leads, with new technology and interviews helping detectives identify the homicide suspect.
Detectives will continue searching for Belanger’s body.
“This case remains open to pursue leads to the location of Ludger Belanger’s body so that his family might bring him home,” state police spokesperson Lt. Aaron Turcotte said in the news release.

title: Cornyn blocks top Justice Department official nominated for judicial vacancy in Texas
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A senior outgoing Republican senator said Wednesday that he will block one of President Donald Trump’s final judicial picks for a court vacancy in Texas, as the GOP-led Senate scrambles to fill all the remaining vacancies in the federal courts before Democrats assume power in January.
Texas Sen. John Cornyn told The Associated Press that he has not returned the “blue slip” for Elliot Gaiser, a top official at the Justice Department who was nominated for the Dallas-area vacancy earlier this month, nor does he plan to. A “blue slip” is effectively a permission slip from home-state senators that allows judicial nominees to advance in their confirmation process, and it gives senators tremendous veto power over a president’s court picks.
“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn said in an interview on Wednesday. “This is part, of course, of the constitutional responsibility of senators in the Senate to provide advice and consent. But it’s hard to provide advice and consent when there’s zero consultation, which happened in that case.”
Cornyn also said the White House has requested information about his preferred candidate, Fort Worth lawyer Steve Fahey. The senator said he did not know whether Gaiser would be formally withdrawn.
“He’s a very bright young man, and I think has a very bright future,” Cornyn said of Gaiser. “I kind of feel bad that he’s been used basically as a pawn in this process.”
The senator stressed that he did not want to leave the court seat vacant. Fahey served in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas from 2003 until 2021, and was a partner at Kirkland and Ellis until starting his own firm in 2024.
Gaiser, who leads the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, was first contacted by Texas Sen. Ted Cruz’s staff about becoming a federal judge on Nov. 4, the day after the election, according to his nominee questionnaire sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee. Cornyn has repeatedly raised concerns about his nomination process, noting that he has not been vetted by a bipartisan federal judicial evaluation committee that is traditionally used in Texas.

SHENZHEN, China (Gray DC) - The leaders of the U.S., Russia and China will meet for a trilateral summit for the first time.
President Donald Trump was greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Shenzhen Airport on Wednesday. Trump and Xi will be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for the trilateral summit.
Nuclear arms control is Trump’s top priority for the summit. He wants to secure a deal that would lead the U.S., Russia and China to reduce their nuclear stockpiles.
Russia’s war in Ukraine, which will soon mark its five-year anniversary, could also be on the agenda. Trump has not been able to end the conflict despite repeated efforts.

title: Standard-offer electricity supply prices to rise in Maine on Jan. 1
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -Many Mainers will pay more for electricity supply starting Jan. 1 after the Maine Public Utilities Commission selected suppliers for next year.
What customers will pay
For the average standard-offer residential customer, the increase is about $4.99 more a month for CMP customers. For Versant customers in the Maine Public District, it is about $2.30 more a month.
Why prices are rising
“The biggest factor in Maine and all of New England is the price of natural gas,” said Patrick Scully, chair of the Maine Public Utilities Commission.
Scully said limited pipeline capacity and global factors, including the Iran war, push up gas prices.
National think tank Third Way projects a Maine household electricity bill could total about $951 from November through March.
How suppliers are chosen
The commission chooses standard-offer suppliers through competitive bids.
“Well, we’re satisfied that it was a competitive process and that these were the best prices that we can get,” Scully said. “Obviously, we’re never happy to see prices go up.”
About the standard offer
The standard offer is the default supply option for customers who don’t choose a supplier. Delivery is a separate charge.
CMP and Versant bill on behalf of suppliers. They don’t play a role in setting the supply price.
The commission will choose suppliers for Versant’s Bangor Hydro District standard offer Wednesday.
