title: Damariscotta hit-and-run suspect previously sentenced to 60 years for Maine murders
text:
A Rockland man accused of a hit-and-run crash that seriously injured a 65-year-old bicyclist earlier this month was previously sentenced to 60 years in prison for the murder of two Sanford convenience store clerks.
John Barczak, 67, was released from prison in March 2024, decades before his sentence would have ended, after earning time off for taking part in work programs, according to Jill O’Brien, spokesperson for the Maine Department of Corrections.
Less than three years later, he was charged with elevated aggravated assault and leaving the scene of a crash that sent a Bremen woman to Maine Medical Center in Portland.
Barczak allegedly fled after crashing his red Toyota Tacoma into Jaja Martin on Nov. 4 in Damariscotta. He also faces a charge of reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
Barczak was taken back into custody after the crash and posted $25,000 bail following his arraignment, according to court records, which note that he is currently under house arrest.
In January 2024, two months before his official release, Barczak was out of prison and struck a deer in South Thomaston, according to state crash records. O’Brien declined to comment on how Barczak was free at the time, saying that information is confidential.
His prison sentence stemmed from the June 1987 murders of Evelyn M. Meyer, 21, and Dawn L. Denny, 26, who worked as clerks at the Lil’ General Store in Springvale, a village within Sanford, according to Bangor Daily News archives.
Barczak, who was 28 at the time, pleaded innocent by reason of insanity. He told police he had drunk 12 beers before the shootings. During his jury trial, a psychiatrist testified that Barczak’s more than decade-long drug and alcohol use had left him with brain damage.
Barczak told police he argued with Denny at the store, went home to retrieve his gun and shot the pair when he returned. He said he initially intended only to scare Denny with the gun but ultimately decided to shoot the clerks.
Barczak was featured in a 2004 New York Times article about felons in Maine and Vermont who are allowed to vote while incarcerated. He told The Times he had voted in every election since he went to prison, describing himself as a moderate independent who was worried about the Iraq war, the economy and the Supreme Court.
He was being held at Maine State Prison, a maximum-security facility in Warren, at the time of the interview.
Martin required several surgeries and is now recovering, according to The Lincoln County News. She told the weekly newspaper that she looks forward to getting back on her bike.
Martin did not immediately respond to a Facebook message from the BDN on Wednesday morning.
“Her injuries were extreme and very severe,” Martin’s lawyer, Lauri Boxer-Macomber, told the BDN on Wednesday. “It’s an example of why people need to be paying so much more attention and [be] aware of who else is on the road.”
Police traced the truck through grille fragments left at the scene and surveillance footage from nearby businesses. That afternoon, police found Barczak’s truck, with matching front-end damage at Hagar Construction where he works, according to a probable cause statement filed in the case.
Barczak admitted to Damariscotta police Officer William Smith that he was driving when he struck Martin, Smith’s statement said. Barczak told the officer he initially thought he had hit a deer, but then saw a reflective vest and realized he had struck a person. He “became scared about returning to prison, which was why he left the scene,” Smith wrote.
Barczak is scheduled to appear in court on Jan. 4.
Peter Rodway, Barczak’s lawyer, was not available for comment Wednesday morning when contacted by the BDN.
BDN writer Daniel O’Connor contributed to this report.

title: Rubio says ‘zero’ information that recent outages in US are linked or related to each other
text:
MANILA, Philippines (AP) - Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the cascade of service outages, which snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications, are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Donald Trump and they prepared to leave the Philippines for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the tech hub of Shenzhen, China.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.
In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for disruptions — and even staunch Trump allies have accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage on Tuesday.
“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila, declaring that “things like that happen.”
But as concern mounted, Rubio appeared to publicly address American worries from the other side of the world.
There has been a steady stream of outages this week
Trump’s nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages was an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
The series of outages began Thursday, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade.”
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related.”
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
Trump’s nonchalance was not shared by some of his allies
Earlier Tuesday, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.
“What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. Later on social media, she praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.
“Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyberattack incident,” Clayton said, explaining that the U.S. government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump’s Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical of the lack of information from the federal government.
“Americans aren’t stupid,” she posted on social media. “We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”
Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, voiced similar concerns.
“Someone high in the administration needs to get on TV and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” McCain, who is also the daughter of late GOP Sen. John McCain, wrote on X. “No one who lived through COVID is believing this is all a coincidence.”
After Trump and other administration officials failed to offer reassurance on those cascading tech problems, Rubio seemed to take on the role of reassurer-in-chief when he appeared unexpectedly in Manila to take questions. The secretary of state is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, though he lately has declined to comment on whether he would consider a campaign to try to succeed Trump.
But Trump’s role in the immediate moment was a pressing concern, even for supporters in his Make America Great Again movement.
“Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack,” Laura Loomer, a right-wing personality known for her incendiary social media presence, wrote on X. “President Trump should come back to the United States.” She did not present any evidence of an attack.
Conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer, writing on X, demanded accountability. “And why does it feel like we’re being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?” she said.
___
AP writers Aamer Madhani in Washington, Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., and Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa contributed to this report.

title: Psoriasis later in life is more than a dry patch — how to treat flare-ups
text:
(Aging Untold) — Psoriasis can develop or flare later in life, and it can show up as more than dry or irritated skin.
Some people notice scaly patches, redness, itching or nail changes such as pitting, discoloration or lifting.
It’s an immune condition, not just a skin condition
“Psoriasis can occur at any age, and it really is not a skin condition. It really is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Swollen or tender joints alongside a rash are a signal to look further.
“Then you have to start thinking further, because it is a clue that you have some systemic inflammation going on underneath, and it is systemic,” Rogers said.
What can trigger a flare
Rogers said genetics play a role.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck has lupus and shared that two of her children have psoriasis. One also has psoriatic arthritis.
“When you have autoimmune diseases already in your genetic history, you have a predisposition, and then something triggers it. Then the inflammatory response takes off, and there you go,” Cradduck said.
Rogers listed stress, infection, skin injury and certain medications as triggers, including beta blockers, lithium and antimalarial drugs.
Cradduck compared stress-related flares to breakouts before a big event.
“That same kind of stress that was causing that can cause these kind of flares in someone with autoimmune,” she said.
Getting sick can also cause a flare because the immune system is already not regulating properly.
Rogers said psoriasis also increases the risk for cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
“So it’s a serious thing that’s telling your body you’re susceptible to some other things,” Rogers said.
Looking at the whole picture
Rogers said traditional and functional medicine play an important role in treating autoimmune disorders.
“I like to say it’s not traditional or functional. It really is integrative,” Rogers said. “If you can understand treating autoimmune disorders, you want to look at nutritional deficiencies and hormonal imbalances and GI infections and cortisol and stress and toxins. All those things play a role.”
She said the goal is not simply to suppress the immune system.
Treatment and when to get help
For daily skin care, aging expert Amy O’Rourke offered direct advice.
“The long, hot shower? Not so much. Use the moisturizer. If you get an infection, get to the doctor right away,” she said.
O’Rourke suggested the National Psoriasis Foundation as a resource.
“I would want people to go there and read up to really enhance their strategy to approach this issue,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck said her daughter has had good results with a cream from her doctor and has not had a flare in some time.
An active flare needs treatment, Cradduck said.
“When you have a flare and you’re active in it, you do have to get that treated and taken care of, because it’s not going to just go away on its own,” she said.
Rogers also cautioned against assuming that skin changes later in life are psoriasis.
“Don’t just think, ‘Oh, it’s psoriasis.’ Now you have to look at other things, like maybe a fungal infection, or are you having a reaction to medicines?” Rogers said.
If joints are involved, Rogers said the search should go beyond a dermatologist.
“Once it becomes no longer a skin disorder, this is a systemic disorder,” Rogers said. “If you have one autoimmune disorder, you have others. Go to someone who knows how to look for it.”
Know your triggers and your treatment
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose encouraged viewers to stay curious about what their bodies are signaling.
“Don’t just stay in judgment thinking you know what it is, or it’s only this or it’s only that, because it’s definitely feedback that your body’s giving you,” Ambrose said.
Rogers urges people with psoriasis to pay attention to things that trigger or worsen it, because those will be different for everyone.
Cradduck said approaches that may help include meditation, de-stressing, medications and oatmeal baths.
Resource
The National Psoriasis Foundation is a nonprofit psoriatic disease research organization.
The website has resources on causes and triggers, treatments, diet and lifestyle information and more.
Key takeaways
- Psoriasis is more than skin deep. It is a sign of immune system inflammation that appears through the skin and nail beds.
- Don’t self-treat or assume. Later-in-life skin changes can have other causes, such as a fungal infection or a reaction to medication. Monitor unexplained nail changes and consult a dermatologist.

The information provided should not be used for diagnosing or treating a health problem or disease, and those seeking personal medical advice should consult with a licensed physician. Always seek the advice of your doctor or other qualified health provider regarding a medical condition. title: QUINN QUESTIONS: Should everyone carry a business card?
text:
I just ordered new business cards, and I look refreshed. But maybe that’s because I used my ten-year-old retouched photo instead of a current one.
Even if you don’t have a job, a card lets you display credentials. You never get a second chance to make a first engraved impression.
Sadly, folks often rank us by what we call ourselves. I have alternately titled myself an analyst, strategist, and thought partner. I don’t know what all those words mean, but I think I can define two out of three.
My friend Bob works only part time, and he takes lots of naps. But his business card claims he’s a “futurist,” so you’ll consider him a forward thinker.
Educational titles on cards impress me. If you’ve got more degrees than a thermometer, a calling card is the place to display them.
Also, if you are certified in a field nobody understands, that is also splendid.
How do you make your card stand out? Get it printed on colored paper, make it a “fold-over” card, or put your photo on it.
What’s the most impressive job name? Personally, I always wanted the title of “manager” of whatever corporation I worked for. I don’t really care what I manage…even if it’s just handling out paper clips. It just means I’m in charge of something.
One of my friends started a business, and he selected a title sure to impress anybody.
His business card reads “Galactic Space Commander.”
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Defendant in murder trial for Bayside shooting takes the stand
text:
PORTLAND — During roughly 10 hours on the witness stand Wednesday, Omar Abdelkader was asked by his attorney: Why did he shoot Edgar Cando?
Abdelkader, who is on trial in Cumberland County Superior Court on a murder charge in Cando’s death, testified that he fired his gun because he was afraid of being killed.
Abdelkader, 23, told the jury that Cando had just knocked him to the ground during what was their third fistfight on Oct. 28, 2024, in the Bayside area. Their fights, and the shooting, were mostly captured on surveillance video that has been played multiple times for the jury, albeit from a distance and with poor sound quality.
Abdelkader testified that he had blood spilling from his face and he believed, at the time, that Cando had stabbed him. Abdelkader said that he knew Cando to carry a knife, although Cando’s partner testified last week that he wasn’t carrying a weapon that day.
After Abdelkader got up, video shows, he broke free from a friend who was holding him back, ran toward Cando and fired his gun three times.
Cando had walked away from the fight after knocking Abdelkader down, video shows. A prosecutor said Cando was already more than 40 feet away when Abdelkader advanced.
“That’s what the cameras saw. That’s not what I saw,” Abdelkader said, testifying that his vision was obscured by the blood, and that he had perceived Cando to be much closer, and still a threat.
Abdelkader also told Assistant Attorney General Kate Bozeman he believed he was having a seizure. Abdelkader’s attorneys, Tina Nadeau and Amber Tucker, have said in court that their client has a seizure disorder for which he receives medication.
Abdelkader said that Cando would not leave him alone, despite his efforts to walk away and end their fight.
“I was afraid of losing my life,” Abdelkader testified. “I was afraid of him killing me.”
Nadeau later asked if Abdelkader regretted the shooting. Bozeman objected before he could answer.
Detectives have testified, and a prosecutor has argued, that Abdelkader also instigated some of the fighting himself. He had also fought Cando’s friend about an hour earlier, in an argument about a bike that Abdelkader said he was watching for someone else. Bozeman suggested that’s how the disagreement between Abdelkader and Cando began.
Abdelkader said he shot Cando to injure him, not to kill, and that he didn’t know Cando had died when he turned himself into the police station three hours later.
Bozeman asked why Abdelkader — who could be seen on camera leaving the scene of the shooting with his girlfriend, and later sitting behind a truck in a parking lot — didn’t turn himself in sooner. The couple had a friend drive them to Gorham before Abdelkader asked his family to take him to the police station.
While in Gorham, Abdelkader said he repositioned his nose, which was broken during the fight with Cando.
Abdelkader testified that he didn’t think of the police when he left, and that he left because he was afraid of Cando’s friends.
Bozeman said the video also showed Abdelkader laughing after the earlier two fights with Cando, and high-fiving a friend who had “sucker-punched” Cando from behind. She said Abdelkader could be seen feeling the pocket where he kept his gun.
Abdelkader said he wasn’t reaching for his gun those times. He testified that in earlier fights that day, he never felt the need to use his weapon.
The last altercation with Cando was different, Abdelkader said in court, because he didn’t believe he was safe to retreat.
“Were you able to walk away from that confrontation?” Nadeau asked.
“No,” Abdelkader said. “He would not let me leave.”
The two men were mostly strangers, although Abdelkader testified that he recognized Cando from seeing him around town and they had spoken about six times. Abdelkader also said in court he had seen Cando fighting others around Portland, and that Cando had once shown off his knife during a conversation.
Abdelkader was hanging around the Bayside neighborhood the afternoon of Oct. 28 with his girlfriend at the time, waiting for her sister, who worked at the nearby Pizzaiolo, to be available.
Cando’s partner, Quantia Moran, testified last week that they had been in the area to get something from the nearby Dyer’s Variety Store.
The trial is scheduled to resume Thursday.

title: California high surf washes engagement ring away minutes after proposal
text:
California high surf washes engagement ring away minutes after proposal
A dream beach proposal in Orange County, California, took an unexpected turn when the tide washed away a couple's engagement ring.
It happened on Sunday, minutes after San Clemente's Jace Harrick bent his knee and proposed to his girlfriend with a beautiful diamond ring. The picturesque proposal with the sunset blanketing Calafia State Beach was nearly perfect until the surf washed onto the shore around the couple.
"Initially, I'm like, 'Okay, this is fine. Let's lift her up,'" Harrick said. "I have her phone in my right pocket, my phone, wallet, keys. I didn't want her to get swept away because we have El Niño. We know that can be a bit aggressive."
As he picked up his fiancée, Harrick lost his grip on the ring box. They lost the 4-carat engagement ring in the knee-high water.
Jessica Licon and her family were on the same San Clemente beach at sunset. She said the surf was rough that day. Her husband heard all the commotion a few feet away, thinking that everyone was celebrating the proposal.
"That's when I told him, 'No, the ring is gone. Everyone's looking for it,'" Licon said. "Everyone was looking for the ring, hoping they'd see a box; that way, it was easier to find, but nobody found anything."
A few treasure hunters with metal detectors searched the sand but had no luck either.
Harrick said he'd replace the ring. Looking for the silver lining, he said the engagement was perfect up to that last moment and that his soon-to-be wife was safe.
"Let's control what we can control right now, and that's our attitude," Harrick said. "I'm just grateful she's OK. That's what's important."
A diver has offered to come out and search for the lost ring. Harrick plans to offer a reward to anyone who can find it.

title: Muslims projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world's largest religion
text:
Muslims projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world's largest religion
Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released Wednesday by the Pew Research Center.
Video above: Aaliyah Bilal describes the Black Muslim experience in debut book "Temple Folk"
Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity are growing, but Islam is growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, is that Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups.
“It's the babies,” said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity are much smaller factors than fertility rates.
During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that's considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.
According to Pew's latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew's new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.
The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration.
Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62% of the population, according to Pew, and will fall below 50% by 2065.
In neighboring Canada, Christians are expected to drop below 50% by 2030, Pew said.
In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41% of the U.S. population and to outnumber Christians in Canada.
Muslims and Christians are expected to keep pace with population growth
The world’s population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070, Pew said. Of the religious groups it analyzed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%.
Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew said. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan.
Over the coming decades, Pew said, most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted.
By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world’s Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing threefold to 270 million.
The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline.
For example, the number of people living in Europe will shrink by 17% by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there will drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe's population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6% to 13%.
In the U.S., Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070.
Several mainline Protestant denominations in the U.S. have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations.
Fertility rates are a driving factor
By Pew’s estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020-2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers.
Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline.
If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia — which currently has the most Muslims.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations are “extremely important” in light of the evolving trends.
“The ‘clash of civilization’ theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides,” she said via email. “Many Christians are not happy to see that Islam will be the world’s largest religion and it’s causing even more angst.”
“I hope people seek opportunities for greater interreligious education,” she added. “Personal contact is important — when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanizes’ the ‘other’ in fruitful ways.”
Alan Cooperman, Pew's director of religion research, noted that most of the projected proliferation of Muslims and Christians was occurring in countries where they already are the majority — with conversion playing only a minor role.
“I don’t think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians,” he added. “I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims.”
The 'nones' are growing in some areas
Many countries have seen a steady proliferation of the “nones” — people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of “nones” but faces a sharp decline in overall population, the ranks of “nones” elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070, Pew said.
The “nones” already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.

title: Hakeem Jeffries could become the first Black House speaker after Democratic nomination
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past most skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker with the gavel.
Jeffries secured the nod during closed-door voting, 251-11, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January. Among those opposing him on the secret ballot were a group of progressive newcomers, who said in a statement there is “still work to be done” to ensure their priorities.
Afterward, Jeffries vowed to work hard, through every corner of the Democratic caucus, and said each generation has the opportunity to “show up, speak up, stand up, and help the country march toward a more perfect union.”
“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” he said, “and to get big things done for the American people.”
Jeffries, of New York, ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change in Congress after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Phone calls and social media campaigns have been flooding the offices of Democrats in both the House and the Senate, demanding a fresh start. Protesters heckled Jeffries last week during a Democratic conference in Denver.
Ahead of Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries said he was taking nothing for granted. Yet having led the Democrats to one of the biggest incoming House majorities in decades, he has room to maneuver.
Those opposing Jeffries, including some backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, signaled that conversations are ongoing as they push to deliver Medicare for All, stop harsh actions from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, get money out of politics and end Israel’s war in Gaza.
“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” they said in a joint statement.
Signing on as opposed were members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York and Frederick Haynes of Texas, though he was one of two Democrats who did not vote. Reps-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres of California and Don Leonard of Ohio also said they voted against.
Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed and were elected, as was Rep. Ted Lieu of California, as chairman of the House Democratic caucus.
He will need a simple majority of 218 votes from the whole House to be elected speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. It would be a milestone in the nation’s struggles to create a representative democracy, since the first Black lawmaker was elected to the House more than 150 years ago.
Skeptics question whether leaders are up to the job
Wednesday’s vote was the first of their careers for dozens of members-elect, before they’re even sworn into office in January.
Jeffries was nominated for House speaker by five Democrats essentially representing all aspects of the caucus, including Rep. James Clyburn, the legendary lawmaker from South Carolina.
“This is a historic moment for our nation,” Clyburn told the room, according to his private remarks that invoked voters’ outpouring for a change in the country.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., discounted the naysayers and said: “It is a day in the history of this nation that cannot be diminished in any way. I could never be more proud to be a Democrat than I am today.”
Rep. Kweisi Mfume of Maryland, who first came to Congress in 1987 with the late Civil Rights leader Rep. John Lewis of Georgia, said: “It just means so much in terms of moving the ball forward. Somebody’s got to break the glass, and in this instance that’s exactly what has happened.”
The tally, with 262 votes cast, included those elected to the new Congress and the House delegates.
Returning Rep. Emily Randall of Washington said earlier that she fielded questions about House leadership during town halls in her district and on her Instagram feed. So she decided to start dialing people back.
“People have messaged me asking if Bernie Sanders could be the speaker of the House,” she said, referring to the Vermont independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. “Technically yes, and it would be probably difficult.”
(It’s true that the House can elect anyone speaker, but it’s unlikely to be Sanders because he already has his day job in the Senate.)
She said she was voting for Jeffries. Lawmakers pointed to the livestream from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York trying to explain the role of the speaker and her support.
“There is one candidate in this race: Hakeem Jeffries,” Ocasio-Cortez said earlier at the Capitol.
First leaders of a post-Pelosi era
Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar have risen together, as a team, as the first new generation of leaders after the Nancy Pelosi era and will soon serve as leaders in the majority for the first time.
When Pelosi, of California, stepped aside from leadership in 2022 after the party’s electoral defeat that handed Republicans the majority, it set the stage for this era.
A similar upheaval with Democrats angling for change is happening in the Senate, where Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in elections next month.
Schumer insisted Wednesday he had the votes: “I will be reelected as majority leader.”
Returning Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona said the situations in the Senate and the House “are quite different.”
She said Jeffries has been a collaborative leader who is listening to ideas from progressive caucus members like her and others. “His job is to reflect all of us, not just a faction,” Ansari said.
Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama, who pulled off a stunning victory in a redrawn district favoring the Republican candidate, said before the vote that he’d be supporting Jeffries.
“It’s not even like a complex question,” he said about Jeffries, who he said “led us through what is likely the most tumultuous two-year tenure of any presidency in the history of this nation.”
“I’m not going to not stand by him right here on the precipice of history,” he said.
___
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

title: Mother accused of faking 2-year-old’s illnesses; child had 175 doctor visits, underwent invasive surgery
text:
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. (WDTV/Gray News) — Three people in West Virginia are accused of faking a 2-year-old’s medical diagnoses, which led to the child receiving medical treatments they did not need.
Munchausen syndrome by proxy is a serious mental health condition and a form of abuse in which a caregiver, most often a parent, falsely claims another person has medical problems, according to the Mayo Clinic.
On Oct. 7, the Monongalia County Sheriff’s Office began an investigation into allegations of child neglect involving a 2-year-old and a 9-year-old.
Detectives said they determined that the 2-year-old had about 175 doctor visits in just over two years after reviewing extensive medical records and speaking with numerous medical professionals.
Emilee Guzman, the child’s mother, repeatedly told doctors that the 2-year-old had an inability or refusal to eat food and that the child had a fear of food (ARFID), officials said.
The information provided by Guzman led to the child undergoing surgical placement of a gastrostomy tube (G-tube) on Oct. 1. Guzman also allegedly told friends and family that the child had rare diagnoses such as microgastria, an extremely rare birth defect where the stomach fails to grow and rotate normally during pregnancy.
During an interview on Oct. 13, Guzman admitted that she knowingly withheld information from doctors concerning the child’s actual food intake. Guzman told officials she misrepresented the child’s eating habits because she feared medical providers would believe she was not properly caring for the child and contact CPS, according to official documents.
On Oct. 27, the detective spoke with the pediatric surgeon who performed the G-tube placement, who said he would not have performed the surgery and instead would have pursued less invasive treatment options if he had the proper information. The doctor said the procedure could be very painful for a child during placement and removal and could also expose the child to serious potential harm, documents said.
After the child was removed from Guzman’s custody, the child was seen eating plenty of food without issue. Foster caregivers also said that the child did not want to let anyone near the G-tube to clean it and was uncomfortable with its placement, according to officials.
Throughout the investigation, officials executed a search warrant at Guzman’s home in Morgantown. Officials said her husband, Milton Guzman Cisneros, and another woman, Caitlin Meredith, were also living in the home.
During the search, officials found deplorable and unsanitary living conditions. The home contained garbage, scattered food, dried feces believed to be from cats and possibly humans, cockroaches and a substantial infestation of flies and gnats, according to official reports.
Officials were particularly concerned about the 2-year-old who had undergone abdominal surgery and required appropriate care and hygiene of the surgical site.
Throughout the investigation, officials also found communications between Emilee Guzman and Meredith that documented “troubling treatment” of the 9-year-old, including ridicule concerning incontinence, threats and descriptions of physical punishment and expectations that the child clean the home.
Emilee Guzman is charged with one felony count of child neglect resulting in serious bodily injury. Meredith and Guzman Cisneros are each charged with two counts of child neglect creating risk of bodily injury.
All three adults are being held in the North Central Regional Jail.

title: Highway patrol to pay $70,000 to former Wild Orchid member in DUI arrest settlement
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) — The Tennessee Highway Patrol will pay $70,000 to Stefanie Fair, a former member of the 1990s pop group Wild Orchid, in a settlement over her DUI arrest.
Blood work later showed Fair was sober at the time of her arrest.
The state Board of Claims approved the settlement, and a payout should result in the next few weeks, according to a spokesman for the attorney general’s office.
Court records show lawsuits by sober drivers are piling up against the state. The claims include reports that a single trooper arrested nine sober drivers for DUI.
Stefanie Fair’s arrest
Fair’s 2024 arrest was featured in WSMV4 Investigates’ “Sobering Problem” investigations.
The trooper who arrested her for DUI said he smelled alcohol.
“There’s a very distinct odor of alcohol that comes from either the person or inside the vehicle,” Trooper Keith Velez said.
“But on my life, I don’t drink alcohol,” Fair responded.
Video obtained by WSMV4 Investigates shows Fair eating ice cream before her arrest.
“I was more scared being with that cop alone than I actually was inside the jail,” Fair said.
Attorney’s comments on the settlement
Fair’s attorney, Ben Raybin, said the state has recognized problems with arrests like hers.
“I think that the state has recognized that a lot of these arrests are just completely legally unsupportable and that if they went to a jury trial, a jury would find against them,” Raybin said.
There is no recourse in Tennessee for sober drivers to recoup costs, even after their DUI charges are dismissed. Raybin said their only option is to sue.
Other lawsuits against the state
Fair is the second sober driver to sue the Tennessee Highway Patrol and settle.
Thomas Manis was paid $75,000 after state troopers arrested him for DUI in East Tennessee.
Other sober drivers who first told their stories to WSMV4 Investigates are also suing the state, including NASA employee Labreesha Batey and former U.S. attorney Jane Bondurant.
WSMV4 Investigates found Bondurant was the eighth sober driver arrested by state trooper James Zahn.
According to a lawsuit filed this year by a Thompson Station man, Zahn also arrested him for DUI while he was sober. That would make him the ninth sober driver arrested by Zahn.
Other agencies
The Tennessee Highway Patrol is not the only agency to settle lawsuits.
Court records show the Rutherford County Sheriff’s Office and La Vergne police have also settled lawsuits from sober drivers arrested for DUI.
Copyright 2026 WSMV via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to LSU-Texas game after ground stop
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop that caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the game a day after all planes were grounded. Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as flights were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
Mullin’s flight comes as the ground stop is garnering increasing scrutiny, with Democrats in the Senate demanding that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it was pausing the installation of the routers that were linked to the ground stop.
Asked on CNBC whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn’t open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
Mullin took over as DHS secretary earlier this year from Kristi Noem, whose tenure was rocked by scandal over spending at the department, as well as an aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. Mullin vowed to serve as a steady hand for the department and keep it out of the headlines.
The Department of Homeland Security said Mullin was required by law to travel on a government plane. It said in a statement that he pays personally for any flight unrelated to government work.
“Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements,” it said.
The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports. The stoppage resulted in thousands of canceled flights and massive disruptions at airports across the nation ahead of the busy Thanksgiving holiday.
President Donald Trump’s administration has said the air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.
“I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said.
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.
___
Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pennsylvania.

title: RSU 63 board accepts superintendent’s resignation at first meeting since Eddington Elementary closure
text:
HOLDEN, Maine (WABI) - The RSU 63 School Board voted Tuesday night to accept Superintendent Sheila Caldwell’s resignation at a special meeting in Holden. It was the board’s first meeting since the vote in favor of the closure of Eddington Elementary School.
The board also welcomed new Special Education Director Kimberly Bennett.
Vote on resignation
The meeting comes amid concerns about a disconnect between the superintendent and the board over what is happening in the schools.
All but one board member present at last night’s meeting, voted to accept the resignation.
Board Chair Rachel Downs voted no.
Public comment
Parents and advocates also spoke at the meeting.
“I hope this board recognizes that our next superintendent will inherit more than a leadership position. They’ll inherit the responsibility of restoring trust, ensuring legal compliance, and addressing systemic concerns that have persisted through multiple administrations. That responsibility must be taken seriously from day one,” one parent said.
“I hope that parents in our district who are angry about the school closure recognize that this decision came after many years of discussion, consideration, and study. I also hope that we can move away from framing this as an Eddington vs. Holden issue. That division is not healthy for our community, nor is it a message we should be sending to our students,” another speaker said.
Interim superintendent task force
The board also appointed four people to a task force to appoint an interim superintendent.
Shelia Caldwell served about a year as superintendent at RSU 63.
The MSAD 17 school district announcing on their website that Caldwell will become the new interim superintendent in Oxford Hills.

title: Explosive device, disguised as video game equipment, detonates inside store
text:
VIDEO: Explosive device, disguised as video game equipment, detonates inside store; business rival charged
Video shows the moment an explosive device, which was disguised as video game equipment, detonated inside an electronics store near São Paulo, Brazil.
The victim suffered only minor injuries. Police say a rival businessman, Everton Lima, is accused of targeting the store. Lima reportedly owns multiple businesses in the same area, and police believe he targeted the new store to get rid of competition.
The explosives were rigged to a timer, but only one detonated.
Lima has been arrested and is being investigated for attempted murder, CNN reported.

title: This Maine designer is dressing the stars
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Instead of yelling “Are we there yet?” over and over, young Elias Matso kept busy on car trips by drawing women’s dresses.
“My parents would put stacks of index cards in the back seat pocket and I would just fill them up with drawings of dresses, as many as I could fit,” said Matso, who grew up in Kittery. “I was just always drawing women in different outfits.”
Now 24, Matso is still drawing women’s outfits, as a freelance designer based in New York City. But now his creations are being worn by runway models and Hollywood celebrities. The dress he created for Jenna Ortega — with thin pieces of metal dangling from it — became a red carpet sensation when Ortega wore it to the New York premiere of her new film, “Klara and the Sun,” on Oct. 19.
A year earlier, movie star Sydney Sweeney had created fashion-world buzz when she wore a sheer silver mesh gown to a Variety event in Beverly Hills, a collaboration between Matso and noted designer Christian Cowan. His work and his creative use of corsets has been written about in publications like People, Women’s Wear Daily and Harper’s Bazaar.
A FAST START
Matso has been working on attention-grabbing apparel for the last couple of years, despite only graduating in May from the Polimoda fashion school in Florence, Italy. While working with Cowan, he helped create a series of gowns for New York Fashion Week. Besides Sweeney, some of the stars and celebrities who have worn his looks or gowns he collaborated on include actors Sarah Paulson, Julia Fox, and Rachel McAdam, and singers Bebe Rexha, Cardi B. and Lizzo.
He says the dress worn by Ortega in October was inspired at least partly by Bob Mackie, the designer who created sparkling, body-clinging gowns for Cher in the 1970s, often with dangling or fringe elements.
The multi-colored dangling metal pieces on the dress are made from the “boning” or structural spine of corsets, Matso said. He wired the boning together with crystal beads and sewed the strands onto the dress.
He says the goal was to take something rigid and make it fluid. There is also a corset hidden beneath layers of fabric in the dress. It took some 300 hours of work.
Another of his red carpet creations was worn by a fellow Mainer. Actor Elysia Roorbach, who grew up in Farmington, wore one of his dresses to the Emmy Awards in September. Roorbach appeared on two episodes of “The Pitt” on HBO Max this year and is cast in the upcoming season of “We Were Liars” on Prime. The form-fitting dress has some of the dangly metal corset spining seen on Ortega’s dress, with a less-adorned flouncy white skirt on the bottom.
Matso is fascinated with corsets and makes them a focus of many of his creations. He used them for drag shows in high school and looks at them as an important “first step” toward creating a garment. He calls it “sort of the motherboard of fashion.” Matso says he tries to work with clients who want to wear a corset dress to make it work for them, so that it’s as comfortable as possible. It’s not for everybody, he says.
MOVIES AND MAGAZINES
Matso says he’s not sure where his passion for fashion came from, but as a youngster he remembers being enthralled by well-dressed celebrities in magazines and flashy costumes in movies like “Victor/Victoria.” In that 1982 film, Julie Andrews plays a singer in 1930s Paris who disguises herself as a man to get work. She wears a sparkling black dress with silver rhinestone fringe and a dramatic headdress in one scene, while she dons a tailored tuxedo in another.
His mother worked as a teacher and educational consultant and his father was a marine biologist at the University of New Hampshire. He traveled with his family fairly often and remembers seeking out celebrity and fashion magazines at airport newsstands.
He went to Kittery public schools, including the Horace Mitchell Primary School. There, even as a kindergartner, his talents for drawing and design were hard to ignore, said Dana Rickerich, a school counselor.
“I still have a picture he drew for me of this amazing fairy with wings that are so intricate for a five-year-old,” said Rickerich. “He’d make all these amazing drawings and little figurines. His creativity was incredible.”
Matso says he’s wanted to work in fashion as long as he can remember. He had an aunt, who was an interior designer, who mentioned the Parsons School of Design in New York as a place where people go to study fashion. By the age of 12 he was “obsessed” with going there.
While in high school at R. W. Traip Academy in Kittery, he designed and wore costumes for drag shows that were “stunning,” Rickerich recalls. Rickerich says Matso’s talent reminded her of a childhood friend, Reed Krakoff, a fashion designer who eventually became the artistic director for Tiffany & Co.
Rickerich had not kept in touch with Krakoff, but decided to write him a letter about Matso and included photos of Matso’s work. She wasn’t sure anything would come of it, but soon she heard from Krakoff’s assistant that Tiffany wanted Matso, who was still in high school, to be an intern.
Tiffany had recently become part of LVMH, a luxury fashion brand. Matso worked with designers, researching and archiving materials and doing random tasks. He got to sketch a little, too.
“It was such a valuable thing for me to be there at that time,” said Matso. “I got to see how a luxury design team works. It was very cool.”
During high school, he had also taken pre-college courses in the summer at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York. After high school, he attended Parsons, but decided it wasn’t the right fit and enrolled at Polimoda. The dress Ortega wore was something Matso made as the finale piece for his thesis collection at Polimoda.
In the summer of 2025, he got the chance to work with New York fashion designer Christian Cowan and created a series of gowns under the name “Christian Cowan x Elias Matso.” The gown Sweeney eventually wore – and created a sensation with – was one of those.
Matso says it’s been “surreal” to see the reaction on social media and in the fashion press to his work, especially the dresses worn by Sweeney and Ortega. He remembers watching Ortega on the red carpet and hearing media members shouting “Who made the dress?” He said Sweeney texted him several weeks after her event to say “that she had never felt as beautiful.”
“The Sydney Sweeney thing was shocking, how it just exploded,” said Matso, from his home in New York. “With Jenna, I saw the paparazzi freaking out about it, asking her who made the dress. It’s all been pretty crazy.”

title: In 2nd year, Cooper Flagg feeling more comfortable and settled with NBA life
text:
BOSTON — Cooper Flagg finished his pregame warmup, but he wasn’t ready to leave the court. He went to the bench, sat in a chair and got into a contest taking seated sideline shots with teammate Dereck Lively II. Then he strolled over to the front row of the stands, where he signed for eager fans in Flagg shirts and No. 32 jerseys.
It was loose, laid-back and easygoing, and a snapshot emblematic of Flagg’s second year in the NBA. Even on the road, the Newport native and Dallas Mavericks cornerstone has felt right at home.
“I definitely feel more comfortable with the system and coaches,” Flagg said after scoring 17 points in a 131-94 loss to the Boston Celtics on Sunday night. “(I got) a lot of time in the summer to sit down and work with everybody. So it’s been good.”
Flagg’s second year has seen an improvement across the statistical board, even from numbers that were impressive enough for him to earn Rookie of the Year honors last season. Through Monday, he was averaging 23.5 points, 6.7 rebounds, 6.2 assists and 1.9 steals per game, all of which equal or surpass last year’s numbers.
The people around him, though, don’t just see a better player. They see a 19-year-old who’s more at ease, more settled, and in more of a rhythm with the hectic and demanding environment that comes with playing in the NBA — let alone as one of its rising stars.
“He just looks like he’s a little bit better in every area,” Mavericks coach Dusty May said. “He looks stronger. He looks just more acclimated to the NBA game. I think last year, he definitely had bright moments, but it was up and down like it is for all rookies. This year, he’s been pretty consistent.”
Flagg’s longtime trainer, Matt MacKenzie, said last year that some of his biggest acclimations to NBA life came off the court. Getting rest was a challenge. So was preserving energy for back-to-back games, or making the best use of downtime.
MacKenzie checks in with Flagg every day and sees him every other week. And he’s seen that this year, Flagg has found his rhythm.
“(He’s gained) a better understanding of what the flow looks like, and the travel, and the back-to-backs, and how much time you have off in between games,” MacKenzie said. “He’s done a really good job of building routines that he knows work well in terms of his sleep habits, in terms of his diet, nutrition, timing of his meals.”
Flagg also is giving his life away from basketball more attention.
“He’s picked some times during his free time where he can get a few swings in on the golf simulator or go out and play a quick round, just to kind of take his head away from the game,” MacKenzie said. “He also has a couple of close friends down there with him right now, so it’s really good for him to be able to kind of have that outlet and have people that he can spend time with.”
Game nights have shown a more settled-in Flagg as well. MacKenzie said he’s been better at getting to the free-throw line — he’s averaging 6.7 attempts per game, up from 4.9 as a rookie — and with his shot selection.
Flagg agreed.
“I’m confident getting to my spots, you know, the shots I want to get,” he said. “Make or miss, I’m happy with the result, and I know where I want to be on the court.”
The numbers have indicated as much. In 14 games, he’s had three where he’s scored over 30 points, including one in which he scored 43. His true shooting percentage, which gives more weight to outside shots in an effort to more accurately assess a player’s ability to shoot efficiently, is up 30 points from last year.
“Man, he’s amazing,” said Mavericks teammate Zaccharie Risacher, who was drafted first overall by Atlanta in 2024, the year before the Mavericks took Flagg with the No. 1 pick. “Just his pace, the way he controls the game, the way he gets to his spot. I feel like that’s really impressive.”
Risacher included another description not often assigned to second-year players.
“He’s a good leader,” he said. “He’s got the voice, but also the energy to put everyone on his back.”
Flagg had an opportunity to use that newfound voice Sunday, as things fell apart immediately for the Mavericks on the TD Garden floor. They were blown out, down 33 points by the end of the first quarter, and Flagg, who shot 5 for 15, could do little to save the day and help prevent a third straight loss.
After the game, though, the player who last year acknowledged difficulty handling these kinds of losses used the defeat to send a message.
“The level they were competing at is something that we need to look at in the mirror, and decide if we’re competing at that same level and if we want it as bad as they did. I don’t think we did,” he said. “This road trip (was) not to our standard, and we’ve got to correct it.”
Flagg has always been a player to lead by example. But being the vocal leader is just another adjustment he’s been able to make with a year behind him.
“I’m fascinated by it, to be honest,” May said. “Just to think, if we all closed our eyes and imagined ourselves at 19. … For (him) to be able to do and manage what he’s done is impressive. And also, it’s fun to watch him, because he’s still getting better.”

title: Giant catsup bottle draws travelers to a landmark with history
text:
COLLINSVILLE, Ill. (InvestigateTV) - Route 66 turns 100 this year, and along the historic highway in Collinsville stands a landmark that is hard to miss: a 70-foot catsup bottle perched on a 100-foot stand.
The structure was built in 1949 as a water tower for a catsup factory — the original home of Brooks Catsup. It holds 100,000 gallons of water.
By the early 1960s, the bottling operation had moved to Indiana. In 1993, Brooks Foods decided to sell the property, and the bottle had fallen into disrepair.
“Major, major disrepair. So they were talking about tearing it down. The Catsup Bottle Preservation Group was formed, they raised a whole bunch of money, and in 1995 had it restored,” said Mike Gassmann of the World’s Largest Catsup Bottle Inc.
In 2002, the structure was placed on the National Register of Historic Places. It has since been inducted into the Illinois Route 66 Hall of Fame.
Gassmann, who holds the title of “Big Tomato” within the bottle’s fan club, said the landmark draws a steady stream of visitors.
“Doesn’t surprise me any day to come by here and see people taking photos,” he said.
As for what’s inside, Gassmann offered no definitive answer.
“I can neither confirm nor deny the reports that it is filled with catsup,” he said.

title: Give thanks for Maine’s independent movie theaters – and these films
text:
It’s the time for giving thanks, and as a Maine movie fan, I’m always grateful for the independent Maine movie houses bringing the boldest and most exciting off-the-radar films to our collective backyard. This Thanksgiving season, those Maine theaters are serving up a personal all-time favorite, a Maine-set indie drama, a deeply necessary documentary, the latest from a giant of world cinema, a telling historical tale and a true cult classic in the making.
Starts Friday, Nov. 20, PMA Films, 7 Congress Square, Portland, portlandmuseum.org
This fictionalized biographical film from Polish director Pawel Pawlikowski (Ida, My Summer of Love) examines the volatile ashes of post-WWII Germany through the eyes of famous author Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler). Driven through the tumultuous countryside by his headstrong daughter Erika (Project Hail Mary’s Sandra Hüller), a writer in her own right, the aging Mann, who fled the Nazis before the war, must confront a defeated country still teetering on the abyss of fascism and contemplating unthinkable crimes. A sobering yet bracing drama from one of the world’s great filmmakers. Plus any trailer that includes a scene of a kick-ass woman shouting, “Shut up, fascist scum!” is worth a watch.
‘In Transit’
Sat. Nov. 21 and Sun. Nov. 22, Colonial Theatre, 163 High St., Belfast, colonialtheatre.com
Restless desire forms the basis of a relationship between an older, creative blocked artist on retreat in Maine and the local female bartender who agrees to become her model.
Filmed in Maine by director-writer Jaclyn Bethany, this compellingly intense indie drama stars Alex Sarrigeorgiou and the always outstanding Jennifer Ehle (“Saint Maude,” “Zero Dark Thirty”), who looks uncannily like a younger Meryl Streep and is just about as talented.
Saturday, Nov. 21, Space, 538 Congress St., Portland, space.538.org
One of the chief pleasures of the recent blue wave midterms win for Democrats was the repudiation of candidates (including many Maine Republicans) who flooded the airwaves with a toxic spill of ads demonizing transgender people.That still doesn’t mean an easy time for trans youth, who, as reported in the trailer for this deeply necessary documentary from directors Lexi Bean and Logan Rozos, attempt to take their own lives at truly horrifying rates, thanks in part to such open abuse all around them. Taking on the stories of two trans boys who did in fact take their own lives, the film attempts to present the harsh and often unsupported realities of trans youth while offering glimmers of hope and warmth for the future. Sponsored at Space by mainetrans.net.
Sunday, Nov. 22, Apohadion Theater, 107 Hanover St., Portland, apohadiontheater.org
Ultra-cool concert and event venue The Apohadion is the perfect place to screen the new, impossible-to-describe film from Cory McAbee. The actor-writer-director-animator made the outstandingly weird sci-fi musical Western “The American Astronaut” in 2001, a movie I found as enjoyable as it was baffling to all but the weirdest and coolest customers, when I showed it on the store TV at the late, lamented Videoport. McAbee will be in attendance at the showing of his new flick, an assemblage narrative about the assassination of Abraham Lincoln told through silent clips from scores of films and scored by the creator himself. A true, original American indie artist, McAbee’s movies are like nothing you’ve seen before.
Wednesday, Nov. 25 and Saturday, Nov. 28, Kinonik, 121 Cassidy Point Drive, Portland, kinonik.org
All thanks to the film-on-film angels at Kinonik for bringing out their precious copy of Wayne Wang’s 1995 indie drama. When I worked at Videoport (no, I will never stop reminding people about the joys of a great video store), this was a go-to recommendation whenever someone said, “Just give me a great movie.” (It was admittedly an uphill battle because of Miramax’s truly terrible poster art.) The definition of a slice-of-life ensemble drama, the film stars Harvey Keitel, William Hurt, Forest Whitaker, Stockard Channing and Harold Perrineau Jr. as denizens of the same nondescript Brooklyn neighborhood whose seemingly unconnected lives intersect via Keitel’s corner tobacco shop. Written by novelist Paul Auster, Smoke is poetic but grippingly ordinary, a true forgotten ’90s indie classic acted impeccably by a never-better cast. The final scene re-contextualizes the story over a couple of cigarettes and a Tom Waits song, and I get goosebumps just thinking about it.
‘Bitter Christmas’
Starts Wednesday, Nov. 25, Maine Film Center, 93 Main St., Waterville, watervillecreates.org
There’s no filmmaker working whose movies are a guaranteed watch for me more than Spanish auteur (and provocateur) Pedro Almodovár (Favorites, in no order: “The Skin I Live In,” “Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown,” “All About My Mother,” “Talk To Her,” “Matador”). So his latest film (his 27th), a typically ticklish drama about two creators whose latest works bring erotic chaos to the thinly veiled real people they’re writing about, mixes self-reflection, artistic rumination, sex, conflict and sexy conflict, all in the inimitable Almodovár style.

title: Obituary: Elden Charles McKeen
text:
WINDHAM – Elden Charles McKeen passed away peacefully on Nov. 12, 2026, following a lengthy battle with dementia.
Elden was born in Portland, Maine, on Dec. 4, 1938, to Adna Charles McKeen and Barbara Viola (Jackson) McKeen. He was the oldest of three brothers, with two younger brothers, Richard and Kenneth.
He graduated from Windham High School in 1957 and went on to attend Portland University before serving his country in the United States Army from 1958 to 1960.
Elden had a passion for baseball and enjoyed coaching in Windham, where he taught hundreds of young people not only how to play the game but also the importance of teamwork, dedication, and good sportsmanship.
He spent 38 years working as a clerk for the Maine Central Railroad where he was a proud member of BRAC/Machinists Union and the Southern Maine Labor Council. In addition to his professional career, Elden dedicated himself to public service, serving two terms in the Maine Legislature representing Windham, Westbrook, and Gorham.
On May 21, 1962, Elden married Patricia Corliss. Together, they settled in Windham, where they raised their three children and built a lifetime of memories.
Family was everything to Elden, and the legacy he leaves behind will continue through the generations. He is survived by his loving wife, Patricia; his daughter Debra and her husband Tom Matthews, and his daughter Susan and her husband Dan Walker. He was predeceased by his son, Thomas, in 2021.
Elden also leaves behind seven grandchildren, Sean, Nicole, Justin, Derek, Dylan, Asya, and Lela; and 11 great-grandchildren, Conall, Eimilie, Aedan, Spencer, Honor, Calvin, Delaney, Erin, Blake, Hattie, and Harlie.
Beyond his immediate family, Elden was fortunate to have many lifelong friends whom he considered family. Those friendships and the memories they created were an important part of his life.
A memorial service will be held on Saturday, Nov. 21, at 4 p.m. at the Windham Community Center, 8 School St., Windham, Maine.
The family would like to extend its sincere gratitude to the staff at Maine Medical Center and Cape Memory Care for their compassion, dedication, and the comfort and excellent care they provided Elden throughout his stay.
Elden will be deeply missed by his family, friends, and all those whose lives he touched. His dedication to family, community, and service will remain a lasting part of his legacy.
In lieu of flowers,
the family requests that donations be made to one of the following organizations:
Windham Democratic Scholarship Fund
503 Falmouth Road
Windham, ME 04062 or to:
AgeMaine
30 Barra Road
Biddeford, ME 04005
